entries.section: 1. The source of wisdom and its characteristics

paragraphs.text: 1 All wisdom is from the Lord, and is with Him for ever. 2 Who can number the sand of the sea, and the drops of rain, and the days of eternity? And who can measure the height of heaven, and the breadth of the earth, and the deep? 3 And who can search out wisdom, which is before all things? 4 Wisdom was created before all things, and the understanding of prudence from everlasting. 5 The fountain of wisdom is the word of God in the highest, and her ways are everlasting commandments. 6 To whom has the root of wisdom been revealed, and who has known her subtlety? 7 To whom has the knowledge of wisdom been made manifest, and who has understood her great experience? 8 There is One who is wise, greatly to be feared, sitting upon His throne. 9 The Lord Himself possessed her, and saw her, and numbered her, 10 and poured her out upon all His works; she is with all flesh according to His gift, and He has given her to those who love Him.
All wisdom is from the Lord, and is with Him for ever. [1]

True wisdom is from the Lord [1]; He gives it to those who seek it, and it never departs from Him; it is the Son, the Word (1 Cor 1:24). The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of wisdom (Isa 11:2); whoever has the Spirit dwelling in him has wisdom (2 Tim 1:7).

When the Lord entered into dialogue with Job, He revealed to him his need of divine wisdom. Job expected God to ask him about certain sins he had committed, and did not expect Him to ask him about matters concerning the wonders of creation, which God made for the sake of every man, and whose secrets man cannot fully know (Job 38). In this God exposed Job's ignorance of how the earth was created (Job 38:4-7), his ignorance of the setting of bounds for the seas (8-11), and of how the light of dawn appears (12-15), and of perceiving the shadow of death and the darkness (16-21), and the clouds, the hail and the thunder... (22-30), the stars and their effect on the earth (31-33), the power of God in the air and in natural phenomena (34-38), and God's care for the irrational animals (39-41).
v Our divine Teacher is to be trusted, for He is marked by three wonderful characteristics: prudence, goodness and authority.

entries.section: 1. The source of wisdom and its characteristics

paragraphs.text: As for prudence, we say that He is the wisdom of God the Father. "All wisdom is from the Lord, and is with Him for ever." As for authority, we say that He is God the Creator. "All things were made by Him; and without Him was not any thing made that was made" (Jn 1:3). As for His good will, He alone gave Himself as a sacrifice for us. "The good shepherd giveth His life for the sheep" (Jn 10:11). Truly He gave Himself. What is good will but the desire for good for the benefit of one's neighbor? [3]

St. Clement of Alexandria The theme of the whole book is the believer's enjoyment of heavenly wisdom. The book begins with the expression "all wisdom," as though the book wishes to affirm that there are different kinds of wisdom, and that the source of all of them is the Lord.

A. Natural wisdom, which the Book of Ben Sirach says is created with the faithful in the womb (Sir 1:12). This wisdom, which believers value as a divine gift, God offers to all humanity without partiality to believer or unbeliever, giving it to each as is fitting. The believer receives it from the hand of God, and so continually offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving in a spirit of humility. The unbeliever boasts of it as a quality peculiar to himself and to no one else, so the ego swells in him, and he falls into arrogance and pride. Many express this by saying that every man admires his own mind, and is neither pleased nor satisfied with what he has of possessions, as though he were marked by pride together with greed.

Natural wisdom is characterized by the following: 1. It is a divine gift, yet it is affected by the lives of the parents and their possibilities, abilities and gifts, so the factor of heredity cannot be ignored. 2. What occupies God's mind is not the quantity of the fruits of this wisdom, but the degree of man's faithfulness in what has been given to him of wisdom and its capacities. A person may be crowned with glory even though, by our human judgment, he does not enjoy exceptional brilliance like others. 3. It is fitting for us to respect and appreciate the variety of these abilities: parents may excel in medicine and gain renown for it, while their son feels that his gift lies in industrial, commercial or administrative work, or skill in one of the arts, or exceptional ability in learning new languages.

The beauty of the family and of society, as of the Church, lies in the variety of gifts, so that each person feels his need of his brother, and that his success rests on his appreciation of the gifts of his brothers. This variety supports man in humility, as he feels his need of others, and it also helps the spirit of unity and cooperation, so that all work together as a team (team work). 4. This natural wisdom can be developed with a spirit of piety, together with striving and a desire for continual renewal and growth; it can also be allowed to decline until it almost disappears through negligence and failure to kindle the gift.

B. The wisdom of study and learning, and also of benefiting from the experience of others and from one's own personal experience in the past. Every man can enjoy this, even if he is an atheist, but the believer realizes that the mind itself is a gift from God, and that all the circumstances surrounding him did not happen haphazardly or by chance, but that the hand of God is at work in all his life, even to the hairs of his head, which are numbered before God. So he is indebted to God for his mind and for his ability to learn and to enjoy the experiences of others and his own experiences.

Man enjoys the wisdom of study and learning and the enjoyment of experience without partiality. Truly, by directing natural wisdom toward uprightness, and by not deviating from the free divine gift, we enjoy growth through study and experience. On the contrary, many have buried their natural gifts because of the deviation of their aim and the misconduct of their behavior.

C. Heavenly wisdom: It pleases God our heavenly Father that every believer bear the icon of the only-begotten Son, "the wisdom of God" (1 Cor 1:24), which the believer treasures through his enjoyment of the grace of sonship. This wisdom is peculiar to the believer who cleaves to God, for he is united with the wisdom of God, or the Word of God incarnate, and so bears heavenly wisdom. The Apostle James says: "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him" (Jas 1:5). It is written in the song of wisdom sung by righteous Job:
"But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?
Man knoweth not the price thereof; neither is it found in the land of the living... seeing it is hid from the eyes of all living...
God understandeth the way thereof, and He knoweth the place thereof, etc." (Job 28:12-23).

St. Augustine sees that the believer seeks wisdom through his realization that he needs union with the Lord Christ Himself, the wisdom of God. So instead of being confined to himself, man enjoys fellowship with the wisdom of God.

entries.section: 1. The source of wisdom and its characteristics

paragraphs.text: v Truly in these books which they study with zeal they read: "For the Lord giveth wisdom: out of His mouth cometh knowledge and understanding" (Prov 2:6). They receive from Him that zeal for study, if it is granted with godliness [4].

entries.section: 1. The source of wisdom and its characteristics

paragraphs.text: v Unless a man comes out of himself, he will not become wise, but through God he acquires wisdom [5].

entries.section: 1. The source of wisdom and its characteristics

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine v He (Christ) is called Wisdom, as Solomon says... and He is also called "the Firstborn," for the Apostle Paul says of Him: "the firstborn of every creature" (Col 1:15). The Firstborn, then, by nature is not different from Wisdom, but is the very same. Finally the Apostle Paul says: "Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God" (1 Cor 1:24) [6].

v There is with God an understanding that you cannot find anywhere except in Christ Jesus. For all the divine attributes are represented in the Lord Christ: He is the wisdom of God; the power of God; the righteousness of God; holiness; and He is salvation; and the understanding of God. Although He is one with the Father in essence, He bears many names that refer to different things. For you do not grasp the same meaning concerning the Lord Christ when you look at Him as Wisdom and when you look at Him as Righteousness.
When you look at Him as Wisdom you understand from that His knowledge of divine and human things.
And when you look at Him as Righteousness you understand from that His ability to give everyone his due.
If you look at Him as Holiness you understand His ability to sanctify all who believe in Him and are consecrated to Him.
And you will also perceive Him as Understanding, for He knows good and evil and what is neither good nor evil.
Origen Who can number the sand of the sea, and the drops of rain, and the days of eternity? [2]

After the wise man calls us to cleave to the Lord so as to enjoy His wisdom, he asks us to touch this surpassing divine wisdom through creation itself, which God brought into being to serve man. He alone numbers the sand of the sea, the drops of rain and all time.
Who can search out the height of heaven, and the breadth of the earth, and the depth of the deep (the seas), and wisdom? [3]

The wisdom of God is surpassing, and His knowledge is beyond all limits, for He numbers the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the days of eternity. Nothing is hidden from Him, for He knows the dimensions of heaven, the size of the earth, and the depths of the seas.
Wisdom was created before all things, and prudent understanding from everlasting [4].

Some see that the created wisdom given to man is the light that God created on the first day (Gen 1:3). God gave us the light of wisdom so that we may walk as ambassadors for Him in wisdom, discernment, understanding and prudence.

And some scholars see that this text concerns the wisdom of God who became incarnate in the fullness of time, although the plan of the Incarnation was in the mind of God before the creation of all things. The incarnate wisdom of God came to save mankind so that they might enjoy the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Rom 8:21-23; Eph 1:10; Col 1:15-17).
As for his saying "from everlasting," it shows that the wisdom of God is eternal, without beginning.

The wise man links the wisdom created before all things, which He gave to the heavenly beings and to men, with prudent understanding, for it is the eternal hypostasis of Wisdom. Holy Scripture has affirmed that Jesus Christ, the incarnate Word of God, is the wisdom of God the Father (1 Cor 1:24), one with the Father in the same essence.
St. Augustine emphasized the distinction between the wisdom of God the Creator and wisdom as a divine gift.

v Wisdom was created before all things, and it is certainly not the wisdom that is co-partner and equal to You, O our God, its Father, and by whom all things were made (Jn 1:3), and in whom, as the Beginning, heaven and earth were created (Gen 1:1)... This is called wisdom although it is created. Just as the Light (God) who illumines is different in power from the light which is illumined.

entries.section: 1. The source of wisdom and its characteristics

paragraphs.text: How great is the difference between the wisdom that creates and that which is created! It is a great difference, like the difference between the righteousness that justifies and the righteousness that is accomplished by justification? [7]

v As God it was said: "Before all the hills He begat me" (Prov 8:25), that is, before all the exceedingly great creatures. "Before the morning star I begat You" (Ps 109:3) LXX; that is, before all ages and temporal things. And as the servant it was said: "The Lord possessed me in the beginning of His way" (Prov 8:22).
As God He said: "I am the truth," and as the servant: "I am the way."

entries.section: 1. The source of wisdom and its characteristics

paragraphs.text: For since He is the firstborn of those who have fallen asleep (Rev 1:5), He prepared the way for His Church to the Kingdom of God and to eternal life; this is the Head who grants immortality to the body. Thus He created in the beginning of the ways of God for His works (or His dispensation) [8].

entries.section: 1. The source of wisdom and its characteristics

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine Fulgentius, a disciple of St. Augustine, sees that the wisdom which was created before all things is the wisdom that God gave to the angels when He created them [9].
St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that the word "created me" here concerns the humanity, not the divinity.

entries.section: 1. The source of wisdom and its characteristics

paragraphs.text: v The expression "created me" refers not to His divinity (and simple nature), but He says so since He assumed our created nature by His divine plan [10].

St. Gregory of Nyssa Heavenly wisdom is distinguished by giving the believer a life of fellowship with God, so that he tastes the Fatherhood of the Father and responds to the sweetness of His care under all circumstances, and experiences the salvation of the incarnate Word of God, and rejoices as he sings: "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Gal 2:20). And he touches the work of the Holy Spirit, who renews and sanctifies him who has enjoyed the new birth in the waters of Baptism, and he experiences the new mercies of God every morning.

By the work of the Holy Trinity the believer is prepared for eternal life with the earnest of heaven (Eph 1:14), and as the Apostle says: "he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting" (Gal 6:8).
To whom was the root of wisdom revealed?
And who has known her wise counsel? [5]

Through fellowship with God, the believer enjoys intimate friendship with Him, and the Lord reveals to him the secrets of His wisdom, and gives him knowledge and understanding; he discovers God's wise plan in his own life as well as concerning mankind.
There is One who is wise and greatly to be feared, and He sits upon His throne [6].

Who is this One who is wise, sitting upon the throne, but the Lord of glory, of whom the Apostle says: "But unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God" (1 Cor 1:24).

entries.section: 1. The source of wisdom and its characteristics

paragraphs.text: v He who truly believes is fully united with Him in whom are truth, divinity, essence, life and wisdom, and sees in Him all these, which are not in him who does not believe. For without the Son of God you would have neither existence nor name, and the strong man becomes without strength, and the wise man without wisdom. For Christ is "the power of God, and the wisdom of God" (1 Cor 24:1), so whoever thinks that he sees the one God without power, truth, wisdom, life or true light, either sees nothing at all or surely sees what is evil [11].
St. Gregory of Nyssa The Lord is He who created her, and saw her, and numbered her, and poured her out upon all His works [7].
Here he speaks of the wise plan of God concerning His rational creation in heaven and on earth.
God poured out wisdom upon all His works, meaning that the Father created all things by the Son, the Word. As the Evangelist says: "All things were made by Him" (Jn 1:3).
She is with all flesh (man) according to His gift, and He gave her (abundantly) to those who love Him [8].

Ben Sirach says that wisdom dwells with every man (believer) according to what is given to him, and God gives it to those who love Him. This gift is not static, but ever-growing (dynamic). He who fears the Lord grows in wisdom and increases in it, as it is said in the Book of Proverbs: "A wise man will hear, and will increase learning; and a man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels" (Prov 1:5).

The Lord gives man His blessings and distributes them according to man's needs and abilities, and also according to his love and the breadth of his heart. If God offers everything, even wisdom, by a certain measure, then on our part it is fitting for us in every work to walk with wisdom, balance and moderation, without exaggeration on the right or on the left.

entries.section: 1. The source of wisdom and its characteristics

paragraphs.text: v He who receives the teachings of wisdom in addition to the first teachings, since he is already wise, receives the following teachings in matters in which he was not previously wise, and so becomes wiser. As it is also said: "When the wise man hears these things, he becomes wiser" [12].

St. Basil the Great

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: 11 The fear of the Lord is glory, and boasting, and gladness, and a crown of rejoicing. 12 The fear of the Lord delights the heart, and gives gladness and joy and length of days. 13 He who fears the Lord will be well at the last, and will find favor in the day of his death. 14 The love of the Lord is glorious wisdom. 15 And those to whom she appears love her when they see her and contemplate her wonders. 16 The beginning of wisdom is the fear of God. She was created with the faithful in the womb, and has made her nest among men for ever, and will entrust herself to their seed. 17 The fear of the Lord is the worship of Him with knowledge. 18 Worship keeps the heart and justifies it, and gives gladness and joy. 19 He who fears the Lord will be well, and will find favor in the day of his death. 20 The fullness of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; she makes men drunk with her fruits. 21 She fills all her house with desirable things, and her storehouses with grain. 22 The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; she makes peace and healing and health to flourish, 23 and she saw wisdom and numbered it, and both are a gift from God. 24 Wisdom pours out knowledge and the understanding of prudence, and exalts the glory of those who possess her. 25 The root of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and her branches are length of days. 26 In the treasures of wisdom are understanding and worship with knowledge, but to sinners wisdom is an abomination. 27 The fear of the Lord drives away sin. 28 The wrath of the wicked cannot be justified, for the burden of his wrath makes him fall. 29 He that is longsuffering will endure for a time, and afterward joy will return to him. 30 The sensible man hides his words for a time, and the lips of the faithful will praise his understanding.

The book made clear that the beginning of the enjoyment of wisdom is the acquisition of the fear of the Lord, by which the believer is prepared to receive wisdom as a divine gift. The fear of the Lord is not unjust, but leads to honor; indeed it is a crown of glory, exaltation, happiness and constant rejoicing for man even to the moments of death. Ben Sirach distinguishes between the fear that causes shame and disgrace, and the fear that gives honor and glory (4:20-21) together with constant joy. The first fear afflicts man like a psychological illness, driving him into a state of frustration, and the holy fear, which he distinguishes by the title "the fear of the Lord," is a good gift that God gives to His children.
The fear of the Lord is glory and boasting and gladness and a crown of rejoicing [9].

The fear of the Lord is the source of the believer's delight and joy [11-13]. The fear of the Lord is the feeling of honoring Him with deep spiritual thought, together with walking in the Spirit of the Lord in moderation and propriety. The blessings of holy fear are:
A. It is a boast, in which the believer glories as he shares with the heavenly beings who praise God in the spirit of glorious holy fear [9].
B. It gladdens the heart with a joy that time cannot shatter [10].
C. It kindles the heart with longing for the last day of the Lord, so the believer does not fear death [11].

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: D. This fear can be granted to the children of believers while they are in the womb, as happened with John the Baptist (Lk 1:44), and Jacob the son of Isaac (Rom 9:11-13), and Samuel the son of Hannah [12].

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: E. Heavenly wisdom gives inward satisfaction, and gives health to the soul as a medicine for it [16].
F. He who fears the Lord is kept from falling into sins and evil thoughts that seem natural, over which man has no authority.

The link between wisdom and the fear of the Lord lies in the fact that the wisdom books are in essence a call to cleave to the Lord Christ, the wisdom of God, and to enjoy His icon through the daily work of the Holy Spirit in us, so that we enjoy the constant divine presence in our life. This divine presence moves us to the fear of the Lord, so that we are made worthy, more and more, of an abundance of divine work in us.

v Where God is, there is the fear of the Lord, there is gentle seriousness, watchful care and eager concern for others, testing with good examination, fellowship that has its weight, fitting progress, obedience with piety, service with a spirit of consecration, unaffected appearance, a renewed church life, and everything that is divine [14].

Tertullian v Question: Why is there sometimes a kind of sorrow of heart and contrition in the fear of the Lord that comes upon the soul without great effort, and happens spontaneously, and at other times there is in the soul a kind of dullness, so that even if a man forces himself, he cannot feel any contrition of heart?

Answer: Such contrition is a gift from God, for He stirs up the desire, and the soul tastes the sweetness of such contrition that is stirred up, and so adopts it (adopts the grace given to it). Or it is to prove that the soul is able, through intense zeal, to be in continual contrition. Thus he who loses this grace through his laxity has no excuse.

But sometimes we force ourselves (to contrition), yet we are unable to obtain it, as evidence of our earlier neglect on other occasions. For it is impossible for man to succeed in a work merely by coming to it without giving it intense care together with diligent training with others, and his soul is shown to be disgusted with the vices and passions that hinder the practice of what is fitting. This is according to the teaching spoken by the Apostle, who said: "But I am carnal, sold under sin. For that which I do I allow not: for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I" (Rom 7:14-15). He also says: "Now then it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me" (Rom 7:17).

God allows this very thing to happen to us for a good purpose, that the soul, by means of the things it suffers involuntarily, may perceive the things that assail it, and as it learns the ways by which it became enslaved to sin against its will (Rom 6:20), it awakens again, and guards itself against the snares of the devil (1 Tim 3:7; 6:9), and discovers that God's mercy urges the support of those who truly repent [15].
v For my sake You turned my mourning into joy for me, You tore my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness" (Ps 30:12).

The joy of God does not settle in all souls, but in those souls which wept over their sins with continual tears, like one who has lost someone dear to them. God turns the mourning of such a soul into joy, and sorrow is profitable here...
The prophets weep over us, and call us to weep until we discover our faults in the light of their prophetic words; then we weep over our perdition, and subdue our body with striving and discipline.
The man who walks in such a way, his sackcloth is torn, and he puts on the adorned wedding garment so as not to be cast outside the wedding (Mt 22:11-13) [16].

St. Basil the Great Thus the book transfers us from dry rational wisdom to the holy practical wisdom set forth in Holy Scripture. It is not fearful cowering, but godliness, consecration to God and glorying in Him (Prov 2:1-5). The believer does not separate divine love from the fear of the Lord (Deut 10:12; Sir 2:15). The fear of the Lord is not foreign to the believer; it is granted to him while he is still a fetus in the womb [12].

The fullness of wisdom is the fear of the Lord [16]. It makes believers drunk with its delightful fruits, and satisfies their souls with its choice food, and fills their storehouses with its produce, and gives them inward peace and perfect health.

The fear of the Lord is not only the beginning of wisdom, but its fullness and its crown. By the fear of the Lord the believer receives the abundant harvest of wisdom. Among the blessings of the fear of the Lord is that it drives away sins, and removes all anger from the soul, for "the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Prov 15:18; Jas 1:20).
Thus the book links wisdom, the divine commandment and the fear of the Lord. At the same time it warns against wavering between pagan Hellenistic ideas and faithfulness in fellowship with God.

v In any case, it is beneficial to fear Him alone, not as one who is unjust but as God who is righteous. For a man fears one who is unjust lest he destroy him by injustice, and fears the righteous one lest he sin and be punished.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: By your fear of Him you are freed from all harmful fears. For unless you fear the one Lord, the Creator of all, you become a slave to all the evils that harm you, I mean you become a slave to demons and (spiritual) diseases and everything that can harm you in one way or another [17].
v Fear God, for He is just, but whether you fear Him or love Him you must not sin...

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: He who fears Him can gain victory over evil desires, and does not covet what belongs to others, but practices tenderness and dignity and works justly! [18]
The Clementines By the fear of the Lord we enjoy the blessed life; St. Arsenius says that he who fears the One (God) will not fear many.
v As a lamp lights a dark room, so the fear of the Lord, when it penetrates the heart of a man, illumines it, teaching it all the virtues and the commandments of God.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: One of the Desert Fathers v Blessed is he who walks in all things in fear through reverent modesty. For he stands firm in the truth, able to say: "I advanced and saw the Lord before me at all times, for He is at my right hand, that I should not be moved" (Ps 16:8) [19] LXX.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great St. Barsanuphius gives us a practical training for obtaining the crown of rejoicing, for he wrote: [Labor with all your strength, and then God will help you by the prayers of your fathers. For He thirsts for your salvation, since He swore by Himself that He does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he return and live" (Ezek 18:23)... Contribute like the widow with the two mites that you have, and He will be pleased as He was with her (Mk 12:42). Hasten with your boat to the ship of your fathers, and they will lead you to Jesus, who alone can give you humility, strength, prudence and the crown of rejoicing [20].]

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: v Rejoice in the Lord, rejoice in the Lord, rejoice in the Lord. May the Lord guard your soul and body and spirit from all evil, and from every opposition of the devil, and from all wearisome imaginings. May the Lord be your light and your protection and your way and your strength and the crown of your rejoicing and your everlasting support. Take heed to yourself, as it is written: "even the word that is gone out of my lips shall not be changed" (Ps 89:34) [21]

St. Barsanuphius The Lord's word in the Book of Malachi concerning the men of the priesthood shows His divine work in their lives, for He fills them with fear as an ornament with which the priests are adorned, so that they enjoy glory and rejoicing, and are adorned with holiness.

v "I do this so that he (the priest) may be filled with fear toward Me; I work in such a way that he trembles before My name" (Mal 2:5) LXX. He counts in a fitting manner all the exalted adornment of the priesthood, which he obtains through the teaching of the Law. He inspires first and before everything the fear of the Lord in the service of divine worship, making them drawn to tremble before His name with fear and trembling when they hear the name of the Lord, and brings them into the experience of inclining toward reverence (of the Lord), not as a matter of no importance, but with seriousness, for there is nothing more important than it... It was said: "The fear of the Lord is glory and boasting." Thus he secures safety for him who practices the priesthood with holiness and in truth.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: He did not ask them merely to be refreshed by fear, but to be completely filled with fear, that is, that the fear of the Lord fill all the heart and the soul [22].

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: v Consider how God uses a means fitting to Him: instead of punishing us, He displays the effects of His wrath on human bodies, preferring to alarm us with simple outward terrors and slight losses [23].

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: St. Cyril the Great v The starting point in the service of God [as slaves] is being filled with the spirit of fear, when the person is still called a child. For children in particular, fear is the tutor. Therefore the Apostle says of such a child: "Now I say, That the heir, as long as he is a child, differeth nothing from a servant, though he be lord of all; but is under tutors and governors until the time appointed of the father. Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world" (Gal 4:1-3) [24].

Origen St. Ambrose, in his discourse on Cain and Abel, compares what the world offers with what the Church offers. The world is unable to give the soul true pleasure and inward joy, whereas the Church, where the wisdom of God and the fear of the Lord are, makes the soul drunk with the joy of the Spirit, together with wisdom and prudence from God.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: v "Come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine which I have mingled" (Prov 9:6). Do you find delight in songs that enchant listeners at banquets? Listen to the voice of the Church, which urges us not only in the Song of Songs: "Eat, O friends; drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved" (Song 5:1), but this drunkenness makes men sober. This drunkenness is grace (from God) and not madness of the mind [25].
St. Ambrose The fear of the Lord gladdens the heart, and gives gladness and joy and length of days [10].
The blessings of the fear of God extend in the life of man in this world to the moment of his death, when he meets the Lord Christ face to face.

v If anyone wishes to obtain the love of God, let the fear of the Lord be in him, for fear begets weeping, and weeping begets strength. And when all these are perfected in the soul, the soul begins to bear fruit in everything. And when God sees in the soul these good fruits, He smells them as the fragrance of sweet incense, and He and His angels rejoice in it, and He satisfies it with joy, and keeps it in all its ways until it reaches its place of rest without suffering harm.
When Satan sees the great heavenly Guardian surrounding the soul, he fears to approach it or attack it because of this great power.

Therefore acquire this power so that the demons may be terrified before you, and your works become easy, and you may delight in the divine work, for the sweetness of the love of God is sweeter than honey.

Truly many monks and virgins in the communities have not tasted this divine sweetness, and have not acquired the divine power, supposing that they have obtained it, although they have not striven. But he who strives for it obtains it surely through the divine mercies, for God is no respecter of persons.

So he who wants to have the light of God and His power must despise the honors of this world and its defilement, and hate all the things of the world and the pleasure of the flesh, and cleanse his heart from all evil thoughts. And he offers to God fasts and tears night and day without relenting as pure prayers; then God pours out upon him that power.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Strive to obtain this power, so that you may do all your works with ease, and have great boldness before God, and He will give you all that you ask [26].
St. Anba Anthony the Great He who fears the Lord, it shall go well with him at the last, and in the day of his death he shall be blessed [11].

When we speak of Jacob's ladder, by which Jacob enjoyed the opened heaven and fellowship with the heavenly beings, we recall that Jacob suffered from fear. He was in complete isolation, with no father or mother or brother or friend to accompany and support him. He was on his way, fleeing from the violence of his brother, suffering many dangers and an unknown future. Jacob leaned on the stone, a type of the Lord Christ, to sleep, and he enjoyed the heavenly vision, and touched the fear of the Lord, for he said: "How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God" (Gen 28:17).

When we suffer from the fear of the flesh or the fear of the world that crushes the soul, we lean on our Christ, the cornerstone, and He replaces destructive fear with holy fear. Instead of our fear of the world with all its harsh circumstances, we see the glory of God and His holiness and His love, so we look forward with joy to the day of our departure from the world, and we realize that while we are on earth we dwell in the house of God, indeed we have become "of the household of God" (Eph 2:19); how much more blessed then will be the day of our death.
The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; it is created with the faithful in the womb [12].

God's care for man goes back to the moment of the beginning of his conception, and continues while the fetus is in his mother's womb. The Lord Christ showed His concern for the faith of infants and children (Lk 18:15-17).
St. Philoxenus distinguishes between different kinds of fear: the fear of slaves, the fear of hired servants, the fear of friends, and the fear of sons.

v There is one who fears being beaten, and this is the fear of slaves; and there is one who fears losing his wages, and this is the fear of hired servants; and there is one who fears being deprived of the inheritance, and this is the fear of sons; so although fear has only one name, the differences among its kinds are many.
The holy prophets feared God, and the Jewish people also from time to time feared God; but how great is the difference between the two fears!

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: For the prophets feared to grieve God as His friends, because they loved Him; while the Jews feared His discipline and punishment as slaves [27].

St. Mar Philoxenus Our Christ wants to raise us by His grace until we reach the fear of sons. So we do not fear God as slaves who fear their master, carrying out the commandment not from their depths but for fear of punishment.

Nor do we fear Him as hired servants who fulfill the commandment for the sake of the wages or for fear of being deprived of them; thus God would be a means and not an end, and we would submit to Him to obtain His blessings and not to possess Him and enjoy fellowship with Him.
Nor do we fear Him as mere friends who seek to please their friend.

But we fear Him as sons, fulfilling the commandment so that the image of our Father may be formed in our depths, and so we are prepared for fellowship in His glories. We possess Him and He possesses us, and we live with Him eternally in His embrace!
St. Augustine sees that the way begins with fear and raises man up the ladder of holiness until he reaches wisdom: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord."

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: v The prophet Isaiah presents to us the seven well-known spiritual gifts. He begins with wisdom and ends with the fear of the Lord, as though he were descending from the heights to our own level. He does this to teach us to climb up again. Thus he begins from where we want to arrive (wisdom), and comes to the point of beginning. He says: "The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and godliness, the spirit of the fear of the Lord" (Isa 11:2). So he descended from wisdom to fear, not to slip backward, but to teach us to climb from fear and ascend to wisdom. We do this so that we may advance, "for the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom [28]."

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine v It is fitting for the souls of those who wish to speak wisdom first to be purified by the divine fear. For distributing the sacraments of salvation to the common people and receiving all persons on an equal footing (without wise discernment), including those whose lives are not adorned with purity, and who have not been tested nor prepared to use the sacraments reasonably, is like pouring precious ointment into a filthy vessel [29].

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great v Just as among the pagans there are those who abstain from the pleasures before them, either because it is impossible to obtain what they see, or for fear of men, or to obtain greater pleasures, so also with regard to the faith, some practice self-control, either because they await the promise of God or for the fear of the Lord; such self-control rests on knowledge and on the enjoyment of better things, and is counted as striving for perfection. It is said: "The fear of the Lord is the head of wisdom" (Prov 1:7) [30].

St. Clement of Alexandria v The beginning of wisdom is fear, for it is fitting that we not begin with (spiritual) contemplations and leave fear. For unrestrained contemplation may drive us to the edge of a precipice. Rather we must be broken and purified, so that through fear we become light in weight, and rise to the heights.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: For where there is fear there is keeping of the commandments, and where there is keeping of the commandments there is purification of the flesh from the cloud that covers the soul and does not allow it to see the divine ray. And where there is purification there is illumination, and illumination is the satisfaction of the desires of those longing for great things, or for things that surpass all great things [31].
St. Gregory of Nazianzus v Let us not allow the beast (sin) to be unbridled; let us hasten to it and put a strong muzzle on every side, which is the fear of the coming judgment.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: When a friend or one of your household causes you to stumble and you become angry, consider that your disobedience is against God, and that the kindness you show to those who trouble you will be repaid to you at your judgment by God's kindness to you [32].
St. John Chrysostom She made a foundation for life among men, and continues to be trustworthy with their descendants [13].

The blessings of the fear of the Lord are: 1. "It makes men drunk with its fruits" [14], so he who fears the Lord does not feel a hunger for the glory of the world and its desires and treasures, but feels satisfied, for his depths are filled with the fruit of the fear of the Lord. 2. "It fills all their houses with desirable things" [15]. For the fear of the Lord brings him into the divine embrace, and he discovers that His mouth is most sweet and He is altogether desirable (Song 5:16). 3. It fills "their storehouses with its produce" [15]; the rich fool wanted to build larger storehouses and fill them with good things so as to eat and be satisfied, but his soul was required of him that very night before he moved to build the storehouses (Lk 12:20); but he who fears the Lord, the Spirit of God raises up from his depths a dwelling for God the Father and His only-begotten Son, and his depths become a kingdom of God (Lk 17:21), so what does he lack? There dwells in him the Lord of glory, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom (Col 2:3). 4. The one who fears the Lord is crowned with the crown of wisdom [16], so peace increases in him without ceasing, and he experiences healing, so no sin wounds him, and no wicked thought steals into his mind! 5. God is pleased with the one who fears the Lord, so He numbers what he has enjoyed, and rains upon him the waters of knowledge, learning and practical wisdom (prudence), and raises him from glory to glory [17]. 6. The one who fears the Lord will not fear the departure of wisdom from him, for the fear of the Lord is the root of wisdom and its roots planted in him, and its branches will never wither [20].
The delight of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and it makes men drunk with its fruits [14].

St. Wissa, disciple of Anba Shenouda, the Archimandrite, sees that wisdom works not only in the life of the wise man but also in the lives of those around him, and on the contrary folly destroys the man and those who deal with him.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: v "Every wise woman buildeth her house: but the foolish plucketh it down with her hands" (Prov 14:1). This means that the wise woman encourages her neighbor in the fear of God and with the love in her heart toward her sister and sisters. On the other hand the foolish woman pulls down with her hands, by her words full of bitterness and hatred and contempt. As it is written: "In the mouth of the foolish is a rod of contempt" (cf. Prov 14:3) [33].

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: St. Wissa v It is altogether unfitting that the beatitudes begin from another source (other than poverty in spirit and the fear of the Lord), where the summit of wisdom is attained, for the crown (beginning) of wisdom is the fear of the Lord (1:16), and on the other hand pride is described as the beginning of every sin (10:13). Let the proud man strive for the kingdoms of the earth and love them; but "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" [34].

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: v For him who strives for wisdom, there is nothing like the saying: "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom" [35].

v Listen to Holy Scripture: "The crown (beginning) of wisdom is the fear of the Lord" (Sir 1:16). Therefore he begins with the fear of the day of judgment: by fear he reforms himself, to strive against his enemies, that is, against his sins. Let him begin to renew his life inwardly, and mortify his members which are upon the earth, as the Apostle says: "Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth... (Col 3:5).

He calls the spiritual matters of evil "members upon the earth," for he continues explaining this: "covetousness, uncleanness," and so on. So that man who begins with the fear of the day of judgment to mortify his members which are upon the earth extends to the height of his heavenly members and their strengthening. He practices goodness with his heavenly members. And as the heavenly members are raised, longing begins toward the fear. He fears that Christ may come upon this wicked man who wishes to curse him... Now the pure soul which desires to embrace her Bridegroom, and renounces the adulterer, begins to long for the coming of Christ.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: She becomes a virgin in her depths through this faith and hope and love. Thus the soul has confidence in the day of judgment, and does not resist itself when it prays: "Thy kingdom come" (Mt 6:10). For he who fears the coming of the kingdom of God may be seized by fears lest his prayer be answered [36].
St. Augustine She fills all their houses with desirable things, and their storehouses with her produce [15].
The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, which gives peace and healing for flourishing [16].
The Lord saw her and numbered her, and rained down the power of understanding, and honors the glory of those who hold fast to her [17].
The root of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and its branches are length of days [18][37].

The fear of the Lord is the steering wheel of the soul; the Holy Spirit of God gives it to us, He who alone is able to bring us from glory to glory, and to give us grace upon grace, through our fellowship with the Lord of glory, the holy Jesus. The fear of the Lord brings us into the royal way, so we do not swerve toward sin, nor toward self-righteousness. It keeps us from the blows from the left and from the right, until we enter into the bosom of the holy heavenly Father.
v The fear of the Lord urges the soul to keep the commandments, and through keeping the commandments the house of the soul is built.
v Let us fear the Lord and build houses for ourselves, so that we may find shelter in the winter where there is rain and thunder, for he who has no house suffers great dangers in the time of winter.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Father Dorotheus v Fear the Lord and keep His commandments, which strengthen you in all your affairs, so that there is none like your works... Do not fear Satan if you fear the Lord, for your fear of God gives you authority over Satan [38].
Hermas St. Clement of Alexandria sees that the Lord often speaks and threatens before He disciplines, so that man may turn back from his evil.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: v The Lord often speaks before He carries out the work (the discipline). He says: "I will spend My arrows upon them; they shall be burnt with hunger, and devoured with burning heat, and with bitter destruction. I will also send the teeth of beasts upon them, with the poison of serpents of the earth. The sword without, and terror within, shall destroy" (Deut 32:23-25). This does not mean that the Divine Spirit becomes angry, as some suppose. He often shows restraint along with encouragement, and shows us what we ought to do. He uses this effective means, which lies in stirring up fear in us, so that we do not commit sin [39].
St. Clement of Alexandria Unjust anger cannot be justified, for the sure effect of anger causes its downfall [19].

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: v In truth, just as madmen and fools do not notice this when they cast themselves into the abyss, so it is with those who lose their gentleness and are struck by anger. This is why the wise man, who wishes to expose the destruction of this intoxication (anger), says: "The wrath of man turns the scale of the balance to his own destruction." Observe how he binds himself in slavery to the work of this passion, destructive in its weight [40].

v Anger is a ravening beast, a violent and raging beast. Let us then prescribe for ourselves a soothing draught taken from Holy Scripture, and say: "Why (how) is he proud who is dust and ashes?" (Sir 10:9), the weight of his anger destroys him (cf. Sir 1:19)... Nothing is more shameful, nothing is uglier than a face inflamed with anger. When you stir up mud, you smell a foul odor. And when a soul is disturbed by passion, it becomes exceedingly foul [41].

v The passion of anger is ravenous, fiercer than any flame. For this reason we need to hasten very quickly to prevent the flame, and not allow it to blaze up on high. For this sickness becomes the cause of many evils. It brings down whole houses, dissolves old friendships, and causes calamities that cannot be remedied in a short time. It was said: "The wrath of man turns the scale of the balance to his own destruction" [42].
St. John Chrysostom The long-suffering man bears patiently until the right time, and afterward joy returns to him with power [20].

Ben Sirach distinguishes between a man who is wronged and so becomes angry and rages, and another who falls under wrong and endures with long-suffering. The first, although his anger rests on a wrong that has befallen him, is burdened by his own anger, and so he falls, even if he thinks he is justifying himself. The second endures for a time in silence, and then joy returns to him, and many bear witness for him while he is silent and does not defend himself.
He holds back his words until the right time, and the lips of many tell of his understanding [21].

31 In the treasures of wisdom are the parables of knowledge, 32 but to the sinner the worship of God is an abomination. 33 My son, if you desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord will give her to you. 34 For wisdom and instruction are the fear of the Lord, and that which pleases Him 35 is faith and meekness, and He will fill him who has them with treasures. 36 Do not disobey the fear of the Lord, and do not come to Him with a double heart. 37 Be not a hypocrite in the sight of men, and keep watch over your lips. 38 Exalt not yourself, lest you fall, and bring dishonor upon your soul, 39 and the Lord reveal your secrets, and cast you down in the midst of the congregation, 40 because you came not to the fear of the Lord, but your heart is full of deceit.
In the treasures of wisdom are the parables of knowledge, but godliness is an abomination to the sinner [22].
If godliness is an abomination to the sinner, how much more can the enemy of good, the devil, not bear it, and so he rages against the godly; yet he has no authority to harm them.
v If (the demons) had authority, they would not hesitate to use it, but would practice evil at once, since this is their aim, especially against us.

Behold, we are gathered together speaking against them, and they know it, that the more we advance, the weaker they become. If they had authority, they would not have allowed any of us Christians to live, for the service of God is an abomination to the sinner (cf. Sir 1:22). But since they have no authority, they harm themselves, for they cannot carry out anything of what they threaten. This obliges us not to fear them [43].
St. Athanasius the Apostolic If you desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord will give her to you [23].

The philosophy discovered by the Gentiles is the product of human understanding, but Holy Scripture proclaims that understanding is from God Himself, who gives it to him who believes in His commandments.
v Do not forsake the commandment of the Lord, but keep what you have received, neither adding to it nor taking away from it [44].
The Didache (the Teaching of the Twelve Disciples)
v I have been absorbed in the commandments that You gave me, and meditated on them with wisdom; I believed in them until I kept them.
Grant me, then, wisdom by teaching me goodness, discipline and knowledge.
This petition agrees with the saying: "My son, if you desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord will give her to you" (cf. Sir 1:23).

St. Didymus the Blind v The (first) Psalm draws for us the way of virtue with knowledge and skill. Turning away from evil is the beginning of good. If you ask from the beginning for the perfection of virtue, you will draw back before you start; but the Psalm prepares the way for us to face it with courage.

And I believe that growth in the love of God is like the ladder that the blessed Jacob once saw, which was on the earth on one side and on the other side was reaching toward the life of virtue, where a man begins by climbing the first rungs of the ladder, and after that rises to a higher rung with deliberation and patience, until he reaches what human nature can attain.
So, by climbing the first rungs of the ladder, we rise above the earth, to live the life that God wills for us.

And the beginning of progress is to keep away from evil, where such keeping away is easy, as in: "You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal" (Ex 20:13-15); this does not require any positive work. But when we are required to keep that commandment: "Love your neighbor as yourself," "Sell what you have and give to the poor" (Mt 19:21), "Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two" (Mt 5:41), these works are done by the wrestler who has tested his strength by divine wisdom, who through small works leads us to perfection.
For he sets before us three things that we must avoid: walking in the counsel of the wicked, standing in the way of sinners, and sitting in the seat of the scornful.

This order begins with making the decision and then carrying out the beginning, here in pure thought. For the foundation of the works of the flesh springs from purity of heart; adultery begins in the lustful soul and ends in adultery of the body. Therefore the Lord said: "That which defiles a man comes out of the heart" (cf. Mt 15:18) [45].
St. Basil the Great Origen sees that wisdom begins with upright conduct, or keeping the divine commandment.

v If anyone meditates in the law of the Lord day and night (Ps 1:2), and is like the mouth of the righteous that speaks wisdom (Ps 37:30), he will be able to ask with care and find. So it will be, on condition that he asks in a sound manner, and by his asking knocks at the door of wisdom, to ask God to open it to him, and is made worthy to receive by the Holy Spirit the word of wisdom and the word of knowledge, and becomes a companion of the wisdom of Solomon [46].

v "I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded" (Prov 1:24). It is reasonable that he said that He (God) stretches out His words in his heart (the heart of Solomon)... because God gave him a large heart.
He is able to explain, in brief, what is stated in the mysteries, within the broad, harmonious and confirmed teachings of Holy Scripture, since he has a large heart.

Therefore, in agreement with the teachings of the wise Solomon, it is necessary for the person who desires to know wisdom to begin with training in conduct, so that he may understand what is written: "Do you long for wisdom? Keep the commandments, and it will be given to you by God" [47].
Origen v Wisdom is good; it fills with joy those who possess her, and brings down those who do not practice (the commandments).

But what does Holy Scripture say? The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (cf. Sir 1:12). Who does not love to reign? And in the Psalms there is the counsel of the Spirit: "Now therefore, O you kings, be wise; be instructed, you judges of the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling." This is the reason for Paul's saying: "Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling" (Phil 2:12). And we read: "If you desire wisdom, observe justice, and the Lord will grant her to you [48]."

v You must order your life by the commandments of God, which we receive to help us walk the good life, beginning with godly fear, for "the fear of the Lord is the head of wisdom" (Prov 1:7), while human pride breaks and weakens [49].

The commandments are those that concern the good, that is, bring the good; and the good is faith without doubt. Hence wisdom is the reward of pure faith. And the reward will be what eye has not seen [50].

St. Augustine v People are commonly called "wise," with a misuse of the word "wise." For the wise are not those who study the sayings and writings of the early wise Fathers, but those whose souls are rational, able to distinguish between what is good and what is evil. They avoid what is evil and harmful to the soul, and wisely take care of what is good and profitable to the soul and practice it with great thanksgiving to God. These alone are truly those whom we should call "wise" [51].
St. Anthony the Great v The knowledge of goodness is not enough for blessedness for him who does not put goodness into practice; true godliness toward God is the beginning of knowledge [52].
St. Didymus the Blind For the fear of the Lord is wisdom and instruction, and that which pleases Him is faith and meekness [24].

v In truth the divinity is not angry, as some suppose; rather, when God uses many threats, He does this as an appeal, showing mankind the things that will come to pass. These are measures that are certainly good; He plants fear to keep us from sin. "The fear of the Lord drives away sin, and he who has no fear cannot be justified." The punishment that God imposes is not from anger but from justice; and he who neglects justice makes no progress [53].
St. Clement of Alexandria Do not disobey the fear of the Lord, and do not come to Him with a double heart [25].

An undivided mind: to enjoy the holy fear of the Lord, which gives wisdom, it is fitting for the believer to keep the divine commandments, for they support his faith in God, and also grant him to be adorned with meekness, so that he does not fall into arrogance even toward unbelievers [27]. And on the other hand, he clings to God with all his heart, without duplicity.

As he speaks of wisdom and its connection with the divine commandment, he calls us to the life of simplicity as the key to obedience to the commandment, warning us against the double heart. If simplicity directs our hearts to the way of truth without deviation, the double heart makes man lose his aim, so that he gives an hour to the Lord and an hour to amusement and temporal pleasures.
As St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, speaks of the virtues, he puts simplicity of heart first, which is the opposite of duplicity of heart, saying:

v Concerning the elements of virtue, which kind of them it is fitting to regard as the greatest, and which of them we need to practice more than the others, this is their order; these things cannot be put into words. For they all have the same dignity, and lead the one who practices them to the heights by way of each one of them.

For simplicity opens the way to obedience, and obedience to faith, and faith to hope, and hope to righteousness (justice), and righteousness to service, and service to humility. By this is achieved the kindness that leads to grace, and grace to love, and love to prayer. Thus every virtue depends on the other virtues. And the virtues lead us to the summit of what we desire. Just as the crown of evil leads its friends to ever-increasing evil... Besides this, it is necessary for us to continue steadfastly in prayer (Rom 12:12). For prayer is like the leader of the chorus of the virtues [54].

St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa Let us follow God with our whole being, or with all our heart and all our mind: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind" (Lk 10:27).

v These alone receive within them the greatness of the commandment and its priority: not only do they love the Lord their God, but they set themselves to accomplish this by three conditions; that is, with all their heart they hold within them the perfection of this love, its thoughts and its works; and with all their soul, that is, they are ready to give it up for the service of God who created all things, when the spreading of His word requires it; for God is loved with all the soul when no part of the soul is held back outside the keeping of the faith; and they love Him with all the mind, so that they think of nothing and speak of nothing but the divine things [55].

Origen v I believe that the wise man counsels divided persons, likening them to those who approach the way of God, when he says: "Do not come to the Lord with two hearts," but draw near to His way as one who sows and another who reaps [56].

St. Isaac the Syrian v The virtuous life is truly the source and root of wisdom, just as iniquity has folly as its source. I say this because the boaster and the slave of lust is taken captive by these vices as the fruit of lack of wisdom... Every sin begins with a lack of wisdom, just as the virtuous person who fears God is the wisest of all. For this reason the wise man says: "The fear of the Lord is the head of wisdom" (Prov 1:7). If the fear of the Lord is to be wise, and the evildoer does not possess this fear, then he is truly stripped of wisdom, and he who is deprived of wisdom is truly the most foolish of all [57].

St. John Chrysostom v It is fitting for the Christian to think thus of his heavenly calling, and that his life be worthy of the gospel of Christ (Phil 1:27). It is fitting that the Christian not be of a double mind (Lk 12:29), nor be distracted from remembering God and His purposes and His judgments [58].
St. Basil the Great Be not a hypocrite in the sight of men, and keep watch over your lips [26].

It was said of the pride of the hypocrite that it lifts him up as if to heaven; with his arrogant thought he seems as one who leads himself to the heavenly life. In hypocrisy he thinks that his head has reached the clouds, for he thinks that his thinking mind is equal to the merits of the saints who went before him.

v Hypocrisy is hateful to God and abhorred by men; it brings no reward, and is of no use at all for the salvation of the soul, but rather destroys it. If someone flees into hypocrisy so that his matter may not be discovered, it is only for a time, for it does not last long; rather, everything is revealed, and brings shame upon its owner. Thus he is like an ugly woman whose outward adornment, put on her by artificial means, is stripped from her. Hypocrisy, then, is foreign to the saints, since it is impossible for anything of what we do or say to escape the eyes of the divinity, for it was said: "There is nothing covered that shall not be revealed, neither hid that shall not be known" (Lk 12:2). If all our words and works will be revealed on the day of judgment, then hypocrisy is wearisome and without profit. It is fitting for us to be proved as true worshippers who serve God with sincere and open countenances [59].

St. Cyril the Great v There may be one who gives his alms before men yet avoids making a show of it, and there is also one who does not give it before men yet boasts of it in secret. For God does not reward almsgiving according to how it is done, whether before men or not, but according to the intention of the one who does it [60].

v Everyone sees the thief, "hypocrisy," carrying everything before his eyes, and he rejoices in it! What a new kind of robbery, which attracts people and delights them while they are being robbed! [61]

St. John Chrysostom v What is the place of the hypocrite (Job 20:9) but the heart of his flatterers? For he rests in the place where he finds those who love him... But as long as he lives, he does not cease to teach his followers the same things that he practices, and through the boldness of his sinful way he begets others also in the likeness of his own vain deceit.
v Hypocrites appear fruitful and green in the eyes of their fellow creatures, but in the sight of the hidden Judge they appear fruitless and withered.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Do not exalt yourself, lest you fall, and bring dishonor upon your soul.
And the Lord will reveal your secrets, and strike you down in the midst of the congregation, because you truly did not come to the fear of the Lord, and your heart is full of deceit [27].
Wisdom is a free gift that He offers to the humble; He offers it without partiality, and gives it to those who enjoy the fear of the Lord and take care to keep His commandments [27].
v Hate greatness, for it is the fruit full of death.
For Adam ate of it in Eden, and it gave him death.
And by it Satan fell from the beginning. By it the house of Adam fell from Paradise.
There is nothing with God so vile and hateful as the love of greatness, and him who exalts himself in pride.

St. Jacob of Serugh v Observe these proud and reckless people; observe the ox as it is prepared for slaughter, left to roam in freedom, destroying what it wishes, until the day of its slaughter... Holy Scripture points to it in another place as a sacrifice, and that it is left to an evil freedom (Prov 7:22) [62].

St. Augustine v Satan fell from his heavenly rank because of his pride; therefore he always does all he can to make fall all who wish to advance toward God with all their hearts, using the same means by which he himself fell, I mean greatness and the love of vainglory. By this and the like he fights us, in the hope of drawing us away from God...

What moved our Lord Jesus Christ to lay aside His garments, and gird Himself with a towel, and pour water into a basin, and wash the feet of those who were beneath Him (Jn 13:4 etc.), if not to teach us humility?! He showed us humility by the example He gave. Therefore those who wish to return to their first rank will not be able to do so except by humility. For pride is the cause of the fall from heaven in the beginning.
And so he who lacks deep humility, from all the heart and mind and spirit and body, does not inherit the Kingdom of God [63].

v Many have lived a long time as monks and virgins, and have not learned how to acquire purity. This is because they despise the teaching of their fathers and follow the desires of their own hearts. Therefore the evil spirits that destroy souls gained mastery over them, wounding them night and day with their unseen arrows, and giving them peace nowhere; rather they occupy their hearts now with pride, and now with vainglory and evil jealousy and slander and anger and fury and quarrels and many other passions. These have their portion with the five foolish virgins, for they passed their time in folly, and did not bridle their tongues, nor keep their eyes pure, nor keep their bodies from lusts or their hearts from impurities and the like [64].
St. Anthony the Great Inspired by Sirach 1

entries.section: Let me possess You, O wisdom of the eternal God!

paragraphs.text: v You are the wisdom of God, Creator of heaven and earth!
You are the wise One, greatly to be feared, sitting upon Your throne!
Who, of the heavenly orders or of men, can search out the mysteries of Your creation?!
Who can search out Your nature?
You are the wisdom of God; You came down to me that I might possess You, and become wise through You.
You are the Giver of wisdom and of every blessing; You have become a gift to me. I possess You within me and I cherish You!
v You gave me reason together with freedom of will so that I might contemplate the works of Your love; but when I stood helpless, You came down to me to dwell in my depths!
You came down to me to carry me in Yourself, and to prepare for me a place in Your heavens.
I meet You face to face, and my insight remains in amazement.
I depart to Paradise, and enjoy the eternal glories and their mysteries, without ceasing!
v My soul blesses You, who have given me the instinct of holy fear.
As I come to know You, Your holy fear is fixed in me, and my depths are glorified by Your dwelling in them.
I glory in You, my joy and the gladness of my heart!
Your fear leads me on the journey of my sojourn until the day of my departure from the world.
Your fear joins me to the orders of the heavenly ones, and I praise You with them with fear and trembling.
Your fear turns the dry wilderness of my heart into a paradise full of the fruit of the Spirit.
Your fear cleanses me from the fear of the devil and the fear of men!
By Your fear I defy the devil and all his forces and all his works, so that no evil thought can steal into me, nor idle word, nor wicked conduct!
Your fear is a tree of life, whose branches extend to my emotions and senses and words and conduct.
I pluck from it, and I am sanctified within and without.
I pluck from it Your love, and I love all mankind, even those who oppose me!
v You made with me a wonderful covenant of love, which You recorded in Your holy book.
You gave me Your book to meditate in, and my soul is filled with Your sweetness!
Your commandments are the precious jewelry that adorns my soul!
Your commandments prepare me for the eternal wedding.
My soul sits as a queen adorned with Your commandments, and the heavenly ones marvel at her!
For every perfection I have seen an end, but Your commandments are exceedingly broad.
Since You presented Yourself to me as a heavenly friend, You gave me Your wisdom and Your fear and Your commandment!
How can I suffer isolation, when You accompany me throughout the journey of my sojourn?
How can I complain of my poverty and need, when I am rich in You!
v Glory to You for Your companionship with me, so that I turn neither to the right nor to the left.
My heart will not know duplicity, for it is in Your hand.
Your love fills my whole heart, so the devil will find no place in it!
Glory to You, O All-wise, Giver of holy fear, and Your commandment full of sweetness!

Appendix to Sirach 1 The fear of the Lord The fear of the Lord is manifested in obedience to His commandments, and he who keeps His commandments enjoys inner glory, and lives in the joy and gladness of the Spirit, and receives a crown of rejoicing. Some claim that God's commandments and judgments humiliate man, because they have not experienced the truth of the commandments, which restore to man the image of God so that he becomes in His likeness, and so lives in joy.
The goal of the commandment is that God may dwell in us and in our midst (Zech 2:5). Therefore the fear of the Lord is glory and pride and gladness and a crown of rejoicing.

"The fear of the Lord was created with the faithful in the womb" [12]. Thus the parents' care for their children begins before their birth. For when Zacharias the priest and Elizabeth were sanctified, and St. Mary visited them and brought the incarnate Word, the child John leaped and ran rejoicing in the Lord, and enjoyed the fear of the Lord while still in the womb.
a. There is a relation between wisdom and the fear of the Lord. Both bring happiness and blessing. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom and its fulfillment and its crown [12, 16, 18].
b. Wisdom is a mother and bride to him who fears the Lord: "She will meet him as a mother, and receive him as a wife married in her youth" (15:2).
c. The eyes of the Lord are upon him who fears the Lord: "And He knows every work of man" (15:19).
d. Those who fear the Lord are filled with blessings and hope: "The fear of the Lord is like a paradise of blessing" (40:27).
e. Those who fear the Lord and the word of God: "They that fear the Lord will not disobey His words" (2:15).

The possibilities of him who fears the Lord: "He that fears the Lord shall fear nothing, and shall not be afraid, for He is his hope" (34:14). "There shall no evil happen to him that fears the Lord; but in temptation He (the Lord) will deliver him again and again. A wise man hates not the law, but he that makes a show of keeping it is like a boat in a storm. A man of understanding trusts in the law, and the law is faithful to him, for it is a divine revelation" (33:1-3).
f. The honor of him who fears the Lord: "What seed is honorable? They that fear the Lord" (10:19).
g. The fear of the Lord is the pride of the elders: "Much experience is the crown of old men, and the fear of the Lord is their glory" (25:6).
h. The fear of the Lord surpasses every good: "The fear of the Lord surpasses all things" (25:11).
i. A good wife is a gift to those who fear the Lord: "A good wife is a great portion, and shall be given to him that fears the Lord" (26:3; cf. 27:3).

entries.section: Between those who fear the Lord and the wicked

paragraphs.text: "He that fears the Lord will receive instruction, and they that seek Him early shall find favor. He that seeks the law shall be filled with it, but the hypocrite will stumble at it. They that fear the Lord shall find judgment, and shall kindle righteous works as a light. A sinful man will not be reproved, but finds an excuse according to his will" (32:14-17).

entries.section: The fear of the Lord and economic life

paragraphs.text: 1. He speaks to us of riches and poverty; riches are good for him who is holy, and poverty is hateful in the mind of the wicked (cf. 13:23). Riches give a man authority and self-confidence, but not like the fear of the Lord and good counsel.

"Gold and silver make the foot stand sure, but counsel is esteemed above them both. Riches and strength lift up the heart, but the fear of the Lord is above them both. There is no loss in the fear of the Lord, and it needs not to seek help" (40:25-26). 2. The rich and the poor: "The rich man does wrong, and yet he proves himself the one wronged, while the poor man is wronged, and is obliged to apologize" (13:3).

He warns us of the importance of work in the spiritual and economic life even to old age: "Hate not laborious work, especially husbandry, which the Most High has created... Have you cattle? Look to them" (cf. 7:15, 22). "My son, lead not a beggar's life; for it is better to die than to beg. When a man looks to the table of another, his living is not to be counted for a life. He loses his self-respect by another man's food, but a man who is wise and well instructed will guard against it. In the mouth of the shameless begging is sweet, but in his belly there burns a fire" (cf. 40:28-30). 3. He warns us of just weights and measures: "A merchant will hardly keep himself from doing wrong, and a huckster shall not be freed from sin" (cf. 26:20). 4. True wisdom and work without planning: "Strive not in a matter that concerns you not, and sit not with sinners in their judgment. My son, meddle not with many matters, for if you multiply them, you shall not go unpunished; and if you pursue them, you shall not overtake them, nor escape by fleeing. There is one that labors, and takes pains, and makes haste, and is so much the more in want" (cf. 11:9-11). 5. The right use of money: "Watching for riches consumes the flesh, and the care of it takes away sleep... The rich man toils in gathering money together, and when he rests, he is filled with his delicacies. The poor man toils in lack of living, and when he rests, he becomes needy. He that loves gold shall not be justified, and he that follows corruption shall be filled with it... It is a stumbling block to them that sacrifice their lives to it, and every fool shall be taken by it. Blessed is the rich man that is found without blemish, and has not gone after gold" (cf. 31:1, 3-5, 7-8).

entries.section: Let us begin with the primary fear

paragraphs.text: v No one can attain to perfect fear unless he first has the primary fear. For the wise Ben Sirach says: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord... the crown (head) of wisdom is the fear of God" (Sirach 1:12, 16), meaning by the word "head" the primary fear, which is followed by the perfect fear of the saints.

The primary fear depends on the state of our spirit, and it keeps the soul from every fall, for it was said that by the fear of the Lord everyone departs from evil. But the man who is rid of evil because of his fear of punishment is like a slave who fears his master, and gradually he begins to do good willingly.

In the beginning he works as a hired servant who awaits his wages for his good work. If he continues thus, avoiding evil because of fear like a slave, doing good in the hope of receiving the reward like a hired servant, then he abides in doing good and gains a particular taste for spiritual good, so that he no longer wishes to be separated from it. Then he reaches the work of a son, and loves good for the sake of good itself; and though he fears, he works because he loves. This is the great, perfect fear.
Father Dorotheus

entries.section: The fear of the Lord and the ladder of the life of faith

paragraphs.text: St. Philoxenus presents to us the ladder of the practical life of faith, beginning with its three steps: faith, simplicity and the fear of the Lord. There is no fellowship with God without faith, and faith cannot stand except through the simplicity that God gave to the soul so that it might meet Him as a simple child who believes in his father and clings to him. This simplicity that begets faith is what preserves it, so that the soul, by the grace of God, continues firm in its faith.

Through this faith the soul enjoys the fear of the Lord. It believes in Him and perceives His greatness, and so it fears Him, honors Him, and keeps His commandments. Faith, then, begets "the fear of the Lord"; so the believing man keeps the commandment and obeys it out of fear of punishment... and as he grows by grace he obeys the commandment as a son who fears to wound his father's feelings... He fears that his nature, which he holds in the image of his God and Savior, may be disfigured.

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: 1 My son, if you come to serve the Lord God, stand fast in righteousness and godliness, and prepare your soul for temptation. 2 Direct your heart and endure. Incline your ear and receive the words of reason, and make not haste in time of calamity. 3 Wait patiently for what you wait for from God; cleave to Him and do not turn aside, that you may be increased in life at your latter end. 4 Whatever comes upon you, accept it, and be patient in the changes of your lowly estate, 5 for gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation. 6 Believe in Him, and He will help you. Order your ways aright and hope in Him. Keep His fear, and abide in it until your old age.
My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation [1].
The word son (or child), teknon, occurs 36 times in this book.

"My son": Sirach regards his school as a family that has its role in the life of society. So he calls his disciples "his sons," at times in the plural, a sign of the unity of the disciples with one another and of his relation to them as a father, and at times he speaks in the singular, "my son," to bring out the personal side of each one of them. Sirach wishes to walk in the spirit of God, who deals with the community, whether leaders or people, as all being the people of God, the object of His special love and care. At the same time he sees in each son a particular member who has his own place in his father's heart.

Sirach presents two complementary ideas: that wisdom shows itself in the service of the Lord, and also that it is impossible to attain wisdom without long-suffering in temptations. These two ideas never leave Sirach's thought.

The subject of "temptations" in the life of the young must be discussed, for it is fitting for the young man to learn in some detail not only about the blessings promised to those who strive to please the Lord, but also to know that temptations accompany him during his striving. He must know beforehand what may befall him. This is what the Apostle James affirmed in his epistle: "Behold, we count them happy which endure.
