paragraphs.text: The most beautiful offering with which parents are pleased is the humility and meekness of their children. The more the son humbles himself in his conduct toward them, the more he grows in greatness in the eyes of God and people. God is glorified in the humble person, because he knows his weakness and trusts in God, who raises up the weak as a hero (see Joel 3:10). The believer does not seek visions and the working of wonders and miracles; what concerns him is walking according to the divine commandment [21-22].

entries.section: 4. The family is a school of meekness

paragraphs.text: As the eye must be opened in order to receive the light [25], so the mind ought to be opened to receive wisdom (Prov 28:14).
a. Meekness does not stop at certain words or particular behaviors, but ought to be blended into and shine forth in all the works of the believer [17].

b. The believer does not seek worldly honor, but whenever he receives honor or authority or success in his works he ought to grow in humility, counting what he receives as free gifts from God, so he finds favor with the Lord, and honor even from people [18].

c. The believer ought not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think (Rom 12:3), but to recognize the truth of his abilities and capacities. So he does not seek what is beyond him, nor search into hidden matters through useless theoretical, disputatious dialogues [21-24]. When Pope Athanasius was asked by a person to show him his God so that he might believe in Him, he answered him: "Show me your spirit, and I will show you my God!"
d. Beware of falling into intellectual stubbornness.
My son, conduct your affairs with meekness, and the people whom the Lord approves will love you [17].
The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find favor with the Lord [18].

If the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, then arrogance is the beginning of folly. Ben Sirach had in mind what pride had done, not only to individuals but also to nations, for Assyria fell, then Babylon, then Persia. He also lived through the fall of Carthage in 201 BC.

Humility is the disposition fitting for those who fear the Lord, who honor their parents. The more a person receives honor, whether on the ecclesiastical or the worldly level, the more he needs to double his humility, so that he may become the object of God's pleasure and not of people's approval. The archbishops used to fear pride lest they lose their salvation. So St. John Chrysostom would repeat in the depths of his heart, as among the bishops, his famous saying: "I marvel at a bishop who is saved!" At the beginning of the celebrations of the ordination of Pope Shenouda, he would sometimes open his speech by repeating what Chrysostom said, so that words of praise might not distract him from his eternity. The saying of our beloved father Fr. Bishoy Kamel is: The servant of church education is the servant of the children of his Master, and the priest is the servant of the servants, the children of their Master; how much more must this be the feeling of the bishop and the patriarch.
What grieves our hearts is that a priest thinks he is the head of the Church and that what he says must be obeyed without dialogue, and likewise the bishop and the patriarch.
* Often the ecclesiastical order and the Levitical work are a cause of falling into pride for one who forgets that he received this honor in the bosom of the Church.

How many men of the priesthood, when they became head, forgot that they must be humble, as though their ordination had exempted them from humility. On the contrary, they must keep humility carefully, because they are granted such great honor, according to the saying of Scripture: The greatest among you, let him be the most humble.

The community chooses you, so bow your head in greater humility. It has chosen you as a leader of others, so do not feel that you are glorified! Be among them as one of them (Lk 22:27). You must be humble and meek. Flee from pride, the source of all evils[5].

* The evil one fights us not only that we should commit sin with persistence..., but that we should be proud and feel that we are perfect. But God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (Prov 34:3; Jas 6:4; 1 Pet 5:5). Therefore the more you humble yourself, the more you are lifted up and find mercy with God [18]...

Whoever turns aside from the commandment does not follow it, since the commandment of God is upright. "Cursed are they that turn aside from thy commandments" does not refer only to those who do not work them, but even to those who deviate from them a little.

Origen * "LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me" (Ps 131:1). Let us say this more clearly, and be heard. I am not proud. I did not wish to be known among people for wonderful powers, and I did not seek anything beyond my strength. In this I boast among the foolish... May no man be proud of God's gift to him, but keep humility, and so fulfill what is written: "The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find favor with the Lord" [18]. How much fear is needed of pride in God's gift. We must press ourselves more and more[6].

St. Augustine * Let our glory be in humility, and our boasting in not loving (vain) glory. And let our desire be in those things that please God and satisfy Him, keeping in our minds what the Wise Man says to us: "The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find favor with the Lord" (Sir 3:18). For He rejects the proud, and regards the arrogant as His enemies. But the meek and the humble in heart He crowns with honors[7].
St. Cyril the Great For the power of the Lord is great, and the humble glorify Him [19].
Do not seek what is too hard for you, nor search into what is beyond your power [20].

Pride reaches its extreme when a person becomes arrogant through his philosophical studies, and does not take into account that the gift of the mind is from God. With all its wonderful greatness, he realizes that it is limited and cannot come to know the mysteries of the Unlimited, nor His plan, without enjoying the work of His divine grace.

It befits us to seek wisdom and to grow in the knowledge of it, without relying on mere rational thought, for God, who treasures man as His ambassador on earth, does not withhold knowledge from him, but offers him what is for his edification according to man's capacities, and also reveals to him His divine will.

The danger that Sirach feared was that there had seeped into the holy land a disregard for the word of God and an indifference to the will of God, through Hellenistic ideas. This atmosphere created Jewish leaders who were arrogant in their thoughts and conduct.
* Deep meditation on the good life and care for the soul beget good people who love God.
Whoever seeks God finds Him, by overcoming all lusts through constant prayer. Such a person does not fear the demons[8].
St. Anthony the Great St. Ambrose presents Arius as an example of one who claims to be possessed of knowledge in what goes beyond human ability.

* It was said to Arius and to all men: "Do not seek what is far too hard for you." Moses was forbidden to see the face of God (Ex 33:23), and Arius thought he was qualified to see Him in a mystery... Paul speaks of lower matters: "For we know in part, and we prophesy in part" (1 Cor 13:9). But Arius says: "I know God with full knowledge, and not in part." Thus Paul is less than Arius. The chosen vessel knows in part, and the vessel of destruction knows all. Paul says: "I knew a man... whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth; how that he was caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words" (2 Cor 12:3-4). Paul was carried up to the third heaven and did not know himself, while Arius wallows in filth and knows God.
Paul says of himself: "God knoweth," and Arius says of God: "I know"[9].
St. Ambrose Meditate on what you have been commanded, for you have no need of hidden things [21].

* The Holy Bible warns us: "Meditate on what you have been commanded, for you have no need of hidden things" [22]. "Do not seek what is too hard for you, nor search into what is beyond your power" [21]. Of course we cannot use words that ascribe vain curiosity to the Holy Spirit. We must only say that searching into the hidden matters of God is a portion of his nature[10].

St. Epiphanius, Bishop of Salamis * Do not seek what is too hard for you, nor search into what is beyond your power [20]. This does not mean that these matters are forbidden to us, for the Lord says: "There is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; and hid, that shall not be known" (Mt 10:26). But if we continue in the way we have undertaken, as the Apostle tells us, God will not only reveal to us what we do not know and ought to know, but will reveal whatever we care to know (Phil 3:15).

The way we have undertaken is the way of faith. May we keep it without hesitation. May it bring us into the mysteries of the King, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col 2:3)...

It befits us to proceed in progress and growth until our hearts become qualified and receive what we are unable to receive now. And if we find, on the last day, that we have advanced sufficiently, then we shall learn what we cannot know here[11].
St. Augustine Do not meddle in (searching) what goes beyond your works, for what has been revealed to you exceeds the understanding of man [22].
What is it that goes beyond your work? Searching into what cannot be comprehended, such as the essence of God or even the essence of the human soul.

* We read in Isaiah about Christ: "Who shall declare his generation?" (see Isa 53:8). When the blessed prophet speaks of God the Word, he uses the word "generation" instead of saying "essence" or "being." In truth, who can declare the being of the Only-Begotten Son? And what language can explain the unspeakable begetting of the Son from the Father? And what mind does not stand helpless and powerless before this concept? In truth we know and believe that the Word was begotten of God the Father. But we say that to entertain any question about this matter in discussion is extremely dangerous... We must not search into matters that exceed our mind and knowledge, not for us alone but for every creature, including those who are spirits[12].

St. Cyril the Great * God has not made all things revealed to you, nor has He permitted all things to be unknown to you. For He does not permit all things to be unknown to you, lest you say that the things that exist are not from (divine) providence. Nor does He permit all things to be known to you, lest the greatness of your knowledge stir up pride in you. So, at least, the wicked Satan pushed the first man to recklessness through the hope of greater knowledge, stripping him of the knowledge that he already had. Therefore the Wise Man advises us, saying: "Do not seek what is too hard for you, nor search into the things that exceed your power, but meditate with reverence on what you have been commanded, for the greater part of His works are done in secret" (see Sir 3:21-22)[13].

* "What has been shown to you exceeds the understanding of man" (Sir 3:22). But he says this for the consolation of the grieving, rebellious man, because he does not know everything. For even these things that (man) observes, and which he is permitted to know, are far greater than your understanding, since you could not attain them by yourself, but God taught them to you. Therefore be content with the wealth (in knowledge) that has been given to you and do not ask for more; rather give thanks for what you have received, and do not be angry about the things you have not received. Give glory for what you know, and do not stumble because of the things you do not know. For God made both equally profitable, and He reveals some things and hides others for the sake of your peace[14].
St. John Chrysostom Many have been led astray by their conclusions, and their evil suppositions made their thoughts slip and fall [23].
The stubborn heart ends in ruin, and he who loves danger perishes in it [24].

Fulgentius sees that the Wise Man is speaking here of the stubborn heretic, so he calls him to return to the Catholic Church, in which is the love that covers a multitude of sins through the gift of the Holy Spirit.
* Question: If one will fall under many blows, while another under few blows (Lk 12:47), how do some say that the punishment is infinite?

Answer: The things that were said in a veiled and obscure manner in certain places of the inspired book of God have been made clear in explicit terms in other places. The Lord declares once that these go away into eternal punishment (Mt 25:46), and again that He sends persons to the everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Mt 5:22), and adds: "Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched (Mk 9:48), which the prophet said rightly long ago: "their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched" (Isa 66:24).

Since many such sayings are found everywhere in the inspired Holy Bible, this is certainly one of the strategies of Satan: that many people, by ignoring these valuable and weighty words and declarations of the Lord, reassure themselves that the punishment has an end, so that they may commit sin with great boldness. If there were an end to eternal torment, then surely life would not be eternal.

Now if we cannot bear to think in this way about eternity, by what logic is it possible to give eternal torment an end? The attribute "eternal" is attached equally to both elements. Therefore He says: "And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal" (Mt 25:46).

From the viewpoint of the explicit sayings, we must understand that those who are beaten with many blows, and those who are beaten with few blows, this does not mean an end to the torment, but points to different degrees.

If God is a just Judge, not only for the righteous but also for the wicked, who "will render to every man according to his deeds" (Rom 2:6), therefore one deserves an unquenchable fire, which can burn quietly or slowly, and another may deserve the worm that dieth not, and this can be moderate or great according to exactly what the person deserves.

A third may deserve Gehenna, in which there is a different kind of torment, while another deserves outer darkness (Mt 8:12; 22:13; 25:30), where all he does is weep, and another suffers gnashing of teeth because of excruciating pain. And outer darkness certainly indicates that there is also an inner darkness.
Moreover it is said in Proverbs about the depths of hell (Prov 9:18), which shows that some of those in hell are not in its depths, but receive less torment instead.

This can be clarified now by taking into consideration the condition of the body. One may suffer from fever with other symptoms and pains, while another suffers from fever but not like the former. And in another way a third, who differs from the first person, does not suffer from fever, being sick, but has pain in his limbs, which may be greater or less.

Now in the present case the "much" and "few" that the Lord spoke follow the customary style with different expressions. And for us this manner of speaking is applied to one afflicted with some illness, as we say in wonder concerning a person who suffers only from fever or from a sharp pain in his eyes: how long has he been suffering, or what troubles he suffers.
Again I say that punishment, severe or mild, is not related to the lengthening or shortening of time, but to the difference of the punishment[15].
St. Basil the Great The stubborn heart is burdened with pains, and the sinner adds sin to sin [25].

entries.section: 4. The family is a school of meekness

paragraphs.text: The disease of the proud has no cure, for the plant of evil has taken root in him [26].

Ben Sirach affirms the danger of stubbornness, which touches the depths of man before it appears in behavior; he attributes it to the heart as well as to the mind. If the fruit of stubbornness is ruin and deviation from sin to sin, he counts it as the root of a hidden plant which inevitably yields its bitter fruit in due time, and without ceasing. This stubbornness has no cure by a mere human decision to stop it, but needs grace, able to change and renew the thick and hardened heart (Mk 8:17; Heb 4:7).

The intelligent man reflects on the discourses of the wise, and makes his ears attentive to the voice of the Lord, so he enjoys with Moses the prophet the divine presence when he drew near to the bush burning with fire and not consumed, and through this presence came to know the mystery of the incarnation of the Word of God. The wise man sings in the spirit of humility with the Psalmist, saying: "LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me. Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child" (Ps 131:1-2).

* I am not proud: I do not wish to be known among people for wonderful powers, and I do not seek anything beyond my ability, of which I boast among the foolish. Like Simon the Magician, who wished to advance in wonders beyond his abilities, and therefore was the more pleased with the authority of the Apostles than with the righteousness of Christians[16].
St. Augustine The heart of the intelligent reflects on the proverb[17], and the attentive ear is the desire of the wise [27].

entries.section: 5. The family is a school of giving

paragraphs.text: 33 Water quenches a flaming fire, and almsgiving atones for sins. 34 Whoever has done good is remembered in his latter end, and finds support in the day of his fall. Holy family life is a school of giving. 1. The doer of kindness and the giver of alms enjoys the compassion of God, who forgives sins, so he walks in safety because what he offers today supports him in the future in the midst of affliction (3:30-31). 2. Sirach urges us not to be slow in caring for the needy, so that we may practice our sonship to God, the lover of giving, and be the object of His love. God's love for the giver is greater than a mother's love for her son. 3. Whoever ignores the needs of the poor becomes a victim of the curse issuing from their sighs. 4. It befits us to respect all: the noble and the poor! 5. Whoever is given authority should realize that authority is a talent and a responsibility, and requires him to do justice to the oppressed. 6. God is the father of the orphan who has no father, and the judge of the widows who have no one to defend them (Ps 68:6).
Water quenches a flaming fire, and almsgiving atones for sins [28].

Ben Sirach regards almsgiving as like an ambassador who goes before a man, preparing the way for him to God, and sees it also as a credit for the believer that supports him in time of affliction and distress.

* After prayer with struggle there is a need for many almsdeeds, because these especially give power to the medicine of repentance. And just as among physicians there is a medicine made from many herbs, yet there is one medicine that is the main herb, indeed it is counted as though it were everything. Therefore hear what the Holy Bible says: "But rather give alms of such things as ye have; and, behold, all things are clean unto you" (Lk 11:41). And also: "By almsgiving and works of faith sins are purified" (Prov 16:6) LXX. And "Water quenches a flaming fire, almsgiving atones for great sins" (Sir 3:28)[18].

* What is said to the person whom a poor man provokes? To bear with the weaknesses of others, and to set the petitioner right before giving him the gift, by showing him gentle looks and kind words[19].

* Fasting brings us no little relief, and frees from entangled sins, on condition that the person devotes himself to showing compassion to others, and quenches the flame of God's wrath (1 Tim 2:1). For "Water quenches a flaming fire, and almsgiving atones for sins" (Sir 3:28)[20].

* Let us use every means to wash away defilement. But first the font washes, and after that there are many means of every kind. For God, being merciful, afterward (that is, after Baptism) provided various ways of reconciliation, the first among all of them being almsgiving. It is said: "By almsgiving and works of faith sins are atoned for" (see Sir 3:28)[21].

St. John Chrysostom Salvian, priest of Marseilles in the fifth century, reveals that giving in itself does not bestow eternal life, even if the person bequeaths the distribution of all that he has while at death's door, unless he walks in Christ Jesus in repentance.

* I do not think that wealth helps anyone if he lives continually in the pleasures of the body, or that he can obtain eternal life, unless he resists sin unto death; even if he bequeaths all that he has while at death's door, unless he truly gives up his sins, and takes off his defiled garments filled with his fornication, and puts on the garment of repentance and holiness from the hands of the Apostle who counsels him (Rom 2:5)[22].
Salvian, priest of Marseilles In one of his moral essays, St. Cyprian presents almsgiving and works of righteousness as another path to forgiveness after the forgiveness of sins in Baptism.

* The Holy Spirit speaks in the Holy Scriptures and says: "By almsgiving and faith iniquity is covered" (see Prov 16:6), and also says: "Water quenches a flaming fire, and almsgiving atones for sins" (Ben Sirach 3:33). Here it makes clear that just as the fire of Gehenna is quenched by the water of salvation, so by almsgiving and righteousness the flame of sins is put out (for those who believe in the blood of the Lord Christ). For since forgiveness of all sins is granted once in Baptism, the continuous work without interruption, following the example of Baptism, grants God's mercies again.

The Lord also taught us this in the Gospel, for when it was pointed out to the disciples that they eat without washing their hands, He answered, saying: "He that made that which is without made that which is within also. But rather give alms of such things as ye have; and, behold, all things are clean unto you" (Lk 11:40-41). He teaches the washing of the heart, not of the hands, and that rather the defilement of the inside is to be removed, not the filth of the outside, and that once the mind is purified, then a man begins to clean his body. And as He counsels us how to wash and be purified, He said that it is necessary to give alms.

That compassionate One teaches us and urges us to show kindness. For as He seeks the salvation of those for whom He offered a sacrifice of such measure, He pointed also to those who, after receiving the grace of Baptism and committing sin, can be cleansed anew[23].

The Martyr Cyprian * Some husbands scatter on the tombs of their wives violets, roses, lilies and purple flowers, and calm the grief of their hearts by performing this gentle duty. Our dear Pammachius watered the holy ashes and the venerated bones of Paulina, but in truth with the balsam of almsgiving. This is the sweet preparation and the perfumes by which the ashes of his dead wife are immortalized, knowing what is written: "Water quenches a flaming fire, and almsgiving atones for sins" [28][24].
St. Jerome * Why do the first inherit the kingdom? "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat." Why do the others go to eternal fire? "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat."

I ask, what does this mean? I see that those who inherit the kingdom were given as good and faithful Christians, not despisers of the words of the Lord, having firm hope in the promises, so they did, for if they had not done so, that barrenness would not have accorded with their good life. They may be pure, not deceivers nor drunkards, keeping themselves from all works of evil, but they do not add to this good works and so remain barren. Because they wanted to be kept far from evil, "but they did not want to keep themselves, and do good" (Ps 34:14), yet He did not say even to these "Come, inherit the kingdom" because you lived pure and did not defraud anyone, nor wrong a poor man, nor trespass on anyone's boundary, nor deceive anyone with an oath. He did not say this, but He said "inherit the kingdom, for I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat."

O the distinction of this one above all the rest (of the virtues), for the Lord did not point to all but to it alone! Likewise He says to the others: "Depart ye into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels."

How many things He could raise against the wicked when they ask: Why do we go to eternal fire? Why? Do you ask, O fornicators, murderers, deceivers, desecrators of temples, blasphemers and unbelievers? Yet He mentioned not one of these, but "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat."

I see you marveling as I do. And truly it is a marvelous matter. But I shall gather, as much as I can, the reasons for this marvelous matter, and I will hide nothing from you. It is written, "Water quenches a flaming fire, and almsgiving atones for sins" (Wisdom of Joshua 3:30), and it is also written: "Shut up alms in thy storehouses: and it shall deliver thee from all affliction" (Sir 29:12)[25].
St. Augustine * [In his praise of St. Paula, mother of Eustochium]
Many married women used to offer gifts to those who praise (the trumpet-blowers). While they spend excessively on a few, they close their hands on the many.

Paula was completely free from this error. She gave what she had to everyone according to his need, not according to her own desires, but to supply wants. No poor man left her empty-handed. She was able to do all this not because of the greatness of her wealth, but because of her wonderful management. Such phrases were always on her lips: "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy" (Mt 5:7).

"Water will quench a flaming fire; and alms maketh an atonement for sins" (Sir 3:28). "Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations" (Lk 16:9). "But rather give alms of such things as ye have; and, behold, all things are clean unto you" (Lk 11:41) [26].
St. Jerome He who repays a kindness with a kindness thinks of the future, and in the day of his fall he finds a support [29].

v I ask you that we not speak evil against our teachers, nor call them to account in strictness, lest we bring evil upon ourselves. Let us examine ourselves, and not speak evil of others. Let us honor that day on which we were enlightened (by Baptism). Whoever has a father, whatever his faults, let us cover them all. For it has been said: "Glory not in the dishonour of thy father; for thy father's dishonour is no glory unto thee... and if he lose his understanding, be longsuffering with him" (cf. Sir 3:10-13). If this was said about our fathers according to nature, how much more regarding our spiritual fathers. Honor him because every day he serves you, and reads the Holy Bible to you, and prepares lodging for you, for all his worship is on your account [27].
St. John Chrysostom Inspired by Sirach 3

entries.section: Sanctify my family as Your church

paragraphs.text: v Your descent to our earth has sanctified all our life.
You make of my heart a holy temple for You, and of my family a church of Your own, indeed of the whole world a new heaven rejoicing in Your presence!
Glory to You, who hold the children of men dear!
v You instill in every leader the spirit of fatherhood or motherhood toward others.

So he lives cherishing his younger brothers. He does not pick up their weaknesses or faults, but learns from every person what builds himself up, and regards his presence among men as a constructive divine gift!
v What concerns me is the salvation of the whole world.
In a spirit of hope I await the day of the Church's meeting with You on the clouds.

I see all believing humanity, from Adam to the end of the ages; I take pride in being a member of Your family, which You cleansed with Your precious blood, and sanctified by the guidance of Your Holy Spirit over it.
v Train me with all my brothers in the language of heaven and its constitution.
Let my tongue speak the sweet word to old and young, and let my heart meditate on true love for the good and the bad, and let my will go forth in harmony and submission to Your divine will.
I offer honor to my parents and my brothers and my children.
I see all of them on the way, wearing the garment of Your righteousness.
And the heavenly beings marvel at the beauty of Your bride, humanity.
The heavenly beings rejoice because their prayers for us, since the first man, have borne fruit in splendor and beauty for mankind.

v It does not concern me to bury my father at his death (Lk 9:49-60); or to bid farewell to my family in order to follow You (Lk 9:61-62); but that we all go forth together on our journey to heaven with Your presence in us!
v If anyone grows old or is struck with loss of memory, I will deal tenderly with him, reckoning that what has befallen him may befall me.
What I deal out to them will be returned to me one day. What I offer them, I offer to You, O Lover of mankind.
v You descended, O fearsome Lord, to the human family.
You became for us a model of meekness and humility of heart. May we be united with You, and taste the greatness of meekness in our family life.
St. Mary did not exalt herself that she was the only one chosen as Your mother.
But by Your incarnation from her she grew in humility through You. Grant us that whenever our success increases by Your grace, we may rise with more humility.
Whenever we receive honor in the family or the Church or the world, adorn our souls by multiplying humility and meekness.
May every member realize that his honor is from the honor of his brothers.
Let us learn from Archbishop John Chrysostom, who feared pride for himself, and used to repeat:
I marvel at a bishop who is saved!
O priest, you are the father of all humanity.
O bishop, there is no episcopate without a people!
Grant us all this mind, full of love, meekness and humility!
v As a member of the holy human family, grant me not to think beyond my capacities (2 Cor 12:6).
I do not seek dry rational knowledge that I may boast of it.
Nor do I desire to perform a miracle or work a surpassing sign.
Paul confessed that he knows in part, so shall I count myself possessed of knowledge and learning?!
He was caught up to the third heaven, and counts himself the chief of sinners.
So what shall I call my wretched soul?!
Grant me that You keep me in the faith, and that I not seek what exceeds my ability.
I do not search into Your divine essence, but I cast myself into Your embrace.
I do not ask how Your eternal birth was accomplished, but I melt with love for the Spirit of adoption which You have given to believers!
I am not concerned with knowing the ranks of the heavenly beings, but I fly with joy at joining their wonderful choir.
v In You and by You I enjoy my membership in the family.
You are the divine Father of the family.
The head of the whole family, which includes the heavenly orders and the congregation of believers!
I thank You for the knowledge You have given me about Your mysteries.
And I praise You for what You hide from me for my edification.

entries.section: 1. Our responsibility toward the needy as toward the great

paragraphs.text: 1 My son, do not deprive the poor of his living, and do not make the eyes of the needy wait. 2 Do not grieve the hungry soul, and do not provoke a man in his need. 3 Do not add more trouble to the provoked heart, and do not delay giving to him who is in need. 4 Do not refuse to give the wretched his request, and do not turn your face away from the poor. 5 Do not turn your eye away from the needy, and do not do anything that brings upon you the curse of man. 6 For if he curses you in the bitterness of his soul, his Maker will hear his prayer. 7 Be affable to the congregation, and bow your head to a great man. 8 Bend your ear to the poor, and answer him gently and meekly. 9 Deliver the oppressed from the hand of the oppressor, and be not fainthearted in judging. 10 Be as a father to the fatherless, and instead of a husband to their mother; 11 so you will be as a son of the Most High, and He will love you more than your mother does.

"My son, do not deprive the poor of his living, and do not disappoint the looks of the needy" [1]. It is stated in the Didache, or the Teaching of the Lord to the Gentiles by the Twelve Apostles (4:5-8): [Do not stretch out your hands to receive, and close them when giving (Sir 4:31). If you have anything through the labor of your hands, give a ransom for your sins (by giving). Do not hesitate to give, and when you give do not grumble, for you will know who is the good Rewarder. Do not turn away the needy, share everything with your brother (Acts 4:32-37). And do not say that you have anything of your own. For if you share in the things that are immortal, how much more in those that are mortal? (Rom 15:27)]. 1. Giving is for living, not for luxury and comfort [1]. 2. If the believer is unable to give materially, he does not blame the poor man or rebuke him [2]. 3. Giving is not appraised by quantity and money, but by its practice with joy, and he does not delay the needy man [3]. 4. He fixes his eyes not on what he will give, but on the heart of the needy man, so that both may enjoy salvation [4]. 5. He gives the poor man what he needs, and offers honor to those to whom honor is due [7]. 6. He gives the needy man a sweet word that lifts up his spirit [8]. 7. The believer behaves without partiality toward a rich man or a man of authority [9]. 8. As a son of the Most High, the believer opens his heart to all, imitating his heavenly Father [10].
My son, do not deprive the poor of his living, and do not disappoint the looks of the needy [1].

When we meet a poor man we remember that God has given us goods as a deposit that we return to Him, and as His children we imitate Him by giving generously, and enter into friendship with Him and cleave to Him.
v What need is there to mention the virtues of this craft and its excellences? It teaches you how to become like God, and this is the head of all good things.

v Almsgiving is strong and has authority, so that it looses bonds and chains, and dispels darkness, and quenches the blaze of the fire of Gehenna, and its effectiveness qualifies one to become like God, as He said: "Be merciful, as your Father who is in heaven is merciful."
v Mercy raises man to a lofty height, and gives him eloquent boldness before God.

For just as when a queen wishes to enter the king's place, none of the courtiers dares to prevent her or ask her where she wishes to go, but all of them receive her with rejoicing, so he who practices mercy and almsgiving appears before the throne of the King without hindrance, for God loves mercy exceedingly, and she remains near Him; therefore the Scripture said: "Upon thy right hand did stand the queen." This is because mercy is preferred by God, since it made Him become man for our salvation.
v Nothing makes us so near to God and in His likeness as this good work!

entries.section: 1. Our responsibility toward the needy as toward the great

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom Do not grieve the soul of the hungry, and do not anger a man in his despair [2].

As it is fitting to offer food to the man who is hungry in body, we must offer hope to the man whom despair is crushing. Instead of rebuking him for his gloomy outlook full of deadly despair, we support him with the spirit of hope, the giver of joy amid afflictions. We bear witness to the tenderness of the Savior, who forgives sins, whatever our sins may be.

v Question: Does he fall into despair of his salvation who has been caught in many evils, and sinned after his baptism? Or what is the measure by which a man may continue in his hope in the love of God for mankind through repentance?

Answer: If you can balance the surpassing tenderness of God, or the weight of the greatness of God's mercy, against the number of sins and their weight, there is no room for despair. But if it is reasonable that the latter is subject to measure and number, while it is impossible to measure God's mercy or count His tenderness, there will never be any place for despair. Rather, by the knowledge of mercy and the condemnation of sins, there is forgiveness in the blood of Christ, as it is written (Mt 26:28).

Yet there are many places and ways through which we learn that we must not despair. Consider especially the parable of our Lord Jesus Christ concerning the son who took his father's wealth and squandered it in sins. From the words of the Lord Himself we learn what kind of feast, and how great, is fitting for repentance (Lk 15:22-24).

Add to that God's saying through Isaiah: "Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool" (Isa 1:18). This is fulfilled when our repentance deserves it, if it proceeds from our hatred of sin, as it is written in the Old and New Testaments, and bears fruits worthy of it [1].

entries.section: 1. Our responsibility toward the needy as toward the great

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great Do not add more trouble to the provoked heart, and do not postpone your gift to the needy [3].
Postponing giving to one who is truly in distress stirs anxiety in his soul, so we add to his material need his deprivation of inward peace.

entries.section: 1. Our responsibility toward the needy as toward the great

paragraphs.text: Do not turn away the suppliant in his distress, and do not turn your face away from the poor [4].
The needy man looks not only at the gift you give him, but gazes at your face to see whether he sees in it the icon of God, who gives generously and cheerfully.

v It is not enough to show mercy, but it is fitting that we offer it generously, with a bountiful spirit, and not only with a bountiful spirit but with a joyful and cheerful spirit... (The Apostle) stressed this same point strongly when he wrote to the Corinthians to urge them to generosity, saying: "He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully" (2 Cor 9:6). And to correct their mood he says: "not grudgingly, or of necessity" (2 Cor 9:7)... For if you grieve while you are showing mercy, you are harsh and violent.
If you are sad, how can you support those who are in sorrow?...
This is the reason for his saying: "He that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness" (Rom 12:8), for how can he be sad of countenance who receives the Kingdom?!
Who remains sad of countenance while he receives the forgiveness of his sins?

So do not think of your spending of money (the work of mercy) but of the abundance you receive through the spending. For if he who sows rejoices although he sows uncertain about the harvest, how much more he who tills the heavens? For you give only a little to receive much... By the two mites the widow was reckoned to have surpassed those who offered many talents, because of her generous spirit [2].

entries.section: 1. Our responsibility toward the needy as toward the great

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom Do not turn your gaze away from the needy, and do not give a man an opportunity to curse you [5].

St. Mar Jacob of Serug calls us to receive the Lord Christ through our meeting with the poor and needy. And we reckon that what we offer of love and concern we offer to the Lord Christ Himself. It is a wonderful opportunity to express our honor to the Lord Himself.
v By these works of righteousness which you give him, he asks you to receive him with joy.
If you give him a crust of bread and a cup of water, let your thought be joyful and with love.
He is weak and tired and distressed and tormented and coming to you, so give him lodging and rest, and rise and serve him gladly.
He is greatly tormented by poverty and bears sicknesses, so show him great love lest he be distressed.
Has he stood as a poor man at your door? God Himself has come to you, so open to him cheerfully that he may enter.
If he had come to you through a rich man you would be ashamed, and you would not be able to receive him.
He came and visited you in humility and lowliness, and when you fill his belly with bread you find life.
Give him of what is his, and do not give him of what is yours, for you have nothing to offer him of what is yours.
It is He who came, and through the poor He asks you to trade with the Kingdom in every case.
He gave you His body; offer Him bread because He is hungry, and you drink His blood, take and bring Him a drink because He is thirsty.
He gave you to put on brightness and splendor from the water, so do not withhold from Him ragged clothes and humble garments.
All that you give through the poor who ask you, He rewards you for with a garment of light in the new world [3].

entries.section: 1. Our responsibility toward the needy as toward the great

paragraphs.text: St. Mar Jacob of Serug For if he curses you in the bitterness of his soul, his Maker will hear his prayer [6].

A man may despise the poor man through the features of his face, or the manner of meeting him, and the soul of the poor man groans without uttering a word, but his Maker looks upon the bitterness of his soul within, and responds to it.

entries.section: 1. Our responsibility toward the needy as toward the great

paragraphs.text: Be beloved of the congregation, and bow your head to a great man [7].

If the Holy Scripture in both its Testaments is concerned with our meeting with the poor and supporting them materially, spiritually and psychologically, on the other hand we must offer honor to whom honor is due. "Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour" (Rom 13:7).

entries.section: 1. Our responsibility toward the needy as toward the great

paragraphs.text: Bend your ear to the poor, and answer him words of peace with meekness [8].

Since the Word of God became incarnate and dwelt among us as one of us, He called us to learn from Him, saying: "Learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart" (Mt 11:29). Ben Sirach offers us practical touches for a life of meekness and humility for the believer to live out in his small family as well as in society as the greater family.

entries.section: 1. Our responsibility toward the needy as toward the great

paragraphs.text: A. Meekness does not stop at certain words or actions, but it is fitting that it be blended with and shine forth in all the works of man [17].

entries.section: 1. Our responsibility toward the needy as toward the great

paragraphs.text: B. The believer does not seek worldly honor, but whenever he receives honor or authority or success in his works it is fitting for him to grow in humility, reckoning that what he receives is free gifts from God, so he finds favor with the Lord, and honor even from men [18].

C. It is fitting for the believer not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think (Rom 12:3), but to know the truth of his abilities and capacities. So he does not seek what is impossible for him, nor inquire into hidden matters with useless theoretical disputations [21-24]. When Pope Athanasius was asked by a man to show him his God that he might believe in Him, he answered him: "Show me your spirit, and I will show you my God!"

v Do not lower your tongue... fill it with blessing and the giving of abundant alms. For you can give alms even by speech. "Thus a word is better than a gift" (cf. Sir 18:16). And also: "Incline to the poor, and answer him words of peace with meekness" (cf. Sir 4:8) [4].

St. John Chrysostom v The divine voice counsels us in the language of the Holy Scriptures: "Honour the LORD with thy substance" (Prov 3:9)... The Lord says that the owner is you; and lest our souls be proud, He said: "Pay your debt" (Sir 4:8) [Vulgate]...

If a man is consecrated, he gives (to the poor) as from what is his own, and if he does not consecrate himself he is asked to return the money to its original owner, as though what he has were not his. God has truly established the Law, by the desire to give voluntarily, or by payment of necessity. God wishes to say: "Give if you wish, otherwise you will return it to the original owner upon refusing to give" [5].
Salvian, priest of Marseilles Deliver the oppressed from the hand of the oppressor, and be not a coward in judging in his favor [9].

It is fitting for the believer to realize that every ability he has is a gift from God on behalf of society as far as he is able, whether money or a position of leadership or authority or strength and health. All his life is turned into instruments of righteousness on behalf of the Kingdom of God, so if an opportunity is given him to do justice to the oppressed, but in his partiality to the oppressor for one reason or another he did not do justice to the oppressed, he is condemned for that. He may not show partiality to anyone because of blood kinship or his social position or wealth or nationality or religion or friendship with him, for God is a lover of all humanity.

v It may be said to one who has authority: Why do you not help the widow and orphans when injustice befalls them? Are you without strength? Can you not support them? I appointed you thus for this purpose, not that you may sin, but that you may prevent injustice [6].

St. Ambrose v Love must be equal toward all without partiality... For those who walk thus, blood relationship will not find room to offer greater love because of the tie of blood, as in dealing with a brother or son or daughter according to the flesh, so as to offer greater love because of the blood relationship than the love toward others. He who follows nature in these matters (that is, favoring relatives) gives clear testimony that he has not yet withdrawn completely from nature, but is still subject to the law of the flesh [7].
v Improper disputes and private love are alike; both must be removed from the monastery. For enmity arises from quarrels and private friendship and divisions that arise from suspicion and jealousy.

In every instance the loss of equality (in dealing) is the root and foundation of all envy and hatred on the part of those who are slighted. For this reason we received the Lord's command to imitate His goodness, who makes the sun rise on the just and the unjust (Mt 5:45). If He gives a share of light without partiality to all, so it is fitting for His followers to send forth the rays of love with equal splendor upon all alike.
But if "God is love" (1 Jn 4:16) as John says, then of necessity Satan is hatred. And just as he who has love has God in consequence, so he who has hatred embraces Satan within him [8].
St. Basil the Great Be as a father to the fatherless, and as a husband to their mother, and you will be as a son of the Most High, and He will love you more than your mother's love for you [10].
What occupies the believer's heart is not the quantity of the giving he offers, but that in all his conduct he be "as a son of the Most High," enjoying partaking of the divine nature (2 Pet 1:4).

v Let us look upon the poor as benefactors to us, able to offer us a fundamental principle for our salvation. And let us give generously and with a spirit of joy without delaying in our offering, but speaking to them with great reverence, showing great meekness (Sir 4:10) even before offering your gift, so you lift up his spirit from the gloom caused by his extreme need, by your gentle words. The Scripture says: "A word is better than a gift" (cf. Sir 18:16). For speech can lift up the spirit, and give rest [9].
St. John Chrysostom

12 Wisdom brings up sons for herself, and takes to herself those who seek her. 13 Whoever loves her loves life, and those who rise early to her are filled with gladness. 14 Whoever possesses her inherits glory, and wherever she enters, there is the blessing of the Lord. 15 Those who worship her serve the Holy One, and those who love her the Lord loves. 16 Whoever listens to her judges the nations, and whoever attends to her dwells securely. 17 If he commits himself to her, he inherits her, and his descendants remain in possession of her. 18 For at first she walks with him by crooked ways; 19 she brings fear and dread upon him, and tests him with her discipline until she trusts his soul, and tries him with her judgments. 20 Then she returns and deals with him uprightly and gladdens him, 21 and reveals her secrets to him, and gathers in him treasures of knowledge and understanding of righteousness. 22 But if he goes astray, she forsakes him and delivers him to his ruin.

This poem personifies wisdom (that is, looks upon her as a person), reckoning her as a mother and those who seek her as sons. At the beginning wisdom allows the one who seeks her to enter into trials so that he may be proved, and declare whether he chooses wisdom or folly. And when he succeeds in the trial, wisdom declares to him her secrets, and as a divine teacher she teaches. 1. The believer begins his way with affliction in the company of God, the gladdener of hearts and revealer of divine secrets [17-18]. 2. He takes care that wisdom does not depart from him while he is on his way to eternity [19]. 3. Wisdom offers on the way her blessings, among them the following:
A. Pride in glorious sonship to God [11].
B. Love of the way of love and rising early to it [12].
C. Tasting the earnest of eternal glory [13].
D. The believer drinks from the Holy One the spirit of holiness and love [14].
E. He bears witness to God, and so judges the nations [15].
F. What concerns him is acquiring the wisdom of God Himself, for He is the giver of gifts, and at the same time offers Himself as a gift [16].
Wisdom exalts her sons, and takes to herself him who seeks her [11].

Since the believer is asked to be in the position of a father to the orphan and a guardian to the widow [10], he may feel unable to accomplish that with all his heart, so he asks that wisdom dwell in him, and so he bears the spirit of spiritual motherhood or fatherhood, by which he who possesses her longs to lift up others as his children, regardless of age. With his heart the believer embraces every man by the wisdom dwelling in him. We can say that Mother Wisdom is far from withdrawing from others; she embraces him who seeks her, and gives him of her characteristics, and he in turn embraces the hearts of others.

Those who seek her: The enjoyment of divine wisdom is not static, but requires growth in it, so we must seek her [11], and love her and rise early to her [12], and possess her, that is, take pride in her [13], and serve her [14] and obey her [15] and turn to her or devote ourselves to her [15] and trust in her and rely on her [16].

The wisdom that Ben Sirach praises is the one who truly deserves praise, the wisdom of God, that is, the Savior; whoever loves Him loves life at an eternal level. For the Lord Christ is the wisdom of God and the power of God (1 Cor 1:24). He magnifies His children who believe in Him, revealing to them by His Holy Spirit the divine mysteries, and gives them continual growth in knowledge, and fills their lives with the joy of the Gospel message. Whoever loves the incarnate wisdom of God loves life, for he keeps His commandments, and so receives eternal life (Jn 12:50). That is, he enjoys in the world the earnest of eternal life, as he experiences the life of constant inward joy. Thus is fulfilled in him the saying of Wisdom: "Blessed is the man that heareth me, watching daily at my gates, waiting at the posts of my doors. For whoso findeth me findeth life, and shall obtain favour of the LORD" (Prov 8:34-35).
Whoever loves her loves life, and those who rise early to her are filled with gladness [12].

Wisdom opens the heart with love as she opens the mind to holy understanding, so she reflects on the believer the spirit of gladness. Wisdom calls all, perhaps they will accept belonging to her, and become her sons, who seek her and she takes them to her fatherly bosom. In the Book of Proverbs we see wisdom lifting up her voice in every place, and calling everyone (Prov 5:1-21).

v In the first instance, while wisdom calls everyone, she calls the simple to understand with prudence, and the unlearned to use their hearts, so that the zealous and watchful reader may establish the meanings of the distinct and different words. She teaches that all things must be practiced and understood and praised and perceived according to their (sound) methods and plans [10].
St. Hilary of Poitiers Whoever possesses her inherits glory, and the Lord blesses whatever place she enters [13].

v Paul testifies that he was sent to proclaim a hidden wisdom which the great men of this world did not know, and therefore they are called foolish. The wisdom of God is hidden, because it is not in words but in power. It is impossible to set it forth in human expressions, but it is believed by the power of the Spirit. God foresaw the sins of the coming world and therefore established this wisdom in a manner baffling to those who want to turn His wisdom into their foolishness, and also to glorify us who believe in Him [11].

Ambrosiaster v The work of the Father which pervades all existence is glorified, and becomes exceedingly great when every man advances and reaches the highest stature of growth through fellowship with Christ "Wisdom" and "Knowledge" and "Holiness."

The same thing is accomplished when man is sanctified and purified and reaches the highest degrees of perfection through fellowship with the Holy Spirit, and thus becomes more worthy to receive the grace of wisdom and knowledge, so that all stains of defilement and ignorance are removed from him, and he reaches this progress in perfection and purity. Thus the life he received from God is worthy of God, that is, pure and perfect. So the creature deserves this (holy) life (after the likeness of the Creator); for the man whom the Creator wills for him receives from Him the power to exist eternally.
Origen Those who serve her serve the Holy One, and those who love her the Lord loves [14].
He who obeys her will judge the nations, and he who turns to her dwells securely [15].

The wise man who walks in the spirit of love and humility enjoys true discernment, and so understands the secret of the fall and rise of nations, and lives in confidence. He realizes how great empires collapse because of their pride, so he takes care for the spirit of humility and surrender into the hand of the Lord. The Book of Ben Sirach touches the Jewish tradition of prophecy which declares what lies behind historical events. The believer senses that historical events did not come haphazardly, but that God Himself is the governor of history with a purpose that surpasses human thought.
If he relies on her he inherits her, and his descendants remain in possession of her [16].
At first she walks with him in troublesome ways, and brings fear and dread upon him, she torments him with her discipline, until she trusts his soul and tests him with her judgments [17].

Divine wisdom is a free gift which the grace of God offers to the believer, so she allows the believer to enter into afflictions so that his soul may be purified, and he learns on the way of suffering in the company of the Crucified, and in this company he enjoys the risen life in Christ who rose from the dead.
v "If you do not return, He will sharpen His sword."

This he says by way of threat, to urge those slow to repent to return (conversion). He does not threaten immediately with wounds and blows and death, but sharpens weapons with a certain preparation as for vengeance.

By this action he points to attack as in a war. Therefore you long for a stop to God's movement toward vengeance; the Holy Scripture says that He sharpens His sword, He bends His bow, and makes it ready, and in it He prepares the instruments of death (Ps 7:13). The instruments of death are the powers that destroy the enemies of God.

"He makes His arrows fiery" (Ps 7:13). The Creator made fire for materials that burn. Certainly it was not made for steel, which does not melt in the fire, but for wood, which burns; so also God made arrows for souls that can be kindled...
Those, then, who were accepted beforehand, and held fast within themselves the fiery arrows of the devil, are those who receive the arrows of God. For this reason "He makes His arrows fiery."

Sensual love burns the soul, and so does the desire of the love of money, and fiery wrath, and sorrows that inflame the soul and melt it, and fears foreign to God. He who is not struck by the arrows of the enemy, and puts on the armor of God (Eph 6:11), remains unaffected by the arrows that bring death [12].
St. Basil the Great Then she returns to him directly and gladdens him, and reveals her secrets to him [18].

Ben Sirach spoke of those who wish to acquire wisdom that they are first exposed to testing and discipline, and if they pass the examination with patience, wisdom returns to them and gives them herself and becomes a guide for them, and offers them her secrets, so they enjoy a life of inward joy and gladness. Some see in this verse a hidden reference to the fall of Solomon the wise, though he returned and repented of his sins.
Then she returns to him directly and gladdens him, and reveals her secrets to him [18].
And if he goes astray she forsakes him, and delivers him to his ruin [19].

Some see that Solomon the wise speaks of his fall by the tongue of wisdom, which forsook him in his fall and then returned to him at his repentance: "Because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded; but ye have set at nought all my counsel, and would none of my reproof... when your fear cometh as a storm, and your calamity cometh as a whirlwind; when distress and anguish cometh upon you. Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me: for that they hated knowledge, and did not choose the fear of the LORD: they would none of my counsel: they despised all my reproof. Therefore shall they eat of the fruit of their own way, and be filled with their own devices. For the turning away of the simple shall slay them, and the prosperity of fools shall destroy them" (Prov 1:24-32).

entries.section: 3. The holiness of the universal family and being on guard against evil

paragraphs.text: 23 My son, observe the time, and beware of evil. 24 And do not be ashamed concerning your own soul, 25 for there is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that is glory and grace. 26 Do not show partiality, for that is harmful to your soul. 27 And do not be ashamed with a shame that is your ruin. 28 Do not refrain from speaking in the time of salvation, and do not hide your wisdom when it is fitting to display it. 29 For wisdom is known by speech, and instruction by the utterance of the tongue. 30 Do not contradict the truth, but be ashamed of your ignorance. 31 Do not be ashamed to confess your sins, and do not struggle against the current of the river. 32 And do not abase yourself to a foolish man, and do not show partiality to the face of the mighty. 33 Strive for the truth unto death, and the Lord God will fight for you. 34 Do not be harsh in your tongue, nor slack and negligent in your works. 35 Do not be as a lion in your house, and as a madman among your family. 36 Let not your hand be stretched out to receive, and closed when it should give.

As the believer guards against evil, he avoids the shame that prevailed in the Hellenistic world (Sir 5:13-6:1; 31:16-42:8). Ben Sirach distinguishes between the shame that evil brings, and the shame because of meekness that leads to honor. It is not fitting for the wise man to stop speaking wisdom at the right time for fear of false shame.
Observe the right time, and beware of evil, and do not bring shame upon yourself [20].

It is fitting for man to observe the right time. Now is the moment you are living, and are aware of, and are able to take the decision befitting you, and set out to carry out the decisive decision, but the coming moment is not yours, and you do not know whether you will be, in your consciousness, able to take the sound decision or not.

"To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven" (Eccl 3:1). Our life with all its circumstances and conditions proceeds according to an ordered plan and design, so that God's purposes are fulfilled at the right time. We must perform our duties faithfully at the right time, and prepare for the future, to see God's plan for us. God created the world for our sake by a wonderful plan, and at the right time He sent the fathers and prophets and gave us the Law, and at the appointed time salvation was accomplished by the Cross, and with heavenly wisdom God cares for every small and great thing in your life, even the number of the hairs of your head does not escape His care.

In other words the history of the whole world and the history of your own life in particular, with all its minutes, are links of events that God arranges. You must live in a spirit of faithfulness, working with all your energies, and living with joy and gladness trusting in God who orders your life, for you by yourself cannot do anything whatever your desire and whatever your abilities.

Origen says: ["To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." There is a time for gathering goodly pearls, and another time after gathering them for discovering the pearl of great price, when it is fitting for a man to go and sell all that he has to buy that pearl. For just as a man who wants to become wise in the words of truth must first learn the principles and then pass beyond through the elementary instruction, which he esteems with all esteem yet does not remain fixed at that point, but reveres it at the beginning of the matter and then seeks perfection. He acknowledges the favor for what he was taught at the outset, because it benefited him much! So the Law and the Prophets are understood with perfect accuracy as elementary teaching for the understanding of the Gospel in its fullness and the understanding of the meaning of all the words and works of Christ [13].]

If God as a Creator who loves mankind "hath made every thing beautiful in his time" (Eccl 3:11), and all that He created is good and by good ordering, yet He lifts us above time... He submitted to time in order to lift us above time, for He "has put eternity in their heart, without which man does not perceive the work that God does from the beginning to the end" (Eccl 3:11).
For there is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that is glory and grace [21].

Glorious modesty accompanies holiness, not the destructive shame before God [21]. St. John Chrysostom noticed in one of his homilies that those present were fewer than usual, and when he learned that the reason was the presence of a banquet of food before the meeting, the saint commented on the words of Ben Sirach: "For there is a shame that bringeth sin, and there is a shame which is glory and grace" (4:21), saying: It is not shameful for a man to share in the spiritual feast of the word of God after sharing in the feast of food. For the feast of the word of God has no fixed time; man may share in it whether he has previously partaken of food or his stomach is empty. The Apostle Paul says: "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season" (2 Tim 4:2). Furthermore Luke the Evangelist relates to us that Paul, being ready to depart from Troas on the morrow, continued his speech until midnight, and a young man named Eutychus sat in the window, weighed down with deep sleep, and fell down from the third loft (Acts 20:7-9). Chrysostom asked: [Was time a problem for him? Did time hinder him from continuing his preaching? [14]]

v "I have made your face hard like their faces, and your forehead hard like their foreheads" (Ezek 3:8). Just as shame is praiseworthy when confronting evil, it is blameworthy when used toward what is good. When the face reddens with shame because of evil, this is the work of the wise person, but the reddening of the face with shame because of doing good is a matter of folly...

He who is ashamed, repenting of an evil he committed, enjoys the freedom of life; and he who is ashamed of having done good falls from his upright position (1 Cor 10:12), and inclines toward the curse. And as the Savior says: "For whosoever shall be ashamed of me and of my words, of him shall the Son of man be ashamed, when he shall come in his own glory" (Lk 9:26).

Some carry what is good in their minds, but since they are not confident in it they cannot defend the truth. He who is not afraid or ashamed to speak what he thinks uprightly is able to defend the truth [15].
Pope Gregory (the Great)
v The shame that brings sin is a man's being ashamed to change his inclination to sin, lest he be accused of being fickle in mind or lest he be judged by his own testimony that he is mistaken [16].
St. Augustine Do not show partiality to anyone that harms your soul, nor honor toward another that leads to your fall [22].

In the service of fallen souls St. John Chrysostom demands that the servant of these souls be committed to bending down to take the fallen man by the hand on the ground and lift him up. But he must first plant his feet firmly on the ground, that he may lift his brother from the ground in safety, and not himself fall with his brother thrown on the ground.

Do not withhold a word in the time of need for it [23]. Ben Sirach warned us often of the slip of the tongue, and of the sin of idle talk or vain speech. This drives some to try to train themselves in silence. This training, to which the pious commit themselves, if used at an unsuitable time becomes evil silence. So when the believer feels the necessity of speaking at a suitable time for the edification of his brother, he is committed to speak. Just as there is evil speech, there is also evil silence; and just as there is holy silence there is also holy speech. The work of wisdom is to give the believer the spirit of discernment, so that he knows when to speak and when to be silent.
v You are the Word who gives a word to those who speak, through You all who speak speak for Your sake.
A ray and a radiance and a great light shone upon me that I might look at You. By my looking at You the soul is enlightened, and so acquires goodness.
And when the soul departs from You it is filled with darkness, and if it gazes upon You, it puts on light so as to speak the words of Your tidings...
Silence and speech stand over me and demand of me. O Lord, order my life according to Your will.
If I am silent I marvel, for I feel my insufficiency (for speech). Let me be silent in wonder, and not in vain arrogance.
And if I speak, may my word be according to Your glory and for Your sake.
When the soul is filled with silence in wonder at You, this silence is a discourse full of every benefit.
And if the soul is moved to glorify You with love... then I move by love, and I move to glorify You. And in wonder I am silent and do not cease from glorifying You.
Grant me, O Lord, wonder and word, that I may be enriched. And every day I wonder, and every day I move with speech!

St. Mar Jacob of Serug v Set, O Lord, a guard upon my mouth, and a strong door upon my lips" (Ps 141:3). He did not say: "a strong barrier, but "a strong door." For a door is opened as it is also shut. If this is a door, let it open and shut. It opens for the confession of sin, and shuts for the forgiveness of sin. For it is a door of safeguarding, not of destruction [17].

St. Augustine v In silence you see your mind, but when you use your mind, you speak within yourself. For during silence the mind begets the word, and the word of thanks that is offered to God is the salvation of man [18].
St. Anba Anthony the Great In a letter of Mar Philoxenus to the monks of Amid, which he wrote from his exile and in which he urged them to strive for the upright faith, he said in it:
[The monk who is silent about the faith is a hypocrite who does not know God...
The monk who is with everyone like him (changes color and conforms to everyone) is a hypocrite who wears the face of a devil.
The monk who puts on Christ and is silent about the truth, his garment is the leprosy of Gehazi.]

entries.section: 3. The holiness of the universal family and being on guard against evil

paragraphs.text: For wisdom is known by speech, and instruction by the word of the tongue [24].

entries.section: 3. The holiness of the universal family and being on guard against evil

paragraphs.text: Do not oppose the speaking of the truth, but be ashamed of your ignorance [25].
The good tongue is the holy tongue and the one under control. The wise man will not yield the truth, nor fear to confess his ignorance [25] or his sin [26].

entries.section: 3. The holiness of the universal family and being on guard against evil

paragraphs.text: Do not be ashamed to confess your sins, and do not stand before the current of the river [26].
Truth resembles an unceasing current [25-26], so a man does not cover up his sins. Confessing a fault does not cause shame, but ignoring it in stupidity is the real shame.

v The lot fell upon (Jonah), and he became subject to accusation on the basis of fact. Perhaps he was afraid, but in truth the accusation became clear (and certain) by his confession. Therefore the wise counsel for those who wish to keep it is: "Be not ashamed to confess your sins" (Sir 4:26) [19].

St. Cyril the Great v It is necessary that we confess our sins to those to whom the stewardship of the mysteries of God has been given. Those who showed repentance in ancient times offered it before the saints. It is stated in the Gospel that they confessed their sins to John the Baptist (Mt 3:6), and in the Book of Acts they confessed to the Apostles by whom they were also baptized (Acts 19:18) [20].

v When you are occupied with some sin, be an accuser of yourself (Prov 18:17), and do not wait for others to bring the accusation. Thus you become like a righteous man who accuses himself in his first speech in court, or like Job, whom the crowd of the people in the city did not hinder from declaring his crime before all [21].
v Confess to the Lord with the lute, with a harp of ten strings sing to Him" (Ps 33:3)

We begin by confessing to the Lord with a harp, that is, by ordering our bodily conduct, for if we have sinned with our body, when we presented our members as an instrument for sin to do evil, our body ought to confess the fault by using the same instrument to wipe out sin (Rom 6:19)
Have you insulted anyone? Speak well of him!
Have you abused your authority? Return what you took!
Have you satisfied the desire of your belly? Fast!
Have you been proud? Be humble!
Have you refused to take for the sake of your dignity? Ask!
Have you killed? Bear the sufferings of martyrdom or what is equivalent to them.
Break your body by open confession. After this open confession, you deserve to praise the Lord with a harp of ten strings.

You must first treat the sins of your body so that you may walk in harmony and concord toward perfection through the word of God, and rise until you behold spiritual goods. For the soul that seeks heavenly goods is called a harp, and it has the shape of the harp, since the notes come from its upper part, and the works of the body confess to God from below, but the mysteries that are revealed to knowledge come from above, and in the soul is the echo of the Spirit.
He who works by all the commandments forms from them a beautiful symphony. He sings to God on a harp of ten strings, referring to the Ten Commandments written in the Law [22].
St. Basil the Great

entries.section: What is our attitude toward him whom his conscience does not condemn (so he does not confess his sins)?

paragraphs.text: v Question: What if (the person) says: "My conscience does not condemn me"?

Answer: The same thing also happens with bodily diseases. For there are many diseases that those afflicted with them do not perceive. Yet they trust the physician's diagnosis more than their own personal lack of feeling of the disease. So also with the diseases of the soul, that is, sins. If someone is unaware of his sin, so he does not condemn himself, yet he must trust those who can see his condition more clearly. This is shown by the holy Apostles, who, despite their conviction of their sincere inclination toward the Lord, yet when they heard: "One of you shall betray me" (Mt 26:21), preferred to trust the word of the Lord, and yielded to His saying, saying: "Lord, is it I?" (Mt 26:22).

As for St. Peter, he teaches us more clearly, for although in the zeal of his humility he refused the service of his Master and God and Teacher (to wash his feet), when he heard the words of the Lord: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me" (Jn 13:8), he was convinced of the truth as it came in the words, and said: "Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head" (Jn 13:9) [23].
St. Basil the Great Do not subject yourself [24] to a foolish man, and do not show partiality to the face of a ruler [27].

It is good that a man walk in the spirit of humility, but for the sake of the believer's concern for his own salvation and the salvation of his brothers he must not hand over the leadership of his life into the hand of a fool, who corrupts his mission and brings him into troubles; and it also stirs in the fool the spirit of pride and his failure to review his follies.
The spirit of humility does not mean cringing before any leader whatever his role at the expense of the needy and the oppressed.

entries.section: What is our attitude toward him whom his conscience does not condemn (so he does not confess his sins)?

paragraphs.text: Strive for the truth unto death, and the Lord God will fight for you [28].

The wise man urges us to (spiritual) striving for the truth unto death [28]. And he who lays down his life for the truth, the Lord fights on his behalf. So he is not ashamed to witness to his faith, whatever the cost.

v "Strive for the truth unto death" (Sir 4:28). From the very same spiritual treasures are made the crowns of the martyrs for the truth, to be set upon their heads, and that with everyone who takes part in the spiritual battles, so (the believer) treads upon those who kindle conflicts and those known as the rulers of the world and the authorities over the darkness of this age and the spiritual hosts of wickedness (Eph 6:12; Sir 4:28; Song 3:10) [25].

St. Didymus the Blind v He who takes part in the Olympic games is crowned not by his victory over one or two or three players, but after his victory over all of them. So he who wishes God to crown him must learn chastity, not only with respect to bodily passions, but also to overcome in the temptation of the love of money and the desire to cling to what is not his, and envy and the love of pleasures and vainglory and being accused of base things and when mortal dangers befall him, and so on [26].

v Let us strive in the good life and the God-loving life, not for the praise of men, but for the salvation of our souls. For death stands before our eyes every day, and because everything human is unstable [27].
St. Anthony the Great St. Augustine distinguishes between three kinds of witnesses to the Lord Christ.
v These three classes are:
The first class includes him who believes in Christ and scarcely whispers His name.
And the next class is he who believes in Christ and confesses openly.
And the third is he who believes in Christ and confesses Him, and is ready to die for Christ.

The first is weak and his shame rests on his fear, the second bears courage on his face but not to the shedding of his blood, the third has all strength and lacks nothing he desires; he is truly as it is written: "Strive for the truth unto death" [28]

St. Augustine Origen sees in the ritual of the tabernacle of meeting or the temple the existence of two altars, one visible and the other invisible. The visible altar is the bronze altar on which the burnt offerings are offered, referring to our spiritual striving for the divine truth unto death. For if our Christ offered His body given up to the death of the cross, we are crucified with Him, and practice the mortification of the body through the burnt offering of pure love. As for the hidden altar, the high priest enters to it in the Holy of Holies, which refers to heaven and entry to the divine throne.

Thus Origen presents to us a symbolic interpretation of the burnt offering in his inner depths as a symbol of the mortification of the body through the fiery Holy Spirit of God, where he renounces everything for the sake of divine truth and love, bearing the cross like his Master with joy and delight; we quote from him the following:
v Each one of us also has himself as a whole burnt offering, and he himself kindles the altar of the whole burnt offering so that it may be consumed.

If I renounce all that I have (Lk 14:33), and take up my cross, and follow Christ (Mk 8:34), I offer a whole burnt offering on the altar of God. Or if I deliver my body even to martyrdom, I offer myself as a whole burnt offering on the altar of God.
If I love my brothers, and lay down my life for my brothers (1 Jn 3:16), if for righteousness and truth I strive unto death (Sir 4:28), I offer a whole burnt offering on the altar of God.

If I mortify my members from every lust of the flesh (Col 3:5), if the world has been crucified to me and I to the world (Gal 6:14), I offer a whole burnt offering on the altar of God, and I myself become a priest of the offering [28].

v You also have a calf that you must offer. This unruly calf is your body; if you wish to offer it to the Lord as an offering, keep it ascetic and pure, lead it to the door of the tabernacle of meeting, where you can hear the reading of the Holy Scriptures there.
Let your offering be a male... so that there may be in it nothing of pampering or lack of firmness.

Lay your hand upon the burnt offering that it may be acceptable to the Lord, and slay it before the Lord, meaning that you set limits of chastity and do not abandon the subduing of the body, but be like him who laid his hand upon his body when he said: "I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway" (1 Cor 9:27).
Slay it before the Lord and do not hesitate to mortify your members (Col 3:5)...

Let there be within you a priest and his sons, that is, the spirit that is in you and its senses, for through them there is understanding of the Lord and perception of divine knowledge. Then offer your body to the Lord in asceticism but with spiritual understanding, as the Apostle says: "a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service" (Rom 12:1)...

entries.section: What is our attitude toward him whom his conscience does not condemn (so he does not confess his sins)?

paragraphs.text: Some offer their bodies as a burnt offering but as though without a priest, that is, without fullness of knowledge...
