And her yoke will be an ornament of gold, and her fetters a cord of blue [30].
You will put her on as a robe of glory, and wear her as a crown of great rejoicing [31].

If you acquire wisdom she becomes a source of pride for you, and becomes like a crown that adorns the head, and necklaces that adorn the neck: "an ornament of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck" (Prov 1:9). For wisdom, represented whether in good speech or conduct, is a cause of delight both to the wise man and to those around him. Therefore kings, rulers and governors in many kingdoms surrounded themselves with the wise and the philosophers, adorning their councils, their courts and their palaces with them, and perhaps the manifestations of wisdom embodied here (strong protection, robe of glory, golden ornaments, purple garments, scarlet, crown of rejoicing) remind us of what Pharaoh of Egypt gave to Joseph: the ring, the garment, the fine linen and the gold chain (Gen 41:45). The blue cords in particular point to the Law. It is stated in the book of Numbers that the Israelites were bound to put a ribband of blue on the fringe of the borders of their garments, so that they might see it and remember all the commandments of the Lord and do them (Num 15:38-39). But here the devout see the fetters of wisdom as a golden ornament with a blue ribband, and they wear a robe of glory and carry a lofty crown (6:30-31). Truly heavenly wisdom makes of the believer a priest who offers the sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving (Rev 1:6), wearing a glorious robe (50:11) and a splendid crown (Prov 4:9)[26].
The requirements for acquiring wisdom are: A. The desire for continual learning [32].
B. The desire to listen [33] more than to speak. C. Cleaving to the wise who have experience [34].
D. Listening attentively to the divine commandment [35]. E. Earnestness and frequenting the places of the wise [36].
F. Sanctifying the mind at all times, which makes it steadfast, not shaken by every strange wind [37].
If you will, my son, you will learn, and if you give yourself, you will become shrewd [32].
Ben Sirach longs for the hearts of believers to be kindled with longing to learn wisdom, so that all may become wise.
If you love to listen you will acquire knowledge, and if you incline your ear you will become wise [33].
He made clear that wisdom is not attained by much talking, but by listening to the wise and acting upon wisdom through the study of the Law.

v It was said: "Wisdom is in the understanding of the faithful." Xenocrates, in his treatise on "Intelligence", says that wisdom consists, according to scientific knowledge, first in the causes and in the rational being. He looks at "intelligence" from two sides: the practical and the theoretical, the latter being human wisdom. Therefore wisdom is a kind of intelligence, but not every kind of intelligence is wisdom...

Heraclitus attacks human beings who lack faith, saying: "They do not know how to speak and how to listen." Doubtless he drew help from the text: "If you love to hear, you will gain knowledge, and if you incline your ear you will be wise" (cf. Sir 6:33).
St. Clement of Alexandria: Stand in the assembly of the elders, and cleave to him who is wise [34].

Ben Sirach links the divine commandment with enjoying the experiences of the saints in the Lord. Besides enjoying the commandment of the Lord as a source of wisdom, he advises his disciples to choose good friends. For friendship or fellowship with the wise has its effect on a person. "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed" (Prov 13:20).
Be ready to hear every divine discourse, and do not let the proverbs of understanding escape you [35].
The need for the law of God, the source of wisdom. This is what distinguishes wisdom full of godliness from philosophical wisdom.
And if you see a man of understanding, rise early to him, and let your steps wear out the threshold of his door [36].

He who desires to learn wisdom must frequent the places of the wise, and whenever he hears of one of the wise he must go to him and visit his door until his feet become familiar with the thresholds of his door.

St. Augustine sees that the man of understanding here is the Lord of glory Jesus. He asks us to rise early to Him and cleave to Him and ask Him: "Master, where dwellest thou?" (Jn 1:38), so that we may abide with Him all the days of our life.

In St. John Chrysostom's discourse on the eunuch, the minister of Candace queen of Ethiopia (Acts 8:30-31), who longed to understand what Isaiah the prophet had said, he says: [He showed us virtue in his conduct by his invitation (to Philip): he was a pagan minister sitting in his chariot, and he called a man lesser than himself in appearance, wearing despised clothing, to come up and ride with him. Do you see his zealous spirit? Do you see his surpassing devotion? Do you see a God-fearing pagan fulfilling the saying of the wise man: "If thou seest a man of understanding, get thee betimes unto him, and let thy foot wear the steps of his door" (cf. Sir 6:36)? Do you not see how he became worthy not to be slighted? Do you not see how he became worthy to receive a privilege from on high? Do you not see that he neglected nothing on his part? Therefore through his teacher he received a distinguished knowledge of the effect of what is written in the Holy Bible, and light shone upon his mind[27].]

St. Augustine sees that this saying explains what is stated in verse 34, namely the endeavor to cleave to the wise. He gave us an example in the Lord Christ's call to Peter and Andrew (Mt 4:19). They followed Him and did not leave Him; they asked Him: "Where dwellest thou?" (Jn 1:38), and He disclosed to them where He dwelt[28].
Think on the ordinances of the Lord, and practice His commandments, for He strengthens your mind at all times, and the desire for wisdom is given to you [37].

He ends this chapter by affirming the role of our Lord Jesus in enjoying true friendship: 1. Meditation on the ordinances of the Lord, or the divine commandment, lifts the believer's heart as it were to heaven, and he sees that its constitution is true love; God Himself is love. "And we have known and believed the love that God hath to us. God is love; and he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him" (1 Jn 4:16). And we come into touch with the heavenly orders who glorify God for His love for mankind and His wonderful work on the Cross for their salvation. 2. By practicing His commandments in our daily life we taste the sweetness of friendship with God and the heavenly orders and with one another. 3. The Lord establishes our mind at all times, so that events cannot shake our friendship, but develop it and make it firm. 4. The Lord gives us the desire for wisdom, as He sanctifies our will so that it is in harmony with His divine will.
Inspired by Sirach 6

entries.section: Shine upon me with the light of Your love, that I may cleave to You, O Friend of mankind

paragraphs.text: v How my soul longed to meet You in the garden of Eden with Adam and Eve.
I hear Your voice as You walk in the garden, and I feel that I am carried on Your arms!
Heaven is not far off; even the wild beasts seek my friendship, for I am Your beloved and Your friend.
My first parents accepted the counsel of the enemy of good, so rebellion took possession of my heart, and my friendship with You turned into enmity!
Even the heavenly orders stood in amazement at what I did, I who am dust and ashes!
Disgrace and shame came upon me, my nature was corrupted, and corruption settled in my depths!
Darkness settled in my heart, and enmity entered with it!
v In Your love You came down to me, and by Your Cross You planted me by the streams of living water.
I have come to suffer a struggle within me.
Will the first friendship return, and my will be in harmony with Your holy will?
By Your grace You gave me sonship, and established Your Kingdom within me.
You poured Your meekness into me, that I may draw my brethren by sweet speech and a gentle tongue.
You made me a member of Your Church, so that those who are at peace with me became many.
But among the thousand, I find You a faithful and mighty counselor.
v Friendship has been corrupted in the world, and there is the friend who seeks what is for his own benefit.
And there is one who befriends me in the time of ease, and ignores me in the day of distress.
He exerts all his effort, not to support me but to hinder my steps.
v You are the faithful Friend, my strong refuge.
You are my eternal treasure and the medicine of life; in place of earthly things You give me heavenly things.
And in place of corruption You give me immortality and incorruption.
You establish Your Kingdom within me, and You have become nearer to me than my father and mother.
Your commandment gives me an easy and sweet yoke?
You grant me to walk in Your company, O Crucified One; I set out on the narrow way to the crown of joy!
You turn the fetters of the commandment into precious ornaments with which my soul is adorned.
v With every morning I sing of Your new mercies.
You shine upon me with the light of Your knowledge and Your mysteries.
You teach me and train me, and I become wise in You.
In You my mind will not be shaken, but increases in understanding, wisdom and knowledge.
You carry me from victory to victory, and from glory to glory.
You prepare me as a heavenly bride sitting at Your right hand, O King of kings and Lord of lords.
Glory to You, O Wisdom of God, for You became incarnate for me and for all my brethren.

Appendix to Sirach 6: A faithful friend is the medicine of life (Sir 6:16). 1. The need for a friend: Who are the friends whom the sweet voice of the Crucified drew, if not the believers from all the nations? And who are those at peace with us, if not the heavenly orders who rejoice in our salvation.

"A faithful friend is a strong refuge, and he who has found one has found a treasure. A faithful friend has no equal, and there is none who can weigh his loftiness. A faithful friend is the medicine of life, and those who fear the Lord will find him" (6:14-16). 2. Sincere friendship: St. Augustine says: ["A faithful friend is the medicine of life" (cf. Sir 6:16). There is no remedy so effective in healing pains as the sincere friend who comforts you in your afflictions, manages you in your problems, rejoices in your success and grieves in your calamities. He who has found such a friend has found a treasure. For the faithful friend has no like, and the weight of gold and silver does not equal the goodness of his faithfulness (cf. Sir 6:14-15).] 3. Friendship and the fear of the Lord: He who carries the fear of the Lord in his heart, and walks in the spirit of godliness in the wisdom of the Spirit, obtains good friendship even with the heavenly orders. 4. Friendship with wisdom herself: "My son, choose instruction from your youth, and you will find wisdom in your old age. Come to her like the plowman and the sower, and wait for her good harvest, for you will labor a little in her work, and will eat of her fruit soon" (6:18-19). 5. Care to preserve friendship: St. John Chrysostom says: [Let us follow love, for it is a safety valve that does not allow us to suffer any evil. Let us bind ourselves to one another. Let there be no deceit among us and no lie, for where friendship is, there is nothing of the kind. Another wise man tells us this: "Though thou drewest a sword at thy friend, yet despair not: for there may be a returning to favour. If thou hast opened thy mouth against thy friend, fear not; for there may be a reconciliation: except for upbraiding, or pride, or disclosing of secrets, or a treacherous wound: for for these things every friend will depart" (cf. Sir 22:21-22).] 6. False friends: St. Ephrem the Syrian says: [If you have a friendship with one of the brethren and harm comes to you because of your association with him, hasten and cut yourself off from him. I do not say this to you, beloved, so that you may hate people, no. But so that you may cut off the causes of vice.]

1 Do not do evil, and evil will not overtake you. 2 Keep away from the unrighteous, and the unrighteous will turn away from you. 3 My son, do not sow in the furrows of iniquity, lest you reap it sevenfold.

The only holy Friend, who is able to dwell in our hearts and establish His Kingdom in them, is the Lord of glory Jesus. He reigns over the heart, so the enemy of good finds no place in us, and flees from us. In this way evil or iniquity has no authority over our hearts or minds or emotions, but our depths are turned into a sanctuary for the Lord. We are sanctified by divine grace, and we draw many to enjoy divine friendship, and friendship with human beings in the Lord.

This is on the side of the holy and mighty divine Friend; yet He does not storm our life by force, but grants us to have our own part, which reveals our desire for the holy life. It is fitting for us to seek holiness and strive with a spirit of vigilance, so that we expel every evil thought and seek to acquire the holy thought. For evil does not impose itself on us.
v Those who strive to have a virtuous life and a life of love for God must give up self-reliance and all empty vainglory. They must also strive for the reformation of their life and their hearts.
The steadfast mind that loves God is a guide and a way to God[2].
v He who is purified from evil and sin is called a saint. For the absence of evil from a person is a greater perfection of the soul and pleases God greatly[3].
St. Anthony the Great: Moreover the Holy Bible has drawn for us the way of perfection by presenting negative commandments and positive ones, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit of God.

v The (first) Psalm draws for us the way of virtue, with knowledge and art, for withdrawal from evil is the beginning of good; if you seek perfect virtue from the beginning, you turn back before you begin, but the Psalm prepares the way for us so that we may face it with courage.

I believe that growth in the love of God is like the ladder that the blessed Jacob once saw, which on one side was on the earth, and on the other side was rising toward the virtuous life, where a person begins by climbing the first rungs of the ladder, and afterward rises to a higher rung with deliberation and patience until he reaches what human nature can attain. So, by climbing the first rungs of the ladder we rise above the earth, to practice the life that God wants for us. And the beginning of progress is withdrawal from evil, where such withdrawal is as easy as "Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not steal" (Ex 20:13-15); this does not require positive action. But when we are asked for that commandment: "Love thy neighbor as thyself", "sell that thou hast, and give to the poor" (Mt 19:21), "whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain" (Mt 5:41), these works are done by the wrestler who has experienced strength through divine wisdom, and through small works he leads us to perfection.

For he sets before us three things that we must avoid: walking in the counsel of the wicked, standing in the way of sinners, and sitting in the seat of the scornful. This order begins with taking the decision and then carrying it out; the beginning here is in the pure thought, for the foundation of the works of the flesh springs from purity of heart, and adultery begins in the lustful soul and ends in adultery of the body, so the Lord said: "Those things which defile a man come out of the heart" (cf. Mt 15:18)[4].
v Question: How can a person come to hate sins (Ps 119:163)?

Answer: Hatred rises in people from hateful and grievous events toward those who cause such disturbance. Therefore if someone is thoroughly convinced of the gravity of the many evils that sins cause, he spontaneously, without anyone urging him, and by an inward inclination, experiences hatred for them, as the psalmist showed: "I hate and abhor lying" (cf. Ps 119:163)[5].
v Question: How is the soul fully convinced that God forgives it its sins?

Answer: When it observes within itself the inclination of him who said: "I hate and abhor lying" (Ps 119:163). When God sent His only-begotten Son for the forgiveness of our sins, He forgives them to us as long as we believe in His role.

St. David sings of mercy and judgment (Ps 101:1), and testifies that God is merciful and just (Ps 115:5), so it is necessary that there enter into us what the prophets and apostles say in the passages concerning repentance, that the judgments of God's righteousness (Ps 119:62) are manifest, and His mercy is perfect in forgiving sins[6].
St. Basil the Great: Do not do evil, and evil will not take hold of you [1].
Evil does not impose itself on a person; rather it is the person who seeks it, and he who plants the seed of evil in its furrows, then iniquity multiplies and gains authority over him.

Iniquity is merely a seed; when a person plants it, it becomes a weak plant that grows with time and becomes a mighty tree, and then he reaps sevenfold. He who sows evil reaps evil multiplied. An example is the troubles that came upon the household of King David, which were the fruit of the evil he committed with Bathsheba (2 Sam 12:9-12). With every slackness toward sin, it gains the right to break into our depths with more power. And with every refusal of the deception of the enemy, the soul increases in boldness, strength and authority over the devil and his wiles and works.

It is fitting for the believer to be faithful in the uprightness of his life, not making light of evil and receiving it in his mind or heart or inner feelings, as in his words and outward conduct. Let his life be in Christ, whether personal, family or public. Let him not seek success or gain or fame at the expense of his principles in the Lord.

v Depart from evil, and evil itself will depart from you. Do not sow the seed of evil deeds in the furrow of injustice, so that you will not reap it multiplied sevenfold... Do not say: "His mercies are great, He will forgive the multitude of my sins"...

It is stated in Proverbs: "His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be holden with the cords of his sins. He shall die without instruction; and in the greatness of his folly he shall go astray" (Prov 5:22-23)[7].

Fulgentius: v Those who fully understand that all their work must aim at attaining the good life, and yet are distracted by temporal blessings; these I liken to people who seek a cure and medicine but do not know how to use it, and are not troubled about (their ignorance of using it). Therefore let us not excuse our sins that we commit by the pretext of the circumstances of the environment or by attributing them to another person, but let us lay the blame on ourselves. For if our souls surrender willingly to sloth, they cannot escape defeat[8].

v He who advances in a godly life does not allow evil to enter his soul, and when his soul is freed from evil, he is in peace and safety. And wicked demons or sudden accidents have no authority over him, but God delivers him from every evil, and he lives under invisible protection, because he is a lover of God. If someone praises such a person, he does not care about it, and if someone reviles him, he does not defend himself against his reviler, nor is he angered at any of his sayings[9].

St. Anba Anthony the Great: v He who flees from worldly pleasures and passions becomes an impregnable tower against the demon of murmuring. For murmuring is caused by the feeling of deprivation of some pleasures that exist or are expected. We cannot overcome it as long as we are bound with earthly bonds. Whenever Satan looks at us and sees us bound by them, he sets his nets for us to stir up murmuring in us.
Father Evagrius the monk: Keep away from iniquity, and it will turn away from you [2].
My son, do not sow in the furrows of iniquity, and you will not reap it sevenfold [3].

Keeping away from iniquity and fleeing from it carries a spirit of strength, because the enemy of good asks us to enter into dialogue with him so as to cast deception into our hearts as he did with Eve. He who goes of his own free will to the furrows of iniquity, and there sows a small plant of iniquity, this planting grows and multiplies, and is not easily uprooted after it has been planted. For the seed of iniquity sprouts and grows until it becomes a tree that is hard to uproot. When we open the door to the enemy, he enters and then storms the place of the steering wheel, and drives us wherever he wishes.

entries.section: 2. Divine love and fitting conduct in public affairs

paragraphs.text: 4 Do not seek of the Lord a place of leadership, nor of the king a seat of glory. 5 Do not claim to be righteous before the Lord, nor wise before the king. 6 Do not seek to become a judge, lest you be unable to root out injustice; perhaps you will fear the face of the mighty, and so put a stumbling block in the way of your uprightness. 7 Do not sin against the assembly of the city, and do not cast yourself down among the crowd. 8 Do not return to sin a second time, for you will not be held guiltless of the first. 9 Do not be fainthearted in your prayer. 10 And do not neglect almsgiving.
Do not seek of a lord a place of leadership, nor of a king a seat of honor [4].

The heavenly Friend calls us not to seek the chief seats, and also warns us against the love of leadership, so that we may not be distracted from our salvation by a spirit of pride. The Lord Christ says: "When thou art bidden of any man to a wedding, sit not down in the highest room; lest a more honourable man than thou be bidden of him; And he that bade thee and him come and say to thee, Give this man place; and thou begin with shame to take the lowest room" (Lk 14:8-9). It is fitting for the believer not to rely on his own understanding or his own abilities, nor to seek temporal honor, so that he seeks neither vain glories nor temporal authority, nor justifies himself before God. The divine Friend came down from heaven and took the last ranks of humanity, becoming the crucified servant between two thieves, stirring in us a spirit of rivalry to hasten toward Him that we may take the last ranks with Him.

entries.section: 2. Divine love and fitting conduct in public affairs

paragraphs.text: Do not declare yourself righteous before a lord, nor show yourself wise before a king [5].

Through the divine friendship, what occupies us when we stand before a lord or a king is not to display our righteousness or our wisdom, but that our conduct bear witness to the righteousness of Christ and His divine wisdom. The wise man commands us: "Put not forth thyself in the presence of the king, and stand not in the place of great men: For better it is that it be said unto thee, Come up hither; than that thou shouldest be put lower in the presence of the prince whom thine eyes have seen" (Prov 25:6-7). It is not wise for a man to justify himself before God, because all have sinned (Ps 143:2; Rom 3:9-10). And as the psalmist says: "If You judge, who will be justified before You?" And it is foolish for a man to boast of wisdom before the king or ruler, because it is hard to perceive what is in his intentions (Prov 25:3).
The judge has a serious obligation to root out evil by persisting in resisting the powers of evil (Lev 19:15).

entries.section: 2. Divine love and fitting conduct in public affairs

paragraphs.text: v Nothing generates haughtiness like a good conscience when we are not careful. Therefore, since Jesus knows that if we do anything faithfully this tendency rises in us, He said to His disciples: "When ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants" (Lk 17:10)... And Solomon also says: "Do not justify yourself before the Lord"[10].
St. John Chrysostom: Do not seek to become a judge, if you are not able to root out iniquity.
Lest you show deference to the presence of the mighty man, and make concessions of your integrity [6].
In the Hebrew text it is: "to become a ruler".

entries.section: 2. Divine love and fitting conduct in public affairs

paragraphs.text: v "Seek not to be made a judge, being not able to take away iniquity" (cf. Sir 7:6). Much more we say here: "Do not seek to be a teacher, if you are not qualified for the dignity of this office, and even if you are drawn into it, refuse it[11].

St. John Chrysostom: v We do not advise you to leave him who entrusted you with the care of the holy churches of God (2 Cor 11:28), but we ask you to take care of yourself in the fear of the Lord. Do not accept gifts from anyone (Prov 15:27), and do not be crooked in judgment (Sir 20:29). Do not be ashamed before a man of authority, and do not acquit the guilty or condemn the innocent (Susanna 53) LXX. Flee from covetousness, the root of all evil (1 Tim 6:10), which in truth has been called a kind of idolatry (Eph 5:5). And do not be proud, that you may be a disciple of the Apostle who said: "Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate" (Rom 12:16). Do not try to please men, for you know with whom those who did so ended; they became strangers to the service of Christ. Indeed the Apostle says: "If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10). And submit to the Lord who says: "Learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls" (Mt 11:29).

entries.section: 2. Divine love and fitting conduct in public affairs

paragraphs.text: Quench anger and put it away from you, for it is destructive to a person. Do everything according to the counsel of God, and you will find Him a helper to you. Always fear death, for it is coming upon us all. Remember the hour of your departure, and do not sin against God. If you reach the point of quietness, you will find rest and grace wherever you decide to withdraw[12].
Sts. Barsanuphius and John: Do not sin against the inhabitants of a city, and do not humiliate yourself before the people [7].

It is fitting for the believer to work for the building up and salvation of the community, and not to shatter his energies and deviate from his mission toward it, lest he humiliate himself before the crowd, especially on the great day of the Lord.
Do not repeat your sin, for you will be punished even for (the sin of) one [8].

Among the traits of him who despises God's long-suffering, makes light of his brother's love, and ignores the building up of the community is that he sins against God, the salvation of his soul and the edification of his brethren, and after repenting of what he has committed he returns and repeats the error.

Even in our dealings with leaders or rulers, we may err because of our human weakness and the Lord covers us, but if we become lax and repeat the fall, the Lord lifts His hand from us, and our first sins, which the Lord covered in order to rescue us from the hands of the leaders, are exposed, and we are called to account for the former and later errors! If God does not discipline us when we sin once, that is not a reason for repeating sin in reliance upon His long-suffering. God does not condemn us because we have sinned, but condemns us if we do not repent after we have sinned, and this is confirmed by our repeating the sin in slackness. One of the desert Fathers says: "I do not remember that the demons led me astray twice in a single matter."

entries.section: 2. Divine love and fitting conduct in public affairs

paragraphs.text: v He who is disciplined for his former sins and obtains forgiveness, let him prepare himself for a wrath more severe than the first if he sins again... "Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee" (Jn 5:14)[13].
v Question: What must one do who repents of a sin and then falls again into the same sin?

Answer: He who repented once and committed the same sin again, let him first be convinced before himself that he has not removed the chief cause of the sin, as from a corrupt root, and so necessarily the same evils sprout again. He is like one who wishes to cut off the branches of a tree, leaving the root as it is, and since the root remains stored in the earth, the same (sin) sprouts again to a lesser degree. Therefore, since there are certain sins whose origin is not in themselves but which proceed from other sins, he who wants to purify himself entirely from sin must cut off the very first causes of those sins. For example, strife and envy (Rom 13:13) do not spring from themselves, but from the root of haughtiness and love of (vain) glory; so he who seeks glory from men competes with one who has great fame surpassing his own, and envies him for it.

entries.section: 2. Divine love and fitting conduct in public affairs

paragraphs.text: Therefore he who falls into the vice of envy or strife, and returns and falls into it again, let him realize that the primary cause is the love of glory of which we spoke before. In this let him take care of this sickness, for he needs to be healed of it, and that by its opposite, that is, by humility, performing simple services, practicing humility. In this way, once he is established in the virtue of humility, he does not fall again into the products of haughtiness and love of glory[14].
St. Basil the Great

entries.section: 3. Between divine love and worship in a spirit of godliness

paragraphs.text: 11 Do not say: "God will look upon the multitude of my offerings, and when I offer them to the Most High He will accept them."

Our heavenly Friend does not need a multitude of offerings, nor of prayers and almsgiving; rather He smells in the offerings the incense of holiness and purity. And He delights in the fervent heart rejoicing in love in prayer, and in offering the sweet word with joy along with every gift or alms. The way of godliness is not impossible, but by love for God in earnestness we enjoy the virtuous life.

entries.section: 3. Between divine love and worship in a spirit of godliness

paragraphs.text: v It is fitting for us not to say that it is impossible for a person to walk in the virtuous life, but to say of it that it is not easy. Truly (the virtuous life) is not obtained by all in equal measure, since only the devout who have a mind that loves God obtain it. The ordinary mind is earthly and changeable, out of which come good thoughts and evil thoughts, and it is variable, inclined toward material things, but the mind that loves God shatters the evil that comes to human beings because of their unintentional negligence[15].
St. Anthony the Great: Do not say: "God will look upon the multitude of my offerings, and when I offer them to the Most High He will accept them" [9].

God has no need of the offerings and sacrifices that we present; rather the offerings and sacrifices of the Old Testament were symbols of the sacrifice of the Cross that the Messiah the Savior offered for reconciliation. It is a sacrifice of love on the part of the Lord to atone for our sins. As for the sacrifices of praise and thanksgiving that we still offer in the New Testament, in their reality they are a yielding of our bare human will and a thanksgiving to the will of the Lover of mankind, the Savior of the world. Thus offerings and sacrifices in themselves do not bring God's good pleasure, and will not be the object of His delight unless they are offered with faith and trust in God who forgives sins.
Do not be fainthearted in your prayer, and do not neglect almsgiving [10].
The wise man warns us against our mistaken reliance on almsgiving. For it is not fitting for the believer to do evil relying on the idea that giving many alms will forgive him all the evils he does.

The Church took care that she should have her positive and constructive calendar in the life of worship at the daily, weekly, monthly, yearly and jubilee levels, etc., not in dry literal practices, but in living encounters with God and enjoying the pledge of heaven. We mention in a few lines examples of this:

The daily level: practicing the canonical hours interacting with personal prayers, in which we remember our life with Him who was born in the manger (the prayer or praise of Prime), and the descent of His Holy Spirit (the praise of the Third Hour), and His crucifixion (the Sixth), and His death for us (the Ninth), and our departure to Him (the Eleventh), and our repose in the Lord (the Twelfth), and our waiting for His last coming (Midnight).
The weekly level, such as the fast of Wednesday and Friday, and fellowship in the sacrament of the Eucharist, that is, the Divine Liturgy.
The monthly level, such as the celebrations of the feasts of St. Mary and the archangel Michael, etc.
The yearly level, such as the feasts of the Lord and the feasts of the saints.
The jubilee level, for our renewal by the Spirit of God and tasting godliness.

v Hire the poor... and they will prepare for you a high place in the world of light, in which you will lay your treasures. They will build you a great chamber, full of good things, that you may enter it and dwell and find all your treasures. They will be a company surrounding you on the road, and by that great declaration they will ask for you and save you... They will open the door of the Bridegroom before you knock... Be a friend to them so that they may receive you into their tents...
St. Jacob of Serugh

entries.section: 4. Uprightness in speech, work and conduct

paragraphs.text: 12 Do not mock a man in the bitterness of his soul, for there is One who humbles and exalts. 13 Do not devise a lie against your brother, nor contrive it against your friend. 14 Do not desire to lie about anything, for the habit of lying is not for good. 15 Do not multiply words in the assembly of the elders, nor repeat words in your prayer. 16 Do not hate laborious work, nor farming, which the Most High ordained. 17 Do not number yourself among sinners. 18 Remember that wrath does not tarry. 19 Humble yourself greatly, for the punishment of the ungodly is fire and worms. 20 Do not exchange a friend for something temporal, nor a true brother for the gold of Ophir.

Since our heavenly Friend calls us to uprightness in our words, works and movements, He came down to us that we may walk in His footsteps, and He even works in us that we may be a living icon of Him in all our conduct. The wise man advises us to righteous conduct and humility. He who mocks a wretched person is foolish, because God who raised you up allowed the other to go down, and He can do the opposite to make a balance [1-6].
Vain words without meaning are unfitting in any gatherings with others or in prayer. And manual work was appointed by God for humanity (Gen 2:15; 3:19), and therefore it is honored (38:24-34).

entries.section: 4. Uprightness in speech, work and conduct

paragraphs.text: The rabbis say that the study of the Torah must be joined with manual work[16]. This is plain in practice from Paul the Apostle and Aquila and Priscilla, since they were tentmakers. In the monastic systems work is counted obligatory for spiritual benefit.

Since the Lord reigns over the heart, the soul is filled with the spirit of hope and joy with trust in God's work in it and through it. The believer feels the richness of God's surpassing grace, which makes of him a king with authority even over his thoughts, and he also draws from the wealth of the traits of the incarnate divine Wisdom, so that he walks in a spirit of meekness and humility, and pride has no place in him.

Our meeting with the divine Friend, wonderful in His love, fills our inner being, and leads us to walk in heavenly wisdom. This love is reflected in the believer's relation with his brethren, so that he overflows with love toward them in the Lord.
Do not mock one who is bitter of soul, for there is One who humbles and exalts [11].

Among the most important evils that befall society is making light of one who is bitter of soul. Nothing increases this person's bitterness like mockery of his person, especially if it is because of a personal incapacity in him. It is fitting for the believer to put himself in this person's place and in the same circumstances, and so share the bitterness of his soul, and support him with love and a spirit of hope, and raise him from the bitterness of his life to sweetness. One of the articles of the heavenly Friend's constitution is: "With what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you: and unto you that hear shall more be given" (Mk 4:24). So he who makes light of a person bitter of soul, the bitterness returns to him, and he falls into humiliation, while he who is bitter of soul is exalted. Perhaps by one bitter of soul is meant the person whom want and need have humbled. And as the wise man says: "Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker" (Prov 17:5).

"He humbles and exalts", and as Hannah said: "The Lord killeth, and maketh alive: he bringeth down to the grave, and bringeth up. The Lord maketh poor, and maketh rich: he bringeth low, and lifteth up. He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory" (1 Sam 2:6-8). This does not mean that He shows partiality between persons, but as was said by the Virgin Mary: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree" (Lk 1:52). Christ died once for the whole world, without distinction between classes of people or distinction between races. He offered the Cross for the little infant and the old man, the man and the woman, the Jew and the Gentile.
Do not devise a lie against your brother, and do not do the like against your friend [12].

The life of society rests on trust among its members, so that all are bound together by the bond of love. The person who slanders his brethren with lies does not deserve to live in society. He commits a hateful crime, because he who does this wrongs the very society that covers the weaknesses of all. He who slanders others falsely is like one who pours deadly poison into society.
Beware of every lie, for the habit of it will bring no good [13].
The heavenly Friend is the Truth, so he who cleaves to Him does not lie to a neighbor or a friend.
Do not speak vanity in the assembly of the elders, and do not repeat words in your prayer [14].

entries.section: 4. Uprightness in speech, work and conduct

paragraphs.text: He who speaks vanity in the presence of experienced elders sins; how much more he who does so in the presence of God, who searches the hearts and knows the hidden thoughts. This evil comes from the soul's haughtiness and lack of humility [17]. The truly humble person deserves to live in society and to have his constructive effectiveness in the life of his brethren.
It is fitting for the believer to sit in the presence of the devout elders to learn, and not to be puffed up with his knowledge, experience and learning.

It is fitting for us to control our tongue and sanctify it. For chatter and much talking are snares that the enemy sets so that our tongue may slip and utter vanity. As for prayer, God seeks the fervent heart steadfast in faith, not much speaking and length in prayer.

v Wisdom advises us well: "Use not many words in a multitude of elders" (cf. Sir 7:14). Again He asks us to limit vain chatter even in our relation with God by setting a limit with this commandment: "Do not repeat words in vain".
St. Clement of Alexandria: Do not hate laborious work, especially farming, which the Most High created [15].

Work is a beautiful gift, with many blessings. The Lord Christ says: "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work" (Jn 5:17). And it was said of the angels: "that do his pleasure" (Ps 104). And God created Adam to work in the garden (Gen 3:15). The earnest person does not despise simple tasks, but rejoices if he has the bodily strength to complete them.
Do not be prominent in the assembly of sinners, and remember that wrath does not tarry [16].

Sitting with sinners exudes upon us their evil traits, and makes us lose calmness of soul and care for our salvation. This is reflected in our thoughts, words and conduct, and brings upon us the curse that awaits them, and since their jesting and sins attract us, we must remember that God's wrath is coming and will not tarry, so that we perish with them. The psalmist takes care for the purity of his life, so he sings: "Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners" (Ps 1:1-2).
Humble yourself greatly, for the punishment of the wicked is fire and worms [17].

Humbling the soul here is controlling oneself by keeping away from the assemblies of the scornful (Ps 1), for man by nature finds pleasure in practicing sin. When a person humbles himself by repenting of his sins, he escapes eternal judgment.

Fire and worms: It was said: "For their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched" (Isa 66:24). The talk here about the worm is a rebuke to sinners who care only for their bodies, for in the end the worm will feed on them.

v Sin carries in it the very bread of death, and offers it to those it calls from among the lovers of pleasures and the foolish. "Stolen waters are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant" (Prov 9:17). As soon as someone touches it, "he knoweth not that the dead are there; and that her guests are in the depths of hell" (cf. Prov 9:18).

When a person thinks of tasting pleasure, the outcome of the refreshment in it is not sweet in the end. This is what the wisdom of God affirms: "Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel" (cf. Prov 20:17). And also: "For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil: But her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a twoedged sword" (Prov 5:3-4). So eating of it and enjoying it is for a little while, after that the worm devours him and his soul becomes far away, for the fool does not know that those who are far from God perish[17].

entries.section: 4. Uprightness in speech, work and conduct

paragraphs.text: St. Athanasius the Apostolic: Do not exchange a friend for money, nor a true brother for the gold of Ophir [18].

There is nothing that equals friendship and love, for "charity never faileth" (1 Cor 13:8). One of the grave evils in public life that must be avoided is betrayal of friendship for material gains. Judas became an example of betrayal of friendship for silver, and it was said of him that it would have been good for him if he had not been born (Mt 26:24).

Ophir: in the south-west of Arabia, famed as a source of gold in the ancient world. It was said of the Church sitting at the right hand of the Lord Christ: "Upon thy right hand did stand the queen in gold of Ophir" (Ps 45:9).

21 Do not part from your wife, if she is wise and good, for her grace is above gold. 22 Do not mistreat a servant who works faithfully, nor a hired man who gives his life. 23 Let your soul love a wise servant, and do not deny him his freedom. 24 If you have cattle, take care of them, and if they are of use to you, keep them with you. 25 If you have sons, discipline them, and bow down their necks from their youth. 26 If you have daughters, guard their bodies, and do not show a cheerful face to them. 27 Give your daughter in marriage, and you will have accomplished a great matter, and give her to a man of understanding. 28 If you have a wife after your own heart, do not cast her off, but the hated one, do not give yourself to her. 29 Honor your father with all your heart, and do not forget the pangs of your mother. 30 Remember that through them you were born; what can you give them in return for what they have done for you?

In speaking of the family, Ben Sirach does not stop at the marriage bond or blood kinship, but commends the servant who works in the family, and the flocks of sheep that the family tends, and the training of the children, and care for their inner peace, and the prevalence of a spirit of faithfulness and sincerity among all, and the honoring of parents.

When the Word of God became incarnate and became man, He lived as a child in a humble and holy family. Its relation to Him made it a holy family, and opened the door for every family that He may dwell in its midst and sanctify it. When He says: "The Son of man hath not where to lay his head" (Lk 9:58), He asks us to invite Him to rest in our family, like the house of Mary and Martha and their brother Lazarus, and to lean on His breast with St. John the beloved.
Sirach explains with all clarity the obligation toward the members of society: the family, friends, priests and the needy.
As for friends, they cannot be exchanged for money. And Ben Sirach also demands good treatment of the faithful servant in the house (33:31-33), and of the laborer (Deut 24:14).
The wise servant must be loved by the believer as himself (Lev 19:18), and freedom is to be given to him in the seventh year as the Torah commanded (Ex 21:2; Deut 15:12).
Animals had their importance and were a source of wealth for the people, so they must be cared for (Prov 27:23-27).
Raising sons requires disciplining them (Prov 13:24), and bowing their necks to the yoke of obedience (30:12-13).
Do not disregard a wise and good wife, for her grace is better than gold [19].

In speaking of family love, he highlights that marital betrayal is graver than the betrayal of a friend. For if it is fitting for society as a whole to be bound by the bond of faithfulness, sincerity and loyalty to others, how much more must this be observed at the family level through the marriage bond. He who betrays his wife imitates the traitor Judas.
The heavenly Friend cares for the wise and good wife, for she enriches the whole family by the grace she enjoys.

The talk begins with the good wife as a treasure, whose grace is better than gold. The good wife is able by meekness to win her husband for the heavenly Friend, and she also has priority in influencing the conduct of her sons and daughters.

v "Every wise woman buildeth her house: but the foolish plucketh it down with her hands" (Prov 14:1). This means that the wise woman encourages her neighbor in the fear of the Lord and in the love that is in her heart toward her sister and sisters. And on the other hand the foolish woman destroys them with her words full of bitterness, hatred, evil and contempt[18].
St. Wisa the Copt: Do not mistreat a servant who works faithfully, nor a hired man who gives himself for you [20].

After speaking of the wife, we expected him to speak of the sons and daughters; but he spoke of the faithful servant and the hired man who is earnest in his work and gives himself in his conduct for the master of the house. For the servant and the hired man in the house or in the field leave the imprint of their uprightness on the sons and daughters.
Let your soul love a wise servant [19], and do not deprive him of freedom [21].
A wise servant's enjoyment of freedom urges the children to care for learning and to behave wisely, as children of the Most High.

Ben Sira calls leaders and employers to recognize the value of the simple worker, the hired man, or the servant when he is faithful in his work, so that they may count him as their own self, and if he is a slave, that they set him free from bondage. For wisdom and prudence together with faithfulness in a person's life cannot be valued at any price.

The ancient systems gave the master freedom to do as he wished with the slave, and the slave had no right to defend himself. But the Law came requiring the master to restore the slave's freedom after six years of work and to treat him well (Ex 21:2; Lev 25:39; Deut 15:12-18).

Many slaves have gone ahead of their masters. The Apostle Paul appointed Onesimus, the slave who had stolen and run away from his master, as a bishop after he accepted the faith and lived in a spirit of godliness (see the Epistle to Philemon).
Have you cattle? Look to them, and if they are profitable to you, keep them [22].

The faithfulness of the wise man does not stop at the members of the family, or friends, or people in general, but extends to caring for the animals that he owns (Prov 27:23-27; Deut 25:4; Prov 12:10).
Have you children? Instruct them, make them obedient from their youth [23].

If the Lord calls us to care for animals, how much more must we care for our brothers among men. The Apostle Paul says: "Doth God take care for oxen? Or saith he it altogether for our sakes?" (1 Cor 9:9-10). The aim of discipline is that the children be marked by a spirit of obedience, so that they become like the Lord Christ when He was a boy, for He was obedient to St. Mary and Joseph the carpenter.
Have you daughters? Take care of their chastity, and do not show yourself too lenient toward them [24].

He who loves his daughter does not pamper her in a way that makes her lose concern and care for her chastity, but spares no effort that she may live pure until the day of her marriage. Some have been known for excessive pampering of their children, especially the wealthy, which spoils the happiness of the children themselves and deprives them of fulfilling their mission. Others have been marked by great harshness, especially where there are family problems. Therefore, firmness should be joined with tenderness, and with gentleness and tenderness firmness should be observed in moderation.

Some see that the care for daughters here is as for weak vessels, so that the parents do not put them to work that might rob them of their freshness and youth, which would affect them at their marriage. As for not being cheerful before them, perhaps what is meant is not to spoil their modesty by gatherings in which conversations take place that offend their modesty [20].
St. John Chrysostom warns the shepherds of the Church against pampering girls out of pity, lest the girls misunderstand the shepherds [21].

v Christ, the Educator of humanity, the divine Logos, calls us to spare no effort, with all strength and together with the gift of wisdom, to save our children by rebuke, discipline, calling them to account, warning them, and offering the remedy together with promises and gentleness toward them...
In short, God deals with us so that we ourselves may deal in this way with our children.
Have you children? Instruct them... Our children, whether male or female, you should love above everything else [22].

v In truth the Teacher of humanity, the divine Word, devotes Himself with all His power to save His little ones by every means through the plan of His wisdom: by warning, reproach, rebuke, correction, healing, promises, and giving benefits... In truth God deals with us as we deal with our children: we care for their bodies, and we do not show ourselves too lenient toward them. Yet we cherish a great love for our children, sons or daughters, more than love for anything else [23].
St. Clement of Alexandria: Marry your daughter, and you will have done a great thing, but give her to a man of understanding [25].
Have you a wife after your heart? Do not divorce her, but do not trust yourself to a wife whom you hate [26].

He did not command the husband to love his wife, but indirectly made clear that his not loving her represents a danger to him. If the Law permitted divorce because of the hardness of their hearts, so that the husband would not act rashly toward his wife, here Ben Sira warns the husband against divorcing his wife out of his desire for a woman more beautiful than she. For the highest beauty is in wisdom, understanding, godliness, and good management. But if the husband feels that his wife is unfaithful, let him beware of her lest she deceive him and turn toward evil.
Honor your father with all your heart, and do not forget your mother's pains in childbirth [27].
Remember that you were born of them; and what will you repay them for what they have done for you? [28]

There is no one who wishes for a person good, progress, and success more than they do. God granted the mother to labor with joy and delight for the sake of her children. God presents her love for her children as a likeness of His watchful care over us: "Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee" (Isa 49:15).

entries.section: 6. Uprightness of life and honoring the priests of the Lord

paragraphs.text: 31 Fear the Lord with all thy soul, and reverence his priests. 32 Love him that made thee with all thy strength, and forsake not his ministers. 33 Fear the Lord, and honour the priest. 34 And give him his portion, as it is commanded thee; the firstfruits, and the trespass offering, 35 and the gift of the shoulders, and the sacrifice of sanctification, and the firstfruits of the holy things.

The discussion of man's relation to the priests of the Lord comes after the discussion of family life. This reveals the concept of the priesthood, whether in the mind of the priest or in the mind of the people.

One of the bishops of the Church of England asked me about the reason for the attachment of the youth in Egypt to the Church and the growing desire for consecration to the Lord, whether through the diaconate, the priesthood, or monasticism. My answer was: the first reason is our view of the priesthood. The believer looks upon the priest as a member with him in the same family, opening to him everything that touches his life as a son to his father. And the priest does not feel that he is an employee who demands an annual leave and is sent into retirement. For although it is the right of his family and his own right to spend a special period with the family, it is not as a personal right that he asks for it, but for the building up of himself and his family.
How my soul grieved when I called the pastor of the church in Los Angeles and said to him: "Reverend," and he answered me: I am now "Mr." because I have been retired!

The priest, even on his deathbed, intercedes for his people as his children, and even when he departs to Paradise he presents his children to the Lord that He may bless them and work in their lives. For this reason it is fitting for us to join what Sirach said, "uprightness of life and honoring the priests of the Lord," to the previous section concerning uprightness of family life.

Honoring the priest is realized in his imitation of the Lord Christ, "who washed the feet of His disciples," and in his sharing with his Church family, and indeed, if possible, in sharing the sufferings of every person. The greatness of the priest is not in an authority he demands, but in his attachment to the heavenly High Priest, who cares for the salvation of mankind and lifts them up to the heavenly mind.
Fear the Lord with all your soul, and honor His priests [29].

Ben Sira cared for the life of the Church, liturgical worship, and honoring the priests. He praised Aaron, the first high priest, as he praised the high priest of his own time, Simon son of Onias. The Lord did not will to give them a special portion in the Promised Land, but wished to distinguish them by being Himself their portion.

Ben Sira emphasized the obligation to give the priests their dues, because the spread of Hellenistic culture and the attraction of some to pagan philosophies had an effect on the priests' income, and some of them were compelled to work in farming.
Love Him who made you with all your strength, and do not forsake His ministers [30].
Fear the Lord and honor His priests, and give him his portion, as you have been commanded:
from the firstfruits, and the trespass offering, and the gift of the shoulders, and the sacrifice of sanctification, and the firstfruits of the holy things [31].

v He who honors the priest honors God also, and he who learns to despise the priest, in the course of time blasphemes God. He says: "Honor My priests" (see Sir 7:31). The Jews learned to despise God because they despised Moses and wanted to stone him. So he who moves with godliness toward the priest does this all the more toward God. And if the priest is wicked, God, when He sees you honoring him although he is not worthy of honor, rewards you for your honoring him [24].
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 7. Divine love and our responsibility toward the forgotten

paragraphs.text: 36 And stretch thine hand unto the poor, that thy blessing may be perfected. 37 A gift hath grace in the sight of every man living; and for the dead detain it not. 38 Fail not to be with them that weep, and mourn with them that mourn. 39 Be not slow to visit the sick: for that shall make thee to be beloved.

It is indeed good for a person to be generous with everyone, and to take part in burying the dead (Tob 1:17). Ben Sira also calls us to share the grief of the sorrowful and to visit the sick (Rom 12:15; Mt 25:39-40). Finally, a person's knowing that he is mortal keeps him humble (7:17; 28:6), along with offering due honor to one's neighbor.
Stretch out your hand to the poor, that your blessing may be perfected [32].

The Holy Bible cares for the forgotten groups who have no one to ask about them, and it requires kindness even toward the dead and the sick, so that the believer may bear witness to unbelievers that God is "the God of the forgotten, the suffering, the needy, and the oppressed." Let the believer's hand be stretched out in giving, and his heart in love toward unbelievers, as an ambassador of God, the Lover of mankind.
v [On the widow's mites and almsgiving]

Her love was greater than her offering, for love is better than whole burnt offerings... Therefore she overcame the rich with her offering. The priests of the people receive vows from those who offer abundantly, while the Lord of the priests sat down in a humility they did not perceive. The greedy chief priests care for sacrifices, but our Lord sought love within the soul... The Son of God rejoices in the one in whom there is love.
v The widow was able to know that the Most High has no need of an offering, but seeks a reason to enrich them.

She thought that if He had wished, He would have turned the dust into gold and the waters of the sea into coral, and she said to herself that He does not ask for gold out of need, but that people may share with Him by their offerings. For gold and silver are His, and as it is written, if the sacrifice is great and the love of the one who offers it is small, He rejects it. This woman alone knew how to discern and to offer with a pure heart a complete vow, with discernment... With pure love she knew how to offer! She offered her complete vow better than Jacob. For she did not set apart a tenth of her possessions, but this blessed woman loved the Lord more than herself!
St. Jacob of Serugh: Let her show the tenderness of giving in the presence of all the living; even to the dead let her not withhold kindness [33].

What does he mean by kindness to the dead? Caring for burying them with fitting honor, as Tobit used to do; caring for their families if they had debts; and giving alms to those to whom the dead man was kind.
Do not withdraw from those who weep, and grieve with the sorrowful [34].

The Apostle Paul says: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep" (Rom 12:15). It may be easy for a person to grieve with the grieving and groan with his groaning, but it is hard for some to rejoice with the joy of their brother. This requires a lofty soul, so that he does not envy his brother for his success, but rejoices with him, counting every success of his brother as success for himself. The Apostle says: "And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it. Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular" (1 Cor 12:26-27).

St. John Chrysostom says: [Nothing establishes love so strongly as sharing in joy and sorrow. Because you are far from troubles, do not isolate yourself also from sharing with others. When your neighbor is in distress, count the distress as your own. Share his tears to support his contrite spirit, and share his joy so that the joy in him may become deep and rooted. Establish love, for by this you serve yourself more than you serve him. By your tears you become merciful, and by feelings of gladness you purify yourself of envy and gloom... If you cannot remove the evils from him, share with him by your tears, and you remove half of the evil; and if you cannot increase his good things, share his joy, and you add to him something great [25].]
Do not hesitate to visit the sick, for by such visits you will be beloved [35].

The Lord Christ counts the visiting of the sick as a visit to Himself, for He says: "I was... sick, and ye visited me" (Mt 25:36). As we desire the healing of the sick, it is fitting for us to desire for him also the fellowship of the eternal glories at the proper time.
40 In all your works, remember your latter end; you shall never sin forever.
In all your affairs remember your latter end, and you will never sin [36].

The believer in all his works speaks of nothing, and nothing occupies his heart, so much as his entering into heaven. He becomes like Aaron the high priest, upon the skirts of whose robe round about golden bells were fastened. "And it shall be upon Aaron to minister: and his sound shall be heard when he goeth in unto the holy place before the LORD" (Ex 28:35). So in every work he practices and in every matter he thinks about, what occupies him is his meeting with the Lord and his standing before the divine throne in the heavenly sanctuaries, where he enjoys the eternal glories and is in the company of the heavenly ones and in the fellowship of praise with them.

v Let him also have bells around the hem of his garment, for Holy Scripture says: when he enters the sanctuary he gives a sound and does not enter in silence (see Ex 28:35). These bells, which give a sound, were placed on the hem of the garment. Their purpose, as I believe, is that you must not be silent about the last things and the end of the world, but you must ring the bells continually and converse and speak according to what was said: "Remember your latter end, and you shall never sin" (Sir 7:36) [26].

Origen v says: "Remember your latter end, and you shall never sin" (Sir 7:36). For He who now forgives our sins will judge our sins on the day of judgment. He who died for us will appear again to judge all mankind [27].

St. John Chrysostom v [Speaking of Marcella]: "Remember your latter end, and you shall never sin" (7:36). This is like the precept of the sarcastic writer: "Live with death in your mind, and time flies"... She spent her days and always lived thinking that she would certainly die. Her very garments were as if reminding her of the tomb. And she offered herself a living sacrifice, reasonable, acceptable to God (Rom 12:1) [28].
St. Jerome v Question: How can we do everything for the glory of God?...
If we do everything according to God and His commandments, and do not seek the praise of men [29].

v "Arise, O Lord my God... in the commandment that You have commanded" (see Ps 7:8). This saying can also point to the mystery of the Resurrection, since the psalmist calls upon the Judge to arise to take vengeance on every sin and to fulfill the commandments that He had set for us... Do not take vengeance for me, but for Your commandment which You commanded, and they despised it" [30].
St. Basil the Great: Inspired by Sirach 7

entries.section: Our heavenly Friend and brotherly love

paragraphs.text: v With the boldness of love Moses refused to move unless You, O Lord, went before the whole procession Yourself, for he said: "If thy presence go not with me, carry us not up hence" (Ex 33:15).
And behold, I call You, O my Savior, not only to accompany me, but to dwell within me.
Your presence, O my holy Friend, turns my depths into Your holy Kingdom.
It inflames my heart with longing for continual departure toward heaven with joy and exultation.
Your presence fills my depths with love for all my brothers, the sons of men.
By Your dwelling within me, I will not accept evil, and all iniquity departs from me.
The enemy of good cannot enter into my heart, my mind, and all my depths, and he will not dare to take hold of the steering wheel, for it is in Your hand!
v I will not desire a high position, nor temporal glory. And I will not boast of righteousness.
For everything that is holy is a gift from You, O righteous and holy One.
And if I fall into sin, You raise me up by Your fiery Spirit, and fortify my life so that I do not return to it.
My longsuffering heavenly Friend, I know Your forgiving mercies.
Behold, I ask for Your grace to fashion me, so that I may truly become a living icon of You!
v O You who accept gifts and offerings though You have no need of them. You call me: "My son, give me thine heart."
Receive my heart, and I will converse with You with an open heart. And let my prayer and all my worship ascend like the fragrant smell of incense, a place of Your delight and pleasure.
Let my prayer rise like a fire blazing with love.
And I will not cease giving, returning to You from what You have given me!
v Receive, O heavenly One, all my life and my movements, and allow me to walk in the steps of Your footprints.
In You I will not mock any person, whatever his weaknesses, for he may rise by Your grace, and I may fall through my foolishness!
I cherish Your friendship with me, O Truth, so that the devil, the father of liars, may have no authority over me!
v I will keep silence, especially in the presence of experienced elders.
Even in prayer, what concerns me is not much speaking and eloquence, but the language of the heart, unheard by men.
v I hope that I will not cease working even in my old age and sickness, for You do not take rest in the idle.
I will flee from the gatherings of sinners, where there is no place for You among them!
I will go about with You doing good, and I will gain friends for myself always!
v Enter, O heavenly Beloved, my house and dwell in the midst of the family.
My family is called by Your name, for I am Yours, my Beloved, and You are mine!
Be manifested in the life of the whole family, the old and the young.
Grant all love, wisdom, discernment, and prudence.
So that every member may desire to offer honor to the rest of the members!
v Grant me the spirit of simplicity, that I may see You in every priest and servant in Your Church!
v Let those whom You love be beloved to me.
I will care for the poor as Your little brother, and for the needy, the suffering, and the oppressed, for You declare that You are the God of the forgotten!
I will seek the lost and the outcast, that I may see You bring them back to Yourself and embrace them.
v Be with me until the last breath; prepare me before the agonies of death, and in the moments of death, and after death.
Open my insight, that I may see the heavenly sanctuaries awaiting my weakness and all my brothers!

1 Strive not with a mighty man, lest thou fall into his hands. 2 Be not at variance with a rich man, lest he lay a burden upon thee. 3 For gold hath destroyed many, and perverted the hearts of kings. 4 Strive not with a man that is full of tongue, and heap not wood upon his fire.

It is fitting for the believer to be prudent in dealing with others, so he does not quarrel with persons of authority lest they become his enemies [1]. Nor does he disturb a rich man so that he informs the ruling authorities against him (Prov 17:23). Nor does he argue with a talkative person with a loud throat who speaks much and without restraint (Prov 26:20-21).
Do not resist the mighty man sharply, lest thou fall into his hands [1].

It is not fitting for the believer to enter into a quarrel with a reckless man who brandishes a weapon, or to openly rebuke a ruler or a king and so expose himself to death in vain, unless that is a witness to the upright faith. Exempted from this are those called to martyrdom by a divine announcement, or the prophets called to confront high priests and kings, as Isaiah the prophet and John the Baptist did.

As for the believers among the people and the young priests, it is fitting for them not to destroy their energies in criticism and in trying to reform by colliding with others, but rather to light a candle instead of cursing the darkness.
It is written in the canons of Pope Peter, Seal of the Martyrs (Canon 9):
[(Those who stirred up the adversary in rashness, so as to kindle the fire of affliction, so that they enjoy martyrdom).

Those who were as though in sleep and suddenly leapt up to stir up the adversary, who was like one whose time of labor had been long, these bring upon themselves trials like the tossing of the sea and a flood of waves without number, kindling the fire (coals) of the wicked against their brethren... With these we are bound to have fellowship, because they conducted themselves so for the sake of Christ, though they did not heed His words. For He taught us to pray lest we enter into temptation, but deliver us from evil (Mt 6:13).

Perhaps they did not know that the Master of the house and our greatest Teacher often withdrew far from those who laid snares for Him, and sometimes did not walk openly because of them. And at the time of His passion He withdrew and did not deliver Himself up to them, waiting for them to come to Him with swords and staves, saying: "Are ye come out as against a thief with swords and staves for to take me?" (Mt 26:55), and they delivered Him to Pilate (Mt 27:2).

What happened with Him was repeated with His disciples who imitated Him, remembering His divine words which He spoke to strengthen us at the time of persecution, saying: "Beware of men: for they will deliver you up to the councils, and they will scourge you in their synagogues" (Mt 10:17). He says that they deliver us up, and we do not deliver ourselves up. You are brought before governors and kings for My sake, not you who present yourselves. He wants us to pass from place to place where the persecutors are, and that for the sake of His name.

Again He says: "When they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another" (Mt 10:22), as though He wants us not to thrust ourselves upon the servants of Satan and his followers, so that we may not be the cause of their double death, nor drive them to cruelty by force so that they commit deadly deeds, but He wants us to wait and be on our guard with watching and prayer, lest we enter into temptation (Mt 26:41).

Stephen (the first deacon and martyr) followed in the footsteps of the Master and endured martyrdom when the rebels seized him in Jerusalem and stoned him after bringing him before a council. He was glorified for the sake of the name of Christ, praying: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge" (Acts 7:59).]
Do not quarrel with a rich man, lest he resist thy strength, for gold hath destroyed many, and corrupted the minds of kings [2].
Do not cling to the great and the wicked rich, lest evil cling to our nature as rust clings to iron and dust to the body.

v As rust is not the work of the smith, and dust is not placed there by the parents, so evil is not from God. Rather, God gave man a conscience and a mind so that he might avoid evil, which show him that evil is harmful and brings torments. Therefore it is fitting for you to be more careful. When you meet a man of greatness and wealth, leave the demons no room to deceive you so that you are led by him, but set death at once before your eyes, and then you will not desire anything evil or earthly [3].

St. Anthony the Great v "They that trust in their wealth, and boast themselves in the multitude of their riches." The prophet addresses this statement to two kinds of persons: to the earthborn and to the rich. He speaks to the former so that they may put away their wrong ideas of their power. And to the latter, who boast of their possessions. He says: You who trust in your strength.

These earthborn trust in the strength of the flesh, and believe that human nature is sufficient to accomplish skillfully what they wish. He says: And you who trust in the uncertainty of riches, listen. You need a ransom to be transferred to the freedom of which you were deprived when you were overcome by the power of Satan, who drew you under his dominion, for he does not leave you in freedom from his tyranny until a mighty Savior works in you, who wishes to exchange you. The ransom is not of the same kind as that which fell under his dominion, but altogether different from it, if he truly wishes to set free the captives from bondage.

Therefore the brother is unable to redeem you. No man can urge Satan to remove his dominion from him who once submitted to him! Likewise the (brother) is unable to offer to God an atonement for his own sins, so how could he have the authority to do this for others?

And what precious thing does he possess in this world that suffices to be given in exchange as the price of a soul that is precious by its nature, this soul that was created in the image of its Creator? And what work in the present time suffices to be offered to the human soul as a means and help to it in the life to come?

We may count these things as simple. For even if a man appears to have great authority in this life, even if a great number of possessions surround him, these words teach him to come down from such thinking and to humble himself under the mighty hand of God (1 Pet 5:6), not to rely on the authority of someone famous, nor to boast in the abundance of his riches. Yet he may rise a little in thought, and, with regard to those who rely on their authority or boast in their wealth, may think of the powers (and authority) of the soul, how imperfect they are in themselves to accomplish salvation. For if there were found one perfect among the sons of men, if he lacked the wisdom of God, let him not boast in anything. For even if he has gained many theories from the wisdom of the world, and gathered much of the wealth of knowledge, let him hear the whole truth of the matter: every human soul has bowed under the yoke of the bondage imposed by the common enemy of all, and being deprived of the very freedom which it received from the Creator, sin led it captive. Every captive is in need of a ransom for his freedom.

Now, a brother cannot redeem his brother, and no one can redeem himself, for he who redeems must be better than the one who was defeated and became a slave. In fact I have no man who has authority before God to make atonement for a sinner, so long as he himself is subject to sin: "For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus" our Lord (Rom 3:23-24) [4].

St. Basil the Great: Dealing with the poor and the rich: The believer who feels the burdens of the trials of his poor brethren is gentle with them in their sufferings and humiliation. When the Lord commands through Isaiah concerning the barren woman who did not bear (that is, the suffering soul), He does not use rebuke and reproof but encouragement, saying: "O thou afflicted, tossed with tempest, and not comforted, behold, I will lay thy stones with antimony, and with sapphire will I found thee..." "Fear not; for thou shalt not be ashamed; neither be thou confounded, for thou shalt not be put to shame: for thou shalt forget the shame of thy youth, and shalt not remember the reproach of thy widowhood any more. For thy Maker is thine husband; the LORD of hosts is his name" (Isa 54:11, 4).

As for the rich, let the shepherd (or the believer) instill in them the spirit of fear of pride and arrogance, for excessive gentleness with them increases their pride and makes them lose their true life. For this reason we find our Lord Jesus rebuking the rich (who trust in their riches): "Woe unto you that are rich! for ye have received your consolation" (Lk 6:24). And the Apostle Paul instructs Timothy his disciple, saying: "Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches [5], but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy..." (1 Tim 6:17). He says to him "charge," and not "hope" or "request of them." But sometimes there is a need to use David's soothing harp to drive the spirit of evil from the heart of proud Saul. Not the harp of flattery and hypocrisy, but the harp of singing in the name of the Lord, the harp of love and gentleness together with prayer, so that the Lord may give him the spirit of humility.

Nathan used the same harp with David at his fall, when he was rich. He hid the bitter medicine in his garment, using gentleness in presenting the case of the man who seized his brother's ewe lamb, and when David realized his error, Nathan was able to offer him the medicine. This is what Ben Sira suffered in the statements before us.
Do not sharply strive with the talkative man, nor heap wood upon his fire [3].
He who enters into a quarrel with a talkative person risks his reputation.
5 Jest not with a rude man, lest thy ancestors be disgraced. 6 Reproach not a man that turneth from sin, but remember that we are all worthy of punishment.
Do not jest with an ill-bred man, lest thy ancestors be disgraced [4].

He warns us against keeping company with jesters, for jesting is unseemly, since it drives the fear of the Lord out of the heart and corrupts the talent of sanctifying time. St. Jacob of Serugh sees that God created the mouth and the tongue to train in praise and in fellowship with the heavenly beings in a life of thanksgiving. Jesting, in his view, is a deviation of the tongue from its holy work for the sake of the Kingdom of God. It is fitting for the wise man to be marked by dignity and seriousness together with gentleness, and in his kindness to be dignified and God-fearing.
Do not dishonor him who has turned away from sin in repentance, and remember that we are all worthy (of punishment on account of our sins) [5].

It is written in the Mishnah: "If a man repents, he is not told: Remember your past deeds" [6]. If someone has repented of a sin he has committed, we must not make light of him. St. Abba Moses the Black says: "Do not be hard of heart toward your brother, for we are all overcome by thoughts." But this urges us all the more toward serious repentance in the Lord.

He who understands and holds fast to godliness says: "Lord, who shall abide in thy tabernacle? who shall dwell in thy holy hill? He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart. He that backbiteth not with his tongue, nor doeth evil to his neighbour, nor taketh up a reproach against his neighbour" (Ps 15:1-3). But we reproach those who repent and those who are converted, although Holy Scripture says: Do not reproach him who has repented of sin (see Sir 8:5) [7].

v There is a man full of faith who comes toward the congregation accusing himself, disclosing to everyone the sin he has committed. Yet those who have no fear of the coming judgment of God, when they hear his words, instead of sharing his sufferings, and instead of caring for him, trouble him, and instead of falling with the fallen, they say: Get away from me and do not come near me, for I am clean! Then they begin to curse him whom they had formerly admired (when his sin was hidden), and withdraw their friendship from him.

He did not want to hide his crime. With conviction he says of those who reproach him: "My friends and my companions drew away from my plague, and my kinsmen left me" (Ps 38:11) LXX...
