He who, after committing a sin, desires the salvation of his soul, and does not care about the rebukes of those who do not think about their own sins and who do not remember the words of the divine Scriptures: "Do not reproach the penitent from sin, and remember that we are all worthy of punishment" (see Sir 8:5). Do not be troubled on account of these things, but be troubled on account of yourself, and pray to God to hear you and raise you after your fall, so that you may be able to say afterward: "I know my iniquity, and I grieve over my sin" (Ps 38:19) LXX [8].
Origen

7 Dishonour not a man in his old age: for even some of us wax old. 8 Rejoice not over thy greatest enemy being dead, but remember that we die all. 9 Despise not the discourse of the wise, but acquaint thyself with their proverbs: 10 for of them thou shalt learn instruction, and how to serve great men with ease. 11 Miss not the discourse of the elders: for they also learned of their fathers, 12 and of them thou shalt learn understanding, and to give answer as need requireth.
Do not dishonor a man in his old age, for some of us also will grow old [6].

A society that makes light of the elderly makes light of its own future. It is fitting for us to benefit from the experience of those who preceded us in life, for the new generation will benefit from our experience, while acknowledging that they will be more advanced than we are. The sign of a society's vitality is continuous progress. This progress rests on what their predecessors strove for, and the new generation learns not only from the progress we have attained but also from our mistakes. Thus the generations remain in constant progress that corrects mistakes, for there will be no one perfect in everything. The present offers what is new to the future without ignoring the past.

Let us remember what the elders offered in the time of their youth, and let us not criticize them because of their bodily weakness and the weakness of their memory and their inability to practice some acts of worship, for we too may grow old one day like them. The Apostle Paul advises us: "Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father; and the younger men as brethren" (1 Tim 5:1). And it is written in the book of Leviticus: "Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD" (Lev 19:32). Ben Sira calls the elders to act in a way that suits their experience and physical ability to the last breath, so that they may not fall into a feeling of despair because of idleness.
Do not rejoice over the death of a person, and remember that we shall surely all die [7].

After he has commanded us to respect the penitent sinner and the old man who is unable to work, he called us to respect the dead and his family, for he who rejoices over a dead man falls into judgment, because he does not know what was in the heart of the dead man before his death, and does not perceive God's plan for him. By death a person is joined to those who went before, so let no one rejoice over the death of his brother, for he will meet him in the life to come. Sirach sees death as a gathering with those who have gone before [7] (Gen 25:8; Judg 2:10).

v One thing is impossible for man, and that is to escape death. But if a man has fellowship with God, this is possible for man if he knows the way. If he wishes, and knows the way, he can, by faith and truth, experience the good life and be united with God [9].

v The soul that knows what the world truly is, and desires to be saved, has a strict rule, which is to think every hour within itself, saying: "It is an hour in which (death) comes, and judgment comes, when you cannot (O my soul) bear (the gaze of) the Judge, and behold, you are about to perish." By this thought the soul keeps itself from shameful pleasures [10].

What is mortal is secondary to what is immortal, and serves it, meaning that matter (the material body) serves man, and this by the compassion of God the Creator and the goodness of His being (since He granted that the body should serve the soul) [11].
St. Anthony the Great: Do not despise the words of the wise, but be diligent in their proverbs.
For from them thou shalt learn instruction, and to serve among the nobles [8].

The true believer is like the bee which gathers the nectar of various flowers and offers it as sweet and useful honey for others. Solomon the Wise says: "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be hurt" (Prov 13:20). Ben Sira prizes the opportunities that were offered him during many journeys, where he served some of the great, yet he did not exalt himself in this work, but gathered wisdom in his thoughts and in his practices.

The story of the Lord Christ's meeting with the sinful woman in the house of Simon the Pharisee (Lk 7) reveals the existence of banquets among the notables of the Jews, where they would invite one of the teachers and hold a banquet for him, not merely to set a table for eating, but he would open the door of his house and those who wished to enjoy what was discussed with the teacher would enter.

v A man can say of those who do not wish to learn what is useful and good for them that they are not in sound health. As for those who have learned the truth and yet dispute it shamelessly, of these it is said that their sense is dead, their nature has become animal, and they do not know God, nor have their souls been enlightened by the light [12].
St. Anthony the Great: Do not ignore the saying of the elders, for they learned from their fathers, and from them thou shalt acquire understanding, and be able to answer at the proper time [9].

The ancient Jewish society esteemed the elders and their view of life through their long experience and their knowledge of the tradition handed down from the generations before them (25:4-6). Openness to learning from the elders and the wise (Lev 19:32) moves the new generation to continuous progress (Prov 22:29). For taking care to sit with the elders teaches people what they have gathered from the generations before them. It is as though sitting with a wise elder adds much to one's life, through the enjoyment of the experiences of those before, in very short periods. This is what is called tradition, where we receive from them what they received from the earlier generations, especially the living faith and the sound conduct. By this a person knows how to answer the questions that arise in his mind or that are put to him by those around him.
The ability to give the right and fitting answer is the product of listening to the tradition from the elders (Prov 22:21).

v The Lord asks of us (as believers) what He does not ask of everyone. The community of mankind lives according to the customs it receives, but the Christian's rule in life is the commandment of the Lord and the imitation of the ancient saints whose greatness of soul was manifest above every trial!

In the end it is fitting for you to leave an example for those who come after you of steadfastness (endurance) and sincere confidence in what you hope for, showing that your grief will not overcome you, but you rise above your sorrows, and are patient in sufferings, and rejoice in hope [13].
St. Basil the Great

13 Kindle not the coals of a sinner, lest thou be burnt with the flame of his fire. 14 Rise not up against a reviler, lest he lie in wait to entrap thee in thy words. 15 Lend not unto him that is mightier than thyself; for if thou lendest him, count it but lost. 16 Be not surety above thy power: for if thou be surety, take care to pay it. 17 Go not to law with a judge; for judgment is given for him according to his opinion. 18 Travel not by the way with a rash man, lest he bring trouble upon thee: for he goeth after his own will, and thou perish with him through his folly. 19 Strive not with an angry man, and go not with him into a solitary place: for blood is as nothing in his sight, and where there is no help, he will overthrow thee. 20 Consult not with a fool; for he cannot keep counsel. 21 Do not practice a secret matter before the stranger, for thou knowest not what he will bring forth. 22 Reveal not what is in thy heart to every man, lest perhaps he give thee no thanks.
Do not kindle the coals of a sinner, lest thou be burnt with the flame of his fire [10].

It is fitting for us to deal with the sinner with wisdom and love, so that we do not kindle his coals more, and so are ourselves struck by the fire of his flame. He who kindles his passions and emotions reaps extremely dangerous fruits (Prov 26:21).
Do not stand before an arrogant man, for he will provoke thee, lest he lie in wait, expecting to make thy words an ambush against thee [11].
He points to not speaking with the arrogant man, lest he provoke us to anger and we sin in our anger, and he finds an opportunity to catch the slips of our tongue.

v What need have you to cry out before the judgment? It is good to keep silence as long as the Judge is waiting; it is well not to return insult for insult, lest we too be counted among those who despise others.

Thus it is fitting for us to follow the example of that man (Job) who refuted those who attacked him by his silence. Truly he showed the strength of his spirit, since the insults did not affect him, and showed the innocence of his conscience, because he paid no heed to the accusations directed against him, but laughed at them as though they were foreign to him.

In truth, when reproaches are directed against us, and we wish to justify ourselves, we become angry and want vengeance, and by this we offer confirmation (of the accusations), for Scripture says: "Let us keep away from insult, take thy garment away, for a harmful man is passing by." And so you keep silence until he passes and does not rage and burn your garment, for it is written: "Do not kindle the coals of a sinner, lest thou be burnt with the flame of his fire" [10]. Therefore the saint keeps silent even if a servant wrongs him; and the righteous man keeps silent if a poor man reviles him; and the righteous man laughs if a sinner pours out his reproaches; and the righteous man blesses if a weak person curses him.
David kept silence when Shimei the son of Gera cursed him (2 Kgs 16:5-14). And Job laughed (Job 19:7) LXX, and Paul blessed, saying: "Being reviled, we bless" (1 Cor 4:12) [14].
St. Ambrose: Suretyship and the responsibility of the sponsor: Do not lend to one who is stronger than thou, and if thou lendest him anything, count it as lost [12].

It is good to support our brethren by giving generously, and at the same time with wisdom, lest we give an opportunity to one who is not in need to borrow from us and not repay the loan. By this we would have sinned against him, since we open for him the door of greed and exploitation of others, and against ourselves, since we are counted unfaithful in what God has given us.
Do not be surety above thy power, and if thou be surety, take care as one who is bound to pay [13].

Suretyship was a common custom in Israel, and the proverbs warned against practicing it carelessly or beyond our ability. Though the believer is bound to love everyone, the practice of love requires prudence and conduct with wisdom. Here he warns us of two matters concerning suretyship:

First: a man should not lend to one who is stronger than he [12], that is, one who is on a higher social level than he. Truly God requires us to give to widows and orphans and those who are in distress out of need, but he who gives to one who is not in need and who is a man of authority, as a kind of display of wealth, expecting that the debt may not be returned to him, is unfaithful in the management of the money the Lord has given him, while the needy were more deserving of this money.
Second: let no one stand surety for anyone for what he is not able, as surety, to return to the creditor.

v Beloved dear ones, consider those who offer themselves as sureties for someone with regard to money (or a loan), how they expose themselves to great danger... Indeed, if the person who received the loan has shown himself good, he returns what he borrowed to the one who guaranteed him. But if he turns into a wicked person, he causes disaster to the one who stood surety. Therefore the Wise Man warns us: "If thou be surety, take care to pay it" (see Sir 8:13).

If this is the case with the surety concerned with money, who is bound to be responsible for everything, how much more those who stand surety in spiritual matters and in the matter of virtue, since he is bound to show great vigilance and watchfulness, by urging and showing fatherly tenderness. It is fitting for (the sponsors) not to take the matter lightly, for you are in danger.

The benefit will be shared if they offer personal counsel to lead the person in the way of virtue, while their judgment will be grave if they neglect this. For this reason it has become customary to call these (sponsors) spiritual fathers [15].
St. John Chrysostom: Do not go to law with a judge, for judgment is given for him because of his position [14].

This does not mean laxity in claiming our rights even from men of the judiciary, but we must use the lawful channels with deliberation and prudence. It is fitting for the believer to realize that it is impossible to win a case he brings against a judge.
Do not travel on a journey with a rash man, lest by his weight he bring thee down.
For he goeth after his own will, and thou perish with him through his folly [15].
One must not accompany a rash man on his journeys, lest he push us into venturing without consideration, which causes us troubles.
Do not fight with the angry man, nor go with him into the wilderness, for to him the shedding of blood is as nothing, and where there is no helper for thee, there he will overthrow thee [16].
Let us beware of the man filled with hatred and fury, for he is driven even to shed blood. Rather, it is fitting for us to stand far from the man who gives himself over to anger.
Do not consult with a fool, for he cannot keep the secret [17].

It is fitting for us not to share our thoughts with those who are not worthy of trust [17-19]. Otherwise, in the wrong of simplicity, we ask counsel of a foolish person who does not keep the secret. Nor is it permissible to disclose our secrets to everyone, and therefore the Church asks that a person be frank with his father of confession, who has no right to divulge the secrets of the penitent to anyone, whatever his worldly or ecclesiastical position, neither openly nor by hint.
Do not practice a secret matter before a stranger, for thou knowest not what he will bring forth [18].
It is wise not to utter secret matters before a stranger whom we do not know to what extent he keeps a secret.
Do not reveal thy heart to every man, lest he show thee no harshness [16] [19].
It is wise not to disclose what is in our heart to a man whose nature we do not know, for he may turn into a fierce enemy.
Inspired by Ben Sira 8

entries.section: Let me deal with everyone in Your presence!

paragraphs.text: v My God, my Savior and my Leader, beloved of my soul, I need Your divine presence that I may walk in the spirit of wisdom.

Sanctify my mind, my heart, my mouth, and my whole being, that I may know how to deal with each person in love together with wisdom, with kindness and tenderness without laxity, so that no one perishes, but all see You manifested in all my conduct.
v I do not fear a mighty man who has authority, but without partiality I love him, and seek the salvation of his soul.
And with wisdom I do not enter into strife with him, lest I waste my time and destroy the purity of my heart and mind.
Let him see You as the secret of my strength and my authority!
Rather, I crush the devil under my feet in a spirit of courage together with humility.
Let him see me hidden in You, so that he dares not come near me.
v In a spirit of tenderness I draw near to the rich man, not desiring anything of what he has, for You are my riches and my eternal wealth.
Let the rich man touch my inner peace and my constant joy, and feel his need of You, O Giver of the riches of spirit, soul, and body!
Let him realize the passing away of the first heaven and earth, and look forward to enjoying the new heaven and the new earth.
Let the whole world become small in his eyes, and let him ask You for the speed of Your coming that he may be enriched by Your heavenly glories.
v I look upon the talkative man, and I ask You to set a guard over my mouth and a strong door over my lips.
Who is the guard but Your Holy Spirit, who will not allow a vain, useless word to come out of my mouth.
And who is it that sanctifies my lips and teaches me when to be silent and when to speak, and what to utter.
v Let the words of unrestrained jesting pass by, so that I do not find them pleasant, but find sweet Your commandment which gives me comfort and joy.
v Remove from my mind the sins of the repentant man, so that I do not remember his weaknesses, but see him clothed in the garments of Your righteousness, O my God.
Let me see him go before many, hastening toward eternal glory.
I do not make light of his repentance, but seek the salvation of my own soul and the salvation of all my brethren.
v If I see an old man unable to stand for prayer, or to practice fasting and prostrations, let me remember that old age is not far from me, and sickness may strike me in moments.
I realize my weakness and pray for the old and the sick, asking growth for all the sons of men.
v If I take part in the prayer for one of the departed, I long for the hour of my departure from the world to arrive.
I do not recall his sins, but I count him blessed because he is going to You, sharing with the heavenly beings and with our beloved departed in a wonderful heavenly choir.
v As for the wise and the self-sacrificing servants, I count meeting them a gift from You.
I count myself a little bee that gathers nectar from every flower, offering it as sweet and useful honey to many, with no merit of mine in it.
v If I meet a furious man, I do not criticize him, lest his anger be kindled all the more and I be burned with him by the fire of his flame.
And if I meet an arrogant man, I remember my former weaknesses, and keep silence while praying fervently for him.
v I do not lend to a man who is not in need and who is stronger than I.
For what You have given me is a trust for the needy and poor.
v Take hold of my hands and lead me, that I may walk in You, and complete all the days of my sojourn in joy and peace.
1 Be not jealous over the wife of thy bosom, and teach her not an evil lesson against thyself. 2 Give not thy soul unto a woman, lest she rule over thy strength.
Be not jealous of the wife in thy bosom, so that thou givest her an evil example that harms thee [1].

Ben Sira begins by affirming his esteem for marriage. At the same time he reveals a grave plague that corrupts the purity of the family, namely the creeping in of suspicion toward one of the members of the family, especially the wife. The wife may act with some simplicity, and it is fitting for the husband to deal with her wisely, lest by his extreme jealousy he spoil her simplicity, and she think that his suspicion of her is the fruit of the impurity of his own heart. Nor is it fitting for the husband to be jealous of his wife for the gifts, abilities, and potentials she enjoys, lest he become an evil example in her eyes.

Mutual trust between the spouses: Solomon the Wise says: "Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies. The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, so that he shall have no need of spoil. She will do him good and not evil all the days of her life" (Prov 31:10-12). Origen says that the wife is like the Garden of Eden, in which are the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil [1].
Do not give thy soul unto a woman, lest she tread upon thy strength [2].

Suspicion of the wife is often a kind of extremism, causing tension in the whole family, yet on the other hand a person's giving up his soul to the other party, that is, to the wife or the husband, is often at the expense of the family's spiritual building up. He who places himself under the authority of a woman (he probably means his wife) will have her despise his dignity (Prov 31:3). The partnership between them does not mean that one dominates the other, and humility does not mean leaving matters without management.

3 Meet not with an harlot, lest thou fall into her snares. 4 Use not much the company of a woman that is a singer, lest thou be taken with her attempts. 5 Gaze not on a maid, lest thou stumble by her beauty. 6 Give not thy soul unto harlots, lest thou lose thine inheritance.

St. John Chrysostom sees that the enemy uses his wiles and powers to destroy man's inner purity, and therefore it is fitting for the believer to set out like a bird soaring in the heavenly places, so that he cannot be captured by a satanic snare.

For the sake of purity of heart, Ben Sira asks his disciples to avoid clinging to a strange woman, who may catch him in her net (Prov 7:23), and to avoid gazing at a virgin with lustful thoughts, lest he stumble and be exposed to punishment.
Do not meet an adulterous woman, lest thou fall into her snares [3].

What is meant here is a lewd woman frequented by those of wealth and authority. Ben Sira often warned his disciples against forming relationships with women through indulgence and carelessness (25:13-26; 18; 42:9-14). He warns of the moral danger of associating with licentious women. It is written in the book of Proverbs: "Give not thy strength unto women, nor thy ways to that which destroyeth kings" (Prov 31:3). "For a whore is a deep ditch; and a strange woman is a narrow pit" (Prov 23:27). "For by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life. Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned?" (Prov 6:26-27).
Do not tarry long with a dancer, lest thou be caught by her wiles [4].
He asks them that none of them prolong his stay with a licentious dancer [4].
Do not gaze on a virgin, lest thou stumble and cause her harm [5].

He does not ask his disciples to close their eyes, but not to gaze at her. As the Lord Christ says: "Whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart" (Mt 5:28). Ben Sira fears falling into sin with a virgin, for the penalty for that in the Old Testament was most severe (Deut 22:28-29). Righteous Job says: "I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?" (Job 31:1).
Do not give thy soul unto harlots, lest thou lose thine inheritance [6].

He calls them not to give their souls to lewd women, for their souls are holy brides in the hand of the holy heavenly Bridegroom. Samson the mighty gave himself to Delilah, and she was able to humble him; she gave the enemies the opportunity to put out his eyes, and he worked in the mill like an ox (Judg 16:4-21). St. Jacob of Serugh says:
[Alas for Samson the Nazirite, who became a mockery, a laughingstock and a disgrace to the generations to come.
The mighty in valor who overcame the lion in battle fell into the hands of a woman, O the great shame!
Like a serpent she bit the Nazirite, and his hair fell from him, and he became weak, wretched, helpless, and reeling.
No sooner had the Philistines snared the lion than they gathered to mock the man who had multiplied their slain.
In their rage they plucked out his eyes, and humbled his splendor, and put out his shining lamp and his sight.
They laid upon him a dreadful and conspicuous stain, and the great one was brought down to great disgrace.
They took him and bound him, and he ground in the prison house, and it was an occasion of great celebration for the Philistines [2].]

entries.section: 3. Purity on the public road and at banquets

paragraphs.text: 7 Look not round about thee in the streets of the city, neither wander thou in the solitary places thereof. 8 Turn away thine eye from a beautiful woman, and look not upon another's beauty. 9 For many have been led astray by the beauty of a woman, and by it love is kindled as a fire. 10 Every woman that is an harlot shall be trodden under foot as dung in the way. 11 Many have been bewitched by the beauty of a strange woman, and their lot was disgrace, for converse with her is kindled as a fire. 12 Sit not at all with another man's wife, nor lean with her on the elbow. 13 And be not a companion with her in wine, lest thy soul incline unto her, and so thou slide with thine heart into destruction.
Do not let thine eyes roam in the streets of the city, nor wander in its desolate corners [7].

Ben Sira did not forbid his disciples to walk in the streets of the city, but calls them to sanctify their sight like Joseph the pure young man, whose garment Potiphar's wife seized, but he realized that the eyes of the Lord were looking upon him (Gen 39:13). It was said of him: "a goodly person, and well favoured" (Gen 39:6), and by leaving the garment in the hands of his mistress he revealed his purity and the beauty of his soul and the sweetness of his heart, and as Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles, says: [Joseph was more beautiful within than without, radiant with the light of his heart more than with the beauty of his body, for the eyes of this woman could not penetrate and enjoy his beauty [3].] And St. John Chrysostom says: [Joseph was stripped and became more radiant than others, as though he had returned to the state of Adam naked in Paradise and not ashamed, because of his purity [4].] And St. Clement of Alexandria calls us to control and sanctify the senses, for it is not fitting for the believer to let his eyes roam here and there like one lost in the streets, nor for the feet to wander in desolate corners. [What is the desolate corner? "The desolate place is the place where there is no pure person, even if there is a noisy crowd in it [5].] It is fitting for us to sanctify the eye by Christ the light of the world (Jn 8:12), and the feet by Christ the Way (Jn 14:6).
Turn thy gaze away from a beautiful woman, and do not gaze at a strange beauty.

entries.section: 3. Purity on the public road and at banquets

paragraphs.text: For the beauty of a woman has led many astray, and by it lust is kindled like fire [8].
He asks not to gaze at a beautiful woman, because the sin is not in her beauty, but in gazing with an evil will.

v And if you want to know the reason, look within yourself, for the beauty of a woman has led many men astray, and by it lust is kindled like fire. The friendship that begins in fire, which is called passion, cannot be quenched in its sin, but returns to the fire [6].

St. Clement of Alexandria v Where do the Holy Scriptures speak of sin and its causes? They accuse those who lived before the Flood of practicing impure relations. Hear how it shows the cause: "The sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives (of them)" (Gen 6:2).

v Was beauty the cause of the sin? That cannot be! In truth, beauty is the work of the wisdom of God, and the work of God will not be the cause of evil. Then was their sin that they looked at them? No, seeing is a natural act. What then? They looked at them with an evil intention, which is truly the fruit of an evil will. For this reason Wisdom gives us this counsel: "Do not gaze at a beautiful (strange) woman." It did not say: "Do not look," not because this happens spontaneously. Rather it says: "Do not gaze," meaning the deliberate scrutiny, the disturbing gazing and the long-range thinking that comes from a corrupt soul which is the prey of lust.

And what is the loss, if a person looks and is able to withdraw from it? Following this comes "the love that is kindled like fire." Indeed, after fire catches the stubble and the straw at once and without need of time, it catches the wood and kindles a blazing fire. So also the fire of lust that is in us, after it becomes a flame in a beautiful and lofty image through the work of the eyes, at once burns the souls of those who gaze [7].

v One of the (wise men) gives this counsel: "Do not gaze at a strange beauty, nor meet with a woman who is addicted to adultery" (see Sir 9:3, 8). For honey drops from the lips of the harlot, who for a time seems smooth to your throat, and afterward you find her more bitter than gall, and sharper than a two-edged sword (Prov 5:3-4). For the harlot does not know how to love, but only how to hunt. In her kiss there is poison, and her mouth is a deadly narcotic. If this does not appear at once, she must be avoided all the more for this reason, because she conceals destruction, and covers over that death, and does not allow it to appear at the beginning [8].

entries.section: 3. Purity on the public road and at banquets

paragraphs.text: v He did not say only: "He who desires," for a person can desire even if he is sitting alone on the mountains. Rather Jesus said: "He who looks with lust," meaning that a person thinks of another merely out of the desire for lust, he who is under no compulsion allows the wild beast to enter by force into his thoughts while they are calm. This intrusion does not come from nature, but from laxity toward the soul. The Old Testament corrects this from the beginning, saying: "Do not gaze at the beauty of another" (see Sir 9:8) [9].

entries.section: 3. Purity on the public road and at banquets

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom v It is right, before everything, to flee from looking at women, for sin is not in touching only but in seeing also, and we must train ourselves to avoid it. "Let thine eyes look right on, and let thine eyelids look straight before thee" (Prov 4:25). It is possible for one who looks at women to remain steadfast, but he needs to guard against falling. It is possible for one who looks to fall, but it is impossible for one who does not look to fall into sexual lust. It is not enough for the chaste to be pure, but he must strive to pass beyond the sphere of blame and be free of all earthly preoccupations for the sake of fulfilling purity. Not only that we may be believers but that we may be worthy of the trust. For this reason St. Paul the Apostle says concerning taking care: "Avoiding this, that no man should blame us in this abundance which is administered by us: Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men" (2 Cor 8:20-21). Holy Scripture says: "Turn away thine eye from a beautiful woman, and look not upon another's beauty" (see Sir 9:8). And if you want to know the reason for this saying of Scripture, it adds: "For many have been led astray by the beauty of a woman, and by it love is kindled as a fire" (see Sir 9:8). The feeling that arises from fire, which we call love, leads to a fire that is not quenched, and that is the end of sin [10].

St. Clement of Alexandria: Do not dine with a woman who is married to another, and do not join her in parties with wine, lest thy soul incline unto her, and thou go down with thy spirit into destruction [9].

He called them not to take pleasure in wine, especially with a woman married to another. The mother of Solomon counseled her son: "It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine; nor for the great strong drink" (Prov 31:4).

v It is a good commandment that Wisdom offers: "Sit not at all with another man's wife, nor lie back on a couch with her," that is, do not dine or eat much with her. Then he added: "Do not take pleasure in wine with her, lest thy heart incline unto her, and thou go down with thy desire into destruction" (see Sir 9:9).

entries.section: 3. Purity on the public road and at banquets

paragraphs.text: Drinking without restraint is dangerous, because it can easily bring thee down into licentiousness [11].
St. Clement of Alexandria
14 Forsake not an old friend; for the new is not comparable to him. 15 A new friend is as new wine; when it is old, thou shalt drink it with pleasure.
After he commanded reserve on the public road and at banquets and parties, he urged believers to practical counsels, among them to prize the old friend and not to abandon him [10].
Do not forsake an old friend, for the new is not equal to him.
A new friend is like new wine; when it is old, thou shalt drink it with pleasure [10].

Forming a friendship with someone and then abandoning him reveals that he built the friendship on temporal benefit. Friendship is not used for temporary profit, but is the pledge of the heavenly love which not even death destroys, but which grows without ceasing, and which we live in eternity. Loyalty to the old friend is regarded as a great virtue. St. Augustine sees the old friend as prizing the Old Testament, which announced the New Testament by prophecies and types: [Were it not for the Old Testament I would not have believed in the New Testament.] And his disciple Fulgentius came to declare the New Testament's esteem for the role of the Old Testament.

v It is fitting that the Old Testament be kept with honor in such a way that it is neglected in no way. This, as it seems to me, is what Ben Sira meant, when he commands under the figure of the old and the new friend, saying: "Forsake not an old friend; for the new is not comparable to him." The divine Scripture spoke by the mouth of Jeremiah, looking to the difference in the mysteries of the two covenants: "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah" (Jer 31:31) [12].

Fulgentius: This friendship with the eternal God is manifested through the relationship of Moses the prophet with Him, for it is said: "And the LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend" (Ex 33:11). St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, says: [O Caesarius, man of God, I have written you this briefly concerning what pertains to the perfection of the virtuous life, and I have sketched something like a pattern of the life of the great Moses, so that each of us may imitate the image of the beauty that appears to us in it by imitating the manner of life of Moses. And there is no evidence that Moses attained perfection more than the divine voice which said to him: "Thou hast found grace in my sight, and I know thee by name" (Ex 33:12, 17), and also that he was called the friend of the Lord: "And the LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend" (Ex 33:11) [13].]

And in the New Testament St. John the Baptist said of himself that he was the friend of the bridegroom (Jn 3:29), who rejoiced as he saw many gathering around the Lord Christ, as the bride sanctified by the Lord. The role of the friend of the bridegroom among the Jews was important and indispensable, and he was exempted from some religious obligations to devote himself to helping the newly married, especially in the first seven days of the marriage. His work before the marriage was to care for the betrothed and guard her and give testimony to the bridegroom about her; and he served as the link between them, carrying the messages of each to the other, since the betrothed was not allowed to leave the house. After the marriage he strengthened the personality of the bride; he slept in a flat next to the dwelling of the couple to prevent any harm from befalling the bride. And he did not allow either party to deceive the other, and it was his duty to examine the purity of the bride, and when he was assured of that he exulted and rejoiced. Perhaps this is what St. John meant by his saying: "This my joy therefore is fulfilled" (Jn 3:29). He presents the gifts that come to the couple, and finally takes part in the joyful celebration of the marriage for seven days. After this celebration the friend of the bridegroom becomes like the defender of the bride (2 Cor 11:2), and he settles any problems that arise between them.

v It is as though John the Baptist said: I would have suffered much had this not come to pass. If the bride had not come forward to her bridegroom, I would then have been pained and distressed by it, but I am not grieved now that my hopes are fulfilled, and everything we wished has been accomplished, and the bride has known her bridegroom, and you have testified to it, and since I have seen this request fulfilled, I am glad and rejoice (as a friend of the bridegroom).

entries.section: 5. Purity in our view of the successful wicked

paragraphs.text: 16 Envy not the glory of a sinner: for thou knowest not what shall be his end. 17 Be not pleased with the pleasure of the hypocrites. Remember that they shall not be justified unto Hades.
Do not envy the honor given to a sinner, for thou knowest not what his end shall be [11].

The Psalmist asked: "Why does the way of the wicked prosper?", and the answer came: "Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity. For they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb. Trust in the LORD, and do good; dwell in the land, and feed on faithfulness" (Ps 37:1-3).
Do not rejoice in what pleases the wicked, and remember that even in the abode of the dead they are not justified [12].

v "Fret not thyself because of evildoers, for they shall soon wither like the grass." Tell me, what is the fate of him who plunders and robs after his departure? Was not all that he had a dream and an illusion?!... But such is not the state of the saints; you cannot utter the same words about their state, and do not say that what belongs to them is a dream and a legend [14].
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 6. Dealing carefully with the wicked mighty

paragraphs.text: 18 Keep far from him that hath power to kill, and the fear of death will not come into thy mind. 19 And if thou come near him, do not offend, lest he take away thy life. 20 Know that thou goest in the midst of snares, and walkest upon the bulwarks of the cities.
He encourages his disciples to associate with the wise, the pious, those who fear the Lord (Prov 13:20).
Keep far from him that hath power to kill, so that thou be not troubled with the fear of death.
And if thou come near him, do not provoke him, lest he put an end to thy life.
Know that thou steppest among snares, and walkest around the archery towers of the city [13].
It is well that his disciples keep away from those who have the power to kill, and so avoid the danger of death [13].

v If we use every means and spare no effort to avoid the death of the body, how much more must we strive to avoid the death of the spirit?! For there is no obstacle before a man who desires salvation, except the neglect and slackness of the soul [15].

St. Anthony the Great v Know that thou walkest in the midst of snares, and that thou goest to an archery tower beside the city [13]. Everything is full of snares; Satan fills everything with nets. But when the Word of God comes to you... you will say: "Our souls are escaped like a sparrow from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we are escaped. We are blessed in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth" (see Ps 124:7)...

Jesus prepares the way for you. He came down to earth and subjected Himself to the nets of the world. When He saw the great flock of humanity imprisoned in the nets, and saw that He alone was able to tear them, He came to the nets, and took a human body and subjected it to the nets of the mighty enemy, and tore them to pieces for your sake [16].

Origen v "Know thyself," that is, examine yourself from every corner. Keep the eyes of your soul as sleepless guards, for you are walking in the midst of snares (see Sir 9:13). The enemy has set hidden nets in every place. Look at yourself in all directions, and so you will be saved like the swallow from the traps and the sparrow from the snares (Prov 6:5). But the gazelle cannot fall into a snare because of the strength of its sight [17].

St. Basil the Great v In truth we need more defense, seeing that there are ambushes on every side. This is as Solomon says in counsel: "Know that thou goest in the midst of snares, and walkest upon the walls of the cities." How many good things this saying means!... Let each of us write it in his mind, and let us carry it always in our memory, so that we do not fall easily into sin... Even boys hide snares in the ground; so Satan covers our sins with the pleasures of life... There are snares in the house, snares at the table, and snares in social relations [18].

v As the birds, so long as they cling to the upper layers of the air, cannot be easily caught, so you, as long as you look to the things above, cannot be captured, whether in a snare or by any other means.

entries.section: 6. Dealing carefully with the wicked mighty

paragraphs.text: The devil is a fowler of birds. Soar on high above his arrows [19].
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 7. Purity in social gatherings and banquets

paragraphs.text: 21 Test men as much as thou canst, and consult with the wise among them. 22 Let just men be thy companions at table, and let thy glorying be in the fear of the Lord. 23 Make thy company with the prudent, and let all thy talk be in the law of the Most High.
At family and church banquets it is fitting for us to choose to sit with righteous people whom we may imitate and whose blessing we may seek, and what occupies us is the law of God.
Assess thy relatives as much as thou canst, and consult with the wise [14].
Let thy talk be with the wise, and all thy words in the law of the Most High [15].

The firm and strong friendship is that which is based on the Lord's dwelling between the two friends, and their guidance according to the divine commandment. Holy friendship is concerned with speaking of the great things of God and exchanging spiritual experiences.

v Christ says: "Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures" (Mt 22:29). And Paul also said: "That we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope" (Rom 15:4). And also: "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable" (2 Tim 3:16). "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly" (Col 3:16). And the prophet says: "In his law doth he meditate day and night" (Ps 1:2). And in another place: "Let all thy talk be in the law of the Most High" (Sir 9:15)... Believe me, nothing strong, nothing useful comes forth from us [20].

v Let us adorn all the rest of your time also with practice in the laws of God. "Let... all thy talk be in the law of the Most High" (see Sir 9:15). As we adorn ourselves thus, let us come to our King, and fall on our knees, not only with the body, but with the mind also. Let us consider who this is to whom we draw near, and on whose account, and what we are accomplishing. We draw near to God, upon whom the seraphim gaze, covering their faces, unable to bear His splendor, He before whose sight the earth trembles [21].
St. John Chrysostom Let the righteous be thy companions at table, and let thy glorying be in the fear of the Lord [16].

entries.section: 7. Purity in social gatherings and banquets

paragraphs.text: Besides our concern to choose wise men who love the law of God in social gatherings, family banquets and church occasions, it is also fitting that the fear of the Lord prevail in them, and that they bear witness to a life of righteousness in the Lord. St. Basil was concerned with a special order and arrangement for the table, as he was concerned with table manners, and laid down the following principles [22]:

entries.section: 7. Purity in social gatherings and banquets

paragraphs.text: a. He requires all to partake of food with thanksgiving to God [23].

entries.section: 7. Purity in social gatherings and banquets

paragraphs.text: b. During the meal a reading from the Holy Bible is read [it must be listened to with greater pleasure than the pleasure we have as we eat and drink, so that our minds may appear undistracted by bodily pleasure, but rather rejoice in the words of the Lord, like him who found them "sweeter than honey and the honeycomb" [24].]
c. To sit, as far as possible, in the last place at the table in a spirit of humility.
d. To keep quiet in movements and voice.
e. The believer does not allow himself to fill his stomach and be satisfied.

f. He does not enter into idle discussions, even in choosing the last place, and if he sees a man seeking the place, he leaves it to him. And if he senses quarrels over the last place, he is bound to obey the one responsible for preparing the table. Obedience to him is better than choosing the last place through useless disputes.

entries.section: 8. A life of purity and dealing with the various classes of the people

paragraphs.text: 24 The work is commended for the hand of the artificers, and the ruler of the people is wise for his speech. 25 A man of ready tongue is feared in his city, and he that babbleth in his talk is hated.

The purity of the believer is evident even in his esteem for every person, whatever his class, education, or work, for we need the simple worker and the wise ruler. Without workers and craftsmen the city does not stand. What concerns us is that all be faithful in the little that is in their hands. While avoiding the talkative man, and also the rash in his speech [18].
The work of the hands of the craftsmen is commended, and the leader of the people is wise for his speech [17].

All humanity will stand on the great day of the Lord for judgment, and what distinguishes them is the measure of their faithfulness in the little that was in their hands in the world, that they may be entrusted with the much that is given in eternity to the faithful.
The talkative man is feared in his city, and he who is rash in his speech is hated [18].
v Beware of coarseness in speech, for humility and chastity are among the marks of the wise...

entries.section: 8. A life of purity and dealing with the various classes of the people

paragraphs.text: The thought that loves God is a light that shines for the soul, as the sun shines for the body [25].
St. Anthony the Great
Grant us the spirit of purity, O Holy One!
v When humanity joins the choir of the heavenly ones, they sing, saying: Holy, holy, holy! May all sanctify You in their lives wherever they may be!
v Remember, O Lord, every family, and dwell in it!
In purity the husband is not jealous over his wife or of her. He does not envy her gifts and abilities.
Nor does suspicion enter between the spouses, so that the whole family is made worthy of the simplicity of the heavenly ones and their love and mutual esteem among them!
v Be, O my God, the leader of the family, so that neither of them gives himself up to the other, but You lead all.
And neither makes light of the other, for all are Your children, longing to be Your icon!
v Grant us the spirit of wisdom filled with love and purity in seriousness!
So that no one clings to a harlot in indulgence and carelessness, and no one wastes his time in licentiousness and slackness.
Let not the eyes of a young man gaze at a virgin, lest he stumble! Nor let him give himself up to a harlot who destroys his inheritance.
v Let our eyes gaze upon You and be filled with radiance. Let the inner vision be sanctified and be lifted up to glories.
We do not loiter in the streets of the city, for the gates of the heavenly Jerusalem are open to us, and the heavenly ones are occupied with us!
v Open our inner sight, that we may see, in the spirit of purity, the table which You prepare for us!
It is no man who gives us enjoyment, but You are the desire of our hearts!
What parties offer us entertainment? Rather Your banquet fills our depths with joy and delight!
v What friend loved us before our creation as You did? And who died on the cross to raise us to the eternal glories?
You are the old Friend who satisfies all our depths. You give us love and purity, so that our heart is enlarged for all mankind.
v You used to converse with Moses the prophet as a man speaks to his friend (Ex 33:11).
Your friendship has given us a new creation; You removed evil from us and gave us Your divine righteousness!
Our meeting with You raises up from us wise and prudent men!
v Take hold of my hand, and turn my life into a joyful journey toward heaven!
Lift me from glory to glory until I meet You.
Lift me from the dust of the world, and rescue me from the devil's snares, hidden and manifest.
v Grant me to meet Your wise children, that I may learn purity from them, and enjoy a constructive friendship.
It is sweet for us to speak together about You and about Your law.
We hold fast to Your divine promises, and grow in Your fear, and find Your love sweet!
I do not despise a poor man nor a simple worker, for I see Your image shining in their hearts, and Your joy manifest on their faces.
v Let me be silent, that I may hear the voice of my heart, and listen to Your words.
I do not find chatter with a man sweet, nor do I walk in a spirit of rashness.
By Your Holy Spirit my being is shaped day by day, that Your icon may shine forth in me, and I be made worthy of the heavenly wedding feast!

1 A wise judge will instruct his people; and the government of a prudent man is well ordered. 2 As the judge of the people is himself, so are his officers; and what manner of man the ruler of the city is, such are all they that dwell therein. 3 An unwise king destroyeth his people; but through the prudence of them which are in authority the city shall be inhabited.
The wise leader teaches his people, and the government of a prudent man is well ordered [1].

God created man to be a leader of himself before he leads others, and whenever he assumes a position of leadership, whether on the family, social, military, or religious level, he must all the more adorn himself with wisdom, for he becomes responsible for those under his leadership, and he becomes a model for them, which they follow.

What occupies Ben Sira's mind concerning the ruler or the heads of cities is not merely their political, economic, or recreational administration, etc., but rather concern for the peace of the people and their building up, so that a generation with a sound character may arise. The successful leader raises up, if possible, from all his people leaders who realize their mission and their role in a spirit of moderation and joy.

The wonderful example in the history of Israel is King Solomon the Wise, who by his broad mind and wise leadership drew even the kings around him to learn from him. For example, the queen of Sheba came to prove him with hard questions (1 Kgs 10:1), and it was said of her: "And when the queen of Sheba had seen all Solomon's wisdom, and the house that he had built, and the meat of his table, and the sitting of his servants, and the attendance of his ministers, and their apparel, and his cupbearers, and his burnt offerings... there was no more spirit in her" (1 Kgs 10:4-5). She said: "Happy are thy men, happy are these thy servants, which stand continually before thee, and that hear thy wisdom" (1 Kgs 10:8).

But the wicked kings destroyed themselves and drew woes upon the people, for from the time of Rehoboam son of Solomon the kingdom was divided into two kingdoms, the separated kingdom of Israel and the kingdom of Judah, that is, the northern kingdom and the southern kingdom, and often one of them joined foreign nations to resist its sister. The first fell under the captivity of Assyria and the second under the Babylonian captivity, and idolatry entered both kingdoms, even into the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem.
As the leader of the people behaves, so do his ministers, and all the inhabitants of the city are the mirror of their ruler [2].

The leader is a teacher to those around him and those under his authority. He teaches not by words but rather by his management and conduct. His role does not consist only in the good management of affairs, but he leads them in godliness, especially in the fear of the Lord. Perhaps the greatest example in the Old Testament is David's stand when his military companions asked him to kill King Saul, who was pursuing him and had fallen into his hands; he gave them a practical lesson in not taking vengeance on him who had devoted his royal powers to killing him (1 Sam 24:1-8).

St. John Chrysostom stands in amazement, asking in his depths: Was pious David a commander of a battle, or a teacher, or a priest or a bishop? He sees him as the good teacher, careful that neither he nor any of his men should stretch out a hand to evil. The soldiers accompanied David to protect him from the plots of Saul and his attempts to kill him, and he accompanied them to protect them from any unholy action or thought. He cares for the salvation of his own soul as for theirs.

He sees him also as the priest or the bishop, for wherever pious David was, he considered himself in the presence of the Lord, as one in a holy temple. The cave was in his eyes a holy church in which he practiced the work of teaching; he spoke with his companions as with Saul to guide them to the way of their salvation. He preached the truth and was careful for the salvation of all.

Chrysostom sees him as like a bishop or priest offering the sacrifice of love and the offering of meekness and mercy. He also sees him as like a ransom, offering his life poured out by his pardon of his opponent who sought his soul, and he sees the cave as like a holy altar and a temple of the Lord, which does not allow any unseemly thought to have a place in it [1].

v You see that it was not possible without the work of God that (David) should succeed in mastering these men of great fury; the grace of God was found on the lips of the inspired man, offering a kind of these persuasive words. In any case David's contribution was not small, for he had formed them in the past, and therefore found them in the decisive moment ready and willing (in what they had learned from him). You see that he was not like a commander of troops (an army) giving them orders, but like a priest, and the cave was a church on this occasion.

He was like one consecrated a bishop giving them a homily. And after the homily he offered a kind of wonderful, extraordinary sacrifice, not by offering a bull as a sacrifice nor by slaying a lamb, but something greater than both: he offered to God meekness and mercy, slaying the (hidden) rage that did not work in him, killing anger, and putting to death the members which are upon the earth. He acted as ransom and priest and altar. Everything came forth from him, the thought which offered kindness and mercy, and meekness of heart, the things which he made offerings (to God) [2].

v Let no one say: I have a wicked, corrupt, and stubborn enemy, who arouses disgust. Whatever you say about him, there is none more wicked than Saul, whom David rescued on many occasions, who personally devised countless plots, and yet David offered him kindnesses in return for his evils, while he persisted in his evil. What plea do you present after this? Have they seized part of your land, have they broken into your possessions, and trespassed on the borders of your house, and stolen your servants, and harmed you, and been greedy, and brought you down to poverty? Yet they did not take your life, which was what that man (Saul) was determined upon. And if they were determined to take your life, perhaps they tried this on one occasion, not time after time like him. And if they repeated it several times, still they did not receive such benefits from you, for they did not fall into your hands once or twice and you spared them. And if this happened, David is still more generous.

It was impossible for a man under the economy of the Old Testament to attain deep values, but now, after the coming of grace, such wonderful excellences have been given. David had not heard of the parable of the ten thousand talents and the hundred denarii (Mt 18:23-30). Nor did he hear the prayer which says: "Forgive them what they owe, as your heavenly Father forgives you" (see Mt 6:14). He did not see Christ crucified, nor the precious blood flowing, nor did he hear the countless words about sound values. He did not benefit from the countless blessings of sound values. He did not benefit from the blessings of the wonderful sacrifice, nor partake of the blood of the Lord. Instead he was brought up under the imperfect laws which did not require these things, and yet he attained the summit of the sound values of the age of grace.

While you are often offended by past injuries and murmur, he on the contrary, with fear of what would happen in the future, and with full awareness that if he saved the man's life the city would lose its immunity as far as he was concerned and his own life would perish, yet did not cease to show care (for his enemy). He did all in his power to protect him who bore him enmity. Who could have acquired greater patience than this?

As for you, learn also from what happened in our days. In any case, we can be reconciled with every person who bears enmity toward us if we wish. What can be fiercer than the lion, and yet men tame it. For skillful training brings out what is better in nature, and the fiercest animal, which is reckoned a king, becomes gentler than a flock of sheep, and moves about in the marketplaces without causing terror to anyone. What excuse then do we have? What plea do we have if wild beasts are tamed, if we claim that human beings cannot be calmed or drawn to take a friendly attitude toward us?

In truth fierceness in animals is due to nature, but in the human being it is against nature, so if we overcome nature, what excuse do we have when we claim that free will cannot be reformed?... Let us concentrate on one thing, not on our not suffering the harm that comes to us from our enemies, but on making them unable to harm our souls. For we are not troubled even if they measure out to us troubles without number. David suffered nothing, though he was driven out and became a wanderer, and was the object of plots to end his life; instead he became all the more famous and revered more than the other (Saul), and became all the more beloved by everyone, not by men only, but by God Himself. Above all this, what harm came to the saint from enduring all this from Saul at that time? Are his psalms not sung to this day? Did he not become famous on earth and still more in heaven? Do not indescribable good things await him, even in the Kingdom of Heaven?

And on the other side, what good did this wretched, miserable man gain by his terrible plots? Did he not lose his royal position, and a pitiable death befell him and his son, and he fell under accusations directed at him by all, and what is worse than this, the eternal punishment awaits him which he will meet? [3]
St. John Chrysostom: An unrestrained king destroys his people, but through the wisdom of its rulers a city becomes habitable [3].
We saw King David rescuing his men from falling into vengeance on King Saul (1 Sam 24:6-7), while King Saul with his corrupt heart spread corruption among those around him.

entries.section: 2. The Lord, giver of wisdom to the administrator

paragraphs.text: 4 The kingdom of the earth is in the hand of the Lord, and in due time he setteth over it one that is profitable. 5 The success of man is in the hand of the Lord, and upon the face of the scribe he layeth his honour. 6 If thy neighbour wrong thee in any thing, be not wroth with him, and do nothing of the things of insult.
The kingdom of the earth is in the hand of the Lord, and He sets over it the fitting man at the fitting time [4].

Ben Sira affirms the Lord's care for all nations and peoples, so kings and rulers are not set up in random ways, but with God's permission for good. A people careless of their salvation and resisting the truth, God permits them to choose an evil leader, that they may realize that what befell them is the fruit of their evil, that perhaps they may repent of corruption and injustice. When the evil of the Babylonians increased and they thought that there was no power in the world that could, now or in the future, stand before them, He permitted Belshazzar, the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, probably his daughter's son, who did not benefit from the lessons of his fathers, to reign over them (Dan 5). Belshazzar defied God Himself and deliberately wished to insult Him. As St. Jerome says: [He was not sober when he did these things, but rather was drunk, forgetting the punishment that befell his predecessor Nebuchadnezzar [4].]

Belshazzar was occupied with holding a banquet for a thousand of the great men who came from every place, with his wives and concubines. He thought it impossible for Cyrus or anyone else to breach the walls of the huge city, so he let him besiege it, in contempt of him and his army. The walls of Babylon, as Herodotus reports, were no less than 87 feet in width and 350 feet in height, with 250 towers rising another 100 feet in the air. Therefore Belshazzar thought that no one could invade Babylon.

The effort Belshazzar made in holding the banquet and the resources that were provided cannot be estimated. And this in defiance of God, for instead of fasting during the time of the siege and crying out to God to save him and his city, he held a banquet, and used the holy vessels for drinking to defile them in an atmosphere of corruption and licentiousness. And while Belshazzar was opening the banquet, the army of Cyrus was at the gates of Babylon. Cyrus had diverted many channels of the Euphrates and suddenly broke into the city, and the kingdom of Babylon came to an end. Belshazzar was responsible for those under his command, and they, together with the rest of the people, were for their part wicked, for God often permits the discipline of a people through the setting up of a wicked leader. And God has often changed the hearts and thoughts of wicked leaders through the prayers of the subordinates and their fear of the Lord and their holy conduct.

entries.section: 2. The Lord, giver of wisdom to the administrator

paragraphs.text: The success of man is in the hand of the Lord, and He gives his glory to the person of the scribe [5].

God in His justice gives success to those who strive, and raises up from among them great leaders. Some see that the word "scribe" here means the decision maker, or the ruler. The class of scribes among the Jews was educated, copying the Holy Scriptures and interpreting them and teaching by them. In the days of the Lord Christ they were looked upon as an exalted class, and many of the priests in Jerusalem served as scribes. They joined special schools and studied particular curricula. Among them were the Jewish historian Josephus, and also Hillel, who was a scholar and became a famous teacher.

7 Pride is hateful before the Lord and men, and its way is the committing of iniquity before both. 8 But the kingdom is transferred from nation to nation because of injustices and insults and riches. 9 No one is more hideous in guilt than the miser. Why is dust and ashes proud? 10 No one is greater in iniquity than he that loveth money, for he maketh his own soul also a thing for sale, and hath cast away his bowels during his life. 11 Every authority is short-lived. A long sickness is a burden to the physician. 12 So the physician cuts off the sickness before it lengthens; thus the king reigns today and tomorrow he dies. 13 And man at his death inheriteth vipers and beasts and worms. 14 The beginning of man's pride is his departing from the Lord, 15 when his heart turneth away from his Maker. For pride is the beginning of sin, and he in whom it is rooted overflows with abominations. 16 And therefore the Lord brought upon them that have it strange calamities, and destroyed them utterly.
Be not wroth with thy neighbour for any harm he has caused, and do not practice any of the acts of insult [6].
Ben Sira learned from the conduct of David the prophet, who did not allow even his men to stretch out their hands in evil against Saul.

When David was vexed with Nabal who insulted him and gave him nothing to eat, him and his young men who had guarded his possessions and his sheep, he drew his sword, and with him about four hundred men with drawn swords, to fight him. The Lord sent him Abigail, Nabal's wise wife, to turn him back from this deed with wisdom and dignity. She fell at his feet, and said: "That this shall be no grief unto thee, nor offence of heart unto my lord, that thou hast shed blood causeless, or that my lord hath avenged himself." David answered her: "And blessed be thy advice, and blessed be thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood, and from avenging myself with mine own hand" (1 Sam 25:33).

Ben Sira warns us against making any decision when a man is stirred up and agitated. Malice, hatred, and wrath are among the fruits of pride. The humble man has compassion on every person, even him who wrongs him (Lev 19:17-18).

v The (believer) must not be angry with his neighbor without cause, nor adopt resentment against anyone, nor repay evil with evil. It is fitting for him to be reviled rather than to revile, to be struck rather than to strike, to be wronged rather than to sin, and to be robbed rather than to rob [5].

v Anger makes tongues unbridled, and talk without restraint. Likewise physical violence and acts of mockery, abuse, accusations, beating and other countless evil deeds are born of anger and resentment [6].

v Hateful and ugly is that soul which has given itself to its passions. Who can look at a man in his anger and his ugly form? And who can look at a sorrowful man, feeble before his own enslaved soul?...
Let us then be careful of our beauty, so that the Bridegroom, the Word, may receive us with welcome with these words: "Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee" (Song 4:7) [7].

v The chaste in the desire for honor is humble. The chaste in riches is content, and attains the measure of the Gospel in poverty. He who controls resentment and anger is gentle. In truth the observance of true chastity governs the tongue and sets a limit for the eyes and cleanses the ears from listening to gossip with curiosity. But he who does not keep all this is not chaste but unruly [8].
St. Basil the Great: St. Pachomius says that he who teaches the wrathful to become meek has cast a demon out of him.
Haughtiness is hateful before the Lord and men, and injustice is shameful to both [7].

The haughtiness of the ruler drives the nation to collapse. Examples of this are what befell Egypt of plagues in the days of Moses because of the pride of Pharaoh (Ex 7-11). Ben Sira learned this lesson from the fall of Assyria (612 BC) and the kingdom of Babylon (539 BC) and Persia (331 BC) and Greece (323 BC), etc.
v O distinguished one, do not exalt yourself over your neighbor; humble yourself before him, and if possible fall before his feet.
Picture before your eyes the humility of the Son of God, and as He humbled Himself, humble yourself also to your equals.
Look at Him humbled as He washes the feet of the members of His household, and being God, He loved humility and hated boasting.
What the Son of God hates, do not approach, for if you approach it, it will kill you and corrupt you.
Hate the pride which the Son of God hated and rejected: it is the evil from which all evils spring.
Love humility, and hate boasting; if you are a disciple, all the demons cannot approach you.
Humility cast them down from their ranks, and if they find humility in you they flee from you.
Humility is the house of divinity, and where it is, God dwells in it...
Be humble that the King may come and dwell with you, and all the power of the enemy will not harm you.
The house of the king is not plundered by thieves, because his soldiers guard its gates with care.
If you are humble, behold the Kingdom dwells in you, and neither robbers nor thieves will rob you.
If you are humble, the tree of all evil is plucked out of you, and our Lord plants in its place the blessed Tree [9].
St. Jacob of Serugh: The kingdom is transferred from nation to nation because of injustice, arrogance, and money [8].
Nothing corrupts any kingdom, state, or family like injustice, arrogance, and the love of money.

v We read, beloved dear ones, in the Holy Bible: "Blessed is the rich man who does not run after gain... he could transgress and did not transgress, and do evil and did not do it" (see Sir 10:8-10). Well, brethren, let us ask our consciences and see whether we despise covetousness in a way by which we share in this blessing [10].
Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles: How can he who is dust and ashes be proud?
For even during his lifetime his bowels stink? [9]
Ben Sira stands amazed at man, created of dust and ashes, for while he is still in this life, as he is occupied with earthly things instead of his inner life, his depths become corrupt and foul!

v The man who turns toward outward things changes into what is worse, and while alive he casts out his bowels (see Sir 10:9). By this he appears to the world to be in a better state, to those who think on earthly things (Phil 3:19), when the sinner is praised for the desires of his soul and the unjust man is called blessed.
v He changes for the better when his interest gradually turns away from the earthly things that appear in this world, and he places his glory in the inward things on high [11].

St. Augustine: It is wonderful that man, while remaining dust and ashes, is proud even toward his Creator, and when he is united with the Most High he becomes heaven and is humble, imitating the Lord Christ who says: "Learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart."

St. Augustine says that if the devil has no justification for his pride, though he is not dust and ashes, then how will man justify his pride? It is wonderful that when man casts off his (foul) inward parts, the reaction is not contrition and humility but covering himself with pride and arrogance.

v It is said: "There went up a spring from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth" (Gen 2:6). It went up from that land of which Scripture said: "Thou art my hope, my portion in the land of the living" (Ps 142:6). When the soul was watered by such a spring it had not yet thirsted for its inner depths by pride. For the beginning of man's pride is the departing from God (see Sir 10:12). And when it is puffed up by outward things through pride, the soul ceases to be watered by the inner spring. Therefore we are rightly mocked by the words of the prophet who says: "Why is he proud who is dust and ashes, and whose bowels have stunk during his life?" (see Sir 10:9).

From the Fathers of the Iberian Peninsula v "For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him?" (1 Cor 2:11). And yet there are things of man which the spirit that is in him does not know. But You, O Lord, who made him, know him completely. In truth, though I am the object of Your sight, I despise myself and count myself nothing but dust and ashes. I know something that is Yours, and I do not know myself. Surely we see in a dark mirror "and not face to face" (1 Cor 13:12). As long as I am far from You I am nearer to myself than I am to You [12].

v I tremble, for the cause of the soul's estrangement from God is that it is proud. I do not doubt this. It is written: "Pride is the beginning of sin" (see Sir 10:13), and the beginning of human pride is distance from God. It is written that this is firm and true. And so what was said of the pride of transient humanity, wrapped in the worn-out rags of the flesh, weighed down by the corruptible body (Wis 9:15), and for a while man exalts himself, forgetting what the very skin is which he wears. Why does he exalt himself? Let the Holy Scriptures tell us: "Because his bowels have stunk" [9]... The proud man gets rid of his bowels, but the humble man longs zealously for his depths. If by pride we are driven out, by humility we return [13].
St. Augustine v Someone may say: How can he who falls into the sin of frivolity acquire the devil in his soul? What we say, beloved dear ones, we prove from the Holy Scriptures.

Listen to Holy Scripture, which says that the proud man is full of the devil: "Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD" (see Prov 16:5), and "Every pride is the beginning of departing from God" (see Sir 10:12). What does departing from God mean but separating from Him? Moreover, the man who withdraws from God necessarily unites with the devil. Scripture also says that the envious man cannot be without the devil. "Through envy of the devil death entered into the world and they that follow him take his side." The prophet says: "The spirit of whoredoms hath caused them to err" (Hos 4:12).

Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles v Pride, haughtiness, and arrogance are the sins of Satan, and because of these faults he left heaven for earth [Satan fell from heaven]. Therefore "God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble" (Jas 4:6). For he who is arrogant forgets what he will become, what frailty will befall him, and in what filth he will sink, and what dung heap continually comes out of his body. What do the divine Scriptures say? How can he who was made of dust and ashes boast? By the corruption of man's inward parts. Pride is the most dangerous of all sins, the chief fault of Satan [14].
Origen

All rational creation in the heavens and on earth is in need of the divine grace which binds it to God, so that it does not fall into pride, and consequently does not isolate itself from Him as the source of its goodness. When one of the heavenly orders isolated itself from God by accepting pride, it was deprived of divine grace and became powers of darkness, unable to bear the light. And likewise when our first parents rejected grace and clung to the promises and guidance of the devil, they fell into pride. He who departs from God or isolates himself from Him perishes, for he walks according to his own evil will, not according to the holy will of God.
Fulgentius, disciple of St. Augustine, sees that the first man was in need of divine grace.

v In truth human nature could not by its own power achieve this possibility, that is, doing good, even for the first man before he was wounded by sin. Therefore, how could man regain his health without the help of the physician, if while in health he was not able to succeed in guarding his health at that time? For this reason dust and ashes ought not to boast, because deep thought in this life has forsaken it (Sir 10:9), and it was not possible for the wounded to act as one in full health, counting that his wound had been healed. Rather he needed in humility to reveal his wounded heart and the stench of his wounds. So he declares with the prophet: "My wounds stink and are corrupt because of my foolishness" (Ps 38:5), and he is able to receive healing not by his merit, but through the gift of free divine mercy. In truth how can man possess what he has not received? And since he has received it, why does he glory as if he had not received it (see 1 Cor 4:7)? [15]

v Man began to sin through isolating himself from God. It is written: "The beginning of pride is departing from God" (see Sir 10:14), and in another place: "For, lo, they that are far from thee shall perish: thou hast destroyed all them that go a whoring from thee" (Ps 73:27). Those who depart from God and commit adultery perish... God does not wish their destruction by His judgment unless they destroy themselves by their iniquities [16].

Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe v Let the humble listen to the voice of the royal Truth: "He that humbleth himself shall be exalted," and let the proud know that "every one that exalteth himself shall be abased" (Lk 18:14). Let the humble know that "before honour is humility" (Prov 15:33), and let the proud know that "before destruction is pride" (Prov 16:18). Let the humble know that: "To this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word" (Isa 66:2), and let the proud remember the saying: "Why is dust and ashes proud?" (see Sir 10:9). Let the humble know that "The Lord is high, yet hath he respect unto the lowly," and of the proud He says: "But the proud he knoweth afar off" (Ps 138:6). Let the humble know that: "The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister" (Mt 20:28), and let the proud know that "Pride is the beginning of sin (and he in whom it is rooted overflows with abominations)" (see Sir 10:15). Let the humble know that our Savior: "humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross" (Phil 2:8).

Let the proud know what is written of their chief: "When he raiseth up himself, the mighty are afraid" "he is a king over all the children of pride" (Job 41:25, 34). By the pride of the devil judgment came upon us, and by the humility of God the covenant of our salvation was accomplished. For our enemy, a creature like all creatures, wished to exalt himself above all, but our Savior deemed it right to become small among all, and thus remained exalted and great above all. Therefore let the meek know that they are raised up to be like God when they humble themselves. And let the lofty know that by their conceit they descend to the likeness of the rebel angel. There is nothing lower than the conceit that casts man down from the state of true exaltation. And how exalted is humility which, by descending to the depths, is joined to the Creator who is above all in the heights [17].
Pope Gregory (the Great)
A chronic illness puzzles the physician, and the king of today dies tomorrow [10].
When a man dies he inherits creeping things, beasts, and worms [11].
The beginning of man's pride is his departing from the Lord, for his heart withdraws from his Maker [12].

v The children of God and the children of the devil are not distinguished from each other except through humility and pride. When you see a proud man do not doubt that he is a son of the devil. And if you see a humble man you must believe and trust that he is a son of God... What cast down the devil but pride, and what raised Christ is humility, for He set the healing of humility for the wound of pride. Therefore if we wish to avoid pride we must always withdraw into the medicine of humility. Let us listen to the Lord who says: "Learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart" (Mt 11:29). He did not say learn of me the creation of the world, or the raising of the dead or the working of other miracles.

Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles v He who is proud suffers the same punishment as the devil, because: the beginning of man's pride is his departing from the Lord (see Sir 10:12). Pride is the beginning of sin, and it is the first impulse and movement toward evil. In truth perhaps it is both the root and the foundation. For the beginning means the first impulse toward evil or the background of evil. It is like a person saying that the beginning of purity is abstaining from looking at unseemly things, for this is the impulse. But to say that the beginning of purity is fasting, this is the foundation which establishes purity. So pride is the beginning of sin, because every sin begins with it and it supports it [18].

v Had Satan not been struck by this disease (arrogance) he would not have descended and become Satan, for he was not formerly Satan. This is what cast him from that confidence, this drove him into the pit of fire, this is the cause of all his woes [19].

St. John Chrysostom v The beginning of human sin is rebellion against God, and the beginning of every sin is pride.
