The Apostle spoke of this matter concerning sin, saying: "Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened" (Rom 1:21). The darkened heart has its punishment in itself. But from where did this happen? "Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools" (Rom 1:22). They said that what they received from God came from themselves. Or even if they knew from whom they received this, they did not give glory to him from whom they received.

v Misery is the seeds of iniquity, but sin is the conception of misery; for the first sin is departing from God [12]. He who conceives misery travails with injustice. Iniquity itself is like injustice, it brings forth that with which it has travailed [20].
St. Augustine: For the beginning of man's pride is sin, and he who holds to it overflows with abomination.
And therefore the Lord brings upon the proud exceeding trials, and destroys them utterly [13].
It is not necessarily so that every sin is accompanied by pride, but every sin has as its first cause pride and man's isolating himself from his God, and his rejecting the divine will.

v He who has learned well the steps of overcoming vices knows that this vice of vainglory must be avoided entirely... for that by which the soul first fell rules the rest. "For the beginning of all sin is pride," and also: "The beginning of man's pride is his departing from God" (see Sir 10:12-13) [21].

v When the soul loves its own authority it descends from what is common to all to what is its own. Had it followed God as its leader in the universal creation, His laws could keep it at the highest level of exaltation [22].

v Blessedness needs nothing else whatever, since it needs to attain the highest wisdom. "But the fear of the Lord is the head of wisdom" (Ps 111:10) LXX. On the other hand pride is called "the beginning of all sin" (see Sir 10:13). The proud man seeks the love of earthly kingdoms, but "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Mt 5:3) [23].

St. Augustine v I beseech you that we be zealous to turn away from this inclination (pride), lest we fall into the same condemnation, and submit ourselves to the same punishment, and share in the vengeance. He says: "Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil" (1 Tim 3:6). He who is puffed up suffers the same punishment as the devil. "The beginning of pride is not knowing the Lord" (see Sir 10:12) [24].
v A wise man says: "Pride is the beginning of sin" (see Sir 10:13), that is, its root, its source, and its mother [25].

v In truth there is nothing so alien to the mercy of God, and casts into the fire of Gehenna like the tyrant of pride. If we possess it within us, our life becomes defiled, even if we practice purity and virginity and fasting and prayer and almsgiving or any virtue whatsoever. Scripture says: "Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD" (Prov 16:5). Therefore we must press down this haughtiness of the soul, and cut off this tumor, if we wish to be pure and be rid of the punishment prepared for the devil [26].
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 4. The greatness of the meek is the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: 17 The Lord hath overthrown the thrones of the sultans, and set the meek in their place. 18 The Lord hath plucked up the roots of the nations, and planted the humble in their place. 19 The Lord overturned the lands of the nations, and destroyed them to the foundations of the earth. 20 He made some of them dry, and destroyed their inhabitants, and removed their memorial from the earth. 21 The Lord blotted out the memorial of the proud, and left the memorial of them that are humble in spirit. 22 Pride was not created with men, nor wrath with them that are born of women.
The Lord destroys the thrones of the sultans, and seats the meek in their place [14].

The Apostle says: "And that he died for all, that they which live should henceforth not live unto themselves, but unto him which died for them, and rose again" (2 Cor 5:15). The statement here is an echo of what is stated in (Prov 3:35) and in (1 Pet 5:5-6).
v Our Christ came to reconcile us with God (the Father) by His humility, since we had strayed from Him by our accursed pride...

entries.section: 4. The greatness of the meek is the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: "Pride is the beginning of all sins." Likewise we read: "The first of man's pride is the fall by departing from the Lord" (see Sir 10:13-14). Therefore may no one live for himself but for Christ, and do His will, and not the will of man himself, and abide in His love, and do the will of his Father and dwell in His love (Jn 15:10) [27].

entries.section: 4. The greatness of the meek is the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine v Is there another proud man? Let him hear: "God resisteth the proud" (Jas 4:6). And "Pride is the first beginning of sin" (see Sir 10:13). "Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD" (Prov 16:5) [28].

St. John Chrysostom: St. Jacob of Serugh presents us with a wonderful picture of the pagan king of Nineveh as he saves his kingdom by his faith with a spirit of humility and repentance. 1. In humility, he did not despise a man without weapons (Jonah), poor and appearing in his looks as lowly. 2. He left the royal throne, offering repentance in contrition and sincere repentance. 3. He gathered the people so that all might take part, even the little children, in the battle. 4. He realized that the weapon of the infants and children is greater and stronger than every weapon, for by them they win the battle, and seize the great mercies of God.
St. Jacob of Serugh depicts for us the meeting of Jonah the prophet with the king of Nineveh, saying:
v Jonah said: There is no means of averting the wrath, for iniquity has grown strong and the overthrow has come to shatter you.
Evil is decreed and the appointed end has arrived; affliction has drawn near, and the fall is at the door.
The Lord sent me, that Mighty One who bears creation, to proclaim the overthrow, and with a cry of terror upon your walls.
That Strong One who by His command terrified all creatures, and looks upon the earth, and it trembles before Him because He is its Lord.
He who disciplined the earth with the waters of retribution and destroyed the sinners from it and they did not escape.
He who scattered the peoples in the regions from the days of Babel, and when they sinned against Him confused their tongues and destroyed them...
These voices struck the king of Nineveh, and he was terrified when he heard the fearful tidings.
He feared Jonah more than thousands of mighty men, and the king fell before that lowly man.
He rose from his splendid throne, and cast the crown from him, and put on sackcloth, and prepared himself for repentance.
He saw that Jonah did not wish to retract what he said, so he thought to nullify his words by contradictions.
He found that the prophet threatened much and strongly, so he girded up his loins (resolved his matter) to face the danger with might.
He knew what that battle required, so he prepared himself to set up the front like a valiant man.
He realized that this battle was not like the usual battles, so he gathered his people and urged them to strive.
He gathered his soldiers and drew them up for supplication, and supplied the ranks of the soldiers with prayers to close the gaps.
He made men and women and children hold to fasting, each according to his strength, to line up for the fight against the wrath.
The king said to his soldiers such words as these to his armies gathered together for the supplication.
A new fight we are entering, unfamiliar. Let us awaken our souls to victory by virtue.
Lay down the weapons, and take sackcloth instead of armor, and leave the arrows, and let the voice of supplications pour forth from us.
Let the children and the elders arise and line up against the wrath, and let men and women fight against destruction.
And let not even a one-day-old be kept from the battle, for the fight is fierce, so let us not show weariness in it.
A boy who has not sinned defeats a thousand in this battle; let them come with us, for the whole war is won by them.
Behold the Hebrew threatens and waves to destroy us; let us confront him lest he rejoice over us when he overcomes us.
Infants at the breast take part with us here among the ranks and support us, until evil is driven back from us.
In this fight the boys are stronger than the men, and the children strive more easily than the mighty.

entries.section: 4. The greatness of the meek is the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: The children who have not sinned defeat thousands in this battle, and take part with us, and through them the struggle becomes better [29].
St. Jacob of Serugh: The Lord plucks up the roots of the nations, and plants the humble in their place [15].

When a believing man dies we feel that his memory lasts forever, because he is in the presence of God, but the wicked, whether on the level of individuals or nations, end as though they had never existed before.

entries.section: 4. The greatness of the meek is the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: v It is customary to say of the proud man that he has lofty spirits. And this is true, because the wind is called spirit. And so it is written: "Fire, and hail; snow, and vapour; stormy wind (Spirit of tempest)" (Ps 148:8). Indeed the proud man is called puffed up, as if he were exalted with the wind. And here the Apostle says: "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth" (1 Cor 8:1)... Let us understand in truth that the poor in spirit are the humble and those who fear God, that is, those who do not have the spirit that is puffed up. In truth the Beatitudes could not begin with anything other than this beginning, since they are set for the attainment of the high wisdom "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom" (Ps 111:10), and on the other hand "Pride is the beginning of sins" (see Sir 10:5). Then let the proud man seek and love earthly kingdoms, but "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" [30].
St. Augustine: The Lord overturns the lands of the nations, and destroys them to the foundations of the earth [16].
He shakes some of them, and destroys their inhabitants, and removes their memorial from the earth [17].
Pride was not created for men, nor the fierceness of wrath for those born of women [18].
Man was created in the image of God in meekness and humility. As for the pride that has befallen us, it is from our carelessness and our isolating ourselves from the grace of God.

entries.section: 5. True honor and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: 23 Which seed is honorable? The seed of man. Which seed is honorable? They that fear the Lord. Which seed is base? The seed of man. Which seed is base? They that transgress the commandments. 24 Among brethren their chief is honored, so in the eyes of the Lord are they that fear him. 25 The rich, and the glorious, and the poor, their glory is the fear of the Lord. 26 It is not right to dishonor the wise poor man, nor is it fitting to honor the sinful man. 27 The great, and the judge, and the mighty are honored, and none of them is greater than he that feareth the Lord. 28 The wise servant shall be served by the free, and the prudent man will not murmur.
Which kind of seed is honored? The seed of man.
Which kind of seed is honored? Those who fear the Lord. Which seed is not honored? The seed of man.
Which seed is not honored? Those who transgress the commandments [19].

If the fear of the Lord is before man, he enjoys honor by clinging to the Lord, or if before him he transgressed the divine commandment, he brings dishonor upon himself by separation from God. Since Noah feared the Lord (Heb 11:7), he and his household enjoyed deliverance from the Flood, and he even entered into a covenant with God that there would not be a flood to destroy the whole earth.

entries.section: 5. True honor and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: v Distance from keeping the commandments of God is distance from God; and this is the essence of sin, which is separation from God and distance from union with Him [31].
St. Basil the Great: The chief among brethren is honored, and those who fear the Lord are honored in His eyes [20].
The fear of the Lord precedes the pursuit of authority, but in violence and pride is its loss [21].
The rich and the dignified (eminent) and the poor are on an equal footing; their boast is the fear of the Lord [22].
The greatness and dignity of a man are not in his possessions, nor in his position or abilities, but in his fear of the Lord, his piety and his wisdom, however great his poverty.

entries.section: 5. True honor and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: v Poverty is not a permanent source of pride, but rather voluntary poverty for the sake of the Gospel. This is perfection! Many have been deprived of wealth, yet in their depths they desire it. They were not saved because they are poor, and their inner intention condemns them. He is not happy who lacks everything, but he who considers the commandment better than the treasures of the world. Thus the Lord blesses him: "Blessed are the poor in spirit" (Mt 5:3). Not those who lack wealth, but those who chose poverty from within their souls. Happiness comes only to him who chose it. For every virtue, especially the virtue of poverty, is a voluntary act [32].
St. Basil the Great It is not just that the wise poor man should be dishonored, nor is it fitting that the sinful man should be honored [23].
The noble and the judge and the ruler will be honored, and none of them is greater than he who fears the Lord [24].
The free render service to a wise servant, and the man of understanding does not murmur at it [25].

The wise Solomon says: "A wise servant shall have rule over a son that causeth shame, and shall have part of the inheritance among the brethren" (Prov 17:2). And the Apostle Paul says: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus" (Gal 3:28). And also: "Where there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian, Scythian, bond nor free: but Christ is all, and in all" (Col 3:11).

v "He that is called in the Lord, being a servant, is the Lord's freeman" (1 Cor 7:22). The person who is delivered from the sins, which in truth refer to "slaves," becomes the Lord's freeman. For he who walks without wisdom is a slave...

entries.section: 5. True honor and the fear of the Lord

paragraphs.text: This is also the opinion of the ancients, who used to call the wise free, and all who are not wise slaves. It is said: "The free serve a wise slave" (see Sir 10:25). Therefore he who believes, though a slave for a time, becomes the Lord's freeman, because by his faith in Christ he walks in wisdom. Sins create slaves, like Ham the son of Noah, who became a slave because of his sin and his lack of discretion (Gen 9:22-24). And when one receives forgiveness of sins he becomes free [33].
Father Ambrosiaster

29 Do not excuse yourself from engaging in work, and do not be puffed up in the time of want. 30 For he who busies himself with every work is better than one who goes about or is puffed up while he is in want of bread.
Do not show off your wisdom when doing your work, and do not exalt yourself in the time of your distress [26].

v Those who spend their lives in small and humble efforts become free from dangers, and have no need of special precautions, and find the way that leads to God with ease, through their constant victory over the passions [34].
St. Anthony the Great He who works while possessing much is better than he who boasts but is in need of bread [27].

However great a man's wealth, he is in need of work. According to St. Basil the Great, work is necessary for the following reasons: 1. Work is a divine commandment and a divine gift, for God created man to work (Gen 2:15). Without work man loses the taste of life. St. Basil affirms that there is no excuse for the lazy man who lives in idleness while he is able to work. It is fitting for him to imitate those fishes that cross the seas in a wondrous way in search of food [35]. 2. Work helps us to do good, so that we share our resources with those who lack them. It is fitting for the believer to work not only in order to eat, but also for his spiritual edification, and to offer from the work of his hands to the Lord Himself through the needy. 3. He who does not work does not deserve his food (Mt 10:10; 2 Thess 3:10). 4. Work spurs us on to diligence.
v Whoever is able, let him work and give to the needy; and whoever is unwilling to work is condemned, and is counted unworthy even to eat (Mt 10:10; Acts 20:35) [36].
v We must, when possible, work, so that we may share our resources with those who lack them [37].
v The prohibition of excessive concern for the needs of our body does not abolish concern and work altogether.

For it remains for us to work for ourselves, not for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life (Jn 6:27), not for our bodily needs only, but also to relieve our neighbor (Eph 4:28). And the Lord will say to us on the day of judgment: "I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink..." (Mt 25:35). What we do for those who have consecrated themselves to Him is counted as if we were working with them, and the heavenly Kingdom is given to us for it. On the contrary, those who did not work and did not toil to help the weak and serve their neighbor will be punished (Acts 20:4, 35), and He will send them to eternal torment (Mt 25:41–46) [38].
St. Basil the Great

31 My son, glorify your soul with meekness, and give it the honor it deserves. 32 He who sins against himself, who will justify him? And who will honor him who dishonors his own life? 33 The poor man is honored for his work, and the rich man is honored for his riches. 34 He who is honored in poverty, how much more in riches? And he who is dishonored in riches, how much more in poverty?
My son, glorify your soul with humility, and give it honor according to its worth [28].

In the garden of Gethsemane the Lord bowed down to receive the cup of suffering from the hand of the Father, assuring us that in Him we seek the glory that God prepares for us: "Glorify thou me..." (Jn 17:5). And as Ben Sira warns us against self-importance, he also warns us against faintheartedness, which drives us into a state of frustration.

v When you insult, it is you who are insulted. Most people know this in part, when they say to one another: "Come, let us withdraw; do not dishonor yourself." Why? Because the difference between you and him is great. For when you insult him greatly, he counts this as credit to himself. Let us put this down in all cases, and rise above insults. I will tell you how.

Is it fitting for us to enter into a quarrel with one who wears purple? Let us reckon that when we insult him we are only insulting ourselves, since we are qualifying ourselves to be in shame. Tell me, what do you mean by this? When you are a citizen of heaven and have the heavenly philosophy, do you dishonor yourself with that man who minds earthly things? (Phil 3:19). For even though he possesses countless riches, and even though he has authority, yet he does not know the good that is in these things. Do not insult yourself by your insult of him... Honor yourself, not him. Is there not such a saying: that he who is honored honors himself? Because of what is good, he who honors honors not the other but himself. Hear what the wise man says: "Glorify your soul with honor from that source" (see Sir 10:28) [39].
St. John Chrysostom Who will justify a man who sins against himself, his soul?
And who will honor a man who dishonors his life? [29]
Ben Sira warns us against a man's belittling of him to whom God has given abilities, gifts and potentials.
The poor man is honored for his knowledge, and the rich man is honored for his riches [30].
There is that for which the poor man is honored, namely knowledge, wisdom and piety.
If a man is honored while in poverty, how much more while in wealth?
And if a man is dishonored while in wealth, how much more while in poverty? [31]

A wonderful, musical poetry that needs no interpretation. For if he who receives honor while poor because of his wisdom, what if he were to become rich? And if he who is dishonored because of his folly and his evil while rich, what if he were also to become poor?!
Inspired by Sirach 10

entries.section: Grant me the spirit of wise leadership!

paragraphs.text: v O my God, You are the King of kings, You came down to raise up even from among children leaders full of love and wisdom.
You created human beings not that some of them should be slaves, but that all should bear the icon of wise leadership!
Everyone who cleaves to You becomes a king, with authority over his depths.
And by love even little children become mature heroes.
Teach me, train me, O You who are all meekness and humility.
Pour out Your grace within me, that I may enjoy the spirit of attractive leadership!
Sanctify me, that my inner Jerusalem may be sanctified by You. Let Your Kingdom be established within me!
v You raised the boy David to be king, and many long to be counted sons of David the successful leader.
And King Saul exalted himself, and his depths were filled with a spirit of vengeance against the one who rescued him again and again!
He corrupted his household, and he and his sons died in shame, and the throne was withdrawn from under him.
v Keep me lest I be lax with Belshazzar king of Babylon (Dan 5), who collapsed, he and his kingdom, in marvelous shame!
Truly You permitted him to be set up as a corrupt king over a corrupt people, so that the nations might be disciplined throughout the ages.
You are wise, O Lord, You who govern history, You send to every nation a leader for its edification or for its discipline!
v Grant me the spirit of earnestness without laxity, that Your hand may be stretched out and carry me successfully on the way of truth.
David listened to Your voice through the wise Abigail.
David blessed her, for she kept him from avenging himself on her husband Nabal the fool.
Grant me, O Lord, to listen with David to Your law, whoever the speaker of it may be!
Let not wrath creep into my heart toward him who causes me harm. And do not allow my mouth to utter a word of insult.
Lead my heart and my mouth Yourself, and set a strict guard over them. Sanctify them, that I may bear witness to You, O Holy One!
v Remove from me the spirit of anger, and grant me of Your meekness! Break down in me all pride, that I may enjoy Your humility!
Let Your Kingdom dwell within me, and be revealed in my depths.
I long to see every child a king and a leader, trampling under his feet the enemy of good and all his powers, and no thief able to steal his glory!
v Help me not to lose Your gift to me, for You want me to be a loving, humble and chaste leader.
Take away from me hatred and pride and the love of money.
You created me from dust and ashes, and granted me that my heart should be lifted up to Your heavens! Let me cleave to You, and not turn back from You!
Draw my depths up to Your heavens, that I may not wallow in the mire of this world.
Do not take from me Your grace that upheld the heavenly orders.
Lest sin drag me down to the abyss, and I join the powers of darkness.
v Rescue me from the tyrant of pride, who is the beginning of every sin, and grant me to fulfill Your holy will and not my evil will.
Grant me a zealous and humble heart, that I may not fall under punishment with the arrogant devil.
v Grant me what You gave to the Gentile king of Nineveh.
In humility he did not despise Your prophet Jonah, simple in his appearance.
He left the throne of the kingdom and put on sackcloth in sincere repentance.
He realized that there is no salvation except through the people's fellowship with their leaders, so that even the children took part in crying out to You.
The pagan king believed that the cry of the simple children and infants is stronger than every weapon!
Grant me, by the spirit of humility, to seek Your great mercies together with all the people.
v Grant me not to know old age, but to work for You and by Your grace until the last breath.
Let me work even on my deathbed!

entries.section: 1. True wisdom and appraisal by appearance

paragraphs.text: 1 The wisdom of the lowly lifts up his head, and seats him among the assembly of the great. 2 Do not praise a man for his beauty, nor despise a man for his appearance. 3 The bee is small among the birds, and its harvest is the chief of all sweetness. 4 Do not boast of the wretchedness of your clothes, nor exalt yourself in the day of honor; for the works of the Lord are wonderful, and His deeds are hidden from men. 5 Many of those in authority have sat on the dust, and the obscure has worn the crown. 6 Many of the mighty have suffered the utmost disgrace, and the honored have been delivered into the hands of others.
The wisdom of the humble man lifts up his head, and his seat will be among the great [1].

The most dangerous thing in social relationships in general is appraising persons by outward appearance without careful study of the reality of their characters. For a man is often deceived by physical beauty, a gentle voice, elegance of dress, and a person's material level or social position. It would be fitting for a person to look at his brother or friend with regard to his true wisdom.

The wisdom of the humble person is like a passport by which he passes through life, whether in poverty or wealth, in distress or relief, in sickness or health. He sets out, and true, humble wisdom seats him among the great. But the fool supposes, by his possessions and wealth and gifts and studies and strength and outward appearance, that he is able to storm the councils of the great ones of the world, and even to sit at their head, not knowing that what he does reveals his weaknesses and folly and pride, so that he goes down in the eyes of God and in the eyes of many to sit as on a dunghill. This is what led the Apostle Paul to advise us that a man ought not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think soberly (Rom 12:3).

He who acquires wisdom goes forth in a spirit of humility to the last rows with the Lord of glory Jesus, who became a servant and was crucified between two wicked thieves, and so the Lord of glory carries him, and he enters with his heart and mind into the heavenly sanctuaries. But he who walks in pride, in folly, collapses with the devil unless he returns to himself by repentance.

When God delivered Hannah from the humiliation she suffered from her rival Peninnah, she praised Him, saying: "The bows of the mighty men are broken, and they that stumbled are girded with strength... The LORD killeth, and maketh alive: he bringeth down to the grave, and bringeth up. The LORD maketh poor, and maketh rich: he bringeth low, and lifteth up. He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory: for the pillars of the earth are the LORD's, and he hath set the world upon them (1 Sam 2:4-8).

v Be vigilant and be steadfast in the Lord. If you keep these sayings you will be good in everything. For it is written: glory goes before the humble (Prov 23:29); and also: "The wisdom of the humble lifts up his head" (Sir 1:11); and also: "But to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word" (Isa 2:66).

v It is also written: "The crushed bones rejoice" (Ps 8:50) (LXX); and also: "The prayer of the humble man is quickly accepted" (see Sir 32:17). And it is also written: "Look upon mine affliction and my pain; and forgive all my sins" (Ps 18:25). See then the measure (of the greatness) of humility. If you have acquired humility you have acquired everything.

entries.section: 1. True wisdom and appraisal by appearance

paragraphs.text: St. Abba Paula of Tamouh On humility Do not praise a man for the beauty of his appearance, and do not shun a man for his looks [2].

True glory does not rest on outward appearance, which often deceives a man, whether in choosing a life partner or the staff to work with him, even though history reveals the deception of appearances. We do not learn from the mistakes of former generations.

The prophet Samuel was amazed at the beauty of Saul the son of Kish and his stature, for it is said: "And he had a son, whose name was Saul, a choice young man, and a goodly: and there was not among the children of Israel a goodlier person than he: from his shoulders and upward he was higher than any of the people" (1 Sam 9:2). "But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the eyes, but the LORD looketh on the heart" (1 Sam 16:7)

v Why are you troubled at a lack of beauty, since this is not shameful? Hear the saying of the wise man: "Do not praise a man for his beauty, nor shun a man for his appearance" (see Sir 10:2). Rather let God be the one who admires (you), the greatest Artist, not man, who has no merit in the make-up in which he was created. Tell me, what are the benefits of beauty? None. It exposes its possessor to great and dangerous trials, regrettable incidents and suspicions. For he who lacks beauty is spared suspicion, while he who possesses it must guard himself in an extremely unnatural way, and gives a poor account. And worse than this is the suspicion of the husband, who has less enjoyment by holding on to her beauty, and also suffers the troubles of jealousy over her. Her beauty becomes dim in his eyes because of her modesty, and she suffers in her character from the weak and from those given to amusement and licentiousness, so that her spirit collapses and she is filled with vanity [2].

entries.section: 1. True wisdom and appraisal by appearance

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom The bee is small among the flying creatures, but its fruit is the first among sweet things [3].

St. Augustine sees that the bee resembles some flying insects in outward appearance [3]. But how great is the difference between the bee that provides us with honey and some insects that cause us diseases.

The bee also, in its appearance, is a dangerous insect that stings a man and causes him pain, while it provides humanity with useful food, which is counted a considerable wealth for the nations. And St. John Chrysostom sees that the talk here is for the husband who sees that his wife lacks beauty, looking to another, for he says:

v "That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, that he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish" (Eph 5:26-27). By the washing, or in the font, He washed her from defilement. And by the word, what word? "In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Mt 28:19). Not only did He adorn her, but He made her "glorious, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing." Let us then seek this beauty for ourselves, and we can bring it about.

Do not ask of your wife's hand things which you cannot acquire. Do you not see that the Church has everything in the hand of her Lord? By Him she became glorious, and by Him she became pure without blame?

entries.section: 1. True wisdom and appraisal by appearance

paragraphs.text: Do not turn your back on your wife because of a deformity in her. Hear what the Scripture says: "The bee is little among such as fly, but her fruit is the chief of sweet things" (see Sir 11:3). She is the work of God. Do not accuse her, but accuse her Creator, for what can a woman do? Praise her not for her beauty, for praise rests on the beauty that belongs to the soul... Let her seek the beauty of the soul. Imitate the Bridegroom of the Church. Outward beauty is full of deception and great dissolution, it drives people to envy, and it drives you to expect hideous things [4].

entries.section: 1. True wisdom and appraisal by appearance

paragraphs.text: v Solomon also does something similar, for he returns to one who lives as in an idle life and confronts him with the ant (Prov 6:6-8), and here he confronts him with the bee [5].

entries.section: 1. True wisdom and appraisal by appearance

paragraphs.text: v If you see a huge man with good qualities, and tall, surpassing others in the length of his limbs, do not marvel at him until you are sure of the state of his soul. It is fitting for us to proclaim a man and call him blessed not for the beauty of his appearance, but for the beauty that relates to the soul. David was small in his body, and short in stature, and though he was so short and small of body, and his arms bare (without weapons), he brought down upon a great army with a single blow that body which was like a tower, without hurling an arrow or drawing a sword from its sheath, but did all this with a little stone. For this reason we were advised thus: "Do not praise a man for his beauty... The bee is small among the flying creatures, but what she gathers is the chief of all sweetness" (see Sir 11:2-3) [6].
St. John Chrysostom Do not boast of your splendid clothes, and do not exalt yourself on the day when you are glorified, for the works of the Lord are wonderful, and His deeds are hidden from men [4].

Sometimes a man's character can be discovered from his dress, yet some exaggerate in wearing luxurious clothes to hide their meager characters. Some great philosophers, men of learning and those consecrated to service are not much occupied with their clothing. These are content with simplicity of appearance without vulgarity or noticeable neglect. He who realizes the value of the beauty of his soul, which the Holy Spirit of God adorns, feels an inner satisfaction, and does not wait for a word of praise for his outward appearance.

v Our teacher advises us plainly: "Do not boast of the clothes you wear, and do not exalt yourself on the day of your glory, for it does not last" [4]. And more plainly he speaks mockingly of those who wear soft clothing, saying in the Gospel: "Behold, they which are gorgeously apparelled, and live delicately, are in kings' courts" (Lk 7:25). He means these earthly courts that crumble, where vanity and empty glory and flattery and error dwell. But those who serve the heavenly court of the King of all sanctify their bodies, which are the worn-out garments of their souls, and clothe them with incorruption [7].

entries.section: 1. True wisdom and appraisal by appearance

paragraphs.text: v Let us pursue that (true) glory, and not that in which there is something grand. Let us leave the glory of the world as a trifle. "Do not boast of the clothes you wear" (see Sir 11:4). Truly, dancers and harlots and actresses wear brighter and far costlier clothes than you. Besides, this boasting is of the kind that the moth attacks, and it can rob you of your joy [8].
St. John Chrysostom Many of the tyrants sit on the dust, but he who was not in the reckoning wears the crown [5].
Many rulers are overtaken by the utmost disgrace, and the glorified are delivered into the hands of others [6].

"He leadeth counsellors away spoiled, and maketh the judges fools. He looseth the bond of kings, and girdeth their loins with a girdle. He leadeth priests away spoiled, and overthroweth the mighty. He removeth away the speech of the trusted, and taketh away the understanding of the aged. He poureth contempt upon princes, and weakeneth the strength of the mighty" (Job 12:17-21).

entries.section: 2. True wisdom and not being hasty

paragraphs.text: 7 Do not blame before you examine. Understand first, then rebuke. 8 Do not answer before you hear, and do not interrupt a man's speech before he has finished.
Do not condemn before you examine the case, but first understand, then judge [7].

entries.section: 2. True wisdom and not being hasty

paragraphs.text: Do not answer before you hear, and do not interrupt a speaker while he is speaking [8].

entries.section: 2. True wisdom and not being hasty

paragraphs.text: v Do not let the stirring up of quarrels, through our love of empty victory, creep in among us. Our aim is to exclude every dispute. Surely this is the meaning of the phrase: "Peace be unto you" (Jn 20:19, 21), "Do not answer before you hear" (11:8). The indistinct voice is the voice of a womanish man; at any rate the voice of the self-controlled man is moderate in its tone, so that it is neither too loud nor talkative, nor does he speak rapidly, nor is he long-winded in speech [9].
St. Clement of Alexandria

entries.section: 3. True wisdom and work without planning

paragraphs.text: 9 Do not dispute about a matter that does not concern you, and do not sit in judgment with sinners. 10 My son, do not busy yourself with many works; for if you multiply them you will not be free from blame. If you pursue them you will not overtake them, and if you outrun them you will not escape. 11 There is a man who labors and toils and strives, and only becomes more in want!
Do not dispute about a matter that is not your concern, and do not sit with sinners when they judge a case [9].

By the spirit of discernment the man of God realizes the truth of his obligations, and so works wisely within the limits of his responsibilities, instead of wasting his time on what is not his concern. Here he calls us to avoid dealing with two groups that waste time: the group of those who love disputing about matters that are not our concern, such as analyzing political events and arguing about them, while he is unable even to express his opinion because he does not know the facts. And the second group is keeping up with unjust judges in a kind of hypocrisy and partiality.

entries.section: 3. True wisdom and work without planning

paragraphs.text: My son, do not let your work include many things, for if you multiply them, you will not continue without punishment; even if you advance in them, you will not overtake them, and you will not escape by fleeing [10].

It is fitting for us not to be occupied with many works and achievements, but to keep to faithfulness until we hear the divine voice: "You have been faithful over a few things, I will make you ruler over many things" (Mt 25:21).

entries.section: 3. True wisdom and work without planning

paragraphs.text: There is a man who works and works and keeps on working, yet becomes poorer [11].

Many are occupied with the number of hours they spend at work, and not with working faithfully and wisely so that it may be fruitful. Let us remember our need to seek the blessing of the Lord; for in many works a man can accomplish in one hour a work that previously needed a whole day. It is said that one day with the Lord is as a thousand years (2 Pet 3:8). This is felt by the student when he is troubled and realizes that his achievement in study is weak, and when his soul is filled with peace and joy his achievement in study is very good. Also, at times a man works diligently and strongly, but with pride and arrogance, and so loses much, and even loses the salvation of his soul and his eternity.

entries.section: 4. Between true wisdom and divine help

paragraphs.text: 12 And there is a man who is slow, in need of help, lacking strength, in great poverty, 13 yet the eyes of the Lord looked upon him for good, and raised him up from his lowliness, and lifted up his head so that many marveled at him. 14 Good and evil, life and death, poverty and wealth are from the Lord. 15 Wisdom and knowledge and understanding of the Law are from the Lord. Love and the ways of good works are from Him. 16 Error and darkness were created with sinners, and those who delight in evil grow old in evil. 17 The gift of the Lord remains with the godly, and His good pleasure prospers forever.

And there is another who is lazy and needs help, strength is lacking in him and he grows poorer, yet the eyes of the Lord look upon him for his good, and He restores his good from his lowly state [12]. Many, even among the famous and the great and the heroes, when they compare the praise of people for them with the truth of their capabilities, fall into a state of frustration, and it turns into a psychological illness. Here He offers them the remedy, which is faith that God fixes His eyes on man because he is His beloved; by His grace He raises him up and grants him self-confidence.

entries.section: 4. Between true wisdom and divine help

paragraphs.text: He lifts up his head, and many are amazed at this [13].

The wise Solomon looks at history and sees horsemen famed for courage and for the ability to enter battles, who won victories, yet some of them fell suddenly in defeat. For this it was fitting for them to realize that victory is from the Lord. "The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but victory is of the LORD" (Prov 21:31)

entries.section: 4. Between true wisdom and divine help

paragraphs.text: Good and evil, life and death, and poverty and wealth are from the Lord [14]... [10]

The Holy Bible affirms two truths that touch man's life: that God gave man freedom of will so that he might be responsible for his actions, and the second, that the mind is a surpassing gift so that it may manage man's life with understanding.
Concerning freedom of will, it is said:

v God, as good and loving (generous), gave man freedom with regard to good and evil, granting him a mind by which he is able to behold the world and all that is in it, and so to know God for whose sake He created everything. As for the evil man, he may desire this (the knowledge of God), but he does not understand, rather he perishes through his unbelief and his thinking that contradicts the truth. This is man's freedom with regard to good and evil [11].
St. Anthony the Great v (Adam was free to pluck or not to pluck the deadly fruit).
Try what I say by these things that are your own, so that the solution of your doubts may come from your own thinking.
You have authority to plant or not to plant a plant, and in your hands is the possibility of doing either of the two.
If you wish to plant a vine it becomes a vine, and if you do not wish, you will not plant it and it will not become so.
Thus the Just One gave freedom to Adam whom He formed; it was within his authority to keep himself from harms.
That command was appointed for that freedom, that it might be led by its own will to where it wishes.
He set a fence for it: that Law, lest the evil seed enter into it like a stranger who does not belong to it.
She opened the door and the crafty one entered and cast his seed, and the land of the soul, which had been a paradise, was corrupted.
Evil grew and became a tree full of death, and it returned and gave the fruits of death to the one who planted it.
As Moses guided the people while teaching them (saying): Look to your heart, let there be no abominable iniquity in it.
Thus the Father commanded Adam not to eat, that is, do not receive in yourself an evil seed [12].
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh As for the relation of the mind to the soul and the body, St. Anthony the Great speaks to us, saying:

v Life is a union between the mind (spirit), the soul and the body, and a bond among them, while death is the tearing apart of this unity, but there is no perishing of all these (elements), rather God preserves them even after the separation [13].

v The mind that pleases God flows before the soul and counsels it to despise the temporal, material, perishable things, and to love the eternal, incorruptible spiritual blessings, so that man, while still in the body, perceives the heavenly and divine things with his mind and contemplates them. By this the mind that loves God is profitable to the soul and its rescuer.

v The souls that are not bridled by the mind, and not governed by the intellect, which suppresses their passions of pleasures and pains, and manages them and directs them (rightly), these souls perish like the irrational animals. For their minds are drawn by the passions, as unruly horses drag their drivers.

v The soul is in the body, and the mind is in the soul, and the Word is in the mind, and by the Word we contemplate God and glorify Him, who gives immortality to the soul and grants it eternal, incorruptible happiness.
St. Anthony the Great v The adornment of the body is the mind, and the adornment of the mind is God [14].

St. Augustine The view of the wise man toward wealth: when the believer is in touch with the Lord's care, he is not disturbed by poverty, nor does he exalt himself because of wealth. All that occupies him is cleaving to the Lord.

entries.section: 4. Between true wisdom and divine help

paragraphs.text: v If you regard wealth and the fullness of its enjoyment as nothing but a deceptive show of pride for a short time, and you know that the virtuous life that pleases God is better than wealth, and you hold fast to this belief and keep it in your memory, then you will never sigh nor murmur nor rebuke anyone, but you will give thanks to God in every circumstance, even if you see people worse than you being praised for their eloquence or knowledge or wealth. The desire for wealth with greed and for pleasures, and the love of lust and vainglory, joined with ignorance of the truth, bring the worst sufferings of the soul [15].
St. Anthony the Great The gift of the Lord remains with the godly, and His good pleasure brings prosperity forever [15].

The wise man says: "Good and evil, life and death, and poverty and wealth are from the Lord" (see Sir 11:14). Some ask whether God is the source of evil as He is the source of good. Is God, the Giver of life, the fountain of life and the fountain of death? Is the Giver of gifts the source of poverty as of wealth?

entries.section: 4. Between true wisdom and divine help

paragraphs.text: v The cause of death is Satan, he who deceived man, but God brought upon him the punishment of death not as one who first issued (the command of death), but as a (natural) punishment for sin. You yourself answered the question perfectly when you said that man was left to himself, and so he became a torment to himself, through the judgment of God, and this was accomplished by his free will. There is no contradiction in the fact that man himself is the source of his punishment, and that God takes vengeance on sin [16].
St. Augustine v Open to us, O Lord, the treasury, at the prayers of our supplications.
Let our prayers serve as an ambassador for us, and reconcile us with Your divinity.
Hearken, O wise men, and give heed, all you who are learners.

entries.section: 4. Between true wisdom and divine help

paragraphs.text: Seek understanding and knowledge, seeing that you are learners and wise (in the Lord) [17].

St. Mar Ephraim the Syrian v When you see a corpse carried in the market, followed by orphaned children, and a widow beating her breast, and servants wailing, and friends depressed, consider the triviality of present things, and that they do not differ at all from a shadow or a dream. Does this not suit you? Think of those who were very rich and perished in the war. Look at the houses around you, which belonged to famous great men, and now have come down to the ground.

entries.section: 4. Between true wisdom and divine help

paragraphs.text: Consider how powerful they were, and now no memory at all has been left for them. And if you wish, you will find every day examples of these things: from the quarrels of rulers, and the confiscation of the property of the rich. Many tyrants have sat on the dust, and he who never thought of it has put on the crown" (see Sir 11:15). Are not our affairs like a wheel? [18]
St. John Chrysostom

18 There is a rich man who has grown rich by his care and thrift, and this is the portion of his reward, 19 when he says: "I have found rest, and now I will eat of my goods," 20 and he does not know how much time will pass until he leaves it to others and dies. 21 Stand fast in your covenant, and be busy in it, and grow old in your work. 22 Do not marvel at the works of sinners. Trust in the Lord and abide in your labor. 23 For it is easy in the eyes of the Lord to make the poor man rich suddenly, in an instant. 24 The blessing of the Lord is in the reward of the godly, and in a moment He makes his blessing flourish. 25 Do not say: "What need have I, and what good shall come to me from now on?" 26 Do not say: "I have enough, so why should I toil from now on?"

The Lord Christ explained this saying to us by the parable of the rich man who thought that his possessions would give his soul satisfaction for many years, and did not know that his soul would be required of him that very night (Lk 12:16-21).
There is a man who grows rich by his care and thrift, and this is the portion of his reward: [16]
when he says: "I have found rest, and now I will share my goods," and he does not know how much time will pass until he dies and leaves that to others [17].

It is among the most grievous things that a man should spend all his life preparing what he will possess for the future in this world, not knowing what will befall. His position is very pitiable, since he puts his hope in the wrong place. For wealth can keep a man from many troubles, but it cannot drive death away from its owner. Death robs a man of what he consecrated his life to acquiring. This is what the parable of the rich man affirmed, who built many of his storehouses to eat and drink and be merry, and he heard the voice of the Lord: "Fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?" (Lk 12:16-20). This parable presents two warnings: preparation for passing from this world; and avoidance of covetousness.

The catastrophe is not in the person's death but in his lack of preparation for passing from the world, and the loss of his whole life in gathering what he will leave behind involuntarily; therefore the Lord called him "fool" (Lk 12:20).
Stand fast in your covenant, and care for it, and reach old age in your work [18].

v Let no one think that the Apostle differs from these words of ours by saying: that they work quietly, and eat their own bread (2 Thess 3:11-12). This commandment is directed to the stubborn and the slack, and it means that it is better for every man to serve at least himself, and not be a burden on others and live idle... Again, his saying: "We wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you" (2 Thess 3:8), carries the same meaning. In the name of brotherly love the Apostle bore the burden of work, besides his obligation toward those who were committed to him, with the aim of eliminating disorder. He who strives passionately for perfection is bound to work night and day, "that he may have to give to him that needeth" (Eph 4:28). The man who relies on himself, or even on another person who is bound to supply him with his needs, and thinks that his own activity and the activity of him who is gathered with him is enough to help him in his livelihood, falls into danger, for he puts his hope in a man, and so falls under the curse that says: "Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD" (Jer 17:3).

Now by the saying: "trusteth in man," the Holy Bible forbids a man to put his hope in another. And by saying "maketh flesh his arm" it forbids him to rely on himself. In both cases there is a turning away from the Lord (that is, his heart departs from the Lord). Then it joins the two together by saying: "For he shall be like the tamaric in the desert (wilderness), and shall not see when good cometh" (Jer 17:6). The Holy Bible declares that any man who makes his reliance on himself or on anyone else turns himself away from the Lord [19].
v The prohibition of excessive concern for the needs of our body does not abolish concern and work altogether.

For it remains for us to work for ourselves, not for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life (Jn 6:27), not for our bodily needs only, but also to relieve our neighbor (Eph 4:28). And the Lord will say to us on the day of judgment: "I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink..." (Mt 25:35). What we do for those who have consecrated themselves to Him is counted as if we were working with them, and the heavenly Kingdom is given to us for it.
And on the contrary, those who did not work and did not toil to help the weak and serve their neighbor will be punished (Acts 20:4, 35), and He will send them to eternal torment (Mt 25:41–46) [20].

St. Basil the Great Do not marvel at the works of the sinner, but trust in the Lord and persevere in your work, for it is easy in the eyes of the Lord to make the poor man rich suddenly in an instant (without expectation) [19].
The blessing of the Lord is in the reward of the godly man, and in a moment God makes His blessing flourish [20].
Do not say: "What need have I?
And what good things shall I receive in the future?" [21]
Do not say: I am independent [21]. From now on what evil will befall me?" [22].

Man by nature, from childhood, tends to be self-sufficient, not depending on others. This inclination has its blessings if it is used with moderation and wisdom, and through it he feels a kind of independence. But if he isolates himself from God and does not trust in Him, this drives him to a kind of dictatorship and arrogance.

God upholds man that he may enjoy a sound personality, one of whose requirements is self-confidence, through the work of His divine grace, but not in conceit of himself and arrogance toward his Creator who cares for him.

entries.section: 6. True wisdom and awaiting the end

paragraphs.text: 27 Afflictions are forgotten in the day of good things, and good things are not remembered in the day of afflictions. 28 For it is easy for the Lord to repay a man according to his ways on the day of death. 29 An hour of evil makes one forget pleasures, and at a man's death his works are revealed. 30 Call no one blessed before his death. A man is known by his sons.
In the day of good things, afflictions are forgotten, and in the day of afflictions good things are not remembered [23].
Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Job, in the midst of his afflictions, remembers the works he had done before, so that his soul might not be drawn to despair, but might take refuge in secure hope.
v (In a letter in which he speaks of the history of the sin of Fabiola and then of her repentance)

As I find my soul dashing against the weaknesses of Fabiola's sin, I have spoken much of it and of her repentance, that I may open a broad and calm way, unhindered, in order to describe her praise. She returned to communion before the eyes of the whole Church. What did she do? In the days of good things she forgot the afflictions (see Sir 11:23). And when her ship was wrecked she did not wish to face the dangers of the sea again. Therefore instead of returning to board the ship of her former life, she sold everything she could lay her hand on of her possessions (for they were great, befitting her rank), and turned it into cash and offered it for the benefit of the poor. If someone set up a hospital that gathered the sufferers in the streets, she would nurse them, and all the victims of diseases and want [22].
St. Jerome For it is easy for the Lord to reward a man on the day of his death according to his ways [24].
The hour of harsh treatment makes a man forget luxury, and at the end of a man's life his works are revealed [25].
It is hard to judge a person while he is still breathing, and even after his death the Church does not hasten to consider a person a saint.

v Nothing is against philosophy (wisdom) like a life of pleasure, and on the other hand, nothing is so profitable to philosophy as pain. Consider what the state of the covetous man will be. For it is said: "An hour of evil makes a man forget pleasures" (see Sir 11:25) [23].
St. John Chrysostom Do not consider anyone happy before his death, and a man will be known in his children [26].

The praise of the departed is better than the praise of the living: the wise, godly man, who fears the Lord, is praised at the close of his life, for a man's praise at the end of his life is better than his praise during his life.

v It is written that wisdom is known at death, meaning that the life of the wise man is praised at the end of his life. Therefore we read elsewhere: "Do not praise a man during his life, and do not call a man blessed before his death" (see Sir 11:26-28). Suppose a man says: I will praise a man after his death, because praising a living man can be an occasion for vainglory, because of the commendation of him or for flattery by him who offers the praise.

In every case, praise of the dead is useful, first because, the person being absent, who will reward us for our praise of him? It is necessary that all the glory be referred to the Giver of grace. Second, admiration of virtue remains without doubt free from flattery. Therefore the praise of the dead that is proclaimed in the holy assembly of the believers is full of edification and free from any kind of flattery [24].

Hilary, bishop of Arles v "Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth" (Prov 27:1). It is written: "Call no one blessed before his death." For as long as we live we are busy with a battle, and there is no sure victory such as appears in the life to come [25].

St. Jerome v How can you know him who is unknown even to himself?... Where then is the assurance? Here there is no assurance in this life, save only in hope of the promise of God. But there, when we arrive, we shall be in complete safety, where the doors are shut, where the bars of the gates of Jerusalem are strengthened (Ps 147:13). There is truly perfect exultation and great joy. You do not feel safe in praising any kind of life: "Call no one blessed before his death" (see Sir 11:26) [26].

St. Augustine v Death, which was hated, has become a subject of praise and is proclaimed as a blessed thing. What was at one time a cause of pain and sorrow and tears and gloom appears as a source of joy and festival. All the servants of God enjoy the blessed death, because the end of their life brings security where God welcomes them. In truth they become perfect, and this perfection restores to them their blessedness and gives them the firmness of virtue, as the teaching affirms: "Judge no one before his death" [26][27].
Father John of Damascus

entries.section: 7. True wisdom and caution against the wicked

paragraphs.text: 31 Do not bring every man into your house; for the schemes of the deceiver are many. 32 Like a decoy partridge in a cage, so is the heart of the proud, and he is like a spy watching for a fall. 33 For he lies in wait, turning good into evil, and stains the chosen with blemishes. 34 From one spark a fire is multiplied, and the sinful man lies in wait for blood. 35 Beware of the wicked man who devises evils, lest he bring upon you a disgrace forever. 36 Receive a stranger into your house, and he will upset your affairs with trouble, and drive you out of your own.

With Sirach's continual speaking about giving, almsgiving and love, he nevertheless wants the believer to keep to wisdom and moderation in every action for the edification of himself and of those with whom he deals. So he warns against the wicked exploiting the service given to strangers, the poor and enemies.

Ben Sira refuses giving to one who insists on evil, like one who takes alms to buy a weapon with which to kill, or to buy drugs, etc. [12:1-2]. Our Christ calls us in the Sermon on the Mount to give with love even to enemies (Mt 5:44-45), so that we bear witness to the love of God for sinners who have entered into enmity against God. St. Augustine sees that love moves us to give in the spirit of wisdom, so that if we know that the gift will be used to harm the one who asks alms or those around him, we ought to give him not money but, in a spirit of love and tenderness, offer him holy counsel in the Lord. In this we imitate the Lord, who even in His discipline offers love, with a longing for the wicked man to return from his wickedness.
Do not bring every man into your house, for the schemes of the deceiver are many [27].

It is fitting for the believer, with his love of hospitality to strangers, if a man is known to be a slanderer who spreads rumors and lies, not to invite him to his house, lest he spoil the purity of the hearts of the household. For the slanderer turns even good into evil, and by his false and lying words kindles a fire in the midst of the family whose consequences are not to be praised (Jas 3:5-6). The wicked man works to isolate his listener from his society, whether family (the household) or Church. St. Clement of Alexandria sees that he does not leave his house unguarded, hosting a deceitful man who may corrupt his purity and the purity of the members of his household [28].

v It is written: "Do not bring every man into your house" (see Sir 11:27). So when a stranger approaches you, first pray to God, and after that ask him about his concerns, where he came from and where he is going. If it appears to you that you ought to welcome him, receive him and ask him to depart after the meal, and do not give him anything else. For if you enter with him into material dealings beyond your capacity, you will not be able to bear him afterward [29].

St. Barsanuphius and his disciple John v I do not mean to diminish the virtue of our forefathers, especially hospitality. In truth it is among the loftiest virtues the fathers practiced, this which inclines toward piety. One of them received God the Savior at his table, and another received angels. One received a reward and had a son in his old age, and the other enjoyed salvation as he fled from Sodom (Gen 18-19). This is what the Apostle spoke of when he urged us to imitate him: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares" (Heb 13:2).

At any rate, let the person who offers hospitality have the wisdom of the serpent and the simplicity of the dove (Mt 10:16), obeying the Lord's double commandment: "Give to every man that asketh of thee" (Lk 6:30), "Do not bring every man into your house" [27]. This is so that you do not bring the danger of a wolf into a dwelling where a lamb lives (Mt 7:15), or a bear where there is an ox (Isa 11:7), which turns gain into loss.
First of all, it is necessary to take into account your ability to tolerate very difficult characters.

Finally you must consider who it is that you are receiving to obtain benefits from you, whether he is rich or poor, in good health or weak, in need of food or clothing. These are the fields in which mercy is practiced. In truth the blessed Abraham did not receive in his house (tent) counselors and leaders, the dominant persons of this passing world, who have horses... Abraham dwelt in an empty place receiving passers-by; those who travel in the desert came to the father, drawn toward his virtue, and some of them had become beggars in extreme poverty. In the same way Lot, who lived in the most wicked city in this desert, truly welcomed all passers-by, to preserve them from the customs of its inhabitants [30].
St. Palladius The heart of the proud is like a partridge set as a decoy in a cage, and like a spy watching for your fall [28].

It is stated in (Jeremiah 17:11): "The partridge utters its voice (the Septuagint), it gathers what it did not lay, he who gets riches unjustly; in the midst of his days he will leave them, and in his end he will be a fool." This was often a common proverb at that time, meaning that a man thinks he possesses, yet as he toils and labors he loses much, and wealth leaves him while he is still in the world in the midst of his days, but at his end he realizes that he walked in folly. This is the literal interpretation of the passage; and before we shed light on it through the deep spiritual meaning, we wish to clarify that the partridge is a wild bird, called in Hebrew "Qore," which means "the one who cries out or calls." And perhaps for this reason it came in the Septuagint version: "the partridge utters its voice" or "gives its voice"; it is one that has voices but no true work! So the rich man, in his bitter striving to enjoy wealth materially or to be satisfied bodily, is like one who gives a voice without work, for he leaves everything and goes out naked from this world.

St. Hippolytus sees that this bird is arrogant, for when the partridge sees the nest of another partridge with young ones without their mother, it makes a sound imitating the mother's voice and calls the young ones to it, and takes them and runs off with them. And it rejoices proudly that it has seized them, but when the true mother comes and calls with her voice, the young ones discover the deception of the first, and leave the deceiver and go to the true mother. This will happen when the Antichrist comes, for he draws humanity to himself by deception to reign over those who are not his, and promises them salvation though he is unable to save himself [31].

The partridge signifies the devil and his hosts, especially the heretics; it gives its own voice, and does not utter what belongs to God, while the children of God utter what belongs to God and not what belongs to themselves, as the Apostle Paul says: "Since ye seek a proof of Christ speaking in me" (2 Cor 13:3).

entries.section: 7. True wisdom and caution against the wicked

paragraphs.text: St. Gregory of Nyssa speaks of the man who is bound to the wiles of the devil and falls under the deceptions of the enemy: [The true good God and Father is no longer God and Father to him who by his corruption becomes an outlaw... and in place of the Father comes one who seems to be a father, who is falsely called the partridge that gathers what it did not lay, as Jeremiah says [32].]
Origen sees that Satan is the partridge, like Pharaoh who did not want the people to leave his land to worship the Lord.
For he lies in wait, and turns good into evil, and in the best of things finds fault with what the good man chooses [29].
From one spark a fire is kindled in the coals, and the sinful man lies in wait to shed blood [30].
Beware of the wicked man and his schemes, lest disgrace overtake you forever [31].

entries.section: 7. True wisdom and caution against the wicked

paragraphs.text: v Just as the simple and unlearned mock the sciences and refuse to listen to anything of them, because knowledge to them is folly, and so they wish that all should be ignorant like them, so also those who are dissolute in their life and morals have a great longing that all should be worse than they, thinking that by this they find an excuse for themselves, since the wicked are many [33].
v The wise man, or he who has begun to reform himself, is alone he who deserves to be called a man... for this quality (incorrigibility) does not befit a man, and such a man must be shunned.

entries.section: 7. True wisdom and caution against the wicked

paragraphs.text: Those who are pleased with iniquity will have no portion among the immortals [34].
St. Anthony the Great Receive a stranger into your house, and he will grieve you with troubles, and estrange from you the members of your household [32].
Inspired by Sirach 11

entries.section: Grant me the spirit of love, management and security!

paragraphs.text: v Your divine presence sanctifies my family and my friends.
Often I relied on my human wisdom, and outward appearances deceived me in everyone I met.
Reveal Your presence within me, O You who are wonderful in Your humility!
In You I walk in the spirit of wisdom in humility.
Your wisdom carries me across from the last rows, and seats me in the council of the heavenly ones.
It removes from me the folly that brought me down to the dunghill.
v In You, O incarnate Wisdom of God, I am not deceived by a man's beauty and appearance.
And I mock no one because of a defect in his body!
The prophet Samuel looked at the beauty of Saul and his tall stature, and thought him the best fit to be king.
And You looked at the heart of the boy David, and prepared him to sit on the throne of Your people.
v Many look at the bee as a small insect that stings, and have not realized that many nations live on the honey it produces.
So many look at persons who seem to have no beauty, and do not realize that they will receive a glorious throne from Your hands.
A husband sometimes regrets that his wife lacks beauty of body, and has not realized that she surpasses many women in beauty of spirit and mind.
In his eyes she is a burden he wishes to be rid of, and in Your eyes her heart is a second heaven, rejoicing!
v Grant me prudence and not to be hasty in judging others.
Grant me not to cease from work until the last breath, imitating the angels who never tire of continual work according to Your will.
Grant me not to be troubled with many works, but to take care to be faithful in little, so that I may be made worthy to receive much in eternity.
Let me work with joy, and look forward to the day of my departure from the world rejoicing.
Grant me wisdom, that I may not allow everyone to enter my house, lest You, O Holy One, depart from it.
Grant me, in the midst of distress, not to desire failure for him who caused it to me.
Grant me, in the midst of my pains, to thank You for the former days of relief.
v In Your love You gave me free will; who can sanctify it and establish it except You?
In You I defy evil and embrace good; in You I thank You even if I become poor, and I serve You with what You have given me of possessions.
In You I defy death, and find sweet the life in You!
In the time of famine I do not forget the days of plenty, and in the time of prosperity I share with my brethren what You have given me!
v Let the days of my sojourn pass while I am in Your company, and let me look forward to death in the spirit of hope.
On the way of sojourn I neither criticize anyone nor praise him, for I look forward to Your grace with every morning.
Do not allow my heart, in my sojourn, to be proud.
Like the partridge shut up in a cage.
It does not cease its annoying cry without work!
Instead of this voice, let me enjoy Your sweet word.
For not by bread alone do I live here, but by every word that proceeds out of Your mouth.
Finally, sanctify me, O Holy One, and sanctify every family and all friends, indeed the whole world.

1 If you do good, know to whom you do it, and your kindness will be acceptable. 2 Do good to the godly man and you will receive a reward; if not from him, then from the Most High. 3 There is no good for him who persists in evil and does not give alms, for the Most High hates sinners, and has mercy on the repentant. 4 Give to the godly man and do not help the sinner; for He will take vengeance on the hypocrites and sinners, but He keeps them for the day of vengeance. 5 Give to the good man, and do not support the sinner. 6 Do good to the humble man, and do not give to the hypocrite. Hold back your bread and do not give it to him, lest he be strengthened by it against you, 7 and you meet with evil twice as much as all the good you did to him. For the Most High hates sinners, and repays the hypocrites with vengeance.

The Apostle Paul warns us against hosting people who may cause us, as well as others, spiritual troubles, saying: "For of this sort are they which creep into houses, and lead captive silly women laden with sins, led away with divers lusts" (2 Tim 3:6).
Ben Sira offers us practical counsels on doing good to others:
a. In the spirit of wisdom we must get to know those to whom we do good, so that we offer them what is for their edification and ours and the edification of others.

b. Since we see in the needy man who receives the kindness the Savior of the world Himself, we must therefore care the more for the godly or for those who long for a life of godliness. This is what the Apostle called us to by saying: "As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith" (Gal 6:10). In this we offer the gift to the Most High Himself [2]. And on the other hand, it is fitting for us, even in our material giving, to offer the food of the spirit in a spirit of love and humility.
c. Not to be deceived by appearance, for a person may seem humble for a time, but time reveals his depths [11].
d. To take care that the person does not use the kindness for evil to himself or to others [3-4].

e. We support the needy so that he may not fall into evil, and so that he may not misuse the tenderness of the giver, especially if begging has turned into the practice of tricks in society. For instead of enjoying the kindness his evils increase and multiply [5].
If you do good, know to whom you do it, and you will be thanked for your good works [1].
St. Ambrose sees that every kindness offered to a poor or needy person is counted as fellowship with the woman who poured the ointment on the feet of the Lord Christ (Lk 7:38).

v Christ died once and was buried once, and yet He wishes that the ointment be poured on His feet every day. Who are counted as the feet of Christ, on whom we pour the ointment, except those of whom He said: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." These are the two feet that the woman mentioned in the Gospel refreshed, and washed with her tears [1].
St. Ambrose Do good to the godly man, and you will receive a reward; if not from him, then from the Most High [2].
v It appears that mercy toward the poor is truly the pouring of oil on God's sacrifice, while the service offered to the saints adds the sweetness of incense [2].

Origen v When someone preaches and you serve him, you share his crowns. For even in wrestling it is not the victor alone who takes the crown, but his trainer shares it with him, and those present and all who prepared the wrestling ring. Those who truly lead and train him share his victory... If we serve the saints with a good heart we share their reward. This is what Christ also tells us: "Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations" (Lk 16:9) [3].

St. John Chrysostom v When the blessed Apostle Paul helped the brethren in the needs of his affliction he said that these good works are sacrifices to God... So when one has compassion on a poor man he lends to God, and when he gives to the little ones he gives God spiritual sacrifices of a sweet-smelling aroma [4].

The Martyr Cyprian Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles, sees that man needs alms, not only of money with which to acquire food for his stomach, but also of the word of God so that his mind may be satisfied with the food of the spirit. Let us offer alms from the word of God, and not wait for anyone to repay it to us, but the Lord Himself will repay it to us.

v Perhaps a man has no bread to offer as alms to the needy, but there remains what is greater, that a man should have a tongue able to give. For he who refreshes the mind to live forever with the food of the Word is greater than he who satisfies with earthly food the stomach of the body that dies.

Therefore, brethren, do not refrain from offering the alms of the word to your relatives. Paul says: "If we have sown unto you spiritual things, is it a great thing if we shall reap your carnal things?" (1 Cor 9:11). "Do good to the godly man, and you will receive a great reward; if not from him, then surely from God" (see Sir 12:2) [5].
Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles There is no kindness to him who persists in evil, or who does not give alms with joy [3].
v Alms are given, but with wisdom to the deserving, that we may receive a reward from the Most High.

And woe to those who assume a deceptive appearance, and those who are able to help themselves and ask from others, for he who has means and pretends with a deceptive appearance or asks because of laziness is condemned [6].

St. Clement of Alexandria v Give to everyone who asks of you without return (Lk 6:30). For the Father wants all to share in the blessings that we have. Blessed is he who gives according to the commandment, for he is blameless. Woe to him who receives without need. If one receives out of want he is counted blameless. But if he receives without want, he will give account of the reason and the purpose for which he received. He is cast into prison, and is questioned about his conduct, and does not come out from there till he has paid the uttermost farthing (Mt 5:26). But it is also said in this regard: Let your alms sweat in your hands [7], until you know to whom you give [8].
The Didache Give to the godly man, and do not help the sinner [4].

Perhaps someone asks: How can one fulfill the commandment: "Give to him that asketh thee" (Mt 5:42) and also: "If thine enemy hunger, feed him" (Rom 12:20); and at the same time: "Do not help the wicked (the sinner)" [4]?

v Let mercy be exercised toward the wicked, not as being wicked, that is, do not receive the wicked as wicked, do not receive him because you incline to his evil and approve it. For it is forbidden to give to the wicked... But how do we listen to the saying: "Give to him that asketh thee" (Mt 5:24), and also: "If thine enemy hunger, feed him" (Rom 12:20)? Perhaps there seems to be in this a kind of contradiction, but let us open to those who knock in the name of Christ, and the matter becomes clear to him who asks...

If a sinner asks me, I give him, not as being a sinner. When do you give to him as a sinner? When you give him what makes him a sinner, and you are pleased when you give him... Would that those who give to a man who fights with wild beasts would tell me why they give to him?.. When you give, give to him so as to put him to shame, not to boasting (in error) [9].

v It seems at the end of the passage that it condemns kindness, for it says: "Do not help the sinner." You must understand that "the sinner" here represents sin symbolically, so that what we cease to help is his sin [10].

St. Augustine v It is written: "Place your bread and your wine on the tomb of the righteous, and do not eat or drink of them with sinners" (Tob 4:18), and he who offers bread and wine to the wicked offers help to the wicked for the sake of their wickedness. There are some rich men who feed the clowns of the theater lavishly, while poor Christians starve. But he who offers bread to the ungodly because he is a human being, and not because he is ungodly, in truth feeds a righteous beggar and not a sinner, for he loves in him his human nature and not his sin [11].
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Do good to the humble man, and do not give to the wicked.
Hold back his bread, and do not give it to him, lest he rule over you by it.
And you will reap from evil twice as much as all the good you did to him [5].

"Do good to the humble man." This commandment, as Pope Gregory (the Great) says, is directed to the rich who flatter the prodigal at their banquets, while the poor suffer from hunger [12].
