It is fitting for us to give to the poor as human beings and not as sinners; and if we realize that he uses the gift for evil, we may not support him.
For the Most High also hates sinners, and repays the wicked with punishment [6].
The Lord punishes sinners who persist in their evils and do not return to Him in repentance.
Give to the good man, and do not help the sinner [7].

The work of the divine commandment is to raise man gradually, especially in the practice of love and giving and not attacking others. This is what St. John Chrysostom and St. Augustine and others made clear. To clarify this we present in a few lines the degrees of the ladder of love:

a. At the bottom man tends to attack others without cause, so some tribes would attack neighboring tribes merely to seize some of their possessions or to dominate them. As we observe, some children, before they learn to speak, tend to snatch what is in the hands of other children even though they make no use of what they snatch.

b. As man ascends the ladder of love, he does not attack his brother without cause, but if the brother attacks him he returns the attack with a doubled attack in order to discipline him so that he does not repeat it.

c. The Mosaic Law rejected the two former degrees, and permitted man, because of his human weakness, to control himself, so that he returns the attack only in equal measure: "Eye for eye, tooth for tooth."
d. The believer can rise higher, so that he returns the blow with less than it, merely for discipline and not for punishment.
e. What is higher is that a man forgives his brother for what he did against him.

f. The Lord Christ came and called us to the glory of the liberty of the children of God to return evil with good, and not merely for the believer to give up his right. It was not possible to reach the last degree before the coming of the Lord Christ and our receiving the grace of sonship to God. Therefore the commandments in the Old Testament came to do good to the godly man, and permitted him not to do good to the wicked.

The commandment forbade doing good to the sinner not out of hatred for him, but so that he might review himself and turn back from his evil, and seek the life of godliness. The Apostle wanted the believers to support their brethren to grow in the holy, godly life, for he says: "As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith" (Gal 6:10).

8 A friend is not known in prosperity, nor is an enemy hidden in adversity. 9 In a man's prosperity his enemies are grieved, and in his adversity even his friend departs. 10 Never trust your enemy, for his wickedness is like the rust of copper. 11 Even if he is humble and walks with bowed head, take heed to yourself and beware of him; for you will be with him as one who has polished a mirror, and you will know that its cleanness from rust does not last. 12 Do not make him stand near you, lest he overthrow you and stand in your place. Do not seat him at your right hand, lest he covet your seat. And in the end you will understand my words and be pricked by my sayings. 13 Who will pity a charmer bitten by a serpent? Or who will have compassion on those who go near wild beasts?

In difficult circumstances we can sort out the sincere friend from the enemy disguised in the garment of friendship. With wisdom the believer discerns the true friend from the enemy who has sweetness on his lips while he plans his friend's descent into a pit. The enemy's eyes may shed tears as one who pities him, while within him lies a desire to shed his blood.
As Ben Sira offered practical counsels in the spirit of wisdom and godliness concerning doing good, here he offers counsels that the believer ought to observe in choosing a friend, and they are:

a. Distress sorts the friend from the enemy. The first, with all his heart and capabilities, wants to help, while the second shows in his features and conduct the spirit of enmity, such as leaving him and ignoring him in the midst of distress [8-9].
b. Not to be hasty in choosing a friend, until time reveals him and distinguishes him.
c. Not to be deceived by appearance, for a person may seem humble, but time reveals his arrogant depths [11].
d. Not to give him the opportunity to draw near to him as long as he is set on evil, lest he overpower his friend [12].
e. We beware of him who is like a serpent that waits for the opportunity to bite charmers, or like a beast that devours him who approaches it [13].
f. We must not be deceived by the smile or tears of him who within desires to shed blood [15-16].
A friend is not known while you are in prosperity, nor does the enemy hide himself while you are in adversity [8].
In a man's prosperity his enemies grieve, and in his adversity even his friend departs from him [9].
Never trust your enemy, for as copper rusts so is his wickedness [10].

The enemy of good does not cease to oppose the children of God, using human beings or wicked angels to oppose them. Therefore Ben Sira warns us of these enemies, as instruments of iniquity who work for the kingdom of darkness.

The Christian is not a man isolated from society, but positive toward it, a servant of all and a lover of all. But he does not keep pace with the children of the world in their evil, that is, he does not practice love at the expense of the salvation of his soul or theirs. Therefore Holy Scripture demanded the necessity of care in choosing friends (Ps 1:1; 1 Cor 10:33; 1 Cor 5:6-7).
v Keeping company with those who are not wise shatters the heart, and conversation with the virtuous is a sweet spring.

v Do not stoop to the slack, or you will have made yourself of the lowest degree, but let your converse be with lovers of good, that your dwelling with them may be on high. Let your station be, with courage, in the places where the highest knowledge is. Go to the city of light, and do not go down to the sinners.

Mar Isaac the Syrian v This is the fuel of Satan who wrestles with us, who kindles the fire that burns us: corrupt talk with laymen... And the mother of evils is the throat and association with idle brethren. If our souls are stripped of this burning fuel, they will not fall into the snares of our wrestlers, and they can quickly fly to God, and through Him be delivered from the schemes of the devil.

The friendship of companions in idleness and amusement fills you with gluttony and evil. Oh, what unclean love and polluted act is this?! Flee, my brother, from those who are accustomed to this. Do not eat with them, and do not befriend them. Their table is unclean, and the demons are helpers in preparing it; the lovers of Christ the Bridegroom do not taste it. The banquet of the gluttonous man who is diverted by delicacies... defiles the soul of the meek, while a dry crust of bread from the table of the pure of soul cleanses it of all pains and defilements. The smell of the table of evil corrupts the intention of the pure, and the child is drawn to it like the dog to the butcher's house. And he who persists in prayer at all times, his table surpasses the fragrance of musk, and he who loves God longs for it like a treasure.
The Spiritual Elder v If someone loves me and I love him exceedingly, and I know that a lack has come upon me because of his love, I cut him off from me, and I cut myself off from him entirely.

Abba Agathon v If you have a friendship with one of the brethren and you suffer harm because of your association with him, hasten and cut yourself off from him. I do not say this to you, beloved, that you should hate people, no. But that you may cut off the causes of vice.

Mar Ephraim the Syrian v Hear what the Lord says: "Wherefore if thy hand or thy foot offend thee, cut them off, and cast them from thee: it is better for thee to enter into life halt or maimed, rather than having two hands or two feet to be cast into everlasting fire. And if thine eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee: it is better for thee to enter into life with one eye, rather than having two eyes to be cast into hell fire" (Mt 18:8-9).

He did not say this about the members, but for the sake of the brethren and relatives who are to us in the position of necessary members... So he says that nothing is more harmful than bad company and wicked association, for friendship often harms or benefits... So He commands us with great plainness to cut off those who harm us...

He did not limit Himself to pronouncing woe on him through whom offenses come, but showed us the way by which a man is saved from offenses. What is this way? He said: Cut off the friendship of the wicked, even if it is in the forest... and do not gain them and destroy your soul with them.

St. John Chrysostom v I charge you, my son, not to walk on the road with a man from whom you have no spiritual benefit, lest you stumble on your journey. And do not keep company with an angry man or a hot-tempered one.
And do not associate with a slanderer or a talkative man.
Do not walk with the envious, for "the meek shall inherit the earth" (Mt 4:5).
Do not walk on the road with a slack man.
And do not befriend a confused man, nor one who has a friendship with a woman.
But watch yourself according to your strength that you have no friendship with a woman.
And do not walk on the road with one who is younger than you, lest you come to the rear.
St. Stephen of Thebes And even if he humbles himself and walks with bowed head, take heed to yourself and beware of him.
Be with him as one who polishes a mirror, and you will know that it is not spoiled forever [11].

v Do not spoil God's commandment for the sake of anyone's friendship. Do not return again to the city in which you sinned against God. Do not abandon worship, lest it become a snare and a stumbling block to you.
The blessed Abba Anthony Do not let him stand beside you, lest he throw you down and occupy your place.
Do not seat him at your right hand, lest he covet the seat of your honor, then you will understand my words at last, and be pricked with sorrow by my words [12].

St. Basil warns us against envy, because it offers an odious kind of friendship that does not know true love, rather all that occupies the friend is that he covets what his friend has, whether money or honor or privilege.

v There is no passion in the heart of man so corrupting as envy. Nothing harms a man like him who is afflicted with it. And as rust corrupts iron, so envy corrupts the man afflicted with it. Envy is a sorrow born of the neighbor's happiness. So the envious man is never without occasions for sorrow. Is the neighbor's field fertile? Is his house pleasant? Is he happy? All this drives the envious man to nurture his disease and to increase his torments. He is like a naked man at whose wound the arrows of everything are aimed. Is there someone strong and in good health? It is a blow that strikes the envious man. Is there a beautiful man? It is a new wound. Is a man intelligent, successful in his works, and doing good? All these are arrows that strike the envious man in the very core of his heart.

The hardest thing in this disease is that it is a shameful disease. The envious man complains of his condition and his strength declines, but if you ask him the cause of his illness, he is ashamed to confess it: "I am envious, and I feel bitterness in my heart, and I suffer from my friend's happiness. I cannot bear the success of others, and my neighbor's happiness seems to me a disaster." This is what he ought to say. But he prefers to say none of this, and to keep in the very depth of his heart his illness that wears him out.

There is no physician or medicine that heals this patient, for the only relief he awaits is the ruin of those he envies. And his hatred has only one object, which is to see his neighbor turn from happy to wretched. Then he gets up and shows friendship as soon as he finds him shedding tears. He does not know how to rejoice with those who rejoice, but only to weep with those who weep, and he is sorry for the calamity that has befallen, not out of a feeling of sympathy, but to increase the weight of the pain by reminding him of what was lost... Just as vultures hover over meadows and pleasant, fragrant places, and swoop down only on carcasses, so the envious man cannot stop at the splendor of a life and the greatness of the works accomplished, but sees in all of it only the blemishes. And if a mistake is made, which is hard to avoid in human undertakings, he publicizes it at once, and on it he bases the definition of every man, as if he were a caricaturist who sees in the portrait of a man only a deformed nose, or a hump on the back, or a natural or accidental defect in the face.

Moreover, he is an expert in deceptive distortions by which good can be mocked, and virtue defamed by means of the similar opposite. The courageous becomes the reckless, the wise the stupid, the just the hard-hearted, and the thrifty the miser. In a word, virtues are turned, in his view, into the vices that oppose them" [13].
St. Basil the Great Who will have pity on a charmer bitten by the serpent, or on all who go near wild beasts? [13]

v It is said: "Who will pity a charmer bitten by a serpent?" (see Sir 12:13) It is fitting for us to know his violent tyranny, so that we may flee from that slavery, and crush the dangerous longing for it. Someone says: "And how is that possible?" By introducing another longing, that is, the longing for heaven. For he who desires the Kingdom mocks the demon of greed and despises him. For he who becomes a slave of Christ no longer is a slave of greed, but its master [14].
St. John Chrysostom

13 So he who keeps company with a sinful man is mingled with his sins. 14 He stays with you for an hour, and if you waver he does not stand firm. 15 The enemy shows sweetness with his lips, and in his heart he plots to throw you into the pit. 16 The enemy's eyes shed tears, and if he finds an opportunity he will not be satisfied with blood. 17 If evil befalls you, you will find him there before you, 18 and while he pretends to help you, he trips your foot. 19 He shakes his head and claps his hands, and whispers many things, and changes his countenance.
So no one pities him who keeps company with the sinful man and is entangled in his sins [14].

v As the fierce beast devours a tender and noble body unable to defend itself, so pride plants its violent fangs and pours into you its poison and its extremely foul smell. It tears off some parts after disfiguring them, and cuts off other parts and cuts them to pieces, and devours other parts. It throws the body to the ground, and hurls itself upon it with its eye on all its members. It attacks everyone who approaches the body, and does not leave it. Who can drive away this beast? (God), who permitted this battle, sends His angels when we beseech Him, and they break the beast's boldness, and bridle its mouth, and drive it away. But He intervenes in the battle on the condition that, when it is driven away, we do not return to it.

So after driving it away He commands it to remain far from us, if we, after we have been delivered from its young ones, which were driven off to their cave, still suffer from thousands of wounds and want to return to it and wake it and provoke it. Then He no longer has mercy on us and rescues us." "Who will pity a charmer bitten by a serpent, and all who go near wild beasts?" [15]
St. John Chrysostom He stays with you for a while, and if you stagger away from him he does not stand to support you [15].
The enemy speaks with sweetness on his lips, and in his heart he plans to throw you into the pit.
The enemy sheds tears, and if the opportunity arises, he is not satisfied with shedding your blood [16].
It is fitting for us to beware the wiles of the deceiving devil, who draws us to the wicked by their honeyed words, while in their heart they want to push us to destruction.
St. Cyril the Great warns us of the nets of the heretics who with their honeyed words corrupt the work of faith.
If evil befalls you, you find your enemy there before you, appearing to help you, and he trips your heel [17].
In rebuking the serpent, the Lord said to it: "He shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel" (Gen 3:15).

Behold the deceitful friend who bears the spirit of enmity: when he finds his friend in distress he hastens to him and appears jealous for him, wanting to rescue him, and behold, he trips his heel [17]. What does tripping his heel mean? If our Savior has granted us by the Cross to crush the head of the old serpent, the devil, behold this false friend trips his friend's heel so that he may not crush the head of Satan!

Faithful friendship, through which the Crucified One declares His dwelling in the two friends, so that they crush enmity and anger and deceit and guile, that is, all that belongs to the old serpent. The deceitful friend cannot bear the crushing of the head of his father the devil, therefore he trips his friend's heel.
He shakes his head, and claps his hands, and whispers many things, and changes his features [18].

The deceiving friend, when he sees his friend in distress, shakes his head and claps his hands and whispers... These outward movements are an expression of inner gloating (Ps 22:7; Job 16:4; Ezek 25:9).
This enemy does not stop at deceiving through the false smile or the lying tears, but hastens to add pains to the person's pains; he pushes him on and on toward destruction.
Inspired by Sirach 12

entries.section: Grant me, O Lord, the spirit of discernment!

paragraphs.text: v I call upon You, O Lover of mankind, to grant me the spirit of discernment.
By Your grace I know how to offer kindness to my brethren, and to whom I offer it? And what are its limits?
All virtues without the spirit of discernment turn into vices.
My soul longs to offer You to them, for You are the satisfaction of hungry souls and the wealth of needy souls.
What good can I offer except the cleaving of all to You, O Maker of good things?!
Grant me to have compassion on sinners, as You have compassion on me, the sinner.
Grant me not to do good in ignorance and folly, lest by my kindness I push the wicked man on, and his evil is multiplied.
v Let me love sinners, and hate sin! You called Your betraying disciple Judas "Friend," yet You did not flatter him, but in firmness You said:
"Friend, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?"
Grant me not to flatter anyone, but in earnestness with tenderness to seek their salvation.
Let my friends be to me as a mirror.
I meet them, and so I realize my faults. And without deceit they discover their own faults.
v Let me imitate You who came down to us.
You took the last row of the rows of humanity.
You were crucified as a slave between two wicked thieves, whom society wanted to be rid of.
You were near them in the body; Your cross approaches their cross to within a few meters.
Dismas the thief believed in You as his Lord and King. He longed that You remember him in Your Kingdom, and You sent him at once to Paradise.
The heavenly ones were amazed that he gained the right of fellowship in the divine glories.
The other thief was at the same distance from Your cross in body.
But he was in a great chasm, for he surrendered himself to evil and rejected faith.
He became a son of the abyss, unable to meet You, depriving himself of enjoying Your majesty and Your glory!
The first thief gained boldness with You, opening his heart to You that You might establish Your Kingdom in it.
And the second bore a spirit of hatred of the truth, so he deprived his insight of seeing Your glories.
Grant me the grace of cleaving to You and to all Your true believers.
When shall I see You face to face?!

entries.section: 1. Caution against the rich and those in authority

paragraphs.text: 1 He who touches pitch is defiled, and he who keeps company with the proud becomes like him. 2 Do not lift a weight beyond your strength, and do not keep company with one who is stronger and richer than you. 3 How can an earthen pot be joined with a cauldron? If it is struck, it breaks. 4 The rich man does wrong and storms, and the poor man is wronged and entreats. 5 If you are useful, he exploits you, and if you are barren, he abandons you. 6 If you have money, he lives with you and drains your money, and he does not tire. 7 If he has need of you, he deceives you and smiles at you and promises you and speaks to you of good, and says: "What do you need?" 8 And he serves you food that shames you, until he drains your money two or three times, and finally he mocks you and sees you after that and abandons you, and shakes his head at you. 9 Humble yourself before God, and wait for His hand. 10 Beware of being deceived and humbled in your folly. 11 Do not be humbled in your wisdom, lest humiliation draw you into folly.
He who touches pitch is defiled, and he who keeps company with the proud becomes like him [1].

Most of the counsels in this book concern the young who have not yet enjoyed true spiritual experience, and who do not realize the danger of their clinging to some wicked friends, especially the rich among them.

Ben Sira presents an example, the young man who touches pitch, to confirm how dangerous defilement is through a sinful friendship; the pitch here is not the person of the friend nor wealth but evil and pride. His message is a warning to the young against certain categories of people, affirming that it is wise to avoid entering into friendships with them and clinging to them.

It is fitting for the believer to separate himself from the wicked in their evil conduct, and the places of their evil and deviations, so he avoids choosing the wicked as friends, in walking with them on the way and being absorbed with them in their thought.

v We read in the book of Sirach, Ecclesiasticus: "He who touches pitch is defiled by it" (see Sir 13:1). As long as we are occupied with the affairs of the world, as long as our souls are bound by possessions and money, we cannot think of God freely. "For what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness? And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel?" (2 Cor 6:14-15), says the Lord: You cannot serve God and mammon (Mt 6:24) [1].
St. Jerome St. Cyril the Great sees that the pitch that stains the soul is the gatherings that do not observe holiness.

entries.section: 1. Caution against the rich and those in authority

paragraphs.text: v Now we must take care, we who have been justified in Christ and have enjoyed fellowship of the Holy Spirit through faith in Him, not to mingle with a people whose thoughts are perverted, of an unholy mentality. Such a people are in truth strangers, speaking a strange language, and speaking words perverted from the truth. Everyone who mingles with them is utterly defiled. Scripture says: "He who touches pitch is defiled" [2].
St. Cyril the Great Do not lift a weight beyond your strength, and do not keep company with one who is stronger and richer than you.
How can an earthen pot be compared with an iron cauldron?
The cauldron strikes it and it breaks [2].

The danger of friendship between a young man and a young man richer than he: that the poor young man is bound to keep up with the rich young man, as in exchanging gifts or banquets, so that the poor man finds himself obliged to spend what is beyond his means [2]. Sometimes a person is dazzled by his friend's wealth and tries to keep pace with him, and so is like an earthen pot that collides with an iron vessel and is shattered.

entries.section: 1. Caution against the rich and those in authority

paragraphs.text: The rich man sins and proves himself the one wronged, and the poor man is wronged and is obliged to apologize [3].

A man's friendship with one who is richer than he exposes him to the shattering of his psyche, for the rich man sins and justifies the wrong he committed and his justification is accepted, while the poor man is wronged by the rich man, and is obliged to apologize to the wrongdoer.

entries.section: 1. Caution against the rich and those in authority

paragraphs.text: If you are useful he (the rich man) exploits you, and if you are in need he abandons you [4].

entries.section: 1. Caution against the rich and those in authority

paragraphs.text: If you have money he keeps company with you, and drains your money without feeling sorry for you [5].

It would be fitting for the rich man to thank God for His gifts by offering a sacrifice of thanksgiving through helping the needy, but some rich men, instead of supporting the needy, exploit them, as by offering them loans in return for high interest or usury. And in their selfishness, feeling that they have no need of the poor friend, they abandon him.

v When man does not put God before his face, what is before his eyes but the world? In other words he gathers money upon money, and is concerned to increase the flock, and his storehouses are filled, and he says to himself: "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry" (Lk 19:12).

v Rightly is the man sick with dropsy compared to the covetous rich man. The first, the more he receives unnatural moisture the more his thirst increases, so the covetous rich man who has received riches in abundance misuses them, and his passion for the love of wealth increases [3].
St. Augustine v Truly man's life does not consist in his possessions through the abundance he has, but he is counted blessed and with glorious hope who is rich toward God [4].
St. Cyril of Alexandria v The life of man does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses [5].

St. Clement of Alexandria v If you offer to God a part of what you acquired unjustly and by seizure, He will not accept your gift... Have mercy on him you have wronged, showing him mercy and love... For God does not share in our greed, nor does He share with thieves and robbers; He is able to feed the poor whom He entrusted to us, but He seeks the fruits of righteousness and love of people.

Pope Athanasius the Apostolic v "He labors in vain and without profit, he who clings to the wealth which he will not taste" (Job 20:18) LXX. What is the use of the splendor of a palace dripping with gold if the wicked man himself is buried six feet beneath (the earth)? What is the use of an abundance of garments of joy and a variety of clothing for a person whom the vermin strip?
Father Hesychius of Jerusalem v Does wealth make you live longer? Why then do you show evils for the sake of an unsure comfort?

Father Theophylact v We must know that covetousness sometimes steals into people by way of pride, and sometimes by way of fear. Therefore some aim at appearing with greater authority, and burn to obtain what belongs to others. Also there are people who fear lest they come to be in want of the necessities of life, so they give their minds over to covetousness to seek what belongs to others, imagining that what they have is not enough for them.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 1. Caution against the rich and those in authority

paragraphs.text: If he has need of you he deceives you, and smiles at you, and gives you hope and speaks to you of good, and even says: "What do you need?" [6]
He shames you with his foods, until he drains you two or three times, and finally mocks you.

entries.section: 1. Caution against the rich and those in authority

paragraphs.text: And if he sees you after that he forgets you, and shakes his head at you [7].

Ben Sira calls us to flee from the table of the wicked, for while he offers you food and drink he does not carry within him true love, but what occupies him is the cost of the table he offered you, or how to exploit the offering of the banquet to push you to evil. The wise man says: "Do not boast before the king, and do not stand in the place of great men: for better it is that it be said unto thee, Come up hither; than that thou shouldest be put lower in the presence of the prince whom thine eyes have seen" (Prov 25:6-7). The Lord Christ gives us counsel at invitations to banquets, saying: "When thou art bidden of any man to a wedding, sit not down in the highest room; lest a more honourable man than thou be bidden of him; And he that bade thee and him come and say to thee, Give this man place; and thou begin with shame to take the lowest room. But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher: then shalt thou have glory in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee. For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted" (Lk 14:8-11). It is fitting for the believer to be adorned with self-control and comprehensive chastity: chastity of the belly, and chastity of the hand and tongue and senses.

entries.section: 1. Caution against the rich and those in authority

paragraphs.text: Beware lest you be led astray, and be humbled in your folly [8].

12 If a powerful man invites you, withdraw; for thereby he will increase his invitation to you. 13 Do not push forward, lest you be driven away, and do not stand far off, lest you be forgotten. 14 Do not venture to converse with him, and do not trust his many words; for by his much speaking to you he tests you, and by smiling at you he examines you. 15 He is without mercy. He does not carry out what he promised, and does not refrain from harm and fetters. 16 Be on your guard and take great heed; for you are on the brink of falling. 17 And if you hear these things in your sleep, wake up. 18 In all your life, love the Lord and call upon Him for your salvation.
If a ruler invites you, be slow in accepting the invitation, for often he will increase his invitation to you [9].
Do not press him, lest you be rejected, and do not withdraw, lest you be forgotten [10].
Do not intend to converse with him as his equal, and do not trust the abundance of his words, for he tests you by much talk, and while he smiles he examines you [11].

Ordinarily there is an innate sensitivity in man toward one who is his peer, that is, equal to him in age or education or work. For man deals with compassion with one who is younger than he without being jealous of him, and also with one who is older than he without resentment, because his age gives him the right to precede him. Ben Sira warns the poor young men not to speak much, and not to disclose their secrets before the rich young men and those in authority.
He who does not guard your words is without mercy, and does not hesitate to harm you or imprison you [12].
Keep your words to yourself and take heed, for you are walking on the brink of your fall [13].

19 Every living creature loves its like, and every man loves his neighbor. 20 Every creature keeps company with its kind, and a man associates with his like. 21 Does the wolf associate with the lamb? So is the sinner with the godly. 22 What peace is there between the hyena and the dog? And what peace is there between the rich and the poor? 23 Wild asses in the wilderness are the prey of lions, and so the poor are the pastures of the rich.

God gave most beings to love what resembles them. By this nations and tribes were formed, as a people live together and sympathize with one another because of unity of language and similarity of color and culture. And in the kingdom of animals we see them going out together: lions walk together in one herd, and so do leopards and bears and deer, and we do not find a lamb grazing among wolves or foxes, nor a cat among snakes or a dove flying in a flock of ravens. So we are not surprised to see groups of one kind of bird flying together and also migrating together, and in the migration of fish, fish of a certain kind set out together. But in the Church of the New Testament, human beings sympathize together not on the basis of unity of language or color of skin or culture, but the heart of the believer is enlarged, sympathizing with the children of men, longing that all become the icon of God and that the whole world become "a holy nation" (1 Pet 2:9); that is, the one Kingdom of God.
Every living creature loves what resembles it, and every man loves his neighbor [14].

v God planted in our nature an attraction that binds us to one another by love. "Every beast (creature) loves its own kind, and every person loves his neighbor" (see Sir 13:15). Behold, there are in our nature seeds that incline us to virtue; while the seeds of vice are contrary to nature. If the latter are dominant, this is nothing but a testimony to our extreme sluggishness [6].

v We all by nature adopt a friendly attitude, so we feel indignation with those who are treated with contempt... and we sympathize with those who enjoy help and protection, and are overcome by the trials that befall others, as we have a common tenderness. For although painful events seem as though they drive to a kind of cowardice, yet we harbor a kind of common tenderness. One speaks of this, explaining: "Every living creature loves its own kind, and every man loves his neighbor" [7].

St. John Chrysostom v "Every creature loves its own kind, according to the saying: "People seek to be united with those like them." It seems very desirable even among us to live with those who have the same habits as we, so how can we escape the thought that this is the case with God? For being good by nature, and the beginning of all virtues and their source, He takes up His dwelling not in lovers of evil, but in doers of virtue, and rises above defilement [8].

St. Cyril the Great In a sermon of Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles, on the feasts of the holy martyrs, he sees that celebrating the holy martyrs is realized in practice by fellowship with them and by imitating their conduct, as the wise man says: "Every creature loves its own kind" (see Sir 13:14).

v As we desire to celebrate the feasts of the holy martyrs, the blessed martyrs want to recognize some of their virtues in us, so that they may be pleased with us and seek God's mercy on our behalf... For like keeps company with like, and what is not like withdraws far from it. Look at our holy patron, whose feast we zealously want to celebrate rejoicing; he is self-controlled, so how can a drunkard keep company with him? What fellowship is there between a humble soul and a proud soul [9].
Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles Every body associates according to its kind, and every man clings to him who is like himself [15].
The goal of dealing with those of our kind is not jesting and amusement but our eternal salvation.

v Do not talk with just anyone about mercy and the virtuous life. And I do not say this out of envy, but because I reckon that you will be in the eyes of the fool like a jester. A man agrees with one who resembles him, and the hearers of such (spiritual) talk are few, or rather very rare, so it is better not to speak, for (mere talk with them) is not what God wants for the salvation of man [10].
St. Anthony the Great What harmony is there between a wolf and a lamb?
So is the sinner with the godly man [16].
What peace is there between the hyena and the dog?
And what peace is there between the rich and the poor? [17]
Wild asses in the wilderness are the prey of lions, so the poor are the pastures of the rich [18].

Sirach turns to the world of animals to illustrate the grave contrast between kinds of people, for in the animal world they devour one another. The wolf devours the lamb [17]. There is nothing the lamb can offer to remedy the wolf's attitude toward it except to flee from his company. At the same time, on the positive side, wealth itself is not evil, but the evil lies in man's thought and his wicked will.

Since sin entered the world, even some irrational creatures were corrupted. The strong lion does not cease to devour animals weaker than he, such as wild asses. And the rich exploit the poor and count them their pasture. Ordinarily we do not find the poor man dwelling beside the rich man, because the rich man often exploits the poor man, and by one means or another lays his hand on what the poor man owns, if he does not also lay his hand on the poor man himself! As King Ahab and his wife Jezebel did with Naboth the Jezreelite (1 Kgs 21), taking away his vineyard, and the queen devised a plot to kill Naboth. A very few control the great positions of leadership, while the price is paid by the poor; so the rich grow richer, and the poor poorer.

v They do not care about righteousness; instead, looking to (their own) profit, they tyrannized over the needy, to profit from the wretched and use them as sandals (Amos 8:6). Scripture says: "The poor are the pastures of the rich" [18]... Love of neighbor is bound up with the accomplishments of righteousness, for truly "Love worketh no ill to his neighbour" (Rom 13:10) [11].
St. Cyril the Great

entries.section: 4. Between the rich and the poor

paragraphs.text: 24 Humility is an abomination to the proud, and so the poor man is an abomination to the rich. 25 When the rich man is shaken, his friends hold him up, and when the humble man falls, his friends drive him away. 26 The rich man slips and many help him. He speaks outrages and they acquit him. 27 The humble man slips and they rebuke him. He speaks with sense, and they give his words no place. 28 The rich man speaks and all listen, and they lift his speech to the clouds.
Ben Sira sees the danger of the great disparity among people in regard to wealth and power, especially if society lacks true wisdom.
The proud man loathes lowliness of station, and so the poor man is an abomination to the rich [19].

The proud man sees in humility uncleanness, and at the same time sets himself up as a god, so he becomes like the Antichrist who claims divinity, and sets up the abomination of desolation in the temple.
If the rich man totters his friends support him, and if the poor man falls his friends push him [20].

When the rich man is exposed to stumbling (tottering), he relies on his wealth and his friends to offer him help. But the man of God finds in God Himself and His rich grace the true help and heavenly comfort that penetrates his depths.

v I reckon that a life passed in fellowship with some persons in the same dwelling is more useful in many respects. The reasons for this are: first, none of us is self-sufficient with regard to material needs, but each one asks the help of another to meet our needs. The foot, for example, has one kind of strength and lacks another. And without cooperation with the other members of the body it finds itself unable to carry on its activities independently of the others for a long time... So in the life of solitude, what is in the hand becomes of no use to us, and what we do not have we cannot achieve, since God the Creator ordained that we must help one another as it is written, so that we may be gathered together [12].
St. Basil the Great When the rich man slips many help him, and when he speaks wicked words they acquit him.
If the poor man slips they rebuke him all the more, and when he speaks with understanding no place is given to him [21].

If the poor man falls no one supports him, but his friends push him down all the more to be rid of him. This is what happened with the Lord of glory Jesus at His trial, so that His disciples might not wait for help or praise from people.
When the rich man speaks everyone is silent, and they lift his word to the clouds.
And the poor man speaks and they say: "Who is this man?", and if he stumbles they push him down all the more [22].

entries.section: 5. Wealth is good for him who uses it well

paragraphs.text: 29 The poor man speaks and they say: "Who is this?" And if he stumbles they overthrow him. 30 Wealth is good for one who has no sin, and poverty is hateful in the mouth of the hypocrite. 31 A man's heart changes his countenance, either for good or for evil. 32 A cheerful countenance comes from a good heart, and the devising of proverbs wearies the thoughts.
Wealth in which there is no sin is good, but poverty is evil in the mouth of the wicked [23].

Lest anyone suppose that all the rich are wicked or harsh or exploiters of the poor, he made clear that wealth is good for him who uses it well, and ugly for him who misuses it. If a man's face sometimes bears a sweet smile and attractive features when the heart is pure, and sometimes bears marks of violence and harshness or anger when the heart is angry, so it is with wealth.
Is wealth a sin? What occupies the believer is the sanctification of his heart, which is reflected even in his features.

v Let us all teach our children to prefer virtue to anything else, and not to give importance to material wealth... Abraham was rich and so was Job; these two not only suffered no harm from wealth, but also enjoyed a good reputation... because they did not use it for their own enjoyment alone, but also for the comfort of others, relieving the pains of need, and opening their house to every stranger [13].
St. John Chrysostom St. Anthony the Great calls us to the moderate life.

v The more a man is moderate in his life the more he is at peace, for he is not full of concern for many things, such as servants and hired hands and sheep... Yet when we cling to such things we become exposed to the troubles that flow from them, which lead us to murmur against God.
And so the passion that springs from our own will (to acquire many things) fills us with disturbance, and we flounder in the darkness of the life of sin, not knowing ourselves [14].
St. Anthony the Great A man's heart changes the features of his face, either to good or to evil [24].

With Ben Sira's concern for man's inner life, and his warning against judging a man by outward appearances, he affirms that the inner life has its effective influence on man's outward features. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, and the joy that man's features bear is only a reflection of the peace of the heart. It is said: "A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken" (Prov 15:13).
A cheerful face is a sign of a heart full of goodness, but devising proverbs requires laborious thought [25].

How great the difference between a man who records maxims and proverbs quoted from the words and writings of others, and one who records them as the fruit of an experience he lives out in his thought and conduct. Therefore Ben Sira, who has tested the upright life in the Lord, says: "Devising proverbs requires the labor of thoughts."

v He also says: "Your face is beautiful." You can understand what kind of "face" this is that the word of God praised and described as beautiful, if you understand what Paul meant by the face in his saying: "But we all, with open face beholding..." (2 Cor 3:18), and his saying also: "but then face to face" (1 Cor 13:12). It is without doubt a kind of face that is renewed day by day (2 Cor 4:16), after the image of its Creator (Col 3:10), having no spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but being holy and without blemish, like the Church that Christ presents to Himself (Eph 5:27).

In other words it means the souls that have reached perfection, those that form the body of the Church; this body appears truly beautiful and handsome when the souls of which it is composed persevere in obtaining the beauty of perfection. For just as the soul, when it is in turmoil, distorts the shape of the bodily face and makes it agitated, while if it is calm it gives the face a shape that bears peace and gentleness, so also the face of the Church is beautiful or ugly according to the traits of the believers and their aspirations.

It is written that the cheerful face points to a prosperous heart [25], and in another place it is said: "A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the countenance is broken" (Prov 15:13). The heart is joyful when the Spirit of God is in it, whose first fruit is love, and the second is joy (Gal 5:22). And I think that the worldly wise have taken their ideas from these truths, since they said that the wise man is beautiful, and every wicked man is ugly [15].
Origen Inspired by Sirach 13

entries.section: Let me lean on Your breast, not the breast of a man!

paragraphs.text: v Your breast, O Savior of the world, is wide enough for every man!
You are the humble rich One; every humble man cleaves to You!
Grant me not to lean on a rich man nor on one in authority.
He may welcome me, but I do not know what is in his heart toward me.
But You are all love, You pour out of Your riches and Your grace into my heart.
v Many of the rich were drawn by money, and they have friends who honor them for their wealth and authority.
When they stumble many hasten to support them.
And when they sin, people flatter them, and justify their errors.
But I in my weakness cleave to You, for You truly love me and help me.
Reveal Your presence in my depths, that I may meet Your heavenly servants and the company of the saints.
In You I am enriched and never in want of anything!
v He who forms a friendship with a wicked, proud rich man is like one who touched pitch and was defiled.
And he who forms a friendship with You, his heart is lifted up to Your heavens.
The devil dares not creep in to him, nor set his snares for him on the way.
With every morning he enters into new glories, and his soul rejoices in his journey in Your company.
You overshadow him, and protect him from the sun of trials.
And by Your Holy Spirit he flies as on the wings of an eagle.
He is not taken to the Promised Land as happened of old, but You carry him to the heavenly Canaan, and the heavenly orders marvel at him and call him blessed.
He who keeps company with the wicked rich man becomes wicked like him.
He who keeps company with You, O Holy One, finds sweet the union with You!
v Clinging to the rich is a burden on the poor.
They suffer from them, and are broken as the earthen pot is broken by the metal vessel.
And clinging to You offers him sweetness, for Your yoke is sweet, and Your burden is very light.
v Clinging to the wicked rich exposes the poor man to injustice.
And by clinging to You he enjoys Your righteousness, and enters into Your depths through the wounds of Your love.
Your cross has become a divine chariot that carries us and sets out with us to You without hindrance.
v Clinging to the wicked rich man exposes me to his withdrawing from me.
He abandons me and counts me a stranger to him.
I feel isolation and suffer from deadly loneliness.
But clinging to You, O Holy One, makes me a member of Your holy body.
I meet You face to face, and enjoy the Fatherhood of the Father and the sanctification of Your Holy Spirit.
I shall never feel isolated as long as I am in Your presence.
And I find sweet the fellowship with the heavenly ones and the saints.
v My soul will not be at rest when a powerful ruler invites me.
He may invite me once and twice, but what, I wonder, does his heart hold toward me?
If I sit at his table I will not look at the splendid food, for I cannot keep pace with him in his temporal wealth.
And if he speaks to me with a smile, I do not know whether he truly loves me or is testing me.
But You, O heavenly Bread, offer me a heavenly table.
You do not send me manna from heaven, as You did in the wilderness.
But You came down to me offering me Your holy Body and Your precious Blood.
By them I receive from Your hands the fellowship of the divine nature.
You grant me the fruits of the Spirit: love, joy and peace, goodness, meekness and chastity, wisdom, understanding and discernment.
O Your surpassing, free table that satisfies my heart and my mind and all my depths!
In truth I become like You, and am a living icon of You.
v My depths cry out to You:
My tongue is unable to express the power of friendship with You, and the blessedness of the mystical fellowship with You, O You who are wonderful in Your love and Your friendship.

entries.section: 1. Chastity of the tongue and its sanctification

paragraphs.text: 1 Blessed is the man who has not slipped with his mouth, and is not stung by remorse for sin. 2 Blessed is he whom his conscience has not condemned, and who has not fallen from his hope.
Blessed is the man who does not slip and fall because of his mouth, and is not stung with pain because of his sin! [1]

Sirach begins his discourse on chastity and holiness with the chastity of the tongue and its sanctification. For if sin corrupts a person's inner peace, those who desire chastity and holiness are often preoccupied with ridding themselves of evil, lustful thoughts, especially the young, and they count deliverance from them exceedingly difficult. But Sirach holds the key to the thought that causes looseness of the tongue among friends. For under the cover of "love, friendship and familiarity," a person does not realize the importance of the sanctity of speech and conversation, even in times of merriment, entertainment or jesting. It befits the believer, as an ambassador of the Lord Christ, to place in his heart that he is always in the presence of God, and to ask that God's grace work in him, so that every good word comes forth for the edification of his own soul and the edification of his friends, and indeed of society. He is a man of God! The Apostle James speaks of the tongue as a small member, yet like the small rudder that steers the whole ship. Our life on earth is a period of training in the school of life, how to enjoy the sanctification of the tongue, so that by grace it may direct the whole being of man to enjoy the eternal heavenly wedding.
v Surely "Blessed is the man who does not slip with his mouth, and is not stung by remorse for sin" [1], or at least repents of the sins of the tongue [1].

entries.section: 1. Chastity of the tongue and its sanctification

paragraphs.text: v If we meet at feasts for the sake of love, and if the purpose of these festivals is to create a holy fellowship among the guests, and we use eating and drinking as instruments of love, does it not befit us to keep a manner that shows self-control of mind?... And if we gather in order to show good will toward one another, why do we stir up ill will through jesting and sport at the expense of others? Keeping silence is better than entering into a quarrel and using a coarse manner with error in deed. Surely: "Blessed is the man who does not slip with his mouth, and is not defiled by remorse for sin" (cf. Sir 14:1), or at least turns back from his sins that he committed by speech, or converses without causing pain to anyone [2].
St. Clement of Alexandria Many of the Fathers speak to us about the chastity of the senses and of all the members of the body:

v Striving to obtain perfect purity requires the striving of soul and body together in works of repentance, in harmony and equality. If the mind is granted some grace, it can then wrestle against the passions without relaxing or slackening, and receive the thoughts, directions and consolations of the Holy Spirit, and it can drive out of the soul the defiled inclinations that arise from the lusts of the heart. And by virtue of the fellowship between the mind or soul of man and the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit helps man to carry out the commandments he has learned, and guides him to drive all the passions out of the soul, whether those that arise from the soul itself independently of the body, or those that attached themselves to it by way of the body.
The Holy Spirit teaches man to keep his whole body - from head to foot - in harmony: he keeps the eyes so that they look with purity.
And he keeps the ears so that they listen in peace, or give heed to the things that belong to peace, without taking delight in talk about others, slanders and the disparagement of others.
And he keeps the tongue so that it speaks only what is good, giving weight to every word, and does not allow anything defiled or lustful to mix with its speech.
And he keeps the hands so that they move naturally, and are lifted up in prayer and in showing mercy and generosity.

And he keeps the stomach so that it has fitting limits for eating and drinking, according to the measure sufficient for the nourishment of the body, so that it does not let lust or gluttony turn it aside, and it exceed its limits.
And he keeps the feet so that they walk in righteousness according to the will of God, for the purpose of doing good works.

entries.section: 1. Chastity of the tongue and its sanctification

paragraphs.text: In this way the whole body becomes accustomed to every good work, and becomes subject to the authority of the Holy Spirit, and is gradually changed until it shares, to some extent, in the end in the qualities of the spiritual body that it receives at the just resurrection [3].
St. Anthony the Great v Adam was more glorious than a crown in his great beauty, and no other beauty was found among creatures to equal him.
His Maker set the two eyes of light on the top of the crown, that he might look at the creatures around him as from on high.
And He fashioned for him below two feet to run like a chariot, and by them he walks wherever he wishes to go.
And He fashioned at his sides two hands, with the ten fingers on them, by which he takes possession of sea and land and the whole world.
And He fashioned the brain, the house of the mind, to be there, and to dwell in the upper story like a god.
And He made for him a palate to examine foods, and set taste in it to distinguish between the sweet and the bitter.
And He opened the sense of smell to be a path for scents, by which he perceives (distinguishing) the foul odor from the pleasant.
And He pierced the hearing, and surrounded it with the pattern of the snail, that sounds might circle in it and enter with delight.
In his breast the heart, in which all thoughts are gathered, to distribute all the treasures as from a great treasury.
In his mouth the word, and in his lips the distinguishing of sounds, and the forehead as a sign; and He adorned the hollow of the eye with the two eyelids...
The Wise One of the worlds composed and arranged a different function in each member in the image of beauty when He perfected it.

entries.section: 1. Chastity of the tongue and its sanctification

paragraphs.text: The Creator made from nothing something great, that he might become lord of all things by wisdom [4].
v When the Creator created the mouth, He placed in it voice and word, that it might move to praise.
So everyone who feels the existence of the Creator must praise the Lord who created him.
The mouth of man is not given authority to use trivial news and unseemly words.

entries.section: 1. Chastity of the tongue and its sanctification

paragraphs.text: When the Creator created the mouth, He perfected it for His praise, and not to utter vain things [5].
St. Jacob of Serugh "and is not stung with pain because of his sin" [1].

We expected Ben Sirach, as he pronounced blessed the one who does not slip with his mouth, to say: "but keeps his tongue holy," but instead he said: "and is not stung because of his sin." Why? He warns us against the extreme of looseness in vain or evil speech, even if it is a sort of jesting, and against excess in grief and pain while offering repentance for every idle word. For just as frivolity is a danger to the holy life, so also remorse without hope destroys a person.

Ben Sirach often speaks of the joy of the Spirit even with the shedding of the tears of repentance, because hope drives a person to move constantly toward the pledge of heaven while we are still in this world.
Blessed is he whom his own soul does not condemn, and who has not been disappointed in his hope [2].

Control of the tongue with a spirit of joyful hope: it is good for a person to condemn himself for the looseness of his tongue, but while he offers repentance with tears of remorse, these tears are mingled with tears of joyful hope, because he meets the Forgiver of sins and Sanctifier of souls from corruption. The Apostle Paul warned us not to do anything with murmuring, lest we fall into the pit of despair. So it was with Judas, who repented and cast down the silver before those who had delivered him over, but did not open his heart in hope to the Savior of mankind as Simon Peter did, who said: "Lord, thou knowest that I love thee" (Jn 21:15).

This is what St. John the Beloved affirms when he says: "If our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart" (1 Jn 3:20). That is, if our inner life declares to us that our motives are not sound, let us cast ourselves upon God, confessing to Him our weakness in spite of the praise of men for us, and He is greater than our hearts, for He alone is able to set right our motives.
3 Riches are not becoming to the miserly man, and what is the profit of wealth to an envious man? 4 He who gathers at the loss of his own soul gathers for others, and another will revel in his goods.
Wealth does not suit the narrow-minded man, and what is the purpose of money to the envious man? [3]

After warning us against looseness of the tongue, he warned us against looseness of thought and its lack of breadth. For in a life of frivolity a person does not care about the sanctity of his tongue, and through narrowness of mind he does not seek what is heavenly and eternal, but is occupied with gathering money, looking at heavenly things as imagination, an escape from reality and a loss of happiness. On the other hand, Ben Sirach links narrowness of mind with miserliness. For the miserly person's mind is narrow, so he does not practice giving with joy, and if he does practice it, it is under great pressure. Some reach such miserliness that they deprive themselves even of the necessities, and so they gather a fortune that others use, whether by seizing it, or by squandering it unwisely, or by leaving it to heirs after their death.
For he who gathers for himself gathers for others, and another enjoys his goods [4].

The miser desires to gather for himself all the possessions he can, and is seized with envy, desiring to acquire for himself what others have, and suffers from a constant thirst for all that is in the hands of others. So it is hard for him to give, but he always wants to take; therefore the Lord Christ said: "It is more blessed to give than to receive" (Acts 20:35).

v He who loves sin loves many possessions, and neglects righteousness, and does not think of the passing of life and its instability and the shortness of its term, and does not remember the certainty of death, which cannot be bribed. And if a person shows this shamelessness and lack of feeling until he reaches old age, he is like a rotten tree of no use [6].
St. Anthony the Great

5 He who is evil to himself, to whom will he be good? Does he not take no pleasure in his riches? 6 There is none worse than he who envies himself; that is the recompense of his wickedness. 7 And if he does good, it is by oversight, and in the end he shows his wickedness. 8 There is none more wicked than he who envies with his eye, and turns away his face, and despises souls. 9 The eye of the miser is not satisfied with his portion, and the iniquity of the wicked dries up his soul. 10 The evil eye envies bread, and at his own table he is in want.
Sirach highlighted the harm a person does to himself when he practices unholy conduct, such as:
a. Money possesses him instead of his possessing money [5].
b. He is miserly even to himself [6].
c. If he gives alms, it is without love [7].
d. He feels that what is in his brother's hand ought to have been his, so he envies his brother what he possesses.
He who is evil to himself, to whom will he be good?
And he does not enjoy his wealth [5].

When a person enslaves himself to money, money becomes a god to him. And instead of money serving him, he becomes its captive. He rejoices for a while when his balance increases, and does not know that money is a tyrannical master. For its sake a person sometimes falls into anxiety, and because of it he sometimes loses tenderness and mercy toward his brother. It brings him down from the joy of the Spirit to a state of disturbance. He loses the fruit of the Spirit, and deprives himself of moving freely toward heavenly things.

v If you look upon wealth and the perfect enjoyment of it as nothing but a deceptive show for a short time, and you know that the virtuous life that pleases God is better than wealth, and you hold fast to this belief and keep it in your memory, you will never groan or murmur or rebuke anyone, but will give thanks to God in every state, even if you see people worse than yourself praised for their eloquence or knowledge or wealth. The lust for wealth with greed, and pleasures, and the love of lust and vainglory, joined with ignorance of the truth, bring the worst sufferings of the soul [7].
St. Anba Anthony There is none worse than he who envies himself; that is the recompense of his vice [6].

In some translations the word "envies" came to mean being stingy, so one who is stingy toward himself is concerned with acquiring without spending for the salvation of his soul through giving; in this way he deprives himself of enjoying his wealth by hoarding it. Thus sin bears its fruit in itself, for he who envies himself, by enslaving himself to the love of possessions, receives the pledge of its fruit while still on earth, as he loses his inner peace and the joy of the Spirit.
And if he does good, it is without intention, and in the end he reveals his vice [7].

If he offers a kindness or alms from what he has by oversight, that is, not with the intention of giving joyfully, then when he corrects himself in the matter he shows his vice, that is, he reveals that he did not give the gift out of love. And since giving lacks the element of love, he loses his being and existence, and the person's life and growth are disrupted. The Apostle says: "And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor... and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing" (1 Cor 13:3).
v Give from what you own in righteousness, because you cannot offer a bribe to Christ your Judge.
v If you are sad as you give, you lose both the bread and the merit, because God loves a cheerful giver [8].

St. Augustine v If you stretch out your hand while your heart is empty of tenderness, you are doing nothing. The measure is not in the giving but in the joy in giving, and if there is no possibility of giving, tenderness alone is enough for those whom we love.
St. Anba Anthony v It is the intention that makes the gift precious or cheap [9].
St. Ambrose He is wicked who envies with his eye; he turns away his face and despises souls [8].
When a person envies his brother, counting that he is not worthy of what he has, he disdains his brother and despises him.

St. Basil the Great says that covetousness is the measure by which a person gauges his depths, whether covetousness has crept into them, and whether his love for himself is greater than his love for his neighbor.
v Question: By what measure is covetousness judged (Lk 12:15)?

Answer: When a person transgresses the limits set by the Law. According to the Old Testament this appears if a person thinks to take more than his neighbor, for it is written: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself" (Lev 19:18; Mt 22:29). According to the Gospel, when one is concerned to take of the necessities more than he needs, beyond the need of the present day. Because of this someone heard: "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided? So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God" (Lk 12:20-21) [10].
St. Basil the Great The eye of the greedy is not satisfied with his portion, and useless iniquity dries up the soul [9].
v It is said: "The eye of the greedy is not satisfied with his portion" (cf. Sir 14:9). Such a one cannot be corrected, and it is right to turn away from him [11].

St. John Chrysostom v Someone said: "No one is worse than lovers of money." This is the person who puts a price even on himself. He goes about like a public enemy of the world, complaining that the earth does not bear gold instead of wheat, or that there are springs instead of water channels, or mountains instead of stones. He is troubled if anyone gains a common benefit from anything.

He shuts every road that brings no monetary reward. He deals with anything from which he takes even two mites. He hates everyone, rich or poor. He hates the rich because he does not have what they have, and he counts all that others have as taken from him. It is truly his own, and he (the rich man) has seized it from him; so he is pleased with no one. He does not know the means of feeling abundance, and has no experience at all of being satisfied. He is the most wretched of all, as one who has nothing at all, and the practice of self-control is the thing most enviable to him [12].

v It is said: "The eye of the greedy is not satisfied with his portion" (cf. Sir 14:9)... For nature came into the world naked, and goes out of it naked. Therefore we do not seek luxuries, since we brought nothing with us, and we take nothing with us [13].
St. John Chrysostom The evil eye of a man envies his bread, and so he is in want at his table [10].

Envy is the natural fruit of selfishness, where a person wants to be the center of everything, and counts that he has the right to take from his brother what he has, even a crumb of bread. This selfishness strips him of the blessing of the Lord, so that instead of taking what is in his brother's hand, he loses even what he has. The envious person feels hunger and thirst, and there is no food or drink or possession that can satisfy him, even if he took the whole world in his hand.

11 My son, spend on yourself according to what you have, and offer to the Lord offerings that are fitting for Him. 12 Remember that death does not delay. Has not the covenant of Hades been made known to you? 13 Before you die do good to your friend, and according to your ability stretch out your hand and give to him. 14 Do not lose a good day, and let not the portion of a good and desirable thing pass you by. 15 Shall you not leave your labors to another, and what you toiled for to be divided by lot? 16 Give and take, and justify your soul. 17 Before your death work righteousness, for there is no way to seek food in Hades. 18 All flesh wears out like a garment, for the covenant from the beginning is that it shall die the death. For as the leaves of a thick tree, 19 some fall and some grow, so is the generation of flesh and blood, some die and some are born. 20 Every corrupt work perishes, and its worker goes with it. 21 And every chosen work is justified, and its worker is honored for its sake.
My son, according to what you have treat yourself well, and offer to the Lord fitting offerings [11].

As Ben Sirach urges us toward the blessed life through the chastity of tongue, thought, conduct and so on, he urges our hearts toward the blessed heavenly life so that we may prepare for it. It is a celebration at an eternal level, where we meet the Bridegroom of souls, the Lord of glory Jesus, and it is a wedding that does not grow old or become ancient, but remains as though new throughout all eternity.

What occupies the human bride and groom in the last moments before the celebration of joy is the moments in which they unite to become one flesh; each forgets all his affairs for the sake of this lasting union. So our expectation of the heavenly wedding occupies us even above the needs of the body, as we see the heavenly Bridegroom preparing for us the eternal wedding. Even His heavenly servants await this great day with longing to see us a bride, a heavenly queen.

With every moment of eternity - if the expression is right - we feel as though for the first time we enjoy the mysteries of the glorious eternal wedding. On the Bridegroom's part, He offered His precious blood as a dowry for our souls, and on our part we offer Him offerings that are fitting for Him. What are these offerings but that we take of what is His and offer it to Him! During our life on earth, by striving that works through love. The Holy Spirit shapes us, and raises up from us the bride, the living icon of Christ. This is the daily offering according to His divine good pleasure. What are the offerings that are fitting for the Lord? 1. The offering of practical love: In a comment by St. John Chrysostom [14] on (Mt 5:23-24), "Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift," he says:

v What goodness this is! What surpassing love shown to mankind! For the sake of our love for our neighbor, He gave no importance to the honor due to Him. What saying is more tender than these words? He says: "Stop the service you offer Me, so that your love may continue. When you are reconciled with your brother, offer a sacrifice to Me." Yes, for this reason Jesus did not say "after the offering" but "before the offering." Rather, precisely, while the offering itself is there before you, He sends you to be reconciled with your brother... What is His motive for this immediate matter? It seems to me He has two aims that He indicates and prepares. First, He wishes to declare how much He exalts the value of love and counts it the greatest sacrifice, so that He does not accept the sacrifice of worship without the sacrifice of love. Second, He magnifies the necessity of reconciliation without leaving room for any excuse [15].

St. John Chrysostom 2. The offering of obedience: Another offering fitting for the Lord is obedience in the Lord. Saul thought that the Lord was pleased with burnt offerings, so Samuel said to him: "Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams" (1 Sam 15:22). 3. The offering of humility: "For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise" (Ps 51:16-18).
Remember that death does not delay, and that the covenant of the netherworld has not been revealed to you [12].

Death is a reality that no sensible person will ignore, and no one will know when it will come upon us, but it does not delay. Even if a person lives a thousand years, it is counted, in relation to eternity, as a drop of water from a sea or a grain of sand in a desert. To the bride it is a day of rejoicing in her wedding, and to the rebel he feels bitterness when he hears the name of death.
The principal clause of the covenant of the netherworld, or its charter, is that death comes upon a person without being bound to a set appointment, and it is not fulfilled according to man's desire.

Like all true sages, Ben Sirach reflects on the danger of being entangled in wealth, remembering the day of his death when he leaves all that he gathered or had to another. So it befits a person to spend on himself, that is, not to be preoccupied with hoarding it but to kindle it for his peace and his eternal salvation; therefore he offers to the Lord offerings fitting for Him as Creator and Savior and the One who cares for him.

v If the wicked man is converted and sighs, all his iniquities are no longer remembered (Ezek 18:21-22). It was also said: Do not postpone returning to the Lord. If the first promise gives you security, the second plea makes you anxious. Listen to the Holy Scripture, which says: "Remember, my son, that death does not delay" (cf. Sir 14:12), and do not say: "His mercy is great, and He will forgive the multitude of my sins. For with Him are mercy and wrath, and His indignation comes down upon sinners" (5:6-7), that is, those who persist in their sins. If we attend faithfully and carefully to the remedy of healing by repentance without delay, we can escape eternal punishment, and enjoy the eternal rewards.

Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles v Dear beloved, let us think wisely and profitably about the judgment and the day of reckoning, with sighs and groans in sorrow over grave sins and faults throughout the days of our life...

v If you confess your sins, God forgives them to you. Let no one despair, and likewise let no one think of hope in a spirit of arrogance. The person who believes that even if he repents of his sins God's mercy will not forgive him sins by despair. As it was said to the despairing: "In the day in which the sinner returns, all his sins are forgiven" (cf. Ezek 18:21). As it is said to the arrogant: "Do not delay to turn to the Lord" (cf. Sir 5:7).
Beloved, may all people give heed to these words, men and women, clergy and laity, young and old, boys and girls [16].

v I urge you, as I often do, dear beloved, always to strive to think of the day of our death and the dreadful judgment. There is no remedy so useful for the wounds of all sins as that each one remember the hour in which he departs from this world. So the Scripture says: "My son, remember that death does not delay" (cf. Sir 14:12), "Remember the end of your life and cease from enmity" (cf. Sir 28:6). If one pays careful attention how severe his examination will be before the judgment of Christ, where He repays each one according to his work (Mt 16:27), his sins and faults cannot bring him pleasure [17].

Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles v It is impossible for us to escape death by any means. And since the wise truly know this, they practice the virtues and think of the love of God, and face death without sighs or fear or tears, thinking that death is on the one hand inevitable, and on the other hand that it frees us from the diseases to which we are subject in this life [18].
St. Anthony the Great Before you die do good to a friend, and according to your ability stretch out your hand and give to him [13].

As we prepare for the heavenly wedding, it befits us to offer to the heavenly Bridegroom what is fitting for Him [11], and to realize that the wedding will not delay, for the hour of our departure from the world has drawn near [12]. We need to take delight in the Bridegroom until the last moments of our life on earth by giving to our brothers, especially the brothers of the Lord [13]. It is good for the believer to use his wealth in practical love for his friend, stretching out his hands in giving as far as he is able, before he dies and every opportunity for him passes away.
Do not allow a day to pass without a good deed, and do not let the carrying out of a good desire escape you [14].

Our life is a series of opportunities for preparing for the wedding; we must not allow time to play with us as though we were a ball in its hand; in the morning we say we shall do good at night, and at night we postpone it till tomorrow, and so time makes sport of us.

God placed in the hearts of men an inclination toward eternity, and they are drawn to it even if one denies it in his conversations with others. This inclination is what enables him to interpret temporal events, and reveals to him God's plan for him and for all humanity. Without the expectation of eternity, humanity loses its mission and its hope and lives in a state of confusion.
v Do not give all the days to iniquity; as long as you have authority, set aside time for righteousness.
We sinned yesterday; let us weep today over our crimes, lest sin spread and destroy us [19].

v Look at the day, how swift it is! And contemplate the night, how it pursues! Though they are quiet, they are busy with their works, and though they promise nothing, they carry out their tasks. They do not speak, and they complete their course. If the sun promised to rise and did not rise, it would not have lit the world by words (that is, by a bare promise)...

v Works are not accomplished by words (promises). Creatures come into being by deeds. The sun rises while silent, and lights the earth without speaking. So say nothing without doing it, but do what you say [20].

v If a good thought comes to you in the evening, begin to carry it out that night. And if the memory of good things awakens in you in the morning, do not refrain from doing good deeds, because the day does not prevent you from completing your works. Attend to your work before the day goes down [21].

v Do not close your eyes in slumber without having opened your mind to prayer. You have seen how the day was hurrying to go; hasten to leave your sins with it! And let your righteousness rise with the morning! Do not put off today's work until tomorrow.

v Behold, the days are buried like the dead. Yesterday we buried yesterday, and here we advise today that it will also be of benefit. Weep, then, over yesterday, which no longer exists, and raise your voice over today, for it too will pass away. Behold, the days snatch you away, and life flees. When the evening buries you, the morning raises you. They put you to death daily so that you may know that you will die [22].

v Yesterday's life has fled from you, and here today's life is quickly passing. Whether you are awake or asleep, the night does not stop its course, and the day does not rest from completing the journey of its way.

Your life here is being plundered, so plunder from it the benefit. Do not rely on the morning because it is bright, if your mind is not enlightened by God so that it may shine. Do not think the evening is for rest, as long as your soul is tormented by the pains of evils [23].
v Until today you have not been your own king, but a slave of the world. Be king over yourself, and serve it...
If a thief robbed you, you would wail, while your life is being stolen from the life of God and you do not grieve over it [24].
St. Jacob of Serugh Will you not leave all the toil of your work to another, and the fruit and all the toil of your work to be divided by lot? [15]
A time comes for every person when work ceases, as he departs from this world, and all that he owned becomes an inheritance for others.
Give and take and control yourself, for there is no way to seek luxury in Hades [16].

Giving is the sure way to receiving. The more we open our hearts and our storehouses to our brothers, the more we find the hand of God stretched out to give generously, and His storehouses open for us to draw from them.
All flesh wears out like a garment, for the covenant from the beginning is that "thou shalt surely die" [17].

v Of this wrath he says: "We were by nature the children of wrath, even as others" (Eph 2:3). And of it Jeremiah says: "Cursed be the day wherein I was born" (Jer 20:14). Of this wrath Job also says: "Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble. He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down... and never continueth in the same state. And upon such an one thou hast opened thine eyes, and broughtest me into judgment with thee. Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Not one; though his life be but one day upon the earth" (Job 14:1-5) LXX... And of this wrath it is said in Ben Sirach: "All flesh wears out like a garment, for the law of the world from the beginning is that thou shalt surely die" (cf. Sir 14:17)...

Of this wrath came the voice of the Apostle: "The creature was made subject to vanity" (Rom 8:20). And of it the psalm laments: "Behold, thou hast made my days as an handbreadth, and mine age is as nothing before thee: surely every man is made a breath" (Ps 39:5) [25].
