Even so, if your brother is in an uproar against you, you can show him mercy and support him in the midst of his agitation, considering that the common enemy (the devil) is mistreating him, and instead of answering him with a harsh word and increasing his confusion, be silent and be gentle with him and with yourself, that you may snatch it away from the hand of the enemy.

Even if the brother returns to agitation against you again, you can be gentle with him and pardon his sin against you so that you may enjoy forgiveness from God. In truth God says: "Forgive, and ye shall be forgiven" (Lk 6:37), and by this you find help and mercy for your brother's soul by pardoning his sins against you [16].

entries.section: 3. The kind word accompanies the gift

paragraphs.text: Father Dorotheus of Gaza v If someone is compelled to beg alms because of hunger, and because of his begging is forced to walk in shame, and because of his shame bears disgrace, then under the weight of dejection he feels a complication accompanied by a darkness that descends on his soul. It befits the one who cares for such people to be longsuffering, and not to behave in a way that increases their dejection and provocation. It also befits him to lighten by encouragement his nature marked by dejection [17].
St. John Chrysostom The fool insults the other and shames him, and the gift of the envious man darkens the eyes [17].

The foolish man does not know how to be gentle in order to win others with tenderness and wisdom, but criticizes continually in a spirit of violence and harshness, and so crushes the souls of those he deals with.

As for the envious man, although he offers gifts to his brothers, he lacks sincere love, so he does not desire their success and progress because of his hidden selfishness; these gifts darken the eyes of others, as they do not perceive what is in his thoughts and what is in his heart of envy, as they also darken his own eyes, so he thinks that he has performed his duty in the fullest way by offering gifts without reforming his heart.

entries.section: 3. The kind word accompanies the gift

paragraphs.text: St. Jerome [18] sees that the Latin word for the envious is invidus, which came in Greek with more force, meaning one who casts a sorcerer's spell, spellcaster. The envious man is harmed by the success and progress of others. If through the envy of the devil death entered the world, he does not cease to instill the spirit of envy in man, not for the benefit of what he acquires, but to stir up his hatred against the successful.
Before you speak learn, and before you become ill take care of your health [18].

entries.section: 3. The kind word accompanies the gift

paragraphs.text: And before you judge examine yourself faithfully, and you will find atonement in the hour of visitation [19].

As man cares for his bodily health, especially when he suffers from illness, it befits him to prepare himself for eternal glory, that he may enjoy complete pardon in the day of the Lord's visitation [19].

21 Before sickness be humble, and in the time of sins show your repentance. 22 Let nothing hinder you from paying your vow in due time, and do not hold back from works of righteousness until death, for the reward of the Lord remains forever. 23 Before you pray, prepare yourself, and do not be as one that tempteth the Lord. 24 Remember the wrath in the days of the end, and the time of vengeance when He turns away His face. 25 In the time of fullness remember the time of hunger, and in the days of wealth remember poverty and need. 26 From morning until evening the time is changed, and all things are quick to change before the Lord. 27 The wise man is wary in all things, and in the days of sins he guards against offenses. 28 Every man of understanding knows wisdom, and confesses to him that finds her. 29 Those who are of understanding in sayings complete their works with wisdom, and pour forth sound proverbs.
Before you are sick, be humble, and when you commit sins, prove your return (to God) [20].

v Whoever loves earthly things and their lusts does not think of being with Christ after his departure, and cannot say: "I am a stranger in the earth," for he is concerned with what is of the earth. But whoever says "Hide not thy commandments from me" is a saint... Therefore the prophet asks God to reveal to him the greatness of His commandments for the heavenly life [19].
Origen Let nothing prevent you from fulfilling your vow without delay, and do not wait for death to be righteous [21].

The psalmist says: "Praise waiteth for thee, O God, in Sion: and unto thee shall the vow be performed" (Ps 65:1); "Vow, and pay unto the Lord your God: let all that be round about him bring presents unto him that ought to be feared" (Ps 76:11). What does paying the vow mean but offering the sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving with joyful obedience to the beloved commandment of God!

v "Unto thee shall the vow be performed" (Ps 65:1) in Jerusalem. For we shall be there perfect, that is, we shall be perfect in the resurrection of the righteous. There all our vow will be paid, not only with respect to the soul but the body also, no longer corruptible, for it will no longer be in Babylon, but will now become a heavenly body and be changed...

Peace will prevail, and war will end. And when peace prevails, that city called the vision of peace (Jerusalem) will prevail. There will no longer be a struggle with death. But now, how grave is the death with which we struggle!

v Do not delay in the vow, for you will pay the vows not by your own strength. You will fail if you depend on yourselves. But if you depend on Him to whom you vow, you will be secure and pay the vows. "Vow, and pay unto the Lord your God." What must we all vow? To believe in Him, and hope from Him for eternal life, and live in godliness according to the measure befitting all men [20].

St. Augustine v What do we vow and pay, brethren? Believe in Him, hope from Him for eternal life and for the good life according to the common level. There is a common level for all men. "Thou shalt not commit adultery" is a commandment for the married as for the unmarried... Therefore all of us must vow what concerns faith and justice and chastity or mercy, and by the help of Him to whom we vow this we pay...

Some vow that they will not permit themselves or desire to know anyone in the future, even if they are presently unmarried. Their vow is greater than the former. Others vow this virginity from the beginning of their life, so that they never practice, unlike those who tried but afterward abandoned it; these are the greatest of all [21].
Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles Before you vow, prepare yourself, and be not as one that tempteth the Lord [22].
Man should not tempt the Lord in his prayers and vows in choosing a particular way, nor hasten in vowing (Judg 11:29-40).
Remember His wrath in the day of your death, and in the time of punishment when the Lord turns away His face [23].
It befits us to ask God for counsel and grace that we may walk according to His good pleasure until the last breath, and hate what He hates.

v Hate hypocrisy, and everything that does not please the Lord. Do not forsake the commandments of the Lord, but keep what you have received, without adding or taking away. Confess your transgressions in the Church, and do not come to your prayer with an evil conscience. This is the way of life [22].
The Didache In the time of fullness remember the time of hunger, and in the days of wealth remember poverty and need [24].
It befits the believer in the time of his fullness to remember God's gifts to him, but while using wealth for his satisfaction, to remember the hungry!

v Since we see that God does not allow us to be swallowed up in the flood of those troubles when they come upon us, may we not allow ourselves to become careless when they pass. Let us remember that when we were sorrowful He comforted us. Let us thank Him now that we are rejoicing. In our sufferings He gave us rest and did not leave us. May we not betray ourselves in the time of ease by turning aside to laziness. One says: "In the time of fullness do not forget the time of hunger" (see Sir 18:24). Therefore let us think in the time of trial of the day of relief. And with regard to our sins let us act in the same way. If you have sinned and received forgiveness, give thanks, but do not forget the sin, not in order to goad yourself by thinking of it, but to teach yourself not to be negligent, and relapse again into the same snares (Heb 6:4) [23].
St. John Chrysostom From morning to evening the time is changed, and all things pass quickly in the presence of the Lord [25].

v You do not know what any day will bring you: "Between morning and evening the weather changes." In another place we are advised with a useful commandment: "Let us walk while we have the light, lest darkness overtake us" (see Jn 12:35).

The negligent person says: When I become old I will resort to the remedy of repentance. This wretched one does not know that when a person grows accustomed to committing sins while waiting for repentance, he will not be qualified to obtain the fruit of repentance, or will be qualified for it with difficulty [24].
Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles v Here the times are riding on wheels to pass on, and through them wealth and poverty are distributed daily.
Whoever is rich today perhaps tomorrow will become poor, and the one who is poor now perhaps will soon become rich?
The sick man is healed, and the one who is healthy becomes sick, for this world and its activities are woven upon changes.
The child grows up, and the man grows old, and the old man dies, for there is no stature complete without change in the world.
The morning has passed, and noon comes, and the sunset draws near, and evening comes, and takes its place.
The day is delightful and its sight is loved and its beauty radiant, and the night walks in and enters in its stead and spoils it [25].
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh The wise man has the fear of God in all that he does, and in the days of sins he guards against offenses [26].

v The fear of the Lord is the bridle that stops man's rush toward committing evil, and draws him backward when he is enslaved to running after his hateful lusts, not only in his outward life but especially in his hidden inner life [26].

v The man who lives in remembrance of God at all times is filled with fear, so that even when he resists a thought of lust passing over his soul, he becomes terrified because of this thought. But the thought flees at once before the fear of the soul, like a bird that flees before the man who disturbs its rest. Fear and respect for the laws of men preserve the body against lusts. And fear and man's shame before God preserve the soul against evil thoughts. For since he knows that God sees him at all times, he watches himself continually lest he sin [27].
St. Mar Philoxenus Every intelligent man knows wisdom, and praises him who finds her [27].

The wise man says: "Happy is the man that findeth wisdom, and the man that getteth understanding" (Prov 3:13). It befits the intelligent believer to seek wisdom and be diligent in searching for it and ask the Lord to acquire it, and to praise everyone who acquires it, for it gives the blessed life, and also presents to him true and lasting riches and glory.
St. Chrysostom asks: Was St. Peter poor, that he had nothing to give to the lame man? Origen sees that the wisdom we acquire is the Law of the Lord, and it is more precious than gold and silver.
v This means: The law that proceeds from Your mouth is better for me; which is Christ. I disdain the pieces of gold and shining silver, that I may take delight in the law of Your mouth and enjoy it.

We can say that "the law of the mouth" is the order of the words that proceed from the mouth of God: the first words were spoken to beginners, while the following words were spoken to those who had received the first, until they reach perfection [28].
Origen The wise in words make others wise, and rain down sound proverbs [28].

As man strives to be wise, let him realize that God grants him wisdom when he strives by his prayers and conduct that his brothers may enjoy wisdom from God, for what he desires for his brothers in earnestness opens the door for him and for them.

30 Do not go after your lusts, but refrain yourself from your appetites. 31 For if you give your soul the desires that please her, she will make you a laughingstock to your enemies. 32 Take not pleasure in many banquets, neither bind yourself to the expense thereof. 33 Make not yourself poor with banquets, spending upon them from borrowing, when there is nothing in your purse; for thereby you lie in wait for your own life.

St. Basil likens the soul to the horseman who knows how to tame his horse and lead it, so that he and the horse are safe. But if the horseman is inexperienced, by his wrong leading he causes harm and destruction to himself and the horse.

v The souls that are not bridled by reason, nor dominated by the mind, which suppresses their passions of pleasures and pains, and manages and directs them (soundly), these souls perish like the dumb animals. For their minds are drawn by the passions, as unruly horses draw their drivers [29].

St. Anthony the Great v Look now, beloved, at what I say: know that just as a horse is good only with respect to its swiftness in the service assigned to it, but needs a trainer who rides it and turns it to the place he wants, because the beast alone does not know what ought to be done. And just as, if the horse is ridden, it must use the things natural to it, I mean to leap and jump, so if its rider manages the causes of its movements well, the harm disappears and the benefit is obtained.

And just as it is not enough for the rider to manage the horse only, but also to acquire knowledge and habit of staying on it, then thereby the need and safety of the rider and the ridden are fulfilled. But if he does not manage it well, and is not knowledgeable and accustomed to staying on it, the horse in many instances turns aside from the straight way... and goes out into steep, rugged roads, and stumbles and falls, with its rider, and both of them come into distress. And the cause of all that is the negligence of its rider, either because he did not know how to train it, nor was accustomed to staying on it, or because he neglected its governance and management and returning it to the straight way.

So also by this example God created man, and placed in him a mind with which he reasons, in honor of the soul He created with the body. So if the soul manages well, and exercises the work of leadership as it ought, and bridles the movements of the body, it is saved and saves the body from falling into distress. But if it is negligent, and does not manage the movements of the body as it should, and is heedless and lazy and lets go of the bridle of the body, then because it has no thought, it goes out into the rugged roads and the soul falls with it into these evils. This is not because of an evil in the body - God forbid - but because the soul did not manage it as it ought [30].

v The light of the body is the eye, and the insight of the soul is the mind created in it by nature, and I do not say that the mind is other than the soul as though they were separate from each other. No, but the soul and the mind are bound by union. For the mind is a natural power of the soul. It is its inward parts, created with it, not foreign to it nor having entered it after a time [31].

v If the soul moves toward its rational faculty which is the mind (that which the Holy Trinity, Creator of all things, made implanted in it from the time He formed it), and the mind thinks of what is fitting and proper to God, then the soul becomes saved, and flees from all uses of the passions.

And when the soul goes first and observes the movements of the body and controls them, then it is in a calm and piety befitting it. And if it comes into virtuous sights according to its nature, it remains contemplating all the works of God and His glory with fear and calm, without anxiety. Rather at times you find it in amazement, looking before it to the Trinity, thinking of the glory of the divinity which cannot be comprehended because of the greatness of its light. And it remains contemplating that blessed light and wisdom without end and absence of disturbance. So if the soul keeps its mind vigilant according to its nature, and thinks of what it should, the mind must be in theoria (contemplation) of the glorified works and all that is of peace [32].
St. Basil the Great Do not follow your passions, but restrain your lusts [29].
In speaking of self-control, he warns us against deviating toward lusts and passions and a life of luxury. He also requires us to be prudent in facing material responsibilities.

v If those who are compelled by necessity to cross wide seas, when they are alert, preserve their lives, for even if the waves are raging while their boats sail, they save themselves by holding on to anything on the shore. But if they are drunk, even if they make countless attempts to swim to the shore, the wine overcomes them, and they drown amid the waves and depart from life.

So also the soul, if it falls among raging waves in the midst of the whirlpool of the currents of life, by its own striving cannot overcome the love of the body, just as it is unable to know (by itself) that it is a divine, immortal soul bound to a material, mortal body full of lusts... and that this is the touchstone for testing it, so if it allows itself to be defiled by bodily lusts, it perishes, and its perishing and going out of the circle of salvation is the result of its negligence and its drunkenness with ignorance and its contempt for goodness. The body is like a river which often swallows us up with base pleasures [33].

v Sin finds help for itself in matter, and the body becomes a throne for it. But the rational soul, when it understands this, casts off from itself the burden of matter, and rises from under its weight, and perceives God Almighty, and washes the body carefully without entrusting it, since it is an enemy and adversary to it. By this God crowns the soul, as it overcomes the lusts and evils [34].

v The free man is the one whom (bodily) pleasures do not enslave, but who controls the body with good discernment and chastity, content with what God gives, however little, thanking Him with all his heart.

When both the mind that loves God and the soul come to understanding, then it (the body) is easily tamed even against its will, and the soul by means of the mind can quench every animal movement [35].

v Those who are not content with sufficiency, but seek more (with lust), enslave themselves to the passions that disturb and bring into them all evil thoughts and apprehensions, that is, all that is evil, although we need to obtain new good things. And just as garments that are excessively long hinder travelers from walking, so excessive desire for possessions hinders the soul from striving and being saved [36].

St. Anthony the Great St. Augustine addresses the Lord in prayer, asking for the work of grace in him, since by his own personal abilities he cannot be freed from passions and lusts; so in his Confessions he declares his need for God's work in him, that He may fulfill what He commands him.

v I heard a divine voice commanding me: "Take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness" (Lk 21:34). Wine is far from me; have mercy on me lest drunkenness come near me.
In any case gluttony sometimes tries to creep in to seize Your servant. Have mercy on me, that it may depart from me! For no one can be chaste unless You give it to him (Wis 8:21).
You give us much when we pray. And all that we have received of good things even before prayer, we received from You. And the truth we learned lately is that we received it from You.

I was never a drunkard, but I know many drunkards who through You became exceedingly lofty men. For it is Your work that these, who were never thus and who ought not to have been thus, have become thus. They are Your works, that they may learn from Him who worked in them thus.
I have also heard another statement from You: "Do not follow your passions, but restrain your lusts" (see Sir 18:29).

Through Your help I heard another statement that I loved very much: "For neither, if we eat, are we the better; neither, if we eat not, are we the worse" (1 Cor 8:8). In other words, the first does not make me rich, nor the last poor.
I also heard another statement: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content... both to abound and to suffer need.
I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me" (Phil 4:11-13)... He strengthens me so that I am able to do that. Grant me, You who commanded, and command what You will.
This man (St. Paul) confessed that he had received this, therefore he glories in the Lord (1 Cor 1:31).

I heard another man pray in order to receive, saying: "Remove from me the gluttony of the belly" (see Sir 23:6). It is clear from this, O holy God, that You are the one who gives, and that You do what You have commanded to be done [37].

v It befits man to be spiritual in order to keep the Law spiritually; this is not through the Law but by grace, that is, not through the commandment but through the free gift, not through the impulse of the letter but the impulse of the Spirit. Now man begins to be renewed inwardly according to grace, on condition that he does not follow what he loves in his mind, nor agree with what the flesh presses upon him and which he hates. This does not mean that he is entirely free of evil lusts, but that he does not follow them (18:30) [38].
v Obeying the commandment "Thou shalt not covet" (Ex 20:17) is one thing, and trying to refrain from practicing it is another. Where man follows what is written: "Do not follow your desire".

And so that you may know that without the grace of the Savior no one can carry out the first commandment or the other. In order to practice righteousness in the true worship of God, fight in an inner struggle against the inner evil of lust, and to attain perfect righteousness by there being no adversary at all. For whoever fights is always exposed to danger, and sometimes is wounded even if he does not fall. But he who has no enemy enjoys complete peace.

And it is rightly said that he is without sin in whom sin does not live. Nor does the one who refrains from evil works declare: "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do" (Rom 7:20) [39].

v What is the accomplishment of goodness but ceasing from evil and ending it? And what is ceasing from evil but what the Law says: "Thou shalt not covet" (Rom 7:7; Ex 20:17)? Coveting is not the fulfilling of goodness, for it is the finishing of evil... Therefore he says: "But how to perform that which is good I find not" (Rom 7:18).

I am unable to accomplish what is said: "Thou shalt not covet." What then do I need? To accomplish: "Do not follow your passions" (Sir 18:29). Do this as long as unlawful lusts are present in your body... Do not give yourself over to your lusts, for if you follow them you give them strength. And by giving them strength, how will you triumph over your enemies when you support them against yourself by your strength? Then what is perfect freedom in the Lord Jesus, who said: "If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed"? When does perfect freedom exist? When there are no enemies, and when "the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death" (1 Cor 15:26)...

Let us, the wounded, beseech the Physician, that we may be carried to the inn so that we may be healed [by the Good Shepherd (Lk 10:30-35)]. It is He who promises health, who has compassion on the man left half dead on the road by the robbers [40].

St. Augustine Father Fulgentius, the disciple of St. Augustine, links this statement with the saying of the Lord Christ: "He that loveth his life shall lose it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal. If any man serve me, let him follow me; and where I am, there shall also my servant be" (Jn 12:25-26).

v How does he who loves his life lose it? He does this who follows his obstinate passions, he who pleases them more than he should. Therefore the Holy Bible warns us in the words: "Do not follow your passions" (Sir 18:29). If you follow them you lose yourself, for this behavior is off the road that leads to virtue. That is like the opposite behavior: he who hates it in this world saves it... Truly, unless you die you bear no fruit for yourself [41].

Father Fulgentius v Pleasant is the present life and full of many pleasures, but not for all, only for those who are drawn to it. If someone looks to heaven and sees the beautiful things there, at once he disdains this life and does not care for it. Just as the beauty of anything is admired when nothing more beautiful is seen, but when something better appears the former is disdained. Therefore if we choose to look to that beauty, and observe the loftiness of the Kingdom there, we free ourselves from the present bonds, for sympathy with things, as Christ says, brings us to this: "He that loveth his life shall lose it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal; if any man serve me, let him follow me" (Jn 12:25-26).

The words seem like a riddle, but they are not, but are full of great wisdom. But how: he who loves his life loses it? When he practices its improper lusts, when he satisfies his lusts where it was necessary to do otherwise. Thus one advises us: "Do not follow your desire" (see Sir 29:18) [42].
St. John Chrysostom If you fill your soul with lust in pleasure, it makes you a mockery of your enemies [30].

v Not only is this self-control worthy of praise in moderation in food, but also moderation in lust. For it is written: "Do not follow your passions, but restrain your lusts, for if you allow yourself satisfaction in lust, it will make you a laughingstock to your enemies" (see Sir 18:29-30). And he says afterward: "Wine and women lead the wise astray" (see Sir 19:2). Paul teaches us moderation in marriage itself, so whoever is not chaste in marriage, this is counted a kind of adultery, and breaks the law of the Apostle [43].

St. Ambrose v Man, though he is ahead of all these (creatures) in dignity, did not understand and ignored following God and the desire to be like his Creator, and became a slave to the lusts of the body. "He is compared to the dull beasts and has become like them."
At one time he resembles a lustful horse, neighing after his companion's wife (Jer 5:8).
And at another time like a ravening wolf, lying in wait for strangers (Ezek 22:27).
And at another time, because of his deceiving his brother, he makes himself a base fox (Ezek 13:4).

Truly there is increasing folly, for he who was created in the image of the Creator is likened to the beast that has no reason. He does not know his structure from the beginning, nor desires to understand the great dispensations made for his sake; at least to learn his dignity from them, but he does not care for the truth, casting off from himself the image of the heavenly to take the image of the earthly. And that he might not remain in sin, for his sake "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us" (Jn 1:14), and "emptied Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross" (Phil 2:8).

If you do not care for your first origin, then for the sake of the price that was paid for you accept at least some thought of your dignity, and look to what was offered in your place, and be assured of what you have been qualified for. You were bought with the precious blood of Christ, so do not be slaves to sin. Understand your dignity, and do not be like the dull beasts.

"This their way is a stumbling block to them" (Ps 48:13) LXX. God who manages our affairs hinders us from walking in evil, so He places obstacles and hindrances that we may shrink from the unreasoning life, after which we rejoice with our tongue. With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession of faith is made unto our salvation (see Rom 10:10). Paul persecuted the Church of Christ; he despoiled it, and pressed on his part with evil (Acts 8:3), and afterward he rejoiced in his understanding, declaring to the synagogue that this is the Christ (Acts 9:22) [44].
St. Basil the Great v "Like sheep they are driven to the abyss; death shall feed on them" (Ps 49:14).

This is he who leads into captivity those who resemble the beasts, and are compared to the dull flocks like sheep, which have no reason nor ability to defend themselves, and he is the enemy who brought them down to his prison, and delivered them to death to shepherd them. For death reigned over them from the days of Adam until the leadership of Moses (Rom 5:14), until the true Shepherd came and laid down His life for His flock, and raised them together and led them (Jn 10:3-18) from the prison of the abyss to the dawn of the resurrection, and delivered them to the righteous, that is, to His angels, to shepherd them.

"And the upright shall have dominion over them in the morning." Every believer is accompanied by an angel worthy to look upon the Father in heaven. These upright ones, then, have dominion over them when they are freed from the harshest bitter bondage, and have dominion over them in the morning, that is, when they advance in the rising of the light.

Consider all the groups of words written. When man was in dignity he did not understand, he became like the dull beasts. He who has dignity, and did not know himself because of the sin dwelling in him, became like the dull beasts. Therefore, since he became estranged from the Word of God and became a dumb beast, the enemy drove him like an unattended flock, and cast him into the abyss, and delivered him to death to shepherd him.

Therefore when he is saved from this, and freed from the evil shepherd (death), he says: "The Lord is my shepherd" (Ps 23:1). It is no longer death but life, and instead of falling there is resurrection, and instead of deception there is truth.

[And their help shall wear away in the abyss] (Ps 49:14) LXX. Perhaps he speaks here of death, for with all its help it cannot preserve those it shepherded, this one whom (Christ) who has authority over death destroys (Heb 2:14), for all their help is old and weak. At that time the help of those who were deceived in mind, and were proud because of wealth or glory or power, appears vain.

"Shall wear away in the abyss" as their weakness is realized. Or perhaps the help of the righteous who were saved by the Lord dissolves in the abyss, since they have not yet received the promises, for God has provided some better thing for us, that those who preceded us "without us should not be made perfect" (Heb 11:40).

"But God will redeem my soul from the hand of the abyss, for He will receive me" (Ps 49:15) LXX. It is clear that he prophesies of the descent of the Lord into hell, who saves the soul of the prophet with others, and he does not remain there [45].
St. Basil the Great Do not enjoy excessive luxury, so that you do not bind yourself to its expenses [31].

v What are we to do about this fact, that the Apostle himself gave us a huge list of vices, and pointed out among them drunkenness and concluded it with a warning not to eat bread with those who sin in such things? [46]
v It is a matter that arouses pity, reminding us how serious it is to eat with those who sin by gluttony even in their homes [47].
St. Augustine Do not become a beggar by holding banquets and do not borrow money, when there is nothing in your purse [33].

Regarding gluttony or greed or the lust of the belly, many of the Fathers, especially the ascetics, count the taming of the lust of the belly as giving victory over all thoughts and temptations. St. Mar Philoxenus, Bishop of Mabbug, devoted, in his Memre, thirteen discourses to speaking of gluttony. In them he highlighted that the lust of the belly is the most defiling of the passions, deprives us of prudent thought, and is the door of all evils, enslaves the soul as well as the body, and hinders tenderness, and being against fasting it destroys prayer and causes sluggishness [48].

St. Mar Philoxenus distinguishes between hunger and the lust of the belly: hunger is a gift from the Creator that supports health without falling into the lust of the belly, which destroys man's authority and enslaves him to other lusts. God created man a god over his belly, feeding it and not being enslaved to it.

St. Mar Philoxenus presents to us the problem of the lust of the belly through three serious examples: Adam in his simplicity through the lust of the belly (Gen 3:6), and Esau lost his birthright and its blessings for the same reason (Gen 25:34), and the people of Israel through the lust of the belly worshiped the golden calf and forgot God (Ex 32:19).
The following are some excerpts from this discourse:

v The person who submits to this base lust cannot accept the yoke of discipleship to Christ... As soon as the stomach becomes master over the body, it commands and subdues all its will, and instead of the road ascending to heaven, it shows him the other road that descends to the abyss [49].

v This lust of the belly is baser than all the passions. As soon as a person becomes its servant and carries its yoke on his shoulders, it no longer allows him rest from serving it. He serves it night and day, and it sends him everywhere it desires like an exhausted servant, not on a clean road but on roads full of stumbling blocks, and to a place where there are harmful things, a lover of the lust of things who has no eyes that see the light, because even if he wishes it, the weight of food makes them grow dark. The day for him is night, and the night is double death [50].

v God created the animals for two things: while all that belongs to their life is eating, they also do a service for the human race, but the gluttonous man eats and does not work. While he is zealous for the table, he is stripped of all important works. The soul that serves the belly does not perceive God, for it is dead to all thoughts of knowledge, and to contemplation of God, since the knowledge of the soul proceeds from the illumination of the body and the members of the body. And the illumination of the body proceeds from reducing food, but surely the gluttonous man is burdened with two yokes, namely the darkness of thoughts and the weight of the body [51]
St. Mar Philoxenus Inspired by Sirach 18

entries.section: I praise You, O great Creator, for Your dispensation!

paragraphs.text: v Allow Your earthly creation to emulate the heavenly creation, O my wonderful Creator!
I stand with the whole universe, as in a chorus unable to express Your wonderful dispensation!
You provide the earthly body with its needs, so it is satisfied and quenched, and for my soul love and tenderness and joy and immortality.
You embrace me with Your care, so I lack nothing.
v My sin brought me down to deprivation of life; the abyss opened its mouth to swallow me and there was no rescuer.
You came down to earth, and became incarnate that I might draw near to You.
You accepted death, that by Your resurrection I might tread on death under my feet!
You accepted the wounds in Your body, so You clothed it with glory instead of disgrace and shame.
The crown of thorns was placed on Your head, and it blossomed and offered me heavenly roses.

Your side was pierced with the spear and poured out blood and water. By Your blood You cleansed me, O Righteous One, from my sins, and by the water You gave me, by Your Holy Spirit, the spirit of adoption.
Whenever I look to the dispensation of Your salvation I stand in bewilderment; who can describe Your love and Your mercies?!
You offered me complete pardon, and clothed me with the garment of Your righteousness.
Even if my days reach a thousand years, they are like a drop of water from the sea of eternity, and a grain of sand in the desert.
You revealed to me Your longsuffering and the overflowing of Your mercy!
v In Your love for all mankind You rebuke and discipline and train and teach, and bring back the lost sheep not to the Garden of Eden but to Paradise, to join them to the chorus of the heavenly ones.
v Your kindness to men is indescribable, and Your giving is beyond estimation.
Grant us kindness, that we may offer our brothers of what You have given us:
The sweet word with spiritual and psychological and material gifts.
Whatever we offer, we draw from the storehouses of Your love that we may be enriched and offer to our brothers.
Grant us Your longsuffering, that we may judge no one before the time.
Grant us of Your humility, that however much honor we offer our brothers, we shall not reach the last row which was reserved for You alone, O You who were crucified for us!
v Your being lifted up on the cross is the only remedy to heal the diseases of my soul.
For my sake You sanctified Yourself, You who are Holy, and as a member of Your body I vow my life to You, desiring that all mankind be sanctified with me.
Gladden my heart by my returning to You with all mankind.
Let us hear Your wonderful voice:
Today you shall be with Me in Paradise.
Let my heart ascend to it now, and I will not postpone even for a moment.
Truly from morning to evening the time changes.

You have shone upon me, O Sun of Righteousness, so I do not wait until evening, but throw myself into Your embrace, and cry out with Jacob my father: "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me" (Gen 32:26)!
v Accompany me, that I may enjoy Your divine presence all the moments of my life.
I do not follow my passions, for Your love sanctifies me.
Who restrains my lusts, except the desire to enjoy union with You?!
I no longer suffer from gluttony, for the bread of this world does not give life.
I do not spend on the pleasures and tables of the world, for my heart and my thought and my senses and my emotions and all my energies are completely absorbed in Your love!

entries.section: 1. Attention to great and small things

paragraphs.text: 1 A laboring man that is a drunkard shall not be rich; and he that despiseth small things shall fall little by little. 2 Wine and women will make men of understanding to fall away. 3 And he that cleaveth to harlots will become impudent. Moths and worms shall have him to heritage, and the impudent soul shall be taken away. 4 He that is hasty to give credit is light-minded; and he that sinneth offendeth against his own soul. 5 Whoso taketh pleasure in wickedness shall be condemned; but he that hateth to be talked to lessens his sins.

He begins with negligence in drinking wine, while practical experience confirms that the life of the drunkard is filled with misery; negligence in improper bodily (sexual) matters is tragic, and association with fornicators corrupts a man's life. Negligence in these matters causes material loss, the misleading of the mind, loss of reputation, corruption of the body, instability of the soul, and falling under judgment. All this calls us to a healthy self-control.
A drunken laborer will not become rich, and he who despises small things will fall little by little [1].

The Apostle says: "Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities" (1 Tim 5:23). Wine was permitted within the narrowest limits as a medicine, and in some cold regions because of the bitter cold.

The scholar Tertullian says that Timothy [abstained from wine, not out of a rule, but because of his consecration.] Wine in itself is not forbidden by a rule, but it is unbecoming, especially for those consecrated to the service of the Lord. St. Clement of Alexandria sees that Timothy used wine as a tonic suited to his sick and weakened body. As for the emphasis on using "a little" of it, it was lest the sick forget themselves through much wine [1].

entries.section: 1. Attention to great and small things

paragraphs.text: Some used it as a drink of hospitality, and within the narrowest limits, lest children become accustomed to it, and others without limits; but the Church preferred to forbid taking it, especially since abstaining from it does no harm to a person, whereas taking it may cause him to become addicted to it. The problem with wine is that when it brings the drinker to the point of drunkenness, he turns into another person, lacking dignity, balance and a sense of responsibility, and even unaware of the seriousness of drunkenness. It makes a person lose his covering and exposes him even before his own sons, as happened with Noah (Gen 9:21). St. Jerome says: [No one may say that drunkenness is not a sin; we read of Noah that he was drunk once, but God warns us not to suppose him a drunkard and an addict of wine [2].] He also says: [In one hour of drunkenness he was laid bare (Noah), who for six hundred years had remained covered with dignity [3].] He also says: [After his drunkenness his body was laid bare; for the pampering of the soul leads in the end to falling into lust: the belly is first gorged, and then the members rise up in revolt [4].] And St. Ambrose says: [O the power of wine! It made him whom the waters of the flood did not overcome to become naked! [5]]

entries.section: 1. Attention to great and small things

paragraphs.text: v The monks were celebrating one of the feasts in Scetis, and they gave one of the elders a cup of wine, but he refused it, saying: "Take this death away from me." When the others who were eating with him saw what he had done, they too refused to take any of the wine [6].
Paradise of the Fathers The lust of drunkenness makes a man unable even to buy the food he needs. The wise man says that wine and dissolute women make a person overpowered (Prov 23:31-33).

entries.section: 1. Attention to great and small things

paragraphs.text: He who controls himself does not squander his money in drunkenness, nor is he negligent even in small matters. St. Augustine says: "Faithfulness in small things is not a small matter." St. Augustine sees that our Lord Jesus often proclaims "Watch" (Mt 24:42; 25:13; 26:38, 41; Mk 13:37), and also says: "Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you" (Jn 12:35), since He keeps us from the gradual approach of the serpent, who instills evil in us [7].

entries.section: 1. Attention to great and small things

paragraphs.text: v Let us not make light of our sins because they are small, but fear them because they are many. The drops of rain are small, but because they are many they can shake mountains [8].

Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles v Just as the water that gathers in the hold of a ship and rises gradually and imperceptibly has the same effect as if the ship were in the midst of a storm, so also the inflammations are small when the pustules appear scattered over the members of the body; but when they spread and cannot be counted, they may destroy life as if it were one great and dangerous wound afflicting the chest. Therefore we read what is written: "A laboring man that is a drunkard shall not be rich, and he that despiseth small things shall fall little by little." Those who neglect sorrow and repentance and do not avoid small sins not only fall from the state of righteousness, but descend little by little and far, until complete ruin.

entries.section: 1. Attention to great and small things

paragraphs.text: v Those who constantly transgress with small sins should think well that sometimes the worst sins are committed in small matters rather than in greater ones. We recognize the greater sins more quickly, and so they can be healed more quickly. But the smaller sins we do not look at, nor do we even regard them as sins. Thus they grow and become worse, since we show little concern when committing them. Likewise it always happens that when the soul becomes accustomed to these small things, it no longer fears the great one among them [9].
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 1. Attention to great and small things

paragraphs.text: v (St. Zosimas) added: St. Ignatius the God-bearer said: I need the meekness by which I destroy all the power of the ruler of this age. The sign of our renunciation of the world is that we are no longer troubled by anything. For it may happen that after a man has left millions, he becomes attached to a small needle with a sick attachment, so that he is troubled on its account. The needle has taken the place of the millions, and thus he becomes a slave to this needle, or to a cap, or to a garment, or to a book, and is no longer a slave of God! [10]
Paradise of the Fathers Wine and women lead the wise astray, and he who associates with fornicators becomes more unstable [2].

v The evil of drunkenness appears clearly in the case of Lot and his daughters. When he was drunk with wine he lay with his daughters and did not care about it. Pharaoh also, being drunk, hanged the baker on a cross.

entries.section: 1. Attention to great and small things

paragraphs.text: Add to this the Jewish people, of whom we read: "The people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play" (Ex 32:6). They drank much wine, and afterward they asked for idols to be made, and in honoring these idols they began to dance, bending their limbs in frenzy with movements of every kind. Herod also, being inflamed with much wine, ordered the killing of St. John the Baptist as a reward for a single dance performed by a girl [11].
Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles Rot and worms shall inherit him, and his reckless soul shall be uprooted [3].

entries.section: 1. Attention to great and small things

paragraphs.text: v By fornication are understood all bodily and animal lusts. Holy Scripture speaks of idolatry as fornication, and the Apostle Paul calls covetousness idolatry, and therefore it is fornication. So every evil lust is rightly called fornication, because the spirit is corrupted by leaving the lofty law that governs it and sells its honor for a base lust that does not befit the loftiness of the spirit [12]!

entries.section: 1. Attention to great and small things

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine v The custom of marrying sisters ceased from the time of Abraham. And the contracting of marriage with many wives ceased from the days of the prophets. As we read: "Go not after thy lusts, but refrain thyself from thine appetites" (8:30). And in another place: "Let thy fountain be blessed, and rejoice with the wife of thy youth" (Prov 5:18), for it clearly forbids polygamy. And Jeremiah plainly gives the name of neighing horses to those who desire other men's wives [13].

entries.section: 1. Attention to great and small things

paragraphs.text: Father Methodius v Above all it befits the monk also to abstain from the company of women and from drinking wine, for wine and women lead astray even the wise (see Sir 19:2) [14]
St. Basil the Great He who is quick to trust is not wise in heart, and he who sins is a criminal against himself [4].

entries.section: 1. Attention to great and small things

paragraphs.text: v My heart rejoices in you, my dear son. May the eternal God and the Lord Jesus Christ guard you! Do not believe everyone, nor place your confidence in all, nor let anyone gain the upper hand over you through flattery and praise. There are many who serve Satan: "He that is hasty to give credit is light-minded..." (see Sir 19:4) [15].
St. Ignatius of Antioch He who rejoices in iniquity shall be condemned [5].

6 He that sinneth against himself repenteth, and he that taketh pleasure in evil shall be condemned. 7 Repeat not that which is evil, and thou shalt lose nothing. 8 Whether it be to friend or foe, talk not of other men's lives; and if thou canst without offence, reveal them not. 9 For he heard and observed thee, and when time came he hated thee. 10 If thou hast heard a word, let it die with thee; and be bold, it will not burst thee. 11 A fool travaileth with a word, as a woman in labor of a child. 12 As an arrow that sticketh in the thigh of a fleshy man, so is a word within a fool's belly.

St. Mar Jacob of Serugh warns women as well as men against chattering in the holy Church. Control of the tongue requires not chattering, not passing on words to any person however much a friend of yours he may be, and keeping to caution and reserve. The proper use of the tongue is shown in the following: 1. Avoiding chatter keeps us from evil. 2. Being careful not to pass on to others what we hear, unless silence would mean harm, loss and injustice to a person! 3. Let our depths be like a grave in which we bury what we hear, lest we travail with a word that becomes the embryo of evil.
v The world met me bearing woes to distribute to me. My Lord, I will not take from its gift, which is full of harms.
In the world chatter and noise are acquired along with curses; give me Your word, that in its company I may find quiet.
It is a second sea, and behold, it troubles me with its storms. O Harbor of life, give me rest in Your pure place.
The world is mire, and he who goes down into it makes his soul stink. My Lord, by Your teaching wash me, for I am defiled by the world [16].
v The Pharisee, who was righteous according to the Law, became beautiful in his own eyes, and stood to recount his good deeds.
He looked at the tax collector, who had also gone up to pray, and despised him and rejected him, and directed mocking words at him.
He thanked the Lord with a spirit full of chatter, and compared himself with the tax collector, and found that he was greater than he.
He said: God, I thank You that I am not like this tax collector, for he forgot that it was a prayer (Lk 18:11) [17].
v Women sit in the holy temple of prayers (the Church), with their mouths gaping with excessive talk.
The prophets cry out to teach the earth good things, while they chatter with vain and unseemly news.
Satan himself blinds the eyes of men, and at every opportunity he tries to kill them.
The giant found that everyone whispers quietly in prayers between himself and the Lord, and in place of the course of prayers he put the whispers of vain news in the mouths of the women.

O wretched woman, whisper in prayer, and uncover your wound to the hidden Physician, who dresses the wound and does not expose it... The evil one wishes to disturb with chatter this work, which dresses the wounds of all sinners.
He makes a man chatter with his neighbor in the holy temple, to relate vain news without benefit.
Satan gathers and brings in some words from the leftovers that error has left in men.
He reminds you of words you had forgotten before you entered, so that you utter them at the time of prayers [18].

St. Mar Jacob of Serugh St. Mar Jacob of Serugh sees the tongue of the holy believer as a fruitful mother, who does not bear chatter but praises to God the Creator: 1. It does not cease to bring forth new praises, not in respect of the words, but in respect of their character as a hymn of love that never grows old. 2. The rock that followed the people in the wilderness poured out upon them flowing living waters; so the sanctified tongue brings forth rivers of living water. 3. It does not befit the tongue of the believer to be like the slothful servant who hid his master's silver in the earth and did not trade with it, so that it did not gain (Mt 25:14-30). 4. If the tongue ceases to praise, God calls the stones to praise Him, as happened on the day of His crucifixion, when men ceased to praise, and the sun and moon and earth and rocks and tombs set out to praise Him, each in its own language.
And he who hates chatter, his sin is lessened [6].

God did not create the tongue for chatter, but that we might place it in His hands, so that He sanctifies it and makes of it a spiritual harp on which His Holy Spirit plays a joyful symphony of love. God is concerned for man's tongue and offers it a heavenly guard, yet not by compulsion, but at man's request.

v Men were created to praise much, and perhaps they would remember praise every day in abundance! The shining sun does not shine for itself or run its course for itself, but it has light to give light to men.
And for their sake the luminaries (the stars) came to be in the atmosphere, and (the enlightened men) benefit from the days and the nights.
To men belong discernment, knowledge, the word and the voice, that they may give praise to the Most High in His place.
The mouth of man is made perfect, as though for the praise of the Lord, and he who ceases to praise becomes ungrateful.
And for this you have a mouth, that you may praise with it, give thanks with it, rejoice with it, and bless with it.
Praise, for you have the praising word; and rejoice, for you have the voice full of melodies.
Give thanks, for you have mind and discernment; and bless, for you have become a rational vessel and not a silent one.
You were nothing, and mercies made you something great... So give thanks with wonder; why are you silent?
Enter into yourself and look at your person within you, for in you are all the wonders of the creative power [19].
v My Lord, may the lowly mouth that rejoices in You and the tongue that chants Your praise, though unworthy, rejoice in You.
My Lord, may the speaker also rejoice in You, and the hearers, for You have gladdened them by Your birth; to You be praise [20].
v He made for him a mouth to praise the Lord his God, and through it he takes foods for his whole body [21].
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh Never repeat a word, and you will never be a loser [7].
Do not tell it to a friend or an enemy, and do not reveal it unless you would sin by keeping it [8].
Someone may hear you and guard against you, and hate you when the time comes [9].
Have you heard a word? Let it die with you.
Be bold! For it will not make you burst [10].

v You heard a word from a man while he was in a state of anger, pained and resentful; let the word die in you. Why do you repeat it? Why do you proclaim it? It does not tear you apart if you leave it inside you. In any case, speak with your friend who wishes to make you an enemy of another friend of yours. Speak with him and treat him with a soothing remedy, as for a sick soul.
Say to him: Why do you want me to become an enemy of that man? He may answer you: He is my enemy!

Say to him: Do you want me to be an enemy of your enemy? I want to be an enemy of your sin. The one whose enemy you want me to be is a man. There is an enemy of you both, and I must be his enemy if I am your friend.
He answers you: Who is this other enemy of mine?
- It is your evil.
- And what is my evil?
- The hatred with which you hate your friend.

In this be a physician. For the physician does not love the sick man unless he hates his sickness. He fights against the fever to free the sick man from it. Do not love the vices of your friends, if you love them [22].

Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles v I do not know from where this disease fell upon men. We have become chatterers, keeping nothing in our minds. Hear the counsel of a wise man, who says: "Hast thou heard a word? Let it die with thee; and be bold, it will not burst thee" (see Sir 19:10). Again: "A fool travaileth with a word, as a woman in labor of a child" (see Sir 19:11). We are ready to bring accusations and prepared for condemnation. Even if we commit nothing else evil, this is enough to destroy us, and it carries us to hell, and occupies us with ten thousands of evils. And that you may know this for certain, hear what the prophet says: "Thou sittest and speakest against thy brother" (Ps 50:20).
St. John Chrysostom At a word like this the fool travails, as a woman in labor of a child [11].
As an arrow that sticketh in the flesh of the thigh, so is a word in the belly of a fool [12].
v Man is mortal in his body, but in his mind and his word he is immortal.

In silence you see your mind, but when you use your mind, you speak within yourself. For during silence the mind begets the word, and the word of thanksgiving offered to God is the salvation of man [23].
v He who speaks foolishly has no mind, for he speaks without thinking about all matters. Therefore examine what is useful for you, for the salvation of your soul, so that you may do it [24].

v The reasonable word that benefits the soul is a gift from God, but the empty word that merely investigates the measures of heaven and earth, and the distance between them, and the sizes of the sun and the stars, those who occupy themselves with that... are like those who draw water with a sieve, for men cannot discover (all) this [25].
St. Anthony the Great

13 Admonish a friend, it may be he hath not done it; and if he have done it, that he do it no more. 14 Admonish thy friend, it may be he hath not said it; and if he have, that he speak it not again. 15 Admonish a friend, for many times it is a slander. 16 And believe not every tale. There is one that slippeth in his speech, but not from his heart. 17 And who is he that hath not offended with his tongue? Admonish thy neighbor before thou threaten him.
When you hear that someone is speaking about you something bad, it is advisable to speak with him directly in love and meekness, without speaking with others about what you heard.
Ask your friend, perhaps he did nothing, and if he did it, he may not do it again [13].

Ben Sira urges us to be careful in examining matters. In a spirit of love and wisdom, if he hears of a friend or neighbor who has spoken evil of him, he should examine the matter without agitation. With wisdom he should speak with the friend or neighbor so that he does not repeat it concerning anyone else. Let him always walk according to the Law of the Most High [17].
Ask your neighbor, perhaps he did not say anything, and if he said it, perhaps he will not repeat the saying [14].
Ask your friend, for it is often slander, and do not believe every word (you have heard) [15].

v If anyone accuses a person of having wronged him, may he not keep that in his mind, whether it was against his neighbor or against us. I ask of you a kindness, that you come to us, and present the accusation, and receive from us our defense of ourselves. It is said: "Ask him, lest what you heard about him he did not say. Ask him, lest he did not do (what you accuse him of). And if he did it, let him not repeat it." For we will either defend ourselves, or if we are at fault we will apologize and strive not to fall into the same errors. This is for your benefit and ours, for you may have accused us without cause, and when you know the truth of the matter you will correct what you supposed; and we, if we have wronged you without knowing, will mend our ways [26].

v "I will go down now, and see whether they have done altogether according to the cry of it, which is come unto me; and if not, I will know" (see Gen 18:21). What the Father says is this: "A report has come to me, but I wish once more to test this rumor more precisely in the light of the facts. I do not do this because I do not know whether I am doing it, but because I wish to teach men not to concern themselves with talk alone, nor to believe it carelessly if someone speaks it against another." It befits men to believe what they hear after they have made a careful examination and found proof in the light of the facts. This is the reason that God said in another place: "Believe not every tale" (see Sir 19:15). For nothing ruins the life of men like their believing everything that people say [27].
St. John Chrysostom A man may slip without intending to; and who is he that has not offended with his tongue? [16]
Ask your neighbor before you threaten him, and let the Law of the Most High take its course [17].

v We read in the Holy Scriptures, beloved, that good counsel preserves those who are eager for the salvation of their souls, as the divine word says: "Holy counsel shall preserve thee." If holy counsel preserves a soul, then unholy counsel not only fails to preserve it but kills it [28].
Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles

18 And give place to the Law of the Most High. All wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and in all wisdom is the fulfilling of the Law. 19 But the knowledge of wickedness is not wisdom, neither at any time the counsel of sinners prudence. 20 There is a wickedness, and the same an abomination; and there is a fool wanting in wisdom. 21 He that hath small understanding, and feareth God, is better than one that hath much wisdom, and transgresseth the Law. 22 There is an exquisite subtlety, and the same is unjust. 23 And there is one that turneth aside to make judgment appear; and there is a wicked man that hangeth down his head sadly, but inwardly he is full of deceit. 24 Casting down his countenance, and making as if he heard not; where he is not known, he will do thee a mischief before thou be aware. 25 And if for want of power he be hindered from sinning, yet when he findeth opportunity he will do evil. 26 A man may be known by his look, and one that hath understanding by his countenance, when thou meetest him. 27 A man's attire, and excessive laughter, and gait, show what he is.

At some length Ben Sira warns us against the false appearances of wisdom, as a kind of cunning that works in the service of injustice and evil under the cover of deceptive appearances. It is not practiced in the fear of the Lord, and it does not care to keep the Law of the Lord practically and seriously from the depths of the heart.
All wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and in all wisdom is the fulfilling of the Law [18].
Wisdom does not stop at merely advising sinners. The wise man is committed to keeping the Law of the Lord and walks in the fear of the Lord.
The knowledge of wickedness is not wisdom, nor is discernment in the counsel of sinners [19].

v Those who are full of evil and whom ignorance has made drunk do not know God, for they are not lofty in spirit. But God is known only by the mind (that is, by the loftiness of our spiritual understanding), and although He is invisible, He is clearly perceived in the things that are seen, like the spirit that appears in the body. And just as the body cannot live without the spirit, so nothing visible and existing can subsist without God [29].
St. Anthony the Great There is a cleverness that is an abomination, and there is a fool who lacks wisdom [20].

It is better for a man to be ignorant but to keep himself from sin, than to have knowledge and misuse it. The man who fears (God) and lacks understanding is better than he who has abundant prudence and transgresses the Law [21].
There is an exquisite skill and yet it is unjust, and there is a man who deceives to establish his right [22].
There is a wicked man who walks bowed down in sorrow, while his inward part is full of deceit [23].
He hides his face and pretends to be deaf, and when no one is aware of him he overcomes you [24].
And if he is prevented from wrongdoing because he lacks strength, he does evil afterward when the opportunity comes to him [25].

v Many have the appearance of humility, but they do not have the virtue. Many present the appearance on the outside, but within they fight against it. They put on a play of humility, but they reject the truth, because "there is a wicked man that goeth bowed down under the weight of evil, but inwardly he is full of deceit" (see Sir 19:23). Such a person is very far from humility [30].

St. Ambrose Truly it befits us to concentrate on our inner life, because it is reflected in our outward conduct. At the same time we do not ignore the outward appearance, for it too can reveal the inner wisdom.
A man is known by his appearance, and the wise man is known by the features of his face when you meet him [26].
A man's clothing, and the way he laughs and walks, indicate who he is [27].

Seriousness with gentleness in all appearances, dress and movements, even the way of walking and laughing, reveals the character of a man. It does not befit the wise man to behave like a buffoon or a jester.

The true believer does not need anyone to bear witness to his godliness and conduct in Christ Jesus; rather even his outward appearance or his holy body language, such as his dress, his smile and his way of walking, bears witness for him while he is silent. For the true Christian is distinguished from others, sanctified within and in his outward conduct.

v The true prudence of the soul and its virtue appear in a man's glances, his way of walking, his voice, his smile, his conversation and his manners. For everything in such a soul has been changed and has become the best it can be, and its thought, which loves God, becomes a watchful guard over it, preventing the entry of evil, shameful thoughts [31].

St. Anthony the Great v Once we are inscribed in the spiritual assembly of the Church, we rightly do not allow ourselves to practice the same deeds that others practice, but always show the control of our tongue and the purity of our mind, and our members learn not to undertake any work that is not profitable for the soul.

What shall I say? We use the tongue only in praises and thanksgiving and in reading the divine commandments and spiritual conversations. As it is said: "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers. And grieve not the Holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed" (Eph 4:29-30). Do you know that if you fail in this you grieve the Holy Spirit? Therefore I ask you to try not to do anything that grieves the Holy Spirit.
If we must go out, let us not take part in dangerous gatherings that go beyond all bounds and are full of folly.

Rather, prefer nothing to the Church of God, the houses of prayer, and discussion in spiritual gatherings. Let every work be extremely dignified. As it is said: "A man's attire, and laughter of the mouth, and gait, show what he is" (see Sir 19:27). The outward appearance shows clearly the state of the soul. Truly the movement of the member proclaims its beauty in a certain way... "If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature" (2 Cor 5:17) [32].
St. John Chrysostom v Let her glances, her love, her speech, her way of walking and her dress tell of virtue [33].
St. Jerome
28 There is one that reproveth, and it is not comely; and there is one that holdeth his tongue, and he is wise.
(The commentary is in the next chapter) (*).
Inspired by Sirach 19

entries.section: My depths cry out to You: Sanctify me completely!

paragraphs.text: v To You, O Holy One, I complain of myself; who can control my depths but You?!
Grant me not to be careless in what I count as small things, lest I be careless also in the great!
You have set me up as a holy temple in which Your Holy Spirit dwells.
Let Him be my sanctifier, and my keeper and guard.
Who will keep me from what is wrongly called the white lie?
And who will grant me seriousness, so that I am not drawn to a word of jesting, and no mockery slips from my tongue by way of playfulness.
You paid Your precious blood as the price for sanctifying every thought or word or movement, hidden or manifest.
v Grant me not to be careless and drink a cup of wine on one occasion or another.
Our father Noah celebrated the new world that the flood had washed.
He drank wine to excess and was laid bare; and his son Ham made light of him, he whom he had rescued together with his two brothers Shem and Japheth and the rest of the family.
Let Your Holy Spirit pour out His joy in my heart, so that I do not share with Noah in his drunkenness, but share with the heavenly hosts in their praises full of jubilation.

v Samson, who killed a lion without a weapon, and enjoyed honey from the lion's carcass, he and his parents, dallied with Delilah, and became lowly before the enemies, grinding like an ox; they put out his eyes, and he realized that he had lost his inner sight.
Grant me seriousness, so that I may have no wrongful familiarity under the cover of innocent kindness.
v Grant me wisdom from You, so that I do not choose a friend for myself without examination and study!
You have made my heart a treasury in which You deposit Your divine secrets; let me not leave its door open without heavenly guard.
v Let me hide in You, O Way, Truth and Life, so that I do not walk in the way of sinners, nor take part in the seat of the scornful.

Let me not open my mouth in frivolity in talking with one fallen in sin, but keep to Your dwelling in my heart and my mind, so that I utter no word unbecoming to Your son, nor distort the features of my face by playing with a reckless person!
v Who will sanctify my tongue to be like a mother that bears praises and thanksgivings, that praises You continually with the new song.
Let my tongue bear sweet words that carry the sweetness of Your commandments.
And let it not bear the chatter of vain speech that has no benefit.
Your Holy Spirit plays upon all my strings:
the tongue, the heart, the mind, the senses and the emotions, so that a symphony of love comes forth, which a fragrance of pleasure breathes in.
v Grant me wisdom from You, so that my silence together with my words may reveal Your work in me!
Let there be no place for folly in my depths, so that I do not practice vain or corrupt silence, nor let unseemly words come out of my mouth!
Let me hide in You, so that I do not respond to words that I hear hastily, but meet You continually, for You are my divine Counselor.

If a man tells me that his brother wronged me by speaking slanderously about me, with deliberation I will admonish my brother, not that he may apologize to me, but that he may be filled with love, meekness and gentleness.
If he confesses his fault, I will pray for him and for myself, that the Lord may purify us all from every weakness and sin.
v Truly I cry out: In Your light I see light. Reveal to me Your secrets, for I wish to see You, and to know Your wonderful plan, Your love and Your care.
I wish to keep Your commandments, and enjoy their sweet yoke, so that I may prepare for the day of my meeting with You!

Grant Your commandments to shine forth in my thoughts and emotions and in my hidden and outward conduct; Your commandments lead even my smile and the manner of my eating, drinking, sleeping and recreation.
v Grant me not to judge anyone by his outward conduct, for no one knows what is in his heart but You.

entries.section: 1. There is a time for silence and a time for speech

paragraphs.text: (Sir 19:28) There is one that reproveth, and it is not comely; and there is one that holdeth his tongue, and he is wise. 1 How much better is it to reprove, than to be angry secretly! and he that confesseth his fault shall be preserved from hurt. 2 As is the lust of an eunuch to deflower a virgin; so is he that executeth judgment with violence. 3 And so is he who gives an unjust judgment. 4 How good is it, when thou art reproved, to show repentance! for so shalt thou escape wilful sin. 5 There is one that keepeth silence, and is found wise; and another by much babbling becometh hateful. 6 Some man holdeth his tongue, because he hath not to answer; and some keepeth silence, knowing his time. 7 A wise man will hold his tongue till he see opportunity; but a babbler and a fool will regard no time. 8 He that useth many words shall be abhorred; and he that taketh to himself authority therein shall be hated.
There is a rebuke that is not in its time, and there is one who keeps silent and has discernment [1].

Neither speech nor silence is a virtue or a vice in itself; rather the use of silence or of speech at the proper time and in a manner befitting the sons of the Lord is counted a virtue. For a man may be silent while his heart is not pure, and he may also speak while his heart is not pure.

v He who has acquired the truth, Jesus speaks with him, and he is able to listen even to His silence (the silence of the Lord Christ), and so he becomes perfect and acts by His word and His silence (the silence of the believer who is aware of the silence of the Lord Christ) [1].

entries.section: 1. There is a time for silence and a time for speech

paragraphs.text: St. Ignatius the God-bearer v Keep away from listening to worldly tales, lest your souls be stained in any way with mire. Do not be eager to hear the words of others, nor to throw yourselves into the discussions of others, so that you do not make yourselves a subject of mockery and cause others to commit slanders [2].

entries.section: 1. There is a time for silence and a time for speech

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great v Those who are unsteady and untried must not try to subject the wise to mere questioning (their concern should not be merely their asking), for the wise man is one who seeks to please God, and is much in silence, and if he speaks he speaks little, uttering what is necessary and pleasing to God [3].
St. Anthony the Great v It is better for you to remain among thousands of men with a loving heart than to hide in caves alone with hatred in you.
St. Evagrius How much better is rebuke than raging with anger [2].
He who confesses his fault is saved from loss [3].
Rebuke with love and wisdom is a declaration of the Church's love for the sinner and her hatred of his sin; therefore the pastor must take care, while rebuking, that:
a. It proceed from a fatherly heart full of compassion and meekness (1 Cor 21:4).
b. It be given according to the state of the sinner and his capacities, and discipline be offered in a flexible form, not in the form of a rigid law or a dry compulsion.
c. Discipline must end in repentance full of hope.

v I ask: who among men was more corrupt than the king of Babylon (Nebuchadnezzar)... Many opportunities for repentance were given to him. The first was that miracle which took place in the furnace of fire (that is, the appearance of the Son of God with the three young men in the midst of the fire) (Dan 3). The second was those visions that appeared to him, which Daniel interpreted for him, visions able to crush any heart of stone (Dan 4), and after that the counsels of the prophet himself.

In all this God did not punish him but was long-suffering toward him, counseling him at one time by visions and at another by the tongue of His prophet; but since no correction came to him by any of these means, at last He poured punishment upon him: "And he was driven from the sons of men; and his heart was made like the beasts, and his dwelling was with the wild asses: they fed him with grass like oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven" (Dan 5:21). And this punishment was not for vengeance, for He restored him again to his first position without any loss befalling him, but he benefited as greatly as possible.

St. John Chrysostom v The Apostle Paul teaches us not to abandon those who have committed a sin unto death, but to bind them to the bread of tears (that is, repentance), yet let their sorrow be moderate. And this is what the phrase means: "Thou hast given them tears to drink by measure" (Ps 130:5); their sorrow must be by measure, lest the penitent be swallowed up by excessive grief. This is as he said to the Corinthians: "What will ye? shall I come unto you with a rod, or in love, and in the spirit of meekness?" (1 Cor 4:21). He uses the rod, but without cruelty, for it is said: "Thou shalt beat him with the rod, and shalt deliver his soul from hell" (Prov 23:14). And what the Apostle means by the rod appeared when he struck against the sin of fornication (1 Cor 5:1), warning against immorality with relatives whom it is forbidden to marry, rebuking their pride, for those who ought to have mourned were puffed up. And finally, speaking of the offender (who wished to marry his father's wife), he commanded that he be removed from the congregation and delivered to Satan, not for the destruction of his soul, but for the destruction of his flesh.

entries.section: 1. There is a time for silence and a time for speech

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose v It is necessary that we confess our sins to those to whom the stewardship of the mysteries of God has been given. Those who showed repentance in ancient times offered it before the saints. It is recorded in the Gospel that they confessed their sins to John the Baptist (Mt 3:6), and in the Book of Acts they confessed to the Apostles, by whom they were also baptized (Acts 19:18) [4].

entries.section: 1. There is a time for silence and a time for speech

paragraphs.text: v When you are occupied with some sin, be your own accuser (Prov 18:17), and do not wait for others to bring the accusation. In this way you become like a righteous man who accuses himself in the first words of his speech in court, or like Job, whom the multitude of the people in the city did not hinder from proclaiming his offense before all [5].
St. Basil the Great Like the lustful eunuch who deflowers a maiden, so is he who uses violence in carrying out justice [4].
For it is impossible for the eunuch to fulfill his desire toward a virgin; he suffers repression and a sense of failure, and he who thinks that he achieves justice by violence fails completely.
There is one who keeps silent and is counted wise, and there is a man who is hated for his much speaking [5].

He speaks of a person who does not know how to deal with some matter, or does not know the answer to a question put to him; if he admits his ignorance within himself and keeps silent, he is counted wise. But if he tries to answer in order to appear as one who knows, this speech of his makes him hated.

entries.section: 1. There is a time for silence and a time for speech

paragraphs.text: There is one who keeps silent because he finds no answer, and one who keeps silent because he knows the proper time for speaking [6].

Two keep silent: one because he does not know the answer, and it is wise that he be silent; the second has knowledge but is silent because the time is not suitable for speaking. The latter speaks at the proper time.

entries.section: 1. There is a time for silence and a time for speech

paragraphs.text: The wise man keeps silence until the proper time for speaking, but the proud and the foolish miss the proper time for speaking [7].

The wise man offers the proper remedy at the proper time, so his word brings fitting fruit; but the proud and the foolish are silent when they ought to speak, as though they do not offer the remedy at the proper time, so they are late in answering, which causes the problem to swell and become complicated.

v In truth, when a man sees that what his neighbor is doing is evil and keeps silent, it is as though he withholds the balm from the wounds he sees, and thereby leads him to death, to the extent that they withhold the healing when it was within their power. In this case the tongue should not be completely bound, but we should control it with discretion and wisdom, for it is written: "A wise man will hold his tongue till he see opportunity (but a babbler and a fool will regard no time)" (see Sir 20:7). That is, when speaking what is fitting is suitable, the restraint of silence must be removed and one must speak so that help may be given with every effort. And it is also written: "A time to keep silence, and a time to speak" (Eccl 3:7), meaning that there are various times about which we must think wisely [6].
Pope Gregory (the Great)

v Now what must we learn before everything else except silence, so that we may be able to speak? Lest my voice condemn me before anything else acquits me, as it is written: "By thy words thou shalt be condemned" (Mt 12:37).
