What do we need that is safer than keeping silence, that we may hasten to guard against the condemnation that comes through speech? How many I have seen fall into sin through speech, while scarcely anyone falls through silence. And so it is much harder to know how to keep silence than how to speak. It is very rare for anyone to be silent when speaking is not profitable to him. Finally, the wisdom of God says: "The Lord gave me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to speak a word in season" (Isa 50:4) LXX. Well does Holy Scripture say: "A wise man will hold his tongue until the proper time" (see Sir 20:7) [7].

entries.section: 1. There is a time for silence and a time for speech

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose He that useth many words shall be abhorred, and he who forces himself on others shall be hated [8].

After Sirach has dealt with the subject of keeping silence or speaking according to what is profitable, he now points to two kinds of error. The first error is that the person speaks at the proper time and has a good answer, but he repeats the answer for a long while and many times, so his answer does not bear fruit, because the hearer grows weary of the many words. The second error is that the person thrusts himself into the lives of others without being asked to, and so the hearer hates him.

9 There is a sinner that hath good success in evil things; and there is a gain that turneth to loss. 10 There is a gift that shall not profit thee; and there is a gift whose recompense is double. 11 There is an abasement because of glory; and there is that lifteth up his head from a low estate. 12 There is that buyeth much for a little, and repayeth it sevenfold. 13 A wise man by his words maketh him beloved, but the graces of fools shall be poured out. 14 The gift of a fool shall do thee no good; for his eyes are many instead of one. 15 He giveth little, and upbraideth much; he openeth his mouth like a crier. 16 He lendeth today, and asketh it again tomorrow: such a one is a hateful man.

Sometimes the outward appearance hides the truth, and a man may even deceive himself or those around him. The experience of failure may drive a man to review himself so that he may walk in a spirit of success in the future, while the life of a man may be shattered by an appearance of success, as happens when he wins a huge sum in a lottery [8].
There may be success in the midst of trials, and also a gain that turns into a loss [9].

A person may enjoy success or gain, but through his bad conduct his success causes him troubles and leads him into severe trials, and what he gained turns into losses. Therefore it befits a person to know how to meet success or gain with wisdom and study, without haste.

v [Be not thou afraid when one is made rich, when the glory of his house is increased] (Ps 49:16) LXX.. This declaration is necessary for the inhabitants of the world, whether for the earthborn or for the sons of men, for the rich as well as the poor. "Be not afraid when a man is made rich"; he says: when you see the unjust become rich and the righteous poor, do not fear for yourself. Let not your mind be alarmed, as though the providence of God did not look upon human affairs, or as though the divine watchfulness extended to some places and not to the whole earth, to care for our affairs. If there is divine providence, it extends to every man in the manner that suits him. The righteous who understand how to use wealth become rich, and the wicked who use wealth as an instrument of their evil must needs be poor.

Now, since there are many among the Gentiles and among the earthborn who hold such notions, and because of the apparent contradiction in the distribution of wealth for life, they think that the world is not the work of divine providence.

Holy Scripture addresses them in order to calm their unsound emotions from the very beginning. It calls them to listen to the teachings. Certainly it refers in particular only to the poor person when it says: "Be not afraid when a man is made rich." These especially need consolation, that they may not tremble before those in authority. For it says that the rich man has no advantages at his death, since he cannot take his wealth with him. At any rate, he reckons that all he possesses is the enjoyment of it, since his soul thinks itself happy in this life through those who flatter him. But at his death he does not take any of those possessions.

It says: he takes only the garment with which he covers his shame, and this, as it seems, is the best that his household offer him when they cover him. He must be content to receive a small piece of ground which they offer him, as those who bury him show compassion toward him, offering it to him for the honor of human nature in general, and not as a special privilege of his own, but for the honor of humanity.

So do not be troubled about present things, but wait for that blessed life. For you will see that what befalls the righteous man of poverty and insult and deprivation of luxury is for his good. Do not be troubled now about what you count as goods, that they are distributed as though unjustly. You will hear what will be said to a certain rich man: "Thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things" (Lk 16:25). But for the poor man, evils befell him in this life; therefore the latter is comforted and the former is tormented.

[And he will praise thee, when thou doest well to him] (Ps 49:18) LXX. This concerns the earthly man, and him who thinks that goods are the advantages of this life, such as wealth, health and authority that is his own. In truth such a man praises God when he is alone with good things, but in dangerous circumstances he utters curses... So also with the accusations that Satan made against Job (Job 1:9), that Job did not honor God for nothing, but received a reward for his godliness: riches and all the rest of his possessions. Therefore, to prove his virtue, God withdrew all that he had, so that man's thanksgiving toward God might shine through everything [9].
St. Basil the Great There is a gift that profits you nothing, and there is a gift that obliges you to repay it double [10].

The scholar Origen speaks of the divine gifts to man, some spiritual and others not spiritual. Spiritual gifts support the wise man and build up his soul as they build up others, while non-spiritual gifts may be misused by a man; though they are not evil in themselves, by their wrong use they become evil.

A man may gain money and misuse it in a life of luxury, drunkenness or association with the wicked. Another finds in money the opportunity to support his family, his friends and the needy. Therefore it befits us to imitate wise Solomon, who asked neither for money nor glory nor victory over enemies, but that God would grant him wisdom for the governing of the life of the kingdom and of his own life.

v When (the Apostle) says: "That I may impart unto you some spiritual gift" (Rom 1:11), he knows that there are gifts that are not spiritual. Certainly the gift of faith is spiritual, and also the gift of wisdom and knowledge and the like, such as virginity. But when he speaks of marriage and virginity he says: "Every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that" (1 Cor 7:7). So in truth he calls marriage a gift, as it is written: "A prudent wife is from the Lord" (Prov 19:14), but this gift is not spiritual. Many other things can also be called gifts from God, such as wealth, bodily strength, outward beauty and earthly kingdoms. For God gives these, as Daniel says: "He removeth kings, and setteth up kings" (Dan 2:21), but these gifts are not spiritual [10].

The scholar Origen Some gifts and talents may profit nothing when a man misuses them or uses them in a spirit of pride and arrogance, for God is able to lift up a humble man and bring low a proud man. He raises men from the dunghill and sets them with the nobles of His people, as He did with Joseph the son of Jacob (Gen 37-50), and as is recorded in the song of St. Mary (Lk 1:47-53).
There is a glory that causes losses, and there is a man who lifts up his head from a state of lowliness [11].

Many fell into pride because of their temporal glory, so the Lord brought them down from their thrones, and they even lost their eternity, while the Lord lifted up the heads of the humble. "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree" (Lk 1:52).

v Great is the power of this medicine, and great the strength of this comparison, in the healing of the disease of pride. Why are you puffed up? Or why does another despise himself? Are we not all one body, the great among us and the small? If in our totality we are one, and members one of another, why do you isolate yourself by haughtiness? Why do you insult your brother? For as he is a member of you, you are a member of him. (The Apostle) has established two things that break the proud spirit: the first, that we are members one of another, not only the small a member of the great but the great also of the small; and the second, that we are one body. Indeed there is a third point, that the gift is from grace, so do not be proud, for it is given to you from God...

Also when he touches on the subject of gifts, he does not say that one is greater and another smaller, but what? The gifts are different! His words are thus: "Having then gifts" (Rom 12:6) are not less and greater but "differing [11]".
St. John Chrysostom There is one who buys much for little, but he pays for it sevenfold [12].

What is mentioned here is suffered by many, since some are preoccupied with buying what they need at the lowest possible price, without a right estimate of what they lose through this choice of theirs. Examples of this:

a. A man buys an old building and tries to repair and maintain it, considering the price less than the price of the land itself. And since the buyer is bound to continual repairs, he finds that he has spent on the building many times what he would have paid had he built it or bought a building in good condition.

b. We often find some people spending long hours to buy something at the lowest possible price; they have wasted much of their time, and they and their family are in need of time more than of what they saved in the price.
c. In choosing the least cost for buying or making something, he may enter into family discussions that spoil the peace of the family, which is beyond price.
The wise man makes himself beloved by his words, and the kindness of the fool is forgotten [13].

The wise man knows the worth of the sweet word that establishes friendships, but the fool may offer kindness and favors, yet since he does not join the favor to a sweet word, the favor loses its value, and the recipient of the favor no longer remembers it.
The gift of the fool will profit you nothing, for he has many eyes instead of one [14].

In his folly the fool exaggerates matters, and so he looks at them as with many eyes. An example of this is the unwise mother, who sees in her son the cleverest of men, and in her daughter the most beautiful of girls. Not estimating matters as one ought spoils a person's peace and crushes those around him. At the same time, in his exaggeration the person thinks that he is the source of their success and their wealth, and so on.

v The eye is the source of the body's sight, and the mind is the source of the soul's sight. And just as the body is blind without the eyes, so that it does not behold the shining sun upon the earth and the sea, and cannot enjoy its light, so the soul is blind without a sound mind and a good life, so that it has no knowledge of God, nor glorifies the Creator, the maker of good things for all humanity, nor is able to enjoy joy through obtaining incorruption and receiving eternal blessedness [12].
St. Anthony the Great He gives little and insults much, and he opens his mouth like a crier.
He lends today and demands it tomorrow. Such a man is hateful [15].

A warning against the foolish man: if he offers a gift, behind it is a measure of insults. He offers a gift and causes more losses than he gave. In his folly the fool offers very little and counts himself the most giving and generous of men. He always expects from those he deals with words of praise, thanks and honor, by one means or another. His mouth is always open complaining of those around him because they have not honored him as is fitting. His life in his own eyes is losing deals, with none to reward him for his gifts.

Such a man is hateful, because he offers little and adds to the offering complaints, grumbling and insults, which causes psychological and spiritual losses both to himself and to the one to whom he gave the offering.

17 A fool will say, I have no friends, I have no thank for all my good deeds, and they that eat my bread speak evil of me. 18 How oft, and of how many, shall he be laughed to scorn! for he knoweth not aright what it is to have; and it is all one unto him as if he had it not. 19 To slip upon a pavement is better than to slip with the tongue: so the fall of the wicked shall come speedily. 20 An unseasonable tale will always be in the mouth of the unwise. 21 A wise sentence shall be rejected when it cometh out of a fool's mouth; for he will not speak it in due season.

After speaking of the deceit of outward appearances, and requiring the wise man to study matters with wisdom, deliberation and depth so that he knows the truths and is not deceived, he spoke of man's need for the grace of God, which leads thought inward so that it comes to know the truth. The man who relies on his own understanding and thoughts, stripped of grace, lacks true discernment. However great a man's intelligence, abilities and studies may be, he needs his depths sanctified by divine grace, not to destroy his thought but to elevate it and sanctify it and reveal to it the transcendent mysteries.
The fool says: I have no friend, and my good works are not met with thanks [16].

Since the ignorant man feels that he has no friend, and that there is none to thank him for his good works, he exerts all his effort to immortalize his name and his memory on earth. He may set up projects that bear witness to his goodness and splendid buildings on which he carves his name. And he does not realize that by his sins he has become dead, cast into the grave. His very body becomes a tomb for his dead soul. St. Basil marvels at those who carve their names on tombs, thus tying their names to death instead of recording them in the book of life. It is as though, having failed to have friends in the heavenly places, they seek friends among the dead. Since the foolish man does not enjoy divine grace nor respond to it, always complaining, he reckons that he is deprived of a faithful friend who would appreciate his good works. He sees that many eat his bread, and instead of offering him thanks they mock him.

v "The ignorant and the dull (the foolish, senseless) perish together, and leave their wealth to others. Their tombs are their dwellings from generation to generation; they call their lands by their own names" (Ps 48:10-11) LXX...

The senseless is in truth he who lacks common sense, and who has no sound insight into ordinary human affairs. In the same way, those who discern in the affairs of life between what is useful and what is harmful are usually called wise or prudent. This is what is expressed in the Gospel: "For the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light" (Lk 16:8). They are not wise in an absolute way, but because of their shrewdness in managing their present life in the flesh, they are also called servants of unrighteousness. In this sense the wise are also vipers, which prepare hidden places for themselves, and in time of danger avoid by every means the blows falling upon the head.

One is called ignorant who lacks the lofty qualities of man. These are the understanding of God the Father, the reception of the Word, Who "was in the beginning with God" (Jn 1:2), and the light that comes from the Holy Spirit.

These persons who have this mind are able to say with Paul: "But we have the mind of Christ" (1 Cor 2:16). Nevertheless Holy Scripture uses the opposite, saying that the wicked man is senseless in these words: "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God" (Ps 15:1). Again it calls what is harmful to life folly, as the Apostle did in speaking of those who fell into foolish and hurtful lusts (1 Tim 6:9).

Thus the senseless and the ignorant go down to one end, which is destruction. And one may say that he who lives like the pagans is called foolish, but he who conducts his life as a Jew with an outward (literal) appearance in keeping the Law is ignorant. For the Lord said to the foolish man because of the godlessness in him: "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee" (Lk 12:20). But Israel, who walked according to the flesh, was called ignorant, as the prophet says: "Ephraim also is like a silly dove without heart: they call to Egypt, they go to Assyria" (Hos 7:11).

Where these perished completely through their ignorance, we strangers have become heirs of their wealth. The commandments became ours, the prophets and the fathers became ours, and so the righteous in the world became ours. These who perished in their ignorance left us their wealth.

At any rate, the houses of these foolish and ignorant have become tombs for them forever. For the tombs of those whose lives were filled with dead works of every kind of sin are their houses forever. He who is dead in sins does not dwell in a house but in a tomb, because his soul is dead.

Now Jacob, innocent in his conduct and simple, dwelt in a house. It is written of him that he was a plain and good man dwelling in a house (see Gen 25:27), but the base man dwells in a tomb, and lays no foundation for regret, because of his dead works; rather he resembles a sepulchre whitewashed outwardly, very splendid, but within full of dead men's bones and all uncleanness (Mt 23:27). Therefore when such a man speaks, he does not open his mouth with the word of God, but he has a tomb; his throat is an open sepulchre. Therefore if anyone believes in Christ and does not practice his works in harmony with his faith, then since he listens to corrupt teachings and blasphemes the meanings of Holy Scripture, he is shattered upon the rock of his tomb [13].

v "Their houses are for ever, their dwelling places to all generations" (Ps 48:12) LXX, that is, their tombs are their houses forever. Then, explaining what he means by tombs, to show that he was speaking of their bodies in which their souls perish through their evils, he adds these words: "their dwelling places to all generations"; for human bodies are always called dwelling places. These also call their lands by their names. For the name of the base man is not recorded in the book of the living, nor is he counted with the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven. Rather their names remain on the earth, since they preferred this passing life of short span to the eternal dwellings. Do you not see how those who build marketplaces and schools in the cities, and set up walls, and construct channels, write their names on earthly buildings?

Indeed some have engraved their names on herds of horses, and made plans to extend their memory over a long time in life; they raised splendid buildings for their tombs and engraved their names on monuments. These are the wise in earthly matters, who care for present glory and reckon that men's remembering them is enough to achieve happiness. For if you see any of those who exalt themselves greatly in what they falsely call knowledge, and devote themselves to corrupt teachings which they have approved, and instead of the name of Christians ascribe themselves to one of the heretics: Marcion or Valentinus or one of the contemporaries of the present, devoting themselves to working on behalf of destructive men, and in short in earthly matters [14].
St. Basil the Great If the foolish do not gain friends for themselves, it is because they do not understand the meaning of true friendship.

St. John Chrysostom often speaks of the love that establishes friends for a man. If he establishes ten friends together, then instead of having two hands with which to work, he has all the hands, that is, twenty-two hands with which each one of them works; how much more if by love he gains thousands to work with him, and they work with him.

v Do you perceive the loftiness of love, how it makes one man who cannot be conquered increase many times over what he is? Do you not see that one man can be present in many places at one time (since each friend of his is counted as though he were himself)? A part of him will be in Persia as in Rome.

What is there that love cannot do? A part of him is present here and another there. Or rather, the whole is here and the whole is there. If he has a thousand friends, or two thousand, imagine again the extent of his strength... (do you not see that love multiplies a man's strength?) It is remarkable that one man carries a thousand of his strength [15].
St. John Chrysostom Those who eat my bread, their speech is without benefit.
How many are those who mock him! And in many ways! [17]
These are the feelings of the fool, for since he walks in malice he thinks of those to whom he does good that instead of thanks they speak against him with a malicious tongue.
A slip on the ground is better than a slip of the tongue; so the fall of the wicked will be swift [18].

Why is the error of the tongue called a "slip"? Because what the fool utters is an unconscious reaction of his folly. The fool errs with his tongue without thinking, but the effect of this slip is grave, and may extend to the great day of the Lord, unless he has offered true repentance for it. It seems as though a slip of the tongue is talk in the air that is of no danger, but Sirach likens it to falling on a pavement, causing him fractures, and it can cause a rupture in the arteries of the brain leading to his death.

v The soundness of the tongue is the tree of life. The tongue that does not err in speech uses soundness of mind. In truth the disease of the tongue is sin. He who is able to control his tongue and not sin is full of the Holy Spirit [16].
St. John Chrysostom The man who has lost grace is like a story told at the wrong time; it continues on the lips of the ignorant [19].

The story of the fool who has lost grace is repeated by the ignorant, but the wise man desires the salvation of the fool by his returning to God before it is too late. We notice in Ben Sira that he often repeats "the proper time"; now is the day of salvation and a proper time for repentance, but postponement is folly, because we do not own tomorrow. He realizes that the one who walks by divine grace is able to study and examine everything, and to deal with others with wisdom, dignity and esteem for them. But the one who has lost grace falls into ignorance and makes light of the commandment of God, while not esteeming those around him.

The one who has lost grace, in his ignorance, does not accept the control of the tongue, the control of the passions and self-control; he does not accept the divine commandment, nor the sincere order of society, nor the experience of godly elders. Ben Sira defines the fool as a man who has lost grace, who may utter words of wisdom that come out of his lips but without experience.
The proverb is rejected from the mouth of the fool, because he does not utter it at the proper time [20].
Since the fool does not return to God that He may grant him the grace of repentance, all his words are counted as offered at an unfitting time.
The wicked cannot bear witness to the righteous, nor can his testimony be effective.

23 There is that is hindered from sinning through want, and in his rest he shall not be pricked. 24 There is that destroyeth his own soul through bashfulness, and by accepting of persons overthroweth himself. 25 There is that for bashfulness promiseth to his friend, and maketh him his enemy for nothing. 26 A lie is a foul blot in a man, yet it is continually in the mouth of the untaught. 27 A thief is better than a man that is accustomed to lie: but they both shall have destruction to heritage. 28 The disposition of a liar is dishonorable, and his shame is ever with him.
There is one whom his want hinders from sin, and in his rest sorrow will not pierce him [21].

God allows some to have want or sickness or any tribulation that keeps them from practicing sin, whereas if they were at ease they would not practice repentance and remorse for sin but would walk in slackness and negligence.
There is one who loses his life from shame, or loses it because of his foolish conduct [22].
Some people are put to shame by what they commit, but they do not set out to repentance in a spirit of joyful hope.
There is one who gives a promise to his friend out of shame, and so gains him as an enemy without cause [23].
Some make promises to their friends while knowing their inability to fulfill them, but they make them because of shame. And when the time comes to fulfill the promise, friends turn into enemies.
A lie is a shameful evil in a man, and it continues on the lips of the ignorant [24].

A lie is considered a stain of disgrace on the character; it arises for many reasons, the most important of which is fear, especially in childhood, when the child wishes to escape the punishment imposed on him; or because of a feeling of inferiority, so that he wishes to appear other than he is. If the lie is discovered, many lose confidence in him in all that he says or appears to be. Satan is called the liar and the father of liars (Jn 8:44). Since the Lord Christ is "the Truth" (Jn 14:6), a lie, which is against the truth, is a mark of the "antichrist." Origen says: [The lie points to the adversary of Him who said: "I am the truth" (Jn 14:6). This is the antichrist, whose father is a liar, being the devil [17].]

v Everyone must give great attention lest "lying" rob him, for the liar is not united with God. The liar is a stranger to God. And Scripture says that the liar is of Satan, since he is "a liar, and the father of it" (Jn 44:8). Thus Satan was called the father of liars, but the truth is God, for He Himself says: "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (Jn 6:14).

Do you not see, then, how we become strangers to God by lying, and with whom we are united (through it)?! Therefore, if we truly wish to be saved, we must love the truth with all our strength and all our zeal, and guard ourselves from every lie, lest it separate us from the truth and the life [18].
Father Dorotheus St. Basil deals with the subject of lying in his answers to questions that appear in the Short Rules.
v Question: Is he condemned who lies deliberately only, or also he who utters something contrary to the truth out of ignorance on his part?

Answer: The judgment of the Lord is also against those who sin out of obvious ignorance, from His saying: "He that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes" (Lk 12:48). And in every case repentance carries the sure hope of forgiveness (Mt 3:8; Lk 3:8) [19]
v Question: If someone only thought to do something and did not do it, is this judged to be a lie (1 Tim 1:10)?
Answer: If what he thought to do is not according to the commandment, the Holy Spirit condemns him not only as a liar but as disobedient, because God searches the hearts and reins (Ps 7:10) [20]

v Question: If someone decided beforehand to do something that is hateful to God, but refrained from doing it, does he cancel his evil decision, or does he complete the sin for fear of being accused of being a liar?

Answer: First: it befits such a man to repent first, because in this he dared and decided by himself to do something, whatever it was (without seeking the counsel of God); he must not do even what is good of himself on his own responsibility.
Second: what is more serious is that he was not afraid to take a decision that does not please God.

As for his having drawn back from what he decided beforehand in opposition to the commandment of the Lord, and not carrying out the decision in practice, this is clear in the case of the Apostle Peter, who decided beforehand and declared: "Thou shalt never wash my feet" (Jn 13:8). And when he heard the judgment that the Lord pronounced: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me," he said... "Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head" (Jn 13:9) [21].
v Question: Is there a special exception through which one may lie for the sake of an expected benefit?

Answer: This cannot be overlooked by the law of the Lord, Who says entirely that a lie is of Satan (Jn 8:44), without distinguishing between one lie and another. There is also the testimony of the Apostle, where it is written: "And if a man also strive for masteries, yet is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully" (2 Tim 2:5) [22].
St. Basil the Great A thief is better than one who lies continually, but both inherit destruction [25].

St. John Chrysostom says: ["Let him that stole steal no more," this does not remove the sin, but how is it removed? If they work, and practice relations of love with others! He does not want us merely to work but to work and toil, that we may practice friendly relations with others. For the thief also has works, but they are evil works [23].]
The state of the lying man brings disgrace, and his shame is with him continually [26].

entries.section: 5. The ways of the wise man

paragraphs.text: 29 A wise man shall advance himself to honor with his words, and he that hath understanding will please great men. 30 He that tilleth his land shall increase his heap, and he that pleaseth great men shall get pardon for iniquity. 31 Presents and gifts blind the eyes of the wise, and stop up his mouth that he cannot reprove. 32 Wisdom that is hid, and treasure that is hoarded up, what profit is in them both? 33 Better is he that hideth his folly than a man that hideth his wisdom.
The wise man exalts himself by his words, and the prudent man pleases the great [27].

We can realize how effective our speech is, for it is said: "By thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned" (Mt 12:37). The Lord Christ says: "Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man; but that which cometh out of the mouth, this defileth a man" (Mt 15:11). And the wise man says also: "Make... a door and a bar for thy mouth" (see Sir 28:29).

St. John Chrysostom speaks of the control of the tongue, saying: [A golden vessel is not used for base things because of the greatness of its price; how much more the mouth, which is more precious than gold and coral, so it is not right for us to defile it with ugly speech, cursing and stabbing others.]

And Father John of Kronstadt says: [Take care of your words, for the word is precious!... Utter the creative word of God, for the Word of God is the cause of all creation, in Him are the present, the past and the future [24].] He also says: [If you are speaking with your neighbor, speak with discretion and dignity and in a constructive way, avoiding every idle word as the venom of the serpent [25].]
He who tills the land increases his harvest, and he who pleases the great atones for the fault [28].
If the abundant harvest is the fruit of effort and toil in tilling the land, then the kind word that pleases the great rescues the wronged.
Presents and gifts blind the eyes of the wise, and like a bridle in the mouth they prevent rebuke [29].
St. John Chrysostom warns us of envy, which pierces even the Church and corrupts it with covetousness, since envy is the mother of covetousness, and presents and gifts move its affairs.

v (Envy) has pierced into the Church. From the beginning it brings countless grave results. It is the mother of covetousness, and the plague that turns matters upside down and corrupts justice. Scripture says: "Presents and gifts blind the eyes of the wise, and like a bridle in the mouth prevent rebukes" (see Sir 20:29). Covetousness makes us slaves instead of being free. We speak of it every day, but we make no progress [26].

St. John Chrysostom Gifts that are offered as a bribe corrupt the sight of the wise and bridle their mouths, so that they are prevented from rebuking the wrongdoer, and cannot behold the truth. And they stop the mouths, so that they do not rebuke the unjust and the wicked; but being occupied with heavenly things and divine gifts opens the eyes to see the mysteries of God and to perceive the divine truth, as it opens the mouths to praise with the angels, and to rebuke the devil and all his powers, and not to flatter the wicked.

v This (love of fame and money) has rushed into the churches. This is the cause of countless deadly things from the beginning. This is the father of covetousness. This disease has turned all things upside down and corrupted justice. It is said: "Presents and gifts blind the eyes of the wise, and like a bridle in the mouth prevent rebukes" (see Sir 20:29). This has made free men slaves. Of this we speak every day without benefit. We have become worse than the wild beasts, we plunder orphans, strip widows, sin against the poor, and add woe to woe. "Woe! The godly man is perished out of the earth" (Mic 7:1) [27].

St. John Chrysostom v A chorepiscopus asked St. Barsanuphius whether he should leave his episcopal work and withdraw to a monastery, and the answer came: I cannot advise you to abandon Him Who entrusted you to care for the holy churches of God (2 Cor 11:28), but to care for your own soul according to the fear of God. Do not accept gifts from anyone (see Sir 20:29; Prov 15:27). Do not hesitate in your judgments (Ex 23:3). Do not be ashamed to appear before any ruler (see Sir 7:6). Do not acquit the guilty, and do not condemn the righteous. Keep covetousness far from you, for it is the root of all evil (1 Tim 6:10)... Do not be proud but be led by the humble (Rom 12:16)... Remember the day of your departure, and then you will not sin against the Lord (see Sir 7:36). And if you reach the point of stillness, you will find rest with grace wherever you withdraw [28].
Sts. Barsanuphius and John v "Presents and gifts blind the eyes of the wise" (see Sir 20:29), and he who accepts them to cause harm to others is not an ascetic.

entries.section: 5. The ways of the wise man

paragraphs.text: Counsels for the ascetics by St. Hyperechius the priest Wisdom that is hid and treasure that is hoarded up, what profit is in them both? [30]

v Those who are able to teach with great effect but who keep away because of excessive humility ought to learn, by reasoning from the consideration of small things, how greatly they sin against the greater and more important duties. Therefore, if they hide from needy brethren the money they have, they undoubtedly spread gloom and sorrow among them. Let them reflect in how great a guilt they are involved, because they withhold the word of teaching from sinful brethren, withholding the medicine of life from souls walking toward death. Therefore the wise man says truly: "Wisdom that is hid and treasure that is hoarded up, what profit is in them both?" (see Sir 20:32). If a famine were to come that destroyed a people, and the people hid their wheat, these would without doubt be heralds and preachers of death. Therefore let those who do not come forward to serve the bread of grace that has been bestowed on them consider, when souls perish from thirst for the holy word, how great the terror of the punishment will be. For this reason it was also truly said by the tongue of Solomon: "He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him" (Prov 11:26); he who hides the wheat monopolizes for himself the words of holy teaching. Such a man is struck by the curse, because by the sin of silence he deserves the punishment of all those who could have walked in what is right because of him [29].
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 5. The ways of the wise man

paragraphs.text: The man who hides his folly is better than the man who hides his wisdom [31].
Let a man hide his folly by his silence; this is better than he who hides his wisdom.
Inspired by Sirach 20

entries.section: Let me cling to You in my silence as in my words!

paragraphs.text: v What occupies me in my silence as in my speech is clinging to You!
In my silence I enter into a secret conversation with You, and with my words I speak according to Your direction for me.
You speak through me, so I bear a spirit of love and long-suffering even toward those who trouble me.
Grant me not to speak in a spirit of folly. Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth and a strong door over my lips.
v Grant me the spirit of wisdom, lest a temporary success draw me to haughtiness.
Let me not rejoice in temporal gains that turn into losses, nor seek the glory of the world, for You are my glory.
v I ask nothing of the fool, lest he count me as his debtor.
He gives me today, and takes from me double!
Remove from me all folly, for what occupies me is Your friendship toward me.
Train me in conversation with You, that my soul may be satisfied with Your love!
Train my tongue, that I may not fall into a slip of the tongue, but let my words be seasoned with the salt of the Spirit; Your grace lifts me up, so that I speak only what I taste and live!
v Grant me wisdom, that I may not give promises that I am unable to fulfill!
Let all my promises and words be true, for You are the Truth and the Life!
Grant me not to steal what is not mine.
v Let every word that comes out of my mouth proclaim Your righteousness.
Let me know when to speak with wisdom and when to be silent.

entries.section: 1. Flee from sin in a spirit of hope

paragraphs.text: 1 My son, hast thou sinned? do so no more, but ask pardon for thy former sins. 2 Flee from sin as from a serpent; for if thou comest near it, it will bite thee. 3 Its teeth are as the teeth of a lion, slaying the souls of men. 4 All iniquity is as a two-edged sword, the wound whereof cannot be healed.
My son, have you sinned? Do not add to it, but pray concerning your former sins [1].

Sin has gained mastery over humanity, because it isolated itself from God, the source of holiness and purity, and so it became in need of the spirit of hope, the giver of joy. Sometimes a man walks for a certain period in a spirit of chastity and purity, and suddenly he is fought by an evil thought or a bad lust or the practice of some sin, and he thinks that he has lost his purity completely, and instead of returning to God he surrenders to sins. Therefore Ben Sira says: "My son, hast thou sinned? Do so no more, but pray concerning thy former sins."

He addresses his speech to the sinner, saying: "My son"; for in wishing to instill a spirit of hope in the sinner he counts him as his son, that he may see in him the image of God his Father. He calls him to prayer in a spirit of hope together with earnestness, instead of surrendering to sin.

v When the soul understands sin, it hates it, (and looks at it) as a wild beast of foul smell. But when the soul is ignorant of sin, sin becomes beloved to it, and enslaves the soul that loves it and takes it captive. The wretched poor man does not see what is able to save him, nor does he even think of this, but welcomes sin with pleasure, imagining that it adorns him [1].

entries.section: 1. Flee from sin in a spirit of hope

paragraphs.text: v The pure soul is sanctified and enlightened by God because of its clarity. Then its mind thinks of what is good, and good inclinations and deeds spring from it. But the soul that is defiled by sin, God abandons it, or rather it is the one that leaves Him, and so it lets evil demons into its thought, and they suggest (to its owner) shameful things: fornication, murder, robbery and other similar evil and demonic deeds [2].

St. Anthony the Great v Remember these things, that with them you may stop the mouths of the lazy, the immoral, the slack and those who hate works of virtue, those who accuse the Master of all. You have sinned. Be silent; but "hast thou sinned? Do so no more." For there is no sin worse than that after you sin you accuse the Master. Know the cause of sin and you will find that no one sinned but you. In every position there is need of a good intention. And I show you this not by reasoning only, but by examples from your fellow servants who walk in this same world. Use this means also...
Is someone a fornicator? Present to him another man who is self-controlled.
Is someone covetous and greedy? Show him a man who gives alms.
Does he live in jealousy and envy? Make known to him a man who is pure of this pain.

entries.section: 1. Flee from sin in a spirit of hope

paragraphs.text: Is he overcome by anger? Bring into the midst a man who walks in wisdom [3].

St. John Chrysostom v To cease from sin is not enough, if we neglect the correction of the old offense. Holy Scripture says: "My son, hast thou sinned? Do so no more!" But lest you think that this alone is safe, he hastened to say concerning the past: "Pray concerning thy former sins" [1]. But what benefit is there in such prayer, if you are not qualified to have your prayer heard because there are no fruits meet for repentance, lest you be cut down like a tree without fruit and cast into the fire (Mt 25:42). If you wish your prayer concerning your sins to be heard: "Forgive, and ye shall be forgiven" (Lk 6:37) [4].

entries.section: 1. Flee from sin in a spirit of hope

paragraphs.text: v In truth repentance for sins reforms men, but it shows no benefit if it is barren of works of mercy. This is what the Truth bears witness to by the tongue of John, who said to those who came to him: "O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance, and begin not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham. And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: every tree therefore which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire" (Lk 3:7-9).. The multitudes asked him, saying: "What shall we do then?" He answered and said unto them: "He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise"... What does this mean except what those on the left hear: "Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels: for I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat" (Mt 25:41-42).. And what will it profit you if you ask forgiveness without preparing yourselves to be heard, by not bringing forth "fruits worthy of repentance," so that you are cut down like a tree without fruit and cast into the fire? If you wish to be heard when you ask forgiveness, "Forgive, and ye shall be forgiven. Give, and it shall be given unto you" (Lk 6:37-38) [5].

entries.section: 1. Flee from sin in a spirit of hope

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine v Some not only do not repent of what they do, but they support their (evil) conduct without ceasing and approve of it. Truly the sin that is supported is multiplied. Rightly one condemns this attitude by saying: "My son, hast thou sinned? Add not to what thou hast done." He adds sin upon sin who adds to what he has done a justification of his fault.. So when Adam, the first man, was asked about his fault.. God's question to him was a call to repentance, but Adam answered justifying himself, saying: "The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat" (Gen 3:12). Adam blames his Creator by implication for his falling into disobedience. It is as though Adam were saying: "You provided me with an opportunity to commit sin, because You gave me the woman." This kind of sin remains evident in the human race to the present time. We still justify our sinful acts [6].
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Flee from sin as you flee from a serpent, for if you come near it, it will bite you.
Its teeth are as the teeth of a lion, destroying the souls of men [2].

The man who is sincere in his repentance, when he sins, immediately resorts to God in prayer seeking forgiveness, looking at sin as a deadly poison, fleeing from it as from the venom of the serpent with the teeth of a lion. The strength of the penitent is in not conversing with sin as Eve did with the serpent; for fleeing from sin is not cowardice but has in it courage, strength and wisdom. The Apostle says: "Flee fornication" (1 Cor 6:18).

He speaks here of the enemy of good who seduces us to surrender to sins, likening him to a serpent with teeth like the teeth of a lion; for Satan fought Eve by the tongue of the serpent, and Peter looked at the enemy of good as a roaring lion walking about seeking whom he may devour (Gen 3:1-7; 1 Pet 5:8).

entries.section: 1. Flee from sin in a spirit of hope

paragraphs.text: v Sin is the unclean thing; let us flee from it and abstain from it. "If thou comest near it, it will bite thee" (see Sir 21:2).. What does it not defile? It defiles the hands and the soul, the very house in which we place the evil treasure. Yet the Jews counted this as nothing. Moses carried the bones of Joseph (which in the eyes of the Jews were unclean), and Samson drank from the jawbone of an ass and ate honey from the lion, and Elijah was fed by ravens. Tell me, if we hold these things dear, what is more unclean than our books made of the skins of (dead) animals? [7]

entries.section: 1. Flee from sin in a spirit of hope

paragraphs.text: v It befits us not to confine ourselves to the outward form and the shadows, but to draw near to the truth and hold fast to it. Sin is an unclean thing. "If thou comest near it, it will bite thee" (see Sir 21:2) [8].

entries.section: 1. Flee from sin in a spirit of hope

paragraphs.text: v Let us avoid every sin completely, for because of it He is blasphemed. It is said: "Flee from sin as from a serpent, for if thou comest near it, it will bite thee" (see Sir 21:2). It does not come to us, but we are the ones who seek it [9].
St. John Chrysostom All iniquity is as a two-edged sword, and there is no healing for its wound [3].

Iniquity is rebellion; the Lord says of it that it is a man's doing what is right in his own eyes (Deut 12:8). If sin is like a two-edged sword, our salvation requires the Word of God, which is like a two-edged sword (Heb 4:13).

5 Terror and violence will waste riches: thus the house of the proud shall be made desolate. 6 A prayer out of a poor man's mouth reacheth to the ears of God, and his judgment cometh speedily. 7 He that hateth to be reproved is in the way of sinners, but he that feareth the Lord will repent from his heart. 8 An eloquent man is known afar off; but a man of understanding knoweth when he slippeth. 9 He that buildeth his house with other men's money is like one that gathereth himself stones for the tomb of his burial. 10 The congregation of the wicked is like tow wrapped together: and the end of them is a flame of fire to destroy them. 11 The way of sinners is made plain with stones, but at the end thereof is the pit of hell.

After calling us to flee from sin in general, he concentrated on the fall of the rich into wronging the poor, and the fall into pride of those who think themselves godly or rich in virtue. It befits the unjust and the proud not to hate rebuke but to fear, so that they return to the Lord with their hearts. But the danger into which the wicked fall is their clinging to one another, so that their hearts grow content with evil, and one draws the other to descend further into the flame of the fire of hell.

If the gate of truth is narrow and its way hard, then the way of sin is wide and paved with smooth stones; once someone slips on it he cannot stand, but descends without stopping. He needs the grace of God, which supports him in keeping the divine commandment and plants in him the fear of the Lord. By this he takes control of his thoughts and enjoys the divine wisdom.
Terror and violence destroy wealth, and likewise the house of the proud is destroyed [4].
God does not accept violence and injustice, and even rejects the alms of the violent and unjust man.

v Why do you revile the Lord by offering Him unclean sacrifices and gifts?!... It is better for you not to strip some men in order to clothe others; do you not wrong those whom you strip? For if you wrong them, even if you give to others what you took from them, this is not mercy.

v If you seize money and give it to others... what is your excuse? Do you want to know the measure of the evil you do? Hear what Solomon says, that he who offers a sacrifice from the goods of the poor is like one who kills a son before his father!
St. John Chrysostom v Enough, O rich man, you have forgotten your formation; let not temporal wealth, which does not save you, deceive you.
O mighty and strong one, rebuke yourself; why do you threaten, when if your heart forgets the Lord, you are weak?
True is the word of prophecy: let not the wise man, nor the mighty, nor the rich man boast.
Let a man boast in the Lord, if he boasts, for he abides forever; to Him be praise [10].
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh The prayer of the poor goes out of his mouth, and reaches the ears of the Lord, and quickly his judgment is executed for him [5].

God is the God of the poor and the oppressed and those who have no one to ask after them; He inclines His ears to all the suffering, needy and forgotten, and hears the cries of their hearts. He is overcome by their prayers, their sighs and their tears; He says to them: "Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me" (Song 6:5).

v Prayer alone is what overcomes God (for He is merciful). But the Lord Christ affirmed that it does not work on behalf of evil, and He gave it all its power when it is used for good. It knows only to give strength to the weak, to heal the sick, to loose those bound by evil spirits, to open the bars of prisons, and to loose the bonds of the righteous.

It also washes away faults and restrains temptations, and extinguishes the fires of persecution, and comforts faint souls, and encourages the downcast, and guides travelers, calms the waves, frightens robbers, refreshes the poor, and restrains the rich.
Prayer raises those who are going down, saves those who have fallen, and establishes those who stand.

Prayer is the wall of the faith. It arms us and shoots arrows toward the enemy who lies in wait for us on every side. So we shall not be unarmed. By day we are aware of our duty, and by night of our watching. And bearing the weapon of prayer we guard the banner of our Commander. And we wait in prayer for the trumpet of the archangel [11].
The scholar Tertullian He who hates rebuke walks in the steps of the sinner, but he who fears the Lord returns to Him with his heart [6].

It is said of the blessings of rebuke: "Turn you at my reproof: behold, I will pour out my spirit unto you, I will make known my words unto you" (Prov 1:23). "My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord, neither hate His reproof" (Prov 3:11). "For the commandment is a lamp; and the law is light; and reproofs of instruction are the way of life" (Prov 6:23). "Rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee" (Prov 9:8). "Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish" (Prov 12:1). "Poverty and shame shall be to him that refuseth instruction: but he that regardeth reproof shall be honoured" (Prov 13:18). "A fool despiseth his father's instruction: but he that regardeth reproof is prudent" (Prov 15:5).

v It often happens that a man breaks down for a time when he is rebuked, and he resists and struggles. But afterward, in his solitude, where there is none but God and himself, he is not afraid of the displeasure of others, so he corrects himself; rather he fears the wrath of God for refusing correction. So he does not again repeat this conduct which his brother disapproved, and he loves his brother, whom he used to regard as an enemy while he was in sin, as much as he hates the sin itself [12].
St. Augustine The one mighty in speech is known from afar, but the prudent man is known when he slips [7].

Ben Sira distinguishes between him who has been given the power of speech and him who enjoys prudence; the first is occupied with his reputation and fame, while the second is occupied with the salvation of his soul, so he realizes his sins and confesses them, returning to God in repentance.
He who builds his house with other men's money is like one who gathers his stones in a storm (or for his tomb) [8].
Among Ben Sira's counsels is his concern for managing financial matters wisely; therefore he warns against taking loans beyond a man's ability and means in order to build his house.
The assembly of the wicked is like a blazing bundle, and their end is a flame of fire [9].

Though the wicked care for being united together like a bundle, it is kindled by the fires of evil, which burn and destroy. Here the wicked man often reaches the summit of his evil, and it is not enough for him to practice evil and boast of it and love it more than good, but he loves the wicked in order to share their evil with them or to urge them still more to practice it with all violence. His pleasure becomes the company of the wicked and consulting with them, for no purpose except that he is pleased by the destruction of men, and rejoices in deceit and lying.
The way of sinners is paved with stones, and at its end is the pit of Hades [10].

What is the way of sinners, paved with hard stones, and at its end the pit of Hades, but the broad way that leads to destruction (Mt 7:13)? As for the narrow way that leads to life (Mt 7:14), in it my soul sings: "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Gal 2:20).
v When a man practices unlawful things, he fears what he has done!
Pope Gregory (the Great)
v The king came out to see those invited guests who had come, and he saw there a man clothed in filthy garments (Mt 22:11-13).
And he said to him: Tell me, friend, who let you in when you are not clothed in the glorious garments of the feast?
Why do you come here in these filthy garments? These garments do not befit the feast.
And the king commanded the servants, and they bound his hands, and tied his feet, and cast him into the fearful darkness.
Where there is great weeping and gnashing of teeth for that one clothed in filthy garments at the feast [13].
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh In the broad way I suffer the shame of nakedness, but in the narrow way I strip off the garments of the world and put on the garment of righteousness.

v The garment of righteousness was given to us formerly in Paradise, and we were stripped of it, and became naked. This nakedness of the prodigal son the father granted that it be covered, for he said at his return: "Bring him quickly the first robe" (see Lk 15:22).

The first robe is the garment of righteousness which man rightly received at his creation, but when he was deceived by the serpent he lost it. Again it is said of this nakedness: "Blessed is he that watcheth, and keepeth his garments, lest he walk naked" (Rev 16:15). For we keep our garments when we keep the commandments of righteousness in our hearts, so that even if we are stripped and appear naked before the Judge by iniquity, by repentance we are covered and the righteousness we lost returns to us.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. Flee from folly and seek wisdom

paragraphs.text: 12 He that keepeth the law of the Lord getteth the understanding thereof. 13 And the perfection of the fear of the Lord is wisdom. 14 He that is not clever will not be taught. 15 But there is a cleverness that aboundeth in bitterness. 16 The knowledge of a wise man shall abound like a flood, and his counsel is like a pure fountain of life. 17 The inner parts of a fool are like a broken vessel, and he will hold no knowledge as long as he liveth. 18 If a skilful man hear a wise word, he will commend it, and add unto it; but as soon as one of no understanding heareth it, it displeaseth him, and he casteth it behind his back. 19 The talking of a fool is like a burden in the way, but grace shall be found in the lips of the wise. 20 They inquire at the mouth of the prudent man in the congregation, and they shall ponder his words in their heart. 21 As is a house that is destroyed, so is wisdom to a fool; and the knowledge of the unwise is as talk without sense. 22 Instruction unto fools is as fetters on the feet, and like manacles on the right hand.

What occupies Ben Sira is the sanctification of the inner man, that the believer may enjoy the spirit of wisdom and discernment in all aspects of his life. Therefore he called us to seek the perfection of the fear of the Lord [11] and to enjoy true knowledge as a fountain of life overflowing upon the mind and the heart [13], and to enjoy divine grace [16], and to remove folly by acquiring wisdom [18], and to persevere in holy teaching as an ornament that adorns the soul [21], and so on.
He who keeps the Law has mastered his thoughts, and the perfection of the fear of the Lord is wisdom [11].

entries.section: 3. Flee from folly and seek wisdom

paragraphs.text: v The difference between wisdom and folly is like light compared with darkness; I think it is fitting that he used the comparison of light for the perception of goodness. And since darkness in its nature is not a reality (has no being)... whereas light can be perceived in its essence. By this comparison he showed that evil has no existence in itself, but consists in the lack of goodness, while goodness is always existing and abiding, and does not consist in the lack of anything higher than itself [14].
St. Gregory of Nyssa Between the traits of the wise man and the traits of the fool:

By the wonderful divine grace the folly of man is shattered and the wisdom of Christ shines forth in his mind and heart and words and conduct. Truly, what comparison is there between him whom the folly of the powers of darkness enslaves and him whom the wisdom of God incarnate frees?!

entries.section: 3. Flee from folly and seek wisdom

paragraphs.text: v The wise person and the foolish person have nothing in common, whether in the terms of human memorials or in divine rewards... The wise man will not share the fate of the fool [15].

St. Gregory the Wonderworker 1. He likens the mind of the fool to a broken vessel in which he keeps nothing [14], and the mind of the wise man to a fountain of sweet and pure water. 2. The fool is like a ruined house, in which nothing good dwells, but some wild beasts and birds dwell [18]. 3. The fool hears the word of God and spits it out, for he counts it an illogical word, unacceptable and without meaning. 4. The fool is like the simpleton; there are fetters on his feet and on his right hand, preventing him from moving and working [19]. 5. The fool laughs with a loud voice, and the wise man smiles in a stillness that reveals his peace and inward joy [20]. 6. Instruction is for the wise man like an ornament that adorns the heavenly bride and a bracelet on his arm that urges him to holy spiritual work [21]. 7. The fool enters the house of one he visits rashly, and the wise man waits for the master of the house to permit him to enter [22]. 8. The fool looks in from the door to see what is inside the house, but the well-mannered wise man stands outside! [23]. 9. It befits the wise man not to intrude on the privacy of others, so he does not eavesdrop on anyone [24]. 10. The wise man weighs his words, so no vain word comes out of his mouth, while the fool repeats his words [25]. 11. The minds of fools are in their mouths, but the mouths of the wise are in their minds; they utter no word without thinking about it.
He who is not clever is not taught, but there is a cleverness that increases bitterness [12].
Intelligence is a gift that God offers to men, but pride turns intelligence into bitterness.
The knowledge of the wise man is like a flood, and his counsel overflows abundantly like a fountain of life [13].

The wise man drinks his fill of true knowledge, and it gives him delight, and it overflows within him like a flood that cannot be measured. It also overflows upon his brethren in sincere counsel like a fountain of life. This is the work of the Holy Spirit in us (Mk 13:11).
The inner workings of the fool (his mind) are like a broken vessel, which retains nothing of knowledge [14].

Wisdom overflows upon man in his depths with knowledge like a flood that does not cease. But the fool is like a broken vessel that will keep nothing within it. Since folly begets evil, the fool suffers emptiness, and becomes like a dumb beast that dies and perishes as though he had never existed at some time. But the wise man, even if he dies, departs to Paradise to enjoy eternal glories and immortality.

entries.section: 3. Flee from folly and seek wisdom

paragraphs.text: v Insensibility and unreasonableness beget in the soul ignorance of God, and this ignorance begets evil. But the knowledge of God brings goodness and saves the soul. Therefore if you remain in a state of loftiness with knowledge of God and an effort not to satisfy your own lusts, your mind turns toward virtue. But if you are drunk with ignorance of God, and enjoy the satisfaction of your evil lusts, forgetting the afflictions that await you after death, you perish like the dumb beast [16].
St. Anthony the Great If a man of understanding hears a word of wisdom, he praises it and adds to it.
But the one immersed in pleasures, when he hears it, hates it and casts it behind his back [15].

How great the difference between the wise man who finds his delight in a word of wisdom and in continual growth in knowledge, and the fool, who cannot bear a word of wisdom, but makes light of it and hates it and ignores it, and counts it as depriving him of his happiness and his temporal pleasures.
The talk of a fool is like a heavy burden on a journey, but grace is on the lips of the prudent man [16].

How great the difference between the wise man and the fool: grace clings to the lips of the first, so no one tires of the words of grace that come from his mouth. But the talk of the fool is without benefit, and whoever accompanies him wishes not to hear his words, because they are heavy and corrupting.

entries.section: 3. Flee from folly and seek wisdom

paragraphs.text: They seek the utterance of the prudent man in the assembly, and ponder his words in their hearts [17].

When the wise man speaks in an assembly, all listen to him, because he instills delight in them and fills them with hope, and urges them to continual progress. They count every word he utters as having its benefit in the life of the hearer as in society.
The word "heart" here, as was previously indicated, means thought or mind. So the hearer of the wise man takes care to keep what he hears and to cherish it, and to ruminate on it continually!

entries.section: 3. Flee from folly and seek wisdom

paragraphs.text: Wisdom to the fool is like a vanished house, and the knowledge of the ignorant is talk that does not stand examination [18].
The fool finds the words of wisdom burdensome; he counts them as an illusion, or as a house in which he does not wish to dwell, indeed as a passing dream.

The day on which a man learns nothing new is not only lost from his life, but it spoils what he had learned before. It is as though man's knowledge will not be static; it either renews itself and grows, or stops, not to remain as it is, but loses its time, and his knowledge weakens, and he falls behind. St. Gregory likens it to one who swims in a sea: either he advances to the harbor or he stops in the middle of the sea, and so sinks and perishes.

entries.section: 3. Flee from folly and seek wisdom

paragraphs.text: Instruction to the fool is like fetters on the feet, and like a manacle on the right hand [19].
Instruction is very heavy to the fool, for he counts it as fetters on his life that deprive him of freedom in conduct and enjoyment.

entries.section: 4. The manners of the wise man

paragraphs.text: 23 A fool lifteth up his voice with laughter; but a wise man doth scarce smile a little. 24 Learning is unto a wise man as an ornament of gold, and like a bracelet upon his right arm. 25 A fool's foot is soon in his neighbor's house; but a man of experience is ashamed of him. 26 A fool will peep in at the door into the house; but he that is well nurtured will stand without. 27 It is the rudeness of a man to hearken at the door; but a wise man will be grieved with the disgrace. 28 The lips of talkers will be telling such things as pertain not unto them; but the words of such as have understanding are weighed in the balance. 29 The heart of fools is in their mouth; but the mouth of the wise is in their heart.

Ben Sira presents to us some traits of the conduct of the wise man, such as the smile instead of laughing aloud [20], a special esteem for instruction, so that he treasures it as the bride treasures the ornaments and jewels that her bridegroom gives her [21}, not being hasty in entering the house of one of his relatives or friends [22], and not eavesdropping at the door [24], and not speaking too much [25], while weighing every word before uttering it [26].
The fool raises his voice in laughter, but the clever man smiles quietly with some hesitation [20].

v If we watch over ourselves with the fear of God when we enter the company of others, and if we care for our hearts in vigilance, we find no cause to be troubled or to laugh. For in the presence of the fear of God there is no one laughing. As for fools, it has been said that they raise their voice in laughter. The words of the fool carry disturbance, but the righteous man speaks only to smile [17].

v If before our encounters with others we prepare our hearts by watching in the fear of God, why should we find any reason to be disturbed or to laugh? In truth there is no one laughing in the presence of a godly fear. It is said of the foolish that they raise their voices when they laugh, and that the talk of the fool is disturbing and leads to the loss of delight. At any rate, it is said of the righteous man that he merely smiles. Therefore if we bring to ourselves the remembrance of God, and fill our thoughts with quiet humility when we are in the company of our friends, then we love them in this manner, and we set before our eyes the fearful judgment of God. For God dwells where there is quietness, gentleness and humility.
Sts. Barsanuphius and John St. Basil made clear the distinction between corrupting laughter and laughter in the sense of the soul's joy and exultation in God.

v Indulging in laughter in an uncontrolled and exaggerated way is a sign of excess and a lack of a man's control over his feelings, and a failure to suppress the soul's levity by using the mind firmly. It is not unseemly to bear witness to the soul's cheerfulness by a joyful smile, if only it illustrates what is written: "A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance" (Prov 15:13). But hoarse laughter, with no control of the movements of the body, is no indication of a soul well ordered, or of personal dignity, or of one who rules himself.

This kind of laughter is condemned by the Preacher especially as destroying the steadiness of the soul, in the words: "I said of laughter, It is mad" (Eccl 2:2). Again: "For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool" (Eccl 7:6). Moreover, the Lord shows that He practiced these necessary emotions that are bound up with the body, as well as those connected with virtue, for example sorrow over the sorrowful and compassion for them, but as we know from the Gospel story He never laughed. On the contrary, He declared that those who give themselves up to laughter are unhappy (Lk 6:25).

Let us not allow the word (laughter) to deceive us, for it has two meanings. Holy Scripture often uses it of the joy of the spirit and the delight of the feelings that follows good works. For example Sarah says: "God hath made me to laugh" (Gen 21:6). And there is another saying: "Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh" (Lk 6:21). In a similar way the words of Job: "Till he fill thy mouth with laughing" (Job 8:21). All these witnesses of gladness point to the soul's cheerfulness instead of boisterous merriment. Therefore he who is master of every passion and feels no agitation in his enjoyment, or at least shows no outward expressions, but tends to control every harmful pleasure firmly, such a one is perfectly chaste, and in truth has clearly been freed from every sin [18].
St. Basil the Great Instruction is to the prudent man like an ornament of gold, and like a bracelet on his right arm [21].
The wise man rejoices in instruction, like the bride who treasures the gifts of her bridegroom that he gives her to adorn herself with.
The foot of the fool is quick in entering a house, but the man of wide experience stands outside with dignity [22].

The wise man moves with dignity and modesty, so he does not hasten to enter the houses of his friends, relying on his close friendship with them, but he knows the limits of friendship and does not transgress them.
He who lacks discernment stares from the door into the house, but the well-mannered man stands outside [23].

entries.section: 4. The manners of the wise man

paragraphs.text: A man shows his lack of manners by eavesdropping at the door, and the prudent man is grieved by that fault [24].

entries.section: 4. The manners of the wise man

paragraphs.text: The lips of fools describe matters in detail, and the words of the prudent are weighed in the balance [25].

entries.section: 4. The manners of the wise man

paragraphs.text: The hearts of fools are in their mouths, and the mouths of the wise are in their hearts [26].

v For a good reason the prophet said: "The tongue (of the wicked) deviseth mischiefs" (Ps 52:4). Contemplation belongs to the living soul through its living feeling, but the tongue was not created as befits the rational nature, but to be a servant of the rational nature. Nevertheless another prophet shows a trustworthy, inspired and perfect saying, for he says: "The minds (hearts) of fools are in their mouths," meaning by this that they utter things at random with no foundation, for they are accustomed not to return to the consideration of the mind after meditating on it in the heart, but walk in a rash movement of the tongue with levity.

If the heart of the fool is in his mouth, it is because he does not speak what he thinks, but thinks after he speaks. This points to the tongue of the fool, but of the tongue of the wise man we read rather: "The mouth of the righteous speaketh wisdom" (Ps 37:30). "My tongue is the pen of a ready writer" (Ps 37:30). The tongue of the wise man is born of meditation on wisdom, therefore it is like the pen of a writer, which never speaks in confusion or with doubt. Rather it submits to what is thought and what is read, and so overflows with keen intelligence according to the judgment of the person [19].
St. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers
30 When the ungodly curseth Satan, he curseth his own soul. 31 A whisperer defileth his own soul, and is hated wheresoever he dwelleth.
If the wicked man curses Satan, he curses his own soul [27].

Some see that the speech here is about one who thinks that someone is a demon and curses him, for the curse returns upon himself. The scholar Origen ascribes every demon to a particular sin, so he who commits many sins is like that man who dwelt in the tombs and in whom a legion dwelt, that is, many demons (Mk 5:9; Lk 8:30).
v If Satan is called "the adversary," then all who are against the will of God can be called devils [20].

v Why does it seem strange that we ascribe a demon to every kind of sin, when it is written that a legion of demons was found in one person? Indeed I recall a similar saying in our interpretation of the passage in a psalm: "I will early destroy all the wicked of the land; that I may cut off all wicked doers from the city of the Lord" (Ps 101:8). It is also said: "a two-edged sword in the hand of the righteous" (see 149:6), without doubt it is used to shatter the opposing powers. But I think that in order to give a stronger and decisive confirmation we cite the word of the Apostle Paul: "And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly" (Rom 16:20) [21].
The scholar Origen The slanderer defiles his own soul, and his neighbors will hate him [28].

The slanderer does not harm others as much as he harms himself. It is reported of St. Augustine that he wrote two lines of verse against slander and hung them in the dining room. It happened that some bishops sat with him at table and began to speak ill of certain people, so he advised them, saying: Either you erase these two lines, or I will rise from the table.

v The man who does not know how to distinguish between good and evil has no right to judge men that this one is good and that one is wicked. He who knows God is good. And if a man is not good, this means that he does not know God and God does not know him. For goodness is the only means of knowing God [22].
St. Anthony the Great v If you hear someone reviling another, flee from him as you would flee from a poisonous serpent, until he is ashamed and learns not to speak this way again.
St. Jerome Inspired by Sirach 21

entries.section: To You I flee, O Savior of the fallen

paragraphs.text: v Your commandment is a wonderful light and a blazing fire, revealing my sins and kindling my heart with the fires of Your love.
The serpent crawls to bite me with its deadly venom, and roars like a lion to terrify me in the wilderness of this world.
To whom shall I flee but to You, O Forgiver of sins, and Giver of joyful hope and righteousness and holiness.
v Your commandment lifts me out of hatred and violence and injustice; so I cling to You and acquire Your love and compassion and humility.

I will not forget that I am dust and ashes, and corruption has crept into me, but You embrace me, You who raise those who are going down, and save the fallen, and establish those who stand, and lift the earthly as to Your heavens.
v You discipline me with Your rebuke to me, so I feel Your love, and return to You.
You grant me Your wisdom, so I do not build my house on the sand of the world, but dwell in You, O Rock of eternity.
I cling to those who give thanks to You, and I do not sit in the assembly of the wicked.
Let not the broad way of sinners draw me, but I delight in being crucified with You, O Way, Truth and Life.
v Your commandments are in their essence a call to possess You, O Word of God.
Do not cease to say: "I am..." that I may know You and possess You.
In You I enjoy wisdom and discernment, and shake off folly and ignorance.
In You I walk in the light, and I hear Your wonderful voice: "Ye are the light of the world" (Mt 5:14).
The frail darkness of sin is scattered, and it has no inward place!
I thank You, for in my folly I was like a broken vessel that does not keep the water of life, and in You I enjoy a fountain of sweet and pure water.
In my folly I was like a ruined house, inhabited by the powers of darkness like wild beasts and birds, and in You I enjoy Your Kingdom within me.
In my folly I mocked Your word, and in You I sing:
"How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" (Ps 119:103).
In my folly I used to laugh with an empty loud voice, and in You my smile proclaims Your dwelling in me.
In my folly I thought Your commandments fetters and a heavy yoke, and in You I see them as the precious ornament that the heavenly bride treasures.
In my folly I was rash in everything, and in You I go forward in quietness as from glory to glory.
v Grant me to find the word of wisdom sweet, and to count it a pearl that I keep in my mind and heart.
I ruminate on it continually, and reckon that I have not yet reached its depths.
Remove from me folly and chatter, that my words may not be a burden to those who hear them.
Grant me Your grace, that I may embrace Your wisdom; fill me with true delight, and let everyone I meet long to possess it and practice it.
Let him contemplate it from time to time, as he tastes its sweetness in his depths.
v Train me to imitate You, O my Creator and Savior.
I am the work of Your hands, indebted to You for all my life.
You ask me continually: "Wilt thou be made whole?" Teach me not to press upon any of my brethren, nor to break into his dwelling without asking his permission.
Sanctify my steps and my words, that I may feel Your company with me in every breath of my life.
Remove from me vain chatter, and guard my tongue from slander.
1 A slothful man is like a filthy stone; everyone hisses at his disgrace. 2 A slothful man is like the dung of a dunghill; everyone who picks it up shakes his hand.

The chapter begins with the two most dangerous enemies of wisdom, namely laziness and indulgence in pleasures. Parents long for their children to be better than themselves in manners, learning, knowledge and success in everything. Therefore he began by speaking of laziness, so that parents may not pamper their children, but that they may grow up serious in their lives. Then he speaks afterward about wisdom, that they may walk in a spirit of prudence in the Lord. He also affirms the discipline of a son if he sins. And he calls on children to flee from corrupt friendships and to cleave to wise friends.

For Ben Sira, slackness or laziness is the prominent mark of the fool. By his laziness the fool is a problem for himself and for others, for laziness has its effects on society. There is no one who wants to cleave to a lazy person.

Ben Sira speaks of the lazy young girl, whom no one wishes to marry, and who spends her life dependent on her parents [3-4]. And the impudent daughter, if she marries, brings shame upon her father and her husband [5].
The lazy man is like a defiled stone; everyone hisses at his shame [1].

Laziness drives a person to shame (Prov 24:30-34). He is like a stone soiled with filth; whoever looks at him is offended by him. It is said: "God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness... male and female created he them" (Gen 1:16, 28). God is the Worker! Perhaps you wonder at this attribute, for rarely does a person fix his insight on God as the Worker. With boldness I say that it befits the image to be conformed to the original and to cleave to him, and to ask for his grace so as to bear the true image, one of whose marks is work!

After the Supreme Artist had brought into being this world, wonderful in its beauty, for the sake of man, and after He had created man as a king in his palace, "the garden of Eden", possessing authority, it is said: "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." God was pleased with what He had made, not out of need of it, but because work pours happiness and joy upon man, whom He loves!

Thus He created us and placed us in the garden of Eden, and we had no need to work in order to eat and drink and take delight. But He wanted us to be like Him, so that we would work and keep the garden. Had our first parents not sinned, we would have worked without weariness, and would have found our joy in offering works of love to those around us, and all would rejoice in the common work of love.
