It is said of God: "And he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made. And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it" (Gen 2:1-2). God's rest on the seventh day is not idleness, for He is always at work: "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work" (Jn 5:17). He completed the creation, and He continues to care for it and to be concerned for the salvation of man, whose nature he had corrupted.

As for us, our rest is not in fleeing from work. Though, for the rest of body and mind, we enjoy holidays, yet we work even in our sleep and our rest, through love. We work with wisdom and balance in every aspect of our spiritual, intellectual, psychological, scholarly, social and physical life, so that a person may enjoy creativity in what God has given him, to complete the work of his brothers in the other aspects.

The Apostle Paul took pride in that he supported himself and those with him through his work (Acts 20:34-36). And in his epistle to the Corinthians (1 Cor 4:8-13) he made clear that he worked and toiled. In this he rebukes them, for in their slackness and laziness they thought of themselves as kings who do not do any work.
v Be occupied with what belongs to the Lord, or busy with your work, but do not be idle [1].

The Didascalia v In the beginning you could have worked without toil... because God Himself wanted this, but you did not allow it. For God did not mix work with toil. Had man experienced toil from the beginning, he would not have been afflicted with it afterward as a punishment. You can work and at the same time not reach the stage of hard labor, as in the case of the angels [2].

St. John Chrysostom v Those who fully realize that all their work must aim at attaining the good life, and yet amuse themselves with temporal blessings; these I compare to people who seek a cure and medicine but do not know how to use it, and are not troubled over (their ignorance of its use). Therefore let us not excuse the sins we commit by pleading the circumstances of our surroundings or by attributing them to another person, but let us lay the blame on ourselves. For if our souls willingly give themselves up to laziness, they cannot escape defeat [3].
St. Anthony the Great The lazy man can be likened to the filth of dung; everyone who gathers it shakes his hand from it [2].

St. John Chrysostom often attacked the lazy who are without work, and he made this clear in his homily In inscriptionem altaris [4]. And when he spoke of the poor he meant the toiling workers. He does not praise them for their poverty, but for their struggle in work, that they weary themselves in order to support their families.

v If you wish to uproot poverty, you will certainly uproot the whole structure of life, you will shatter your life. You will not find a sailor or a ship's pilot or a farmer or a builder, nor a weaver or a shoemaker or a carpenter or a smith or a tanner or a miller; you will find none of these workers nor any others... If all become rich, all will live in idleness, and everything will perish and be dissipated [5].
St. John Chrysostom

3 An undisciplined son is a disgrace to his father, and a daughter only brings loss. 4 A prudent daughter is an inheritance to her husband, and a shameful daughter is a grief to her father. 5 The impudent one shames her father and her husband, and both of them treat her with contempt.
An undisciplined son is a shame to his father, and the birth of a foolish daughter is a loss to him [3].

An obstinate, undisciplined son shames his parents. As for the birth of an obstinate daughter, it is counted a loss in the family. A daughter lacking discipline is not tolerated by her husband and so she shames her parents; neither her husband nor her parents honor her.
A prudent daughter brings an inheritance to her husband, and a shameful daughter is a sorrow to her father [4].
An impudent daughter shames her father and her husband, and is despised by both of them [5].
6 A tale out of season is like music in mourning, but stripes and instruction are wisdom at all times.
A word out of season is like music in a time of grief, but discipline and the teaching of wisdom are fitting at every time [6].

The Lord disciplines His children through love, and in the same spirit parents discipline their child (Heb 12:5-8). It seems that Ben Sira was groaning over the excessive pampering of children, especially in aristocratic circles, and he was also grieved over families that neglect the upbringing of their children. Note that the number of children whom families have spoiled has greatly increased. What occupied families was working with all their energies and praying that the Lord would give them children, without exerting any effort to bring them up as befits them as people of God.

The first one responsible for a child's upbringing is the family; and if the family fails, it befits the teachers to try to guide the children; and if the teachers fail, the police intervene to discipline the undisciplined.
Guiding children and disciplining them in a fitting manner is necessary, lest they grow up fools and lose a worthy life.

v The Lord disciplines human beings not out of hatred, for He suffered for our sake when He was able to destroy us because of our faults. He is the good Teacher who has full power to reprove with words of rebuke.

Words of rebuke are like a whip with which the idle mind of men is scourged. And while He scourges them, it is stirred to advise them. For those who are raised by words of praise are pricked by being blamed. And those whom blame cannot raise to salvation as though they were dead, rise to the truth through their accusation. "But stripes and instruction are fitting at all times for wisdom" [6].
St. Clement of Alexandria He who teaches a fool is like one who mends a broken earthen vessel, and like one who tries to wake a man sunk in his sleep [7].

7 He who teaches a fool mends a vessel of earthenware, 8 and rouses one sunk in his sleep. 9 He who speaks to a fool speaks to one who is drowsy; and when he has finished he says, "What?" 10 Weep for the dead, for he has lost the light, and weep for the fool, for he has lost his mind. 11 Weep less for the dead, for he is at rest, 12 but the life of the fool is worse than his death. 13 Mourning for the dead is seven days, but mourning for the fool and the hypocrite is all the days of his life. 14 Do not multiply words with the ignorant, and do not mingle with the dull. 15 Be on guard against him, lest he trouble you and defile you with his filth. 16 Turn away from him and you will find rest, and his folly will not grieve you. 17 What is heavier than lead? And what is he called but a fool? 18 Sand and salt and iron are lighter to bear than an ignorant man! 19 A framework of timber bound into a building is not loosened by an earthquake; so also the heart that relies on sound counsel is not afraid at all. 20 The heart that leans upon a wise opinion is like an ornament of sand on a polished wall. 21 As stakes set in a high place do not stand against the wind, 22 so the fearful heart of the fool, with its thoughts, does not stand against any terror. 23 The heart of the fool is afraid in its thoughts, but he who continues in the commandments of God at all times is never afraid.
Weeping over the fool is more bitter than weeping over a dead man. Therefore Ben Sira demands that children be kept apart from association with the fool, for the following reasons:
a. Because the life of the fool is worse than death.
b. He does not accept instruction, so speaking with him is a waste of time and causes weariness to the one who speaks with him.
c. Dealing with him is counted a burden on the soul, for he is heavier than lead and sand and salt and a block of iron.
d. The wise man takes a firm decision with which he defies the coming of an earthquake of troubles (Ps 112:7; Mt 7:24-27), but the fool is wavering, and the mere fear of troubles shatters him.
He who tells something to a fool is speaking to a sleeping man, and in the end he says: "What is this?" [8]
If children live faithfully and have what is necessary, they cover over the lowliness of their parents. [9]
But proud children, through scorn and lack of food, stain the nobility of their kin [10].

It does not befit the believer to despise children and infants, for the ill-behaved child does wrong to his family, and the child who walks in the way of truth is a blessing to it and supports it. For it was said of the repentance of the people of Nineveh:

v Oh, the harmony of repentance! What a wise and powerful sorrow! They did not leave even the animals outside the arrangement, but in marvelous ways obliged them also to cry out. They separated the calf from its mother, and deprived the lamb of its suckling.

They took the nursing infants from their mothers' arms. The mothers were put in one place and the infants in another, calling to one another and answering with mournful voices. The hungry infants seek the source of their milk, while the mothers, pricked by the instinct of motherhood, cry out toward their children in grieved voices.

The hungry infants cry out, seized by bitter cries for help, while the hearts of the mothers were tormented by the pains of natural affection. For this reason the inspired Word preserved their repentance as a universal model of how to live.
The elders grieved because of the chastisement with which they were threatened; they were in bitterness, in their old age.
The boys and the little ones lament with greater burning.
The poor sigh, while the rich forgot their comfort and put on the sackcloth that befits the sorrowful.

The king of Nineveh left his glory and his loftiness, turning toward disgrace. He left his crown, and put dust on his head, and took off the royal robe and wrapped himself in sackcloth. He left his high and glorious majesty, and crawled on the ground in lowliness. He left the luxury that belonged to him as a king, in order to grieve with the people. He became one of them when he saw the wrath of the Lord of all [7].
St. Basil the Great Weep for the dead, because he has left the light behind, and weep for the fool, because he has left the mind behind.
Weep with joy for the dead, because he is at rest, but the life of the fool is worse than death [11].
By saying: "Weep with joy for the dead, for he is at rest", he reveals that there is a blessed life after death, and not a cessation of life.

v True prudence is knowing what you do and what you do not do. He who possesses it does not cease from virtuous works, and will not be pierced by the deadly arrow of vice. So he who understands the words of prudence knows the difference between what is enticing and built upon deceit, and what calmly reminds us of the true way of practicing life... Give such prudence to him who builds his house, that he may lay the foundation upon a rock, that is, support it with faith in Christ, so that it is not shaken when the winds blow and the rains fall and the storms assail it (Mt 7:25) [8].
St. Basil the Great v Just as the body without the soul is dead, so the soul without the mind is idle (barren) and unable to inherit God [9].

v In the soul there is a mind that works, while in the body there is instinct. The mind makes the soul divine, and instinct corrupts the body (that is, if we satisfy our instincts and natural desires).
Instinct works in every body, but not every soul has the mind working in it. For this reason not every soul is saved [10].
St. Anthony the Great Mourning for the dead lasts seven days, but mourning for the fool lasts all the days of his life [12].

v If Jeremiah saw that those who were wounded in war deserved continual lamentation, what shall we say all the more for those calamities that befall souls?! (Isaiah) said: "Thy slain men are not slain with the sword, nor dead in battle" (Isa 22:2). I lament the sting of true death, and the gravity of sin, and the fiery darts of the evil one, those which kindle fires fiercely for souls as well as bodies.

Truly the divine commandment groans with a loud voice when it sees such uncleanness creeping over the earth, proclaiming in the Old Testament: "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife" (Ex 20:17; Deut 5:21). And in the holy Gospel it also says: "Whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart" (Mt 5:28). And here it now sees the very Bride of the Lord, she whose head is the Lord Christ, boldly committing the sin of adultery.
Even the congregations of the saints groan over her![11]

St. Basil the Great v Count every person better than yourself (Phil 2:3). Weep over your dead (see Sir 22:11; Jn 11:31). First cast the beam out of your own eye (Mt 7:5). Rebuild your house that was destroyed. Let him cry out: Have mercy on me, Son of David, that I may see again (Mk 10:47-51; Lk 18:38-41). Learn, you, until every mouth is stopped (Rom 3:19), and do not speak with arrogance. Make a bolt for your door (your mouth) [12].

Sts. Barsanuphius and John Do not prolong the discussion with the fool, and do not visit the dull; be on guard against him to avoid weariness, and do not be defiled by him if you come into contact with him.
Turn away from him and you will find rest, and you will not be wearied by his folly [13].
Ben Sira calls us not to enter into a discussion with a fool, lest we be defiled and be struck with a state of disturbance.

v When you meet a man who loves to argue, and he begins to dispute with you about what is self-evident and true, break off the conversation and withdraw quickly, for his mind has turned to stone. For just as water spoils the finest wines, so foolish arguments spoil those who are virtuous in conduct and in character [13].
St. Anthony the Great What is heavier than lead?
And what is his name but the fool? [14].
Sand and salt and a piece of iron are easier to carry than a foolish man [15].
The wooden brace bound into a building is not loosened by an earthquake; so also the firm mind fortified with rational counsel is not afraid of a crisis [16].
A mind established on wise thinking is like a plaster decoration on a polished wall [17].
Ben Sira compares the steadiness of the wise man with the unsteadiness of the fool. This steadiness or unsteadiness touches the life of the person in the midst of the community.
As fences set in a high place do not stand before the wind, so the cowardly heart in the thought of the fool does not stand before any kind of fear [18].

24 He who pricks the eye brings forth tears, and he who pricks the heart brings out feeling. 25 He who throws a stone at birds frightens them away, and he who reproaches his friend breaks off the friendship. 26 If you draw a sword against your friend, do not despair, for he will return. 27 If you open your mouth against your friend, do not be afraid, for he will be reconciled, except in reproach and arrogance and the disclosing of a secret and a wound dealt with treachery; for in these every friend flees. 28 Remain faithful to your neighbor in his poverty, that you may be satisfied with him in his good things. 29 Stand by him in the time of his distress, that you may share in his inheritance. 30 Before the fire come the vapor of the furnace and the smoke; so before bloodshed come insults. 31 I am not ashamed to defend my friend, nor will I hide from his face; and even if evil befalls me from him, 32 everyone who hears of it will be on guard against him. 33 Who will set a guard over my mouth, and a sure seal upon my lips, that I may not fall because of them and my tongue destroy me?

The subject of friendship was very close to the heart of Ben Sira. For he longs to see society, if not the whole world, ruled by unity, love, tenderness and completeness. For wisdom in his mind does not stop at a person's ordering his own private life or enjoying eternal salvation, but touches the life of the community, if not of humanity as a whole!

The first part of this chapter speaks of wisdom, whose dangerous enemy is laziness; for the goal of wisdom and diligence, or constant perseverance, is that all humanity interact together in a spirit of genuine friendship. The fickle fool's evil returns upon the life of the community. Such a person cannot be relied upon. He is unsteady in his loyalty and faithfulness to others, therefore those who wish to form a friendship with him are struck with a state of frustration. There is no one who would like to keep the friendship of a person who is wrathful or abusive [20].
This does not mean that there is no anger between two faithful friends, but in the spirit of faithfulness the anger soon passes, and there may result from it a better love, trust and understanding.
He who pricks his eye makes tears flow, and he who pricks the heart brings out his feelings [19].

The scholar Origen[14] calls us to strike the eye and the heart with prayer in faith; we ask for God's work in us, and we ask for more of His gifts. As it came in the Psalms: "Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it" (Ps 81:11).

The phrase came in his writings: "He who pricks his eye, tears flow, and he who pricks the heart brings out feelings"; by the eye and the heart here he means the inner life. It befits the believer to drink from his inner springs, that is, from his insight and his affections. If the Word of God in His Incarnation dwelt among us, to establish His kingdom within us (Lk 17:21), then He directed our gaze to our depths, that we might see Him working in us. He came not despising us, but honoring us by our union with Him and our enjoyment of His surpassing works.

In the scholar Origen's discourse on the work of the Holy Spirit in man, he asks us to drink the living waters from our inner springs and wells, as it came in the Book of Proverbs (5:15, 18). It befits us to dig in our inner earth, that we may enjoy these living waters.

v Let us work according to the counsel of Wisdom to us, which says: "Drink waters out of your cistern, and running waters out of your well. Let them be yours..." (Prov 5:15, 17). Be assured, O reader, that you have your well and your spring, so that when you take hold of the Holy Bible, you begin to express yourself through your teaching of the text, in harmony with what you have learned from the Church, and also try to drink from your inner spiritual source.

Within you is a spring of living water (Gen 26:19), perennial veins, and an abundant flowing stream, with rational understanding so long as it does not collide with the earth and the remnants of rocks. Continue working to dig your earth and cleanse it of defilement, that you may remove laziness from yourself and drive idleness from your heart. Hear what the Holy Bible says: "Strike the eye and tears flow, and strike the heart and it produces understanding" [19]. You must also purify your spirit, so that you drink from your living springs. In truth, if you receive the Word of God within you, there becomes in you a spring of water overflowing with eternal life [15].

v You have the nature of living waters within you (Gen 26:19). There are in you perennial veins and channels overflowing with prudent understanding, provided only that they are not filled with dust and refuse.

Take care to dig your earth and remove the filth, that is, remove the idleness of your natural power, and drive out the idleness of your hearts. Hear what the Scripture says: "He who pricks the eye makes tears flow, and he who pricks the heart brings out understanding" (see Sir 22:19) [16].

v Continue to dig your earth and cleanse it of filth, that is, remove from it the idleness of your natural power, and drive out from it the idleness of your heart. The Scripture says: Strike the eye and tears flow, and strike the heart and understanding comes forth [17].

The scholar Origen v Preserve, my children, that friendship which you began with your brothers, for there is nothing in the world more beautiful than this. It is a comfort in this life to have one to whom you can open your heart, share your trust, and entrust with the secrets of your heart. It is a comfort to have beside you a trustworthy person who rejoices with you in your prosperity, sympathizes with you in your troubles, and encourages you in persecution.

What good friends were those Hebrew youths whom the flame of the furnace's fires did not separate from their love for one another (Dan 3:16 etc.)! We say of them what was said: "Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided" (2 Sam 1:23) [18].

v He who is not faithful to God cannot be a friend to a person. Friendship is the guardian of godliness and the teacher of equality, making the greater equal to the lesser, and the lesser to the greater [19].
v Friendship cannot exist where there is false flattery [20].
St. Ambrose Throwing a stone at birds makes them flee in fright, and insulting a friend breaks off the friendship [20].

Sirach warns us lest we lose friendship through some trivial behavior that we practice. For friends leave a person quickly when they sense a danger coming upon them, like birds that flee if someone throws a stone toward them.

It befits a person to hasten to apologize for his wrong conduct without justifying himself; if he has uttered a harsh word or drawn a sword against his friend, let him not despair of regaining the friendship if he is earnest about it.
He who draws near to his neighbor in the time of his distress, the friend most often forgets this when he comes into prosperity.
It befits a person not to be ashamed to defend his friend in the time of his poverty or distress, and not to try to flee from him.
If evil befalls you from your friend, take care not to sin with a word against him.
If you draw a sword against your friend, do not despair, for renewing the friendship is possible [21].

v Let us follow love, for it is a safety valve that does not allow us to suffer any evil. Let us bind ourselves to one another. Would that there be no deceit among us and no lie. For where friendship exists there is nothing of the kind. The wise man also tells us: "If you draw a sword against your friend, do not despair, for the friendship can be renewed. If you open your mouth against your friend, do not be afraid, for reconciliation may take place, except in the case of abuse and arrogance and the disclosing of a secret and the treacherous blow. For in these cases every friend flees"... What secret do you have? Do you wish to do evil to your brother? Or do you wish to deprive him of sharing with you some benefits? For this reason the secret must be annulled! [21]

St. John Chrysostom If you open your mouth against a friend, do not be afraid, for reconciliation is possible, except in abuse and arrogance and the disclosing of a secret and the blow of treachery; for every friend flees from conduct like this [22].

When someone discloses the secret of his friend, what concerns the friend is not his material or moral losses because of the disclosure of the secret, but rather the loss of trust and the lack of faithfulness.
v Nothing is good without friendship... Let one person have a hill of talents, and another have a hundred friends; the latter is richer in his resources than the former.
St. John Chrysostom Gain the trust of your neighbor in his poverty, and you may be satisfied with him in his prosperity.
Stand with him in the time of distress, and you may share with him in his inheritance [23].

The true, faithful friend is known by his steadfastness in practical friendship and his concern if the friend is struck by poverty or want or distress. True friendship is manifested when the friend does all in his power to protect him from his enemy [25].
Just as the smoke and vapor of the furnace precede the fire, so insult precedes bloodshed [24].
I am not ashamed to protect a friend, nor will I hide from his face [25].
And if evil befalls me because of him, everyone who hears of it will be on guard against him [26].
v If friendship proceeds from the fountain of good will, do not hesitate to endure great dangers in life for the sake of the friend. It is said: If evils befall me from him, I will bear them [22].

v Surely, if there is a necessity to give testimony, whoever knows a fault in a friend of his must rebuke him privately, and if he does not listen he must do so openly. For rebuke is good, and is often better than silent friendship. Even if the friend thinks that he has been hurt, you must rebuke him. And if the bitterness of the wounds to his mind is for his correction, do not cease from rebuking him; do not be afraid!

"Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful" (Prov 27:6). So rebuke your erring friend, and do not abandon the innocent. For friendship must be faithful and settled in true affection. It befits us not to exchange our friends in a childish way for a trivial passion [23].

v In necessity we endure even troubles for the sake of the friend. Even enmity can be endured for the innocence of the friend. We endure even insults if someone defends and answers for a friend who wrongs him and charges him with (false) accusations. Do not be afraid of such troubles, for the voice of the righteous man says: "And if evil befall me from him, I will bear it for the sake of the friend" (see Sir 22:6).

In the time of hardship also the friend appears, for in the time of ease all seem to be friends. And just as patience and endurance are required in the time of trial, so in the time of ease the strong influence (of friends) is required to examine and refute the arrogance of the domineering friend [24].
St. Ambrose Who will set a guard over my mouth, and the seal of prudence upon my lips, that I may not fall because of them, and my tongue not destroy me?
v It does not befit a person to open his mouth for what is unseemly, but to open it for speech that bestows treasures of God's goods.

Fr. Anthimus of Jerusalem v Let us keep in mind, concerning the mouth and the tongue, that we offer our prayer while keeping them free from evil. If you have a vessel of gold or made of precious metal, you do not choose it to use for a shameful matter; how much more those whose mouths are more precious than gold and pearls, how can they defile them with shameful ugliness and corruption and mockery. You do not offer incense on an altar of bronze or even of gold, but what is more precious than this in a spiritual temple, for the material of the former is lifeless, while God makes His dwelling in you, you who are members of the body of Christ... Let us guard our mouths always; let us set a mind over them to close them, so that they are not kept closed continually, but it opens them at the proper time.

There is a time when silence is more precious than speech, and there is also a time when speech is more precious than silence... It is necessary, as you see, not only that we keep silence and speech at the proper time, but that it be with great love. For this reason Paul also says: "Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man" (Col 4:6).

Bear in mind that this is the member with which you enter into converse with God, and with which we offer the praise. This is the member with which we receive the awesome Sacrifice, for the faithful know what I am saying [25].
St. John Chrysostom Inspired by Sirach 22

entries.section: O Holy One, sanctify my children and my friends!

paragraphs.text: v Your descent to our earth has turned my heart into a sanctuary for You, from which You establish a temple in which Your Holy Spirit dwells.
You removed the dust from it, and springs of living water burst forth within me!
My heart has been kindled with the fire of Your love, so I see in the young my children, and in the old friends and beloved ones.
How my depths long that the whole new generation (the children) be sanctified, and with it the present generation (the friends).
v I confess to You my laziness and slackness, for I caused my children to stumble.
Remove the stumbling block from them, and instead of laziness let them work by You, O Almighty.
For their sake You did not cease working for their salvation.
You loved them and were crucified for them, and here You are preparing for them glorious mansions in Your heavens.
Fill them with the spirit of wisdom, that they may walk in purity and chastity and love and longsuffering.
They will become a living icon of You, so that the heavenly ones marvel at Your work in them.
v Shine the light of Your knowledge in their hearts, that they may reject folly and ignorance.
They will accept from You rebuke and discipline for their edification on a heavenly level.
Glory to You, who stretched out Your hands on the Cross; here You embrace all generations.
v And what shall I say of my brothers? They are my friends and my beloved.
Burst forth in their hearts springs of spiritual water, that will turn their dust into holy, fruitful spiritual gardens.
v Sanctify my tongue and theirs, that they may become instruments of righteousness bearing witness to Your salvation.
Instead of idle chatter and harsh words and the disclosing of others' secrets, grant me and them the holy tongue, the sweet words, and the constant smile.
We will not entrust the guard of our tongues, able to tame our mouths, to any but Your Holy Spirit.
How easy it is to tame wild beasts and teach birds, but the taming of our tongues is Your work alone!
v Grant us the spirit of trustworthiness and faithfulness, so that in the distress of our friends we find an opportunity to serve them with joy, to express by it our pure and sincere love for them.

entries.section: 1. A prayer for the sanctification of the senses and the enjoyment of wisdom

paragraphs.text: 1 O Lord, Father, Master of my life, do not abandon me to the counsel of my lips, and do not let me fall by them. 2 Who will set scourges over my thoughts and the discipline of wisdom over my heart, so that my follies are not spared and my sins are not overlooked? 3 Lest my follies be multiplied and my sins abound, and I fall before my adversaries and my enemy rejoice over me. 4 O Lord, Father, God of my life, do not abandon me to the counsel of my lips. 5 Do not let me lift my eyes in pride, and turn desire away from me. 6 Let not the desire of the belly nor fornication take possession of me, and do not give me over to an impudent soul.
O Lord, Father and Master of my life, do not abandon me to their counsel (my tongue and my lips), and do not let me fall because of them [1].
To whom do we pray? To the Lord, the Father and Master of my life; I have the boldness of sonship and the confidence that He gives me life instead of death.
And what do I ask? I entrust no one but the Father of my life to strike my thoughts with scourges!
I confess my sins, especially the sins of arrogance, evil desire and gluttony.

A person often feels that the commandments concerning the sanctification of the senses, the thought and the heart are higher than his spiritual stature; indeed it seems impossible for a person to fulfill these commandments while he has no authority over his senses, and indeed over his whole inner man. At the same time it befits us to realize God's love, for in the full freedom of our will we ask Him to sanctify our free will and to grant us longing together with zeal for holiness. No one is able to control his senses and sanctify them, therefore he must cry out to God, who alone is able to sanctify the lips and the thoughts and the mind and the eyes and all the desires, so that he does not fall before his adversaries, that is, the devil and his angels.
The prayer for wisdom in this chapter corresponds to a prayer of St. Ephrem the Syrian, which some Orthodox churches use in the Great Lent:

v My Lord and Leader of my life, take from me the spirit of laziness and faintheartedness, and the desire for power, and idle talk, but give to Your servant instead of these the spirit of purity, humility, patience and love.
Yes, O Lord and King, grant me to see my own faults, and not to judge my brothers.
For You are blessed from generation to generation. Amen.
St. Ephrem the Syrian Ben Sira mixes wise sayings with prayer: "O Lord, Father, Master of my life, do not abandon me to the counsel of my lips, and do not let me fall by them" [1].

a. Turning back from evil: "Return to the Lord and forsake your sins. Pray before His face, and lessen your offenses" (see 17:25). "Flee from sin as from a serpent, for if you come near it, it will bite you" (see Sir 2:21).

b. Honoring parents: "He who honors his father will be gladdened by his children, and in the day of his prayer he will be heard... For kindness to a father will not be forgotten, and will help in atoning for your sins" (see Sir 4:3, 14). Honor your father with all your heart, and do not forget the pains of your mother in childbirth. Remember that you were born of them, and what can you repay them for what they have done for you? (see Sir 7:27-28)
c. Preparing for the meeting with God: "Before offering a prayer prepare yourself, and do not be like a man who tempts the Lord" (Sir 18:23).
d. Serving as pleases the Lord: "He who serves the Lord according to His good pleasure will be accepted, and his prayer will reach to the clouds" (see Sir 35:16).

e. Meekness and humility: "The prayer of the humble pierces the clouds, and he is not comforted until it reaches the Lord" (see 35:17). "The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find favor before the Lord" (see Sir 18:3). "The wisdom of the humble lifts up his head, and seats him among the great" (see Sir 11:1).
f. Rising early for prayer: "He sets his heart to rise early to the Lord who made him" (see Sir 39:5).
g. Not repeating words in vain (Mt 6:7): "Do not repeat words in your prayer" (see Sir 7:14).
In his prayer Ben Sira asked the Lord, the Father and Leader of his life, to protect him from his tongue, and that the Lord would refine his mind and his heart and keep him from falling into error.
Ben Sira calls the Lord the Father and Master of my life; with the boldness of sonship he speaks with the Lord as a father to him, while He is his Master and Creator.

entries.section: 1. A prayer for the sanctification of the senses and the enjoyment of wisdom

paragraphs.text: Who will subject my thoughts to scourges, and my heart to the discipline of wisdom, so that it does not spare my faults, nor neglect me in my sins? [2]

He asked the "Father and Master" of his life to subject his thoughts and his heart to scourges, as though Ben Sira wished to present himself as an example before his disciples. For he is no better than they, since he has no authority over his thought and his heart, that is, over his inner man, but needs God, his Father and Teacher and Trainer and Refiner, to take hold of the scourge in order to straighten his inner depths. If the wise Sirach declares his need of scourges from the Lord to set him straight, how can any of his disciples think that he is able to avoid sins of thought and emotion by his own effort?!

v "Who will subject my thoughts to scourges, and my mind to the discipline of wisdom, so that he does not spare my faults, nor overlook my sins? [2] Note in particular: "Who will subject my thoughts to scourges?" So there are scourges which scourge thoughts. They are the scourges of God, for the Word (the Logos), when He leads the soul to realize how it has sinned, scourges it. He scourges the blessed man who suffers from the scourgings, because the words (of rebuke) touch him and he does not complain against the one who rebukes him. But there are some without feeling, of whom it is said: "You have scourged them, but they did not grieve" (Jer 5:3) [1].

v Let us see what was said about sinners: "I scourged them (with whips), yet they felt no pain" (Jer 5:3). Earthly whips, when we strike living bodies with them, cause pain to those who are struck, whether they wish it or not. But the scourges of God are not so, for some of those struck feel pain and others do not... The wretched are those who do not feel pain from the blows of God, and the happy are those who feel pain from these blows.

The Book of Wisdom says in this matter: "They were only pricked that they might remember Your words, and then were quickly saved, lest they fall into deep forgetfulness and be deprived of Your kindness." As it was said: "Who will set a whip over my thoughts, and the words of the wise upon my lips, lest they be lenient with me in my faults, and I perish because of my sins" (see Sir 23:2).

Look carefully at these words: "Who will set a whip over my thoughts?" So there are whips for striking thoughts. It is God's scourges that strike thoughts, for the Word "Logos", when He takes the soul aside and pushes it and presses upon it until its conscience is awakened to the faults it has committed, scourges it.

So He strikes the blessed (wise) man, who feels pain under the blow, because the words of God have affected his soul, and he did not cast these words aside with contempt because they shamed him. But there is a man of whom it can be said that he is without feeling; of him it is said: "I struck them, yet they did not grieve" [2].

entries.section: 1. A prayer for the sanctification of the senses and the enjoyment of wisdom

paragraphs.text: Origen Lest my faults be multiplied and my sins increase, and I fall before my adversaries, and my enemy rejoice over me [3].

The scholar Origen distinguishes between the whips of the world and the scourges of God. The first are material whips that fall upon living bodies, and everyone feels their pain. But God's scourges, which are for discipline, are of another kind; they fall upon the thought, and some receive them and feel them and offer repentance and return to God, and become blessed. Others do not feel their pains and do not respond to God's call to return to Him; these are struck and do not feel pain (Jer 5:3).

v It is said of sinners: "I struck them, yet they did not grieve" (5:3). The perceptible whips of this world fall upon living bodies, whether those who are beaten accept them or refuse them, and they are painful (to all). But God's scourges are of a kind that causes pain to some, while others do not suffer from them.

Let us explain what it means not to suffer from them. Why do these people of evil natures not suffer from God's scourges, while those who feel pain from them are blessed? Wisdom says: "Who will subject my thoughts to scourges, and set the seal of prudence upon my lips, so that he does not spare my faults, and my faults do not lead me to destruction."

Let us pay attention to the words: "Who will subject my thoughts to scourges." So there are scourges that are particular to striking thoughts. They are God's scourges that strike the thought, where the Word is joined to the soul and leads it to the knowledge of its sins. He strikes the blessed soul, and it suffers, for the Word comes and pierces the soul in its depths... But of him who is dulled with regard to the blow it is said: "I struck them, yet they did not grieve" [3].

entries.section: 1. A prayer for the sanctification of the senses and the enjoyment of wisdom

paragraphs.text: Origen O Lord, Father and God of my life, do not give me haughty eyes [4].
He asked Him to remove from him his haughty eyes, that is, looking to high matters that are above his spiritual stature.

entries.section: 1. A prayer for the sanctification of the senses and the enjoyment of wisdom

paragraphs.text: But turn away evil desire from me [5]

He asked the Lord not to allow the desire of gluttony or fornication to possess him, and not to give him over to an impudent soul (Sir 23:1, 4-6, 13, 15). This prayer describes the character of the wise man. It is prayer in faith, that the believer may be formed in the image of Wisdom herself.

entries.section: 1. A prayer for the sanctification of the senses and the enjoyment of wisdom

paragraphs.text: Do not allow gluttony or desires to rule over me, and do not give me over to an impudent soul [6].

St. Augustine sees that many of these requests appeared among the divine commandments. Here St. Augustine asks why Sirach offers these requests when he knows that they agree with the will of God and His commandments. He answers that it befits the believer to declare his personal desire, affirming that his will is that the will of God be done in him. As though he were saying: "Thy will be done" (Mt 6:10) [4].

In St. Augustine's discourse[5] on grace and free will, he says that the followers of Pelagius think they know something important when they affirm that God commands nothing that He knows human beings are unable to practice. He comments saying: "Who does not know this?" and continues: But God gives commandments beyond our abilities, in order that we may know that we must ask Him, and He will give us the power to carry them out. So in faith we pray that we may fulfill the commandments. The saint presented many of the requests that the wise man (Ben Sira) asks, so that by grace we may practice what is beyond our strength.

St. Augustine sees that all the prayers in the Old Testament do not go beyond the Gospel prayer which our Lord Jesus taught us, and he gave many examples, among them some requests found in the Book of Sirach. The prayer found here: "Let not the desire of the belly nor fornication take possession of me" (see Sir 23:6) is nothing other than "Lead us not into temptation", and the request found in (Sir 36:4), which he translates "May You be sanctified among all men as You are sanctified among us", is nothing other than the request: "Hallowed be thy name" [6]

7 O children, take hold of the discipline of the mouth; for he who keeps it is not caught by his lips. 8 For by them the sinner is trapped, and by them the slanderer and the proud stumble. 9 Do not accustom your mouth to swearing, 10 and do not become familiar with naming the Holy One. 11 For as a servant who is continually examined does not lack bruises, so he who continually swears and names is not purified. 12 A man who swears much is filled with iniquity, and the scourge does not depart from his house. 13 If he does not fulfill it, his sin is upon him, and if he treats it lightly, his sin is doubled. 14 And if he swears falsely he is not justified, and his house is filled with calamities. 15 There is also a manner of speech that is clothed with death. May it not be found in the inheritance of Jacob. 16 All these things are far from the godly; they do not wallow in sins. 17 Do not accustom your mouth to coarse speech, for that is not without sin. 18 Remember your father and your mother when you sit among the great, 19 lest you forget them before them, and the habit of associating with them make you foolish; then you would wish you had not been born of them, and curse the day of your birth. 20 He who is accustomed to words of abuse will not be disciplined all his days.
He concentrates on the faults of the tongue, and often enumerates them, as we have seen.
O my children, listen to the teaching of my mouth, for he who keeps it will not be defeated [7].

If Sirach asks for himself scourgings issuing from the hand of his Father, who is tender toward him and all-wise, in order that he may control his thoughts and his heart and his tongue, this tongue, which can destroy its owner and those around him, if it is sanctified, offers teaching according to the divine mind. Therefore he says to his disciples: "O my children, listen to the teaching of my mouth" [7]

Again he says: "There is a manner of speech that resembles death" [12]. For the tongue can be an instrument of righteousness for the sake of the Kingdom of God, bearing witness to the teaching of the Lord, or an instrument of iniquity that drives others to eternal death.
The sinner is trapped by his lips, and by them the abusive, proud man stumbles [8].
We are in need of a divine guard that keeps our lips from falling into sin.
v Moses taught you by the blood of the lamb which he sprinkled on the doors; it befits you to moisten your lips with the blood of the Son every day.
For the mouth is the door of man, which sends forth both praises and words, glory and abuse, of every kind.
David asked that a guard be set over him. Who is this one who stands as guard when he is asked, if not the Crucified?
David asked, saying: "Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth" (Ps 141:3). It is the Cross that guards the door of the mouth from Satan.
The Cross stood at the doors of the children of the people, and kept them from the slayer of the firstborn on the earth.
You too now, take the blood of the Son of God, and with your fingers trace the sign of the Cross upon your lips.
Make it a guard for your mouth, and be confident of its sure effectiveness, and then when the destroyer sees it he will not come near you.
If its symbol was able to stand at the door and guard them, how much more can He Himself guard the one who seeks Him?
Receive the blood from the divine cup upon your lips, and it will prove to you that it is a trustworthy guard of the door.
The doors of the people were sealed with the blood of the lamb, so seal your door with the blood of the side of the Son of God.
Dye your tongue and your lips and your mind with the blood of your Lord, and He will guard you from harm.
Seek every day this guard for your mouth and your lips; win him with tears, and he will keep you without sleeping.
The blood of the slain Christ is sprinkled upon the mouths of the people; Moses saw this and pictured it in the blood of the lamb [7].
St. Jacob of Serugh Do not accustom your mouth to vows, and do not become familiar with pronouncing the name of the Holy One [9].
For just as the servant who is continually beaten is not without bruises, so he who vows and pronounces the name of the Holy One continually is not cleansed from sin [10].

v "Do not accustom your mouth to swearing, nor let it become familiar with uttering the name of the Holy One" (see Sir 23:9). Why? "For as the servant who is still being beaten does not lack the marks of the blows, so he who swears" (see Sir 23:10).

See the discernment of this wise man. He did not say: "Do not accustom your mind but your mouth", because since this is entirely the work of the mouth, its remedy is easy. For this becomes a habit without intention, as for example there are many who enter the public baths merely by passing by their borders and crossing over them [8].

v It is impossible, entirely impossible, for a mouth that practices oath-taking not to commit false swearing. Therefore I ask all of you to abandon this deadly evil habit, so that you may receive another crown [9].
St. John Chrysostom The man who swears much is filled with iniquity, and calamity does not depart from his house.
If he sins, his sin is upon him. And if he treats the matter lightly, his sin is doubled.
And if he swears falsely he is not justified, and his house is filled with afflictions [11].

In the Old Testament a person was required to swear with dignity and truthfulness to bear witness to his faith in God, in contrast to the pagans who swear falsely by their gods (the idols). So the tongue that pronounces the name of the holy God, if it practices oath-taking often and without wisdom, swears falsely and its oath is counted as iniquity.

He warns us against haste in swearing by the name of the Holy One, lest it become a habit, and a person use it without wisdom and not be cleansed from sin. This habit drives a person to commit a doubled sin [11]: haste in swearing without prudence, and inability to fulfill what he swore to do (Lev 5:4; Num 30:2). Through this haste a person is exposed to blasphemy, whose penalty is death (Lev 24:15-16; Jn 10:33). It befits a person not to accustom himself to haste, not only in swearing by the name of the Holy One but even in the council of great men, lest he behave foolishly and be exposed to troubles, and wish he had not been born, and curse the day of his birth [14] (Job 3:3; Jer 20:14).

In the New Testament, as we have entered into spiritual maturity, the Lord commands us not to swear at all, but let our speech be yes, yes, and no, no. St. John Chrysostom explains this by saying that swearing is like the wind to the ship of anger; without it the ship cannot sail in a person's life. He says: [Lay down a law for a man who is very passionate never to swear, and there will be no need to teach him composure[10].] St. John Chrysostom considers not swearing to be the distinguishing mark of the Christian and his own language: [Let us receive this as a seal from heaven, so that we may be seen everywhere to be the flock of the King. Let us be known who we are by our mouth and our language][11].

v It befits a person never to swear, for it is written: "A man who swears much is filled with iniquity, and the scourge does not depart from his house" (see Sir 23:11). What was said about the scourge that does not leave his house is not to be understood of his earthly house, but of his soul (his soul), which is the temple of God [12].
Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles There is a manner of speech that resembles death. Would that it not be found in the inheritance of Jacob!
For the godly keep away from all these faults, and do not become entangled in sins [12].

Perhaps he means here speech of blasphemy against God, which deserves death and deprivation from the inheritance of Jacob, that is, from the Kingdom. He also means violent criticism that hurts feelings and spoils relationships, and may often develop into something worse than wounding feelings. It does not befit such a person to belong to the eternal inheritance.
Do not accustom your mouth to speak in indecent expressions, for this is sinful speech [13].

Our teacher James the Apostle calls us to control our mouths and our tongues, likening this to putting bridles in the mouths of horses that they may obey us, and we turn about their whole body (Jas 3:3). He also likens the tongue to the small rudder of the ship that moves the whole ship (Jas 3:4-6). He praises him who controls his tongue, saying: "If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body" (Jas 3:2).
Remember your father and your mother when you sit in the council of the great, lest you forget yourself before them, and by habit behave like a fool.
Then you would wish you had not been born, and curse the day of your birth [14].
v Hate greatness, for it is the fruit full of death.
For Adam ate of it in Eden, and it gave him death.
And by it Satan fell from the beginning. And by it the house of Adam fell from Paradise.
There is nothing with God so vile and hateful as the love of greatness and the haughtiness of pride.
St. Jacob of Serugh He who is accustomed to abusive words will not be disciplined all the days of his life [15].

Some think that abuse is to utter improper words against someone, but St. Basil sees that every word, even if it is not evil in itself, which distorts the image of others, directly or by implication, is abuse. St. Basil also warns us against insulting a person even with a general expression and with the intention of joking.
v Question: What is the abusive person?

Answer: Every word uttered with the intention of distorting the image of a person, even if the word itself does not seem to be abuse. This is clear from what the Gospel says of the Jews: "Then they reviled him, and said, Thou art his disciple" (Jn 9:28) [13].
v Question: What is the word "Raca" (Mt 5:22)?
Answer: It is a colloquial word of that nation for a slight, common insult, said by persons known to him without cost [14].
St. Basil the Great

21 There are two sorts of people who multiply sins, and a third sort that brings wrath. 22 The soul that burns like a blazing fire is not quenched until it is consumed. 23 And the man who commits fornication with the uncleanness of his flesh does not cease until he kindles the fire. 24 For to the fornicating man all bread is sweet; he does not tire until he is finished. 25 And the man who transgresses against his bed, saying in himself: "Who sees me? 26 Darkness is around me and the walls conceal me, and no one sees me; so what shall I fear? The Most High will not remember my sins." 27 He fears only the eyes of men, 28 and does not know that the eyes of the Lord are ten thousand times brighter than the sun; they see all the ways of men, and look into hidden places. 29 He knows all things before they are created; so also after they are finished. 30 So this man will be punished in the streets of the city, and where he does not expect, he will be seized, 31 and will be put to shame before all, because he did not understand the fear of the Lord. 32 So also the woman who leaves her husband and provides an heir for him from a stranger. 33 For first she disobeyed the law of the Most High, and second she betrayed her husband, and third she was defiled by adultery, and raised up offspring from a strange man. 34 This woman will be brought to the congregation, and the condition of her children will be examined. 35 Her children will not take root, and her branches will not bear fruit. 36 She will leave behind a cursed memory, and her disgrace will not be blotted out. 37 Then those who are left will know that there is nothing better than the fear of the Lord, and nothing sweeter than heeding the commandments of the Lord. 38 To follow God is great glory, and in being received by Him are length of days.
The gravest things about adultery are three:
a. Adultery is a blazing fire, which is not quenched except by the complete destruction of the person.
b. Despite the things about adultery from which the soul recoils, its pleasure lasts only minutes, offering sweetness to what is corrupt.

c. He who opens the door to adultery through negligence gives adultery a right of ownership over the heart and the mind and the emotions, and it clings to them, and the more negligent the person becomes, the harder it is to drive adultery out than it was. He who is negligent with desires and thoughts has his depths inflamed with a fire that is difficult to put out, and it remains aflame until the fire consumes him.

It seems that Ben Sira distinguishes three kinds of sins of men: 1. Adultery with an unmarried girl; the fire of this passion destroys a person (1 Cor 7:9). 2. Sexual relations between relatives, which the Law of Moses forbids marrying (Lev 18:6). This sin kindles the fire of divine wrath (Num 11:1). 3. Adultery with a married woman (9:9) is like one who eats bread that is pleasing to the soul (Prov 9:17; 30:20), and leads to death.
The one who commits adultery thinks that no one sees him, but God knows all the conduct of men (17:19-20), even if it seems hidden from everyone (Prov 5:21).

By meditating on the fate of the godly and the wicked, the believer is convinced that there is nothing better than life in the fear of the Lord and keeping His commandments (Eccl 12:13; Deut 10:12-13).

"The man who commits fornication with his body does not cease from this evil of his until the fire consumes him. To the fornicating man all food is sweet, and he does not rest until he dies. He who breaks his marriage vows, saying in himself: Who sees me? Darkness is around me, and the walls hide me. And no one sees me; so what shall I fear? The Most High will not notice my sins. He fears the eyes of men, and does not know that the eyes of the Lord are ten thousand times brighter than the sun; they see all the ways of men, and penetrate into hidden ways" (see 23:16-19). "Do not gaze at the beauty of any man... for from garments comes the moth" (see 42:12-13).
There are two sorts of people who multiply sins, and a third sort that brings wrath [16].

The danger of not controlling the tongue, and also of falling into desires, appears in that both strike the whole society, because the relationships among the members of society are often based on dealing by the tongue, and on sex as the biological basis of marriage and the formation of the family, which is the pillar of society and the chief element in establishing the community.

Corruption of speech destroys trust among people, and corruption of sex destroys the family order on which all humanity rests and which gives it unity. If there is no control of sex, there is no control of the tongue either. Adultery is not only a sin against purity but also against justice, for adultery is a violation of the human covenant. When a person commits adultery he does not offend only against his family but also against society. The chief remedy for these sins is the enjoyment of the fear of the Lord.
The soul that burns like a blazing fire is not quenched until it is consumed.
And he who gives over his whole body to fornication does not stop until the fire burns him.
To the fornicating man all food is sweet, and he does not stop until he dies [17].

v Let us provide wives (for our sons) at an early age, so that the brides may receive their bodies pure and undefiled, and their love may be more ardent. He who is pure before marriage is all the more pure after marriage; and he who practices fornication before marriage practices it after. "To the fornicating man all food is sweet" (see Sir 23:17).

Crowns are usually placed on the heads of bridegrooms as a symbol of victory, indicating that they approach the marriage bed not defeated by pleasure. But if he is a captive of pleasure and has given himself to a harlot, why does he wear the crown while defeated?![15]

v It is a passion that has no limits. Again, those who take pleasure in fornication cannot cease from it. It is said: "To the fornicating man all food is sweet" (see Sir 23:17). He does not stop until he is devoured. For it is a passion![16]

St. John Chrysostom v He who thinks that he hides his crime is lost through an empty hope, for this is a false saying and there is no truth in it. And the false speech that sinners utter is hateful (see Sir 27:13). It produces not fruit but a burden. For the talk of the fool is like a load on the road (see Sir 21:17). And what is sin but a heavy load? It is heavy, carried by the fugitive in this life, where he is greatly weighed down by the heavy load of his crime. If he does not wish to fall under the burden, he must give heed to the Lord who says: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mt 11:28) [17].
St. Ambrose The man who transgresses against his marriage bed, saying in himself: "Who sees me?
Darkness is around me, and the walls of my house hide me. And no one sees me; so what shall I fear? The Most High will not remember my sins" [18].

v Let us always walk honestly, as in the day (Rom 13:12), and renounce the works of darkness. We know that the night has been appointed for the rest of the body, not for work and activities, therefore we spend the night in sleep in comfortable forgetfulness, and we do not spend it in feasting and drunkenness and revelry and immodesty. It befits us not to say: The darkness and the walls hide us, for the Most High observes us and sees us. Instead of this let us love the light and walking in the sunlight, and desire that our works be radiant in the presence of God [18].

v Every person who avoids the light loves the darkness, seeking to hide, although he cannot hide from God, who knows not only what actually happens, but even what is thought, whether in the depths of a place or in the minds of men. So the Book of Jesus son of Sirach also says: "Who sees me? Darkness is around me, and the walls conceal me. And no one sees me; so what shall I fear?" (see Sir 23:18) [19].

St. Ambrose v He who seeks mere sexual pleasure turns his marriage into adultery. He forgets the words of the Teacher: "The man who breaks his marriage vows, saying in himself: Who sees me? Darkness is around me, and the walls hide me. And no one sees me; so what shall I fear? The Most High will not notice my sins" (see Sir 23:18). Such a man is utterly wretched, for he fears only the eyes of men, and thinks that he is hidden from God. "He does not know what the Scripture tells him: that the eye of the Lord is brighter than the sun... they see all the ways of men, and penetrate into hidden ways" (see Sir 23:19). At another time the Teacher warns us through Isaiah: "Woe to you who make your counsel in secret, and say: Who sees us?" (Isa 29:15) LXX.

The light that the senses can see may pass and we do not notice it, but that which enlightens the mind cannot be ignored... May we not allow ourselves to be swallowed up by darkness by any means, for the light dwells in us, and the darkness cannot overcome it (see Jn 1:5). The night is turned to day by pure prudence.

Holy Scripture calls for a day by pure prudence. Holy Scripture calls the mind of the good man a lamp that cannot be put out (Wis 7:10). In fact, the very attempt to cover over what a person does is a sign that the person realizes he is committing a sin [20].

St. Clement of Alexandria The eyes of men are his fear, and he does not know that the eyes of the Lord are ten thousand times more radiant than the sun; they see all the ways of men, and observe even the hidden places [19].
v Such a person is utterly wretched, for he fears only that people will notice him, and thinks that he is hidden from God [21].

St. Clement of Alexandria In a letter that St. Ambrose sent to St. Irenaeus he affirmed that those who think that God does not see them because they practice evil in the darkness, and that the depths cover them, their hope is in vain, for God sees the hidden depths that cannot be fathomed; everything is exposed before Him before it happens.
He also made clear that the prophet Elijah chose to dwell in the mountains, and his disciple Elisha used to dwell in the upper room.

v Elijah and Elisha did not live in dwellings below the surface of the earth. One of them carried the dead son of the widow to the upper room where he was dwelling, and there he restored him to life (2 Kgs 17:22). The other had a chamber prepared for him in the upper room by the great Shunammite woman, as the Scripture testifies... What shall I say of Peter, who went up to the housetop at the sixth hour and learned the mystery of the baptism of the Gentiles (Acts 10:9)? On the other hand the criminal Absalom set up for himself a pillar in the king's valley, and he was thrown into a pit when he was killed (2 Kgs 18:7).

Thus the saints go up to the Lord, and the wicked go down into sin. The saints are on the mountains, and the criminals are in the valleys, for He is the God of the mountains and not the God of the valleys (1 Kgs 20:28) [22].

v Let us walk honestly, as in the day, and leave the works of darkness (Rom 13:12-13). We know that the night passes in sleep and forgetfulness so that the body may find rest. The night was not appointed for the practice of any work or any dealings. Let us not take part in parties and drunkenness... Let us not say: "The darkness and the walls cover us; who knows whether the Most High sees us" (see Sir 23:19). Let there be in us a love of the light and our appreciation of goodness, so that we may be like one who walks in the day, desiring that our works shine in the presence of God [23].
St. Ambrose He knows all things before the world was created, and the end of all things is also known to Him [20].
This adulterer will be punished in the streets of the city, and where he does not expect, he will be seized [21].
So also is the woman who leaves her husband and provides an heir for him from a stranger [22].
As for the adultery of the woman [22-27], her sin is three-sided:
a. Breaking the law of God (Deut 5:18; Ex 20:14).
b. Sinning against her husband.
c. Bearing children who are not from her husband.

According to the Mosaic Law the woman is stoned to death (Deut 22:22; Additions to Dan 13:36-41), and deprives herself of practicing motherhood and enjoying her grandchildren (Wis 3:16-19; 4:3-6). Instead of being honored after her death, her memory becomes a disgrace (Sir 41:5-9).
For first she disobeyed the law of the Most High, and second she sinned against her husband, and third she was defiled by adultery, and bore children by a strange man [23].
This woman will be brought to the council, and an investigation will be made into the matter of her children [24].
Her children will have no roots, and her branches will not bring forth fruit [25].
She will leave behind a cursed memory, and her disgrace will not be blotted out [26].
Then those who remain after her will know that there is nothing better than the fear of the Lord, and nothing sweeter than care for the commandments of the Lord [27].

v O you who love teaching and long to listen, receive once more the holy words, and delight yourselves with the honey of wisdom, for it is written: "Good words are a honeycomb, and their sweetness is the healing of the soul" (Prov 16:24) LXX. The work of the bee is very sweet and benefits the soul of man in many ways, but the divine, saving honey makes those in whom it settles skilled in every good work, and teaches them the ways of spiritual progress [24].

St. Cyril the Great v Do you love pleasure and delights? Look to the commandments of the Lord, for to the sound soul they are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb![25] It is the charm of the truth which the psalmist expressed, affirming it when he said: "How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" The yoke of Christ is sweet, and its burden light in refreshing those who submit to it, but everything foreign to the teaching of the Gospel is heavy and wearisome (Mt 11:28-30) [26].
v Question: How can one who has become slack in the commandment regain his zeal and watchfulness?

Answer: By being convinced of the presence of the Lord God, who watches over all things everywhere, and by setting before his eyes the threat against the slack, and the hope of a great reward from God, who promised it through Paul the Apostle, saying: "Every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour" (1 Cor 3:8), and similar expressions which encourage zeal and patience in everyone for the glory of God [27].
v Question: How can a person fulfill the commandments of the Lord by an inner impulse and with zeal?

Answer: By nature, through the experience of what is sweet and beneficial, and the expectation of anything of this kind, an impulse and a longing for it is born in the soul. Therefore if one hates iniquity and abhors it (Ps 119:163), and is cleansed from every sin, then just as when the body loses appetite and the pleasure of food because of illness, so through the sickness of sin the soul suffers from dullness and aversion to the righteous judgments of God. And if one is fully convinced that God's commandment is eternal life (Jn 12:50), and that all the promises for those who keep them are true, then by this the impulse works in him, for it is said: "The judgments of the Lord are true and righteous altogether. More to be desired are they than gold and very precious stones, sweeter also than honey and the dripping of the honeycomb. Moreover by them is thy servant warned, and in keeping of them there is great reward" (Ps 19:10-12) [28].
St. Basil the Great Inspired by Sirach 23

entries.section: Have mercy on me, my Father, from my own counsel!

paragraphs.text: v To You I complain of myself, O Lord, Father and Master of my life.
Let Your will be done in my life, and let my negligent counsel be crucified.
Who can discipline my negligent thoughts and scourge them with whips but You?
I entrust no one to scourge my thoughts but You.
For You are a compassionate heavenly Father, almighty and knowing all my depths!
With Your firm scourges, full of love, shatter the arrogance of my haughty eyes.
To You alone belongs the authority to uproot my evil desires and gluttony, and all corruption, from their roots.
v Support me and set a strict guard to keep my tongue.
Do not allow a word of abuse or arrogance or haste in vows to issue from my mouth.
Do not allow my defiled mouth to be negligent and swear by Your name, O You who alone are Holy!
Words of blasphemy attack my mouth to occupy it, so that death may come upon me.
As a son of Yours, do not allow cheap, unseemly words to issue from my mouth!
v Extinguish the fires of desires lest they burn me and destroy me completely.
All souls, however corrupt, realize that desires are bad; their pleasure may last for minutes and the soul recoils from them.
But when they take hold of a person's heart and mind, they strike their roots into his depths, and reckon that they have established their kingdom in him...
Who can drive them from the seat of their throne?!
You alone, O Holy One, shine forth with Your righteousness, and the darkness of desires is dispelled!

1 Wisdom praises herself, and glories among her people. 2 She opens her mouth in the congregation of the Most High, and glories before His hosts, 3 and is exalted among her people, and glorified in the assembly of the saints, 4 and is praised in the multitude of the chosen, and blessed among the blessed, and says: 5 "I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature, 6 and I made the light shine in the heavens forever, and covered all the earth like a mist, 7 and I dwelt in the heights, and set my throne in the pillar of cloud. 8 I alone went round the circle of heaven, and walked in the depth of the deeps, and walked upon the waves of the sea, 9 and my foot trod all the earth, and over every people, 10 and every nation I held sway, 11 and by my power I trod upon the hearts of the great and the small. In all these I sought rest, and in what inheritance should I abide." 12 Then the Creator of all commanded me, and he who possessed me appointed the place of my dwelling, 13 and said: "Dwell in Jacob, and inherit in Israel." 14 Before the age, from the beginning, he possessed me, and to the age I shall not cease, and I ministered before him in the holy tabernacle. 15 And so in Zion I was established, and he gave me a dwelling in the beloved city, and my dominion is in Jerusalem. 16 So I took root in a glorious people, in the portion of the Lord, the portion of His inheritance, and in the assembly of the saints is my abode. 17 I was exalted like the cedar in Lebanon, and like the cypress on the mountains of Hermon. 18 Like the palm tree on the shores, and like rose plants in Jericho. 19 Like the fair olive tree in the plain, and like the plane tree by the water courses in the streets. 20 My fragrance spread like cinnamon and sweet-smelling calamus, and my scent was diffused like choice myrrh. 21 Like galbanum and onycha and stacte, and like the incense of frankincense in the tabernacle. 22 I stretched out my branches like the terebinth, and my branches are branches of glory and grace. 23 I am like the vine that brings forth grace, and my blossoms are fruits of glory and wealth. 24 I am the mother of fair love, and of fear and knowledge and holy hope. 25 In me is all the grace of the way and the truth, and all the hope of life and virtue. 26 Come to me, you who desire me, and be filled with my fruits. 27 For my spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance more delicious than the honeycomb, 28 and my memorial endures to generations of ages. 29 He who eats me will come back to me hungry, and he who drinks me will come back thirsty. 30 He who listens to me will not be put to shame, and he who acts by my guidance will not sin. 31 He who explains me will have eternal life.
Wisdom will praise herself, and glory among her people [1].
She opens her mouth in the congregation of the Most High, and glories before His might [2].
What does the wisdom of God say?

a. In calling believers to acquire her, she praises herself and glories among her people, not because she is in need of praise or outward glory, whether from the sons of men or from the heavenly orders, but because she offers what is hers to the believers. As though she were saying to them: What is mine I give to you. For he who finds me bears witness to the glory he receives by being united with me.

b. If the heavenly ones glorify me, I desire to lift up my people, in whom I take pride, that they may be joined to the congregation of the Most High, so that their thoughts and their hearts are lifted up to heavenly things.

c. If the dwelling of Wisdom is in the heights and her throne is in the pillar of cloud, yet she is not far from all rational creation. For if man has descended to the depths of the abyss (the deeps) because of his disobedience and his deprivation of the source of his life, I am not far wherever I may be found, whether on earth or in the seas or in the abyss; I save him and depart with him to my dwelling in the heights, and join him to the congregation of the Most High. Without partiality I work in the life of the believer, whatever his nationality; I have authority over every people and nation.
d. How does Wisdom seek rest? When the beloved rational creature rests in the wisdom of God, she counts every rest of the creature as her own rest, wherever this creature is found.

e. Although the wisdom of God fills the whole world, in heaven and on earth, yet she is concerned for the people of God, and so she pitches her tent in Jacob, and her inheritance in Israel [8]. As though the people of God were her house and her inheritance. This is the condition of every true believer, who sings: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine" (Song 6:3). The Lord Christ, the wisdom of God and the power of God, assures us: "The kingdom of God is within you" (Lk 17:21).
f. The plan of the wisdom of God for our eternal salvation extends to before the creation, and her work continues forever [9].

g. The authority of the wisdom of God over all peoples and nations [6], she counts herself working on behalf of him who receives her and responds to her, and she counts him her beloved city and her holy temple, her portion and her inheritance, and she is his portion and his inheritance [10-12]. She asks to settle in the believing person, and that he settle in her.
I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, and covered the earth like a mist [3].

She refers here to the birth of the Son, begotten of the Father from eternity. St. Ambrose sees that God the Word proceeded from the Father, He who is in the bosom of the Father (Jn 1:18). And that the bosom here means a kind of dwelling wholly deep in the love of the Father and in His nature (not separated from Him), for He dwells in Him always. And He is begotten in His heart, where He uttered the Word, and here He proceeds from the mouth of the Most High, where divine justice (righteousness) proceeds, and from Him wisdom proceeds, and says: "I came forth from the mouth of the Most High" (see Sir 24:3) [1].

v It was said that Wisdom came forth from the mouth of the Most High (see Sir 24:3), not outside the Father, but she is with the Father, for "the Word was with God" (Jn 1:1). Not only "with God", but also in God, for He says: "I am in the Father, and the Father in me" (Jn 14:10). And when He comes forth from the Father He does not come forth from a (particular) place, nor is He separated from Him, as one body is separated from another [2].

v It does not appear that the Son came forth from any place, but God from God, the Son from the Father, and He has no beginning in the course of time, but came forth from the Father as one begotten, just as the Begotten One Himself said: "I came forth from the mouth of the Most High" (see Sir 24:3) [3].

v It is part of the work of His authority that He made us children of God (Jn 1:10 etc.), while the teachings of God reveal to us His begetting with regard to the hypostatic characteristic, for the wisdom of God says: "I came forth from the mouth of the Most High" (see Sir 24:3), meaning not out of compulsion but in complete freedom, not under the bond of authority, but He was begotten with a mysterious begetting, by the hypostatic power of the Supreme Being and the righteousness of authority. Again, of this same Wisdom, who is the Lord Jesus, the Father says elsewhere: "From the womb I begot You before the morning star" (Ps 110:3). He says this not that we should think of a bodily womb, but to show that it is a true begetting, a fitting act [4].
St. Ambrose And I pitched my tent in the heights, and my throne is in the pillar of cloud [4].

v Solomon (Sirach) shows Him to be the Word of God (who came forth from the mouth of the Most High), by whose hands these works of the world were made. He says: "I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn of all creatures. I made in heaven that which shines with a light that does not fade, and like a cloud I covered all the earth; I dwelt in the heights, and my throne is in the pillar of cloud" (see Sir 24:3-5). John says this: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made" (Jn 1:1-3) [5].
Fr. Lactantius I alone compassed the circuit of heaven, and walked in the depths of the abyss [5].

The one speaking here is the Wisdom of the Eternal One, one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, everlasting; by our union with Him we enjoy immortality. The Apostle Paul said of Him: "The blessed and only Potentate (the One with authority), the King of kings, and Lord of lords; who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto" (1 Tim 6:14-16).

St. Augustine distinguishes between the human soul, of which it was said in the creation of Adam: "and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life" (Gen 2:7), and the coming forth of the Son or Wisdom from the mouth of God, for it did not say "the mouth of God breathed" but that He came forth from the mouth of God [6].

v It cannot be said that Wisdom comes forth from the mouth of the Most High (see Sir 24:5) so as to be outside the Father, but with the Father, because the Word is with God (Jn 1:1), not only with the Father but also in the Father. For He says: "I am in the Father, and the Father in me" (Jn 14:10). But when He came forth from the Father He did not withdraw as from a place, nor was He separated from Him as one body is separated from another. And being in the Father He is not counted as a body in a body [7].
St. Ambrose And over the waves of the sea and all the earth, and over every people and every nation I held sway [6].

Wisdom works in the life of the universal Church as her one holy people, as she works in the life of the believer as a member of this people. She directs her speech to the holy congregation as to each member of it.
In all these I sought a place of rest, and in what inheritance should I take refuge [7].
Then the Creator of all commanded me, and He who created me appointed a place for me to live, and said: "Pitch your tent in Jacob, and receive your inheritance in Israel" [8].
This passage came to announce the Incarnation of the Son, the wisdom of God, by saying: "appointed a place for me to live", "Pitch your tent in Jacob", "and receive your inheritance in Israel".

v Another prophet spoke of the Son in the same way: "This is our God, and there shall none other be accounted of in comparison of him" (Bar 3:36). Of whom does he say this? Did he say this of the Father? Of course not! Listen how well he points to the divine plan! For after saying: "This is our God, and there shall none other be accounted of in comparison of him", he added: "He hath found out all the way of knowledge, and hath given it unto Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved.
