Afterward did he shew himself upon earth, and conversed with men" (Bar 3:36-38) [8].
v Jeremiah was the first to say that God becomes man, remaining God. This is our God, and there shall none other be accounted of in comparison of him [9].
St. John Chrysostom Before the ages and from the beginning He created me, and to the age of ages I shall not cease [9].
In His holy tent before Him I ministered, and so I was established in Zion [10].
And He gave me rest in the beloved city, and my dominion is in Jerusalem [11].
So I took root in an honored people, in the portion of the Lord, His inheritance [12].

The people were counted glorious because they enjoyed the word of God and His divine promises; so when the believer embraces the word of God in his heart, and enjoys fellowship with Christ, the end of the Law (Rom 10:4), he enjoys the true treasure, for in Him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col 2:3).
Like the cedar tree in Lebanon I rose high, and like the cypress tree on the mountains of Hermon [13].
In offering what is hers to the believers, she establishes from them a holy garden that includes six kinds of trees with various flowers and fruits:
a. The great cedar of Lebanon (1 Kgs 6:9-11).
b. The cypress of the mountains of Hermon (2 Kgs 19:23). c. The palms of En-gedi (2 Chr 28:15).
d. The shrubs and roses of Jericho. e. The olive tree (Judg 9:8).
f. The plane tree, which rises beside the waters. g. Cinnamon and fragrant calamus (bamboo cane).
h. Choice myrrh with a fragrant scent. i. Galbanum (jalina) and onycha and stacte (mastic).
j. Frankincense as in the tent of meeting [15].
k. Her branches are like the branches of the terebinth, a source of turpentine oil and of tanning materials [16].
l. The vines [17].
Like the palm tree in En-gedi I rose, and like rose plants in Jericho, like the fair olive tree in the plain I rose, and like the plane tree beside the waters I rose [14].
Like cinnamon and fragrant calamus my fragrance spread, and like choice myrrh my scent was diffused, like galbanum and onycha and stacte, and like the perfume of frankincense in the tent [15].
I stretched out my branches like the terebinth, and my branches are glorious branches, full of grace [16].
I am like a vine that brings forth grace, and my blossoms bear fruits of glory and wealth [17].
I am the mother of pure love and fear, and knowledge, and holy hope.
Therefore, being eternal, I am given to all my children who were named through Him (that is, through the Lord) [18].
Come to me, you who desire me, and be filled with my fruits [19].
She calls her children to come to her with longing, and to be filled with her fruits and her harvest (Prov 9:4-6).
For my memorial is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance more delicious than the honeycomb [20].
She assures her children that when they draw near to her and enjoy her fruits, they experience her sweetness, which does not leave their memory, and they inherit what is sweeter than honey.
Those who eat me will hunger for more, and those who drink me will thirst for more [21].
He who eats of her and drinks increases in hunger and thirst for her with great longing. And at the same time he who hungers and thirsts for her enjoys satisfaction by her eternally.

v But you will not cease from love, for he whom you see is like one who confuses you, not with any kind of anxiety, but He satisfies you and also does not satisfy you at the same time. When I say that He satisfies you I fear that you will be like one who is full and wishes to depart, as from a meal or a supper. What then shall I say? That He does not satisfy you? Again I fear that it will seem that He does not satisfy you, and that you will seem like one in need, like one who is empty, and this emptiness needs to be filled. So what shall I say but what can be said, though it can hardly be thought? He satisfies you and does not satisfy you also, for I find both in the Holy Bible. While it says: "Blessed are the hungry, for they shall be filled" (Mt 5:6), again it says of Wisdom: "Those who drink thirst again" (see Sir 24:21). No, it did not say: "another time" but "still", because they thirst again, as they were like one who is satisfied once and departs and digests and then returns to drink [10].
St. Augustine Those who obey me will not be put to shame, and those who work with me will not sin [22].

entries.section: 2. A practical comment on the speech of Wisdom

paragraphs.text: 32 All these things are the book of life, and the covenant of the Most High and the knowledge of truth. 33 Moses commanded the Law, and the judgments of justice, the inheritance of the house of Jacob and the promises of Israel. 34 The Lord promised David His servant that He would raise up from him the mighty King who sits on the throne of glory forever. 35 He pours out wisdom like Phison, and like the Tigris in the days of the harvests, 36 and fills with understanding like the Euphrates, and like the Jordan in the days of harvest, 37 and makes discipline appear like the light, and like Geon in the days of the vintage. 38 The first did not complete the knowledge of Wisdom, nor will the last search her out, 39 for her thought is wider than the sea, and her counsel deeper than the great deep. 40 I, Wisdom, am the one who makes rivers overflow. 41 I am like a channel from the river, and like a conduit that went out into Paradise. 42 I said, I will water my garden, and irrigate my flower bed; 43 and behold, my channel has become a river, and my river has become a sea. 44 For I shine forth with discipline like the dawn and make it known to the ends of the earth. 45 I penetrate all the depths of the earth and look upon all who sleep, and I enlighten all who hope in the Lord. 46 I pour out teaching like prophecy, and leave it behind for the generations of ages. 47 See that my toil was not for myself alone, but also for all who seek wisdom.
All these things are the book of the covenant with the Most High God and the Law which Moses commanded us, an inheritance for the congregations of Jacob [23].
Wisdom binds them to the covenant with God and to keeping the Law as an inheritance for them [23].
Do not hesitate that you are strong in the Lord; cleave to Him, and He will establish you, for the Lord Almighty is God alone. And beside Him there is no other savior. [24]

This chapter is regarded as the center of the book. It rains surpassing blessings upon the souls of believers who seek wisdom. And lest anyone think that what Wisdom says does not concern him, because he is too weak to enjoy her, she encourages him, saying: "Do not hesitate that you are strong in the Lord; cleave to Him, and He will establish you" [24]. For He alone is the mighty Savior. Man himself cannot save himself, nor can his brothers save him.

v "He cannot give to God an atonement for himself, or the price of the ransom of his soul (even if he toiled forever)" (Ps 48:7-8) LXX. So do not ask your brother for a ransom for you, but ask Him who surpasses your nature, for He is not a mere man, but God incarnate, Jesus Christ; who alone is able to offer a ransom to God (the Father) for us all. For God set Him forth as a propitiation through faith in His blood (Rom 3:25). Moses was a brother to Israel, and was not able to save him. Now can any ordinary man save? Therefore the passage declares: "No brother can save?" and another passage asks in earnest: "Shall man be saved?" (Ps 48:7) LXX.

Moses did not free his people from sin, but asked God for exemption from the punishment for sin. At any rate, he was not able to ransom himself when he sinned. For after he had wrought many great wonders and signs that he had seen, he uttered these words that express doubt: "Hear now, ye rebellious doubters: must we fetch you water out of this rock?" (see Num 20:10). For this reason, because of these words the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: "Because ye believed me not, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore ye shall not bring this congregation into the land which I have given them" (Num 20:12), and so he did not offer a ransom to God for himself.

In truth, what great thing can a man find sufficient to offer as a ransom for himself? But one thing was found worthy to be offered for all people together. This was offered as the price for the redemption of our souls: the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, holy and most honored, which He shed for all of us; therefore we were bought with a great price (1 Pet 2:22).

If the brother does not save, can a man be saved? But if the brother cannot save us, then He who saved us is not a man. Therefore do not think, because He dwelt among us "in the likeness of our sinful flesh" (Rom 8:3), that our Lord is a mere man, being unable to perceive the power of His divinity, He who has no need to offer a ransom for Himself, nor to redeem Himself, for "he did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth" (1 Pet 2:22). No one has sufficiency to save himself, unless He come who removes the captivity of men not by ransoms nor by gifts, as it is written in Isaiah (52:3), but by His blood.

And although we are not His brothers, since we became enemies by our disobedience, He who is not a mere man but God, after the freedom He gave us, called us His brothers. He says: "I will declare thy name unto my brethren" (Ps 22:22; Heb 2:12). He who saves us, if you examine His nature, is neither a brother nor a man, but if you examine His condescension to us by grace, He calls us His brothers; He comes down to our human nature, He who does not give God a ransom for Himself, but for the whole world.

He has no need of a ransom; He Himself is the propitiation. "For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens; who needeth not daily, as those high priests, to offer up sacrifice, first for his own sins, and then for the people's" (Heb 7:26-27). Then he says: "And he worked (even if he toiled) forever or lived to the end" (see Ps 49:8-9). For the existence of (the Redeemer) Himself, and His power, and His persevering nature work with toil in this life, and when He was weary from the journey He sat at the well (Jn 4:5) [11].

St. Basil the Great v When I call all these things to my memory (if I speak according to feelings), I am struck with a kind of dreadful fear and cold terror, lest through distraction of thought and preoccupation with vanities I fall from the love of God and become an object of insult to Christ. For he who now deceives us and strives by every means to urge us to ignore our Benefactor through the confusion of the enticements of the world that leap upon us and trample on us to destroy our souls, then, in the presence of the Lord, rebukes us for our impudence, and gloats over our disobedience and apostasy. He who never created us nor died for us counts us among his followers in disobedience and neglect of the commandments of God.

This insult directed to the Lord, and this victory for our enemy, seems to me more terrible than the punishments of Gehenna, because we give the enemy of Christ material for boasting, and an argument to exalt himself over Him who died for us and rose again. For this reason we are debtors to Him in a very special sense, as it is written (Rom 8:12). Therefore it befits us all the more to observe the love of God.
My aim, as I said before, is not to present the whole subject, for that is impossible, but to implant in your souls in brief the remembrance of keeping the divine longing awake within you [12].
St. Basil the Great v Question: What if someone was commanded and refused the commandment, but afterward of his own will left off this refusal and fulfilled the commandment? (Mt 21:29).

Answer: By his refusal he is considered an opponent (of the commandment), and one who provokes others to practice similar evils. Let him realize that he is subject to this sentence: "The rebel stirs up every evil, so the Lord sends a cruel messenger against him" (see Prov 17:11). Therefore let him be convinced that he is not resisting or obeying a man, but the Lord who says: "He that heareth you heareth me; and he that despiseth you despiseth me" (Lk 10:16).
But by remembering the commandment he has shown repentance; let him apologize first, and then, if it is permitted him, fulfill the work [13].
St. Basil the Great This Law fills people with wisdom, like Phison and the Tigris[14] in the days of the firstfruits [25].

Ben Sira used what is mentioned in the Old Testament about the rivers, especially in the garden of Eden, for he sees in them the overflowing through the enjoyment of the characteristics of wisdom (Gen 2:10-14).

He speaks of the small channel that was turned into a great river, through his practical experience, where he looks at what he acquired of wisdom at the beginning of his life, and as he was asking God continually to give him wisdom, the channel of wisdom within him turned into a river that overflows upon many. He offers them the waters of life, than which no river overflows with the like, therefore he presented to them six famous rivers. Four of them are mentioned in the story of creation (Gen 2:10-14) watering the garden of Eden, and the Nile and the Jordan [25-28].

If her waters are better than all the rivers, they are very wide, so that the river becomes a sea, and at the same time, in a spirit of humility, she becomes like a channel from the river or a conduit that waters the garden. She cares for the believer to water him with a channel or small conduit, and when she enters his depths the channel becomes a river, and the river becomes a sea. What are these waters that overflow upon the human soul as from a channel but the divine wisdom that offers a life full of blessings (Isa 58:11; Ezek 47:1-12).
The waters of wisdom are also a light that shines in the soul like the dawn that gleams from afar.
He did not say like the river Jordan, as he mentioned rivers found in the lands of the Gentiles, for Ben Sira often declared what the Gentiles enjoy through the preaching of the Gospel.
v "Hear this, all you peoples; give ear, all you inhabitants of the world. O you earthborn, and you sons of men, rich and poor alike" (Ps 49:1-2).

The place of assembly is enormous, where the psalm calls all the nations to listen, and all who fill the world with their dwellings. I think that by this exalted proclamation he draws not only the earthborn but all the sons of men, rich and poor, and calls them to listen.

What kind of watchtower is this, standing in its height over all the earth to see all the nations from afar, and embracing the whole world with its eyes? What kind of herald is so loud of voice that he cries out and many ears hear him at the same time? What place is able to contain such gatherings? What greatness and what wisdom has this Teacher, to give instructions fitting for this great assembly? Wait a little, and you will learn that what follows is fitting to the promise (made to them). For He who gathers all, and calls them to the proclamation, is the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, who gathers together the prophets and the apostles who are saved. Of whom it was said: "Their sayings have reached all the earth, and their words the ends of the world" (Ps 19:5) LXX. Therefore the Church was gathered from all classes of people (of life), so that no one may be left without help from her.

There are three groups called, which embrace the whole human race: Gentiles, and inhabitants of the world who are earthborn, and the sons of men, rich and poor. Who then was left and not called to listen? Those who are outside the faith are called by the call of the Gentiles. The inhabitants of the world are those who are in the Church.
The earthborn, who are wise in the affairs of earthly things and cling to the pleasures of the flesh.
The sons of men are those who walk with some seriousness and train their minds, for prudence is the mark of man.
The rich and the poor have their identity known from them: the former have increasing possessions of the necessities of life, and the latter stand in need of them.

And since the Physician of souls did not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance (Mt 9:13), in His call He placed first in each group those who are condemned. The Gentiles are worse than the inhabitants of the world, and yet they were chosen first in the call, so that the sick may come first, to enjoy the care of the Physician. And after that the earthborn were placed before the sons of men, and the rich before the poor.
The group that was hopeless and whose salvation was harder was called before the poor. Such is the tenderness of the Physician, offering His help first to those who are weakest.

At the same time, sharing in the summons is union in peace, so that those who until that time were opposing one another, because of differences of customs, by assembling together, grow accustomed to one another in love. Let the rich man know that he is called by the same proclamation as the poor man. It says: "rich and poor alike" (Ps 49:2).

Let arrogance toward those who are in greater need, and the haughtiness of wealth, be left outside; with this enter the Church of God. So let not the rich treat the poor with disdain, nor the poor shrink trembling under the authority of the wealthy. Let not the sons of men despise the earthborn, nor the earthborn isolate themselves from them. Let the Gentiles grow accustomed to dealing with the inhabitants of the world, and the inhabitants of the world through love receive them as friends and guests through the covenants [15].
St. Basil the Great And she fills them with understanding, like the Euphrates and like the Jordan in the days of harvest [26].
This Law shines forth with teaching like the light, and it overflows with teaching like the Nile, like Geon in the days of the (grape) vintage [27].

In speaking of the Law that shines forth with teaching, he does not liken it only to the rivers that watered the garden of Eden, but added to them other rivers such as the Nile, because the divine Law is not limited to the Jews alone. Our Christ overflows upon us with grace, and as the Apostle says: "In whom we have redemption through his blood... according to the riches of his grace; wherein he hath abounded toward us in all wisdom and prudence" (Eph 1:7-8).

v "The stream of the river maketh glad the city of God" (Ps 46:4). The waters of the sea stirred up by the winds swell and rise, but the stream of the river flows without disturbance. It flows quietly, for those who have been counted worthy to receive it. Therefore it makes glad the city of God, and now the righteous man drinks of the living waters (Jn 4:10), but in the future he will drink abundantly when his name is written among those who dwell in the city of God.

Now he drinks as in a mirror, darkly (1 Cor 13:12), for what he takes of divine contemplations is little, but then he will be filled, and his river will be able to overflow with joy in the city of God.

What then is the river of God? It is the Holy Spirit who flows in those who are worthy, who truly have faith in Christ. "He that believeth on me, as he says, out of his belly shall flow rivers..." (Jn 7:38); also he who drinks of the water that I give him, it shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life (Jn 4:13). This is the river that makes glad the city of God. It is the stream of the Holy Spirit [16].
St. Basil the Great Just as the first man did not know Wisdom completely, so the last man does not search out her depths [28].

With the understanding and wisdom with which the first man was endowed, he could not reach the depths of divine wisdom, and humanity remains unable to do so, even the last man. Ben Sira affirms that there is not one person throughout all ages and to the end of the age who is able to comprehend the depths of the wisdom of God.
For her thought is deeper than the sea, and her counsel deeper than the great abyss [29].

Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles, sees that the believer, as he eats and drinks the word of God, enters into a dialogue with God, and this dialogue does not cease, therefore Satan cannot overcome him [17].
And I am like a channel from the river, and like a conduit that went out into a garden [30].
I said: "I will water my garden, and drench the beds of my well-arranged flowers."
And behold, my channel has become a river, and my river has become a sea [31].
What is this channel that became a sea? St. Basil the Great sees that it is the tears of repentance.

v Who prays with streams of tears receives storms of rain at the right time? Who washes away sins, imitating the blessed David, who poured out tears upon his bed? Who washed the feet of strangers and rinsed off the dust of travel, so that even in time of need this person intercedes with God, asking that the drought cease? Who supports a child deprived of parents, that in return God may supply him with wheat, as an orphan shattered by contrary winds? Who cares for a widow struck by the hardships of life, so that the help we need may return to us? Tear up unjust contracts, so that sins also may be loosed.
Remove debts with exorbitant interest, so that the earth may bring forth its ordinary fruits [18].
St. Basil the Great I make discipline shine like the morning, and I make it shine afar [32].

entries.section: 2. A practical comment on the speech of Wisdom

paragraphs.text: I pour out teaching like prophecy, and leave it behind me for the generations to come [33].

v "You shall enter into the generation of your fathers" [19]. I think he is speaking of the sinner who knows God according to what his fathers handed down to him, but has not acquired anything additional by his own thought, nor added to his knowledge of the truth by himself.

He says: "O Lord, You are near", and at the same time he has a great idea of You as existing in the generations of his fathers. While he walks in laziness, and his spirit is occupied with earthly and fleshly things, which stagger in riches and luxury, and his mind is loaded with the cares of life, therefore "he does not see the light" [see 19].

As they entrust their leadership to blind teachers, they deprive themselves of the blessing of the light. This saying, "He enters into the generation of his fathers", carries the same meaning. This is said of those who pass through an evil life, and of teachings issuing from their fathers, but who are estranged from godliness; not only will it punish them, but it drives out those who lay down corrupt teachings. This is what he means by saying: "He enters into the generation of his fathers". Not only he who has blameworthy thoughts about God, but also he who leads others to this destruction. So are those who receive this evil from their forefathers, which is strengthened through persevering in it by habits for a long time, and there is difficulty in cleansing it. "He does not see the light", for they are sent into the outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth (Mt 8:12). This comes upon them according to the just judgment of God, since they hated the light in this life, because they did evil.

"Man being in honor did not understand; he is compared to the senseless beasts, and is like them." What a hateful report! Man? This one whom You made a little lower than the angels" (Heb 2:7), and of whom Solomon says: "Man is a great thing; the man who is pitied is honored" (Prov 20:6) LXX. He is compared to the senseless beasts, and becomes like them", because he does not realize his honor, and bows down to the desires of the flesh [19].

entries.section: 2. A practical comment on the speech of Wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great And as you see, I did not strive for myself alone, but for all who seek wisdom [34].
Inspired by Sirach 24

entries.section: That I may know You, and love You and possess You!

paragraphs.text: v Do You need to glory, O Wisdom of God, You who fill the heavens and the earth?
You glory in Your wondrous love for us sinners, that we may come to know You, and cleave to You and love You.
You went forth with Your Cross to shake the foundations of the abyss, and carry us to Your Paradise, and count us as the congregation of the Most High, and offer us the impossible!
v You came forth from the mouth of the Father, without being separated from Him.
And You gave us the Spirit of adoption, so that we have boldness to speak with You.
You came into the circle of heaven, and You are its Creator.
By Your Spirit You lift us from glory to glory, until we meet You face to face.
v It is wondrous that in Your humility and love You seek rest in us, and ask for an inheritance for Yourself!
Your rest is to establish from our weakness a new heaven, and so rest within us!
And Your inheritance is to turn our hearts into Your divine Kingdom!
v You pitched Your tent in Jacob, and counted Israel an inheritance for Yourself, and here You offer me Your Kingdom within me, that I may sing: "The Lord is my portion, saith my soul!"
Your Kingdom in my heart has no likeness on earth.
With what shall I describe it? Is it a unique garden?
Whenever I stretch out my hands to take of its fruits, my hunger for it increases, and whenever I drink of its waters, my thirst for it increases.
v The more I cleave to You, the more I feel that I am strong.
I sing with the Apostle: "I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me" (Phil 4:13).
You alone are the Lord Almighty; I have no savior but You!
What price is greater than Your precious blood, shed as a ransom for me?
What heavenly creature or what prophet among the prophets atones for my sins but You?
v Truly You are the lover of all mankind, offering Your Law and Your covenant not to a particular people, but to all humanity.
In Your infancy Judaism was stirred up against You, even those who knew the prophecies concerning You.
And the Magi came to You from the East to worship You.
You fled in Your infancy to Egypt, to establish Your Church there.
The world feels Your love and is indebted to You for its salvation.
v Your care for humanity is surpassing; Your grace waters my garden, and the fragrance of its beautiful flowers rises, the heavenly ones smell it and rejoice at Your wondrous work in us.
The channel of Your love overflows with grace to water my depths.
And as the garden widens and grows, Your channel turns into a great river.
And my garden remains thirsty for You more and more, and Your great river turns into a great sea.
And with every growth in understanding and knowledge, I realize that I am still on the shore of the sea of Your wisdom.
Would that all humanity shared with me my experience of Your grace and love and care!

entries.section: 1. Three beautiful things and three hateful persons

paragraphs.text: 1 Three things are an adornment to me, and by them I stood up beautiful before the Lord and men: 2 agreement among brothers, love of neighbor, and harmony between a wife and her husband. 3 Three my soul hates, and I loathe their life: 4 a proud poor man, a lying rich man, and an old adulterer who has lost understanding.
Ben Sira's discourse on the three beautiful things and the three hateful things can be understood through the behavioral, personal interpretation, and also through the symbolic interpretation.
As for the behavioral interpretation of the proverb, we note the following:

a. What is beautiful in the eyes of Sirach is beautiful also in the eyes of the Lord and in the eyes of men. It is as though he affirms that the man of God does not rely on his own individual opinion, but first treasures and esteems the view of the Lord Himself, without isolating himself from people, because he is a living member of the holy congregation. It is good for a person to have his own thinking and his own evaluation of things, and at the same time for his vision to be led by the divine mind and the mind of the Church. His delight is in the Lord's good pleasure and in harmony with the Church of Christ.
b. The secret of beauty is agreement and unity through love. The common factor in the three things is love in the spirit of unity, or unity in the spirit of love.

c. The believer does not separate his family life from his social life and from the life of humanity as a whole. And although the holy and successful family is the secret of the sanctification and success of the community as a whole, he began with the brothers, that is, all mankind, followed by the neighbors and relatives, and finally the family. Thus, in the spirit of love the heart of the believer widens to include all the children of men if possible; and this will not be achieved without his caring for his relatives, and this in turn is not achieved without the sanctification of the family and its unity in the Lord.

v When the wise man enumerates the things that are counted blessings, he mentions among them "a wife who agrees with her husband" [1]; and in another place he mentions among the blessings that a woman dwells in harmony with her husband (see Sir 40:23).

In truth, from the beginning God showed a special concern for this unity, and counted the two as one. He said: "Male and female created he them" (Gen 1:27), and it is said: "There is neither male nor female" (Gal 3:28). There is no relationship between one person and another as strong as the relationship that exists between a man and his wife, if they are joined together in the Lord! Therefore, when the wise man wished to express the overflowing love in his grief for someone dear to him, he did not refer to a father or a mother or a son or a brother or a friend, but said: "Thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women" (2 Sam 1:26). Truly this love is more violent than any violence, for the other kinds (of love) are strong, but this affection is not only strong but also does not wither. There is a certain love settled in the depth of our nature, which binds our bodies to one another in an inexplicable way. From the very beginning the woman came out of the man, and after that every man and woman come forth from man and woman together (1 Cor 11:8).

Do you perceive the strength of the bond and the power of the sign? How God did not permit a different nature to intrude from outside. Observe how the arrangements were filled with divine providence! He allowed the man to marry his sister, no, not his sister but his daughter, not his daughter but something more than his daughter, she is his body! (Here he refers to the marriage of Adam to Eve.)

Thus God created all from one beginning, so that they might be joined to one another like stones in a building in one unity. He did not create her from outside, lest the man feel that she was a stranger to him, nor did He make marriage stop with her alone, lest she be confined to herself and suppose that she is the center of all (here he means that she cannot bear children without the man, otherwise she would have exalted herself over him, and love would not have arisen between them; rather her sense of need for him in order to bear fruit makes the children a sign of the union and love between them). Nothing so joins our lives together with one another as the love of a husband and his wife [1].
St. John Chrysostom As for the hateful things, we note the following:
a. The believer cannot hate persons; he hates only "their evil way of life."

b. Much has been said about caring for the poor with material, moral and spiritual giving, but poverty in itself is not a virtue; rather, if the poor man foolishly supposes that he is better than the rich man in the eyes of the Lord, then by his pride together with his poverty he becomes hateful! Riches also are not in themselves a hateful vice. The truthful rich man who realizes that all he has is a gift to him from God, that he may give from it to the poor, is righteous like Abraham, who was very rich (Gen 13:2), and like Job the rich, from whom praise did not depart even in his trials (Job 1:21). But the lying rich man is the one who reckons that his wealth is the fruit of his own intelligence or his family's, so he exalts himself in his personality or ascribes it to a wealthy family that left him a great inheritance. This rich man is a liar, because what is in his hands may be destroyed in a moment of time!

Likewise, it befits the old man to give the young what he has learned through the length of his life, with love, humility, wisdom and holiness. But if he forgets that he is human, and it befits him not to trust his body while being careless in his conduct, and he walks without wisdom, relying on his old age and long experience, he soon falls into what he did not fall into when he was young; by this he loses understanding. By this he presents a bad example to the young. It befitted white hair to be a model that the young might imitate.
As for the spiritual, symbolic interpretation, we note the following:

In the previous chapter Sirach mentioned that what he writes is prophecy (24:33), which he presents to his contemporary generation as well as to the generations to come. So what he presents here in the two proverbs is a prophecy about the Church of the Covenant, which bears the image of her Bridegroom, the Lord of glory Jesus, and which is ever renewed by the work of the Holy Spirit in her.
First: the Church of the New Testament, the holy bride of Christ.
In the spirit of prophecy he looks to the beautiful Church of the New Testament, marked by the three beautiful things in Christ Jesus:

a. The beauty of the Church is that she opens herself to humanity in love, to present to it the Savior, who is "fairer than the children of men" (Ps 45:2), whom the true believer acquires, so that His beauty is reflected upon him, and the earth becomes in his sight a radiant heaven without blemish, and he experiences a foretaste of heaven and fellowship with the heavenly ones.

b. This spiritual beauty will not be realized unless relatives are sanctified in a spirit of unity and harmony together in the Lord. These relatives are the members of the Church; and the existence of any division in her, especially among the leaders, whether men of the priesthood or monasticism, or servants, men and women, and also disputes at the level of families, or at the level of the one family, indeed at the level of the person himself, where the soul is not sanctified together with the body, and the mind with the emotions, and so on.

In all the beautiful things one notices the communal aspect: "brothers, neighbors, and a married couple." But the three kinds of people whom the soul of Sirach hates are on an individual, selfish, isolated level: "a poor man who is proud, a rich man who is a liar, and an old man who is an adulterer."
There are three things beautiful to see, and they are beautiful before the Lord and men:
Agreement among brothers, friendship among neighbors, and a wife and husband who agree well together [1].

There is no relationship between one man and another as intimate as that between a man and his wife, if they cleave to one another as they ought. Nothing is more precious than love through the wife and his love for her.

entries.section: 1. Three beautiful things and three hateful persons

paragraphs.text: v This is the chief point, which surpasses all, good in the home: "a man and his wife agreeing" (see Sir 25:1). Where this exists, there is nothing that is not delightful. When the head is in harmony with the body, and there is no strife between them, how should all the other members not be at peace? [2]

entries.section: 1. Three beautiful things and three hateful persons

paragraphs.text: v Nothing is more precious than to be loved in this way by a wife, and to love her [3].

entries.section: 1. Three beautiful things and three hateful persons

paragraphs.text: v Indeed, from the beginning God showed a special provision for this unity, speaking to the two as to one person. He said: "Male and female created he them" (Gen 1:27). Again: "There is neither male nor female" (Gal 3:28). For there is no relationship between male and male as intimate as the relationship of a man with his wife, if the two are joined together as they ought [4].
St. John Chrysostom Three kinds of people my soul hates, and I loathe their way of life with utter loathing:
The proud beggar, the lying rich man, and the old adulterer who lacks understanding [2].

What does he mean by the proud poor man? By the poor man he does not mean only the person who suffers material poverty, but rather the word poor or needy means more the person who is in spiritual want. For sin makes a person needy, in need of God's mercies and help; it also carries the person who is not occupied with the temporal things of the world, but fixes his inward sight upon the Kingdom of God. The Lord Christ opened His Sermon on the Mount with His saying: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Mt 5:3).
Origen presents to us, in his homilies on the Book of Judges, how sin drove the people into great distress, and when they cried out to the Lord in their poverty, He answered them.

v Now, these persons who were delivered up (to distress) because of sin and came into suffering, let us see what they did. Indeed it is written: "Then they cried unto the Lord in their trouble, and he saved them out of their distresses. He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and brake their bands in sunder" (Ps 107:13-14).

Add to this that each one of us, if he is small, even if he is very small, even if he is utterly insignificant by worldly standards, can act through the vice of pride, and not be among those who are so foolish and hateful (like him), not among those who are base and contemptible, according to what is stated in the Holy Scripture, like the proud poor man or the lying rich man.

entries.section: 1. Three beautiful things and three hateful persons

paragraphs.text: Sometimes the disease of pride penetrates not only among the poor, but attacks even the order of the priests and Levites. Sometimes we find pride even among us, who ought to have been examples of humility, and who gather around the altar as a mirror for those who observe us, and yet the vice of arrogance sends out its foul and loathsome odor. So it happens that from the altar of the Lord, which requires the offering of incense of sweet fragrance, there comes forth the exceedingly foolish odor of pride and the rays of self-conceit. But this odor, which is utterly foolish, must be driven out, for the sake of heaven. Let it be driven out from the whole holy Church, especially from those who serve in the sanctuaries, that we may say with Paul that we are able to be a sweet savor of Christ (2 Cor 2:15), lest the wrath of the Lord be kindled (Ps 2:12) [5].
Origen

entries.section: 2. The attractiveness of wisdom in old age

paragraphs.text: 5 If you have not stored up in your youth, how will you find in your old age? 6 How beautiful is judgment for gray hair, and good counsel for the old. 7 How beautiful is wisdom for the old, and opinion and counsel for men of glory. 8 Much experience is the crown of the old, and the fear of the Lord is their boast.

If the soul of Sirach hates the adulterous old man [2], it rejoices in the old man who has the virtue of discernment and of giving good counsel, who is adorned with wisdom and understanding, and crowned with experience of great benefit, the secret of whose glory is the fear of the Lord.

Wisdom in the life of the young man: a young man may be careless about cleaving to wisdom, postponing it to the time of his old age. If the young man does not store up wisdom, what will he gain in his old age [3]? He who cleaves to wisdom in his youth presents wise judgment in his old age, and many accept his counsel, which comes from his practical experience. Wisdom weaves a crown for the old man, indeed she becomes his crown [5]. By true wisdom the experienced old man is honored with the crown of the fear of the Lord [6].
If you have not stored up anything in your youth, how can you find anything in your old age? [3]

The young man who is serious in seeking true happiness cares for his study, his work and all aspects of his life, and benefits from the experience of those who went before him. And the young man does not forget that one day he will reach old age, and he will find many old people, men and women, suffering from emptiness with little physical effort, and sometimes suffering from weakness of memory. Therefore it befits him to look toward this coming stage with seriousness and to prepare himself for the blessed life, when in his youth he asks and strives to obtain wisdom from God and the experience of his brothers, so that he will have a reserve in his old age, when wisdom overflows from his holy mouth, and many desire to benefit from his experience. "The glory of young men is their strength: and the beauty of old men is the grey head" (Prov 20:29).

In the spirit of strength the young Daniel cried out when he saw innocent Susanna being led to death unjustly, and in the spirit of wisdom he "cried with a loud voice: I am clear from the blood of this woman" (Dan 13:45, addition). In such a young man the saying is fulfilled: "With the ancient is wisdom; and in length of days understanding" (Job 12:12). And also the saying: "The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness" (Prov 16:31).
Good discernment is the beauty of gray hair, and good counsel belongs to the old [4].

entries.section: 2. The attractiveness of wisdom in old age

paragraphs.text: v Just as helmsmen (those who direct the rudder) and drivers of chariots gain experience in their work through discernment (wisdom in conduct) and continual striving, so also it befits those who truly seek the virtuous life to use discernment with vigilance, and to take care to live as is fitting and as is acceptable to God. For the person who desires this virtuous life and believes that he can attain his desire, receives through faith incorruption (the pure life) [6].
St. Anthony the Great Wisdom is like beauty for the old, and understanding and counsel for men of glory! [5].

Solomon the wise says: "For honourable age is not that which standeth in length of time, nor that is measured by number of years" (Wis 4:8). The honor of the old man is not in his white hair and the length of his years and experiences, for his experiences may be evil, to which he clings, reckoning them wisdom itself.
v The old man is he who goes first and hears about the work.
The old man is he who lives a great age in the faith.

entries.section: 2. The attractiveness of wisdom in old age

paragraphs.text: The old man is he whose age is held in esteem, and whose long time is without wrinkle [7].
St. Ambrose The crown of the old is great experience, and the fear of the Lord is their glory [6].

entries.section: 2. The attractiveness of wisdom in old age

paragraphs.text: v "Much experience is the crown of old men" (see Sir 25:6), and the whiteness of the hair is their crowns that bear witness to that experience. Nevertheless some are ashamed of the advance of years and of the whiteness of their hair [8].

St. Clement of Alexandria v One day Abba Ammon went to visit (Abba Sisoes) and found him grieved over his coming from the desert, and he said to him: Father, it is not good for you to grieve, because you have drawn near to the dwelling place of the brothers, for your body has become weak and you are no longer able to perform those works that you want in the desert.

When Abba Sisoes heard this speech he looked sharply at Abba Ammon and answered him, saying: What is this that you say to me, Abba Ammon? Was not the freedom of thoughts that I had in the desert sufficient to take the place of all the works? ... Tell me, what can you do in the desert in advanced age? And even if I am unfit for the works of the body because I have become weak through my old age, I have more ability to accomplish the works of the mind than I had in my early manhood.
The Paradise of the Fathers

9 Nine things have I counted happy in my heart, and the tenth my tongue speaks: 10 Blessed is the man who is made glad by children, and who sees in his lifetime the fall of his enemies. 11 Blessed is he who dwells with a wise woman, and who has not slipped with his tongue, and who has not served one who is unworthy of him. 12 Blessed is he who has found prudence, and who puts his speech in a hearing ear. 13 How great is he who has found wisdom; yet he is not better than he who fears the Lord. 14 The fear of the Lord is higher than everything. 15 He who possesses it, to whom shall he be likened? 16 The fear of the Lord is the beginning of loving Him, and faith the beginning of union with Him.
Nine thoughts I count happy in my heart, and I will mention the tenth:
A father who rejoices in his children, and a man who lives and sees the fall of his enemies [7].

He presents to us ten examples of blessed people. First, blessed fathers who rejoice in their children as a gift from God (Ps 128:3-5). Next, he who sees his enemies (the devil and his hosts) fallen, having no authority over him (Ps 112:8).

St. John Chrysostom warned us against caring for the upbringing of our children out of pride, that we may be fathers of successful sons, without caring for their eternal life. What gladdens the hearts of the wise is to see their sons wise in the Lord.
A husband who is blessed because he lives with a wise wife, a man who does not slip with his tongue, and a man who does not serve one who is unworthy of him! [8]

The wise wife qualifies herself and her family for the blessed life, that is, she shares with the heavenly ones their blessed life. She reflects this blessedness upon her husband, so that the two live like two angels filled with the life of blessedness and heavenly joy. The wise man says: "House and riches are the inheritance of fathers: and a prudent wife is from the Lord" (Prov 19:14).

It is stated in the discourse of St. Gregory of Nazianzus about his parents that Gregory was drawn by his wife Nonna, not only to believe in the Lord Christ, but also to become a bishop afterward. [Behold, the good shepherd is the fruit of the prayers and guidance of his wife, and from her he learned his ideal pastoral life. With power he fled from the worship of idols, and afterward the demons began to flee from him... They became equal in prudence and splendor, zealous, supporting one another, flying above all... They had two bodies, but it was as though the two bodies had been turned into one spirit, even before their dissolution... They possessed everything and lacked nothing. They rejected wealth, and so became rich in honor... I say only one word about them, that they were truly and justly appointed, each one for his own sex: he was appointed an ornament for men, and she an ornament for women, not only an ornament, but an example of the virtuous life [9].]

"Why is he blessed who does not serve one who is unworthy of him?" He does not mean by this that the blessing arises from not serving the wicked, but from the wisdom exercised by the person who does not show partiality to a wicked man, and who, instead of supporting him to abandon evil, serves him in negligence and flattery, which drives the wicked man to persist in evil.
A man is blessed because he finds discernment!
And a man is blessed because he speaks to listening ears! [9]
When St. Abba Anthony was asked about the best of the virtues, he answered, "Discernment."
As for listening ears, this requires of us that we pray for those who listen to the voice of the Lord that we proclaim.

v You must be careful concerning whom you speak to. If you notice that this person wishes to benefit, then speak. But if not, there is no need to speak. For it is written: "Blessed is he who speaks in the ears of those who listen" (see Sir 25:9).

May you never be found giving what is holy to the dogs, or casting your pearls before swine (Mt 7:6). May the Lord grant you modesty, O brother, that you do not turn aside from the way of humility [10].

Sts. Barsanuphius and John v When St. Paul appeared before King Agrippa to answer the accusations brought against him, he wished to use a clear style for his hearers, and being confident of the success of his reasoning, he began to congratulate himself with these words: "I think myself happy, king Agrippa, because I shall answer for myself this day before thee touching all the things whereof I am accused of the Jews: especially because I know thee to be expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews" (Acts 26:2-3). He had read Joshua (Ben Sira): "Blessed is he who tells the ears of those who listen" (see Sir 25:9). And he knew that the defender has to do with one who has influence over the judge. I also think myself happy that cultured ears should listen to my defense [11].

St. Jerome v Jeremiah was preaching the word, but no one listened to his words. So he was like the physician who wastes his medicines because of the stubbornness of his patients, who do not wish to follow his treatment or take his medicines. It is as though he were a physician saying: "I have done no good, and no one has done me any good." Perhaps the reason for the contradiction in this verse goes back to the feeling of love and affection which the person to whom good has been done bears toward the person who did him this good. It follows from this that he who preaches the word also receives good from his word (that is, he gains the love of those who hear him). And as it is written: "Blessed is he who speaks to an ear that listens" (see Sir 25:9). And the greatest good that the teacher can reap from those who hear him is that they should grow and advance, so that he may have fruit among them (Rom 1:13) [12].

v Those who are great and strong in their souls Scripture mentioned with blessing. When a person is occupied with great works, and has ambitions of worth, and continually sets before his eyes clear goals so as always to live according to the right truth, and does not even wish to look at anything trivial or small, such a person has strength and greatness in the soul. But those others who were "poor," they did not listen to the word of the Lord, as the prophet says; and, to be more precise, they did not listen because they were poor.

Therefore, since this word has been spoken to us also, let us pray to God that we may receive from Him strength and greatness enabling us to listen to those holy words, knowing that those who utter words of rebuke lose nothing as much as those who hear and do not accept this rebuke, and whom Jeremiah accuses of being poor in their minds and thoughts [13].
Origen How blessed is he who finds wisdom!
But there is no one who rises above him who fears the Lord [10].
The fear of the Lord surpasses all things, and to what can it be compared? [11]

v The fear of the Lord is the bridle that stops a person's rush toward committing evil, and pulls him backward when he is enslaved to running after his loathsome desires, not only in his outward life, but especially in his hidden inner life" [14].
v The person who lives in remembrance of God at all times is filled with fear, so that even when he resists a thought of lust passing through his soul, he becomes terrified because of this thought.

But the thought flees at once before the fear of the soul, like a bird that flees from before the person who disturbs its rest. Fear and respect for men's laws keep the body from passions. And fear and a person's shame before God keep the soul from evil thoughts. For since he knows that God sees him at all times, he watches himself continually lest he sin [15].
St. Mar Philoxenus

17 The utmost of pain is pain of the heart, and the utmost of wickedness is the wickedness of a woman. 18 Any pain, but not the pain of the heart. 19 And any wickedness, but not the wickedness of a woman. 20 And any calamity, but not the calamity from those who hate. 21 And any vengeance, but not the vengeance of enemies. 22 There is no head worse than the head of a serpent. 23 And no wrath worse than the wrath of a woman. To dwell with a lion and a dragon is better to me than to dwell with a wicked woman. 24 The wickedness of a woman changes her appearance, and turns her face black as sackcloth. 25 Her husband is grieved among his companions, and when he hears it he sighs bitterly. 26 Every evil is slight compared to the evil of a woman. Let the lot of the sinner fall upon her. 27 As a sandy ascent is to the feet of the old man, so is a woman wicked of tongue to a quiet man. 28 Let not the beauty of a woman cause you to stumble, and do not desire a woman for her loveliness. 29 Wrath, and impudence, and great disgrace 30 is the woman who rules over her husband. 31 A wicked woman is humiliation of heart, a frowning of the face, and pain of the soul. 32 She who does not make her husband happy is but slackness of the hands and loosening of the knees. 33 From the woman sin began, and because of her we all die. 34 Do not give the water an outlet, nor a wicked woman authority. 35 If she does not walk at the beck of your hand, she will shame you before your enemies. 36 Cut her off from your body, lest she harm you continually.
Ben Sira continues to denounce the wicked wife, and each time after denouncing the wicked wife he immediately praises the good wife (26:1-6; 13-18).
Any wound but the wound of the heart, and any evil but the evil of a wife! [12]

He links the wound of the heart with the evil of the wife, to bring out that the wicked woman wounds the depths of her husband's heart and his inner feelings, even if he does not show it in his features. What is said about the wicked woman applies to the wicked husband.
Any misery, but not the misery of those who hate me!
Any vengeance, but not like the vengeance of enemies! [13]

Fierce animals may attack a man, but they bear no hatred toward him. It is said of the lion that when it has preyed upon a man and is satisfied it does not harm those around it, because it attacks the man out of its hunger and not out of hatred. It is also said of some animals and snakes that they do not attack a man when he does not attack them. So what they do by instinct is better than what the rational man does when he hates his brother.
There is no head worse than the head of a serpent, and no wrath worse than the wrath of an enemy! [14]
I would rather dwell with a lion or a serpent; it is better for me than dwelling with a wicked wife [15].

According to some modern scholars, Ben Sira is a hater of women, but other scholars have refuted this opinion, because what he wrote here concerns the wicked woman, especially as he warns his young disciples against haste in choosing a wife merely for her beauty. To the extent that he warned against wicked women, he honored and praised pious, wise women [16].

It is said that the word "head" and the word "venom" are in Hebrew "rosh." It is as though Sirach presents the following marks of the wicked woman: "vengeance" [13], "venom" [14], "preying" [15], "stings" [15], wickedness [16], and violent features [16]. Through these marks we perceive the marks of the good wife as the opposite of those of the wicked one. We find in her kindness and healing tenderness, self-giving and generosity, long-suffering with meekness, and in her love and a sincere smile are manifested.
The wickedness of a wife changes her appearance, and makes her face dark like a bear [16].

The inner wickedness of the wicked wife is reflected in her outward features: "An evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth evil; for of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh" (Lk 6:4; Mt 12:35).
Her husband goes to his neighbors to eat, and against his will he sighs bitterly [17].

As the husband's heart is crushed because of his wife's wickedness, he finds no one to support him except God, so he sighs bitterly. He is often ashamed to complain of his wife to anyone, even relatives.
All wickedness is slight compared to the wickedness of a wife.
May the lot of the sinner fall upon her [18].

God sometimes allows a sinful man a wicked wife, for his discipline. Therefore it befits one who feels that his wife is wicked, before he criticizes her, to examine himself and offer repentance for his sins.
As the climbing of a sandy hill is to the feet of an old man, so is a talkative wife to a quiet husband [19].

The quiet husband finds it difficult to cope with the chatter of the wicked wife, so his state is like that of an old man climbing a sandy hill, for he stumbles in his walking, and his feet sink into the sand, and with great difficulty he is able to move.
Do not fall because of a woman's beauty, and do not desire her beauty [20].

He who has not yet chosen a wife must seek not her beauty, but her wisdom, prudence and holiness, reckoning that dwelling with a ravening lion or a poisonous serpent is better than dwelling with a wicked wife [15-16]. Beauty is a gift from God; if it is joined with beauty of spirit in humility, the husband finds his happiness in his humble wife.
Anger, impudence and great reproach is the woman who spends upon her husband [21].

Each of the husband and the wife has a responsibility and obligation in the family; therefore the husband who in slackness does not strive to manage the financial affairs of the family is exposed to his wife's contempt.
The cause of the dejected heart, the gloomy face and the wounded heart is the wicked wife.
The wife who does not make her husband happy makes the hands limp and the knees weak [22].

The wife has her effective role in her husband's life; with wisdom she can support him so that he enjoys outstanding success, and in foolishness she can shatter his energies, gifts and abilities so that he fails.
From a woman sin had its beginning, and because of her we all die [23].

The Apostle Paul says: "Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the transgression. Notwithstanding she shall be saved in childbearing, if they continue in faith and charity and holiness with sobriety" (1 Tim 2:14). Some see that St. Mary conferred great honor upon women, since she bore for us the Savior. And others see that women, although they have been deprived of public teaching in the Church in the presence of men, nevertheless receive their crowns through bringing up their children in faith, love and holiness with sobriety, which men cannot do. Truly they present to the Church blessed leading members!

v Elizabeth prophesied before John. And before the birth of the Lord and Savior, Mary prophesied. Sin began from the woman, then spread to the man. In the same way salvation began first from women. Thus the rest of women can cast off the weakness of their sex, and imitate as far as possible the life and conduct of those holy women whom the Gospel describes [17].

Origen v Eve, from whom sin began, was formed from the side of the man (Gen 2:21). For she came out of his side while he slept; Christ was hanging and died on the Cross when He was wounded. Sleep and death are joined to one another, and so are the two sides: the side of Adam and the side of Christ. The Lord was wounded from where sin arose. But from the side from which Eve was formed, who by committing the fault brought death upon us, from the side of Christ the Church was formed, bestowing upon us a birth [18].
St. Augustine Give the water no passage, nor a wicked wife boldness of speech [24].

The wise man says: "The beginning of strife is as when one letteth out water: therefore leave off contention, before it be meddled with" (Prov 17:14). Neglect of a small wound can multiply and destroy a person's whole life. And a small breach in a ditch, if neglected, can cause a flow of abundant water that cannot be confronted. So it is with the wicked wife who does not restrain her tongue: she destroys the family.
If she does not walk according to your good direction, separate her from you [25].

v The Mosaic Law did not command divorce, but commanded the one who divorces his wife to give her a bill of divorce, because in giving her a bill of divorce there is that which calms the fury of a man's anger. So the Lord, who commanded those hard of heart to give a bill of divorce, indicated that He did not wish for divorce as far as possible. Therefore when the Lord Himself was asked about this matter He answered, saying: "Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives" (Mt 19:8). For however great the hardness of heart of the one who wishes to divorce his wife, when he knows that by means of the bill of divorce she can marry another, his anger subsides and he does not divorce her. And in order that the Lord of glory might confirm this principle, which is not to divorce a wife lightly, He made the only exception the cause of adultery. For He commanded that all other troubles (other than adultery) be endured with steadfastness for the sake of conjugal love and for the sake of chastity. And the Lord of glory confirmed the same principle by calling the one who marries a divorced woman an adulterer.

The Apostle explained this matter, saying in (Rom 7:2-3) that the wife is bound as long as her husband lives, but if her husband dies she is permitted to marry. I think that by the same rule, if the man leaves his wife, then the woman is not permitted to marry as long as her husband lives, nor the man to marry as long as the woman whom he divorced is alive [19].
St. Augustine Inspired by Sirach 25

entries.section: Set me free from the slavery of the devil, and prepare me for the heavenly wedding!

paragraphs.text: v By my own will I was drawn to sin to enjoy its temporary pleasure, so the enemy of good hunted me and enslaved me for the sake of his kingdom.
Instead of the image of God in which I was created, corruption took hold of my nature.
True love, sincere unity and holiness ceased to be of my nature.
I fell into arrogance, lying and evil desires.
Who sets me free from the slavery of Satan but You?
v In my youth, in ignorance, I did not seek heavenly wisdom.
And the old age of helplessness came upon me while I was still young.
Behold, You open to me the doors of Your love and Your wonderful storehouses.
I cleave to You, and I come to know Your mysteries. I draw wisdom, understanding, prudence and discernment.
You crown me with the crown of love, purity and the divine fear.
I no longer fear old age, but am filled with strength.
For Your dwelling in me grants me the blessed life of the Holy Spirit.
v My thoughts have become joyful in You.
In You I enjoy fatherly love, so that every person finds in my heart a special place; I am not terrified of the devil, for in You I have crushed him under my feet.
You raise up my soul as a heavenly bride who knows no wickedness, and You set a strict guard upon my tongue.
No word will come forth except through You, O Holy One!
You grant me the spirit of discernment, so that I walk with wisdom and good management.
Your fear makes of my weakness something like a seraph or a cherub.
v Who can wound my heart while You dwell in it?!
How can I covet what my brothers have, when You are my portion?
The ancient serpent cannot swallow me, for by Your grace I do not crawl on the earth, but fly as though to heaven.
Let the devil, the savage lion, roar, and let the serpent crawl, for my heart is in Your hands!
How can my face be downcast, when Your Kingdom is established within me?
You grant to my weakness joy, gladness, glory, riches, righteousness and perfection.
I am too small to thank You and praise You!

1 Blessed is the husband of a good wife, and the number of his days is doubled. 2 A virtuous woman delights her husband, and makes him spend his years in peace. 3 A good wife is a good portion, given as a lot to him who fears the Lord, 4 so that his heart is glad, and his face cheerful at all times, whether he be rich or poor.
Happy is the husband of a good wife, for the number of his days is doubled [1].

A good wife gives her husband happiness [1, 2, 4], long life [1] and peace [2]. The holy family that enjoys the peace of God has an effect even upon a person's physical and psychological health. On the contrary, the existence of family disputes, especially between the spouses, shatters the psychology of the husband, wife and children, and affects their bodily health. The wise man says: "A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband: but she that maketh ashamed is as rottenness in his bones" (Prov 12:4).

From the spiritual side, the doubling of the number of a person's days means the doubling of blessing. A person may live to old age, yet his days are counted as nothing, and a child may die and his few days be counted in the eyes of God and the eyes of the heavenly ones better than thousands of years. What the unborn John the Baptist did, while he was not yet complete and had not yet come out into the world, was greater than the works of the high priests and all the leaders at that time. Moreover, on the great day of the Lord we shall be surprised by little children who are counted great heroes, whose days are counted exceedingly long and fruitful in the Lord. It was said of God's godly people such as Abraham, Isaac and Job that they died full of days (Gen 25:8; 35:23).
v How can we express the marital happiness which the Church joins together, which the oblation confirms, and which the blessing seals? [1]
Tertullian A virtuous wife delights her husband, and he spends his years filled with peace [2].

Where there is godliness together with sincerity, family life is transformed into a life almost heavenly, and the family tastes blessing in every work to which their hands are extended, and the joy of the Spirit comes upon them all, and they are filled with inner peace.

If heaven in its essence is a "fellowship of love" and a "life of unity in God, the center of heaven," then true married life in the very core of its being is a unity of marital love, through which the two become one.
v Marriage is greater than being merely human; it is a miniature kingdom, a little house of the Lord.
St. Clement of Alexandria A good wife is a great portion, and she is the portion of him who fears the Lord [3].

The God-fearing husband looks to his good wife and counts her a divine gift. The Lord presented her to him as a great portion in which he delights. Where there is mutual love between God and the godly man, the believer says: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine" (Song 6:3). The believer counts the Lord as his portion (Jer 3:24). And the Lord counts His children as His portion, as was said of the tribe of Levi: "The Lord is his inheritance" (Deut 10:9). Thus the husband counts his wife his great portion, and the wife counts her husband her great portion.

v I do not reject the bond of marriage; rather, I submit to it in a greater love, for by this I bear witness, confessing, to my wife whom the Lord appointed for me, and I honor her, and I do not refuse to be joined to her by the bond of love in Christ, which is never loosed [2].
Abba Theonas A good heart, in rich or poor, is a cheerful face at all times [3] [4].
The bishop and monk St. Ambrose speaks of the married man in his relation to his wife, saying: [A man without a wife is reckoned like one who has no house [4].]
v There is nothing more precious, and nothing more precious can be found, than that a person be loved by his wife and love her!

Scripture says: "A wife who agrees with her husband" (as one of the three blessings that the wise man mentioned) (see Sir 25:1), because where this (love) exists there is wealth and prosperity overflows, and where it is absent nothing else avails, but all things go in the wrong way, and life becomes misery and anxiety.
Let us seek this before everything! He who seeks money seeks nothing. Seek what endures!
Do not seek a wife from among the rich, lest the increase of wealth on her side cause arrogance.

It befits us not to seek a wife for her wealth, but to seek her as a partner for us in life, for the sake of management, to be a helper for the bearing of children. God gave the woman not to bring money but to be a helper! [5]
St. John Chrysostom

5 Three things my heart fears, and for the fourth I made supplication with my face: 6 the slander of a city, the gathering of a mob, 7 and a false accusation. All this is heavier than death. 8 But a woman jealous of a woman is heartache and mourning, 9 and her tongue is a whip that strikes everyone. 10 A wicked wife is a chafing yoke, and he who takes hold of her is like one who grasps a scorpion. 11 A drunken woman is a great wrath, and her shame is not covered. 12 The adultery of a woman is in the lifting up of her eyes, and it is known by her eyelids. 13 Keep a strict watch on the daughter who has little shame, lest she find an opportunity and give herself away. 14 Beware of her impudent eye, and do not wonder if she transgresses against you. 15 She opens her mouth like a thirsty traveler, and drinks from every water that she comes upon, and sits down at every tent peg, and opens her quiver to every arrow.
Among the evil traits of the wife are: jealousy of her rival [6], a biting tongue [6], drunkenness [7], chatter [8] and arrogance [10-11].
Three things my heart fears, and for a fourth I pray.
The slander of a city, the gathering of the common people, and a false accusation: all this is heavier than death [5].
This statement is considered an introduction to his discourse on the wicked wife. Here he presents four things that cause anxiety, yet marriage to a wicked woman is more dangerous than these things.
a. The first thing is the slander of the city, or open false defamation, where a person sees injustice prevailing in the city, and there is no one who can stand before it to defend the truth.
b. The gathering of a mob, the agitation of the rabble, and the occurrence of a state of general disorder.
c. A false accusation.

d. The three preceding things rest on the absence of truth and the prevalence of falsehood and vanity, which makes life tasteless, so that a person desires death, with all its heaviness, rather than life in this gloomy atmosphere. For though a person feels that he is leaving many under the yoke of injustice, it is nevertheless easier than living with the occurrence of the preceding things.

Then he moves on to the fourth grave thing, which happens in secret and not openly like the preceding things, namely a wife's jealousy of her co-wife (in polygamy) or of a woman who has a relationship with the family through kinship or neighborliness. The discourse on the wicked woman, who represents a danger more hideous than the preceding things, brings out the following:
a. The wife jealous of a woman or girl who rivals her, so that her life is turned into a whip that strikes the whole family [6].
b. The wicked wife resembles an ill-fitting yoke that makes the neck of him who bears it bleed, and a scorpion that injects venom into him who holds it [7].
c. The drunken wife exposes herself in a disgraceful shame [8].
d. The adulterous wife, even if she hides her defiled conduct, her impudent eyes bear witness to her uncleanness [9].
e. The young wife [or daughter] of little shame needs serious guarding [10].
f. The wife thirsty for defilement drinks from every water without discrimination [11-12].
There is also heartache and sorrow when a wife is jealous of another woman, and her tongue is a whip that strikes everyone [6].

This woman's heart turns into a raging volcano. For she is jealous over her husband, pursues him and suspects his conduct, whether by speaking frankly with him or in an obscure way. The tongue of the jealous woman does not keep silent, and her thought moves in a closed circle, so the house is turned into an unbearable hell. Even the children, whatever their age, lose peace and joy without knowing the hidden cause of this bitter life.
The wicked wife is like the yoke of a raging ox; he who wishes to restrain her is like one who seizes a scorpion [7].

Ben Sira compares the wicked woman to the loose yoke that moves here and there, which is placed on the neck of the ox; because it moves it causes pain, even if the ox is strong; this loose yoke affects the ox's ability to work. So the wicked woman is like a yoke on her husband's neck, causing him much pain that shatters his energy and spoils his vitality, so that she becomes like a fetter in his life, hindering his work for the sake of the family and its upbuilding. If someone intervenes to set the situation right and approaches her with wise counsel, she injects venom into him and stings him like a scorpion.
A drunken woman is a great wrath, and she does not cover her shame [8].

Evil may drive a woman to drink wine under the pretext that she forgets her cares, and since she knows no limits in drinking, she becomes drunk and loses her consciousness, as happened with Noah, who was uncovered when he got drunk. The drunken wife expresses the evils of her heart by her tongue and her conduct without balance and without prudence. She exposes the corruption of her heart and the deviation of her conduct unawares. The husband is ashamed of her behavior, especially before their children.
The adultery of the wife appears in her haughty looks and her eyelids [9].

He speaks of the impudent wicked wife, who tries to entice one who is not her husband to fall with her into sin, so she is the first one responsible for her fall and for enticing the other party. The adulterous wife denies that she has fallen into sin, but the impudence of her eyes and the movements of her eyelids bear witness against her. Solomon the wise warns against the provocative movements of her face: "Lust not after her beauty in thine heart; neither let her take thee with her eyelids" (Prov 6:25). And St. Clement of Alexandria speaks of adultery through the winking of the eyes.

v No excuse can be offered for a prudent man when he sins, and still more a woman of bad repute of whatever kind, for she brings disgrace. In the words of Scripture: "A drunken woman is a great wrath, and her shame is not covered" (see Sir 26:8), for it is said of her that through wine she has become wanton and the wrath of God comes upon her. Why? Because her shameful conduct is exposed. For as soon as a woman yields to pleasure, she quickly falls into immoral acts [6].

St. Clement of Alexandria v Scripture says: "The light of the body is the eye" (Mt 6:22), for what is within is lit up, and becomes visible by the light shining upon it; therefore "the adultery of a woman is seen in the impudence of her eyes" (see Sir 26:9) [7].
St. Clement of Alexandria Keep a strict watch on the stubborn daughter, lest she find some freedom and use it to her own harm [10].

He demands wise guarding over the daughter (perhaps he means the wife of young age) who has little shame, for leniency with her in her keeping her chastity harms her. He does not ask that she be bound, but that she be supported to keep her purity. What he said about the faults of the wicked wife he sees as doubled in the case of the daughter of little shame.
Be on your guard against her shameless eye, and do not wonder if she sins against you [11].

By being on guard is meant not to go too far or be lax in speaking with her and cleaving to her. This reserve may provoke her to anger against the person, for one who has fallen into adultery cannot bear the conduct of a pure person.
Laxity in bringing up the daughter leads her to disobedience toward her father.
She opens her mouth like a thirsty traveler, and drinks from every water near her, and sits down at every tent peg, and opens her quiver to every arrow [12].

He likens the adulterous wife to an unsettled person always traveling, who suffers thirst and drinks from every water near him. For the sin of adultery makes her thirsty for every person she meets. Whenever she finds a tent peg she sits beside it to meet the one who enters the tent, so she enters with him and entices him to fall into sin.

16 The kindness of a wife delights her husband, 17 and her discipline makes his bones fat. 18 A silent woman is a gift of the Lord, and a disciplined soul cannot be exchanged for anything. 19 A modest woman is grace upon grace. 20 And a chaste soul has no worth that can balance it. 21 The sun rises in the heights of the Lord, and the beauty of a good wife is in the order of her house. 22 The lamp shines on the holy lampstand, and a beautiful face on a sedate stature. 23 Pillars of gold stand on bases of silver, and beautiful legs on the soles of a woman of dignity. 24 Foundations on a rock stand forever, and the commandments of the Lord are in the heart of a pure woman.
After revealing the traits of the wicked wife, he tells us about the blessed wife:
a. She makes her husband glad, and makes his bones fat by her skill [13].
b. She is marked by holy silence and by conduct with good manners [14].
c. She is chaste in soul and modest in her clothing, bearing the grace of purity [15].
d. She is radiant like the sun, as one who rises from the heights of heaven [16], and she walks with management and order.
e. She gives light to those walking in darkness, like the lamp set on the lampstand [17].
f. Her movements are glorious, her feet beautiful like two pillars of gold on two bases of silver [18].

In brief, the blessed wife resembles the heavenly Jerusalem, which presents a blessed life to those who dwell in it. She also resembles the Church, the bride of Christ. Moreover, what applies to the wife, whether good or wicked, applies also to the husband, indeed to every person. In the same spirit St. Peter presents to us the role of the good wife in winning her unbelieving husband (1 Pet 3:1-5).

He began by speaking of the good, faithful, peace-loving woman as a great portion and a blessing given to him who fears the Lord [3]. After that comes his discourse on the wicked wife and the impudent daughter, and then he returns to speak of the blessed wife. It is as though he does not want the husband or father to be hasty in judging the wife or the daughter, so that he justifies to himself a revolt against them. Rather we must look to what is good and blessed in their lives, and so he begins the discourse about them and also ends it.
The traits of the good wife are:
Kindness, which pours gladness upon the husband [13].
Skill: she has her artistic and mental abilities, so she knows no sluggishness and does not fall into smallness of soul, and her husband feels as though his bones within him delight in his wife [13].
Modesty: her dignity and balance pour upon her personality grace upon grace, and her husband admires her chastity and purity [15].
Her beauty does not come from her bodily appearance, but from the splendor that shines out from her as from the sun, like a heavenly grace, and is reflected even upon the order of her house [16].
Like the lofty lampstand, she dispels the darkness and gives light to those around her.

There is harmony between the outward beauty, even of her feet, and the inward beauty of the hidden heart, which no one sees except the Lord. Her feet move upon the earth like a godly woman of God, and with her heart she soars to heaven, where the Heavenly One establishes His Kingdom in her heart. Such a wife cannot be known by anyone through his abstract thought, but she is a gift from the Lord [14].
The kindness of the wife makes her husband glad, and her skill makes his bones fat [13].

The husband sees in his blessed wife a living image of the Church, in whom the heavenly Bridegroom delights. And her skill makes his bones fat; so is the seriousness of believers in putting their skill and gifts to work for the sake of the Kingdom of God.
