A silent wife is a gift from the Lord, and a disciplined soul cannot be valued at any price [14].

The wife who is silent in the Lord, her heart meditates in the law of the Lord, and her mind converses with her Savior, and her disciplined soul submits to her heavenly Bridegroom. This is reflected in the marital relationship, so that her husband feels that she cannot be valued at any price.
A modest wife is grace upon grace, and there is no scale that can weigh a chaste soul [15].

The modesty of the wife does not stop at outward appearance and clothing, but her modesty goes back to her inner life, where the Lord Himself establishes His holy and awesome Kingdom. This inner modesty is reflected in all her outward conduct, even the way she walks and her smile and her voice, so that whoever deals with her senses the overflow of God's grace upon her without interruption. He also feels a complete inability to describe her and to evaluate her life.
Like the sun rising from the heights of heaven, is the beauty of the good wife in her well-ordered house [16].

Everyone who looks at the Church of Christ sees her as an icon of the Sun of Righteousness, all light, shining upon the world and rising upon all who live in her. So the blessed wife shines like the sun from the heights of heaven. The husband and the children feel that her holy life lifts the whole house as though to Paradise. The family sees in this blessed wife that she imitates her Lord, who is not the God of confusion but of peace, as in all the churches of the saints (1 Cor 14:33).
Like the lamp that shines on the holy lampstand, is the beauty of the features in the life of one in good health [8] [17].

St. John the Beloved looked to the Lord Christ sitting on the throne with His Church around Him as seven shining lampstands (Rev 1:12). So the blessed wife, or the holy soul, is lifted by the Spirit of God, the Holy One, from glory to glory, and the heavenly ones see her as a lampstand in heaven around the divine throne.
Beautiful feet together with a steadfast heart are like pillars of gold standing on bases of silver [18].

Sirach did not describe the body of the blessed wife, but was content with her feet and her heart. The beautiful feet point to continual movement night and day, even during her slumber, as it is said: "I sleep, but my heart waketh" (Song 5:2); they move as though on the wings of the Holy Spirit from height to height, until she reaches the sight of the heavenly Bridegroom face to face (1 Cor 13:12). As for her feet, they are like pillars of gold standing on bases of silver, reminding us of the tabernacle and the temple of Solomon, which stood on pillars whose bases were silver. So the husband sees in his blessed wife the temple of God, with the Spirit of God dwelling in her (1 Cor 3:16). As for the heart, it points to the hidden heavenly sanctuaries overflowing with holiness and love.

entries.section: 4. Three things that grieve the heart

paragraphs.text: 25 Two things grieve my heart, and the third makes me angry: 26 a man of war when want makes him helpless, and wise men when they are despised, 27 and one who turns back from righteousness to sin, the Lord keeps him for the sword. 28 Hardly shall a merchant be free from iniquity, and the tavern-keeper shall not be acquitted of sin.

The heart of Ben Sira grieves over two things, and anger rises in him over the third thing. What are these three things? Ben Sira feared that some young men might misunderstand his discourse on the wicked wife, and look at woman with a pessimistic eye, asking: Can a young man find a wife who has these traits? This is what led him to bring out dangerous specimens of wicked young men, such as: 1. A war hero who in his pride deviates into idleness. 2. Young men who insult the wise and despise them [19]. 3. The righteous who through their negligence deviated into sin [19]. 4. Dishonest working merchants, who commit iniquity [20] through their greed and unfaithfulness.

Two things grieve my heart, and at the third anger rises in me: a man of war who is in want because of poverty, and wise men when they are insulted, and one who turns back from righteousness to sin: the Lord will prepare him for the sword [19].

The first thing: a man of war whom poverty has made helpless. If as a man of war he exerted all his effort to protect the state, then in time of peace he must not rely on his reputation as a mighty warrior who loves his country and his people, but he must work without ceasing. Sirach looks to work as a holy matter, not only to satisfy temporal needs, but also to keep the soul striving without idleness. Therefore he demands even of the old that they work according to their ability and means.
The second thing: the insulting of the wise, instead of honoring them by imitating them and seeking their counsel.
The third thing: that a person turn back from the righteousness of God because of a temporary pleasure of sin.

v Even he who fasts for his sins, and walks in his way again and practices the same conduct, who will hear his prayer? Again we read: "If anyone turn back from his righteousness to sin, the Lord will prepare him for the sword," and also: "As a dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly" (Prov 26:11) [9].
St. John Chrysostom A merchant will hardly avoid committing iniquity, and the peddler will not be acquitted of sin [20].
Trade can be a holy work when the seller and the buyer are faithful and care for the salvation of their souls.
a. The Law pointed to exactness in the balance and the measure and to not cheating.
b. Not cheating in goods offered for sale.
c. Caution against the temptation of exaggerated profit.
Inspired by Sirach 26

entries.section: Prepare all as a heavenly bride!

paragraphs.text: v Every believer longs to receive his bride from Your hands.
And every believing woman wishes to see You transfigured in her bridegroom.
Let Your Holy Spirit work in every family.
Let all our life be the object of Your good pleasure and delight.
Grant us Your peace and bestow upon us Your blessings. Let our depths enjoy a foretaste of Your heavens.
And let our conduct and our features bear witness to Your grace!
v Take away from us the spirit of envy and evil jealousy, and give our tongue sweetness.

Let us be drunk with the wine of Your love, so that our heart may widen to all mankind, and our emotions and senses be sanctified by Your dwelling in us. Take away from us every deviation, and nail Your fear in us.
Grant us the single eye, not impudent. Grant me that You accompany me on the journey of my life.
So that I do not desire the waters of the world and its pleasures.
v Establish me in true membership in Your Church.
So that the heavenly ones rejoice in Your kindness to me.
And sanctify all my powers to work for Your Kingdom.
Grant me holy silence: my tongue is silent, and my heart speaks; and my heart is silent, and You, O Holy One, speak within me.
Your holy fear grants me true modesty.
It pours Your grace into me, so that my heart is filled with chastity.
v Rise, O Sun of Righteousness, from Your heavens upon my soul.
Make me a light to the world according to Your divine promise.
Let there be no place for darkness within me, but let me bear the reflection of Your splendor upon me.
v When shall I see all mankind as shining lampstands around Your throne?!
When will You light the lamp of my soul, and lift me upon the lampstand?
Sanctify even my feet, so that I move always toward Your heavens.
Count me a pillar of gold standing upon Your law, the silver base.
Grant my heart steadfastness, so that the winds of the world do not move me.
v Would that I might not grieve the hearts of the saints.
So that I may not be like an idle man of war after the battle, but work continually under the leading of Your fiery Spirit.
And that I may not despise the wise, but seek their counsel, their prayers and their blessing.
And that I may not return to sin again, but hide in Your righteousness.
v Make me a faithful merchant, who does not covet the possessions of the world, nor walk in a spirit of deceit, but sells everything in order to acquire You.
O You, the Pearl of great price!

1 Many have sinned for the sake of the goods of this world, and he who seeks riches turns away his eye. 2 Between the joinings of stones a nail is driven, and between selling and buying sin is wedged in. 3 And iniquity shall be crushed together with the wicked. 4 Unless a man holds fast with diligence to the fear of the Lord, his house shall quickly be overthrown.
Behind grave sins lies a deviation of thought, especially in commercial work. Some businessmen look for suitable opportunities that bring them more profit while giving up some upright principles.

Trade in general is not evil, but if a person practices his trade at the expense of his upright principles for the greatest possible profit, then although his aim is sound, namely to build up his wealth through trade, yet if the person loses the uprightness of his life he sins, even if others among businessmen are accustomed to it.
Many have sinned because of obtaining profit, and he who seeks riches turns away his eye [1].
A nail is driven between fitting stones, and sin is wedged in between selling and buying [2].
He who does not hold fast to the fear of the Lord, his house is quickly overthrown [3].

Just as the nail finds a safe, firm place between fitting stones, so the sin of the love of money hides behind some trading operations, and the remedy is to hold fast to the fear of the Lord. It befits the businessman to walk in the fear of the Lord with faithfulness, truthfulness, sincerity and contentment, even if some businessmen are accustomed to a kind of deceit for the sake of gain. "He that buildeth his house with other men's money is like one that gathereth himself stones for the tomb of his burial (or: in a storm)" (see Sir 21:8).

5 When a sieve is shaken, the refuse remains; so the filth of a man remains in his thinking. 6 The potter's vessels are tested in the furnace, and a man is proved by his speech. 7 The tillage of a tree is shown by its fruit; so the thought of a man's heart is shown by his words. 8 Praise no man before he speaks; for this is how men are tested.
When the sieve is shaken the filth remains; so the filthiness of a man remains in his thoughts [4].

As long as the sieve is still, with wheat or other grain heaped in it, the sand and dust in it do not show; but as soon as it is shaken the grains fall through and the filth remains to be thrown on the dunghill. So man, as long as he is slack in examining his depths and reviewing his aims under the leading of the Holy Spirit, does not perceive his faults, nor present repentance for them.

v It remains now to understand what this commandment contains as addressed to the power of the mind. "Take heed to thyself"; I mean that you observe yourself from every side, that the inner sight of your soul be alert to guard yourself, as you pass through the midst of snares; for the enemy has set hidden snares on every side. Watch everything with all care so that you may "be saved as a gazelle from snares, and as a bird from traps (Prov 6:5) [1].

v When you are occupied with some sin, be an accuser of yourself (Prov 18:17), and do not wait for others to bring the accusation. In this you become like a righteous man who accuses himself in the first speech he makes in court, or like Job, whom the crowd of the people in the city did not hinder from declaring his offense before all [2].

St. Basil the Great v As a man comes out of his mother's womb naked, so also the soul goes out of the body. Some souls go out pure and shining, others stained and degraded, and a third kind defiled with many sins. Therefore the rational soul that loves God, remembering the trials and distresses awaiting after death and meditating on them, lives in righteousness so that it may not be condemned nor subjected to these distresses. But unbelievers do not have such feelings, for they commit sins, making light of what awaits them [3].
St. Anthony the Great As the potter's vessels are tested in the furnace, so a man is tested by his arguments [5].
The martyr Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, sees that this statement is the basis of the view of St. Paul and of all Christians concerning suffering.

v After the shipwreck, after the scourging, and after terrifying torments of the body (2 Cor 11:23-33), the Apostle Paul says that he suffered no harm, but rather benefited from the trial, because indeed he was proved through such terrible sorrow. He says: "There was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure. For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Cor 12:7-10).

When weakness or inadequacy or any ruin takes hold of us, then our strength is made perfect. Therefore if our faith is put to the test it stands firm and receives a crown, as it is written: "The furnace proveth the potter's vessels, and the trial of tribulation proves the righteous." This, in brief, is the difference between us and the others who do not know God: in the day of trial they complain and murmur, but the trial does not let us leave the truth that belongs to virtue and faith, but strengthens us by its sufferings [4].

The martyr Cyprian, bishop of Carthage v God has authority over us as the potter over the clay, to form from the same material vessels unto honor and vessels unto dishonor. Therefore, as for you who answer God in a spirit of haughtiness, it is enough for you to hear these things [5].

Origen v The lion creeps into a hidden ambush to prey upon the righteous, and earthen vessels are tested in the furnace (see Sir 27:5), and the righteous are tested by trials. For in another place it is written: "My son, if thou come to serve the Lord, prepare thy soul for temptation" (see Sir 2:1) [6].

St. Jerome This fire, as St. Augustine says, is the fire of trials, which burns the one whose works were earthly, while it purifies the one whose works were according to the Lord's good pleasure, and increases his splendor [7].

v Earthen vessels become hard by fire; so the strength of the body of Christ is not consumed by fire like straw but grows harder like earthen vessels, through the fire of the sufferings (of Christ) [8].

v The fire tests the quality of each one's work: if his work endures, the work which he built (and it endures if the person is concerned with divine things, how to please the Lord), he receives a reward for his concern; and if it is burned he loses his reward, because he cannot keep what he loves (earthly things), but he himself shall be saved, yet so as by fire (1 Cor 3:15). This last expression means that without the pain of the fire he cannot destroy the pleasures which he loved to build up.

v Here it seems to me that we have a fire which these people do not lose, a fire which brings gain to one person and loss to another, and is a test of both. This fire is not the fire which our Lord means when He says to those on His left: "Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire" (Mt 25:41) [9].

St. Augustine St. Augustine distinguishes between one who is tempted and one who falls into temptation. For in the Lord's Prayer, when we ask "lead us not into temptation," we are not asking not to be tempted, but not to enter into it.

v The prayer here is not that we may not be tempted, but that we may not enter into temptation. It is like one who passes through a trial by fire: he does not pray that the fire may not touch him, but that he may not perish by the fire, for "the potter's vessels are tested in the furnace, and the righteous in the trial of tribulation" [5]. Joseph was tempted by the enticements of an adulteress, but he did not enter into the temptation (Gen 39:17). Susanna was tempted but she did not enter into the temptation (Dan 13:20, addition). And so many of both sexes, especially Job [10].

St. Augustine v After a man among us confesses his fault, he is transformed by his repentance into a change through knowledge, and shows remarkable progress, and so he is tempted by the enemy, and the strength of his soul and the soundness of his purpose are tested. Indeed Scripture says: He who has not been tested is not worthy of trust. No one will reach perfection unless he is first tested by trials [11].

Rufinus v The blessed John the Evangelist, who was certainly not less than St. Jacob (son of Isaac) in merits, declares: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 Jn 1:8). Moreover we read in another place: "A just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Prov 24:16). Therefore, since it was not possible for the blessed Jacob to be without light sins, God wished to destroy these small transgressions in this world by the fire of tribulations. In him was fulfilled the word of God by the Holy Spirit: "The potter's vessels are tested in the furnace, and a man is proved by his speech." Moreover, "God scourgeth every son whom he receiveth" (Heb 12:6) and "we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God" (Acts 14:21). Therefore, in order that God might present the holy Jacob as pure gold on the coming day of judgment, He first removed from him every stain of sin, so that the other witness of fire might find nothing in him to burn [12].
Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles As the fruit shows how the tree was cultivated, so the thought of a man shows his heart [6].
Do not praise a man before he reveals his way of thinking, for by this a man is tested [7].

As the tree is known by its fruit, so a man is known by his speech. For speech is the translation of inner feelings and an expression of the hidden things of the heart: "For by speech wisdom shall be known, and learning by the word of the tongue" (see Sir 4:24). Therefore it is not fitting to praise a man without listening to him. Thus Ben Sira sets great value upon silence and speech: through silence a person listens to his depths and finds the opportunity to know himself and to enter into dialogue with God, and in a person's speech there is a translation of his personality.

9 If you pursue righteousness you will overtake it, and put it on as a robe of glory, and dwell with it; and it will keep you forever, and in the day of visitation you will find support. 10 Birds resort to their kind, and truth returns to those who practice it. 11 The lion lies in wait for the prey; so sins lie in wait for those who work iniquity.
If you pursue righteousness you will obtain it, and put it on as a glorious robe [8].

Ben Sira fears that there may be a conflict between the demands of wisdom and the demands of wealth, so he makes clear the possibility of overcoming this conflict, saying that he who strives to seek wisdom finds it, and even puts it on as a glorious robe [8]. There is no unavoidable conflict between holy righteousness and the practice of trade. The holy God strives toward man and seeks him, and presents to him His righteousness with the crown in His hand, to set it upon him if he responds to Him.
As birds gather to their own kind, so truth returns to those who practice it [9].

One of the factors that make the conflict between the holy life and trade possible to overcome is the existence of good businessmen, who are not as rare as some suppose. These can gather together to sanctify commercial work, for birds gather to their own kind. So the godly in every work support their brothers in the Lord.
The lion lies in wait for its prey; so sin lies in wait for those who work iniquity [10].
The Apostle says: "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour" (1 Pet 5:8).

v Is there anything more terrifying than Satan? Yet we find no armor against him except faith, for it is an unseen shield against an unseen enemy, who aims various arrows in the midst of the night at those who are unguarded. But since he is an unseen enemy, we have faith as a mighty instrument, as the Apostle says: "Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked" (Eph 6:16). When Satan casts a burning spark of base lust, faith shows the image of judgment, and the mind extinguishes the spark [13].
St. Cyril of Jerusalem

12 The talk of the godly man is always wisdom, but the fool changes like the moon. 13 Among the foolish watch for the opportunity, and among the wise be constant. 14 The talk of fools is hateful, and their laughter is in the pleasures of sin. 15 The speech of him who swears much makes the hair stand on end, and his quarrel makes one stop the ears. 16 The quarrel of the proud is the shedding of blood, and their abuse is grievous to hear.
The talk of the godly man is wise at all times, but the fool changes like the moon [11].

The wise godly are marked by their steadfastness in their godliness, their sincerity and truthfulness, and they are counted men of peace; therefore those who work in trade often rest in them and are reassured by their conduct. But as for fools, even if they swear, others do not trust them nor feel secure in dealing with them. Origen sees that the foolish man is like one sick with epilepsy; when the sickness attacks him he becomes like another person, entirely different from what he is.

v Epilepsy attacks its victims at various intervals, and when the sick man suffers from it he seems a person entirely different from himself in good health, when the epilepsy is not at work in him. This same disorder you may find in certain souls, those which are thought to be healthy when they are in a state of self-control and the practice of other virtues. But they become at times as though in a state of epilepsy when their passions provoke them. They fall from the state in which they were, and the deceits of this world and the other lusts draw them away (Mk 4:19). Perhaps you would not be wrong in saying of them that they suffer from a spiritual epilepsy, when they fall through "spiritual wickedness in high places" (Eph 6:12).

They often become sick at the time when the passions attack their souls, and they fall into the fire (Mt 17:15). As it was said by Hosea that they become adulterers "as an oven heated by the baker" (Hos 7:4). And they fall again into the water (Mt 17:15), when the king of all the dragons brings them down from the ark, where they appeared to breathe freely, and they fell into the depths of the currents of the sea of human life.

This interpretation of ours concerning the fool is supported by the one who says in the Book of Wisdom, concerning the traits of the righteous man: "The talk of the godly man is always wisdom," but the fool changes like the moon [14].

Origen The fool changes like the moon: St. Augustine says: [The sun signifies the spiritual, and the moon the carnal... The sun is the wise person, and the moon the unwise person... "The wise man endures like the sun, and the fool changes like the moon" [15].] He also sees that the wise man here points to the wisdom of God incarnate, as the Sun of Righteousness, and the fool is Adam fallen into sin.

v Note now what we read in Proverbs: "The wise man continues like the sun, but the fool changes like the moon" (see Sir 27:12). Who is the wise man who continues, but the Sun of Righteousness, of whom it was said: "The Sun of Righteousness shall rise upon me" (see Mal 4:2)? But the wicked, upon whom He does not rise, will say weeping on the last day: "The light of righteousness hath not shined unto us... and the sun rose not upon us." For God made the sun visible to bodily eyes, rising on the evil and on the good (Mt 5:45)..

Who is the fool who changes like the moon but Adam, "in whom all have sinned" (see Rom 5:12)? Without doubt, when the human mind withdraws from the Sun of Righteousness, I mean from inward contemplation of the unchanging truth, turning all its powers to earthly things, it is struck more and more with blindness to the sight of what is within and of heavenly things. But when it begins to return to the unchanging wisdom, then, to the degree that it draws near to wisdom (God) in holy love, "the outward man perisheth, yet the inward man is renewed day by day" (2 Cor 4:16). Then all the light of its mind which was directed to base aims is turned to lofty aims, that is, it is turned from earthly things so that the person may die more and more to the world, and his life be hid with Christ in God [16].

St. Augustine v Our eyes do not always see (the moon) in the fullness of its size: now it represents the perfection of the round disk, and when it wanes and decreases it shows a lack on one side. And when it grows from a crescent to a full moon it is darkened on one side. And when it is pale the other side disappears.

Now it is not without a mystical reason that the divine Creator of the universe made the moon appear from time to time in different shapes. It is a dazzling parable of our nature. Nothing is stable in man. Here man rises from nothing to perfection... and suddenly he undergoes gradual decline, and is shattered by continual diminishing. So looking at the moon makes us think of the swiftness of the changes of human affairs, and teaches us not to be proud of the good things of this life, nor to boast of our power, nor to be seduced by passing riches, but to despise our body, which is subject to change, and to care for the soul because its goodness is unchanging [17].

v If the moon causes you grief by its diminishing brilliance and its gradual waning, so much the more ought you to be troubled by the soul that has virtue and through negligence destroys its beauty, and does not remain as it was, but is turned about and changed continually through the whims of the mind. Truly Scripture says: "The fool changes like the moon" (see Sir 27:11) [18].

St. Basil the Great v If we feel grief when we see the moon become pale, which recovers what it lost and renews itself, how much more if your soul, full of the fruit of virtue, changes often in its purpose and in its directions colored by rashness. This is the extreme of folly and ignorance, for Scripture says: "The fool changes like the moon," but the righteous continues like the sun (Ps 72:5).

The moon has no share in foolishness, for it does not change like the fool, but the fool changes like the moon... The moon works for your sake, and submits to the management of God's will... But you take upon yourself change by your own choice... Without understanding you often find joy in it [19].

v The wise man is not destroyed by fear, nor changed by power, nor does he boast over good news, nor is he swallowed up by sorrow. Where wisdom is, there is strength of spirit with perseverance and endurance.

The wise man is steadfast in soul, and is not tossed about by the change of events. He does not waver like a child, nor is he moved with every wind of doctrine, but remains perfect in Christ, grounded in love, rooted by faith. The wise man will not be idle and has no experience of change of mood of the mind, but shines like the Sun of Righteousness, who shines forth in the kingdom of His Father (Mt 13:34) [20].
v The foolish man cannot of himself become a disciple of virtue or persevere in his aim, for the fool changes like the moon [21].

St. Ambrose v God dwells in the midst of His saints, and where there is holiness there is the dwelling of God. God gives a dwelling to men in one way, to those who choose the way of one life and persevere in it. Truly the righteous man is steadfast (unchanging), for he takes one decision, and for all time, to live the righteous life. But the sinner, on the contrary, is inconstant: "The wicked is changeable like the moon" (see Sir 27:11) [22].
St. Jerome Limit your time among the foolish, and instead spend it among the wise [12].

It befits the believer to choose the suitable time to speak with the foolish and listen to them. Indeed he takes care to flee from them when necessary, because their talk is sometimes meaningless, their jesting silly, and their stories stumbling blocks that corrupt the soul of the listeners. "Esteem your relatives as much as you can, and take counsel with the wise. Let your conversation be with the wise, and all your talk in the law of the Most High. Let righteous men be your table companions, and your glory in the fear of the Lord" (see 9:14-16).
The talk of fools is hateful, and their laughter is in the pleasures of sin [13].

The talk of fools is hateful, especially their talk about God, for they suppose that He in His heavens has no relation to men while they are on their earth. Fools practice their evils in the darkness, supposing that God does not see them and is not concerned with their lives.

v The man who supposes that he is not seen by Him who sees all things, and that his transgressions are hidden by the darkness, dwells in the shadows. In vain he reckons that there is no one who watches him, for the eye of the Lord is brighter than the sun, it uncovers all secrets, and lights up all darkness, and enters into the knowledge of the depths of the heart, and pierces the heights and the depths (see Sir 23:19).. Therefore he is found out like a fugitive and a wicked hireling (mercenary), known before he hides himself..

He who supposes that he hides his crime falls into a vain hope, utters vain words and not the truth. Truly the talk of fools is hateful (see 27:13), producing not fruits but wailing. For the speech of a fool is like a (heavy) burden on the way (see 21:16). What is sin but a weight? It weighs down the traveler in this world, so that he sinks downward by its weight. He who does not wish to be weighed down, let him look to the Lord who says: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mt 11:28) [23].
St. Ambrose Speech full of oaths makes the hair stand on end at last, and quarreling obliges a person to stop his ears [14].
He who dares to use the holy and awesome Name without reserve or reverence, his talk makes the hair stand on end.
The quarrel of the proud leads to the shedding of blood, and their abuse is grievous to hear [15].
It befits us not to dispute with the proud and reckless, nor to insult them, nor to rub against them, and we should use the methods suitable to them and at the suitable time.

17 He who reveals secrets destroys trust, and shall never find a friend for himself. 18 Love your friend, and be faithful to him, 19 but if you reveal his secrets, do not seek him afterward. 20 For he who has destroyed the friendship of his neighbor is as one who has destroyed his enemy. 21 And just as you let a bird go from your hand, so you have let your neighbor go and you will not catch him again. 22 Do not seek him, for he is far off and has fled, like a roe from the snare. 23 A wound can be bound up, and after abuse there is reconciliation, 24 but he who reveals secrets has no hope.
He who reveals secrets destroys his credibility, and finds no friend for life [16].

It befits a person to be worthy to become a depository of secrets. This requires that he be wise, enjoying spiritual satisfaction and filled with spiritual and social knowledge. For revealing a secret is counted a mark of shame for the one who revealed it. The faithful friend does not reveal secrets even after the death of their owners, but remains faithful to them even after their departure.
Love your friend and be faithful to him, but if you reveal his secrets, do not pursue him closely [17].
Just as a man destroys his enemy, so you have destroyed the friendship of your neighbor [18].
It is difficult for a person to regain the friendship and trust of one whose secret he revealed.
And just as you may let a bird go from your hand, so let your neighbor go, and do not catch him again [19].
Do not pursue him, for he has gone far away from you, and has fled like a hart from the snare [20].

Ben Sira compares the friend who has lost trust in his friend, because he revealed his secret, to the bird that escaped from the hand of the hunter and flew from him so that there is no way to recover it. And like a gazelle that has come out of the snare and gone off without return to the same snare.
A wound can be bound up, and abuse can be forgiven, but he who reveals secrets has no hope [21].
It is almost impossible for the friend to regain his friendship with one who revealed his secret, and if he returns to him he does not disclose his secret to him any more.

25 He who winks with the eye devises evils, and no one can avoid him. 26 In your presence his mouth is sweet, and he admires your words, but afterward he turns his speech, and out of your words he lays a stumbling block before you. 27 I have hated many things, but nothing like him, and the Lord will hate him.
He who winks with his eye plans evil deeds, and there is no one who can avoid him [22].
In your presence his speech is sweet, and he admires your words, and afterward he distorts by his speech what you said, and out of your words he troubles you [23].
I hate many things, but nothing like him, and the Lord also will hate him [24].

The Psalmist speaks of the hypocrite, saying: "The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords" (Ps 55:21). This applies to Judas, who betrayed his Master with a kiss.

v They approached Him to test Him (Lk 2:19-26), hiding from Him their deceitful aim. They addressed Him with soft words, while they were like fierce beasts in sheep's clothing. Such as these the Psalmist also rebuked, saying: "Their words are softer than oil, yet are they sharpened arrows" [24].
St. Cyril the Great

entries.section: 7. Sin bears its fruit in itself

paragraphs.text: 28 He who casts a stone upward casts it on his own head, and a blow struck by deceit wounds the deceiver. 29 He who digs a pit falls into it, and he who sets a snare is caught in it. 30 He who does evil, it rolls back upon him, and he does not know from where it comes upon him. 31 Mockery and reproach belong to the proud, and vengeance lies in wait for them like a lion. 32 Those who rejoice at the fall of the godly are caught in a snare, and pain consumes them before their death. 33 Malice and anger, both are abominations, and the sinful man holds fast to them.
He who throws a stone into the air throws it on his own head, and the blow of deceit wounds the deceiver [25].
The devil supposed that he was able to be rid of the Lord Christ by crucifying Him, and did not realize that by the Cross the authority of the devil and all his powers was shattered.

v Those who delivered Jesus up (to crucifixion) have become forgotten. The high priests no longer exist, and no high priests came after them. The scribes who condemned Him to death, their minds were darkened and their understandings struck with blindness, and they are no longer able to see the meaning of the holy texts.

All those who condemned Jesus to death were delivered up to the enemy of Christ. Those who mocked Him in their turn became an object of mockery when the enemies surrounded Jerusalem and its desolation drew near (Lk 21:20). Those who scourged Jesus were themselves scourged, and have continued so until the time of the fullness of the Gentiles comes in (Rom 11:25).

Truly he who throws a stone into the air, it falls on his own head [25]. All this happened because of God's unceasing concern for them, and they become among those who are saved from the Gentiles together with the chosen remnant (Rom 11:5). Truly, had God not left a remnant, they would have become like Sodom and Gomorrah (Isa 1:9) [25].

Origen v It happens at times that when an arrow is aimed at something smooth it rebounds upon the one who shot it, and wounds him who wished to wound (another). In this the words are fulfilled: "He who casts a stone upward casts it on his own head" [25][26].
St. Jerome He who digs a pit will fall into it, and he who sets a snare will be caught in it [26].

v It is written: "He who digs a pit falls into it"; for though they bind our hands and feet (like the three young men), love has authority to loose us. Note this miracle. Those who bound them, the fire set free. It is as though some persons had been delivered to the servants of their friends, and the servants, because of the friendship of their masters, instead of harming them treated them with all gentleness. So the fire acted when it knew that the three young men were friends: it broke their fetters and freed them, and let them walk, and the fire became a passage for them, falling beneath their feet. Justly were they cast into the fire for the glory of God [27].
St. John Chrysostom He who does evils, they roll back upon him, and he does not perceive what strikes him [28] [27].

entries.section: 7. Sin bears its fruit in itself

paragraphs.text: It is told of a godly Christian slave that the rest of the slaves in the palace hated him and planned to kill him; so one of them went and informed against him to the master, who devised a plot to kill him. He ordered him to go early to some people outside the city who kindle a fire, to bring something from them, and he had agreed with them to kill him by throwing him into the fire as soon as he reached them. But the good slave, on his way that morning, heard the bell of the church, so he went there, intending to do the master's errand after the Liturgy. As for the informer, in the morning, some time after the Christian slave had left the palace, he thought of enjoying the sight of the Christian slave in the fire. When he drew near the fire the men fell upon him and hastened to throw him into the fire without verifying his identity and without listening to his protest. When the Liturgy ended and the Christian slave went toward the place where the slaves were, he found a fire that had gone out and found no one of the people, so he returned to apologize to the master, who was astonished at seeing him. And after wearying himself with thought he learned the whole truth of the matter, that it was nothing but an informing, and the informer was punished by dying in place of the one he had informed against; thus God returned the evil upon its doer [29].
Mockery and abuse belong to the proud, and vengeance lies in wait for him like a lion [28].
Those who rejoice at the fall of the godly are taken in the snare, and pain consumes them before their death [29].

Many of the Fathers of the Church, such as St. Macarius the Great, affirm that sin bears its corruption in itself, so the wicked man who is determined on his evil perishes as a natural fruit of evil, certain to corrupt. The wicked man has no need of one to restrain and punish him, but what he does brings him bitterness and death! He drinks from the same cup that he filled for himself, unless he casts the cup away through enjoying fellowship with his Savior, and his earnest striving through the holy will in the Lord.

entries.section: 7. Sin bears its fruit in itself

paragraphs.text: v If you remain concerned with the dust, you will in the end be turned to it. It befits you to change, you must be transformed, you must become heavenly [30].
Origen Anger and malice are both hateful, and the sinful man possesses both [30].

entries.section: 7. Sin bears its fruit in itself

paragraphs.text: v "Anger destroys even the wise. A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger" (see Prov 15:1). Surely all things depend on our decision, whether to stir up anger or to calm it... "A soft answer turneth away wrath," that is, the way of answering in evident humility and without harshness [31].

entries.section: 7. Sin bears its fruit in itself

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom v Our Lord presented most of His commandments to us by persuasion rather than by commands. Gentle rains moisten the earth and penetrate it, but very heavy rain spoils the surface of the earth and presses upon it so that it is not absorbed. "Grievous words stir up anger" (Prov 15:1), and cause harm. When the harsh word opens a door, anger enters, and harm follows [32].
St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian Inspired by Sirach 27

entries.section: Keep me from the corruption and bitterness of sin!

paragraphs.text: v You gave me mind and thought that I might know You and love You.
In folly I brought my thoughts down to the dust. Grant me to leave the dust and ashes, and to enjoy meeting Your Holy Spirit, who reveals to me my esteem for You, O Holy One.
I return to You that You may sanctify my thoughts in You.
I despise the pleasure of sin, and my heart burns with longing for fellowship with You.
Let me know that my soul is exceedingly precious in Your eyes!
v Let my depths be sifted in the furnace of trials.
You reshape them and restore to me Your image.
By the fires of trials You destroy all that is dust in me, and plant Your Cross within me.
You establish Your Kingdom and shatter all darkness in me!
v Grant me to soar toward the heavenly places with Your saints.
Let us gather together as birds gather to their own kind.
I do not fear the devil who roars to devour me.
I take refuge in You, O Lion who came out of the tribe of Judah.
The snare of Satan is broken, and by You I escape his nets!
v Grant me by Your grace to grow continually, to be enlightened by You, O Sun of Righteousness, and to give light always.
I shall not suffer continual change like the moon, but through You become a light to the world!
I will stay long with the wise, and flee from the councils of fools!
Sanctify my mouth, that it may utter only the truth and know neither the wounding word nor the evil word!
Let me not know the quarrels of the proud nor their abuse.
v Let me cleave to You, O wonderful Friend.
In You I cover the weaknesses of my brothers, and in You I walk faithfully, so that I do not reveal their secrets.
v Take from me the garment of deceptive hypocrisy, and grant me to put on Your righteousness, which covers my weaknesses!
I will not cast a stone into the air, lest it fall upon my head.
Nor dig a pit for anyone, lest I fall into it.
I will not harbor evil against anyone, lest it come upon me!
I will not rejoice at anyone's falling into the snare, nor be glad at the death of a wicked man!
Rather let love settle in my inward parts, in my heart and my mind.
Let love flow in my blood toward all mankind!
Let me taste the foretaste of heaven, so that I know neither malice nor anger.
Set me free from every sin and set free all my brothers, that I may experience the joy of the Spirit with every believer!
1 Whoever takes vengeance will find vengeance from the Lord, and the Lord will keep a close watch on his sins.

Vengeance is among the first sins that man practiced (Gen 4:14-15, 23-24). Sirach begins by observing that those who seek vengeance on their brethren are themselves called to account for the errors and sins they have committed. It was said of Cain: "Whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold" (Gen 4:15).
Whoever seeks vengeance will be overtaken by the vengeance of the Lord, who will surely punish him for his sins [1].

The Book of Deuteronomy recorded the same concept: "To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence; their foot shall slide in due time: for the day of their calamity is at hand, and the things that shall come upon them make haste" (Deut 32:35), and the Apostle Paul confirmed it: "Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Rom 12:19).
St. Basil the Great stands amazed as he looks at man in his state of agitation. He loses his natural characteristics as a human being, even his features change, and he becomes like another person.
One wonders: has the man been transformed into a beast, or has a demon entered him and changed his whole being?!

v Who can describe such an evil accurately?! How the quick-tempered, as soon as some pretext chances to seize them, cry out and shout and attack with a shame no less than the shame of the brute or of the beast that breathes out venom! Nothing stops such a person until immense harm that cannot be remedied has occurred, as if a bubble of wrath were bursting and boiling, pouring out scorching waves without restraint. Neither the edge of a sword, nor fire, nor anything else terrifying can stop and restrain a soul driven headlong by the madness of anger.
No one is able to restrain those possessed by demons; so the wrathful are no different from them, either in appearance or in the inclinations of their souls.

For those who long for vengeance, the blood boils in their hearts, as if it were kindling and breathing out as from a raging, blazing fire. They burst out and their anger appears for all to see, so that the angry man looks different from the man everyone knows and is accustomed to, as if he had put on his face a mask like that worn by one who stands on a stage. Those near him do not see in his eyes those usual expressions, but the marks of madness appear in his gaze, and fires blaze in his eyes. He grinds his teeth like a wild boar going out to battle. His face becomes flushed and full of blood, his body swells and grows heavy, and his blood vessels burst. His breathing quickens savagely, as though a storm were raging within him. His voice rises and trembles and reaches the utmost pitch, and no one understands what he says; it pours out without restraint, rushing along without order or logic and without clarity [1].
St. Basil the Great

2 Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done you; then when you pray, your sins will be forgiven. 3 Does a man harbor anger against another man, and then seek healing from the Lord? 4 Or does he not show mercy to a man like himself, and then ask forgiveness for his own sins? 5 If he, being flesh, holds on to resentment, who will atone for his sins? 6 Remember your last end, and cease from enmity. 7 Remember corruption and death, and abide in the commandments. 8 Remember the commandments, and do not bear malice toward your neighbor. 9 Remember the covenant of the Most High, and overlook ignorance.
Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has committed, and your sins will be forgiven when you pray [2].

Ben Sira does not ask the wise man merely to refrain from vengeance; he requires him to forgive the one who worked to harm him, so that God may hear him and forgive his sins [2]. As the Lord Christ teaches us to pray: "Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors" (Mt 6:12). The Lord Christ comments on this prayer: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: but if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses" (Mt 6:15). The Lord Christ made this principle clear by the parable of the servant who would not forgive his fellowservant (Mt 18:23-25).

Truly God, who is all love and mercy, longs to forgive us our sins, but if we do not forgive our brethren we shall not enjoy the divine love. Our insistence on taking vengeance on those who oppose us hides from us the enjoyment of the spirit of love and humility, and so we are deprived of receiving God's mercies toward us.

v The believer must not be angry with his neighbor without cause, nor harbor wrath against anyone, nor return evil for evil. It befits him to be reviled rather than to revile, to be struck rather than to strike, to be wronged rather than to do wrong, and to be robbed rather than to rob [2].
St. Basil the Great Does a man keep hatred against his neighbor, and then seek healing from the Lord? [3]
Whoever keeps hatred is struck with a grave sickness that deprives him of healing from his sins.

v God prefers love above everything. As in the making of the royal purple robe the flowers and the dye from which the color of the robe is made are counted the most precious thing, so nothing supports love like our not remembering the faults of those who oppose us... It is sweeter to love a person who has wronged us than to hate him [3].

v Why do we imitate madmen, each devouring the other, and wage war against our own bodies? Hear what the Old Testament says, how greatly it concerns itself with this matter: "The ways of the avengers lead to death" (see Prov 12:28) LXX. "Does a man harbor anger against another man, and then seek healing from the Lord?" (see Sir 28:3) [4]

v Do not be wrathful with anyone, and do not bear a grudge, forgiving all their transgressions. For it is said: "Does a man harbor anger against another man, and then seek healing from the Lord?" (see Sir 28:3). "Forgive, and ye shall be forgiven" (Mk 11:25) [5].
St. John Chrysostom Can he refrain from showing mercy to a man like himself, and then ask mercy for himself from God? [4]
In the parable of the Lord Christ in which He declares the universal fall of human nature (Mt 18:23-35), He calls us to show gentleness to the fallen, so that God may show gentleness to us.
If he continually holds on to wrath, being flesh, who will atone for his sins? [5]

v It is fitting and very honorable for a man to practice Christianity and not to demand the blood of his adulterous (wife); we cite to him what is written: "Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done you, and when you pray your sins will be forgiven. Does a man harbor anger against another, and then seek healing from the Lord? Or does he not show mercy to a man like himself, and then pray for the forgiveness of his sins? If he, being flesh, holds on to resentment, who will atone for his sins?" (see Sir 28:2-5). By this we can say: "Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors" (Mt 6:12). And it is said in the Apostle: "Recompense to no man evil for evil" (Rom 12:17) [6].
St. Augustine Remember the end of your life, and cease from enmity; remember destruction and death, and abide in the commandments [6].

The practical way to calm the soul from the desire for vengeance is to remember death and the day of judgment. The Holy Bible and the Fathers of the Church urge us to meditate on the day of our departure and our meeting with Christ on the great day of judgment.

v The remembrance of death is good (Sir 28:6; 41:1), so that man may know that he is mortal and realize that the mortal is not eternal. For he who is not eternal will surely leave this age, even against his will. Therefore, by the constant remembrance of death, man learns to do good by his own free will [6].
St. Barsanuphius and St. John Remember the commandments, and do not vent your wrath on your neighbor; remember the covenant of the Most High, and overlook faults [7].

It befits the believer, through his love for the salvation of all humanity as his brethren, to look at the one who wrongs him as a sick man who needs love, tenderness, kindness and calm as medicines to help him toward the salvation of his soul. In the same spirit St. Augustine invites us to look at the one who wrongs us as a little child stricken with fever, whom we treat gently and are not vexed with, but embrace until he is healed of it.

v The doer of evil must be treated as by a physician, who is not angry with the sick man but fights the sickness. So vice is attacked and the weakness of the soul is corrected... For example, pride is corrected by being required to practice humility, idle talk by silence, laziness by work, gluttony by abstinence from food, and murmuring by withdrawal from the company of the brethren [7].
St. Basil the Great

entries.section: 3. Ceasing from strife and evil speech

paragraphs.text: 10 Refrain from strife, and you will lessen sins. 11 For a hot-tempered man kindles strife, and a sinful man disturbs friends, and casts discord among those who are at peace. 12 As the wood of the fire, so it burns; and according to a man's strength is his wrath; and according to his wealth he increases his anger; and according to the vehemence of the strife it blazes. 13 A hasty quarrel kindles a fire, and a hasty dispute sheds blood. 14 If you blow on a spark, it will glow; and if you spit on it, it will be put out; and both come out of your mouth.
Avoid quarreling, and you will lessen your sins, for the violent-tempered man kindles quarreling [8].

v Drive away by your silence the darkness of the wrathful man whom you see, and you will again acquire joy in your heart, and peace among the brethren, men and women, who are like you in mind, and zeal and care for keeping the churches of the Lord [8].

v Do not treat evil with evil, and do not try to overcome one another in such matters. For in the strife to gain the victory by evil, the victor is always wretched and miserable, for he departs bearing with him his greater sin. For this reason he who repays evil with evil does not become perfect... Stop evil by silence! But when you receive into your heart the storm of that person's anger, you imitate the wind, and strike back at what has blown upon you with a counterblow. Do not use your enemy as a teacher, while you hate him! Do not imitate him in this. Do not be, so to speak, a mirror of the one rushing in anger, showing within yourself the same appearance as his.
His color has turned red; do you want your color to be like the color of wine? His eyes are red as burning coals [9].

v He who is chaste in the desire for honor is also humble. He who is chaste in wealth is content, and attains the measure of the Gospel in poverty. He who controls indignation and anger is gentle. Truly the observance of true chastity governs the tongue, sets a limit for the eyes, and cleanses the ears from listening to gossip out of curiosity. But he who does not keep all this is not chaste but unrestrained [10].

v He who uses his intelligence and skill to destroy others is wicked; but he who works with intelligence and firmness to avoid the harms that others store up for him recognizes wisely what is for his good, acquiring praiseworthy prudence.

entries.section: 3. Ceasing from strife and evil speech

paragraphs.text: Listen diligently to the voice of the prudent soul, and you will know that it has a center that uses prudence to give sound counsel to itself as well as to its neighbor, and this is praiseworthy [11].
St. Basil the Great The sinful man troubles his friends and sows discord among those who are at peace [9].

entries.section: 3. Ceasing from strife and evil speech

paragraphs.text: The fire burns according to the amount of wood; so also the fire burns according to the stubbornness of the quarrel [12].
And according to a man's strength is his anger, and according to his wealth his indignation increases [10].

v The man who makes peace with another immediately after rising up against him heals his anger but does not heal his grudge; therefore he remains resentful toward his brother. For anger is one thing, grudge is another, agitation (upheaval) a third, and disturbance yet another.

And so that you may understand the matter more clearly, I give you an example: in order to kindle a fire a man takes a piece of coal, and this is the word with which your brother wronged you; if you bear it, you will have put out the coal. But if you think: "Why does he say this to me? I too will answer him by saying such and such. If he had not intended to wrong me he would not have said this to me. Therefore I must repay the wrong in kind." By this thinking you put some fuel or the like to start the fire. And thereby it produces smoke, which is disturbance. And disturbance is a movement in the thoughts and a turning of them over, which stirs up the heart and agitates it.
Agitation, however, is a vengeful act against the one who wronged you. And this leads to boldness. St. Mark said: "Ill will, when fed by thoughts, agitates the heart, but prayer kills it."

Yet if you had borne those little words that your brother uttered, you would have put out the little piece of coal before it produced disturbance. And even so, if you wish, you can put out even the disturbance at its beginning by silence and prayer, and even by merely bowing from the heart. But if you persist in fanning the smoke, that is, in agitating the heart and stirring it up with thoughts that say: "Why did he do this to me?.. and I will repay him in kind," then by this the heart is kindled and the flame of agitation is generated. And if you wish, you can also put out the agitation before it reaches anger.

entries.section: 3. Ceasing from strife and evil speech

paragraphs.text: But if you persist in stirring yourself up and agitating yourself, you are like one who adds fuel to the fire. And so you produce a blaze, which is anger. And anger, if it continues, turns into a grudge, from which man cannot be freed except by shedding his blood (that is, his sweat and effort and the toil of his soul) [13].
Abba Dorotheus v Question: What is the difference between bitterness, wrath, anger and clamor (Eph 4:31; Ps 58:5)?

entries.section: 3. Ceasing from strife and evil speech

paragraphs.text: Answer: The difference between wrath and anger, I think, lies in the inclination and the impulse, since the pain of the one who is moved to anger extends only to the inclination (or disposition), as the one who says: "Be ye angry, and sin not" (Ps 4:5; Eph 4:26) clearly shows. But the wrathful man, his impulse extends, since it is said of the wrathful that he is like the serpent (Ps 58:5). Herod was wrathful toward Tyre and Sidon (Acts 12:20). The extension of wrath reaches to clamor, and bitterness is declared with exceedingly terrible determination, with deliberate malice in the heart (Eph 4:31) [14].

v Anger makes brothers ignore one another, and fathers and sons forget the natural bond between them. For wrathful persons begin by ignoring themselves first, and then in truth ignore all their friends. Just as torrents rush down from the top of a mountain and sweep away before them everything in the valleys that stands in their way, so fits of anger that are hard to control sweep away before them everyone who stands in their way. Those possessed by wrath do not respect the aged, nor care for the life of goodness, nor are they concerned with the strong tie of kinship, nor with the kindnesses that people had done them before, nor with anything else honorable.

entries.section: 3. Ceasing from strife and evil speech

paragraphs.text: Wrath is a kind of short-lived madness. The angry often harm themselves in their rush toward vengeance, heedless of their own interests. For as soon as they remember those who grieved them, they appear like men stung by horseflies all over their bodies, so that their wrath is stirred up and leaps within them, and they do not rest until they do something that harms the one who provoked them, and perhaps they themselves receive the harm, just as things violently shattered suffer more severe damage than they would cause when they strike against hard objects [15].
St. Basil the Great A hasty dispute kindles a fire, and a quarrel in zeal sheds blood [11].
If you blow on a spark it will glow, but if you spit on it it will be put out, and both come out of your mouth [12].

Whoever does not flee from the atmosphere of quarreling finds his heart growing more inflamed toward vengeance. And the fires of anger blaze upon his tongue, so that he begins with violent speech, like a spark of which we do not know how far it will inflame the fires of vengeance (Jas 3:5-6).

St. Basil presents to us the cycle of anger; for often the inner feelings of anger turn into conflict and quarreling, and quarreling begets faults, and faults drive to blows, and blows cause wounds, and wounds may drive to death. Stopping anger in its first early stages is far easier than stopping it in its later stages.

How do you stop anger at the start of its stages? Remember that what someone insults you with is in reality not an insult, for Abraham, the father of fathers, said of himself that he was dust and ashes, and David reckoned himself a worm and no man. Let us imitate Moses, whom Aaron and Miriam wronged: instead of thinking of the insult that had come upon him, he prayed for them.
v Tell me, does calm show on your countenance? His voice trembles; is your own voice gentle?

For the echo of a voice in the wilderness is not like what he does who answers the one who wrongs him. On the contrary, the echo answers only a word with a word like it, whereas he who wrestles with another answers him with further words in addition. For what is the nature of the words that quarrelers say together? One says to the other that he is a worthless person, the son of a worthless man, and the other answers that he is a slave, the son of a slave.
One says: He is a poor laborer, and the other says: You vagabond!
One says: You fool, and the other answers: You madman.

And so they exchange insults between them like rebounding arrows. These are the abuses of the tongue that hasten on, and soon vengeance comes upon them through deeds. For wrath begets conflict and quarreling, and quarreling begets fault, and fault begets blows, and blows beget wounds, and wounds often lead to death.

entries.section: 3. Ceasing from strife and evil speech

paragraphs.text: So let us stop evil from the very beginning, very early! Let us remove anger from our souls with every possible effort. By this we can uproot many evils together with the passions, for evil is a kind of root, a kind of source [16].

v Has he spat upon you and counted you as nothing? Receive this thought concerning him, that you are taken from the dust of the earth, and that you will return to the earth and the dust (Gen 3:19). He who applies this thought to himself, truly and from his heart, finds that every contempt toward him is less than the truth. By this you give your enemy no opportunity for vengeance, and you show him that the insult does not shake you. So you gain for yourself a great crown of perseverance, making another's madness the starting point of your wisdom. For this reason, if you listen to his anger, you will of your own will add further insults to yourself...

entries.section: 3. Ceasing from strife and evil speech

paragraphs.text: Does someone call you a fool and a beggar who deserves nothing? Say that you yourself are a "worm" (Ps 23:6), and born of the mire of a "dunghill," as David said [17].
St. Basil the Great

15 The whisperer and the double-tongued are deserving of a curse, for they have destroyed many who were at peace. 16 The third tongue has disquieted many, and scattered them from nation to nation, 17 and has pulled down strong cities, and overthrown the houses of the great, 18 and has broken the armies of peoples, and destroyed mighty nations. 19 The third tongue has driven out virtuous women, and deprived them of their labors. 20 Whoever listens to it will find no rest, and will not dwell in security. 21 The stroke of a whip leaves a welt, but the stroke of the tongue breaks bones. 22 Many have fallen by the edge of the sword, but not so many as have fallen by the tongue. 23 Blessed is he who is sheltered from its evil, who has not been exposed to its wrath, who has not borne its yoke and has not been bound with its bonds, 24 for its yoke is a yoke of iron, and its bonds are bonds of bronze. 25 Death by it is a cruel death, and Hades is better than it. 26 But it has no power over the godly, and they will not be burned by its flame, 27 but those who forsake the Lord fall under its power, and it will burn among them and not be quenched. It will be sent against them like a lion, and it will devour them like a leopard. 28 Fence in your property with thorns. 29 Lock up your silver and gold, and make a balance and a weight for your words, and a door and a bolt for your mouth, 30 and take heed lest you slip by it, and fall before one who lies in wait for you.

Anger causes loss of control over the will and over the senses and the body, especially the tongue. When it rises in the mind or the heart it makes a man lose control over his tongue, so that he utters speech without restraint, and the members of his body rise up in a spirit of violence, and he carries within him the stirrings of mockery and bodily violence, and thus countless evil deeds are begotten from anger and wrath! In short, anger deprives of freedom and makes of itself a maidservant (a slave) without authority!
v Anger makes tongues unbridled and speech without restraint. Likewise bodily violence, acts of mockery, abuse, accusations, blows and other countless evil deeds are born of anger and wrath [18].

v Because of anger tongues are not bridled, lips are not silenced, hands are not bound, but from anger and its passions, and from wrath and its feelings, there are begotten countless agitations, uproars, rebukes, slanders, blows and other things without number. By wrath also the edge of the sword is sharpened, and the hand of man dares to kill a man [19].
St. Basil the Great Curse the slanderer and the deceiver, for he destroys many of those who are at peace [13].
The lack of control over the tongue kindles the spark all the more. Many nations have been completely shattered because of a small spark that came from an uncontrolled tongue.
Gossip unsettles many and scatters them from nation to nation, and pulls down strong cities and overturns the houses of the great [14].

v Envy is the germ and root of evils; from it spring murder, hatred, slander, plunder, desiring harm for others, and the like. Which of you does not know that by envy one imitates the devil, through whose envy death entered into the world?
St. John Chrysostom Gossip drives out virtuous women and deprives them of the fruits of their labors [15].
King Ahasuerus listened to the gossip of the drunken and drove out Queen Vashti, the virtuous (Esth 1:17).
Whoever devotes himself to gossip finds no rest and will not dwell in security [16].

v What does it mean to abstain from eating meat while we do not abstain from eating the flesh of our neighbor by gossip and backbiting? And what does it mean to fast from food while we do not cease from evil thoughts, fornication, grudges and hatred?

Beware of fasting only from meat and thinking that this is what is required of you. True fasting is abstaining from every vice: "Put away all iniquity" (Isa 8:5), and it is the forgiveness of every offense against the neighbor; it is the remission of debts owed by the needy: do not fast in order to quarrel and to go to law before the courts [20].
St. Basil the Great v Could we perhaps find another man like the Apostle Paul, who could say: "I have a desire to depart, and to be with Christ" (Phil 1:23)?

For my part I cannot speak as Paul did, for I know that if I depart, all that is wood, hay and stubble (1 Cor 3:12) in me must be burned. This wood that is in me is gossip, excess in drinking, thefts and other kinds of wood that have piled up upon the foundation that is in my house. All this is hidden from many believers; each one of us thinks that so long as he has not committed adultery or fornication he will be saved; and we do not realize that "we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad" (2 Cor 5:10). And we do not set before us Him who said: "You only have I known of all the tribes of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities" (Amos 3:2), not for some of your iniquities while for the others I will not punish you [21].
Origen The stroke of a whip causes a wound, and the stroke of the tongue breaks bones [17].
Some think that words cause them no harm, but practical experience reveals how dangerous the lack of control over the tongue is, for it has shattered people, families and nations.
Many fall by the edge of the sword, but they are not as many as those who fall because of the tongue [18].

v If only we could see how our inner man has been wounded by every sin!... Have you not read: Swords wound, but not as the tongue wounds [18]. Therefore the soul is wounded by the tongue, as also by evil thoughts and wicked lusts, for it is broken and shattered by the works of sin. If we were able to see all these things and perceive the scars of the wounded soul, we would surely resist sin unto death.

In any case, just as those who suffer delirium and loss of their senses do not feel that they are wounded, because they have lost their natural sensations, so we cannot feel the gravity of our wounds and the extent of the soul's misery that sin causes, if we are struck with the madness of the love of worldly pleasures and the drunkenness of vice [22].
Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles Blessed is the man who is sheltered from it, and is not exposed to the wrath of the tongue, and does not draw its yoke, and is not bound with its bonds [19].
For its yoke is a yoke of iron, and its bonds are bonds of bronze [20].
Death by it is an evil death, and Hades is better than it [21].
The evil tongue has no power over the godly, and they will not be burned by its flame [22].

Godliness, or the fear of the Lord, delivers a man from the yoke of the tongue and its bondage [22-26]. If a man does not master his tongue, the tongue masters him; or he who does not enslave his tongue, his tongue enslaves him.
Those who forsake the Lord fall under its power, and it will burn among them and not be quenched.
It will be sent against them like a lion, and will devour them like a leopard [23].

Just as the farmer protects his property with a fence, so it befits the wise man to guard his tongue from slander. Careless persons who slip by their tongues fall prey to onlookers (Prov 13:3; 21:23).
Behold, fence in your property with thorns, and lock up your silver and gold [24].
Every morning the believer asks: "Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth; keep my lips" (see Ps 141:3).

v Beloved brother Andrew, listen: those who receive pure, unalloyed coins from the king, if they keep them with zeal and care, find that they retain their luster and cleanness. But if they do not take care of them, they are not only soiled but perhaps even lost. For this reason one of the wise said: "Bind up your gold and silver" (see Sir 28:24).

I tell you not only to bind them with unwavering faith, but also to seal them with humility and longsuffering, with the patience by which he who endures is saved. I tell you a bold thing, by God who permits me to do so: the Lord Jesus, the great Mediator, the Son of the blessed Father, the Giver of the life-giving Holy Spirit, tells you through me, the last of all: "Your many sins are forgiven you" (Lk 5:20; 7:48), your sins from your birth until now! By receiving this great and unspeakable joy, you love Him with all your power, bringing forth fruits meet for repentance (Mt 3:8) [23].

St. Barsanuphius and St. John v Let everyone welcome fasting with zeal as the mother of all sanctification, mortification and subjection of the body (1 Cor 9:27), and choose to undertake this work: he fences his property with thorns [24], as one of our wise men says [24].

Pope St. Cyril the Great v Beloved brethren, let us courageously avoid and shun the words of those whose speech spreads as a gangrene (2 Tim 2:17), and as the Apostle says: "Evil communications corrupt good manners" (1 Cor 14:33). So the wise man warns us: Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to the evil tongue [24] [25].

St. Cyprian the Martyr v For whom was it written: "Fence in your property with thorns, and lock up your silver and gold. And make a balance and a weight for your words, and a door and a bolt for your mouth" [24-25]?

Your property is your mind, your gold is your heart, and your silver is your speech. "The words of the Lord are pure words, as silver refined in a furnace (by fire)" (Ps 12:6). A good mind is good property. Accordingly the pure inner life is valuable property. Fence this property, then, with thought; guard it with thorns, that is, with godly care, lest the ravening passions of the flesh rush upon it and take it captive, and violent emotions attack it, and transgress its boundaries and carry off its vines.

Guard your inner life. Do not neglect it, and do not hold it lightly as though it were trivial, for it is valuable property. Truly it is precious; its fruits do not perish after only a while, but remain to be used for eternal salvation [26].

v Bind your words lest they run in rashness and become loose, and sins return through much speaking. Let them be restricted and so return to their limits. For the river that overflows quickly gathers mud... The sobriety of the mind has a bridle that restrains it, leads it and directs it [27].
St. Ambrose Make a balance and a weight for your words, and a door and a bolt for your mouth [25].

St. Cyprian the Martyr sees that the believer fences his ears from the poisons of the heretics by withdrawing from those who fled from the Church. The Apostle commands us: "Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us" (2 Thess 3:6). For there can be no fellowship between the faith and the enemy.

He who is not with Christ is against Christ, and is an enemy of His unity and peace, and cannot be united with us. If they come with prayers and correction, let them be heard; but if they attack with curses and threats, let them be rejected [28].

v It is clear that we defile ourselves when we speak everything that passes through our mind and talk about matters that ought not to be discussed, so that they become a source of sins, although we know that it befits our lips to be closed with understanding (Prov 15:7), and it befits us to make a balance and a weight for our words [25] [29].

Origen v "Shut your door" (Isa 26:20) in the face of the enemy. "Weigh your words in a balance, and make a bolt for your door" (see Sir 28:25). You know how I speak to you, so understand the things I say. Labor to make them firm, and you will find the treasures hidden in them according to God, and give in them fruit worthy of God, and do not put my gray hairs to shame, as I pray for you day and night. May God grant you to understand and to act in His fear, Amen [30].

v Cross over from this world, go up now to the Cross; rise above the earth, shake off the dust from your feet (Mt 10:14), despise the shame (Heb 12:2). Do not join the Chaldeans in kindling the fires of the furnace, lest you be burned with them (Dan 3:23) by the wrath of God. Esteem every person better than yourself (Phil 2:3), weep for your dead (Sir 22:11).. bind your words firmly in the yoke, and make a bolt for your door (see Sir 28:25) [31].

St. Barsanuphius and St. John v Put a door and a bolt on the mouth (see Sir 28:25). For countless evils come from idle talk: families are destroyed, friendships are torn apart, and endless tragedies occur. O man, do not busy yourself with the affairs of your neighbor. But you talk much, and there is weakness in you. Speak of your faults before God. Thus weakness is turned into no weakness, and even into profit. Speak of your weaknesses to your friends who are truly friends and godly, and in whom you trust, that they may pray for your sins. If you speak of the faults of others you will gain nothing and acquire nothing, but you will destroy yourself [32].

v Let us ask His help that we may complete our diligence in action, and keep our mouth, making a bolt for our mind, not always closed, but to be opened at the proper time... Therefore the wise Solomon says: "A time to keep silence, and a time to speak" (Eccl 3:3). If it were necessary for the mouth to be always open, it would not need a door; and if it were necessary for it to be always closed, it would not need a guard. The door and the guard are so that everything may be done in its time. Another says: "Make a balance and a weight for your words" (see Sir 28:29), that is, that we utter our words with care, weighing them and reflecting upon them [33].

St. John Chrysostom v Let your mouth have a door that is closed, and at need is lifted. Let it be shut tightly, so that no one can provoke your voice to anger, so that you return insult for insult [34].
St. Ambrose And take heed lest you slip by your tongue, lest you fall prey before one who lies in wait for you [26].

One way to avoid sins is to flee from disputes, for the man who loves quarreling tears friendships apart (Prov 15:18; 16:28). Quarrelers put fuel on the fire (Prov 26:20-21; Jas 3:5-6), especially if they are rich and men of authority (8:1-3; 13:2), and quarrels may lead to bloodshed (22:24; 27:15).
Inspired by Ben Sira 28
v You gave the first man dominion over all the earthly creation, not that he might display his might, but that he might enjoy Your care for him.
In my stubbornness I lost love, tenderness and mercy, for Your holy image has vanished from my depths.
Instead of grieving over what I have corrupted, the love of vengeance and pride have mastered my feelings and my will.
Our love of vengeance makes us worthy that vengeance be taken on us!
By our love of vengeance we rob You of Your work, for You say: "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Rom 12:19).
v Turn my eyes away from the doings of my brethren, that I may see my own sins, and seek mercy for them and for myself.
Open my heart to love, that I may find sweet the tenderness toward the fallen.
Let me be angry at my sins and the sins of my brethren and not be angry at them, for we all await Your mercy.
Let me hate the sickness, not the sick man, for there is no man who is not exposed to sickness.
v Train me to flee from quarreling by holy silence. Then my heart will rejoice in Your wondrous work in sinners!
Let my heart be released from the battles of the world, and let it join the choir of the heavenly ones.
Instead of entering into disputes and argument, let me seek through love peace, joy and grace for my brethren and for myself!
Cleanse me completely, so that I do not waste my time in quarrels, nor my ears in listening to anger.
v Instead of throwing fuel on the fires of anger, grant me to pour out the waters of love, kindness and tenderness.
Do not allow anger to turn into a grudge, nor the grudge into agitation, nor the agitation into vengeance, but by Your Holy Spirit extinguish in me every unseemly passion.
The sweetness of fellowship with You, O my God, removes the bitterness of my anger against my brother!
v Instead of blowing with my mouth on the spark of anger, grant me to spit with my mouth on the spark so that it is put out!
Grant me to imitate Moses the prophet, who prayed for Aaron and Miriam who had insulted him (Num 12:13).
v Grant that my tongue may not move in my anger, and set a guard from You over my inner tongue.
O Lord, extinguish the spark of my tongue at the beginning of its starting, lest it turn into a deadly furnace.
Remove from me the wood of gossip, lest I be burned by it.
v Keep me from my tongue, and protect me from its harsh yoke, and free me from its bitter bonds, and extinguish the fire of its wrath!
May You sanctify it, that it may be made worthy to praise with the heavenly ones.
If You tame it, it pours out sweetness, gentleness and kindness.
And if it is not tamed, it devours me like a lion or a leopard.
Fence my mouth with Your grace, that no wounding word may come out of it; v set, O Lord, a guard from You over my mouth.
That I may know when to speak and when to be silent.
If I speak, grant that You may speak through me; and if I am silent, may You be revealed within me.
