1 He who shows mercy lends to his neighbor, and he who is generous with his hand keeps the commandments. 2 Lend to your neighbor in the time of his need, and repay what you owe him at its appointed time. 3 Fulfill what you have spoken and be faithful to him; then you will obtain at all times what you desire. 4 Many have counted a loan as a windfall, and have troubled those who helped them. 5 Before he receives, he kisses the hand, and humbles his voice, until he obtains his neighbor's money. 6 But when the time for repayment comes, he delays, and speaks wearisome words, and complains of the turn of the times. 7 If repayment is within his power, he scarcely returns half, and counts what he has returned as a windfall. 8 Otherwise he robs him of his money, and makes him an enemy without cause. 9 He repays him with cursing and abuse, and instead of honor he rewards him with insult. 10 Many have held back because of the wickedness of men, fearing to be robbed without cause. 11 Nevertheless be longsuffering toward the wretched, and do not delay him in giving alms. 12 For the commandment's sake help the poor, and in his need do not send him away empty. 13 Lose your silver for your brother and your friend, and do not let it rust under a stone and be spoiled. 14 Spend your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; it will profit you more than gold. 15, 16 Shut up almsgiving in your storehouses; it will deliver you from all evil. 17, 18 It will fight for you against your enemy, more than a shield of might and a spear of valor.

As Ben Sira speaks of loans that are given to the needy who are in harsh circumstances, he requires both the lender and the borrower to keep the divine commandments. If he who is well-off must support his brother who is in need, then on the other side it befits the borrower not to take advantage of the one who lends to him.
He who shows mercy lends to his neighbor, and he who strengthens him by stretching out a helping hand keeps the commandments [1].

The true motive for lending is mercy toward the one who is in distress and asks for a loan; by this he keeps the commandments. He gives him the loan and does not ask for interest. He who lends to his needy brother at interest (usury), taking advantage of his need, commits a sin.

It befits the believer to distinguish between giving a loan to a person going through a temporary crisis and giving it to a businessman who uses the loan to manage his business, which brings him profit. The first is given the loan without interest. "If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury" (Ex 22:25).
Lend to your neighbor in the time of his need, and when you borrow, repay what you owe your neighbor at the appointed time [2].
On the part of the lender, it befits him not to be slow if the need is certain; and on the part of the borrower, he must keep faith and repay what he owes of loans without delay [2].

v Why then, O rich man, do you desire so late, while you are in hell, what you never hoped for when you were enjoying your luxuries? Are you not the one who ignored the person who was laid at your gate? (Lk 16:20). Are you not the one who despised the poor man (Lazarus), mocking Moses and the prophets? You refused to hold fast to faith in your dealings with your neighbor during his poverty, and now you do not enjoy its pleasant time... This is the way to be in line with the teaching of the Lord: "Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations" (Lk 16:9). There are poor people here who have no dwelling to receive you in. Make friendship with them by the mammon of unrighteousness, the gains that injustice counts as gains. For there are gains that justice counts as gains; these are found in the treasuries of God. "He that receiveth a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet's reward... And whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, verily I say unto you, he shall in no wise lose his reward" (Mt 10:41-42), and so by his good things [1].
St. Augustine Keep your word, and be trustworthy with him, and you will find what you need in every circumstance [3].

It does not befit the borrower to take advantage of the kindness of the lender and be slow or postpone repayment, for he may be in need in the future; and on another side, failure to repay may deprive his needy brethren of finding someone to lend to them.
Many count a loan as a sudden, unexpected gain, and bring troubles upon those who help them [4].
A man should not hasten to ask for a loan without consideration, for he often brings troubles upon himself and upon others.

He kisses the lender's hand until he receives the loan, and to take his neighbor's money he humbles his voice; but when the time of payment comes he postpones, and repays only with words of indifference, and blames the times [5].

It is shameful for a man to use a double standard: when he asks to borrow he speaks with humility and gentleness and joy, and exaggerates the promise of repayment on time; but when the appointed time for paying the debt or returning the loan arrives, he turns into another person, and puts off the creditor and tries to evade him, and offers him excuses and reckons that the time is not suitable, and accuses the lender of harshness and lack of mercy. The creditor is then compelled to press him in order to receive even half of the loan, and the two enter into enmity without cause. Sometimes the borrower insults the one who lent to him instead of honoring him. This is what drives some to refrain from giving loans, lest their money be taken from them and they lose friendship [7].

When the lender is firm with him, he scarcely recovers half of the loan, and counts that as an unexpected gain; and if the borrower repays nothing, he has robbed him of his money, and counts him his enemy without cause. So the borrower repays the lender with curses and abuse and insult instead of honor [6].
Many refuse to lend, not because they are wicked, but for fear of being robbed without cause [7].
Nevertheless, be longsuffering with one who is in wretched circumstances, and do not make him wait for your alms [8].

Ben Sira calls us to be patient with longsuffering when the one asking for a loan is in harsh circumstances. It befits us to help the poor man and so fulfill his commandment, for it is better than gold and silver [8-11].
For the commandment's sake help the poor, and in his need do not send him away empty [9].
Lose your money for the sake of your brother and your friend, and do not let it rust under a stone and be spoiled [10].

The work of mercy keeps a man's possessions from theft or rust (Mt 6:19-21). And when a man ceases to give, he is like one who keeps his money under a stone, and with the passing of time this money is spoiled.
Use your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High, and it will profit you more than gold [11].

This expression is a preparation for the saying of the Lord Christ in (Mt 6:19-21) concerning His call: "Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven." If Ben Sira asks us to keep almsgiving and shut it up in our storehouse [21], that is, in a safe place into which no thief can slip, the Lord Christ came to declare that heaven is our safe place, which all the powers of darkness cannot break into.

In the ancient Latin translation (the Vulgate), among some of the Latin Fathers, it reads: "Shut up (store up) your alms in the heart of the poor man." It is as though, when the believer meets a poor man, he sees in his heart a safe treasury in which to deposit his gifts that spring from his loving heart. It is as though the hearts of the believer and of the poor man meet together in Christ Jesus who works in both. He works in the heart of the capable to give with love, and works in the heart of the poor to receive the gift with thanksgiving to the Lord of glory and His generous believers.
Shut up almsgiving in your storehouses, and it will deliver you from all sorrow [12].
If we wish to preserve what is in our treasury, let us give alms that will keep us in the day of evil. It is a strong weapon for our protection against those who oppose us [12-13].

v The good Teacher taught us how it befits us to cleanse the corruption of our body, saying: "Give alms of such things as ye have; and, behold, all things are clean unto you" (Lk 11:41). Do you not see how many remedies there are! Tenderness cleanses us, the word of God cleanses us, as it is written: "Now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you" (Jn 12:9). Not only in this passage, but in other passages as well you have seen the greatness of grace. "Almsgiving delivers from death" (Tob 12:9). "Shut up almsgiving in the heart of the poor man, and it will deliver you in the evil day" (see Sir 29:12) [2].

St. Ambrose v We have been baptized and yet we are debtors, not because something was left unforgiven in Baptism, but because we do in our life what we need to be forgiven daily. Those who were baptized and immediately left this world came out of the baptismal font without any sin. But those who were baptized and remained in this life commit uncleanness because of their bodily weakness, which, although it does not cause the ship to sink, needs the help of the pump (to bail it out), or else the water enters little by little and causes the whole ship to sink.

Prayer is our calling for help to the pump in keeping the ship from sinking; all voices and hands are used. Now we use our voices when we say "Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors," and we work with our hands when we do this: "To break your bread for the hungry, and to bring the poor who wander into your house" (Isa 58:7). Do a kindness in the heart of the poor man, and he will intercede for you before the Lord (see Sir 29:12) [3].

St. Augustine v The remedy for appeasing God has been given to us in the very words of God, for the divine teachings instruct sinners what they ought to do, namely, that God is satisfied with works of righteousness (through the blood of Christ). By mercy they deserve the forgiveness of sin. And it is written in Solomon: "Shut up almsgiving in your storehouses (in the heart of the poor), and it will deliver you from all evil" (see Sir 29:12).

And also: "Whoso stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor, he also shall cry himself, but shall not be heard" (Prov 21:13). For he who shows no mercy cannot be made worthy of the mercies of the Lord. And he who has no humanity toward the requests of the poor gains by his prayers no share of divine compassion. This is what the Holy Spirit declared in the Psalms, affirming: "Blessed is he who regards the poor; the Lord will deliver him in the day of evil" (Ps 41:1).

Remember what counsel Daniel gave to Nebuchadnezzar the king when he was troubled and afraid of the grave dream, offering him a remedy to obtain divine help that removes evils, saying to him: "Wherefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable unto thee, and break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine iniquities by shewing mercy to the poor..." And since the king did not obey him, he fell under the calamities and evils that he saw, which he could have escaped by almsgiving...

And the angel Raphael bears witness to the like, urging the giving of alms by choice and with generosity, saying: "Prayer is good with fasting and almsgiving, for almsgiving delivers from death, and purges away sins" (Tob 12:8-9). He shows that our prayers and fasts, unless almsgiving helps them, become less profitable. For he who does them without supporting them by good works has little power in them to reach what he asks [4].
St. Cyprian the Martyr It fights for you before your enemy, more than a strong shield and a mighty spear [13].

Virtues without almsgiving become barren and fruitless. For the Lord Christ receives the gift of the capable man, and the one who gives alms stores it up for him in heaven, where the enemy of good with all his powers cannot approach it. It is kept for the great day of the Lord, which the wonderful Judge will declare, saying: "I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat..." (Mt 25:35).

v Those who will inherit the Kingdom are those who help the poor with good things, and they are sincere Christians who follow the words of the Lord and hope in His promises with confidence. Such is their conduct, for without it their lives, fitting as they are to holiness, would be barren, binding themselves to abstain from sins, so that they do not defile purity, and abstain from drunkenness and theft and the practice of any evil. But if they do not add works of love they remain without fruit, for they keep the first part of the commandments: "Depart from evil," and not the other part, "and do good" (Ps 37:27).

So when it is said: "Come, ye blessed, inherit the kingdom" (Mt 25:34), this invitation is not prompted by the fact that they lived in purity, and abstained from theft, nor that they did not exploit the poor, nor seize the possessions of others, nor swear falsely. Rather it is said to them: "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat" (Mt 25:35)... They are saved not because they did not sin, but they were saved from their sins by their good works [5].
St. Augustine

19 A good man becomes surety for his neighbor, and he who has lost all shame forsakes him. 20 Do not forget the kindness of your surety, for he has given his life for you. 21 The sinner flees from his surety, and the mean-spirited forsakes him. 22 The sinner destroys the goods of his surety, and the ungrateful forsakes his deliverer. 23 There are men who become surety for their neighbor, but he loses all shame and forsakes him. 24 Many were prospering, and suretyship ruined them and tossed them like the waves of the sea. 25 It drove mighty men into exile, and they wandered among foreign nations. 26 The sinner who rushes into suretyship and pursues business dealings falls under judgments. 27 Help your neighbor according to your ability, and take heed to yourself lest you fall.

Ben Sira deals with the position of the surety and also of the one who asks for surety [14]. 1. It befits the surety not to be stingy toward his neighbor, so as to refrain from becoming a surety who guarantees him [15-17]. 2. It befits the one whose neighbor has stood surety for him to make every effort to fulfill what is required of him, and not to forsake the one who stood surety for him. 3. A man should not hasten to stand surety for someone who is not trustworthy, nor stand surety for a man beyond his ability. He sums this up by saying: "Help your neighbor according to your ability, and take heed to yourself lest you fall" [20]. In other words, be generous as far as you can, and be prudent for the sake of your peace!
The good man stands surety for his neighbor, and he who has lost all shame abandons him [14].

The good man acts in the spirit of his Savior, who offered Himself as surety for us while we were sinners, and atoned for our sins and granted us His righteousness. Our Christ became an atoning intercessor for us before the Father although there is nothing good in us. If we refuse to stand surety for our brethren who share our weakness and forsake them, we lose all shame by refusing to be an icon of our Intercessor. A story about suretyship is recorded in The Garden of the Monks:

[While a rich young woman was strolling in her garden, she saw a young man trying to commit suicide. She hurried to him and learned from him that he was attempting this because of his many debts and the pressure of the creditors upon him, so he had decided to be rid of life, considering death better than this grievous life. She pledged to pay all his debts even if it cost her all her money. And indeed it cost her most of her wealth. After a little while she became poor and gave herself over to sin. But the merciful God did not will that her labor and love be lost, so He allowed her to fall ill. While she was on her sickbed she came to herself, and repented, and resolved to become a Christian. She asked her neighbors to ask the Pope that she might be baptized, but they doubted her request because of her bad reputation.

One night the angel of the Lord stood by her in the form of the man whom she had pitied, and she asked him to help her to be baptized. He reassured her and brought two other angels who carried her to the church, and the three appeared in the likeness of three well-known archons of the city in the king's retinue. When the priests asked them whether they would vouch for her as sponsors, they answered: Yes. So she was baptized and put on the white garments, and the angels returned her to her house.

When her neighbors saw her wearing the white baptismal garments they marveled and reported the matter to the Pope, who summoned the priests and inquired of them what had happened. They told him that three of the archons had vouched for her, but when the archons were brought they denied any knowledge of this matter. The Pope then knew that the matter was from God. Then he asked her: What good have you done in your life? She said to him: If I was a sinner and a fornicator, what good could I have done? Then she told him the story of the man for whom she had stood surety. At that she fell asleep in peace, and the Pope cried out, saying: "Righteous art thou, O Lord, and thy judgments are very great" [6].]
Do not forget the kindness of the surety toward you, for he gives his life for you [15].

As Sirach insists that we support our brethren wisely as far as we can, so on the other side he requires the person not to belittle his surety and forsake him, taking advantage of his love and squandering his money and ignoring the good deed he has done. It befits the one for whom surety was given to be marked by thankfulness and faithfulness, so as to encourage others to continue in doing good and to give surety as far as they can.
The sinner squanders the goods of his surety, and the ungrateful man deliberately denies his deliverer [16].
Who is the Surety who pays our debts except the Lord Christ? The sinner who does not care for the grace of the Lord and His free work of salvation merely squanders the goods of his Surety.
Suretyship has ruined many of the rich, and tossed them like the waves of the sea [17].
Suretyship has drawn men of influence and authority from their homes, and they wandered among foreign nations [18].

Suretyship has ruined many of the well-to-do who gave their possessions and money as a pledge to rescue those in need, and those they rescued did not care about the position of the surety, who is sometimes compelled to flee from the city.
The sinner who risks suretyship and the man who pursues gain fall under judgment [19].
The sinner who abuses the love of his surety is occupied with exploiting the surety as much as he can. This sinner, if he escapes punishment in this world, is judged on the day of the Lord.
Help your neighbor according to your ability, and take heed to yourself lest you fall [20].
Ben Sira advises offering practical love with wisdom, so that suretyship may not cause harm to both parties.

v God does not ask you to do good to your neighbor beyond your ability, for thus He says: "Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it" (see Prov 3:27; Sir 29:20) [7].

St. Barsanuphius v The truth is that if they distribute all they possess to the poor, the members of Christ, in return for one single sin, there is no profit at all, unless they cease from sin and acquire the love that knows no sin (1 Cor 13:4).

So let anyone who gives alms in return for his sins begin with Love (Christ) Himself. It befits a person to remember the saying of the Lord: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself" (Mt 22:39), so that you may realize that it is not fitting for a person to give alms to his neighbor without having pity on himself. Let us also remember the words: "Have pity on yourself your soul and you will please God." How can a person give alms to his neighbor in return for his sins if he does not give alms to himself that pleases God? In the same sense the text gives us the same lesson: "He that is evil to himself, to whom will he be good?" (see 24:5). Surely prayers help in giving alms. Here appears the importance of heeding the words: "My son, hast thou sinned? do so no more, but pray for thy former sins" (see 21:1), that they may be forgiven. The very purpose of almsgiving is that when we pray for the forgiveness of our sins, the prayer is heard. Its aim is not that we continue in our sins, imagining that by alms we pay the price of forgiveness for our sins [8].
St. Augustine

entries.section: 3. Be content and do not burden anyone

paragraphs.text: 28 The chief things for life are water, and bread, and clothing, and a house to cover shame. 29 The life of a poor man under a roof of boards is better than sumptuous food in a stranger's house. 30 Be content with little and with much; then you will hear no reproach in the affair of the house. 31 Wretched is the life of a man going from house to house, and wherever he is a guest he does not open his mouth. 32 You feed and give drink to those ungrateful for your kindness, and you are their guest, and after that you hear bitter words.

We must not sponge as unwelcome guests, especially by lodging with the rich; for it is better for a man to subsist on what is necessary for life, such as bread and water and clothing and a dwelling that shelters him, and to live in a simple hut, than to sponge on a rich man. By this the believer feels sufficiency and thanks God without murmuring over the deprivation of luxuries.
The essentials of life are water and bread and clothing and a house that provides privacy [21].
St. John Chrysostom sees that Ben Sira was thinking of righteous Noah, how he lost his dignity and composure even in the eyes of his household because of luxuries and drunkenness with wine.
v Noah was the first farmer who tilled the earth and planted a vineyard. He drank of the wine and was drunken, and he lay uncovered in his dwelling.

What a dreadful thing! You, beloved, see in drunkenness a dreadful thing, able to dull the senses and put to death the perception of the mind, although Noah was a sensible man to whom the responsibility for all creatures had been entrusted; he was bound with fetters that cannot be loosed, and fell down and became like a lifeless corpse.

In truth he became worse than a corpse, for the corpse is unable to do good or evil, but the drunkard is unable to do good, yet becomes more able to do evil; he sprawls and becomes an object of mockery for his wife and children and even the neighbors...

What can be more base than a person who is addicted to drink, from whom a foul smell rises to heaven day after day, and who loses his mind? Therefore comes the warning of the wise man: "The life of man is founded on the essentials: water and bread and clothing and a house to cover shame" (see Sir 29:21). So that if anyone falls a victim to drunkenness he does not become a spectacle to the public, and his friends do not look upon him, and he does not become an object of mockery to everyone [9].
St. John Chrysostom The life of a poor man under a shelter of logs of wood is better than sumptuous food in the house of a stranger [22].
The believer feels secure in the Church, his simple home, more than in enjoying the banquets of the philosophers, which seem sumptuous but are in a foreign land.
Be content with little or much, and you will not hear a rebuke that you are a stranger [23].
Wretched is the life of the man who moves from house to house, and wherever he stays he dares not open his mouth [24].
You entertain guests, and give drink to the ungrateful, and above that you hear bitter words [25].

33 Come, stranger, prepare the table, and if you have something in your hand, feed me. 34 Depart, stranger, from before an honored person; my brother has come to be my guest, and I need the house. 35 Two things the sensible man finds heavy: reproach concerning the house, and the insult of the lender.
"Come here, stranger, prepare the table, and if you have something in your hand, feed me [26].
Depart, stranger, from before an honored person; there is a more important guest here than you, my brother has come, and I need my house" [27].
Two things the wise man finds heavy:
Reproach for the household and the insult of the creditor [28].
Wisdom is a free gift that the Lord gives to those who fear Him, who keep His commandments, who walk in faith in a spirit of meekness.

What occupies the heart of Ben Sira is the fear of the Lord, which gives his heart the spirit of simplicity so that he does not walk with a double heart, that is, limping between two ways, at one time walking in the Lord and at another outside the Lord.
Inspired by Sirach 29

entries.section: Do not leave me in my financial dealings

paragraphs.text: v Your wondrous hand, O my God, lifts my heart above financial dealings!
Not to destroy Your financial gifts, but I ask that You not leave me, that I may walk wisely according to Your commandments.
In all my dealings be revealed all the more in my depths, and let me fulfill Your will in everything.
If my brother asks me for a loan I will give it in Your name.
I will neither delay nor hasten, for the sake of the salvation of my soul and the salvation of his soul.
I give the loan, and the balance of my love with You increases.
If he is able I will ask him for repayment lest greed corrupt him, and I will find the opportunity for another in need.
And if I borrow from anyone, let me hasten to repay with sincere thanks from the heart!
v If anyone is truly in need I count him the safe treasury of my possessions, which no thief can assail.
I count wise giving a weapon for me against the enemy.
As I give love and kindness with wisdom and generosity, I hear Your wondrous voice: "I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat."
v Grant me to be a wise surety, offering what is within my means.
You alone are the Almighty Surety; You stood surety for humanity before Your Father, and paid the price on the Cross!
I will not forget Your grace toward me, O divine Surety!
I will not deny Your love, for You granted me Your righteousness in place of the corruption that came upon me!
Through suretyship You went forth with the Cross to hell; it could not hold You captive, but You destroyed its bonds and released the captives to Paradise!
You freed me from the bonds of sin, and You shone upon me, O Sun of Righteousness, so that darkness no longer has a place within me.
Let me take shelter in You, and I long for the whole world to enjoy freedom instead of slavery to sin.
v You are my treasure and my satisfaction and the rejoicing of my soul; my soul desires nothing but You!
If I open my house to one of my brethren, I see You blessing the house and accepting the hospitality.
And if someone hosts me, I do not burden him.
And at his table I cling to You, who take the last place.
As long as I am in this world, wherever I am, I am a stranger and a guest.
And as long as my heart moves toward Your heavens, wherever I am, I am at home.
Your divine bosom is the place of my rest and my stability.
I rejoice in You, for You count me among "the household of God" (Eph 2:19).

entries.section: 1. The right upbringing in raising children

paragraphs.text: 1 He who loves his son multiplies the rod for him, that he may be glad at his latter end. 2 He who disciplines his son will reap the fruit of his discipline, and will boast of him among the notable. 3 He who teaches his son makes his enemy envious, and will rejoice in him before his friends. 4 When his father dies, it is as though he had not died, for he has left behind one like himself. 5 In his life he saw and rejoiced, and at his death he did not grieve. 6 He left behind an avenger against his enemies, and one to repay his friends with kindness. 7 He who spoils his son will bind up his wounds, and at every cry his bowels are troubled. 8 A horse that is not tamed becomes headstrong, and a son who is not restrained becomes foolish. 9 If you pamper your son, he will terrify you, and if you play with him, he will grieve you. 10 Do not laugh with him, lest he bring you sorrow, and in your latter end you will gnash your teeth. 11 Do not give him authority in his youth, and do not overlook his follies. 12 Bow down his neck in his youth, and beat his ribs while he is young, lest he become stubborn and disobey you, and heartache take hold of you. 13 Discipline your son and labor at his instruction, lest he fall into what will shame you.

He offers practical advice on the upbringing of children, and he has already spoken of this matter several times. The father is concerned with three things in the life of his son: he loves him (agapon), disciplines him (paidevon), and teaches him (didaskon). These three elements, that is, love, discipline and teaching, make up one unity in the building up of the new generation. In correction true love must be shown, in discipline godliness, and in teaching the desire that the son grow in spiritual and secular knowledge. Love supports discipline, and discipline leads to teaching.
The man who loves his son multiplies his discipline of him, that he may be glad in him in his last years [1].

He who loves his son is firm with him, so that he becomes a cause of delight and joy to his parents (Prov 10:1; 22:6). The heavenly Father cares for His children: "For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. If ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons; for what son is he whom the father chasteneth not?" (Heb 12:6-7).

Discipline, the rod or the staff is not understood as bodily punishment alone, but means the use of firmness mixed with love and kindness, with wisdom and balance, for he who is excessive in beating his children and in using harshness may lose them.
v No one who is disciplined and corrected as to his state loses hope, for he who loves his son disciplines him (see Sir 30:1). It befits that no one lose hope of a cure [1].

entries.section: 1. The right upbringing in raising children

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose He who disciplines his son will reap comfort in him, and will boast of him among his acquaintances [2].

What St. John Chrysostom laments is that what concerns many in raising their children is not the salvation of their children and their inner edification and true success, but they look at their children through their own vainglory, wanting their success in their works and wealth and their attaining great social positions, with no aim except to boast of them, so that the children become a means of vainglory for their fathers [2]. What concerns Sirach here, however, is the fathers' pride in their enjoying a leading personality able to achieve continual growth in all aspects of life.

entries.section: 1. The right upbringing in raising children

paragraphs.text: He who teaches his son stirs the envy of his enemies, and rejoices greatly in him before his friends [3].
The stirring of the enemy referred to here because of good upbringing means not giving any enemy the opportunity to gloat over the corruption of the children.

entries.section: 1. The right upbringing in raising children

paragraphs.text: When his father dies it is as though he had not died, for he has left behind one like himself [4].

The son whom his parents have disciplined is qualified to occupy his father's place (Tob 9:6). It is as though the role of the parents is to qualify their children to occupy their places with a good reputation (41:13; 44:8). Therefore the good father dies with a peaceful mind, because he has left behind a good, godly, successful son who walks as a man of God.

entries.section: 1. The right upbringing in raising children

paragraphs.text: In his life he saw him and rejoiced in him, and at his death he did not grieve [5].

entries.section: 1. The right upbringing in raising children

paragraphs.text: Against his enemies he left behind an avenger, and one who repays his friends for their services [6].

At his death the father leaves behind a courageous son who challenges the devil his enemy, and does not allow the works of darkness to creep into his mind, and at the same time offers all love to his father's friends, in maturity and in the spirit of strength [6].

Tobias the son is considered a wonderful example, for he resembled his father in every respect, according to the testimony of both Raguel his father-in-law and Gabael who owed his father silver. He was equal to the responsibility, for he bore the hardships of the journey in order to carry out his father's commandment while still a young lad, and became a blessing to his parents; he carried the medicine to his father and restored joy to his mother (Tob 9:6) [3].

entries.section: 1. The right upbringing in raising children

paragraphs.text: He who spoils his son will bind up his wounds, and at every cry his heart is pained [7].

Ben Sira warns parents against pampering their children. For pampering causes wounds in the souls of children. The father who pampers his son drinks of the fruit of his pampering before he dies, that is, he touches his son's failure. So it happened with Eli the priest, who pampered his two sons, and they were slain in the battle, and their father fell dead, and the people were defeated (1 Sam 4).
St. John Chrysostom reveals the danger of a life of pampering, whether a man pampers himself or his son or those under him. True love moves us to strive and to be firm with wisdom and love.

The father has compassion on his son as he disciplines him, fearing for him, so he binds up his wounds and is tender toward him, and his bowels groan over him. Even when compelled to use discipline, he is also tender with him; he strikes with one hand and bandages with the other, for the purpose of discipline is training and not vengeance.

v "Whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it. For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?" (Mt 16:25-26). This means: I decide these things not because I do not care for you, but because I care for you very much.

In fact he who supports his child constantly destroys him, but he who does not so support him saves him. The wise man says the same thing: "If you beat (your son) with the rod, he shall not die; you shall rather deliver him from Hades" (see Prov 23:13-14). And also: "He who pampers his son will bind up his wounds" [7].

This is also the case in the army. The commander who cares for his soldiers and orders them to stay constantly in the city (without military training) causes the death not of them alone but of the others in the city as well...

Do not remain inside, but go out and fight. For even if you fall in the battle you will live. If in earthly wars the person who is ready to be killed has a special esteem above others, is not conquered and is terrifying to the enemy, for even after his death the king who gave him arms cannot bring him back to life, how much more does it befit a person to offer his life to death and find it (Mt 16:15). First, his life is not taken quickly, and second, even if he falls, a higher life is given to him [4].

entries.section: 1. The right upbringing in raising children

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom A horse that is not tamed becomes headstrong, and a son who is allowed to run in debauchery becomes stubborn [8].

The successful horseman is the one who knows how to train horses and lead them and deal with them as in a common language. The rider is pleased when he finds the horse he trains doing its part as it should. How much more does the son need his parents to train him in a spirit of love and tenderness and in kindness without laxity.

v There are two kinds of fear, one kind connected with respect. This kind the citizens feel toward their rulers if they are good, and we feel it toward God as children dealing with their father. The Scripture says: "A horse not broken becomes headstrong, and a son left to himself becomes impudent" (see Sir 30:8).

The other kind of fear is mixed with hatred; this is the fear of slaves, which they feel toward their masters, and which the Hebrews felt when they looked upon God as their master and not as their Father [5].

entries.section: 1. The right upbringing in raising children

paragraphs.text: St. Clement of Alexandria If you pamper your son, he will terrify you, and if you play with him, he will grieve you [9].

How wonderful it is for children to feel that their parents are their friends or like elder brothers to them, and for parents and children to speak with frankness and openness. But pampering or jesting is a kind of extreme opposed to harshness, and both extremes present a danger to the whole family. St. Augustine says that love has its order. The father's love has its limits, and the mother's love also has its limits. Love and openness do not mean laxity or jesting in an unseemly manner.

v This obligation belongs to fathers as it does to mothers also. There are fathers who sacrifice everything to secure for their children teachers of pleasures, and make of them rich heirs. But that the children become Christians and practice godliness they do not care much. What a blindness that must be counted a crime!

It is a foolish neglect, responsible for the confusion that makes society bitter. Suppose you prepare great possessions for them. If they do not know how to conduct their lives, these possessions will certainly not last with them. Rather they are scattered, and perish with their owners, and become a most dangerous inheritance!

entries.section: 1. The right upbringing in raising children

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom Do not laugh with him, lest you be grieved with him, and in your latter end the gnashing of teeth take hold of you because of him [10].

What does he mean by "laugh with him"? It is good for parents to be affectionate with their children in a cheerful spirit through a smile and kindness, but exaggerated laughter corrupts the life of children and parents, where the person loses the spirit of wisdom and moderation under the pretext of creating a pleasant atmosphere. We hear of children who drove out their fathers and mothers in their old age, and disowned them and mistreated them, and that is the fruit of excessive pampering and bad upbringing, so that they reaped thorns in their latter end instead of grapes and thistles instead of figs.

The father needs wisdom and God's guidance so that he knows when to give and when to refrain, when to let his son go out and when to forbid him, when to punish him and when to caress him; for if he gives him money excessively he may spoil him, and if he does not give him he may feel deprived. If he allows him to go out, bad friends may surround him and draw him to what harms him, and if he is not allowed, how will his personality grow and develop practically through society? And if he is harsh with him his personality may weaken and he may become a defeated, withdrawn personality; and if he caresses him pampering may spoil him! [6]

entries.section: 1. The right upbringing in raising children

paragraphs.text: And do not give him authority in his youth [11].

It is good for parents to instill in their children the spirit of leadership and self-confidence together with faith in God, the giver of wisdom, strength and understanding. But exaggeration in the spirit of leadership and falling into the love of domination and insistence on one's own opinion corrupts the soul.
Press upon his ribs in his youth, lest he become stubborn and disobey you (and cause you grief [7]) [12].

entries.section: 1. The right upbringing in raising children

paragraphs.text: Discipline your son and labor with him, lest he confuse you by his conduct [13].

v Let us use the authority of Holy Scripture: "Beat his ribs while he is young, lest he rebel..." (see Sir 30:12). Lest he become unruly and untamed. The aim of such human punishments is to help rid us of ignorance, and to curb our untamed desires [8].
St. Augustine

14 A poor man who is in good health and sound in body is better than a rich man worn out with sicknesses. 15 Health and soundness of body are better than all gold, and strength of body is better than countless wealth. 16 There is no wealth better than health of body, and no pleasure that exceeds joy of heart. 17 Death is better than a bitter life, or continual illness. 18 Good things poured upon a closed mouth are like foods laid upon a grave. 19 What use is an offering to an idol? For it neither eats nor smells. 20 So is he whom the Lord afflicts, and repays for his iniquities. 21 He sees with his eyes and sighs, like a eunuch who embraces a virgin and sighs. 22 Do not grieve your soul, and do not distress your heart with your thoughts. 23 Gladness of heart is the life of man, and the rejoicing of a man is length of days. 24 Love your soul, and comfort your heart, and drive sorrow far from you; 25 for sorrow has killed many, and there is no profit in it. 26 Jealousy and anger shorten the days, and anxiety brings old age before its time. 27 A cheerful and good heart is always at feasts, and his banquets are prepared with care.
Ben Sira feared that a person might be concerned with providing his children with a huge fortune while neglecting their health.

The Lord Christ highlighted man's responsibility regarding bodily health, saying: "Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?" (Mt 6:25). Sadly some destroy their health by excessive work for the sake of increasing wealth. The health of the spirit has its role in the health of the body, though the health of the body can also support the health of the spirit. The wise man can benefit from the health of the body as from its sickness, and he may not destroy the body, because the weakness of the body often affects work for the edification of the spirit.
A poor man who is in good health and sound in body is better than a rich man afflicted in his body [14].
It befits the poor to thank God for bodily health, which many of the rich long for. For the sick rich man longs for the food of the simple and their work.
Health and soundness of body are better than all gold, and strength of body is better than enormous wealth [15].

The body is a talent given to us by God, and care for bodily health is necessary. The Apostle says: "For no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church" (Eph 5:29). The Church prays in her liturgies for spiritual, psychological and bodily health.
There is no wealth greater than health of body, and no pleasure that exceeds joy of heart [16].
Here he links the soundness of the body with the gladness of the spirit, so we thank God for the health of our body and the rejoicing of our hearts in Him.
Death is better than a wretched life, and eternal rest than chronic illness [17].
The loss of health sometimes deprives a man of happiness, so that he longs for death as better than a life full of suffering from sickness.
v Death, for those who understand it, is immortality; but for the foolish who do not understand it, it is death.
We must not fear this death, but fear the perdition of the soul, which is ignorance of God. This is what truly terrifies the soul! [9]
v Just as when you left the womb you no longer remember what happened to you in it, so when you leave the body you will no longer remember what happened while you were in it [10].
v And just as by leaving the womb you came into a better state and your body grew, so when you leave the body pure and undefiled you come into a better state that is incorruptible [11].
v And just as the body must be born when its growth in the womb is complete, so the soul must leave the body when it reaches the end of life in the body at the time appointed by God [12].
v Just as you treat the soul while it is in the body, so it will treat you when it leaves the body.
The man who is lax with his body in this life, giving it every kind of comfort, only prepares for himself sickness after death, bringing judgment upon himself through foolishness [13].

v Just as the body cannot live if it leaves the womb before it is complete, so the soul cannot be saved or have fellowship with God when it leaves the body unless it has attained, by its good life (while in the body), the gaze toward God [14].
St. Anthony the Great Good things set before a closed mouth are like offerings of food placed upon a grave [18].
For one who is sick and unable to eat, abundant good things are of no benefit; foods become for him as though placed upon a grave, with no one to eat them.

St. Augustine criticized the pagan customs in which they bring offerings and place them on the grave of the dead; for just as the closed mouth does not benefit from the good things offered to a man, so the idol worshiper does not benefit from the offerings on his grave [15].
What benefit is an offering of fruit to an idol, for it can neither eat nor smell.
So is he whom the Lord grieves [19].

He who does not enjoy the Lord's pleasure in him is like one who offers fruit to an idol that neither eats it nor smells its fragrance. Daniel mocked the idol Bel, whom the king of Babylon supposed ate and drank what the priests of Bel offered to him [16].
He sees with his eyes and sighs, like a eunuch embracing a virgin [20].
What does the eunuch who embraces a virgin and sighs mean, except that he cannot proceed to marry her? Such is the state of one who sees wealth and riches and precious goods and cannot use them.

v Why do you heap up gold, O mortal? Why do you seek for yourself a bitter slavery? A hard prison? Why do you bring upon yourself harsh anxiety? You think that the veins of gold in the mines or the gold in the palaces can be yours. In truth, even if you have an abundance of wealth, all you do is hide it away. It does not serve you, for if you do not use what you have now, but do not touch it as though it belonged to another than you, what will you do if you get more of it? Usually for the greedy, the more wealth increases and they gather it around them, the more they seek to store it up. Perhaps you will say: "I know that it is mine." In that case your possessions are in your thoughts and not for enjoyment. You may object: "I am great before others." In truth you will appear weak before the rich and the poor and robbers and slanderers and servants, in truth before all who conspire against you...

He who wants to embrace a girl he loves while unable to satisfy his desire suffers the bitterest torments. So does the rich man, who has abundant wealth and it is with him, yet he is unable to satisfy his desire [17].
St. John Chrysostom Do not give yourself over to sorrow, and do not trouble your soul on purpose [21].
The happy life: a man's happiness springs from within him, not from the outward circumstances surrounding him. He who surrenders to sorrow and is confused by his thoughts does not enjoy happiness.
The gladness of the heart is the life of man, and the joy of man lengthens his days [22].
Inner gladness gives life a taste, so the days of his life are lengthened.
Love your soul, and give rest to your heart, and drive sorrow far away from you.
For sorrow has destroyed many, and there is no profit in it [23].

What is the profit of sorrow? It has killed many, and has profited no one. Many complain of their falling under the bitterness of sorrow, as though it storms our hearts or steals into them. Here Ben Sira assures us that sorrow is the fruit of our negligence or our faults. It befits the believer to love his soul and relieve his heart by clinging to the Savior who makes hearts glad. By this he enjoys authority to strip sorrow from his depths.

The Fathers of the Church speak of deadly sorrow, distinguishing between holy sorrow accompanied by inner peace, which the Lord Christ blesses, saying: "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted" (Mt 5:4), and destructive sorrow springing from lack of hope.

Amma Syncletica sees in lust, temporal pleasure and destructive sorrow three springs of evil. They are connected with one another, each spring opening the way for the other. If a man allows lust to proceed from within, and finds it pleasant even in thought, it develops into temporary worldly joy, and so instead of enjoying the joy of the Spirit and longing for the heavenly Bridegroom, he falls into destructive sorrow. He who controls lust by the work of divine grace will not have a fleshly, temporary pleasure, and so deadly sorrow does not shatter him.

v There are three springs of the enemy from which every evil wells up: lust, pleasure and sorrow. They are connected one with another, and each follows the other. It is possible to control pleasure to some degree, but it is impossible to control lust, for the satisfaction of pleasure is accomplished by the body, but lust begins from the soul, whereas sorrow can dwell in both. So do not allow lust to become active, and thus you will dispel the last two (that is, evil pleasure and sorrow). But if you allow the first to emerge, it develops into the second, and then together they form a "vicious circle" from which the soul cannot escape.

Amma Syncletica St. Augustine sees in every work of love offered to the brethren for God's sake that what occupies the believer's heart is that this work touches his own salvation, and this love is love for the person himself, for what he offers is for the account of his own spiritual edification. He who does not love himself spiritually, how can he fulfill the commandment: "Love your neighbor as yourself"?

v Every person who gives alms for the atonement of his sins begins first with love for himself. Let a person remember the saying of the Lord: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself" (Mt 22:39), to realize that it is not fitting to give alms to his neighbor without showing mercy to himself. There is also another reminder: "Love your soul" [24]. How can anyone give alms in return for his sins if he does not give alms to himself that please God? In the same sense: "He that is evil to himself, to whom will he be good?" (see Sir 14:5).
And of course prayers have their role with respect to alms. Here appears the importance of the words: "My son, hast thou sinned? do so no more, but pray for thy former sins" (see Sir 21:1) [18].
St. Augustine Envy and anger shorten the number of your days, and anxiety brings old age before its time [24].
Jealousy and anger and care corrupt life, so that a man grows old before his time.
He who has a cheerful and good heart benefits from the food he eats [25].
The rejoicing man benefits from the food he eats, whatever its kind!
Inspired by Sirach 30

entries.section: Sanctify the new generation and cleanse it from our faults!

paragraphs.text: v O Holy One, sanctify our view of the new generation.
We desire that they be holier and better than we.
If the coming generations are not higher than we, the Church is counted stagnant and sick and bearing the smell of death.
v O Savior, lead us in raising the new generation.
Grant us the spirit of love, care and knowledge.
We love the new generation without pampering and corrupting laxity.
With firmness and seriousness we wish to see them successful leaders.
They realize that they are ambassadors for You, bearing witness to Your divine love.
Who trains them but Your Holy Spirit, that they may not stumble over our weaknesses.
We rejoice in their trust in the power of Your grace and their striving to be an icon of You.
v We thank You, O Physician of souls and bodies.
By You our souls challenge the world with all its allurements and sorrows.
Its possessions cannot enslave us, nor enslave our children.

Whether in bodily health or sickness we bless You, for You lead us to Yourself, and with every morning we and our children experience Your glories; our wealth or our poverty will not turn our eyes from looking to You.
v If the enemy attacks us with sorrow, he will not draw the joy of the Spirit from our hearts.
Our sojourn in this world is joyful, for You are our companion all the more in sorrows.
Our days are very few, as though they were thousands of years, for You bless every day and make it like a thousand years.
v You are the gladness of our heart; You are the door through which we enter into clinging to You.
You are our treasure, so we need nothing else but You.
v O Holy One, sanctify the new generation by Your grace.
Sanctify our body, that we may strive by Your grace, and thank You for the gift of bodily health.
Sanctify our spirits, that we may be made worthy of Your dwelling in them.
Sanctify our joy and rejoicing, that You may accept it as a sacrifice of thanksgiving for Your wondrous works with us.

1 Wakefulness for the sake of riches wastes away the body, and anxiety over it drives away sleep. 2 The wakefulness of anxiety deprives one of slumber, and severe illness is driven off by sleep. 3 The rich man toils in gathering money, and in his rest is filled with delights; 4 the poor man toils for the need of living, and in his rest becomes needy. 5 He who loves gold shall not be justified, and he who follows corruption shall be filled with it. 6 Many have fallen for the sake of gold, and their destruction has come to be before their faces. 7 Gold is a stumblingblock to those who sacrifice to it, and every fool is caught by it. 8 Blessed is the rich man who is found without blemish, and has not gone after gold. 9 Who is he, that we may call him blessed? For he has done wonders among his people. 10 Who has been tried by it and found perfect? Let him glory in it. Who has been able to transgress and has not transgressed, and to do evil and has not done it? 11 His goods shall be established, and the congregation shall declare his alms. 12 If you sit at a bountiful table, do not open your throat wide over it, 13 and do not say, How much there is upon it!

He speaks of the sound use of wealth immediately after speaking of bodily health, because some destroy their health by excessive effort for the sake of wealth. The love of money has gained mastery over many, and has made some careless of the safety of their souls and bodies. Because of the love of money, some are exposed to the following:
a. The ruin of bodily health through wakefulness out of love for money [2].
b. Suffering from anxiety and being deprived of enough time for sleep [1].
c. Some are exposed to bodily illnesses because of luxury and excess in eating [3].
d. The love of money drives God's righteousness out of the heart [5], so that a man loses the blessed life and the money itself [8].
e. He falls into temptations whenever tribulation comes [10].
f. He loses his role in supporting the needy in the holy congregation (the Church).
Wakefulness (sleeplessness) for the sake of wealth wastes away the body, and anxiety over wealth drives away sleep [1].

Wealth in itself is not evil, but it is a burden to the soul that clings to it, causing it to lose its life and tearing it away from its attachment to its Savior. St. John Chrysostom speaks to us of sleep as a gift of God which He gave us by nature for our rest. But we have no pity on ourselves; rather we stand in enmity with ourselves, inventing for ourselves a tyrant stronger than the force of nature, which robs us of the rest of sleep.

* It is said: "Anxiety over wealth drives away sleep" [1]. Behold the greatness of God's providence! He did not leave us the choice to sleep according to our own will, nor according to our need for sleep, but bound us by the necessities of nature, so that what is good for us might come to pass even without our will. To sleep is a matter of nature. But we, like cruel haters of ourselves, like strange enemies and persecutors, invent a tyrant stronger than this necessity of nature, the one that comes from money [1].

* Worse than every burning is what comes upon our souls through the bitterness of grief. Just as the body dries up and is wearied by its struggle against the violence of the sun's rays, and is brought into a shelter in which there are several springs, to be calmed by the gentle breeze, so the night does for us, when our souls are given over to sleep. Indeed, I ought rather to say that it is neither the night nor sleep that does this, but God, who knows how great is the toil and misery of our race. Yet we have no mercy on ourselves, as if we were enemies of our own souls, and we gave ourselves a despot stronger than the natural need for sleep, namely sleeplessness because of wealth... Behold the greatness of God's care. For He did not leave the right to rest to our will, nor the need for sleep to our choice, but bound sleep to the necessity of nature, so that we may practice what is good even without our will [2].

St. John Chrysostom * When one of the passions of your soul rises up in you, remember that those who think rightly and wish to establish what they have upon a sound and firm foundation do not rejoice in corruptible riches, but in the true glory which is in the heavens, and by this they become blessed. For wealth may be plundered or stolen by those who have greater power, but the virtue of the spirit alone is the faithful possession that cannot be taken away, besides that it rescues its owner after death.
Those who think thus are not deceived by the glitter of vain riches and the other delights [3].
St. Anthony the Great The care of sleeplessness deprives one of slumber, and severe illness puts an end to sleep [2].

One of the accumulated troubles of preoccupation with wealth is that anxiety invades the soul and one suffers from sleeplessness, which also causes bodily illnesses. In this the Apostle Paul says: "But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows" (1 Tim 6:9-10).

* Why do you envy the rich man? Is it because he has subjected himself to many cares?... For he is bound like a dog with myriads of chains, that is, his wealth!... And it is as though, in a spirit of enmity toward ourselves, we hand ourselves over to a tyrant stronger than the natural need for rest, that is, the sleeplessness that arises from wealth.
St. John Chrysostom The rich man toils in gathering money, and in his rest is filled with his luxury [3].

St. Ambrose comments thus on the parable of "Lazarus and the rich man" (Lk 16:19-31): [Not every poverty is necessarily holy, nor is every wealth hateful [4].] In other words, poverty is not an end in itself, nor is wealth evil in itself; rather it is the life of man that corrupts the one or the other. The pampered, luxurious life that has no pity on the needy dishonors wealth, and the holy, thankful life adorns poverty.
The poor man toils for the need of living, and in his rest becomes needy [4].

He who is born in poverty is not to blame for his poverty. If he offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God for the faculties He has given him, then although he is in need in temporal things, he is counted rich in his offerings. This is like the widow who offered two mites (Mk 12:42).
He who loves gold is not called righteous, and he who follows the track of gain goes astray because of it [5].

St. Cyril the Great comments on the saying of the Lord Christ: "There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day: and there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores" (Lk 16:19-31), saying: [I ask you to observe closely the words of the Savior... He called him "rich" simply so, but the poor man He pointed out by name. What do we conclude from this? That the rich man, being unmerciful, was without a name in the presence of God, since it is said elsewhere by the voice of the Psalmist concerning those who do not fear the Lord: "I will not take up their names into my lips" (Ps 16:4); but the poor man, as I said, had his name mentioned by the tongue of God [5].]
Many have fallen into disaster for the sake of gold, and their destruction has come to be before their faces [6].

* In the parable of Lazarus and the rich man (Lk 16:19-31), in the end the rich man became a beggar asking of the poor man, and begging from the table of him who had been hungry and cast down to the mouths of the dogs. The situation was reversed, and each one came to know who was truly rich and who was truly poor, for Lazarus appeared richer than all, and the other poorer than all.

As in the theaters the actors put on the masks of kings, generals, physicians, teachers, professors and soldiers, yet in their reality they are not so, so wealth and poverty here are mere masks. If you sit in a theater and see a man wearing the mask of a king, do not envy him, nor consider that he has become a king, nor desire to be like him... So the rich man here is often poor (in his depths): if you take off his mask, and uncover his conscience, and enter into his thought, you will often find in him the poverty of virtue, and find him belonging to the lowest classes [6].
St. John Chrysostom * Hear how the rich man boasted and was glad, he at whose door (Lazarus) was cast down and laid.
His body was sound and he was rich in his possessions, his clothing was fine and his food was good.
His table was abundant, his house resounded, his standing was awe-inspiring; he was rich and healthy, and everyone loved and honored him.
Splendid clothing, a healthy body, a full purse, and a life made pleasant with every good thing, without harm.
Rejoicing in his riches, proud of his garments, all of him splendid, luxurious and healthy, and he did not look upon the poor man.
Lazarus was at the door of this boaster, full of woes, and he saw the good things and did not murmur.
He only longed to be satisfied with the crumbs, and did not ask for the surplus that was there.
He did not desire clothing, nor riches, nor the foods that were abundant on the table.
He needed only the crumbs that the dogs eat; this is what nature requires, and this is what he longed for [7].
St. Jacob of Serugh It is a snare for those who devote their lives to it, and every fool falls into it [7].
When a man devotes his life to the love of the good things of the world, it corrupts his depths, and the good things of the world become evils to him.
* The good things of (the world) are in truth evils, and its evils (its afflictions) are also certainly good things.
All the good things of this world are full of death, and he who endures gathers life from its evils.
He who is at rest in it: torments are prepared and kept for him; and he who is tormented in it: he finds rest in the new world.
The Gospel of our Lord teaches men thus, and whoever wishes not to understand, that rests upon him.
He said plainly: He who finds himself destroys it, and he who destroys himself in the world finds it (Mt 10:39).
He who destroys himself is the one who toils, and is persecuted, and is crushed, and crucifies daily the passions and desires (Lk 9:23; Gal 5:24; 6:14).
And he dies every day for the hope of the world to come, and his life in the world which he does not love is a surplus.
And he who destroys himself here goes and finds a desirable place and a life of light without end.
And he finds his soul full of blessings in the great world, and in it the saying is fulfilled: he finds himself if he destroys it.

That one who boasts, and takes his ease, and sins, and swaggers (in his walk) admiring himself, in whom is the life of the world and all its pleasures, who loves riches, and whose soul is bound to possessions, who hates troubles and flees from torments, and finds himself in a pleasant life without annoyances, this one is destroyed, and makes the soul he has found guilty.
And he goes and inherits the sea of fire, like the rich man who received here all his good things, as it is said (Lk 16:25) [8].
St. Jacob of Serugh Blessed is the rich man who is found without blame, and does not go after gold [8].

There are blessed rich men, such as Abraham the father of the fathers, who was very rich (Gen 13:2). His wealth did not distract him from his attachment to God and the enjoyment of fellowship with Him, from his hospitality to strangers, and from making Sarah his wife a partner in serving them.
* It is necessary that gold follow you, not that you follow it. In truth gold is a good thing; surely God did not create anything evil. Do not be evil, and gold will become good.

Behold, I place gold in the hands of a godly person and of another who is unfaithful. If the unfaithful person takes it, the poor man is oppressed, those in authority are corrupted, the laws are broken, and social life is thrown into confusion. Why? Because the unfaithful man took the gold. And if the godly person takes it, the poor man is supported, the naked is clothed, the oppressed are set free, and the prisoners are rescued. How great is the good that the righteous person reaps from gold, and how many evils happen through the gold that the unfaithful man has taken!...

If you are unfaithful you will follow gold, and if you are godly gold will follow you. What does it mean that gold follows you? That you rule over it and are not its servant, because you possess it and it does not possess you [9].
St. Augustine Who is he, that we may call him blessed?
He does wonders in the midst of his people [9].

I rejoice in Your wonderful works, so that I forget even myself, and I delight in You alone. For what is better than You? In truth You are the great God, You do wonders in the body as in the soul, and You raise up from earthly man a son to Yourself, reflecting Your splendor upon him eternally.

* Wisdom works in everything; it accompanies all that is good. For how could it give good counsel unless justice were with it also, so that it might wrap itself in uprightness, and not fear death, and not draw back at any warning or fear, and not think it right to avoid the truth by any kind of flattery, nor avoid exile, knowing that the world is the homeland of the wise man? It does not fear want, knowing that nothing is lacking to the wise man, but the whole world with its riches is his. Who is greater than the man who knows not to be stirred at the thought of money, scorning wealth and holding it in contempt, like one who looks from a lofty foundation upon the desires of men? Men consider that one who acts thus is too exalted to be merely a man. It is said: "Who is he, that we may call him blessed? For he does wonders in his life" [9]. Surely one must marvel at him who scorns riches, looking to the fact that many care for them more than for their own safety [10].

St. Ambrose * He declares the wonders of God (Ps 1:9) who sees them accomplished not only openly in his body but also invisibly in his soul; indeed these wonders are more sublime and exalted. For men, being earthly, are led by what they see with the eye, and marvel the more that dead Lazarus rose in the body than that Paul the persecutor rose in the spirit (Jn 11; Acts 9). But the visible wonder calls the soul to enjoy the light, whereas through the invisible one a man passes on to understand it, and so speaks of all the wonders of God [11].

* To rejoice in the (wonderful) works of God is to forget even yourself, for you can delight in Him alone. For what is better than He? Do you not see this, that when you return to yourself you return to a sinful thing? "I will remember Your wonders of old" (Ps 11:77)... "You are the God that alone does wonders" (Ps 14:77). In truth You are the great God, You do wonders in the body as in the soul, You alone are the doer of them. The deaf hear, the blind see, the weak are healed, the dead rise, and the paralyzed are strengthened. But these wonders were accomplished at that time in the body. Let us look at those accomplished in the soul. Those who a little while ago were drunkards have become workers, those who a little while ago were idolaters have now become believers, those who formerly robbed others now offer gifts to the poor [12].

* "The heavens shall praise Your wonders, O Lord" (Ps 89:5)... For in every work of mercy toward lost souls, every work of justification of sinners, what do we praise but the wonderful works of God? You praise Him because the dead rise; praise Him the more because the lost have been saved. Yesterday, O man, you saw a whirlpool of drunkenness; now you see the beauty of self-control. Yesterday you saw a blasphemer of God; now you see him praising Him. Yesterday he was a slave of the creature; today he has become a worshiper of the Creator. Thus men have turned away from these dreadful conditions. Let them not look to their own merits. Let them become heavens and praise the wonders of Him who made them heavens" [13].
St. Augustine Who has been tried by it and found perfect? He may glory in it.
Who has been able to transgress and has not transgressed? And to do evil and has not done it? [10]
His goods shall be established, and the congregation shall declare his alms [11].

What commends a man for the Kingdom is not the amount of money, but his faithfulness in using it. Some were helped by money toward the salvation of their souls when they used it for the glory of God and the good of their brethren, being content with only what was necessary for themselves. Blessed, then, is that man who was able to sin and transgress the commandment because of money, but refrained from it through his fear of God. For his goods are established, because his conduct glorifies God.

* Show works of righteousness, for you are able to accomplish works according to your ability. Your fear of God and your obedience to Him are not shown in abstaining from works beyond your strength, but in those in which you are able to violate the Law, yet do not violate it [10]. If you give alms to the poor after having robbed them of what they had, it were better for you neither to take from them nor to give to them. Why do you defile your wealth, which in truth is your own, by adding to it money gained by injustice? Why do you offer a gift out of the injustice which you dared to present as an abomination, with the intention of showing mercy to another poor man? Be merciful to him against whom you have sinned. Show him kindness, and so you fulfill the duty of mercy together with justice. God has no fellowship with greed, and the Lord is not a companion of robbers and thieves. He did not leave the poor to us to feed them because He is unable to do this Himself, but He asks us to do it for our own good, as a fruit of mercy and justice [14].
St. Basil the Great

14 Remember that an evil eye is a great evil. 15 What has been created more wicked than the eye? Therefore it weeps from every person. 16 Wherever it glances, do not stretch out your hand to it, 17 and do not crowd it at the dish. 18 Understand what your neighbor has from what you have, and consider every matter. 19 Eat of what is set before you, as a man eats, and do not be greedy, lest you be hated. 20 Be the first to stop, out of good manners, and do not be insatiable, lest you be rebuked. 21 And when you sit among many, do not stretch out your hand before them. 22 How little suffices a well-bred man, and such a one does not gasp on his bed. 23 Sleeplessness, cholera and colic are for the gluttonous man. 24 The sleep of health is for the man moderate in his belly; he rises early and is master of himself. 25 And if you are forced to eat, withdraw from the midst of the company and rest. 26 Hear me, my son, and do not despise me, and in the end you will find my words true. 27 In all your works be diligent, and no sickness will overtake you. 28 He who is generous with food, lips bless him, and the testimony to his generosity is a true testimony. 29 He who is stingy with food, the city murmurs against him, and the testimony to his meanness is a sure testimony. 30 Do not play the hero in regard to wine, for wine has destroyed many. 31 The furnace tests the tempered iron, and wine tests the hearts of the proud in battle. 32 Wine is life to a man, if you drink it moderately. 33 What life is there for a man who has no wine? 34 What takes away life? Death. 35 Wine was created from the beginning to make men glad, not to make them drunk. 36 Wine is the gladness of the heart and the joy of the soul, to him who drinks of it in its time as much as suffices. 37 Drinking with gentleness is health to soul and body. 38 Excess in drinking wine is strife and contention. 39 Excess in drinking wine is bitterness to the soul. 40 Drunkenness stirs up the anger of the fool to his downfall, and lessens strength and multiplies wounds. 41 At a wine banquet do not rebuke your neighbor, and do not despise him in his merriment. 42 Do not speak to him words of reproach, and do not press him in demanding repayment.

Ben Sirach ties the conduct of man in every sphere to the wisdom that befits a man of God. It befits the believer, who bears the image of God and is an ambassador of the Lord Christ, to bear witness to the blessed, heaven-like life even in his eating and drinking, and indeed in his walking and the movements of his body. When a believer is invited to a table, it befits him to practice self-control and the restraint of the appetite for food, not for the sake of those who share the table with him, but for the sake of the soundness of his inner being. For while we care for the health of the body in sharing in banquets, it befits us to care for the health of the spirit.

He presents to us proper conduct at banquets, such as moderation in food and drink, commitment to godly conduct befitting the people of God, care in conversation during the banquet, and generosity in a spirit of wisdom.

The table is a wonderful school in which all, children and young people, adults and elders, learn how to enjoy the divine presence while they are at the table. We mention, by way of example, the following:

a. Not only does one begin to eat after prayer, but all feel that they are in the divine presence while they share in eating or in conversation during the meal. The godly man knows, during the meal, when to be silent and when to speak, and how to sanctify every breath of his life wherever he may be!

b. Banquets are a wonderful opportunity, not for a man to display his asceticism in food or his sharing it with others, but to express naturally what is in his depths of joy of the spirit and satisfaction with the divine presence.

c. The sanctification of time even in the moments of eating and drinking. I recall, for example, that at one of the church conferences between the Chalcedonian and non-Chalcedonian Orthodox, during the lunch meal in Switzerland, I noticed that His Grace Anba Gregorios, Bishop of Coptic Studies, had turned his eyes for some minutes in a certain direction while silent. I asked him: "What are you thinking about?" He answered me: "I am looking at this small icon on the wall; it is Coptic art! Notice how the cheek of the Child Jesus clings to the cheek of St. Mary! St. Mary has become a unique divine throne upon which He sits and declares His love for mankind in the person of His mother according to the flesh!" And he told me the story of a British man who would not allow himself to sit on a chair in his house because Queen Victoria had sat on it one day. How great is St. Mary, in whose lap the King of kings sat?! This is what occupied the heart of His Grace Anba Gregorios while he was eating.

d. The sitting of children with their parents during a banquet or at home is counted a wonderful occasion for shaping their personalities, so that they may silently take from their parents a life of thanksgiving, of not being gluttonous, of not being preoccupied with food, and of consideration for others, so that they do not fill their plate more than they will eat! They realize that even in the midst of a banquet they are members of a holy congregation, which enjoys the earnest of heaven on every occasion.
e. Greed or gluttony is a great evil.
f. A man eats with good manners, and with deliberation, of what is set before him.
g. Let the believer be the first to stop eating.
h. The believer does not stretch out his hand to eat before the others.
i. Gluttony deprives a man of quiet sleep.
j. Not to exceed in drinking wine, lest a man perish.
k. Drunkenness stirs up anger and adds wounds to the soul.
l. At the wine banquet we do not rebuke anyone nor trouble him with our demands.
Are you sitting at the table of a great man? Do not be greedy, and do not say: "How much there is upon it!" [12].
It befits the wise man not to fix his eyes on the abundance of food or its variety, but on his inner satisfaction, the beauty of his depths, and the health of his spirit before God and heaven.

In the parable of "Lazarus and the rich man" (Lk 16:19-31), the Lord Christ linked the pride of the rich man with a life of luxury, especially his concern to hold banquets. St. Cyril the Great says: [Let us look at the pride of the rich man, who was arrogant because of things of no real value, for it is said: "He was clothed in purple and fine linen," that is, his concern was to adorn himself with beautiful clothing, and his garment was costly. He lived in unceasing banquets; this is what is meant by the words "fared sumptuously every day," besides the word "luxuriously," that is, wastefully... What was the result? It differs little from the forms of statues and paintings, for in truth the rich man was an object of admiration to those absorbed in the senses, but his heart was full of pride and haughtiness; he thought something of himself with arrogance, although there was nothing excellent in his mind, and he offered varied dishes because of his empty pride. His delight was in costly banquets, music and revelry; he had many cooks working to arouse gluttony with appetizing foods; the cupbearers wore beautiful clothes; he had male and female singers; he heard the voices of flatterers. Thus the rich man lived, therefore the disciple of Christ warns us, saying: "For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life" (1 Jn 2:16). Meanwhile Lazarus suffered from sickness and poverty, cast out at the rich man's gate. The rich man dwelt in lofty halls and spacious, magnificent houses, while the poor man was cast outside, neglected, appearing as one who deserves nothing. Deprived of compassion and care, he found nothing to satisfy his hunger, and so he gathered the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table. He also suffered from a grievous disease without remedy, yes, and the dogs licked his sores; and as it seems they did not harm him but comforted him and had compassion on him, for with their tongues they soothed his toils and removed what pained him and eased his sores. But the rich man was crueler than the beasts, for he neither had mercy on him nor comforted him, but was harsh [15].]
Remember that an evil eye is a great evil. What has been created more wicked than the eye?
Therefore it weeps for every face [16] [13].
