The eye, which was created to support the spirit in enjoying spiritual insight, is not satisfied with the whole world if it is offered to it; what satisfies it is its meeting with God and its fellowship with Him, and its readiness to enjoy the heavenly table and the bread of angels.
Do not stretch out your hand to everything you see, and do not crowd anyone at a dish [14].
Taking part by accepting the invitation to the banquet does not mean ignoring self-control; it does not befit the believer to stretch out his hand to everything he looks at on the table.
Understand what your neighbor has [17] from what you have, and deliberate in every matter [15].
Eat of what is set before you, as a man eats, and do not devour it in a greedy manner, lest you be despised [16].
The believer takes care not to be a cause of distress to the host, confusing him with particular dishes that it may be hard for him to provide at that time.
Be the first to stop eating, out of good manners, and do not be greedy, lest you cause offense [17].

He points to the care to be taken in the manner of eating, for some have a disgusting way of eating, and this way often repels those who sit with them and arouses their revulsion, such as making a sound in the throat when gulping down water, and eating in a manner that betrays gluttony and a lack of cleanliness [18].
And when you sit at a table among many, do not stretch out your hand before them [18].
It befits the believer to stretch out his hand to the food after all have begun, and to finish before all.

* The mark of the moderate person is that he takes a small quantity when eating or drinking, but does this at a fitting time; so do not hurry to be the one who begins to eat, nor hesitate here and there to be the first to finish eating, so that you take on an attitude of indifference [19].

St. Clement of Alexandria * The mark of the man who has control of himself is that he takes a small quantity when he eats or drinks, but does so at a fitting time, and does not hurry as far as possible at the beginning of his eating, nor lag here and there. And he is the first to finish eating, and takes care not to display indifference. The Scripture says: "Be the first to stop eating, out of good manners... and when you sit at the table among many, do not stretch out your hand before them" (cf. Sir 31:19).

There is no need to say that it does not befit us not to lean forward in order to begin taking the food out of gluttony, just as it does not befit us to hold back too far and so confess, through our fault, that we have no control over ourselves.

At the same time we do not stand like those who guard their food, like animals that stand poised for their food, nor do we yield to pleasure through the many pleasures of food. It is a mark of self-control that we rise from the table before everyone and withdraw from it in a spirit of humility. It is said: "When the time has come, rise and do not delay; hasten to your house and do not loiter" (cf. Sir 31:11) [20].
St. Clement of Alexandria How little suffices a well-bred man, and on his bed he does not breathe with difficulty [19].
To be content with eating little of what is set before one is not a commandment peculiar to monks; rather it befits all Christians to keep it.
Healthy sleep depends on moderation in food. He rises early with a good spirit.
But gluttony is accompanied by anxiety because of sleeplessness, and by vomiting and colic [20].

Healthy sleep depends on moderation in eating. St. John Chrysostom speaks to us of the vice of the desire for sumptuous food, showing that this pleasure quickly stops when the belly is filled, and sometimes before the feeling of satisfaction, for a man loses the attraction of this pleasure while the food is still in the mouth and has not yet been swallowed.
* Let us first examine the vice of pleasure concerning the sumptuous table, which is exceedingly attractive...

At the moment when a person begins to feel satisfied, the pleasure stops. Indeed sometimes it stops more quickly than the course of a flowing stream. And sometimes the pleasure does not remain until the food itself is swallowed, but stops while the food is between the teeth.

I am not speaking of the evils that follow this, nor of how dangerous the storm is that arises from the pleasures of the table. In truth, the person who abstains (from pleasure) not only feels comfortable, but feels light and more at ease than the one who lies in his bedchamber weighed down with a stuffed stomach. The Scripture says that healthy sleep depends on moderation in eating. Is there any need to summon sicknesses, indigestion, trials and waste? They come from such meals [21].

* We read: "The sleep of health is for the man moderate in his belly"; moderation in eating (cf. Sir 13:20). In whatever you keep the proper measure it is delightful, but he who exceeds the measure loses the pleasure [22].
St. John Chrysostom If you are stuffed with food, rise in the middle of the meal and stop eating [21].

This was a bad habit that was widespread among the Romans: when a person was invited to more than one banquet, he would rise after eating, go into the bath and vomit the food, and then prepare himself for the next banquet. Perhaps here he gives advice to the person who was compelled to eat too much under the pressure of the host.
Hear me, my son, and do not despise me, and you will realize that my words are important.
In all your works be ready, and no sickness will overtake you [22].
Ben Sirach fears that some may despise his words because he enters into the details of daily life, but he wishes the reader to arrive at a state of moderation in everything.
He who is generous in (offering) his food, lips bless him, and their testimony to his loftiness is trustworthy [23].
He who is stingy with food, the city murmurs against him, and their testimony to his stinginess is a true testimony [24].
While he rebukes the greedy guest, he urges the host to offer generously to his guest everything possible.
Do not prove your valor (by drinking) wine, for wine has destroyed many [25].
As the furnace tests the hardness of steel in the process of its tempering, so wine tests hearts in the fighting of the proud [26].

* Those are worthy of pity who withdraw from moderation in their gatherings, thinking that their life is happier when it turns to licentious drinking. Their life is nothing but festivals of licentious drunkenness, full of troubles (headache), marked by idleness and drinking and so on. You see some of them in truth half-drunk, stammering in speech with one another, putting garlands around their necks as though they were bottles (of drunkenness), and under the cover of sincere friendship each one spits wine upon the others... It was well said: "As the furnace tests the hard steel that is cast into it, so wine makes the heart proud" (cf. Sir 31:26) [23].
St. Clement of Alexandria Wine is like life to a man if you drink it moderately; what life is there for him who has no wine?
For it was created to make men glad [27].
Wine is the gladness of the heart and the joy of the soul, to him who drinks of it at the proper time and in moderation [28].

In the Old Testament wine pointed to pleasure and joy (Judg 9:13; Ps 104:15). So when the Virgin Lady came to the Lord Christ at the wedding of Cana of Galilee, she said to Him, "They have no wine," which means that joy had ceased from Israel, and this is what Ben Sirach meant here.
Excess in drinking wine is bitterness to the soul, and brings agitation, stumbling and falling [29].

* The Scripture says: "Do not be excessive in wine, for wine has shattered many" (cf. Sir 31:29). The Scythians and the Celts (an Indo-European race that dwelt in central and western Europe) and the people of the island of Iberia are occupied with drinking without limit, and they were all warlike peoples, and think that they are doing a noble and pleasant work. Let us, the peaceful people, celebrate our feasts and drink the cups of friendship without wine, so that we may be glad without committing sin [24].
St. Clement of Alexandria Drunkenness stirs up the anger of the fool to his hurt, and lessens his strength, and adds to his wounds [30].

* The Tragedian says: "Every man whom wine overcomes falls under his passions and is empty of reason, utters vain babble, and is compelled against his will to hear things that he said of his own will." Before this a warning was written by Wisdom: "Excessive drunkenness stirs up quarrels and causes much ruin" (cf. Sir 31:30) [25].
St. Clement of Alexandria At the wine banquet do not rebuke your neighbor, and do not despise him in his revelry.
And do not utter a word of insult against him, and do not grieve him with demands that you make of him [31].
In the discourse of Pope Gregory (the Great) on pastoral care, he stresses the obligation to act at the right moment. He calls us to act without fear but in a spirit of wisdom [26].

* Since God knows that drinking wine in moderation is healthy and increases discernment, while he who gulps it down without measure engenders vices (cf. Sir 31:30-42), He gave us this creature. He left to mankind the freedom and the possibility of using it abundantly, so that even by using a small quantity it might be a lesson in sobriety, and the condition of human nature bears the error and destruction of its misuse and the commission of the crime of drunkenness. Noah became drunk and reeling because of wine, and fell into a deep sleep (Gen 9:21). In this way he who had acquired glory through the Flood came into shame through wine. Nevertheless the Lord preserved the good qualities in wine by its nature, so that He made its fruit contribute to our salvation, and caused us to receive the forgiveness of sins by its use (in the Divine Liturgy) [27].

St. Ambrose * Let us keep far, far away from jesting, for it is the beginning of abuse, by which fierce quarrels develop, and family enmities, and the rising up of enemies. We believe that arrogance accompanies drunkenness... The Scripture says: "At the wine banquet do not rebuke your neighbor" [28].
St. Clement of Alexandria Inspired by Sirach 31

entries.section: I long to enjoy the heavenly table!

paragraphs.text: * Grant me, O Lord, faithfulness in the little over which You have set me, so that You may set me over the much that You are preparing for me.
By Your wisdom I trade with the talents here, that I may enjoy the glories in eternity.
Take away from me every attachment to temporal wealth, so that I may enjoy Your peace in my waking as in my sleep.
May I enjoy health of spirit as health of body.
I will stretch out my hand to give, not to take.
I will manage what I have with wisdom, so that nothing enslaves me.
I will not be a captive to grief nor to pain, but I will enjoy the glory of the children of God.
Instead of the luxurious life, I put on Your splendid righteousness.
I will not devote my heart to passing temporal things, but to You, O Eternal One.
* You promised me that You go up to prepare a place for me.
What place do You prepare for me except that You make me ready to rest in Your bosom?!
Queen Esther was not pleased to sit at the king's table, but enjoyed the table of heaven!
For the sake of love I share with my brethren, without desire for eating or drinking.
When I begin to pray at the table, I ask that You not deprive me of the bread of angels.
I want to be drunk with Your divine love, that my soul may rejoice.
The food of the world, if it increases a little, confuses my soul and body.
But the food of heaven increases my hunger and thirst for You, O Satisfier of souls!

1 If they make you the master of the feast, do not be lifted up, but be among them as one of them. 2 Take care of them, and then sit down, and when you have fulfilled your duty, recline, 3 that you may rejoice because of them, and receive a crown as an ornament, and be honored by their gifts. 4 Speak, you who are old, for it becomes you. 5 But with accurate knowledge, and do not hinder the music.

In ancient times the leading of a banquet was regarded as a great honor to a person. When a godly man is appointed master of the table, he sets in his heart that he is as one of all those present, marked in his dealing by a spirit of humility and care for all the invited guests, whatever their positions.
Have they appointed you master of the feast? Do not be proud, but be as one of them; take care of them, and then sit down [1].

The aim of banquets is the practice of love, the fellowship of joy, and the practice of brotherhood in a spirit of meekness. Therefore the leader of the table is bound by particular qualities, among them that he does not think himself to be in a position of authority and control over the arrangement of the table, but reckons himself one of those who share in the table, committed to kindness in a spirit of love and wisdom, and that he is invited to serve those present, not to be served.

* Behold how the leader who led them into the holy land, the land of promise, was himself one of the people. He was the successor of Moses, and yet he did not allow himself to claim a portion of the land. Although he was the leader of the people, he waited to take the small portion; he who is called Joshua (Jesus) deserved to build the place which he had received and to take care of its rebuilding, so as to make it truly fitting as a gift of God and a divine inheritance... (Joshua the son of Nun) drew lots for all and left for himself the last place. What do you think, why did he want to be the last? Surely to be first of all (Mt 19:30) [2].
Origen After fulfilling all your duties, sit at the table, that you may rejoice on their account, and receive a crown for your good leadership [2].

It befits the leader to realize his responsibilities regarding the food and its arrangement, and to observe and direct the conversation among those present, neither in unseemly jesting nor in dry seriousness. It befits him that the conversations not be sharp, but cheerful, full of love and profitable. Cheerful conversation is the crown of a table that is properly prepared. Some discussions must be postponed to their proper time, for man shall not live by bread alone (Mt 4:4).
Likewise the table is not the proper place for dry discussions.
Speak, O elder, for you are fit for it, acting with accurate knowledge, and do not hinder the music [3].
In a person's management of the leading of the banquet, it befits him that the banquet be a living icon of the supper of the Lamb (Rev 19:9), in which quiet music prevails, not noise.

6 Do not pour out talk where there is listening, and do not bring forth wisdom out of its time. 7 The strains of singers at a banquet of wine are like a seal of ruby in a setting of gold. 8 The melodies of singers over pleasant wine are like a seal of emerald in a work of gold. 9 Listen while you are silent, and by your modesty you will gain favor. 10 Speak, young man, but seldom, when need calls you. 11 If you are asked twice, answer briefly, 12 expressing much in few words, and be as one who knows and keeps silent. 13 In the company of the great do not make yourself equal to them, and among elders do not be much given to chattering. 14 Before the thunder goes forth the lightning, and before the modest goes favor. 15 When the time has come, rise, do not delay. Hasten to your house, do not be negligent. There amuse yourself, 16 and do what you please, and do not sin by words of pride. 17 And for all these things bless your Maker, who makes you drunk with His good things.
Do not pour out talk at a gathering, and do not bring forth wisdom out of its time [4].
The table is not a field for displaying a man's eloquence, wisdom, gifts and abilities.
* In my opinion limits must be set to speech; if one wishes to practice self-control, his limit is to stop at answering the questions directed to him, even if he is able to speak.
St. Clement of Alexandria A musical gathering at a wine banquet is like a seal of ruby in a setting of gold [5].

In that Sirach prefers quiet music with a little wine, he means that an atmosphere of love and joy should prevail at the table; the table is not a place for talking of profound thoughts that are hard to follow, nor should a spirit of argument prevail there, which may turn into a kind of sharpness of style. Tertullian says: "Argument over the Holy Scriptures profits nothing. This is plain; it only wearies a man's stomach or his mind."
In the early ages Christians were forbidden to eat with heretics, perhaps for fear that the table might turn into an atmosphere of dry disputation.
A musical melody over pleasant wine is like a seal of emerald in a setting of gold [6].
Speak, young man, when need calls you, twice at the most if you are asked repeatedly [7].

He gives us commandments concerning the conduct of the young man at the banquet, for it is not an opportunity to display his cheerful personality in extremes of loud laughter and vain, unedifying talk. Ben Sirach requires him to lessen his talking at the banquet, perhaps that he may be rather a listener and so benefit from the experience of others.
Be concise, and express much in few words, and be as one who knows, yet holds his tongue [8].

Brevity in speech during the meal is effective and practical. Much talking, whatever the subject of the conversation, scatters the mind, especially at the table. The less the young man talks, the more he becomes an object of the esteem and admiration of those present, especially since the great and the elders do not tend to listen for long.

* Let these take heed that when the young of birds try to fly before their wings have grown strong, they fall from above where they were trying to soar. Likewise let them understand that if we place heavy timbers upon the frames of buildings that have not yet become strong, the result is not the living of a life but destruction and death.

Likewise when women bear children whose growth is not complete, they fill graves with the dead, not houses with life. Therefore the Truth Himself teaches His disciples about the power of teaching, He who wished to give an example to His followers not to venture upon the ministry of teaching before their ability for it is complete. And He who could have given strength at once to the one whom He wished to strengthen added at once, saying: "But tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high" (Lk 24:49).

To remain in the city means to withdraw into seclusion between ourselves and our own souls, so that we do not go about as teachers unless we have put on divine power. Only then do we go outside from meditation in the depths of our souls to where we can teach others. Therefore it is said by the tongue of the wise man: "Speak, young man, but seldom, when need calls you. If you are asked twice, answer briefly" (cf. Sir 32:10-11).

For this reason our Savior Himself, who is the Creator and who sits in the heavens, continually teaching the angels by the declaration of His surpassing power, did not wish to be a teacher of men on earth before the age of thirty. And it is clear that He wished to instill a holy fear in those who are hasty, when they see that He who was without sin did not come forward to teach with the grace of the perfect life until He reached the fullness of age. And here the Gospels show: "And when he was twelve years old... the child Jesus tarried behind in Jerusalem" (Lk 2:42-43). And when His parents sought Him, "they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions" (Lk 2:46) [3].
Pope Gregory (the Great)
In the company of the great, do not make yourself equal to them, and if another speaks, lessen your talk [9].
Lightning flashes before the thunder, and favors [4] go before the humble man [10].
The banquet is a wonderful opportunity to show love in a spirit of humility, without expecting words of praise from those present.

* If we bear the holy thought of God like a seal that is not loosened, it is imprinted upon our hearts by constant, pure remembrance. By this we become partakers in the love of God, who inspires us to fulfill the commandments of the Lord, and He Himself remains kept in us without distraction [5].

* This is a testimony that no one can deny, that if we fulfilled all the rites and works of righteousness, and kept all the commandments of the Lord, and performed great wonders without love, they would be counted as works of iniquity and not as gifts of the Spirit, not because there is anything faulty in these works themselves, but because those who perform them have as their whole aim to magnify themselves, as the Apostle says of those who "suppose that godliness is a means of gain" (1 Tim 6:5). And in another place he says: "Some indeed preach Christ even of envy and strife; and some also of good will: the one preach Christ of contention, not sincerely, supposing to add affliction to my bonds" (Phil 1:15-16). And in another place he affirms: "For neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloke of covetousness; God is witness: nor of men sought we glory, neither of you, nor yet of others, when we were able to be in dignity as the apostles of Christ" (1 Thess 2:5-6) [6].
* Each time we bend the knee and rise, we show by this act that sin throws us to the ground, and the love of Christ calls us to heaven [7].

St. Basil the Great * What is the head of the virtues? Humility! Therefore (the Lord Christ) began with it, saying: "Blessed are the poor" (Mt 5:3; Lk 6:20). This head has no long lock of hair, nor hair in curls, but in it is beauty, so that it draws God to it. Of it He says: "To this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word" (Isa 66:2); and "Mine eyes are upon the meek of the earth" (cf. Ps 101:6); and "The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart" (Ps 34:18)... This is the parent of wisdom. When one has it, he has the rest of the virtues also... It pours out great beauty even upon the other members. If someone mixed endless colors, they would not bring about such beauty [8].
St. John Chrysostom Rise to leave the place at a fitting time, and do not linger.
Hasten to your house and do not be slothful [11].

He calls us to observe the sanctification of time, so that lingering and excess in staying up late are not fitting, out of care for a person's health. On the other hand it is fitting that the banquet not be at the expense of the family's joy, especially the children's, or at the expense of a person's worship in his house. Recreation at home is better than staying up late at parties.
There you will be glad, and do what seems good to you, but do not sin by words of pride [12].
And bless your Creator for all these things, who fills you with His good things [13].

If it is necessary to open the banquet with prayer, that the Lord may bless the food and lead those present to joy of spirit in His divine presence even while eating, it befits a person to offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving for the joyful spiritual atmosphere he has enjoyed.

18 He who fears the Lord will accept His discipline, and those who rise early for Him will find His favor. 19 He who seeks the Law will be filled with it, but the hypocrite will stumble in it. 20 Those who fear the Lord will find justice, and will kindle from judgments a lamp for themselves. 21 The sinful man avoids reproof, and finds arguments that suit his desire. 22 The man of counsel does not neglect reflection, but the proud, who is not such a one, is not seized by fear, 23 not even after he has done as he pleased without counsel. 24 Do nothing without counsel, and you will not regret your deed. 25 Do not walk in the way of ruin, and you will not stumble over the stones. Do not cast yourself on a path that you have not tried, lest you make for yourself a stumblingblock. 26 Beware even of your sons, and be on guard against the members of your household. 27 In all your works follow your conscience, for that is the keeping of the commandments. 28 He who follows the Law keeps the commandments, and he who trusts in the Lord will not lose.
He who fears the Lord accepts teaching, and those who rise early to Him obtain His favor [14].

God stretches out His hand all the day long (Isa 65:2); everyone who rises early to Him and seeks Him earnestly finds Him, for he offers Him the firstfruits, and so obtains His favor. "I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me" (Prov 8:17).
He who seeks the Law is filled with it, but the hypocrite stumbles in it [15].

He connects indirectly the fear of the Lord with the seeking of the Law, for he says that the fear of the Lord prepares the believer to accept teaching, and goes on to say that he who seeks the Law is filled with it, and so becomes godly, a fearer of the Lord, and not a hypocrite [15]. The hypocrite here means one who knows the Law and deliberately ignores it in his thought, heart and conduct, even if he practices some outward show of religion. In the age of Ben Sirach some of the Jews boasted of the Law and kept it by heart but did not live it.
Those who fear the Lord discover (right) judgment, and like light they make righteous works shine [16].

In a wonderful sequence and marvelous connection Ben Sirach begins with the divine fear that grants the Lord's favor and His pleasure in His children [14]; the fruit of that is the believer's longing to enjoy the sweetness of the Law and to be filled with it without stumbling, which the hypocrite does not enjoy [15]. By this the fearer of the Lord enters into new depths, and discovers the beauty of discernment and prudence, and practices works of righteousness through divine grace like a light that shines from his depths [16].
The sinful man rejects correction, and finds arguments that suit his desire [17].
The wise man is constantly concerned with the correction of himself, but the careless sinner ignores it.

* It is written in Jeremiah: "Jerusalem hath grievously sinned; therefore she has become a tumult; all that honoured her despise her, because they have seen her nakedness" (Mk 11:8). At any rate, he lessens the severity and harshness of the accusation, showing the sweetness of his teacher, saying: "My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord; neither be weary of his correction: for whom the Lord loveth he correcteth; even as a father the son in whom he delighteth" (Prov 3:11-12), while "the sinful man avoids reproof" [17]. Therefore the Scripture says: "Let the righteous man rebuke me and discipline me, but let not the oil of sinners anoint my head" (Ps 141:5) [9].
St. Clement of Alexandria The man of counsel does not neglect thinking, but the stranger and the proud do not tremble in fear [18].
Do nothing without counsel, and you will not regret your deed [19].

The man who is earnest about the salvation of his soul takes care to think deeply on the Law. And he accepts the counsel of the prudent and the wise. The believer's recourse to counsel instills in him a spirit of humility, so that he does not fall into pride.

* Brother, the Holy Scripture says: "Do all things with counsel, and without counsel do nothing." When you were acting without counsel but by your own will, you were not striving with your mind. For there is no one who does not need counsel except God alone, who created wisdom. But when you sought to cut off your own desire according to the mind of God and to attain humility, and to take me, your very little brother, as your counselor, you stirred up the envy of Satan, the enemy of good, who envies all men continually [10].

* If you have not yet attained the spiritual level, and are still on the bodily level, humble your mind and submit to your teacher, so that he may teach you with tenderness, and "without counsel do nothing," even if it seems good to you, because the light of Satan is revealed at the end to be darkness. So if you hear or think or see something without the least effort in your heart, know that this is from Satan [11].

Sts. Barsanuphius and John * Question: The Lord commands: "Whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain" (Mt 5:41). And the Apostle teaches us to submit ourselves one to another in the fear of Christ (Eph 5:21). Are we then bound to obey everyone, any person who gives us orders?

Answer: The matter differs according to those who give the command; they must not wrong the obedience of those who receive the command. Moses did not refuse to listen to his father-in-law Jethro when he gave him good counsel (Ex 18:19). But surely there is no small difference in commands, for some give commands against the commandments of the Lord, and others corrupt the commandments of the Lord, falsifying them in various ways by mixing them with forbidden things, and others give commands that agree with the commandment. Others again, although they do not clearly agree with the commandment, nevertheless contribute and help toward carrying it out. It is therefore necessary to remember the commandment of the Apostle who says: "Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. Abstain from all appearance of evil" (1 Thess 5:20-21). Again he says: "Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ" (2 Cor 10:5). Thus if we are commanded to do something that agrees with the commandments of the Lord, or contributes to fulfilling them, or supports the soul, we must accept the command with zeal and care according to the will of God, and so fulfill what is written: "Bearing with one another in the love of Christ" (Eph 4:20).

But if we are commanded to do something against the commandments of the Lord, or something that appears to corrupt or falsify the commandment, then it is time to say: "We ought to obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29), and to remember the Lord who says: "A stranger will they not follow, but will flee from him: for they know not the voice of strangers" (Jn 10:5).

It befits us to take into account the Apostle, who wished to reassure us again, and ventured to speak even of angels, saying: "But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed" (Gal 1:8).

From these sayings we learn that even if a person is very dear to us, and perhaps in a high position and an object of admiration, yet makes known to us what our Lord requires, or commands us to do something that the Lord forbids, this person must be rejected, and condemned by all who love the Lord [12].

St. Basil the Great * The hasty destroy every good deed, and fall into evil because of their lack of discernment of good works. Such people do not think about what they are doing nor when they are doing it. They do not realize that something should not have been done until after its time had passed. To these Ben Sirach addresses his fitting saying: "Do nothing without counsel, and you will not regret your deed" (cf. Sir 32:19). And (Solomon) also says: "(Let thine eyes look right on,) and let thine eyelids look straight before thee" (Prov 4:25). And this does not come to pass unless counsel precedes our deeds. And those who do not examine their deeds go forward, but with closed eyes. These fall quickly where they have neglected the eyelids of counsel, and their feet slip [13].
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Do not walk in a way full of obstacles, and do not stumble on stony ground [20].
Do not trust excessively in a way that has not been examined [21].
The wise man avoids ways full of stumblingblocks. And at the same time he must walk with caution, lest there be hidden stumblingblocks [20-21].
And beware of your children [22].
In all your works entrust yourself to the Lord, for that is the keeping of the commandments [23].
* Question: Does the Word permit us to do what is good as each of us pleases?

Answer: He who pleases himself pleases a man, because each one of us is a human being. But then "cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm," and this is plain in him who trusts in himself. And there is added: "and whose soul (heart) departeth from the Lord" (Jer 17:5).

So he who pleases another, or does something to satisfy himself, falls from godliness, and falls into wavering for human benefit. The Lord says: "But all their works they do for to be seen of men" (Mt 23:5; 6:2). And the Apostle confesses: "For if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10). But there is a more serious threat that the Holy Book of God presents, saying: "God has scattered the bones of those who please men (Ps 52:6) LXX [14].
St. Basil the Great He who trusts in the Law gives heed to the commandments, and he who trusts in the Lord suffers no loss [24].

* What is hard, or painful, or impossible in the Lord's saying: "Sell that thou hast, and give to the poor"? If He had charged you to plow the land or to venture in trade, and to bear the labors that follow from it, you would understand the grief that comes over you; but He offers you the gaining of eternal happiness in an easy way, without work or sweat, so why do you not rejoice in the ease of salvation, instead of lamenting and exposing yourself to the loss of the reward for your work?

So if you have not truly killed, as you say, nor stolen, nor borne false witness, you make all your efforts vain, when you do not add to that what can open to you the Kingdom of God. If a physician came to you to set right one of your members, you would not hesitate but would accept it willingly; why then do you grieve and are troubled when the Physician of souls comes to you, wishing to make you perfect by adding to you what you essentially lack?
There is no doubt that you are very far from what the love of neighbor requires, and you bear false witness that you love him as yourself.

What the Lord offers you is conclusive proof of your lack of true love. For if you had truly kept from your youth the commandment of love for your neighbor, and made yourself equal to your brother, could you have this vast wealth? Care for the poor calls for great expense, if we wish each one of them to receive what is necessary, and all men to benefit from the good things of the earth and obtain what meets their need. For he who loves his neighbor as himself ought not to have more than his brother.

It is certain that you have wide possessions, so from where did this inequality arise, if not from your preferring your personal enjoyment at the expense of the happiness of others? The more you increase in riches, the more you fall short in love. If you had loved your neighbor, you would long ago have distributed a part of your money. But you cling to these goods as you cling to a part of your spirit. And it pains you to be deprived of them as it pains you to have a member of your body cut off [15].
St. Basil the Great Inspired by Sirach 32

entries.section: Let my life be a banquet that does not cease

paragraphs.text: * Your divine presence turns my life into a feast that does not end.
What banquet satisfies our souls with joy like Your presence in us?!
You lead the banquet with Your love and Your care, You who in Your humility take the last place.
Your presence on any occasion makes our banquets a fountain of joy, delight and holiness!
You give the elders wisdom and a word, and You draw the young to Your Word.
You pour the wine of Your love into our hearts, so that our souls are made drunk, and our hearts and minds are lifted up to Your heavens!
* Your presence stirs in us the spirit of wise leadership, so that our conduct is the best language in which we express our attachment to You!
You shine with Your light, O Sun of Righteousness, like lightning, and Your voice thunders, shattering every evil in us!
We often count our parties a waste of time, but Your banquet blesses every moment as though it were glorious and fruitful years.
* At every celebration and banquet we are bound to return quickly home for the sake of our children's feelings.
In Your celebration we set out as to our heavenly home, we set out with our children to You, that all may rest in Your bosom!
At Your party the heavenly ones, with the fathers, prophets and apostles, play the quiet music of the Spirit.
Your Holy Spirit reveals to us the sweetness of Your commandments!
The food of Your banquet is heavenly and exceedingly wonderful.

entries.section: 1. Between the sober fearer of the Lord and the light-minded fool

paragraphs.text: 1 He who fears the Lord will meet no harm, but in temptation the Lord will keep him, and deliver him from evils. 2 The wise man does not hate the Law, but he who is a hypocrite in it is like a ship in a whirlwind. 3 The intelligent man believes the Law, and the Law is faithful to him. 4 Prepare your speech, as the righteous do in their questions, and you will be heard. Arrange the meanings of your knowledge and answer. 5 The inward parts of the fool are like the wheel of a cart, and his thought is like a lightly turning axle. 6 The mocking friend is like a stallion that neighs under every rider.
No evil befalls him who fears the Lord, but He (the Lord) delivers him in temptation again and again [1].

The fearer of God, the man of God, is in a unique position; he realizes that he is in the mind of God, as the beloved of the Lord, and is not in fear lest temptation or trials overtake him, for God delivers him and turns the trials into enjoyment, entering into eternal glories. This is our faith which moves us to prayer and stirs in us joyful hope. This was fulfilled the more through the Incarnation of the Word of God, for a great position has become ours; therefore the Apostle exulted, saying: "And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory" (1 Tim 3:16). By Him we enjoy righteousness and defy all the powers of darkness.
* Let us put on our heads the helmet of salvation, lest we be wounded and die in the battle.
Let us gird our loins with truth, that we may not be found weak in the fight.
Let us rise and awaken Christ, that He may calm the waves for us.
Let us take the shield against the evil one, as the preparation of the Gospel of our Savior (Eph 6:15-16).
Let us receive from our Lord the authority to tread on serpents and scorpions (Lk 10:19)...
Let us rejoice in our hope at all times (Rom 12:12), that he who is our hope and our Savior may rejoice in us...
Let us take for ourselves a weapon for the battle (Eph 6:16), which is the preparation for the Gospel.
Let us knock at the door of heaven (Mt 7:7), and it will be opened before us and we will enter in.
Let us ask for mercy with diligence, and we shall receive what is necessary for us...
Let us lift up our eyes on high, to see the radiance that is revealed.
Let us lift up our wings like the eagles, to see where the carcase is (Mt 24:28)...
He who has two wings flies with them away from him (from Satan), so that the arrows which he shoots toward him do not reach him?
The spiritual see him fighting, and his weapon has no power over their bodies.

entries.section: 1. Between the sober fearer of the Lord and the light-minded fool

paragraphs.text: All the children of light do not fear him, for darkness flees before the light. The children of the Good One do not fear the evil one, for He has given them to tread upon him with their feet (Gen 3:15) [2].
St. Aphrahat the Sage He does not hate the Law, but he who claims to keep it is like a boat in the storm [2].

While the believer lives kept in the hands of God and does not fear temptations, the man who is a hypocrite in keeping the divine commandment is never free from anxiety, like a small boat in the midst of a violent storm. It turns a man's life from a pleasant journey in the company of the Lord, going forward quietly toward heaven, into a boat in the midst of a dangerous tempest.

entries.section: 1. Between the sober fearer of the Lord and the light-minded fool

paragraphs.text: The man of understanding trusts in the Law, and the Law is trustworthy to him, because it is a divine revelation [3].

The wise man of God believes in God through His word, and so understands God's plan for him, trusts in His divine promises, and counts himself blessed, because God reveals to him His divine mysteries.

entries.section: 1. Between the sober fearer of the Lord and the light-minded fool

paragraphs.text: Prepare what you say, and you will be heard; gather your knowledge and answer [4].

How does the fearer of the Lord prepare himself to enter into an open dialogue with God, except by gathering all his inner powers? For he is enjoying the greatest moments of his life, as he stands before his Beloved.

* God does not need resounding speeches, nor eloquent words, for He knows what is useful to us. Thus we can define prayer as a work that is accomplished in a man's conscience and within him, and it is a work that extends to all the works that weave a man's life [3].

entries.section: 1. Between the sober fearer of the Lord and the light-minded fool

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great The heart of the fool is like the wheel of a cart, and his thoughts are like the revolving axle [5].

The fool lives in the whirlpool of life; he does not feel his way along the true road, nor does he know where he is going, and he turns around himself all his life. His mind is like a small light cart, with no wise driver to direct it; it does not perceive the straight road that leads to heaven, but remains in confusion and disorder.
The mocking friend is like a spirited horse, which neighs under everyone who rides it [4] [6].
The friend who mocks his friend is like a stallion that neighs under everyone who rides it; he gives out disturbing sounds with no meaning and no purpose.

* When the first man fell and disobeyed God, man became, as the Scripture says, like sheep [for Hades (Ps 49:14)], because he sinned against reason. For a good reason man was counted irrational like the animals. In a similar way Wisdom says: "The pleasure-seeker and the adulterer are like a stallion" (cf. Sir 33:6), because he has become like the animals, without reason. Therefore he added: "which neighs under every rider upon him." Such a man no longer speaks, for he who sins against reason is not rational, but a dumb beast surrendered to desire, upon whom any kind of pleasure can mount and lead him [5].
St. Clement of Alexandria

entries.section: 2. The wise man and the need for God's grace

paragraphs.text: 7 Why is one day preferred to another, when the light of every day in the year comes from the sun? 8 The knowledge of the Lord distinguished them, when the sun was made which keeps the order, 9 and He varied the seasons; so the feasts were celebrated at the appointed hour. 10 Some of them He exalted and sanctified, and some He made among the number of ordinary days. And so all men are of the dust, and Adam was made of the earth, 11 but the Lord distinguished them in the fullness of His knowledge, and varied their ways. 12 Some of them He blessed and exalted, and some He sanctified and brought near to Himself, and some He cursed and brought low and cast down from their station. 13 As the clay is in the hand of the potter, and all its ways go according to his pleasure, 14 so men are in the hand of their Maker, and He recompenses them according to His judgment.
Why is one day better than another, when all the light of the days of the year comes from the sun? [7]

Although the source of illumination of all the days of the year is the very same sun, God has appointed holy days, seasons and feasts, and these days are distinguished from others. So out of the love of the Lord, the Sun of Righteousness, who lights all the days of our life with His divine righteousness, He gives us special days such as Sundays and the monthly and yearly feasts, which present to us declarations of the saving work of God, with a taste of the earnest of the heaven that He prepares for us.

entries.section: 2. The wise man and the need for God's grace

paragraphs.text: It was the knowledge of the Lord that distinguished them, for He varied the seasons and the feasts [8].

God arranged this variety so that we might experience His plan in creation and salvation, and so desire to attain eternal life. And the Church calls us, through the church calendar, from the beginning of each church year to its end, not to cease from enjoying the experience of fellowship with the Holy Trinity, who loves all mankind! With every morning the believer sings with the prophet Jeremiah, whose heart's walls pained him (Jer 4:19) on account of the bereavement of the daughter of his people, whom their disobedience and estrangement from God was shattering; but through his inner experience and his assurance of the work of God, his depths are turned into a second heaven, and he says: "His compassions fail not. They are new every morning... The Lord is my portion, saith my soul" (Lam 3:23-24).

The secret of the exultation of the heart of St. Jacob of Serugh in the midst of his pains was his realization that the mountain of Golgotha is the "wedding of Golgotha"; he is crucified with the heavenly Bridegroom to rise each day with Him, and experiences the embrace of the Lord, the fountain of inner peace and heavenly joy! This is the role of the church calendar.

* It must be realized that it befits each one of us to prove whether he is in the days of good or in the days of evil. And does he possess "the days of Joshua," which are the days of righteousness, or does he possess the days of evil? For if we recognize "the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world" (Jn 1:9), and give ourselves up to Him to be enlightened, and if the "Sun of righteousness" (Mal 4:2) rises in us and lights the world of our souls, we shall possess "the days of Joshua," that is, the days of Jesus Christ, the days of salvation. But if someone gives himself up to "the light that shall be put out" (cf. Job 18:5), the light that is opposed to the truth, he will also possess days, but they are days of evil. He will not be in the days of Joshua, but in the days of Manasseh or Pharaoh, in the evil days of other kings.

entries.section: 2. The wise man and the need for God's grace

paragraphs.text: Origen Some days He exalted and sanctified, and some days He made ordinary [9].

The Church calls us to make all our days the Lord's, so that we may enjoy continual joy, and she has established occasions that renew in us the remembrance of God's saving works and turn our life into a joyful, continual feast. We mention, by way of example, the following:
First: daily joy: in the prayer of Prime we enjoy the gladness of the Resurrection, and in the prayer of Midnight the gladness of the coming of the Bridegroom.
Second: weekly joy: on Sunday we enjoy the gladness of the Resurrection of Christ.
Third: monthly joy: where we enjoy the commemoration of the Annunciation, the Nativity and the Resurrection.
Fourth: yearly joyful commemorations and feasts.

entries.section: 2. The wise man and the need for God's grace

paragraphs.text: And all men are of the dust, and from the earth Adam was created [10].

God deals through human history, distinguishing each man from his brother according to his seriousness in life and salvation, and his faithfulness in employing his powers and using his gifts. Therefore there are vast differences in the lives of men and their aspirations for life, although all are of the offspring of one man created of dust, namely Adam [10].

entries.section: 2. The wise man and the need for God's grace

paragraphs.text: The Lord distinguished them in the fullness of His wisdom, and changed their ways [11].

God in His love for men gave each man his various gifts and abilities so that all might live together, each one completing the other. This variety lends humanity beauty, love and humility; each person needs his brother.

entries.section: 2. The wise man and the need for God's grace

paragraphs.text: Some of the days He blessed and exalted, and some of the days He sanctified and brought near to Himself, and some of the days He cursed and abased and removed from their station [12].

It is clear that by his talk of days here he means the days of man. He made plain that all men are equal since they were created of dust, and God gave them various talents, so He blesses and sanctifies some days, and permits humiliation in some days. By this he calls us to serious thought about our life and our mission.

a. God wishes to bless all days; on His part He spreads out His hands to give us His blessing, but if we give Him the back and not the face (Jer 2:27), even the days of feasts become hateful to Him (Isa 1:13).
b. The assurance that man's life is open to change, so that it befits the believer, if he falls, to return to God in a spirit of hope.

c. To realize that God's wisdom is above human thinking, for God may permit a man to be humbled for no apparent reason, but only that the Lord may carry him over into glory for his own edification and the edification of many, as happened with the righteous young man Joseph the son of Jacob.

d. It befits the rich, the people of authority and the church leaders to adorn themselves with humility, and what they enjoy is a divine gift. When the children of Israel, as the people of God, grew haughty, He permitted them the humiliation of the Babylonian captivity for seventy years.
All His ways are according to His good pleasure, like the clay in the hand of the potter.

entries.section: 2. The wise man and the need for God's grace

paragraphs.text: So men are in the hand of their Maker, and He recompenses them according to His judgment [13].

The Holy Scripture calls us to submit to the will of our Creator, that we may experience His work in us as the Lover of mankind (cf. Isa 45:9; 64:7; Jer 18:6). And the Apostle says: "Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?" (Rom 9:21). God gives us the Spirit of adoption, that we may know His divine mysteries, and so long to enjoy the eternal glory that He prepares for us. And on our part it befits us to realize that we are "a potsherd of the potsherds of the earth. Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou? or shall it say, Thy work has no hands? Woe unto him that saith unto his father, What begettest thou? or to the woman, What hast thou brought forth?" (Isa 45:9-10). St. John Chrysostom [6] affirms that the Apostle wishes to present one aspect of the parable, namely that God works in us and we can do nothing but obey. But He does not take away from us the freedom of our will; if we wish to live with Him, He changes us for the glory of His name, in a manner that surpasses our understanding.

15 Over against evil is good, and over against death is life; so over against the godly is the sinner. And so consider all the works of the Most High; you will find them two by two, one over against the other.
Good is the opposite of evil, and life is the opposite of death, and in the same way the sinner is the opposite of the godly [14].
So consider all the works of the Most High; they appear two by two, the one over against the other [15].

A man's life is either good or evil, he is a sinner or a righteous man; there is no position between the two, "for whosoever hath, to him shall be given, and he shall have more abundance: but whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken away even that he hath" (Mt 13:12). On the other hand, the good God is able to turn evil into good. The Cross of the Lord of glory Jesus is a unique example of bringing forth good out of evil. He presents the grace of salvation through the Cross which the enemy of good prepared for destruction.

St. Augustine sees in this statement a revelation of the purpose of the book, which is to offer good instead of evil, and life instead of death, so that man may look to the works of the Most High, who works in the sinner that he may become godly [7].

entries.section: 4. The scribe, the teacher, gleans behind the grape gatherers

paragraphs.text: 16 I, the last, have awakened, and have inherited these things as they were from the beginning. 17 Like one who gleans behind the grape gatherers, I came with the blessing of the Lord; and I filled the winepress like one who had gathered. 18 See how my labor was not for myself alone, but also for all who seek instruction. 19 Hear me, O great men of the people, and give ear to me, O rulers of the congregation.
I was the last to awaken to glean in the vineyard behind the grape gatherers [16].

In a spirit of humility Ben Sirach presents an example for us to follow; with his surpassing gifts and the wonderful work of God in his life, he did not boast of his wisdom. Rather he reckoned himself as one who gleans behind the grape gatherers. He reckoned himself like Ruth the Gentile maiden, who gathered the ears of grain behind the reapers with care and striving, without slackness, and so became a grandmother of Jesus Christ, the divine ear of grain who gives life, satisfaction and glory to His believers of all peoples, nations and tongues. This is what gladdened the heart of Ben Sirach, that his striving and watching were not enjoyed by him alone, but he offered them to all who seek instruction.

entries.section: 4. The scribe, the teacher, gleans behind the grape gatherers

paragraphs.text: By the blessing of the Lord I arrived at the right time, and filled my winepress like one who gathered grapes [17].

Ben Sirach, as a teacher, observed that some present questions on trivial matters far from the salvation of the soul; so while not despising his students, the teacher tries to direct his students toward what is for edification.

The Lord Christ, who works in good teachers, in His dialogue with the Samaritan woman, who tried to steer the conversation away from the salvation of her soul, spoke to her gently without wounding her feelings as a woman living with a man who was not her husband, and led her to the divine truth. He looked upon the woman as an ear of grain fallen from the reapers which it befitted Him to gather, as Ruth used to do, but He raised her to a better level for her salvation. This is what Naomi did with Ruth, for she accepted her striving in gathering the fallen ears of grain, yet directed her toward the owner of the field, Boaz, and so she became the grandmother of the unique divine ear of grain, Jesus the son of David, the Bread that came down from heaven, the giver of salvation and satisfaction.

In brief, while not despising the gleaning of what falls from the reapers, we must raise those whom we shepherd and serve to a surpassing heavenly level. One of the brothers asked Father the Elder Barsanuphius about a cowl that a brother had sent to him, whether he should accept it or not. The answer of the Elder came to him that this matter should not occupy him, lest he spoil his time in trivial things, but that he must care for the plentiful harvest that is on behalf of the Kingdom of God.

* Brother, I have sent you wisdom: "Be free, what do you want? Turn to yourself: 'The harvest truly is plenteous' (Mt 3:16). Leave everything, and give your time to the harvest and gathering, that you may have fruits of wheat and wine (Ps 4:7; Deut 33:28), that your heart may be strengthened and become joyful in the Lord. As for the cowl, if the brother wishes to give it to you with all his heart, accept it, and condemn yourself as unworthy [8].

entries.section: 4. The scribe, the teacher, gleans behind the grape gatherers

paragraphs.text: St. Barsanuphius Observe well that my labor was not for myself alone, but for all who seek instruction [18].

He compared himself with the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and the prophets, and realized that he was like one who gathers ears of grain behind the reapers. And in a spirit of hope he realized that his labor would not be lost in vain, but by the grace of God all who seek instruction would benefit from it.

entries.section: 4. The scribe, the teacher, gleans behind the grape gatherers

paragraphs.text: Hear me, O leaders of the people, and give ear to me, O rulers of the congregation [19].

Ben Sirach realized by the Spirit of God that all who seek instruction benefit from his work, so he dared to speak with the leaders of the people and the rulers of the congregation. True humility moves a man to work in a spirit of strength, even among leaders and rulers!

entries.section: 5. Do not be under anyone's guardianship!

paragraphs.text: 20 Do not put in authority over yourself in your lifetime your son or your wife or your brother or your friend, and do not give your goods to another, lest you regret it and have to beg him for them. 21 As long as you live and breath is in you, do not give yourself over to any man, 22 for it is better that your sons should ask of you than that you should look to the hands of your sons. 23 In all your affairs keep your preeminence, 24 and do not leave a blemish on your honor. Divide your inheritance at the end of the days of your life, when death is at hand. 25 Fodder and the rod and burdens are for the ass, and bread and discipline and work for the servant. 26 Set the slave to work and you will have rest; slacken his hands and he will seek liberty.

Do not put in authority over yourself in your lifetime your son or your wife or your brother or your friend, and do not give your possessions to another, lest you change your mind and have to beg for them [20].

entries.section: 5. Do not be under anyone's guardianship!

paragraphs.text: As long as you live and breath is in you, do not let anyone take your place [21].

entries.section: 5. Do not be under anyone's guardianship!

paragraphs.text: It is better that your sons should ask of you than that you should look to the hands of your sons [22].

The believer longs to see every man a leader who takes pride in the work of God in him and with him; the wise father gives his sons and his wife the opportunity to share with him in the management of the family's affairs and his administration of all the aspects of the family, for their good as for his own; in a spirit of wisdom he does not hand everything over to them during his lifetime:
a. Sons are sometimes exposed to deviation, as happened with the prodigal son (Lk 15), who squandered all that he received.

b. A person himself may be exposed to a crisis because of illness or the country's economic circumstances, and when he asks his children they may not respond to him. So it is wise to give them a share during his lifetime, and to write a will concerning the rest of his possessions, keeping it with him and informing them of where it is.

entries.section: 5. Do not be under anyone's guardianship!

paragraphs.text: Be distinguished in all your works, and do not disfigure your reputation [23].

Although a father loves his children more than he cares for himself, Ben Sirach wishes the father to keep the authority of love, so that the image of the loving, wise father and manager remains until the moments of his death.

entries.section: 5. Do not be under anyone's guardianship!

paragraphs.text: On the day when you complete the days of your life, and at the time of your death, divide your inheritance [24].

The father does not leave his children to enter into disputes about the distribution of his wealth, but arranges the matter of the inheritance among them with justice, wisdom and frankness before his death if possible.

entries.section: 6. Let each man do what suits his role and gifts

paragraphs.text: 27 The yoke and the thongs bow the neck, and constant work subdues the slave. 28 For the wicked slave there are torments and torture. Compel him to work lest he be idle, 29 for idleness teaches many kinds of wickedness. 30 Put him to the works that befit him; and if he does not obey, make his fetters heavy, but do not be excessive in the punishment of any person of flesh, and do nothing without discernment. 31 If you have a slave, let him be to you as yourself, for you acquired him with blood. If you have a slave, treat him as yourself, for you need him as you need yourself. 32 If you hurt him, he will run away, 33 and if he flees and goes away, in what way will you seek him?
Fodder and the rod and burdens are for the ass, and bread and discipline and work for the servant [25].
While looking upon the slave (or servant) as a brother, the master must care for three things:
a. Providing fodder or bread, so that he does not leave him hungry or deprived of food.
b. The rod, which is understood as the exercise of firmness together with love, so that he realizes his limits without injustice on the master's part.

c. Work in moderation; for to burden him beyond his strength is counted as violence which may drive him to rebellion, and indulgence toward him may drive him to laziness, and this is not for his good spiritually, physically or socially.
Put your slave to work and you will find rest; release his hands and he will seek freedom [26].

If the laws at that time ignored the right of slaves as human beings, the Law did not leave the master to control them in an absolute manner. Directing the slave to work that suits his strength gives the master a kind of rest.
The yoke and the thongs bow the neck, and for the wicked slave there are torments and pain [27].
As Sirach defends the rights of slaves, so he asks for the wise discipline of the rebellious and those who spoil the work, for the good of both parties.

entries.section: 6. Let each man do what suits his role and gifts

paragraphs.text: Compel him to work lest he be idle, for idleness teaches many evils [28].

St. John Chrysostom sees that the expression "idleness" has a wider meaning than mere "not working," for he sees that one who works merely to acquire vain food is counted idle, and he sees that one who exhausts all his strength and energy merely to eat is working for the sake of vain food. St. John Chrysostom calls us to work in order to offer to the Lord Christ food and drink and clothing, for the sake of the Kingdom of Heaven; this food is not vain, but truly remains forever [9].

* The prohibition of excessive care for the needs of our body does not forbid care and work altogether. It remains for us to work for ourselves, not for the perishing food, but for the food that endures for eternal life (Jn 6:27), not only for our bodily needs, but also to relieve our neighbor (Eph 4:28). And the Lord will say to us on the day of judgment: "I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink..." (Mt 25:35). What we do for those who have consecrated themselves to Him is counted as though we did it with them, and for it the heavenly Kingdom is given to us. And those who did not work and did not toil to help the weak and serve their neighbor will be punished, and He will send them to eternal torment (Mt 25:41-46) [10].

entries.section: 6. Let each man do what suits his role and gifts

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great Put him to work as befits him, and if he does not obey, make his feet heavy with fetters [29].

Idleness is harmful to the master as to the slave, to the child as to the old man, even to the sick. It befits all mankind to work according to their gifts, time and abilities. Sts. Pachomius and Basil often affirmed the monk's obligation to work for their spiritual edification.

entries.section: 6. Let each man do what suits his role and gifts

paragraphs.text: And do not behave arrogantly toward any flesh, and do nothing without judgment [30].
Ben Sirach was careful that the students should not fall into the letter that kills, so he requires them to practice everything with prudence and not by the literal execution of the commandment.

entries.section: 6. Let each man do what suits his role and gifts

paragraphs.text: If you have a slave, let him be as yourself, for you acquired him with your blood [31].

Sirach prepares the Jews and the Gentiles for the acceptance of the Lord Christ the Savior, who spreads out His hands to embrace, if possible, all mankind without partiality for race, age, position or abilities. For all were created of dust, and for all the Savior offers Himself as a sacrifice on their behalf, and behold, He prepares places in heaven for everyone who believes in Him and responds to Him.

entries.section: 6. Let each man do what suits his role and gifts

paragraphs.text: If you have a slave, treat him as a brother, for you need him as you need yourself [32].
Without doubt this statement represents a revolt against the system of slavery, not by violence but by sound thinking.

entries.section: 6. Let each man do what suits his role and gifts

paragraphs.text: If you wrong him, and he flees away, in what way will you go to seek him? [33]

He warns against mistreating slaves. He lived in an age when man enslaved his brother in humanity, and there was no law to protect slaves. He is preparing the way for the liberation of slaves! He required the master to reckon his slaves as himself, to treat them as brothers, highlighting their mutual need. This opinion provoked the Roman rulers, because the empire at that time had sixty million slaves, and it was feared that this teaching might drive them to revolt against their masters, which portended a revolution of unwelcome consequences, and perhaps this was one of the causes of the persecution of Christianity. "Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven" (Col 4:1).

* Let social differences be wiped out, so that there is no subjection and authority, poverty and extravagant wealth, nobles and commoners, a degraded family and an honored family, and no room for inequality... Let us judge by political and legislative equality, and let it be distributed to each one in complete freedom, and in a manner full of peace, that he may choose what he wishes [11].
St. Gregory of Nyssa Inspired by Sirach 33

entries.section: Grant me wisdom and good management

paragraphs.text: * Nail Your fear within me, that I may not fear temptations.
I hold fast to Your true promises, and my soul is at peace.
Take away from me all folly, that I may not walk in a vicious circle!
* Let me cling to You, and You will sanctify all my days for You.
You shine with Your light, O Sun of Righteousness, upon my life, and my life is turned into a perpetual feast and glorious joy.
* I am dust and ashes, but Your gifts to me are surpassing.
With every morning my soul sets out from glory to glory.
The touches of Your hand raise me up as a vessel of honor, O greatest Potter.
I confess to You my weaknesses, and You turn my evil into true good, and raise me from darkness to light, and from death to eternal life!
* Count me like Ruth the Gentile, gleaning behind the reapers.
I possess You, O divine ear of grain, and You make me of the household of God.
You promised me that You do not forget a cup of cold water, so accept my service to everyone who seeks true instruction.
* Give me the spirit of wisdom with love, that I may know how to give generously and with good management!
Grant me not to cease from the good fight.
That I may not fall into despair, nor haughtiness come upon me!
Teach me not to despise any man, for You came down to take the last rank of mankind.
You spread out Your hands on the Cross, and embrace sinners and fornicators and sanctify them.
Let every man be as myself, that I may ignore no one.
For I wish that all may become members in Your body, O Holy One!

1 The hopes of a man void of understanding are vain and false: and dreams lift up fools. 2 Whoso regardeth dreams is like him that catcheth at a shadow, and followeth after the wind. 3 The vision of dreams is the resemblance of one thing to another, as the likeness of a man before a man's face. 4 Of an unclean thing what can be cleansed? and from that thing that is false what truth can come? 5 Divinations, and soothsayings, and dreams, are vain. 6 And the heart fancieth, as a woman's heart in travail. If they be not sent from the most High in thy visitation, set not thy heart upon them. 7 For dreams have deceived many, and they have failed that put their trust in them. 8 The law shall be found perfect without lies: and wisdom is perfection to a faithful mouth. 9 A man that is instructed knoweth many things; and he that hath much experience will speak with understanding.

The ancient Greeks often thought of dreams as messages from the gods. As for the Jews, dreams appear in the Old Testament carrying messages from God, and warnings are also given against vain, deceptive dreams.

The Old Testament mentions the dreams that Joseph the son of Jacob saw: in his youth he saw two dreams; in prison he interpreted two dreams for the king's cupbearer and the king's baker; and in the palace he interpreted two dreams for Pharaoh king of Egypt. These six dreams were from God and were actually fulfilled. In the New Testament Joseph the carpenter saw three dreams: the first after the Incarnation of the Word in the Virgin (Mt 1:25), the second for the flight to Egypt with the Child Jesus and His mother, and the third concerning the return from Egypt. As for Daniel, who was nearer to Ben Sirach in time, he was known as a man of dreams; he interpreted many dreams that declared God's plan and included prophecies that were fulfilled in history, and others that prophesied of the coming of the Lord Christ and His second coming.
Nevertheless, the foolish person gives himself over to vain dreams and puts his hope in them.

The prophets of old warned much against the error into which dreams can lead, and stressed not relying on them, especially since a confusion had occurred between them and divination, sorcery and charlatanry. "I have heard what the prophets said, that prophesy lies in my name, saying, I have dreamed, I have dreamed. How long shall this be in the heart of the prophets that prophesy lies? yea, they are prophets of the deceit of their own heart; which think to cause my people to forget my name by their dreams which they tell every man to his neighbour, as their fathers have forgotten my name for Baal. The prophet that hath a dream, let him tell a dream; and he that hath my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the chaff to the wheat? saith the LORD" (Jer 23:25-28; cf. Deut 13:2-6; Eccl 5:6-7; Jer 29:8-9; 27:9-11; Zech 10:2) [1].
The man without understanding has futile and false hopes, and dreams give wings to those without understanding [1].
Corrupt souls, turned aside from the truth, place their hope not in returning to God with a pure heart, an upright life and sincere repentance, but in a vain hope that relies on deceptive dreams.
One who pays attention to dreams is like one who grasps at shadows and pursues the wind [2].
He who walks after the vain world has vain dreams; he clings to them like one who grasps at shadows, and runs after them as after the wind [5].
The vision of dreams is this over against that, and the likeness of face before face [3].
A dream is often merely a reflection of events or imaginings, like the reflection of a man's face in a mirror, as though it did not represent a real existence.
What can be cleansed from an unclean thing?
And what truth can come from a false thing? [4]
We shall not profit from dreams unless our depths are purified, so that God works in us.

He does not mean that all dreams are unclean, but he gives an example: if what is unclean produces nothing pure, so also what appears in a dream does not represent a reality, but is vain and false; can falsehood then produce truth?!
Divination, omens (augury) and dreams are worthless, like a woman in the pains of labor, the heart becomes visible [5].

Ben Sirach sees that seeking after divination, omens and dreams reveals a person's inner disturbance and instability, and the Law forbade them explicitly (Lev 19:26; Deut 18:10-14). While they were counted unfitting for the believer (1 Sam 6:2; Isa 44:25; Ezek 13:6-8; 21:26), the pagans practiced them. Ben Sirach made clear that man's mind pictures divination, omens and vain dreams out of itself, and he thereby highlights the psychological aspect that modern psychologists proclaim.
If visions are not sent from the Most High in a visitation from Him, do not set your heart upon them [6].
The pious, wise person discerns the dreams and visions that come from the Most High, and opens his heart to them, so that divination, omens and false dreams do not lead him astray.
For dreams have led many astray, and those who put their hope in them have fallen [7].

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the images that appear in dreams affect the soul and arise in different ways, so they must be discerned [2]: 1. Sometimes dreams occur because of indigestion. 2. Sometimes they occur as the fruit of illusory imaginings that occupy a person's mind. 3. Sometimes a dream is a revelation of something. 4. There are dreams stirred up by the enemy of good, the devil; therefore Holy Scripture warns us: "For dreams have deceived many, and they have failed that put their trust in them" [7]. It also commanded us: "Neither shall ye use enchantment, nor observe times" (Lev 19:26). 5. There are dreams that are holy revelations. Pope Gregory (the Great) says: [In any case, the saints, by the discernment they have acquired, are able to distinguish between illusions and revelations, and to penetrate the meaning of the words and images in visions. Thus they know what is from the good Spirit and what is from deceptive imaginings. But if the soul is not prudent in the matter of dreams, it finds itself perished in a forest of vanity that is the work of the deceiving spirit, who by his art sometimes presents many true things, and afterward captures it in the snare of a single lie.]

Some scholars also see that dreams are often a reflection of what is within a person, of scenes, events and imaginings, when a person sleeps and the censor over the unconscious is weak. Some are the fruit of sleeping in an uncomfortable position. Some are the fruit of a person's intense preoccupation with a matter all day long, especially in the period immediately before sleep. Sometimes dreams reflect some events or behaviors of the person when he was a child or a youth, which he no longer remembers. And some dreams are deceptions of the enemy of good against a person in order to lead him astray.
The Law is fulfilled without such lies, and wisdom is perfect in the mouth of the believer [8].
Ben Sirach affirms that the Law, as the source of true wisdom, is a safeguard for the believer, who draws from it instead of resorting to deceptive superstitions.

entries.section: 2. Practical experiences and the benefit of travels

paragraphs.text: 10 He that hath no experience knoweth little: but he that hath travelled is full of prudence. 11 He that hath not been tried, what doth he know? and he that hath wandered is full of cunning. 12 I have seen many things in my wanderings, and most of my words come from what I have experienced. 13 Often have I ventured myself in this pursuit, even unto death, and then I escaped.
The man who travels much knows much, and the one of much experience speaks with understanding [9].

If the Law keeps the believer from the deception of illusions and dreams, it nevertheless does not prevent the believer from benefiting from the experience of others. For the Law purifies the heart and the mind, and urges the believer to resort to God with reverence and piety. In this way the believer benefits from his many travels, for he enjoys a spirit of discernment, and so perceives what is true and distinguishes it from what is false.
He who has not been tried knows little, but he who travels increases in prudence [10].

entries.section: 2. Practical experiences and the benefit of travels

paragraphs.text: I have seen many things in my travels, and what I understood is more than I can express in words [11].
God is able to make known His will and counsel by many means, among them travels, to those who are sanctified to Him.

entries.section: 2. Practical experiences and the benefit of travels

paragraphs.text: Often I was exposed to the danger of death, and I escaped because of those experiences [12].

Although Ben Sirach valued learning from the experience of others, which requires travel to meet with different cultures and experiences, he was confident in the Lord who rescued him as from death [12]. He presented his experience of benefiting from the experience of others, and his practical experience of trusting in God who saves and cares for him, so that he is not terrified of anything and fears no one.

v [And bring us not into temptation] In some manuscripts "and lead us not" occurs, and it is equivalent to "bring us not in," because the Greek word carries both meanings. Some pray, saying: "Do not allow us to be led into temptation." For God does not lead a person into temptation, but He permits the one who has been deprived of His help to be led into it, according to God's hidden wisdom and according to the merits of the one whom He allows to be led into temptation.

To be led into temptation differs from a person's being tested. For without temptation no man is approved. He is tried to approve himself, as it is written: "He that hath not been tried, what doth he know?" (cf. Sir 34:11), or he is tried to approve others, as the Apostle says: "Your temptation[3] which was in my flesh ye despised not" (Gal 4:14). For from these circumstances the Apostle knew that they were steadfast, because they did not abandon love on account of the troubles that befell the Apostle in the flesh. As for God, He knows us before we are tried, for He knows all things before they come to be [4].
St. Augustine

entries.section: 3. The fear of the Lord, a harbor of safety

paragraphs.text: 14 The spirit of those that fear the Lord shall live, 15 for their hope is in him that saveth them. 16 Whoso feareth the Lord shall not fear nor be afraid, for he is his hope. 17 Whoso feareth the Lord, blessed is his soul. 18 To whom doth he look? and who is his stay? 19 For the eyes of the Lord are upon them that love him, he is a mighty protector and a strong stay, a covering from the heat and a shadow from the noonday sun. 20 A defence from stumbling and a help when falling. He lifteth up the soul and lighteneth the eyes: he giveth health, life and blessing.
What occupies Ben Sirach in the matter of vain dreams is to reveal the safe way for ordering the believer's life:
a. He highlighted the necessity of enjoying a spirit of discernment in order to be rid of pagan practices such as divination, omens and the interpretation of deceptive dreams [5].
b. Holding fast to the Law to enjoy perfect wisdom [8].
c. Benefiting from the experiences of others through travels.

d. Sure hope is realized through the fear of the Lord, as a harbor of safety from every deception, whatever its source, whether the illusions of the soul, or slipping into pagan practices, or the deception of the enemy of good through misleading dreams.

Now he speaks of the fear of the Lord and its work in the believer's life: 1. The fear of the Lord gives life to the spirit that sin kills [13]. 2. The fear of the Lord gives a spirit of challenge, so that one fears nothing and is not terrified [14-15]. 3.
