The fear of the Lord shows us that the eyes of the Lord are toward those who love Him and keep them from every danger [16]. 4. The fear of the Lord lifts the soul and gives it inner insight, healing, life and blessing [17].

St. Mar Philoxenus recorded for us two homilies (memre) on the fear of the Lord, after writing two on faith and two on simplicity. He presented to us the fear of the Lord as a person born of faith and keeper of faith. He made clear that Adam, and after him Cain, drove the fear of the Lord away from themselves, and so lost their faith.
Those who fear the Lord, their spirit lives, for their hope is in Him who saves them [13].

v He who understands what the body is, that is, that it is corruptible and short-lived, understands also that the soul is heavenly and immortal, that it is a breath from God, and is joined to the body until it advances and rises toward likeness to God. The man who understands the soul rightly walks in an upright life that pleases God, and is wary of the body and does not trifle with it. Likewise, by the mind's contemplation of God, he sees mentally (spiritually) the eternal blessings that God gives to the soul [5].
St. Anthony the Great He who fears the Lord fears nothing and is never terrified, because the Lord is his hope [14].

v Because Cain did not fear God willingly, fear ruled over him by compulsion, and he became terrified, a wanderer on the face of the earth, and under the torment of fear he was begging God to make any man kill him, that he might be rid of this life full of fear and terror!
St. Mar Philoxenus of Mabbug Blessed is the soul of the man who fears the Lord.

entries.section: 3. The fear of the Lord, a harbor of safety

paragraphs.text: To whom does he look? And who is his support? [15]

v The test of the fear of the Lord is within the soul; and only the man himself can know whether he fears God or not. Have you remembered God and trembled? Have you thought of Him and been filled with fear? Have your thoughts trembled along with your members, and your soul with your body? Has your mind bowed your head, and has shame come upon you before God? If these things happen to you, know that the fear of the Lord is in you, and the remembrance of God is indeed present with you [6].
St. Mar Philoxenus of Mabbug The eyes of the Lord are on those who love Him. He is an effective protection and a strong support:

entries.section: 3. The fear of the Lord, a harbor of safety

paragraphs.text: He is a refuge from the heat of the scorching, and a shade from the noonday sun, a protection from stumbling, and a help from falling [16].

Ben Sirach calls those who fear the Lord "those who love Him." He who loves the Lord finds his protection in the Lord, for He supports him from the heat of temptations, saves him from falling, glorifies him, enlightens his inner insight, gives him healing from sorrows, and gladdens his heart with His divine goods. If the Lord is called the Sun of righteousness who enlightens the soul, then the enemy of good is called Satan, in that he pushes men toward burning temptations. Fear supports the believer in his striving against evil, especially in his resisting inner thoughts:

v The fear of the Lord is the bridle that stops a person's rush toward committing evil, and pulls him back when he is enslaved to running after his loathsome desires, not only in his outward life but especially in his hidden inner life" [6: 181].

v The man who lives in the remembrance of God at all times is filled with fear, even when resisting a thought of lust that passes over his soul, and he becomes terrified because of this thought. But the thought flees at once before the fear of the soul, like a bird that flees from the man who disturbs its rest. Fear and respect for men's laws keep the body from lusts. And fear and a man's shame before God keep the soul from evil thoughts. For when he knows that God sees him at all times, he watches himself continually lest he sin [7].
St. Mar Philoxenus of Mabbug (The Lord) raises the soul up [8], enlightens the eyes, and gives healing, life and blessing [17].

v As fear accompanies the childhood of this world and drives it to learn reading and writing, so also the fear of the Lord suits the childhood of the soul, and drives it to carry out the commandments and not to treat the word of God lightly [9].
St. Mar Philoxenus

21 He that sacrificeth of a thing wrongfully gotten, his offering is mocked; and the mockeries of the wicked are not well pleasing. 22 The Lord is alone for those that wait for him in the way of truth and righteousness. 23 The most High is not pleased with the offerings of the hypocrites; neither is he pacified for their sins by the multitude of their sacrifices. 24 Whoso bringeth an offering of the goods of the poor doeth as one that killeth the son before his father. 25 The bread of the needy is their life: he that withholdeth it from them is a shedder of blood. 26 He that snatcheth his neighbour's living slayeth him. 27 He that withholdeth the hire of the hireling sheddeth his blood. 28 One buildeth and another pulleth down; what profit have they but labour? 29 One prayeth and another curseth; whose prayer will the Lord hear? 30 He that is washed from the touching of the dead and toucheth it again, what availeth his washing? 31 So is a man that fasteth for his sins and doeth them again: who will hear his prayer, and what hath his humbling profited him?

Of all the wisdom books, Ben Sirach alone is concerned to speak of the true worship of God. From the beginning of the book the writer declared his concern for the service of the Lord (2:1). In his view the service of the Lord is the true life of man.

The service of the Lord is bound up with the believer's inner life. Like the prophet Isaiah, Ben Sirach perceives that worship and the offering of sacrifices can be practiced with a letter that has no spirit, and so the Lord is not pleased with them; stopping at the letter without purity of heart is a disdain of living communion with the Lord. Like Isaiah, Sirach links the offering of sacrifices with walking in the fear of the Lord [18, 20]. Sirach gives examples of worship and offerings unacceptable to the Lord.

He who approaches the Lord with his heart isolated from his brethren, the Lord will not accept him. The first murder in the world took place during Cain's offerings to the Lord, which were not accepted (cf. Gen 4:3-5). It is to be noted that Luke the Evangelist, who spoke much of prayer, also spoke much of almsgiving. For by practical love and works of mercy and compassion, God smells prayer as a sweet savour of acceptance. Therefore the Lord warned us against offering sacrifices on the altar before we are reconciled with our brethren.
He who offers sacrifices by committing iniquity, the offering is mockery; and the gifts of the wicked are not accepted [18].
The Most High is not pleased with the offerings of the wicked, nor by the multitude of their sacrifices does a man obtain forgiveness of his sins [19].
He who offers a sacrifice from the possessions of the poor slays a son before his father [20].

v He who has turned to bitterness because of the roots of deadly poison cannot bring forth sweet fruit. For this reason the Lord says by the prophet, rejecting even the offerings: "For I the LORD love judgment, I hate robbery for burnt offering" (Isa 61:8). He also says: "The sacrifice of the wicked is abomination: how much more, when he bringeth it with a wicked mind?" (Prov 21:27). They offer to God even the things they take from the needy, but the Lord shows with great reproof how He strips them, saying by the wise man: "Whoso bringeth an offering of the goods of the poor doeth as one that killeth the son before his father" (cf. Sir 34:20). And is there anything more dreadful than killing the son before the eyes of his father? So God looks upon these sacrifices with great wrath, like the grief of a father who has lost his son [10].
Pope Gregory (the Great)
The bread of the needy is the life of the poor, and he who deprives them of it is a shedder of blood [21].
He who takes away his neighbor's living slays him, and he who deprives the hireling of his wages sheds his blood [22].
If one builds and another pulls down, what do they gain but labor? [23]

The statements [23-26] highlight the continual struggle between good and evil. It is good for a man to fast and pray in order to obtain forgiveness, but he must not become careless and fall into that for which he offered repentance.

St. Barsanuphius was asked: If a person is not sincere in his repentance, will his sins be forgiven for the sake of the saints if they pray for him? The saint used this saying, counting the saints as building by their prayers, while the one who is careless in his repentance pulls down, so what is the gain but labor?

v The man who does not practice what he is able to do, and relied on this effort, that is, the prayers of the saints, their prayers do not profit him at all. If they practiced the ascetic life and prayed for him while he lived a life of waste and dissoluteness, what is the benefit of their prayers to him? For the saying is fulfilled: "When one buildeth, and another pulleth down, what profit have they then but labour?!" (cf. Sir 34:23).

Truly, if it were possible for this to happen, that is, for the saints to pray for a man and he be saved, while the latter did not care about it even with a little concern, then nothing would have prevented them from doing so for the sins of the world [11].
St. Barsanuphius v In truth, if those who build are many and the one who pulls down is one, destruction is easy and breaks the many hands of the builders [12].
St. John Chrysostom When one prayeth, and another curseth, whose voice will the Lord hear? [24]
v A man who takes from what belongs to others and gives it to another does not show mercy, but practices great error and injustice.

And as a stone cannot bring forth oil, so cruelty does not bring mercy. When almsgiving is practiced in this way it is not counted as almsgiving. Therefore I urge you not only to consider how we give to the needy, but also not to give from what we have taken from others.
When one prayeth, and another curseth, whose voice will the Lord hear?" (cf. Sir 34:24).

If we guide ourselves so strictly, we shall be able, by the grace of God, to obtain many compassions and mercies and forgiveness for all that we did throughout the long time, and to flee to the Kingdom of Heaven by the grace and compassion of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen [13].
St. John Chrysostom He that washeth himself after the touching of a dead body, and toucheth it again, what availeth his washing? [25]

v If a man gives his wealth to God, but offers himself to Satan, he fulfills what is written: "He that washeth himself after the touching of a dead body, and toucheth it again, what availeth his washing?" (cf. Sir 34:25). Likewise the Apostle Peter made clear: "For if after they have escaped the pollutions of the world ... they are again entangled therein, and overcome, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning" (2 Pet 2:20).

Consider, brethren, the testimony of the blessed Peter concerning sinners: if, after they have begun to be saved from their sins, they return to the mire of vice, their last state becomes worse than the first. What the same Apostle Peter added points to the same people: "The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire" (2 Pet 2:22). In fact Solomon (Ben Sirach) warns us more clearly in more terrifying words: "My son, hast thou sinned? do so no more, but pray for thy former sins, and they shall be forgiven thee" (cf. Sir 21:1) [14].

v Beloved, dear ones, do not allow the divine blessings to be destroyed in you by your following evil deeds, lest vices overtake you unawares, and virtues do not leave your hearts. For what is written is fulfilled: "He that washeth himself after the touching of a dead body, and toucheth it again, what availeth his washing?" (cf. Sir 34:25).

If the virtues withdraw and we accept the vices, we must fear the fulfillment of the words: "When the unclean spirit is gone out of a man, he walketh through dry places, seeking rest, and findeth none. Then he saith, I will return into my house from whence I came out; and when he is come, he findeth it empty, swept, and garnished. Then goeth he, and taketh with himself seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter in and dwell there: and the last state of that man is worse than the first" (Mt 12:43-45) [15].

v According to the greatness of what we receive, it befits us to guard it with more care and attention. It is a grave matter for a pagan to reject the grace of God, but the danger is no less if a Christian, after having received it, returns and loses it. It is not the dignity of the title "Christian" that makes him a Christian. You have no profit at all in the title itself unless you show it by works. So the Lord Himself also says in the Gospel: "And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?" (Lk 6:46). Therefore let us strive to live in purity, righteousness and godliness, so that when we stand before the judgment seat of the eternal Judge, we are not punished with the wicked and sinners, but are made worthy to receive the eternal rewards with the righteous who fear God, by the help of our Lord, to whom belong honor and power forever and ever. Amen [16].

Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles v Those who do not keep the innocence of life after lamentation neglect purity after washing. And those who wash but are not cleansed are none other than those who commit the sins over which they were weeping and still are. Therefore the wise man says: "He that washeth himself after the touching of a dead body, and toucheth it again, what availeth his washing?" (cf. Sir 34:25).

He who purifies himself by weeping is like the one who washes after touching the dead, while he who returns to commit sin after shedding tears over it is like one who returns to touching the dead after his washing. Those who mourn over their sins but do not leave them ought to know that in the eye of the just Judge they are like those who, when they stand before certain persons, grieve with humble supplication, but when they leave them, bear them all hatred and harm [17].
Pope Gregory (the Great)

v Such people do not wash away their sins by their sighs, since they do not cease sinning after their sighing. They sigh because of their crimes, and after sighing they return to them. Of these the Holy Scripture says in the Book of Ben Sirach: "He that washeth himself after the touching of a dead body, and toucheth it again, what availeth his washing? So is it with a man that fasteth for his sins, and doeth the same again: who will hear his prayer?" (cf. Sir 34:25-26). Therefore God rightly says to men: "By returning and sighing ye shall be saved" (cf. Isa 30:15) [18].
Fulgentius (disciple of St. Augustine)
So is it with a man that fasteth for his sins, and doeth the same again: who will hear his prayer?
And what doth his humbling profit him? [26]

v If Eve had practiced fasting and avoided eating of the fruit of this tree, we would not have been in need of this fast, because "They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick" (Mt 9:12). It is our sin that brought sickness upon us. So let us be healed by repentance; but repentance without the practice of fasting is vain: "Cursed is the ground for thy sake ... Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field" (Gen 3:17-18) [19].
St. Basil the Great Inspired by Sirach 34

entries.section: Your fear is my refuge from my weaknesses

paragraphs.text: v My God, how do I distinguish between holy dreams and vain dreams?
Nail Your fear in me, that my heart may be purified by Your grace, and I may enjoy safety as You give me the spirit of discernment.
v Sanctify my mind and my heart, that in earnestness I may experience fellowship with You.
And in my travels let me learn from the experiences of my brethren with You.
v That I may fear You, O Holy One, and so fear nothing, and You open to me the door of hope, and I hide in You!
Your fear leads me to the worship that is pleasing before You.
You open to me the door of heaven, and my heart is lifted up to it.
Let my tongue offer You a sacrifice of thanksgiving, which You smell as a sweet savour of acceptance.
By Your fear I practice my fasts, my prayers and my prostrations (metanoias), and all worship, with boldness before You!

1 He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough. 2 He that taketh heed to the commandments hath sacrificed a peace offering. 3 And he that departeth from iniquity hath sacrificed a sin offering, and hath made atonement for his sins. 4 He that offereth fine flour hath paid his thanks, and he that giveth alms hath sacrificed a sacrifice of praise. 5 To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to the Lord, and to forsake unrighteousness is a propitiation for sins. 6 Thou shalt not appear empty before the Lord; 7 for all these things are done because of the commandment. 8 The offering of the righteous maketh the altar fat, and the sweet savour thereof is before the most High. 9 The sacrifice of a just man is acceptable, and the memorial thereof shall never be forgotten. 10 Give the Lord his honour with a good eye, and diminish not the firstfruits of thine hands. 11 In all thy gifts shew a cheerful countenance, and dedicate thy tithes with gladness. 12 Give unto the most High according as he hath given, and offer the gain of thine hand with a good eye. 13 For the Lord recompenseth, and will recompense thee seven times as much.

The Book of Leviticus, which is considered the book of the call to holiness, since the saying is repeated: "Ye shall be holy unto me: for I am holy" (Lev 11:44; 11:45; 19:2), was concerned to speak in some detail about sacrifices and offerings in the temple of God. And the Book of Ben Sirach came to call every believer to offer spiritual sacrifices and offerings in his life. So he saw that he who keeps the commandments offers a peace offering [1], and he who does a kindness to one in need offers an offering of fine flour [2], and he who gives alms sacrifices a thank offering to God [2]. And he who withdraws from evil offers a sin offering with which God is pleased [2]. He links the service of the temple with the believers' offering of sacrifices and offerings in their daily life in the presence of the Lord.
The man who keeps the Law multiplies his offerings, and he who holds fast to the commandments offers a peace offering [1].

God is pleased with offerings of obedience to the divine commandment and holding fast to it, and counts them offerings and a peace offering pleasing before Him. The peace offering, in the view of Origen, is the offering of the spiritually mature or perfect man who enjoys the perfect peace of God in his inner life and in his inner relationships, as an overflow of peace and thanksgiving springing forth in the Lord Christ Himself, the giver of peace.
v True peace is from above. As long as we are bound to the body, we bear a yoke of many things that weary us.

Seek peace, then, and be freed from the troubles of this world. Acquire a quiet mind, and a calm, unperturbed soul, which passions do not stir up, and false teachings do not attract, so that it defies their allurements to accept them, that you may obtain "the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts" (Phil 4:7).

He who seeks peace seeks Christ, for He Himself is our peace, who maketh the twain one new man (Eph 14:2), making peace through the blood of His cross, whether things in earth, or things in heaven [1].
St. Basil the Great He who requites with kindness offers an offering of fine flour, and he who gives alms offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving [2].

Origen says: if you are unable to offer your whole life consecrated to the Lord as a burnt offering (Lev 1), then offer your daily work, sanctified to Him, as an offering of flour or unleavened bread, crying out to God to pour into you the oil of His mercy without ceasing, that the world may not distract you from your eternity (Lev 2). And he who gives alms is like one who sacrifices a sacrifice of thanksgiving.

v When you lie down on your bed, remember the blessings of God and His care for you, and thank Him for this; for as you are filled with these thoughts you rejoice in the Spirit. Then in the sleep of the body there will be an elevation for your soul, and the closing of your eyes will be a true knowledge of God, and your silence, while you are charged with good feelings, is a glorification of Almighty God with all the heart and all the strength, offering to God a praise that rises to the heights. For when there is no evil in a man, thanksgiving alone pleases God more than costly offerings, to Him who is the glory forever and ever. Amen [2].
St. Anthony the Great v Question: How can a man fulfil his love to God?

Answer: When we are in a state of continual thanksgiving and gratitude for the graces of God... as we see it also with irrational animals. Dogs, for example, love those who offer them food. We also learn this principle from the Lord's accusation of the people of Israel by the tongue of the prophet Isaiah, saying: "I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me. The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib: but Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider" (Isa 1:2-3). As love grows spontaneously in the ass toward its master, and the ox toward its owner, so also we. If we thank God gratefully for His graces that He gives us, how then shall we not love Him who grants us so many of those great gifts?! How is such a virtue not formed in the conscience of the sound soul naturally, without learning it (practicing it), so to speak?! [3]
St. Basil the Great To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to the Lord, and to forsake unrighteousness is a propitiation [3].

Some peoples became acquainted, through tradition, with bloody sacrifices, having received them from Noah and his three sons, but they distorted their concepts and purpose. But the Jewish people alone had the rite of "the great Day of Atonement" (Lev 16), the like of which one seeks in vain among any other people, and it points to the sacrifice of the Cross which the Lord Christ offered for the world. "Atonement" in Hebrew, "kebodit," means "covering" or "concealing," for on this day sins are forgiven and the man is covered by the precious blood, and the high priest makes atonement for himself and for the priests and for all the congregation, and even for the tabernacle and all its contents, a general and collective atonement for that into which the congregation as a whole, or as members, had fallen throughout the year.
Ben Sirach sees that departing from evil is the offering of atonement.
You shall not appear before the Lord empty-handed, for all these offerings are offered because of the commandment [4].

The commandment was often repeated: "None shall appear before me empty" (Ex 34:20), since the temple was committed to helping the needy, and also gave the priests and Levites portions of what was offered to the altar for their living and their families'. So it befits the believer not to appear empty. St. Mary, in her visit to Elizabeth her kinswoman, did not bring gifts in kind on the occasion of Elizabeth's pregnancy, but entered bearing the Lord Christ incarnate in her womb, and the babe leaped in her womb and Elizabeth rejoiced, saying: "And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" (Lk 1:43). So it befits us to follow St. Mary's example and not appear empty, but to bring to our brethren the Lord Christ dwelling in our hearts, He "in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Col 3:3). And when we stand in the presence of the Father we have nothing to offer except Christ our righteousness (1 Cor 1:30).
The righteous and good offering is anointing oil for the altar, and its sweet savour rises up before the Most High [5].

The Apostle says: "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" (1 Cor 3:16). If we are the temple of God, the inner altar in our hearts must be anointed with the anointing of the righteousness of Christ, and the incense of pure prayers be offered upon it, sending forth the sweet savour of Christ (2 Cor 2:15). Thus he links the ecclesiastical rite with the holy life.
The sacrifice of the righteous is acceptable, and the memorial of it shall never be forgotten [6].

The goal of our worship and our communion with the Holy One is that we become holy, bearing the icon of our God. For He has no need of offerings, but that we bear His righteousness and be prepared for eternal glory. His delight is not in the multitude of offerings but in the purity of our hearts, which will be revealed on the great Day of the Lord, and we shall enjoy the fellowship of the eternal glories. The Apostle repeats the saying: "The just shall live by faith" (Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11; Heb 10:38).
Glorify the Lord with your generosity, and do not be sparing of the firstfruits of your hands [7].

Generosity in offering reveals the righteousness of God working in us, and our pride in the glory of the Lord. It is not fitting for the believer to be sparing with the firstfruits and tithes, but to bring them with joy. "He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully. Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver (1 Cor 9:7).
In every gift be of a cheerful countenance, and dedicate your tithes with gladness [8].
St. Irenaeus says: "Judah dedicated the tithes of their incomes to God, but as for those who have received freedom (in Christ), they place all that they have at the disposal of Christ."
Give to the Most High as He has given you; give to Him generously according to your own unexpected gain[4] [9].

The prophet Malachi gives us sincere advice, in the words of the Lord, that we may touch practically how giving generously opens before us the windows of heaven, so that divine gifts flow upon us from where we do not expect. "Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it" (Mal 3:10).
For the Lord is the one who rewards; He will reward you sevenfold [10].
The Lord rewards the one who is generous in giving materially, and gives him inner joy and spiritual blessings.

entries.section: 2. There is no partiality with God

paragraphs.text: 14 Offer not gifts that have a blemish, for the Lord will not receive them. 15 And trust not in an unrighteous sacrifice; for the Lord is judge, and with him is no respect of persons. 16 He will not accept persons against the poor, but will hear the prayer of the oppressed. 17 He will not despise the fatherless that supplicateth him, nor the widow, when she poureth out her complaint. 18 Do not the tears of the widow run down her cheeks? and is not her cry against him that causeth them to fall? 19 For from her cheeks they go up to heaven, and the Lord that heareth will not delight in them. 20 He that serveth is accepted with good-will, and his prayer reacheth unto the clouds. 21 The prayer of the humble pierceth the clouds, and it will not rest till it come nigh, and will not depart till the most High shall visit and judge righteously and execute judgment. 22 For the Lord will not be slack, neither will he be long patient toward them, till he have smitten in sunder the loins of the unmerciful; 23 and avenged himself on the heathen, till he have taken away the multitude of the proud, and broken the sceptres of the unrighteous. 24 Till he have rendered to every man according to his deeds, and to the works of men according to their intents. 25 Till he have judged the cause of his people, and made them to rejoice in his mercy. 26 Mercy is seasonable in the time of affliction, as clouds of rain in the time of drought.
Do not offer Him a bribe, for He does not accept it, and do not offer a sacrifice of injustice [11].

The Lord Christ says: "I am the way, the truth" (Jn 14:6). And St. John the Beloved says: "God is love" (1 Jn 4:8, 16). So He does not accept a bribe from one who ignores the truth, and from one who does not practice love but injustice, and He does not show partiality. What is the connection of acceptable worship with bribery? Some think that by their contributing to houses of worship or by giving alms they obtain forgiveness of their sins without repentance and returning to God, as though they were bribing God.
For the Lord is the Judge, and with Him there is no partiality [12].

The Lord is as a father to the orphans, and as a judge to the widows, a defender of the oppressed, and a shepherd to the needy and suffering; He does not show partiality to the rich who have no pity on their brethren. He is no respecter of persons (Deut 10:17; Job 34:19).
He does not show partiality at the expense of the poor, but hears the petition of the oppressed [13].

There is no partiality with God (Rom 2:11); He cares for the poor and needy and oppressed, but He does not give to the person unwilling to work and the lazy, nor does He support one who counts himself wronged if it is because of his neglect and slackness.
He does not neglect the supplication of the orphan, nor that of the widow when she pours out her complaint [14].

entries.section: 2. There is no partiality with God

paragraphs.text: Do not the widow's tears run down her cheeks, and does she not cry out against him who caused them? [15].
Here he highlighted God's concern for the care of the oppressed classes. His ears listen to the supplications of orphans and widows, and to their tears and cries.

entries.section: 2. There is no partiality with God

paragraphs.text: He whose service pleases the Lord will be accepted by Him, and his prayer reaches the clouds [16].

Because Moses served the Lord faithfully, the Lord answered the cries of his heart before he cried with his mouth (Ex 14:15). Origen said: [God hears the silent cries of the saints by the Holy Spirit.]

entries.section: 2. There is no partiality with God

paragraphs.text: The prayer of the humble man pierces the clouds, and he does not rest until it reaches the Lord [17].
The humble man perceives that his prayer has reached God not only through visible or tangible signs, but, what is more important, he feels a true inner rest; he feels that he is in the bosom of God.

v Remember the pure conscience (of Job) and his blameless prayer: "O earth, cover not the blood of my body" (Job 16:18) LXX, that his prayer might go up as incense toward the Lord (Ps 141:2), and not be deposited in the earth.

The prayer of the saint pierces the cloud (cf. Sir 35:17), but the earth opens her mouth, and hides the prayer of the sinner in the blood of the flesh, as God said to Cain the murderer: "Cursed art thou from the earth, which hath opened her mouth to receive thy brother's blood from thy hand, as long as thou art earth" (cf. Gen 4:11-12) [5].

St. Ambrose v Let us now come to silent prayer, the prayer of Hannah the mother of Samuel. How she became an object of God's pleasure, and opened her barren womb, and removed her reproach, and bore a Nazirite or priest (1 Sam 1).

And Samuel also, when he prayed before his God and showed the wickedness of the Israelites when they asked for a king. Samuel offered a whole sacrifice upon the altar (1 Sam 12:17-18), and the rain came down...

David also prayed before his God and was delivered from the hands of Saul. And he also prayed after he had numbered the people and turned away from them the divine wrath and punishment when the destroyer had gained authority over them (2 Sam 24:17).

Asa also prayed, and his prayer showed great power, when Zerah the Ethiopian came out against him with an army of a million. Then Asa prayed and said: "Your power will be known, O our God, when You destroy a huge people by a few people" (2 Chr 14:12-15). So this great army was defeated by the power of Asa's prayer.
His son Jehoshaphat shattered the enemy's army by his prayer, which defeated them (2 Chr 20:3-30).
Hezekiah also prayed, and by his prayer he prevailed over 185,000 men, the angel acting as the leader of his army (2 Kgs 19:15, 35).

Jonah prayed before his God from the depths of the sea and God heard him (Jon 2), and answered his prayer, and he was delivered without any harm. His prayer pierced the depths, and overcame the waves, and was stronger than the storm. It pierced the clouds and flew in the air (cf. Sir 35:17), it opened the heavens and drew near to the throne of majesty by means of Gabriel who presents prayer before God. As a result the depths cast out the prophet, and the whale brought Jonah safely to the land. Likewise in the case of Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael, their prayers overcame the flame, and quenched the power of the fire, and changed its burning nature. They put out the king's fury, and delivered the righteous men (Dan 3)..

When Daniel also prayed, his prayer shut the mouths of the lions (Dan 6); the devouring mouths were shut before the flesh and bones of a man. The lions spread their paws, and caught Daniel so that he would not fall to the ground, embraced him in their arms, and kissed his feet. And when Daniel stood in the pit to pray, he lifted his hands to heaven, and after the pattern of Daniel the lions followed him and imitated him. That One who received his prayer came down and shut the mouths of the lions. For Daniel said to Darius: "My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me" (Dan 6:22).

And although the pit was covered and sealed, light shone inside it, and the lions rejoiced when they saw the light that appeared for the sake of Daniel. And when sleep overcame Daniel and he wished to doze, the lions knelt that he might sleep upon them, and not on the ground. The pit was more illuminated than an upper chamber with many windows. And in the pit he offered many prayers more than in his upper chamber, where he used to pray only three times a day (Dan 6:10), and when Daniel triumphed and rejoiced, those who had accused him were thrown into the pit instead of him, and the mouths of the lions opened and devoured them and crushed their bones [6].

St. Aphrahat v Above all this, let him observe the words of the Apostle: "For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us" (Rom 8:18), and expect the revelation with David: "in keeping of them there is great reward" (Ps 19:12), and recompense and crowns of righteousness, and the eternal dwelling, and the life without end, and the unspeakable joy, and the unperishing places with the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, who is the true God in heaven, and the meeting face to face, and rejoicing with the angels and fathers and patriarchs and prophets and apostles and martyrs, that we may be numbered with these, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong power and glory forever and ever. Amen.

entries.section: 2. There is no partiality with God

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great And he will not withdraw it until the Most High visits him, and does justice to the righteous, and executes judgment [18].

v Here we overcome the adversary, if we fight with tears and prayers and a broken heart continually. It is written: "The prayer of the humble pierces the clouds ... and does not cease until the Most High visits him." Therefore the weeping of the humble contributes with great power to the destruction of fleshly lust. Tears issuing from the pricking of the heart defeat the enemy and acquire on our behalf the gift of triumphant happiness [7].

Fr. Fulgentius v In ancient times six hundred thousand armed men of the children of Israel went forward against Midian, and all of them were defeated because of the sin lurking in them (Num 11:21). Now the Midianites, victors over six hundred thousand, were struck down by two thousand, that you may know that Israel was not victorious because of the large number of soldiers, but by the righteousness and godliness in which they are.

And in blessing them it was said that if they kept the law of the Lord, one of them would defeat a thousand, and two would put ten thousand to flight (Lev 26:8). Behold then, one saint praying is better than countless sinners in battle. The prayer of the saint pierces heaven (the clouds) [17], how then should it not defeat earthly enemies? For this reason it befits you in every way to labor, first to seek and to keep the righteousness of God (Mt 6:33).

If you obtain (the righteousness of God) and keep it, He will subdue all your enemies to you. If the Apostle says: "Having on the breastplate of righteousness, and your loins girt about with truth, and the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit ... Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked" (cf. Eph 6:14-17). When you are armed with these weapons you are able to fight all the camps of Satan and all his army, and sing with assurance: "Though an host should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear: though war should rise against me, in this will I be confident" (Ps 27:2) [8].

entries.section: 2. There is no partiality with God

paragraphs.text: Origen For the Lord will not delay, nor be slow in helping them [19].

entries.section: 2. There is no partiality with God

paragraphs.text: Until He crushes the loins of those without mercy, and repays with vengeance upon the nations [20]

entries.section: 2. There is no partiality with God

paragraphs.text: Until He wipes out the multitudes of the proud, and breaks the scepter of the unrighteous [21].

With many words the Pharisee offered a haughty prayer, while with few words the tax collector offered a humble prayer. The first was rejected, and the second passed through to the throne of God, for God listens to the words of the humble.

v It is fitting that our petitions be offered to God in humility, for it is our heart that is heard, not our voice. God, who sees our thoughts, is not to be petitioned by shouting, as the Lord affirms when He says: "Wherefore think ye ... in your hearts?" (Mt 9:4). And in another place: "And all the churches shall know that I am he which searcheth the reins and hearts" (cf. Rev 2:23) [9].

entries.section: 2. There is no partiality with God

paragraphs.text: The martyr Cyprian Until He renders to man according to his deeds, and to the works of men according to their thoughts [22].

The heavenly life that we live here is a pledge of the immortal life extending beyond the limits of time, when the Lord Christ the King appears with His angels to recompense each one according to his work. If faith is the foundation of the Kingdom, it must nevertheless be "practical," so that the Lord may give us the eternal crowns, recompensing "each one according to his work."

entries.section: 2. There is no partiality with God

paragraphs.text: Until He executes judgment for His people, and makes them rejoice in His mercy [23].

St. John Chrysostom sees that Moses, with all the esteem he had reached in the eyes of God, cannot grasp the depths of God's wisdom and mercy, as though God were saying to him: [O Moses, it is not for you to know who is worthy of My love for man; leave this to Me. If it is not Moses' right to know, how much more is it so for us?[10]]
Mercy is beautiful in the time of his affliction[11], like rain in the time of drought [24].

While the Lord of glory suffered bodily the sufferings of the Cross, He offered to mankind His mercy, and made atonement for their sins. St. Augustine also says that afflictions bring us into contact with the mercy of God and His care and love.

v "Hear me, O LORD, for thy mercy is sweet" (Ps 69:16).. For the man who is in troubles, he needs to find sweetness in the mercies of God. Concerning this sweetness of God's mercies see what is said in another place, where Holy Scripture says: "Mercy is seasonable in the time of affliction, as clouds of rain in the time of drought" (cf. Sir 35:24)... Even bread is not sweet unless hunger precedes it. For this reason, even when God permits or wills that we be in any affliction, even in this He is merciful. He will not withdraw help, but stirs up in us the longing (for Him) [12].

v "In the daytime the LORD will command his mercy, and in the night He will declare it" (cf. Ps 42:8). In affliction a man has no leisure to hear. Listen when you are at ease. Learn, when you are in quiet, the discipline of wisdom, and store up the word of God as you do with food. For in the time of distress it befits everyone to benefit from what he heard in the time of security. For in the time of ease God commands you His mercy (Ps 42:8), and as you serve Him faithfully, He frees you from distress. Only in the night does He declare to you His mercy which He commanded you in the daytime. When distress actually comes, He will not leave you deprived of His help, but shows you that what He commanded you in the daytime is true. It is written: "Mercy is seasonable in the time of affliction, as clouds of rain in the time of drought" (cf. Sir 35:24) [13].
St. Augustine Inspired by Sirach 35

entries.section: Accept my life as a sacrifice of pleasing love!

paragraphs.text: v You loved me and offered Your life as a sacrifice for my salvation; what shall I render to You, O All-Love!
Grant me to keep Your Law, that my heart may be purified.
Let me keep Your commandment, and my heart will be filled with holiness and peace.
v I see You before me in my brethren, so I walk with them in kindness and generosity.
By Your grace I flee from evil, and enjoy Your righteousness.
I have nothing to offer You, for all that I offer is from You.
Set up for Yourself an altar within me, and anoint it with the oil of gladness.
I offer upon it my prayers, bearing Your fragrance, O Holy One.
That I may possess You and see Your glory, and enjoy Your sweet voice!
v You have no need of my worship and my goodness. Grant me compassion for the poor, and a longing to remove injustice, and a desire to free the captives and prisoners, and to heal the sick.
You are the Father of orphans, the Judge of widows, O God of the forgotten!
v You are pleased with the prayer of the heart; You alone hear it, and are pleased with it, and answer its cries.
And there is no enemy who can obstruct it.
What shall I ask of You, O Giver of good things?
Give my prayer the two wings of the Spirit, that it may fly and pierce the clouds.
It will rest in Your bosom, You will grant me Your free righteousness, and gather me into Your heavenly house!
My God, my heart asks You to hasten Your coming!

1 O Lord, God of all, have mercy upon us, and behold us, and shew us the light of thy mercies. 2 And cast thy fear upon all the nations that have not sought after thee, that they may know that there is no God but thee, and declare thy great things. 3 Lift up thine hand against the strange nations, and let them know thy might. 4 As thou wast sanctified in us before them, so be thou magnified among them before us. 5 And let them know thee, as we have known thee, that there is no God but thee, O Lord. 6 Renew the signs, and work wonders. 7 Glorify thy hand and thy right arm. 8 Raise up indignation, and pour out wrath. 9 Destroy the adversary, and smite in sunder the enemy. 10 Hasten the time, and remember the covenant, and let them declare thy wondrous works. 11 Let him that escapeth be devoured by the fire of wrath, and let them that oppress thy people find destruction. 12 Smite in sunder the heads of the rulers of the enemies, that say, "There is none other but we." 13 Gather all the tribes of Jacob, and take them for thine inheritance, as from the beginning. 14 O Lord, have mercy upon the people that is called by thy name, and upon Israel, whom thou hast made equal to thy firstborn. 15 Have compassion on the city of thy sanctuary, Jerusalem, the city of thy rest. 16 Fill Zion that it may proclaim thy sayings. Fill thy people with thy glory. 17 Give testimony to those that are thy creation from the beginning, and raise up the prophecies that are in thy name. 18 Give reward to them that wait for thee, and let thy prophets be found true. Hear, O Lord, the prayer of them that supplicate unto thee, 19 according to the blessing of Aaron over thy people; that all the inhabitants of the earth may know that thou art the Lord, the God of the ages.

This prayer expresses the feelings of the people who were under oppression, but it is certainly not taken from the public rite which the people practiced; rather it is a prayer coming from the heart of Ben Sirach in the name of the suffering people who await the Savior of the whole world. St. Augustine sees that verses 1-4 are a prayer offered on behalf of the nations that they may enjoy the fear of the Lord, and this was fulfilled by the coming of the incarnate Word of God.
Have mercy on us, O Lord God of all, and behold us, and put Your fear upon all the nations [1].

This prayer came as an expression of intense pain, before the rise of the Maccabean revolt in 164 BC and the purification of the temple. The psalmist says: "God shall bless us; and all the ends of the earth shall fear him" (Ps 76:7).
Lift up Your hand against the strange nations, and allow them to see Your power [2].
By the strange nations he means those that despised Israel, and certain rulers, especially Antiochus Epiphanes, allowed them to offer unclean animals on the altar.
As You were sanctified in us before them, so be magnified in them before us [3].

This happened in former ages, as in the days of Moses the prophet, and now let this power appear once again, so that no wicked nation covets them and they say that their God has forgotten them. It is said: "Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against thee, O Zidon; and I will be glorified in the midst of thee: and they shall know that I am the LORD, when I shall have executed judgments in her, and shall be sanctified in her" (Ezek 28:22). The purpose of disciplining the nations is not vengeance, but enlightenment to know the Lord. It is a petition for the salvation of the nations. Would that they knew the true way! Would that they abandoned their idols!

St. Augustine often gave us examples confirming that the Lord's Prayer given in the Holy Gospel is characterized by comprehensiveness, for all the prayers found in the Old Testament have their counterparts in the Lord's Prayer, among them what is found in this chapter (36:4, 16).
v For example, he who says: "May You be sanctified in all men, as You are sanctified in us" (cf. Sir 36:16), what does he say but "Hallowed be thy name"?
And also he who says: "O God of hosts, turn us again, and cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved" (Ps 80:3-4), what does he mean but: "Thy kingdom come."
And he who says: "Order my steps in thy word: and let not any iniquity have dominion over me" (Ps 119:133), what does he say but "Thy will be done, not my will"...
And he who says: "Let not the lust of gluttony nor fornication take hold of me" (cf. Sir 23:6), but "Bring us not into temptation"...

If you go through the words of the holy prayers, you will find nothing, in my way of thinking, that the Lord's Prayer does not include; therefore when we pray we are permitted to utter the same things but in different words, but it will not be permitted to say different things [1].
St. Augustine Let them know You as we know You, for there is no God but You, O Lord [4].
St. Augustine says: [This prophecy, in the mold of longing in the spirit of prayer, has been fulfilled in Christ Jesus, as we see[2].]
Renew Your signs, and work new wonders, and glorify Your hand and Your right arm [5].

By renewing the signs he means that the Lord should declare His wrath upon these nations, as He did of old to Pharaoh of Egypt, who humbled the people and refused to let them go out to the wilderness to offer sacrifice to the Lord (Ex 3:19-20).
Raise up Your wrath, and pour out Your indignation, and drive away the adversary, and destroy the enemy [6].

When we hear of the wrath and indignation of God it befits us to realize that God, who is all love, does not bear a spirit of vengeance, but is angry at evil, and longs for the purification of the sinner and his sanctification. When He sent Jonah the prophet to declare His wrath upon Nineveh because of its evils, the king and the leaders and the people returned to God with repentance, and so became a wonderful model through the generations of God's purpose in rebuke and discipline, namely His love for sinners that they return to the source of their sanctification.
In every age there were men of God among the pagan nations, such as righteous Job, who was the object of God's honoring him.

v You find many passages in Holy Scripture in which God is likened to the attributes of man. So if you ever hear the words "the wrath of God and His fury," do not think that wrath and fury are emotions and attributes present in God, but it is a way by which God condescends and speaks in order to discipline His children and set them right.

For we also, when we wish to guide our children and correct their faults, appear before them in a frightening form and with a stern and firm face which does not correspond to our true feelings, but corresponds to the manner of discipline.

If we always showed on our faces the tolerance and leniency that exists in our souls and inner feelings toward our children, without changing the features of our faces according to the children's behavior, we would spoil them and drive them to the worse. In this way we speak of the wrath of God: when it is said that God is angry, what is meant by this wrath is your repentance and your reform, for God in truth does not become angry or furious, but it is you who will bear the effects of wrath and fury when you fall into the terrible, harsh torments because of your sins and evils, in the case of God's disciplining you by what we call the wrath of God![3]
Origen Hasten the time, and remember Your oath, and let the people declare Your mighty works [7].

The oath mentioned here refers to the covenant which the Lord established with our father Abraham (Gen 17:21). Since the men of God in the Old Testament were awaiting the coming of the Messiah the Savior, who would fulfill the covenants established between God and men of faith, Ben Sirach asked that the time be hastened so that God might fulfill His promises, and God declare His mighty works through the Cross. At the same time Ben Sirach's prayer came expressing the bitterness of his soul at what the people of God were suffering at that time, while he enjoyed hope for the salvation of the nations from the corruption that had befallen them because of their unbelief.
Let him that escapeth be devoured by Your fiery wrath, and let him who harms Your people meet destruction [8].

If Ben Sirach asks for the swift coming of recompense upon the rulers who resisted the Lord and His people and who defiled the temple of the Lord, then by the spirit of prophecy he asks for the swift vengeance on the devil and his angels who oppose the kingdom of God in the hearts of mankind.

v We have fallen under the authority of our enemies, that is, "the king of this age" and his helpers of the powers of evil. For this reason our need became redemption by the One who buys us that we may return from the state of estrangement from Him. Our Savior gave His blood as a ransom for us... And since "the forgiveness of sins," which follows redemption, was impossible before man was set free, we must first be freed from the authority of him who took us captive and kept us under his control, and be freed beyond the reach of his hand, so that we may be able to obtain forgiveness of our sins and healing from the wounds of sin, so that we may accomplish works of piety and other virtues.
Origen Crush the heads of the leaders of the enemies, who say: "There is none other but we" [9].

Our life is a pleasant journey, even though it is full of trials and the resistance of the devil against us, but the Word of God became incarnate and dwelt among us and gave us by His Cross to crush the ancient serpent, the devil, according to His promise to Adam (Gen 3:15).

The psalmist stood amazed before the marvelous work of God, in the midst of the battle between God and the devil. He saw himself a sparrow with neither might nor power. He cannot escape from the snare of the fowlers, that is, the devil and his angels, but the Almighty helped him, and broke the snare for him and set him free. The psalmist sang, saying: "Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped. Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth" (Ps 124:7).

v What is the snare that was broken? The Apostle says: "(The Lord) shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly" (Rom 16:20), "that ye may recover yourselves out of the snare of the devil" (2 Tim 2:26). Behold, you see that Satan is the fowler, longing to catch our souls for destruction. Satan is the master of many snares and deceptions of every kind... When we are in the state of grace our souls are in safety. But as soon as we play with sin, our souls are troubled and become like a ship tossed by the waves [4].
St. Jerome Gather all the tribes of Jacob, and give them their inheritance as in the beginning [10].

Together with God's care for every individual personally, He seeks to gather the believers together from Adam to the end of the ages, to establish from them the Church, the queen and heavenly bride. The Apostle Paul says: "For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ" (2 Cor 11:2).
O Lord, have mercy on Your people who are called by Your name, and Israel whom You likened to Your firstborn son [11].

Although Cyrus the Persian permitted the Jews to return, few of them returned, in three waves, to the Holy Land, and some remained in Babylon, and many went to the Fertile Crescent, and some to Egypt or Ethiopia. Many Jews settled outside the Holy Land, especially on the shores of the Mediterranean. This dispersion of the people changed many features of the Jewish religion.
v What is said about Israel? "He who sees God." How did they see God who walked among them in the flesh, and they counted Him a man and killed Him?...

"His name is great in Israel." Do you wish to be Israel? Note that man of whom the Lord said: "Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!" (Jn 1:47). If the Israelite indeed is one in whom is no guile, then he in whom there is guile or falsehood is not an Israelite in truth [5].
St. Augustine Have compassion on the city of Your sanctuary, Jerusalem, the city of Your rest [12].

The Jews considered Jerusalem an icon of heaven (Isa 54:10) and the temple the point of meeting of the people with God, and Jerusalem was the focus of the gaze of all the Jews, wherever they were scattered about the world, for it is the city of the great King, the city of peace, the city of Melchizedek (Gen 14:18), the city of David the great king, and in the days of David and Solomon became the religious and political capital. The beloved city of Jerusalem was exposed throughout the ages to demolition, burning and defilement.

It became a symbol of heaven: "Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out: and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God" (Rev 3:12). "And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband" (Rev 21:2).

v Honor the holy Church and love her and praise her, your mother the heavenly Jerusalem, the city of God. She is the one that in this faith which she receives bears fruit and spreads throughout all the world. She is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth (1 Tim 3:15), which in her dispensing of the Sacraments bears with the wicked who at some time are cut off and excluded [6].
St. Augustine Fill Zion with the celebration of Your divine virtue, and Your people with Your glory [13].

In the Old Testament God was preparing Zion that He might become incarnate of St. Mary and offer salvation to the world. Now the Lord cares for His Church, the Zion of the New Testament, as the people of God who share with Him in the divine nature. The psalmist says: "The LORD loveth the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob" (Ps 87:2).
v It seems to me that the gates of Zion are the virtues.
As vice and sin are the two gates of death, I think that the gates of Zion are the virtues [7].

v He does not mean the gates that we see today in dust and ashes, but he means the gates against which hell shall not prevail (Mt 16:18), through which enter the multitudes of those who believe in Christ [8].
St. Jerome Bear witness to what You created in the beginning, and show forth the prophecies that were spoken in Your name [14].
Reward those who wait for You, and let Your prophets be found trustworthy [15].

The men of God in the Old Testament were awaiting the fulfillment of the prophecies concerning salvation and the coming of the Lord Christ. "And I will shake all nations, and the desire of all nations shall come: and I will fill this house with glory, saith the LORD of hosts. The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, saith the LORD of hosts. The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former, saith the LORD of hosts: and in this place will I give peace, saith the LORD of hosts" (Hag 2:7-9). St. John Chrysostom sees that the prophet uttered this statement because many of the Jews found it hard to believe how the old temple would return once again with its gold and silver after it had become dust and ashes, as though the Lord were saying to them: [Why do you not believe, for the silver is Mine and the gold is Mine, I do not need to borrow from anyone to adorn My house?![9]]
Hear, O Lord, the prayer of those who supplicate You, according to the blessing of Aaron upon Your people [16].

Ben Sirach concludes the prayer by asking for the blessing which He promised His people by the mouth of Aaron (Num 6:22-27). The Lord made clear that the blessing that comes upon the people through the priests is God's own gift, offered by the Holy Trinity, and the priests are but a means; they ask God three times that the Holy Trinity bless the people. Thus he affirms that it is He who blesses, not the priests, however high their rank; He keeps and has mercy and it is He who grants peace.
And let all the inhabitants of the earth know that You are the Lord, the God of the ages [17].

With Ben Sirach's concern for the service of the ancient people and prayer on their behalf, he does not ignore the salvation of the nations which is realized by the coming of the Messiah the Savior. Here he asks on behalf of "all the inhabitants of the earth."

entries.section: 2. The need for a spirit of discernment

paragraphs.text: 20 The belly receiveth all meats, yet is one meat better than another. 21 The palate discerneth the meats of venison, and an heart of understanding discerneth false speeches. 22 A froward heart causeth heaviness: but a man of much experience will requite him.

The spirit of discernment is like food that the wise man tastes, and so is pleased with its flavor [18]. It gives sweetness to a man in every circumstance he lives in; he feels as though the sweetness that touches his inner being is unique, he has never experienced sweetness like it.
The stomach receives all kinds of food, but some food is better than another [18].

It is difficult for a man to give a definition of sweetness. It touches his food and drink and words. Material food is taken by the stomach, and the palate distinguishes it with a kind of sweetness that differs from one food to another and from one person to another. This sweetness gives a man a kind of discernment between one food and another.
As the palate tastes the flavor of venison, so the understanding heart discerns false speeches [19].
A man's palate discerns foods, and his heart and ear discern the speech which he utters with his tongue, and as it is said: "The ear trieth words, as the mouth tasteth his meat" (Job 12:11).

The wise man has a heart that discerns good, fitting speech from bad, unfitting speech. Therefore it befits a man not to be hasty in answering or commenting on a matter before his mind and heart examine it.

v He is not speaking of the ear of the body (Job 12:11), but the ear of the spirit. With the bodily ears we hear the sounds of words, but with the inner ears we discern thought and words. Likewise "the palate (especially the taste) tastes food," meaning that it appreciates it with respect to its pleasure. So also the palate of the spirit discerns its benefit.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem v "For the mind nous discerns words"... If God gives us the palate to discern the tasting of food, He also gives us the mind to take our decisions, and time allows us to seek understanding.

St. John Chrysostom v There is one judge who oversees the inside, that is, the power of discernment which belongs to the mind, but through fitting ways that keep the five senses distinct. God works wonders, so the eye cannot hear, nor the ear see, nor the mouth smell, nor the nose taste, nor the hands smell. While all these work through the powers of the one mind, yet no sense can practice other than what the Creator has appointed for it. And so through these outward bodily arrangements, He leaves it to us to gather them within in a spiritual way...

While there is one wisdom dwelling in one man less than in another... yet in itself it bears no differences among them, but by it we practice various different operations, so one receives the gift of wisdom, and another the gift of knowledge, and another tongues, and another the gift of healing...

The blessed Job condemns the inexperience of his friends, and the insolence of everyone who is puffed up, claiming that he has learned in wisdom. For knowing something about God is one thing, and tasting what you know with understanding is another.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
The crooked heart causes grief, and the man of wide experience requites it [20].

"The wicked heart," that is, the impure, brings many troubles upon a man. It is characterized by narrowness, so it cannot bear a word of criticism, and does not rejoice in giving, while the pure heart is spacious, longs to love even those who trouble it, and serves everyone, and is pleased with giving, not taking, therefore it reaps countless blessings.

entries.section: 3. The spirit of discernment and the choice of a wife

paragraphs.text: 23 A woman will receive any man whatever, yet is one daughter better than another. 24 The beauty of a woman cheereth the countenance, and surpasseth all the desires of man. 25 And if there be mercy and meekness in her tongue, her husband is not like the other sons of men. 26 He that getteth a wife beginneth a possession, she is to him the head of riches, and a help meet for him, and a pillar of rest. 27 Where no hedge is, the possession is spoiled; and where no woman is, the wanderer mourneth. 28 Who will trust a thief well girded, that wandereth from city to city? so is the man that hath no nest, and lodgeth wheresoever the night overtaketh him.

In ancient times a woman had no opportunity to choose a husband, and if she had, as happened with Rebecca the wife of Isaac (Gen 24:1-8), it is not comparable with a man's freedom to choose his wife. Usually the parents or those in their place chose the husband and the wife; though this does not mean the deprivation of the spouses of happiness. And the rate of divorce was not high as it is today.

As much as he warned the young men lest they choose a wicked wife, he blesses him who marries one whose tongue is gentle and who is characterized by meekness; her husband feels that he is not like the rest of men, because he lives as with an angel from heaven [23].
He speaks of the importance of the good wife in her husband's life, declaring that she plays a principal role in his life:

entries.section: 3. The spirit of discernment and the choice of a wife

paragraphs.text: a. Richer than anyone who has wealth [24], for she is a precious treasure (Prov 31:10).
b. He does not feel isolation, for she is a helper to him [24].
c. He counts her as a pillar on which he leans while in safety [24].

entries.section: 3. The spirit of discernment and the choice of a wife

paragraphs.text: d. She encircles him like a hedge around him, so her husband does not wander [25].

entries.section: 3. The spirit of discernment and the choice of a wife

paragraphs.text: e. He feels a stability, especially when he returns in the evening to his house and feels her presence with him [26-27].
A woman receives any son[10], but there is a daughter[11] better than another [21].
The beautiful woman makes the man happy, and surpasses all that he desires [22].

Here he praises physical beauty, which without doubt deserves praise, like everything beautiful among men or among creatures, yet all God's creatures are beautiful, and beauty is a relative matter, as there is a difference between physical beauty and the beauty of the spirit.
And if there is gentleness and meekness in her tongue, her husband is not like other men [23].
We can touch Ben Sirach's view of woman through his speaking of the role of the virtuous woman in her husband's life.

The tongue of the wicked wife, as we saw before, utterly destroys the husband's life, while the tongue of the virtuous wife offers the husband gentleness and meekness, and even lifts him above all men, that is, transforms him into the likeness of an angel.
Ben Sirach did not say this about the good husband in the effect of his tongue upon his wife. We have not heard that the good man by his tongue transforms his wife into something higher than all men.

There are other qualities worthy of the woman to be adorned with: such as wisdom, chastity of tongue and bearing responsibilities, those qualities that make the husband a happy person who boasts of her among his friends, for physical beauty may turn to ugliness because of illness, while the good constant qualities remain, and death does not destroy them.
He who marries such a woman has acquired the best possession, a helper like himself, and a pillar to lean on [24].

Ben Sirach exalts the wife in a wonderful way. For although she is often physically weak in relation to the man, yet she is able to lift him above all men, and make him rich by being his precious treasure, and even give him strength, as he leans on her in his weakness as on a pillar!
Where there is no hedge, possessions are plundered, and where there is no wife, the man wanders mourning [25].

A good marriage protects both parties, the husband and the wife, from the snares of the devil. Ben Sirach sees that marriage to a wise woman is better than celibacy, for the wife becomes to her husband a support and helper to him (Gen 2:18). A good woman is a good portion, given to him that feareth the Lord, whether rich or poor, his heart is in gladness and his countenance always bright.

Marriage may help a man to commit to a social life and to preserve his time, his money and his reputation, and not to deviate into harmful paths. The good woman is to him like a hedge, a guard and an overseer; he finds one who cares about his affairs, and fears for him, and the warmth of a happy quiet home will be waiting for him. It is natural that he who has no wife and no children moves easily from place to place and from house to house. This may push him to deviate and to instability.
Who will trust the armed thief who wanders from city to city? [26].

entries.section: 3. The spirit of discernment and the choice of a wife

paragraphs.text: Who will trust the man who has no shelter, and lodges wherever the evening overtakes him [27].
Many look to marriage as a safe shelter for the wife, but Ben Sirach sees that in the virtuous wife the husband dwells in a safe house, in which he sleeps and rests!
Inspired by Sirach 36
v Look upon all mankind, for You are the God of all!
You were sanctified in Your believing children, and through You they became saints!
May You be glorified by the return of all the nations to You!
In Your love You are angry at their evils, and in Your compassion You draw them to You.
Hasten Your coming, that we may meet all the pious believers, and rejoice in Your presence among the heavenly and the earthly.
v You have kindled our hearts with longing to enjoy the Jerusalem above, our mother.
We see You, and so we are truly counted the heavenly Israel.
The prophecies are fulfilled by Your coming on the clouds.
And we enjoy what eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath entered into the heart of man!
v Grant me the spirit of discernment in all my life.
May I know what is good and fitting for me as Your son, and reject what is bad and unfitting for me.

By the spirit of discernment my heart is enlarged with love for all the sons of men, loving giving more than taking, and listening more than speaking; I reject the wicked one, so grief cannot slip into my heart, nor does my soul suffer disturbance.
v My God, truly the good wife makes her husband happy; he sees her as his treasure, his support and his hedge, so he finds stability with her, and by Your Holy Spirit the two become one flesh.
Let wisdom be the bride who embraces me.
Let wisdom occupy my heart, and I shall be in a wedding that never ceases.
Neither the events of the world, nor illnesses, nor all the powers of darkness can spoil my peace.
I shall not move from city to city, for heaven is my dwelling.
And no thief shall assault my mind or my heart or my feelings, for Your divine Kingdom is established within me!

1 Every friend saith, "I also am his friend": but there is a friend which is only a friend in name. Is it not a grief unto death, 2 when a companion and friend is turned to an enemy? 3 O wicked imagination, whence camest thou in to cover the dry land with deceit? 4 There is a companion which rejoiceth in the prosperity of a friend, but in the time of trouble he will be against him. 5 There is a companion which for the belly's sake laboureth with his friend, and taketh up the buckler against the enemy. 6 Forget not thy friend in thy mind, and be not unmindful of him in thy riches. 7 Consult not with him that suspecteth thee, and hide thy counsel from such as envy thee. 8 Every counsellor extolleth counsel, but some counsel for themselves.
Sirach returns to speak about friends, who must be faithful and chosen with a spirit of discernment, offering examples of those who must be avoided:
A. Those who are friends in name only, without deeds (nominalism); that is, their friendship is not genuine [1].

B. The friend who may turn into an enemy, and who is worse than the enemy who is open from the beginning [2]. The bad example in the Bible is Judas the traitor. He is a deceiver [3]. Such a friend leaves a bad mark on the lives of many, for he stirs up suspicion among some friends. The appearance of such a person drives some to examine seriously the motives of the one with whom they will be joined as a friend.

C. A friend who is not steadfast in his friendship, who clings to his friend in his prosperity and ignores him in his adversity. Sometimes he even takes up toward him an attitude of enmity without any real cause.
D. There are friends whose friendship stops at the limits of courtesies, especially in holding banquets and parties on occasions.
Sirach gives a person advice so that he may practise genuine friendship, by being concerned with his friend as one who dwells in his depths, caring for him and supporting him even materially.
Every friend says: "I also am your friend," but sometimes he is a friend in name only [1].

Ben Sira begins the list of those to be rejected from friendship with those who claim friendship but do not practise it in deed. Some, without discernment, are occupied with the number of friends around them, not with their quality. The heart of the believer must open itself in love, if possible, to everyone, but not everyone is a friend to whom he discloses his secrets, for at some time they may wrong him, and they may even destroy him.
Is it not a grief unto death when a companion and friend is turned to an enemy? [2]

The second group is the unfaithful persons who for some hidden reason turn from friendship to enmity. Examples of this are Judas, to whom the Lord Christ gave many blessings, but because of his love of silver he betrayed his Master; and also King Saul, whom the boy David rescued, and when the people loved the boy, he set it in his heart to be rid of him by every means. In contrast to this is the character of David, who met Saul's enmity with love and would not accept to take vengeance on him, but even kept friendship with Saul and his offspring after Saul's death.
It is exceedingly sad when a friend in name, in whom his friend trusts, turns into an enemy to him.
O wicked thought! Why were you drawn in to cover the earth with deceit? [3]

Ben Sira stands grieved at what has befallen the nature of man, which God created good and possessed of authority, how it has been brought low by sin and evil inclinations have crept over it. And man, created in the image of God, has turned from being a friend to his brethren into an enemy! These evil inclinations do not harm the person himself alone, but the fallen nature of man. The Apostle says: "For the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who hath subjected the same in hope" (Rom 8:20). St. John Chrysostom sees that corruption has come down not only upon the nature of man but upon creation as well. And when the nature of man is restored by the work of the Savior, the world is delivered from the bondage of corruption (Rom 8:21), for he says:

[Now, what is this creation? It does not mean you alone, but with you also the lower creation, which does not share with you in reason or sense; this shares your blessings. He says: "It shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption," that is, it will no longer become corrupt, but will walk side by side with the beauty that is given to your body. For just as when your body became corrupt it also became corrupt, so now, when your body becomes incorruptible, it also follows it. And as the Apostle declares this he reaches the conclusion: "into the glorious liberty of the children of God," so that its freedom is fulfilled.

He is like a nurse who is bringing up a king's son: when the son receives his father's authority she enjoys the good things with him, and so it is also with creation together with us. You see that in all things man occupies the position of leadership, for it is for his sake that all things were made. Behold how (the Apostle) soothes the wrestler, showing God's unspeakable love toward man, for he wishes to say: Why are you troubled at your trials? For if you suffer for your own sake, even creation suffers because of you. And he not only soothes, but also shows that what he utters is a matter of importance. For if creation, which was brought into being wholly for your sake, is "in hope," how much more does it befit you to be in hope, you through whom creation will enjoy those good things? Just as fathers, when they see their sons on the way to receiving an honor, clothe the servants in splendid garments for the glory of the son, so God clothes creation with incorruption for the glory of the freedom of the sons[1].]

Man abused the emotions that God gave him, and also the gift of reasoning and true wisdom, and so man fell into treachery, which appeared clearly in Cain, who killed his brother Abel because he was more righteous than he.
There is a companion who rejoices at the joy of a friend, but in the time of affliction he is against him [4].
The third group that must be avoided is the person who exploits his brother: he befriends him where he gains a personal benefit, and is hostile to him when he finds no personal benefit in him.
There is a companion who strives to help a friend for the sake of his belly, and in the time of battle he takes up the shield [5].
The fourth group, persons whose dealings are limited to parties and amusement, and who care neither for the salvation of their own souls nor for the salvation of their families and friends.
Do not forget your friend within your soul[2], and do not neglect him when you distribute your wealth [6].

After warning us against the four preceding groups, he called us to be faithful friends ourselves. The mark of true friendship is that our friend has a special place in our souls, that is, in our hearts, thought and feelings, and that we count what we possess as a divine gift with which we support others.

9 Beware of the counsellor, and first inquire what he needs; for he will counsel what profits himself, 10 lest he cast the lot upon you, and say to you: 11 "Your way is good," and then stand over against you to see what will befall you. 12 Do not consult the hypocrite about godliness, nor the unjust man about justice, nor a woman about her rival, nor a coward about war, nor a merchant about trade, nor a buyer about selling, nor the envious man about giving thanks for kindness, 13 nor the harsh man about tenderness, nor the slothful man about any work, 14 nor the hired man who lives with you about finishing work, nor the idler about much work. Do not give heed to these in any matter of counsel. 15 But keep company with the godly man, whom you know to keep the commandments, 16 whose soul is as your soul, and who, when you fall, grieves for you. 17 And establish counsel with the heart, for you have no counsellor more faithful than it, 18 for a man's soul sometimes tells the truth more than seven watchmen who watch from a high place. 19 And in all these things pray to the Most High, that He may guide you in truth in the straight way.

The counsellor is more serious than the friend, for what a person asks of a friend is that he share his sufferings and joys and not divulge his secrets. But the counsellor, besides what pertains to the faithful friend of these qualities, is wise and marked by a spirit of discernment, so that a person may ask counsel of him, especially in taking a decision that is fateful in his life.
On the positive side, the friend or counsellor must be chosen godly, keeping the commandments, and concerned for his own salvation and the salvation of the one whose friend or counsellor he is [12].
Sirach stresses an important element in all matters, especially in choosing the friend and counsellor, and that is prayer to God, the searcher of hearts, who knows the depths of every person.
Every counsellor extols his counsel, and some give counsel for their own benefit [7].

Ben Sira directs our gaze to the one who claims wisdom and experience in managing affairs and in guiding the one who consults him to the sound choice.
