Yet he is selfish and pretends concern and love, while what occupies him in the decision he advises to the one who consults him is that it should be beneficial to himself, whether materially, psychologically or socially, without caring for the losses that the one who sought his counsel will reap.
Guard yourself against the counsellor, and know beforehand his interest.
For he will think of himself, lest he cast the lot against you [8].

Before a person chooses his friend, he must observe and study what his interests are, whether he has a heart wide with love for those with whom he deals, lest the person be surprised one day that he is advising him to his own harm.
Casting the lot here is meant as harboring evil so that the harm falls upon the friend.
And he says to you: "Your way is good," then stands aside to see what will befall you [9].

Do not make one who is suspicious of you your counsellor, and at the same time it is fitting that you hide your secrets from the one who envies you. By this he has warned us in general against those who are marked by the following: those who care for their own good and are indifferent to the interest of others, those who gloat over others' misfortune, those whom a person suspects, and those who envy him for what he has.
Now he presents to us certain groups that must be avoided when choosing a counsellor:
Do not consult a man who looks at you with suspicion, and hide your counsel from those who envy you [10].

Do not consult a woman about her rival, nor a coward about the battle, nor a merchant about exchange, nor a buyer about selling, nor a slanderer about gratitude, nor an unmerciful man about generosity, nor an idle man about any work, nor a seasonal hireling about finishing his work.
Nor a slothful servant about a great work, so do not listen to these in any counsel [11].
Here wisdom warns us against choosing the counsellor from one of the preceding groups.
A. Do not consult the wife about her rival [11], for her opinion of her is known beforehand; she will not sympathize with her, but heaps accusations and faults upon her.
B. A soldier in a battle must not consult one who is known to be a coward [11], for he weakens hearts and discourages resolve, since he has no ability to face the enemy.

C. One must not seek the counsel of a greedy merchant when he wants to barter with another [11], nor must a seller seek the counsel of the one who buys from him [11]. For what concerns them both is that the deal should go to themselves, so both are biased, and neither will be impartial in his advice.

D. One must not consult a slanderer whom he does not trust with his secret. For such a counsellor himself is not faithful with the secrets of others. This is what happened with wicked Haman when King Ahasuerus consulted him about Mordecai, and how he should reward him for the good he had done him; Haman bore a grudge against Mordecai, but his evil turned back upon his own head.

E. A person must not consult someone about a matter that he is unable to carry out: he must not ask giving of one who is a counsellor without mercy, nor ask the slothful about any work he wishes to complete, nor ask one who seeks a wage for seasonal work about finishing his work.
Instead of this, persevere with the godly man, whom you know to keep the commandments, whose soul agrees with your soul, and who, if you fall, shares your sufferings [12].

After Ben Sira has given advice about avoiding choosing as friends those unfit to give good and fitting counsel, he gives positive advice in choosing the friend. First, that he himself be godly, keeping the divine commandment, and that he choose a friend who agrees with him in godliness and the keeping of the commandments. Second, that he be loving and self-giving, sharing his sufferings. So his counsellor must not be one of those who love frivolity without seriousness, and he must not be a drunkard.
v It is impossible for you to become good or wise in a moment; rather you need study, care, exercise, training and long striving (and above all) a strong desire for the good.
The good man who loves God and who truly knows God never ceases to do, without exception, all the things that please God. But it is rare that we meet such people[3].

St. Anthony the Great v Let us keep away, keep far away from joking, for it is the beginning of the use of abuse; through it dangerous quarrels and growing enmities break out. In our opinion arrogance accompanies drunkenness. A man is condemned not only for his deeds but also for his words. The Scripture says: "Reprove not thy neighbour at the wine, ... and speak not unto him words of reproach" [31]. Surely we were strongly counselled to keep company with the godly man [12]; therefore he who makes sport of a holy man commits a sin[4].
St. Clement of Alexandria And hold fast to the counsel of your heart, for there is none more faithful to you than it [13].

Ben Sira wishes to direct his disciples to their depths, so that their hearts may be sanctified in the Lord and be more faithful to them than friends and counsellors. It is dangerous to think that humility and seeking counsel mean that a person should behave in a spirit of weakness and lack of confidence in himself. For God created man to be a leader in the Lord.

When the Lord Christ became a boy of twelve years, He affirmed His leading role by saying to St. Mary: "Wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" (Lk 2:49). He spent three days in the temple and was sitting in the midst of the doctors, hearing them and asking them questions, and all who heard Him were astonished at His understanding and answers. This conduct is counted a revolution in the world of boys, so we do not belittle them, but respect their mission, their personalities, their potentials and their role.
For a man's soul sometimes tells him more than seven watchmen sitting high on a watchtower [14].

Solomon the Wise stands in amazement before the wisdom of the Creator, which is manifested in raising man up as a leader to rule over the world. For he says: "And ordained man through thy wisdom, that he should have dominion over the creatures which thou hast made, and order the world according to equity and righteousness, and execute judgment with an upright heart" (Wis 9:2-3). Before we seek the support of any man, whatever his abilities, wisdom and love, we must trust in what God has given us of grace and ability to cling to Him, and ask for His leading of us, but not in arrogance and haughtiness, rather in humility and living faith.
And in all cases pray to the Most High, that He may direct your way in truth [15].
If God calls us to have fathers as leaders and wise counsellors, then let God be first in all our decisions.

The Apostle Paul presents himself as an example not only for bishops and priests, but for every true believer, for he says: "We are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised" (1 Cor 4:10). The Apostle finds his delight in being counted a fool for the sake of Christ the Lover of mankind, and counts those he serves as wise in Christ.

20 A word is the beginning of every work, and counsel goes before every action. 21 The countenance shows the changing of the heart. Four things proceed from the heart: good and evil, life and death, and that which rules over these at all times is the tongue. 22 There is one among men who is shrewd, a teacher of many, but he profits his own soul nothing. 23 And there is one who claims wisdom, and his speech is hated. Such a one shall be deprived of all food, 24 for he has not been given favour from the Lord, since he has no share of wisdom. 25 And there is one whose wisdom is for himself, and the fruits of his understanding are good in the mouth. 26 The wise man teaches his people, and the fruits of his understanding are good. 27 The wise man is filled with blessing, and all who see him count him happy. 28 The life of a man is numbered days, but the days of Israel have no number. 29 The wise man inherits the confidence of his people, and his name lives forever. 30 My son, test your soul in your life, and see what harms it, and keep it from that. 31 For not everything is profitable for everyone, nor is every soul pleased with everything.
A word is the beginning of every work, and counsel goes before every action [16].

The word meant here is not that which is spoken by the tongue, but that which the mind and heart adopt. Thinking precedes the work, and the expression of it decides the fate of man, the life of man or his death. "By thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned" (Mt 12:37). So man's life and death are in his speech. "Death and life are in the power of the tongue" (Prov 18:21). And counsel also must precede the work.

v O brother, the Holy Scripture says: "Do all things with counsel" [Prov 24:72 (a) according to the text], and "Without counsel do nothing" (b). When you acted without counsel, but by your own will, you were not striving with your mind. For there is none who has no need of counsel except God alone, who created wisdom; but when you sought to cut off your own will according to God and to reach humility, and to take me, your very little brother, as a guide, you aroused the envy of Satan, the enemy of good, who envies all men continually[5].

v If you are dead to the flesh, how can the natural passions be alive in you? But if you have not yet reached spiritual perfection but are still carnal, and if you are still a little child in the Spirit, then lay yourself down (that is, humble yourself) in the Spirit and submit yourself to a teacher so that he may discipline you with mercy. "Do nothing without counsel" (see Sir 32:19), even if things seem good to you, for the light of the demons becomes darkness in the end. If you hear or think or see anything that leaves even a little disturbance in your heart, know that it is from the demons[6].
St. Barsanuphius Four kinds of things appear as a sign of the changing of the heart [17].
Good and evil; life and death.
And the tongue is the one that rules over these at all times [18].
It befits the mind to take its fateful decision from four choices: good, evil, life and death.
There is a clever man who is a teacher of many, but he does not profit his own soul [19].
There are among men those who are clever, able to teach by word, but their lives nullify what they say.
v For a man's words to be convincing, the life of the speaker has a great effect, more than any loftiness of eloquence, no matter how eloquent[7].
St. Augustine v A good example gives a sweeter and more pleasant voice than the sounds of music and all instruments of entertainment, for people do not weigh what we say as much as what we do.
St. John Chrysostom The man who invents crafty words will be hated; this man will go away hungry [20].

St. Augustine translates it: "He who speaks sophistically is hated," and comments on it, saying: [In any case, the person may not be a deceiver, but he is concerned with adorning speech literally, in a sort of exaggeration and not in earnest, so that his speech is counted sophistical[8].]

v A man ought to be purified before he purifies others, and become wise so that he may make them wise, and a light to shine upon them, and draw near to God to draw them to God, and be sanctified for the sake of their sanctification, and have someone to lead him so that he may himself lead them with wisdom.
St. Gregory of Nazianzus Grace has not been given to him from the Lord, for he is deprived of all wisdom [21].
If we do not care to enjoy God's wisdom, we shall not experience His grace in our lives.
And there is a man who is wise to himself, and the fruits of his understanding are trustworthy when he speaks [22].
It is good that a person's life be a practical lesson, but there is a need for the word by which he expresses his life.
The wise man teaches his people, and the fruits of his understanding are trustworthy [23].
It befits the wise man to teach, for his life proves what he proclaims, so that people trust him.
The wise man is full of blessing, and all who see him count him blessed [24].
What people perceive in the life of the wise man is not only his wise conduct and godliness but also the blessing of the Lord tangibly present in him.
The life of man is counted in days, but the days of Israel have no number [25].
The wise man inherits confidence in the midst of his people, and his name lives forever [26].
My son, test your soul while you live, and see what harms it, and do not give in to it [27].
For not everything is profitable to everyone, nor does every soul enjoy everything [28].

Father Gregory (the Great) said: [The venerable Gregory of Nazianzus has already taught us that the shepherd does not give one piece of advice to all. For one counsel is not suitable for all, since not all have the same character. The advice that benefits some may harm others. Like the pastures on which some animals feed while they are not fit for others. And the gentle whistle that calms the horse may excite the puppy. And the medicine that heals one person increases the diseases of another. And the food that nourishes the strong man destroys the little child.]

entries.section: 4. Self-control and the sin of gluttony

paragraphs.text: 32 Do not be greedy for every pleasure, and do not pour yourself out upon foods. 33 For excess of eating makes the eater sick, and greediness reaches to colic. 34 Many have perished through greediness, but he who is content increases in life.
Truly all believers are called to avoid evil, so how much more does it befit us to choose the friend or counsellor who does not lack self-control, even in food.
Do not be greedy for every delicious food, and do not give yourself over to foods [29].

v Those who are free are not free according to their position, but those who are truly free in their life and character. For example, we may not call the famous and the rich free when they are wicked and fierce, for such are slaves of bodily passions. The freedom and blessedness of the soul are the fruit of true purity and contempt for temporal things[9].
St. Anthony the Great v We must control the belly and keep it under the direction of heaven. For God in the end will destroy all that belongs to the belly, as the Apostle says[10].

St. Clement of Alexandria v How do you see the posture of four-footed creatures? Their head is bent toward the earth, and they look to their belly, searching for the things that please them. But you, O man, your head is raised toward heaven, and your eyes look to the heights. So if you are defiled with the lusts of the flesh, and serve the pleasures of the belly and the lower pleasures, you by this [draw near to the beasts that have no reason, and become like them] (see Ps 49:12).

I set before you the care of another matter that befits you: "Seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth" (see Col 3:1). Rise above the accidents of the passing world, and learn from your bodily make-up, and make it the rule of your life: your city is heaven; your true homeland is the Jerusalem above, and your fellow citizens are the firstborn, whose names are written in the heavens[11].

St. Basil the Great v When the belly becomes the mistress of the body, she commands it and subjects it to her will, and instead of the way that leads to heaven she shows it the other way that brings it down to the abyss...

The passion of love of the belly is the worst of the passions. And the man who becomes subject to it, once he has borne its heavy yoke on his shoulders, does not accept to take a truce during his service to it. For this passion works in him day and night. It sends him wherever it wishes like a wretched servant, not on easy and smooth roads, but on roads full of stumbling stones, and into places where there are heavy losses. For the friend of the passions has no eyes with which to see the light...

The body is heavy by nature, but gluttony adds to it another weight... The animal, when it has filled its belly, leaves the rest of the food and does not store it... But man does not do that, because his desire is not filled when his belly is filled.

Eating out of lust is one thing, and eating out of need is another. He who eats out of fullness eats for the sake of the soul and not for the sake of the body. He nourishes his body so that it may be at every time ready to serve the soul....

It befits the disciple of Christ to flee from this foolish passion and not become a slave to his belly... The Apostle Paul said of the belly: "Whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame" (Phil 3:19)... The man who bows beneath that wicked passion cannot bear the yoke of discipleship to Christ[12].
St. Mar Philoxenus For excess of eating brings sickness, and gluttony leads to illness[13] [30].
Many have died of gluttony, but the man who is careful prolongs his life [31].
Gluttony is not only a sin that harms the soul, but it represents a danger even to the health of his body.
Inspired by Sirach 37

entries.section: Choose for me friends and a counsellor, O searcher of hearts!

paragraphs.text: v Grant me friends and a counsellor in whom I see You manifested.
You are the searcher of hearts, and You know who they are that support me in the salvation of my soul.
I am no better than my brethren; I need one who will support me in You!
Grant my weakness to be a godly friend by Your grace.
Let Your grace work in me and in them, that together we may share in fellowship with You.
v Let Your Holy Spirit work in me, that I may touch Your Kingdom within me.
Grant me confidence and hope in the sanctification of my thoughts and my words, that I may walk in the truth under Your care.
Count me, together with my friends and counsellors, an instrument of righteousness for the sake of Your Kingdom.

May You lead my mind and my heart and also my belly, so that the passions of the flesh may not destroy me, nor my stomach enslave me, but that I may enjoy the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

1 Honour a physician with the honour due unto him for the uses which ye may have of him: for the Lord hath created him. 2 For of the most High cometh healing, and he shall receive honour of the king. 3 The skill of the physician shall lift up his head: and in the sight of great men he shall be in admiration. 4 The Lord hath created medicines out of the earth; and he that is wise will not abhor them. 5 Was not the water made sweet with wood, that the virtue thereof might be known? 6 And he hath given men skill, that he might be honoured in his marvellous works. 7 With such doth he heal [men], and taketh away their pains. Of such doth the apothecary make a confection; and of his works there is no end. 8 And from him is peace over all the earth. 9 My son, in thy sickness be not negligent: but pray unto the Lord, and he will make thee whole. 10 Leave off from sin, and order thine hands aright, and cleanse thy heart from all wickedness. 11 Give a sweet savour, and a memorial of fine flour; and make a fat offering, as not being. 12 Then give place to the physician, for the Lord hath created him: let him not go from thee, for thou hast need of him. 13 There is a time when in their hands there is good success. 14 For they shall also pray unto the Lord, that he would prosper that which they give for ease and remedy to prolong life. 15 He that sinneth before his Maker, let him fall into the hand of the physician.

The subject of medicine is bound up with wisdom, for the physician is committed to studying medicine and drugs, and wisdom is granted to him from God to practise his work; therefore the physician is still called among the common people "the wise man" (hakim). Among the Rabbis, and those who were later known as the Hasidim, that is, the pious, it prevailed that resorting to the physician is a weakness of faith in God, relying on what is recorded in (2 Chr 16:12) that King Asa sought the physicians and not the Lord. These physicians often used magic and divination, and did not turn to God while using the art of medicine. Ben Sira was sympathetic to progress in the field of medicine and drugs, so he spoke of the importance of the physician and his esteem for medicine.

St. Basil the Great, together with his friend St. Gregory of Nazianzus, realized their mission while they were students at the University of Athens, forming a group among the students that had its esteem and respect even among the philosophers, the university professors. This drove him to make prominent that he saw medicine as a gift and endowment from God like all other gifts and arts, so that it is not permissible to resist or ignore it, but to care for the study of this art or craft with esteem and respect for it.

As for the physician, God created him to work according to his gift and study, yet the true healer is God. The physician offers the blessing of health as a gift from God, and this calls us to honor the physician. And medicine is one of the divine gifts offered to men, like the sun and the rain, which are given to sinners as to the righteous, as the Lord Christ said.
v Question: Is resorting to the art of medicine consistent with the practice of godliness?

Answer: Every art is a gift of God, to remedy the defect in nature. An example of this is the art of agriculture, to remedy the produce of the earth when the produce is not sufficient to satisfy our needs. And the art of weaving, to make the clothing necessary for modesty and for protection from the winds. In the same way the art of building. The same is true of the art of medicine; since our body is exposed to various kinds of harm, some attacking from outside, and some from inside because of the food we take, and since the body suffers because of excess of eating or lack of it, the art of medicine was given by God to guide our whole life, as an example of the healing of the soul, leading us to remove what is excessive and to add what is lacking...

When we were commanded to return to the dust from which we were taken, and we came to have a body ridden by pain, whose destiny became destruction because of sin, and for the same reason it was also subjected to sickness, we have the art of medicine to help the sick at least to some extent[1].
St. Basil the Great Give to the physician the honor that is fitting for him, and also according to your need of him, for the Lord created him [1].

By the incarnation of the Word the Creator confirmed His honoring of the body, and in His ministry He healed many so that no one might think that He rejects the body, but rather seeks its wholeness, as He grants it eternal glory together with the soul. And by His saying: "They that are whole need not a physician, but they that are sick: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance" (Mk 12:17), He did not disdain to call Himself a physician. St. Justin sees in the Lord Christ's saying an open door for the body, which some heresies attacked as being a sinner unworthy of resurrection with the soul, for he said: [If the flesh is the sinner, the Savior came for the sake of sinners, for He says: "I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." By this He shows the flesh its value in the eyes of God, and that it is glorified... and it must be saved[2].]
For healing comes from the Most High, and from the king (the physician) receives gifts [2].

God gives the physician understanding and wisdom, and it is He who offers us healing through the physician. If the king honors the successful physician and gives him gifts, it befits the king as well as the physician to thank God, the giver of healing.

v O brother, some people resort to physicians, and others do not go to them. Those who resort to them do so with their hope in God, saying: "In the name of the Lord we entrust ourselves to the physicians, for He grants healing through them." And those who do not resort to them do not do so, and they have hope in the name of God, and He heals them. So if you resort to physicians you do not commit a fault, and those who do not resort to them are not proud[3].
v A person must remember that without God not even the physician can do anything. Rather it is God who grants healing to the sick when He wills it[4].
St. Barsanuphius The skill of the physician lifts up his head, and he is admired in the presence of great men [3].

In speaking of the success of his ministry and the ministry of Apollos in Corinth, the Apostle Paul says: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase" (1 Cor 3:6). So it is with physicians: they provide the medicine, and God is the one who heals. St. Augustine says: [What is the use if we plant or water if God does not give the increase? For neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth, but God that giveth the increase[5].] By the same logic we say: [What is the use if the physician treats the patient if God does not heal?]
The Lord created medicines out of the earth, and the wise man will not despise them [4].

St. Macarius the Great sees in the making of medicines God's wonderful care for man. For if diseases came upon man because of his neglect of the heavenly and his preoccupation with earthly things, God gave the earth so that it might provide medicines from the herbs that grow from the earth.

v God gave the earth and its drugs for the healing of the body, issuing a command that the body that is of dust be treated with things taken from the dust (herbs)... After man fell from Paradise he came at once under the influence of the sicknesses and disturbances of the body... Therefore God gave the world medicine for its relief, for the healing and care of the body, and permitted those who cannot entrust themselves wholly into the hands of God to use it[6].

St. Macarius the Great v Sometimes God sees that it is better to heal us secretly without visible means [such as resorting to a physician and using a medicine] when He sees that this means is useful for our souls. At other times He wants us to use medicines for the treatment of our illnesses, either so as to imprint on our souls the remembrance of His grace which we receive through our slow healing, or, as I said, to offer us an example to imitate concerning care for the soul. For just as in the case of the body it is necessary to get rid of the elements foreign to it and to add to it what is lacking, so in the case of the soul it befits us to get rid of what is foreign to it, and to accept what is in harmony with its nature. For God made man upright (Eccl 7:29) and created us for good works that we should walk in them (Eph 10:2).
St. Basil the Great Was not the water made sweet with wood[7], that the virtue thereof might be known? [5]

Here he refers to what is recorded in (Ex 15:24), when the people felt thirst and murmured against Moses, for they found bitter water that could not quench their thirst. Moses the prophet cast the tree into the bitter waters and they became sweet. Thus the power of God was known through the tree that was cast into the bitter spring, so that its waters became sweet.

Many of the Fathers see in the tree a type of the Cross that works in the waters of Baptism, so that our life is changed from bitterness to sweetness, and instead of bearing the works of the old man we enjoy the new nature that has become ours in Christ Jesus[8]. St. Ambrose says: [Marah was a spring of intense bitterness, but when Moses cast the tree into it, it became sweet water. For water without the preaching of the Lord's Cross is of no benefit for the coming salvation. But after it has been consecrated by the mystery of the saving Cross it becomes fit for use in the spiritual font and the cup of salvation; for just as Moses the prophet cast the wood into that spring, so too the priest pronounces over the baptismal font the testimony of the Lord's Cross, and the water becomes sweet because of the work of grace[9].]
And it is He (the Lord) who gave men skill, that He might be glorified in His wonders [6].
What is the wonder in His giving men skill? He honors man, giving him reason and understanding and the ability to work, while God Himself is the giver of healing through the work of the physician.
With medicines He heals, and takes away pains, and of them the pharmacist makes mixtures [7].

Ben Sira is careful to affirm the need for human work to be in harmony with divine work and sanctified by it, and for our will to be joined to the divine will and sanctified. The physician has his role in obtaining healing and his skill is a gift from God, the medicine is extracted from herbs and plants, and the pharmacist prepares and mixes it.
And the works of God have no end, and through Him health comes upon the face of the earth [8].
My son, when you are sick do not be negligent, but pray to the Lord, and He will heal you [9].

With the affirmation of God's work and our dependence on Him, it is fitting that we not neglect our bodily health, but ask God for healing. Moreover, our being struck by any illness gives us first the opportunity to review our spiritual accounts, confessing our sins, giving thanks to God, and praying so as to enjoy the work of God in us.
v Sickness of the body restrains sin, and luxury kindles the fire of the sin of the flesh[10].

v When we suffer the blows of trials from the hand of God, who directs our life with goodness and wisdom, we must first ask Him to grant us to understand the reason for our being afflicted with these blows, and second ask Him for our deliverance from our sufferings or that He give us patience to bear them to the end, for God gives us with the temptation the way out to bear it (1 Cor 13:10).
St. Basil the Great Leave off your iniquities, and make your hands upright, and cleanse your heart from all sin [10].
The believer seizes every opportunity, among them sickness, for a new start in the spiritual life and for the enjoyment of purity of heart.

v We must also give proof of the reform of ourselves by bringing forth fruits worthy of repentance (Lk 8:3), remembering the words of the Lord: "Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee" (Jn 14:5).
St. Basil the Great Offer a sacrifice of sweet savour, and a memorial of fine flour, and pour oil upon your offering, as though you were to die soon [11].
The offering of the sacrifice of love, thanksgiving and praise does not leave our hearts even in the moments of death, for it is a preparation for our departure from this world.

v When we receive healing from God... we must receive this with thanksgiving. Let us behold God's care watching over us without distinction, whether the healing takes place through an unseen source or through a material thing (medicine), and let us accept the latter healing as a gift from the hand of God.

v Lazarus, in spite of suffering painful sores, never murmured against the rich man, nor asked him for anything, and therefore found rest in the bosom of Abraham, as one who humbly accepted the trials of life (including his sickness)[11].
St. Basil the Great Keep in touch with your physician, for the Lord created him, and do not let him leave you, for you need him [12].
There is a time when success is in their hands [13].
For they too pray to the Lord that their work may succeed in bringing relief and healing, for the preservation of your life [14].

Our faith in God, the Physician of our souls and our bodies, does not call us to neglect our health or not to resort to medicine and drugs. Moreover, it befits the physician to turn to God that He may give him wisdom and blessing in his work.
He who sins before his Maker may fall into the hands of a physician [15].
The Lord permits bodily sickness so that we may care for the sicknesses of the spirit, which we so often disregard.

v When we are granted the blessing of healing, whether by means of wine mixed with oil, as in the case of the man who fell among thieves (Lk 10:34), or by means of a fig, as in the case of Hezekiah, we receive it with thanksgiving. Besides that, we look to God's care watching over us without partiality, whether it is accomplished through an unseen source or a material agency; for in the latter a more vivid awareness is truly born in us of the kindness that comes from the hands of God.

Often the sicknesses that befall us come for our benefit, and our submission to painful treatment is part of the ordering of our life. Therefore sound prudence dictates to us not to protest against amputation or cauterizing, or against bearing the bitterness of an unwelcome medicine, or abstaining from food, or following a diet, and being committed to abstaining from harmful things. We must also keep to our goal, namely our spiritual benefit, as the care of the soul teaches us by analogy (with the care of the body)[12].
St. Basil the Great

entries.section: 2. Mourning for the dead for a time

paragraphs.text: 16 My son, shed tears over the dead, and begin lamentation as befits one who has suffered a great calamity, and shroud his body as is right, and do not neglect his burial. 17 Let your weeping be bitter, and burn in wailing. 18 Hold the mourning according to his rank, a day or two, to avoid slander, then be comforted for your grief. 19 For grief brings death, and heaviness of heart bends strength. 20 In solitude grief grows strong, and the life of the wretched is according to his heart. 21 Do not give your heart over to grief, but drive it away, remembering the last things. 22 Do not forget, for there is no return from there, and you do not profit him, but you harm yourself. 23 Remember that what was decreed for him is decreed for you. Yesterday for me and today for you. 24 When the dead is at rest, rest from remembering him, and be comforted for him when his spirit departs. 1. The Jews surpassed many peoples in their treatment of the dead, such as the Romans and the Etruscons. In Italy, when the Romans gained control over the Etruscons, the latter burned the bodies of their dead and the Romans burned them until they became ashes. In the Bible, in both its Testaments, we hear only of the burial of the dead, and the believers held to the resurrection of the bodies as it came in (2 Kgs 7). The New Testament affirmed this (Heb 11:35; Acts 2:32, 36; 13:31-32; 24:13-15). With the spread of the faith in Hellenistic/Roman culture, the culture adopted the idea of burial instead of the burning of corpses. In Rome there were the burial places in underground catacombs before the building of churches. 2. The Law allowed the burning of the bodies of the dead in two cases: the one who dies under a curse, as in the case of Achan the son of Carmi and his family, who were burned after being stoned (Josh 25:7); and the guilty one who is caught in the sin of adultery (Lev 20:14; 21:9). 3. In general, the Jews were careful to wash their dead as quickly as possible, then to bury them in a ceremony marked by simplicity after a prayer or the hymns of the Kaddish was recited, which is an Aramaic word meaning holy. There are at present four basic kinds of Kaddish. And when the Kaddish is recited as a prayer of mourning for the souls of the dead, the son of the dead man does the recitation, and if there is no son, a mature male of the family, or any volunteer Jew. The chanting of the Kaddish continues for eleven months and one day from the date of death. The reason for the length of this period is the Jews' belief that the punishment of the wicked in Gehenna lasts a whole year, and so the recitation of the Kaddish must stop before the completion of the year so that it may not appear that the deceased was among the guilty; the Kaddish is also recited on the anniversary. 4. Because of the climate, burial usually took place immediately after death, and because they did not embalm the dead like the Egyptians, nor burn them like the Romans. They used embalming for Jacob and Joseph, who died in Egypt, and they were placed in coffins. 5. Jewish cemeteries are called "the house of the living" or "the house of eternity." They regarded the place where a Jew is buried as holy. Perhaps this excessive concern for the body of the dead explains Israel's concern to recover the bodies of the slain. 6. Professional mourning women: the family and friends carry out the lamenting and weeping for the dead, led in this by a professional "mourning woman," so that their clamor and wailing rise resounding and echoing (Eccl 12:5; Amos 5:16). 7. Excessive grief: sometimes excessive grief leads some extremists to inflict wounds on their bodies. The Law forbade the people of Israel from such an act (Lev 19:28; 21:5; 2 Sam 1:11-12; Lam 1:16). 8. The body that is not buried in the earth is considered a shame for the family and brings a curse on the land, so even the bodies of criminals must be buried (Deut 21:22-23). 9. The Jews visit the graves on feast days to offer prayers before the tombs of the dead so that they may intercede for them with God.
My son, shed tears over the dead, and begin to lament as befits one upon whom a grave calamity has come.
Shroud his body with honor as is due to him, and take care of his burial [16].

entries.section: 2. Mourning for the dead for a time

paragraphs.text: When Lazarus died it was said: "Jesus wept" (Jn 11:35). Ben Sira did not ignore the feelings of separation, but he encouraged a quick return to normal life, because the dead man does not benefit from the tears of those who grieve over him. And excessive grief is harmful to body and soul [19-23].

v The Lord wept for Lazarus, whom He was about to raise to life, doubtless in order to allow us by His example to weep for our dead, even though He did not give us His commandment to that effect, this with our faith that they rise to the true life. It was not at random that it was said: "Shed tears over the dead, and begin to lament as one who has suffered great harm," but he goes on a little later to say: "and be comforted for thy heaviness, for of heaviness cometh death, and the heaviness of the heart breaketh strength"[13].
St. Augustine v In order that the Savior Himself might show that He has real human feelings, He grieved for the one whom He was about to raise from the dead[14].
St. Jerome Weep bitterly, and lament with warmth, and hold the mourning according to his rank a day or two, to avoid slander, then be comforted for your sorrow [17].

Bitter weeping here means weeping with sincere feelings, and not for outward show for the sake of those taking part in the funeral service. This sincerity is better than lamentation, for many lament the dead man and praise him not from the heart.

Ben Sira did not forbid mourning for the dead, but within the limit of two days to bring out sincere feelings. After that the person declares his practical consolation by returning to his work and his obligations, taking warning from death as a passage into Paradise.
v Guard against surrounding yourself with the tyrant of grief. You can control yourself, for the storm is not greater than your skill.
v Never be depressed, for there is only one thing to be feared, and that is sin.

v Do not look at the body lying with closed eyes and silent lips, but at the man who has risen and is enjoying the unspeakable and wonderful glory; direct your thoughts from the present sight to the coming hope[15].

v Have you been deprived of meeting him, so that you weep and grieve? Now is this not something unreasonable? If you gave your daughter in marriage and her husband took her to a far country where she enjoys wealth there, you do not count this a catastrophe, but their riches console you for the grief caused by her absence. And now here it is not a man but the Lord Himself who takes your relative, so do you grieve and lament?[16]

v You may grieve and weep, but do not let despair come upon you, and do not be absorbed in complaints. Thank God who took your friend, so that you may find an opportunity to honor the departed, and his separation from you becomes a mourning. If you fall into a state of dejection, you withhold honor from the departed, and grieve God who took him, and harm yourself. But if you are thankful you honor the departed and glorify God and you yourself benefit. Weep as your Lord wept for Lazarus, observing the proper limits of grief, which you must not transgress. So also Paul says: "I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope" (1 Thess 4:13). He says: "Do not grieve like the Greeks, who have no hope of the resurrection, who despair of the life to come[17].
St. John Chrysostom For of heaviness cometh death, and the heaviness of the heart breaketh your strength [18].

There are two kinds of grief: holy grief, which is mingled with a spirit of hope, like Peter's grief after his fall; and extreme grief without hope, like the grief of Judas, which drove him to suicide. Excess of grief brings dejection, despair and weariness, takes away a man's vitality and breaks his heart, and he is counted dead.
v Excessive grief is a dreadful thing that begets death. Therefore Paul says: "lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow" (2 Cor 2:7)[18].

v Satan can destroy even under the appearance of godliness. For he is able to destroy not only by leading a person to fornication but sometimes, on the contrary, by excessive grief that makes despair follow repentance. To snare us by sin is his proper work, but to snare us in our repentance is a refined disgrace, for he fights us with our weapon and not with his own[19].
St. John Chrysostom Also, in affliction sorrow remaineth, and the life of the poor is the heaviness of his heart [19].

entries.section: 2. Mourning for the dead for a time

paragraphs.text: Do not give your heart over to grief, but drive it away, remembering the end of life [20].

v For your sake, O man, He prepared the Kingdom! And for your sake He prepared unspeakable good things, and a portion made ready in heaven, and a life without parallel, and a joy that cannot be uttered!

entries.section: 2. Mourning for the dead for a time

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom Do not forget that there is no return (from there), and you will not profit the dead by grief, but only hurt yourself [21].

St. John Chrysostom presents to us a view of faith that challenges death, through which, instead of excessive grief over the dead, we count him blessed because he has departed to enjoy what surpasses nature.

v In his preaching (the Apostle Paul) grew in honor by accepting insults and persecutions, looking at death as we look at life, accepting poverty as we accept wealth, enjoying labors as we seek rest, preferring affliction to pleasure, and praying for his enemies more than those who pray against them. So he overturned the order of things, or rather let us say that it is we who changed those systems. For he simply kept the laws of God, because what he sought agrees with human nature, while what we seek is against nature[20].
St. John Chrysostom Remember my end, for your end will be like it:

entries.section: 2. Mourning for the dead for a time

paragraphs.text: "Yesterday for me, and today for you" [22].
v Look at me, my companions who accompany me and bury me, and let not the temporal dwelling lead you astray as it led me astray.
Flee from the world, flee from wealth and from iniquity; come and see how the way out of the road has been crossed.
Look at me, my friends, how I ran, and how I became rich, and here I go out stripped of my possessions.
You accompanied me, so remember your own selves because of me; the road is common, so make smooth, make smooth your paths.
The dead man says these things to all his relatives by his silence, and the sight of him is of benefit to the discerning.
Whoever does not profit from teaching by words, let him look at nature (and see) what his end is, and repent.
If the hearer denies the written Law, lifeless nature casts terror upon those who look.
The end of the dead man becomes a good cause for the living, that each one may remember himself and return to repentance.
Behold teaching without discourses or words; blessed is he who by his death despised the world lest he covet[21].

entries.section: 2. Mourning for the dead for a time

paragraphs.text: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh When the dead man is at rest, let his remembrance rest, and be comforted for him when his spirit departs [23].
The talk of the rest of the dead man comes from Ben Sira's faith in life after death.

25 The scribe acquires wisdom in the time of leisure, and he who has little business obtains it. 26 How shall he get wisdom who holds the plough, and glories in the goad, and drives the oxen, and is occupied in their works, and whose talk is of the young of bulls? 27 His heart is on the furrows of the plough, and his watching is in fattening the heifers. 28 So also every craftsman and engineer who spends the night as the day, and those who engrave the signets of seals, who strive in varying the shapes, whose hearts are set on representing the image like its original, and whose watching is in completing their craft. 29 So also the smith sitting by the anvil, bent over forging a massive piece of iron; the blaze of the fire hardens his flesh, and he struggles with the heat of the furnace. 30 The sound of the hammer is continually in his ears, and his eyes are on the pattern of the thing made. 31 His heart is set on completing the works, and his watching is in adorning them to perfection. 32 And so the potter sitting at his work, turning his wheel with his feet; he is ever anxious about his work, and counts all his products. 33 With his arm he kneads the clay, and before his feet he bends its strength. 34 His heart is set on perfecting the glaze, and his watching is in cleaning the furnace. 35 All these rely on their hands, and each of them is wise in his craft. 36 Without them a city is not built. 37 They do not dwell in cities, nor walk about, nor enter the assembly, 38 nor sit on the judge's seat, nor understand the arts of lawsuits, nor expound judgment and justice, nor utter proverbs. 39 But they keep the things of the age in order, and their prayer is for the work of their craft, unlike the one who gives himself to meditation on the law of the Most High.

With the role of leaders, among them the scribes, in the progress of society, Ben Sira honors the craftsmen and those with manual skills, because society depends on them for progress and prosperity. He speaks of craftsmen and those who work in animal husbandry [25-26], carpenters and sculptors [27], metalworkers [28] and potters [29-30]. These provide the materials that the leaders and scribes use. Ben Sira did not belittle any work in society.

If the Jews exempt the Rabbis from some works and crafts, it is not out of contempt for these works, but so that they may devote themselves to pastoral care, service and worship. But often every Jew, whatever his position, learns a manual trade that he practises when necessary. This is clear in the life of Saul of Tarsus the Pharisee, and also Aquila and Priscilla; they were all tentmakers (1 Cor 9:4-11). And in the monastic system manual work is obligatory for all, even if they are heads of monasteries or do intellectual work such as teaching.
The wisdom of the scribe depends on his opportunity for solitude, and when he has little work he becomes wise [24].
v "I sleep, but my heart waketh." I rest from being occupied with activities, but my mind directs all its energies toward the inclination of clinging to God[22].

St. Augustine How shall he become wise who holds the plough? For he glories in the shaft of the goad, and drives the ox, and is occupied with the laborers, and his talk is of the young of animals [25]
The goad is the rod with which we prick some animals; the shepherd uses it in leading sheep and animals.
His heart is turned to the furrows of the plough, and his watching is in fattening the calves [26].

It is good that the farmer be faithful in his work, but he can enjoy wisdom, which is the adornment of life and without which life is not possible. His work confines him to a narrow material circle without enjoying contemplation of God's work with him.

So it is with every craftsman and master workman who works night as day, and those who engrave the signets of seals, who are diligent in varying the shapes; these set their hearts to reproducing a living image, and watch to finish their craft [27].

Society needs those who have gifts in various arts, and it is good that the worker be diligent. However, if these arts are offered by people who walk in the Spirit, they leave beautiful spiritual impressions on many who behold them.
The makers of icons used to fast while painting the icon, and took care of their prayers and worship, so that the icon might have its spiritual fruit.
And so the smith sitting by the anvil examines closely what he is forging:
The flame of the fire melts his flesh, as much as he suffers from the heat of the furnace, he inclines his ear to the sound of the hammer, and his eyes are fixed on the pattern of the vessel.
He sets his heart to finish his works, and watches that he may complete their details [28].

The smith who suffers from the blaze of the fire and the smoke and the sound of the successive blows on the anvil bears that for the sake of finishing his work. With his faithfulness in work he needs rest and contemplation, which grant him a better life and greater skill in his work.

The integration of society is not achieved without craftsmen and their availability, yet setting aside time for study and knowledge to acquire wisdom is necessary in life, for even the trades need wisdom, which God gives to the craftsman, so that his craft comes forth in a form that glorifies God.
So also the potter sitting by his work and turning the wheel with his feet, who is always careful about the quality of his work, and also the quantity of his output [29].
With his arm he kneads the clay, and with his feet he moves the wheel to curve it. He sets his heart to complete its polishing or glazing, and cleans the furnace with precision and care [30].

It befits the potter (or the earthenware maker), who spends his time at his wheel absorbed in making the vessels required of him, then decorating them and painting them and arranging them in the furnace so that they become vessels of various beautiful shapes with wonderful designs, and after that spends the rest of his time cleaning the oven and preparing it for the new batch. It befits the potter, as he prepares the clay to put it on the wheel to shape it, to remember God, the Greatest Potter. And as Origen says of Him:

[As long as the earthenware is raw clay it can be reshaped, but once it enters the fire it becomes hard, and if it is broken it cannot be mended. What does this mean? We understand this in a general way first, then, if the Lord permits, we understand it in detail.

As long as we are in this life, we are counted as vessels of raw earthenware, either made of vice or of virtue. In any case our vices can be broken so as to become new virtues, just as our progress in virtue is liable to reversal and to falling back. But when we pass the present time and reach the other life, we pass through the fire, whether the fire of the flaming darts of the evil one or the divine fire, since our God is a consuming fire, and whether we are wicked or good, after our breaking (our death) it will not be possible to reshape us and we shall not be capable of being mended. So as long as we are in this life we are as in the hand of the potter: if the vessel falls from his hands he can treat it and mend it. Let us repent of our sins that we have done in the body, and let us return to God with all our hearts now, that He may grant us deliverance and salvation while we have an opportunity for repentance, for after our departure from the world we shall not be able to confess our sins and offer repentance for them[23].]
All these trusted in their hands, and each of them is expert in his craft [31].
Without them the city is not fit to live in, nor will anyone travel to it or live in it [32].
Yet they are not sought in the council of the people, and in the assembly they have no distinction.
On the judge's seat they do not sit, and the ordinances of the law they do not understand [33].

They cannot give instruction in discipline and judgment, and among those who utter proverbs they are not found; but they keep the fabric of the world firm, and their prayer is in the work of their craft [34].
Ben Sira looks at the man who is faithful in his work as one who practises prayer, because he bears the mark of faithfulness that befits the godly believer.
Inspired by Sirach 38

entries.section: I glorify You, O Physician of my soul and my body!

paragraphs.text: v I bless You, O Holy One, for You care for my body as for my spirit!
By sin the beauty of my soul vanished, and sickness crept into my body!
You did not forsake us; You gave skill and understanding to the sons of men.
You offered healing to my body through medicine and physicians.
v You brought forth medicines from the earth that You created, and gave skill to man to extract the medicine!
You allow me sickness that I may reassess my life, so that I may seek Your righteousness to qualify me to receive a share in Your eternal glories.
v By Your resurrection You raised my soul from the death of sin, and prepared for me a place in Your bosom, and granted my body to share with the spirit its glory!
In Your love You did not place our hope on earth but in heaven!
So if one of mine dies I weep for a time, as You shared the weeping of Mary and Martha for Lazarus, Your beloved!
I will not give in to grief lest it destroy my soul.
Rather, with the Apostle I will sing: O death, where is thy sting?!
I see in the one who has fallen asleep that he has found rest.
And I congratulate him on his passing and await with joy my own passing.
v O Your wonderful love for all the sons of men.
By Your wise ordering You gave men various talents, so that no one may seek to live isolated from his brethren, and no one may be afflicted with smallness of soul because of his trade.
All can hear at Your final coming:
You were faithful over a few things, I will make you ruler over many things.
We shall see great men who were saved as by fire, and from all trades and positions we shall find those who became as the angels of God!
The heavenly ones rejoice over all the believers in heaven.
They welcome us and glorify the Creator for His salvation of the sons of men!
When shall I see all become the Queen-Bride sitting at Your right hand, O King of kings?!

entries.section: 1. The leader who loves the Law

paragraphs.text: 1 For he searches out the wisdom of all the ancients, and devotes himself to prophecies. 2 He keeps the discourses of renowned men, and enters into the subtleties of parables. 3 He searches out the hidden meanings of proverbs, and is conversant with the dark sayings of parables.

It befits the leader to realize his mission, so that he finds sweetness in his striving and in his continual progress in study and knowledge, especially of the Holy Scripture. This is what Bishop Ambrose presented to us when he said that the bishop must learn all the days of his life. There is only One who teaches and has no need to learn, and that is God.
And in contrast to that, he who gives himself to the study of the law of the Most High, seeking out the wisdom of all the ancients and occupying himself with their prophecies [1].

The leader counts himself an extension of the life of the ancients, so he does not stop learning from those who preceded him in the study of the Holy Scripture and in becoming acquainted with the prophecies of the prophets. Ben Sira reveals the law of the Most High and its distinction from human philosophies, bringing out that the law of the Most High, though presented as a personal dialogue between God and man, yet God, the Lover of mankind, wants His believers, whether leaders or people, to be an image of Him, bearing a heart wide, if possible, for all humanity. Therefore the believer is concerned to study the inheritance he has received from the ancients through the generations. But the philosopher is often occupied with his own selfish thought, as though he were the center of the universe.

v I desire to strive in learning so that I may be able to teach. For there is one Master (God) who alone does not learn what He teaches to all. But men must learn before they teach, and receive from God, their Teacher, what they teach others.

entries.section: 1. The leader who loves the Law

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose He keeps the discourses of renowned men, and penetrates the marvels of parables [2].
By the renowned he means the people of God who fulfilled their mission in a spirit of godliness and witness to the life of faith.

v He mentioned with the greatest precision that the names of the twelve tribes of Israel were written on the breastplate of judgment. For bearing the names of the fathers written on the breastplate makes the priest ever think of the life of the early fathers. Then the priest walks blamelessly in the footsteps of the holy fathers who preceded him, contemplating their life, keeping away from vain imaginings, lest he take an unfitting step[1].
Father Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 1. The leader who loves the Law

paragraphs.text: He searches out the hidden meanings of proverbs, and is occupied with the dark sayings of parables [3].

Ben Sira encourages his disciples, the seekers of wisdom, to travel in order to benefit from the wisdom and experience of others in the Lord. On another side he asks the believer to make his journeys through the ages, from Adam to the age in which he lives, where he studies God's dealings with the great fearers of the Lord, and examines the proverbs and the dark sayings of parables, as well as the Law and the Prophets and the books of wisdom.

entries.section: 2. The role and characteristics of the leader

paragraphs.text: 4 He serves among the great, and appears before the ruler. 5 He travels through the lands of foreign nations, for he tests good and evil among men. 6 He sets his heart to rise early to the Lord who made him, and makes supplication before the Most High, 7 and opens his mouth in prayer, and makes supplication for his sins. 8 If the great Lord will, he shall be filled with the spirit of understanding. 9 He will pour forth the words of his wisdom, and in prayer give thanks unto the Lord. 10 He shall direct his counsel and knowledge, and in His secrets shall he meditate.
He serves among the great, and appears before the rulers.
He travels through the lands of foreign nations, and tests good and evil among men [4].

Whoever considers what is stated in this text [4-11] feels that the writer is presenting a portrayal of the life of St. Paul. Wisdom requires making journeys among cities [4], and among ages [3], and among the books of the Holy Scripture.
Kings and great men were drawn to the wise for the management of the affairs of the state or their private affairs or the upbringing of their children.

Their enjoyment of this fame does not lead them merely to hold fast to their personal experience, but they thirst to become acquainted with the experiences of others, even among foreign nations; therefore they are lovers of journeys.

entries.section: 2. The role and characteristics of the leader

paragraphs.text: He sets his heart to rise early before the Lord his Maker, and makes supplication before the Most High, and opens his mouth in prayer, and makes supplication for his sins [5].

This work, from the geographical, historical and scriptural side, requires of the one who desires wisdom to rise early, and stand in solitude with the Lord his Maker, and make supplication to Him and pray and ask forgiveness of his sins [5], so that he becomes qualified for understanding, knowledge and sound management.

The spiritual leader, more than any other person, needs the life of stillness and quiet contemplation, away from the atmosphere of service and teaching, for his own benefit and the benefit of those he serves, lest in the midst of the sweeping currents of service and the continual, relentless busyness he deviate a little. Then his service turns into routine or duty or into a merely formal service, or a service remote from the Spirit that has no spiritual effectiveness.

v Those who have been entrusted with works of goodness and the care of souls are obliged to bear to people a witness of the other life (the life of contemplation); therefore they must devote themselves to study and to contemplation of the truth and of eternal life.

And just as it is not fair that the life of contemplation should be a cause of hindering a capable person from carrying out the duties of the Church, so also it is not just that a person who is capable of the faithfulness of managing the affairs of the Church, because he is longing and burning for the life of contemplation and the inspiration of wisdom, should withdraw from the field of work and cast himself into the void of endless contemplation.

entries.section: 2. The role and characteristics of the leader

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine If the great Lord will, he is filled with the spirit of understanding, and pours forth the words of his wisdom (the Lord's), and in prayer gives thanks to the Lord [6].
As he receives wisdom as a divine gift he gives thanks to the Lord, for no gift is without increase except that which is without thanksgiving.

entries.section: 2. The role and characteristics of the leader

paragraphs.text: He directs his counsel and knowledge aright, and meditates on (the Lord's) secret things [7].
This study and this gift offered to him from above require walking uprightly, and delighting in contemplating the secret things of God, which are full of love and wonder.

v The eloquent define the orator as "a good man able to speak," for he must be without blemish in his conduct as in his lips (his oratory) so as to be worthy of praise, because the teacher whose words are not supported by his deeds loses all influence on his hearers.
St. Jerome

entries.section: 3. Teaching by the law of the Most High

paragraphs.text: 11 He shows forth the instruction of his teaching, and glories in the law of the covenant of the Lord. 12 Many shall commend his wisdom, and it shall never be blotted out. 13 His memorial shall not depart, and his name shall live from generation to generation. 14 The nations shall speak of his wisdom, and the congregation shall tell forth his praise. 15 If he remain, he shall leave a name greater than a thousand, and if he go to his rest, it benefits himself.
He proclaims the teaching when he teaches, and glories in the law of the covenant of the Lord [8].

John the Baptist was asked: "Who art thou?" And we would have thought he would say: "I am the one to whom Gabriel, who stands before the throne of God, came to announce to my father my birth," or "I am the angel who prepares the way before the awaited Messiah." But he said: "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, Make straight the way of the Lord..." This is my mission as a shepherd: to proclaim the voice of the Lord aloud, and to reveal the law of the Lord to my children, and to teach my brethren how to live! This is what distinguishes the shepherd, that he is able to teach others the way of the Lord.
Many commend his understanding, and it is never blotted out; his memorial shall not depart, and his name lives through all generations [9].
It befits the seeker of wisdom to realize that what God gives is not for him alone, but that many may enjoy with him the wisdom of God.
The nations proclaim his wisdom, and the congregation tells forth his praise [10].
If he lives long, he leaves a name greater than a thousand, and if he enters into his rest, his work is counted complete [11].

Successful ministry shows its fruit most after the repose of the leader, like the early patriarchs and the prophets and the saints in the Old and New Testaments and throughout history also. If his life is long, God permits him to be greatly honored in his life, and many benefit by his virtue. And if he enters into his rest, that is, rests in Paradise, the perfection of his striving and pastoral care is declared, and his memory also endures through the generations.

entries.section: 4. The fragrant aroma of the Law

paragraphs.text: 16 I will yet declare my thoughts, for I am filled as the full moon. 17 Hearken unto me, ye holy children, and bud forth as a rose growing by the brook of the field, 18 and give ye a sweet savour as frankincense, 19 and flourish as a lily. Send forth a smell, and sing a song of praise. Bless the Lord in all his works, I have much to say, I will describe it in detail: for I am full as the full moon [12].
Ben Sira is in a state of illumination like the shining full moon, which no man can hide.
Hearken to me, you holy children, and grow like a rose planted by a stream of water [13].

It befits the one who learns wisdom not to limit his thought to the bounds of his people, but to seek that the nations proclaim the wisdom of God. For the seekers of wisdom are like roses planted by streams of water, who do not hold back the sweet aroma of Christ that is in them [13-14], and like incense that goes forth into the air, which all inhale. St. Clement of Alexandria spoke of God's care for man, how He created for him even the different kinds of flowers for his benefit.

v These flowers and herbs were created for our needs, not for us to abuse them in luxury. We leave room for a simple kind of indulgence, but it is enough that we enjoy their fragrance; we have no need to adorn ourselves with them. God the Father deals with man with great care, placing in our hands all the work of His hands for this one purpose, and as the Scripture says: "The principal things for the whole use of man's life are water, and fire, and iron, and salt, flour of wheat, and honey, and the blood of the grape, and oil, and clothing. All these things are for good to the holy."
St. Clement of Alexandria v By reading the divine writings the soul acquires great wealth if it receives them with love.
They are set like a spring for the thirst of the world, and everyone who is thirsty drinks life from them daily.
The divine books are blessed streams; all you who are thirsty, come, go and drink the water of life.

The rivers are for the drinking of bodies and animals, and behold the readings of the divine writings are for the drinking of souls; O distinguished one, give the body water to drink, and give the soul the Book to read and delight in.
It is thirsty for the spring that is in the books; it puts its mouth and drinks life from them every day.
The soul is tormented by the company of the evil world, and it is filled with senses and unlovely desires...
But if it opens the Book and reads with great love, it is enlightened at once and sees the beauty that cannot be comprehended.
And the light enters from the reading into the mind like a ray from the disk into the hollow of the eye.
And the wind of the Book blows from between the lines, and lifts the smoke of error from the mind.
The more love is joined to reading, the soul becomes pure and full of light and is not troubled.
The evil one envies and knocks (at the door) at once like a ruler, so that the Book may be made void by the disturbing thoughts of the world.
If the soul's love is joined to reading, it will despise and reject all activities for its sake.
And if love of the world increases, reading is made void, and endless deeds enter and the world comes to an end.
O soul that wishes to live well with God, bind your love to the reading of the divine writings.
And silence the troubled banquets of the world, and make them void, and remove them from your mind.
And listen to the Book, which cauterizes the wound, and heals the sickness, and cares for the soul and bandages it and restores it by healing[2].
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh Send forth your fragrance like incense, and flourish like the lily.
And spread abroad your fragrance, and sing a song of praise, and bless the Lord for all His works [14].

The lifting up of incense during worship points to God's pleasure in the offering of prayer, and it is an ancient tradition whose beginning is not known, and extends so that we see it in heaven practised by the bodiless priests. David the prophet wrote: "Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense" (Ps 141:2). And Malachi prophesied that the Gentiles would use it in worship: "For from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same my name shall be great among the Gentiles; and in every place incense shall be offered unto my name, and a pure offering" (Mal 1:11). One of the gifts offered to the Child Jesus by the Magi was incense.

v It befits us to seek "incense" (see Sir 39:14), but not any kind of incense, but that pure kind. The high priest does not wish to take anything dark and base, but asks what is pure. He also asks for galbanum (a resinous gum), which by nature drives away harmful snakes by the strength of its smell. And he asks for "myrrh," for he wants our words and deeds to be holy and pure. He also asks for onyx or the Yemeni agate (onycha) (Ex 30:34), which covers some animals as a kind of shield to protect them so that no harm touches them[3].
Origen

entries.section: 5. The Law of the Most High and praise

paragraphs.text: 20 And magnify his name, and give thanks unto him with praise, with the songs of your lips and with harps, and in praising him you shall say thus in confession. 21 All the works of the Lord are exceeding good, and all his commandments are accomplished in their time, and all of them are sought in their season. 22 At his word the water stood as an heap, and the receptacles of waters at the word of his mouth. 23 At his commandment is all his good pleasure, and none can hinder when he will save. 24 The works of all flesh are before him, and nothing can be hid from his eyes. 25 He seeth from everlasting to everlasting, and there is nothing wonderful before him. 26 A man cannot say: "What is this?" or "Wherefore is that?" for all things are created for their uses. 27 His blessing overflowed like a river, learning wisdom is not separated from the practice of praise [15-35]. It is not a subject of dry theoretical debate but a subject of fellowship with the heavenly ones in their praises. The man of God praises Him for His wonderful works in creation, and is not troubled by the calamities that come, but they drive him to cling to the fear of the Lord and his rejection of evil.
Magnify His name, and give thanks to Him with praise, with the songs of your lips and with harps, and say thus in thanksgiving: [15]

v The confession of sins is the ordinary confession known to you. There is no need for me to speak of the reasons for its use. Therefore it befits us to look at confession in the praise of God and the proofs of it.

People are accustomed to the call to "confession" of sins, and every time they hear the reader say the words: "Confess," they beat their breasts, with a murmur accompanied by an uproar within their consciences, as they remember what they must do.

This often happens, yet it is not always meant as confession of sins. Sometimes a person speaks of confession in praise, as in that passage in the Holy Scripture where it says: "Confess to the Lord, and say thus: The works of the Lord are all exceeding good"... It is clear that this is a confession of praise to the Lord and not of your offenses... Certainly the Lord Jesus did not commit sin, yet it is said in the Gospel: "I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth," and He completed the speech with praise: "because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes. Even so, Father: for so it seemed good in thy sight" (Mt 11:25-26). This is the confession of one who praises God, not of one who accuses himself[4].
St. Augustine All things are the works of the Lord and they are exceeding good, and all His commandments are accomplished in their times.
No one can say: "What is this? And why is that?"
For every question will be answered in its appointed time [16].
All the works of the Lord are exceeding good, but sin has corrupted man's sight so that he sees what is good as bad.

v It befits us to bless the Creator of all things before we partake of food, and so also at celebrations when we enjoy His gifts that He created. It is fitting to sing psalms directed to Him. In truth, to sing a psalm in harmony is a blessing; it is a work of self-control. The Apostle calls the psalm a spiritual praise (Col 3:6; Eph 5:9). Again, it is a holy duty to give thanks to God for His kindnesses and the love He shows us, before we sleep. The Scripture says: "Give thanks to Him with praise, with the songs of the lips, for His commandments that bring forth all kindness, and there is no lack in His salvation"[5].

St. Clement of Alexandria v God is good, without passions, and does not change. Man accepts this saying as a true fact that God does not change, but he is perplexed, asking how God rejoices in the righteous and leaves the wicked, and is angry with sinners and shows them mercy if they repent?! And the answer to this is that God neither rejoices nor is angry, for joy and anger are passions, and it is absurd to think that the Godhead can be benefited or harmed by human behavior. God is good, and does nothing but good. He harms no one and remains as He is always. But as for us, when we are good we enter into fellowship with God by becoming like Him. And when we become wicked we deprive ourselves of God by not being like Him.

When we live a virtuous life we belong to God, and when we become wicked we abandon Him. This does not mean that He is angry with us, but with our sins, which hide His face from us and bind us to the troublers, who are the demons.

But (at repentance), by prayers and doing good (with faith in Him) we obtain the removal of sins. This does not mean that we appease Him and change Him, but by these works of ours and our return to Him we are healed (by His grace) of the evil that is in ourselves, and become able to be partakers with God in His goodness. So also with the saying "God leaves the wicked": we are like one who says that the sun hides itself from those who have lost their sight[6].
St. Anthony the Great At His word the water stood as an heap.
And at the word of His mouth were the receptacles of waters [17].
Here he refers to the separation of the oceans from the earth in creation (Gen 1:9-10).
At His command everything is accomplished according to His good pleasure, and no one can diminish His salvation [18].
v By the tenderness of our Creator there are many ways of salvation, those which calm spirits and lead them toward heaven[7].

St. Anthony the Great v After the first man was deceived by the serpent, and received counsel in sin, and by sin met death, and by death misery, God did not forget him. The goodness of God did not forget us, in spite of our dryness toward the tenderness of God and our violent resistance to the Maker of good things. Yet we cannot blot out His love for us, for we have risen from death, and have become alive by our Lord Jesus Christ Himself... And it was not enough for Him to call us to life anew, but He prepares us for eternal rest, which in the greatness of its joy surpasses all human thought[8].
St. Basil the Great The works of all men are before Him, and nothing can be hid from His eyes [19].
His sight extends to them from age to age, and nothing is wonderful to Him [20].

God formed man, and knows all his thoughts and works, and man must realize this well, for the eye of God follows him to the farthest place, and at all times "from everlasting to everlasting," and nothing is too hard for Him.
No one can say: "What is this? And why is that?"

entries.section: 5. The Law of the Most High and praise

paragraphs.text: For all things were created to perform their work [21].

God created everything for a purpose, so that even what we see as harmful is in reality useful. St. Jerome has an essay on the importance of insects, whose existence some object to, yet which play a role among the rest of the creatures.

entries.section: 5. The Law of the Most High and praise

paragraphs.text: His blessing overflowed like a river, covered the dry land, and watered it like a flood [22].
Perhaps in this there was a reference to the River Nile, whose flood nourished the land in the Nile basin with much fertile silt, so that the land produced a double harvest.

entries.section: 6. Between the position of those who fear the Lord and the stubborn

paragraphs.text: 28 And watered the dry land like a flood. So shall the nations inherit his wrath, 29 as he hath turned the waters into dry land. His ways are straight unto the holy; so are they stumblingblocks unto the wicked. 30 For the good are good things created from the beginning, so evil things for sinners. 31 The principal things for the whole use of man's life are water, fire, iron, and salt, flour of wheat, honey, milk, and the blood of the grape, and oil, and clothing. 32 All these things are for good to the godly; so to the sinners they are turned into evil. 33 There be spirits that are created for vengeance, which in their fury lay on sore strokes. 34 In the time of destruction they pour out their force, and appease the wrath of him that made them. 35 Fire, and hail, and famine, and death, all these were created for vengeance. 36 The teeth of wild beasts, and scorpions, serpents, and the sword, punishing the wicked to destruction. 37 They shall rejoice in his commandment, and they shall be ready upon earth, when need is; and when their time is come they shall not transgress his word. 38 Therefore from the beginning I was resolved, and I thought on these things, and have left them in writing. 39 All the works of the Lord are good, and he will give every needful thing in due season. 40 So that a man cannot say, "This is worse than that": for in time they shall all be well approved. 41 And therefore praise ye the Lord with the whole heart and mouth, and bless the name of the Lord.
As He turns sweet waters into salt, so the heathen inherit His wrath [23].
God pours out His wrath upon the stubborn, and because of stubbornness the earth is defiled, so that sweet waters are turned into salt.
Just as His ways are straight for the holy, so they are a stumblingblock for the wicked [24].
The divine commandments, which are a cause of blessing for His saints, are a cause of condemnation for the wicked.

v The texts of the Holy Scripture lead us to understand that a stumblingblock is everything that draws us away from true godliness in any form of deviation, or committing faults, or failing to observe godliness.
In general it is everything that hinders us from keeping the commandment, even if the result of that is death[9].
St. Basil the Great Just as good things were created from the beginning for the good, so evil things for sinners [25].

The divine works that the saints see as good and so praise Him are the very ones that sinners see as evil. Nothing is unclean, but "unto the pure all things are pure: but unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure; but even their mind and conscience is defiled" (Titus 1:15). So where a man is pure, that is, pure in heart, he sees everything in God's creation as pure. And St. Jerome[10] defines the pure heart as the one at which God looks.
