For by the holy God the heart is sanctified, and God's pure look at everyone and everything becomes its own.

As for how it is purified, St. Augustine says: [The truth is that all are unclean, those who have not been purified by faith in Christ, as the passage says: "purifying their hearts by faith" (Acts 15:9)[11].]
The basic needs of man's life are: water, fire, iron, salt, flour of wheat, milk, honey, the blood of the grape, olive oil and clothing [26].

He speaks of the principal elements in man's life as the Lord provided them for man; these elements may be used for evil, for the water that quenches thirst can destroy, as happens in floods. And iron is used to make instruments of battle. And salt, for preserving, if increased in the food spoils it. Wheat and milk and honey, which points to prosperity, are misused by the covetous. And the blood of the grape, that is, wine, points to gladness and joy, and the wicked get drunk with it.
All these things are good for the godly, but they turn to evil for sinners [27].
Foods differ from one country to another, and from one generation to another; the principal needs such as water, fire, salt, etc., do not change.

v For healing, medicine may make use of some flowers in order to extract from them some ointments and perfumes, and this cannot be overlooked. And if some ask: What use are these flowers to those who do not use them? Let them know that ointments are made from certain kinds of flowers and they are very useful...
All these exist so that we may benefit from them and use them[12].

St. Clement of Alexandria There are spirits that were created for vengeance, and in His (the Lord's) wrath they increase their scourges, and in the time of destruction they pour out their force, and appease the wrath of their Maker [28].
Perhaps it refers to destructive storms, while there are beneficial winds, and gentle winds may turn into destructive storms as a discipline for the wicked.

entries.section: 6. Between the position of those who fear the Lord and the stubborn

paragraphs.text: Fire, hail, famine and death, all these were created for vengeance [29].
Among the fruits of sin are suffering hunger and thirst and calamities, because it isolates man from God, the source of his true satisfaction and quenching.

v Let us return again to the same prophet (Amos) whom we heard at the beginning of the discourse: "And also I have withholden the rain from you, when there were yet three months to the harvest: and I caused it to rain upon one city, and caused it not to rain upon another city: one piece was rained upon, and the piece whereupon it rained not withered. So two or three cities wandered unto one city, to drink water; but they were not satisfied: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the Lord" (Amos 4:7-8).
We must learn, then, that because of our distance from the Lord, and our unconcern for His ways, God has caused us those wounds.

He does not seek our destruction, but rather strives to bring us back to the right way, just as good parents care for their children with firmness, rebuking them when they do something wrong, not because they seek to harm them, but rather because they wish to lead them from childish neglect and the sins of youth to the attainment of mature alertness[13].

entries.section: 6. Between the position of those who fear the Lord and the stubborn

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great The teeth of wild beasts, scorpions, serpents and the avenging sword for the destruction of the wicked [30].

Man was master of the earthly creatures, and the wild beasts were subject to Adam and Eve; but when man disobeyed God in stubbornness, these animals became terrifying to him, and man even came to kill his brethren with the sword. When the people murmured in the wilderness He let the fiery serpents bite them (Num 21:5-6), and when some children mocked Elisha the prophet He allowed two bears to kill forty-two of them, and when the king of Assyria sent pagan people to dwell in the land of Canaan after his taking the people of Israel captive, God sent lions among them to devour them (2 Kgs 17:24, 26). What are these beasts that are let loose upon us but the sins from which God keeps us as long as we are in His presence responding to His voice; for if we give Him the back and not the face He lets the beasts bereave us of our children, that is, our inner fruits, and gnaw our cattle, that is, corrupt our body?!

Origen says: [Many are the swords that pass through our land if we do not keep the law of the Lord and follow His commandments! Let each one enter into himself, and contemplate within himself, lest our land, that is our body, be stirred up by a spirit of fornication or disturbed by a spirit of anger and agitation, or by a movement of covetousness, or by the bow of lust and pleasures... This the Apostle Paul knows, for he says: "Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God" (2 Cor 10:5), so that we do not submit to this sword and those wars, but the Lord keeps our land in safety.]

entries.section: 6. Between the position of those who fear the Lord and the stubborn

paragraphs.text: They rejoice in carrying out His commandment, and make ready for His service upon earth, and when the time comes they do not transgress His word [31].
By natural instinct the wild beasts are subject to the will of God, and do not transgress His word, for God sometimes uses them for discipline.

St. Basil the Great[14] sees that it befits the believer not to fear wild and poisonous animals, etc., for God has permitted them for our discipline as well as for our benefit. The animals bear witness to faith. Have you confidence in God? "Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder (a malignant kind of serpent): the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet" (Ps 91:13). By faith you have power to tread upon serpents and scorpions. Do you not see that the viper that fastened on the hand of the Apostle Paul as he gathered sticks did not harm him (Acts 28:3), because it found the saint full of faith? If you have faith, do not fear the animals more than you fear your unbelief, which makes you liable to destruction.

entries.section: 6. Between the position of those who fear the Lord and the stubborn

paragraphs.text: Therefore from the beginning I was resolved and determined, and I left this in writing: [32]

entries.section: 6. Between the position of those who fear the Lord and the stubborn

paragraphs.text: All the works of the Lord are good, and He will supply every need in its hour [33].

v Be a herald of the goodness of God, for God rules over you in spite of your unworthiness. Although your debt to Him is very great, He is not seen demanding of you full payment; and through your very small works He gives you great rewards. Do not call God just, for His justice is not declared in the things that concern you. And if David calls Him just and upright (Ps 25:8; 145:17), His Son declares to us that He is good and compassionate[15].

St. Isaac the Syrian v His light cannot be hidden, nor can His glory remain without a witness, nor can His goodness go unenjoyed, nor can all that pertains to the divine nature remain unused for the benefit of man, that he may enjoy it and share in it. For if man came into being for this purpose, that is, to share with God in His goodness, then certainly in his creation he was given the capacity to enjoy all that is good. So the eye enjoys seeing the true light by virtue of the ray implanted in it naturally, which draws to itself what is like it by its innate power. Likewise there had to be a likeness of human nature to the divine so that through this likeness it might be joined with what is akin to it. Irrational creatures, whether those that live in water or in air, had to have an order adapted to the environment surrounding each creature, so that each might find its kind and what is akin to it, one in the air and another in the water. So too man, who came into being to enjoy the goodness of God, had to have something in his nature resembling that in which he would share. For this reason man was endowed with life and reason and wisdom and all the attributes that befit God, so that through all of these there might arise in him the desire for what is akin to him[16].

entries.section: 6. Between the position of those who fear the Lord and the stubborn

paragraphs.text: St. Gregory of Nyssa No one can say: "This is worse than that," for all things are well pleasing in their time [34].
God's providence is surpassing; all things work out for good as long as we use them fittingly and at the proper time.

entries.section: 6. Between the position of those who fear the Lord and the stubborn

paragraphs.text: So now sing with all your heart and voice, and bless the name of the Lord [35].
Ben Sira speaks here of God's plan of salvation as the supreme work of God, which He accomplished by the incarnation of the Word of God and by offering Himself as a sacrifice for humanity.
Inspired by Sirach 39

entries.section: Your Law makes my heart rejoice!

paragraphs.text: v Grant me to be faithful in devoting my life to Your Law.
That I may draw from the experiences of the patriarchs, prophets and apostles, enjoy the experiences of the saints and understand their wisdom.
I rise early to You with every morning, I confess my sins and ask for Your wisdom.
I seek Your work even among strangers, O Lover of all nations!

v I glory in Your covenant, and desire the salvation of all humanity. I am careful of every moment to enjoy Your wisdom, so my soul will find rest when it departs from the body! Your wisdom turns my life into a full moon in its light!
Your wisdom is a spring of living water that waters the roses planted within me.
v Your Law turns my life into a spiritual harp.
Your Holy Spirit plays upon it the song of wisdom and the melody of love!
You reveal to me the mystery of Your care for humanity.
All things work for the edification of Your beloved children, and for the one who resists the truth, things are turned to his discipline.
Those who oppose You suffer from it as a harsh discipline.
While Your children count it as surpassing gifts, You are wonderful in Your care and Your plan and Your divine ordering!

entries.section: 1. The fall of man and the heavy yoke of sufferings

paragraphs.text: 1 Great travail is created for every man, and an heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam, from the day that they go out of their mothers' womb till the day that they are buried in the earth, the mother of all. 2 For they have disturbance of thoughts, and fear of heart, and anxious expectation, and the day of ending. 3 From him that sitteth on the throne in glory, unto him that is humbled in dust and ashes. 4 From him that weareth purple and a crown, unto him that is wrapped in coarse linen. And add to that wrath, and envy, and unquietness, and trouble, and fear of death, and malice, and strife. 5 And in the time of rest upon the bed, the sleep of the night, which troubleth a man's mind. 6 So he hath little rest, as nothing, and afterward in dreams, as in the day of watching. 7 He trembleth at the vision of his heart, as one that fleeth from the face of the battle, and when he escapeth he awaketh and marvelleth that his fear is gone. 8 Such is the lot of all flesh, from man to beast, and sevenfold more for sinners. 9 Death, and blood, and strife, and sword, calamities, and famine, and crushing, and the scourge; 10 all these things were created for the wicked, and for their sakes came the flood. 11 All that is of the earth turneth to the earth again, and all that is of the waters returneth to the sea.

Ben Sira presents a lament over what has befallen man in general because of his fall. What was said to Adam: "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread" (Gen 3:19) has been inherited by all his offspring, so that people feel weariness, even those who are not physically exhausted. Life in the world has become marked by pain, and it ends with the death of the body. During the day man is exposed to the following troubles:

entries.section: 1. The fall of man and the heavy yoke of sufferings

paragraphs.text: a. Confusion about the unknown future and the expectation of death [2].

entries.section: 1. The fall of man and the heavy yoke of sufferings

paragraphs.text: b. Everyone suffers from anger, envy, unrest, anxiety, fear of death, rebellion, and strife [4].

entries.section: 1. The fall of man and the heavy yoke of sufferings

paragraphs.text: c. Even on the bed, for the sake of rest, a man thinks about what befell him in the daytime, and sees it in a form different from what he was thinking [5].

entries.section: 1. The fall of man and the heavy yoke of sufferings

paragraphs.text: d. Disturbing dreams weary him [6].

entries.section: 1. The fall of man and the heavy yoke of sufferings

paragraphs.text: e. When he wakes he expects hard things, but he does not find them real [7].

Hard labors were created for every man, and a heavy yoke was laid upon the sons of Adam, from the day they came out of their mothers' womb until the day of their return to the mother of all men (the dust) [1].

Since human life has become harsh, Ben Sira called it a heavy yoke laid upon the sons of Adam. The book comes to point to the coming of the Messiah, the Savior, who carried the yoke of our sins on the cross, offering to His believers His yoke, saying: "My yoke is easy" (Mt 11:28-30), and some translate it: "My yoke is sweet," since He offers us the sweetness of salvation by the cross.

Ben Sira looked at the believers, the children of the new Adam, and saw them moving on toward the mother of all men, as the Apostle Paul says: "But Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all" (Gal 4:26). For the Lord Jesus freed us from the yoke of bondage, and granted us the freedom of the glory of the children of God".

Man brought upon himself the yoke of sin, so he lost the soundness of his soul and the ability to cleave to the Holy One. He deprived himself of the spiritual bread, the garment of faith was taken off him, and he suffered the wounds of bodily lusts. Man's life was turned into a journey of misery and weariness. "Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble" (Job 14:1). This outlook changed after the coming of the Word of God, for we enjoyed divine grace and sonship to God in the waters of Baptism, and our life became a delightful journey in the company of God. Before the fall there was no conflict between the desires of the spirit and the desires of the flesh; rather, the body and the spirit were in harmony in the love of God and obedience to Him.

v "I am a stranger in the earth" (Ps 119:19). I know that "the life of man upon earth is a trial" (Job 7:1), and that "a heavy yoke is laid upon the sons of Adam" [1]. But we say that we are sojourners or strangers on the earth, since we find our city above. Here we receive the pledge, and when we arrive there we shall not depart from it [1].

St. Augustine v Of this wrath (which came upon us by the disobedience of Adam) it is said: "We were by nature the children of wrath, even as others" (Eph 2:3). Of this wrath Jeremiah says: "Cursed be the day wherein I was born" (Jer 20:14). And of this wrath the righteous Job says: "Man that is born of a woman is of few days and full of toil. He cometh forth as a flower and is destroyed, and doth not continue in the same state. Upon such a one hast thou set the pupil of thine eye, and me hast thou brought into judgment with thee. Who shall bring a clean thing out of the unclean? No one, even if his life be but one day upon the earth" (Job 14:1-15) LXX.

Of this wrath the Book of Sirach also says: "All flesh waxeth old as a garment: for the covenant from the beginning is, Thou shalt die the death" (see Sir 14:17), and also: "Of the woman came the beginning of sin, and through her we all die" (see Sir 35:24). And also: "Great troubles are created for every man, and an heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam, from the day that they go out of their mothers' womb till the day of their burial in the mother of all" (see Sir 40:1). Of this wrath the Preacher says: "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity. What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun?" (Eccl 1:2-3) [2].

v Now the forgiveness of sins relates chiefly to the judgment to come. For in this life what is written is still being fulfilled: "An heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam, from the day that they go out of their mothers' womb till the day of their burial in the mother of all" [1]. So we see even little children, after they have been washed in the font of the new birth, suffering many evils, and thus we understand that the effect of the sacraments of salvation is suited rather to the hope of the good things of the age to come than to the keeping and possessing of the present goods.

Likewise many sins seem now to be overlooked and to pass without punishment, because the punishment for them is reserved for the life to come; so it is not in vain that that day is called the day of judgment, when the Judge of the living and the dead shall come... The Apostle says: "For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged. But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world" (1 Cor 11:31-32) [3].

v In truth, nothing prevents the fulfillment of the prophecy: "An heavy yoke..." (see Sir 40:1). For even the children who have been set free by the font of regeneration from the bond of sin that held them, that is, original sin, suffer many troubles, and sometimes some of them even suffer the attack of evil spirits. What a joy, that even this attack (God forbid) will not be able to harm them, even if the attack reaches the point of death [4].
St. Augustine The awareness of the things to come and of the day of death confuses their thoughts and terrifies their hearts [2].

v Death, for those who understand it, is immortality, but for the foolish who do not understand it, it is death. We must not fear this death, but fear the destruction of the soul, which is the ignorance of God. This truly terrifies the soul!

v It is impossible for us to escape death by any means. And since the wise truly know this, they practice the virtues and think upon the love of God, and they face death without sighs or fear or tears, thinking that death is on the one hand inevitable, and on the other that it frees us from the sicknesses to which we are subject in this life.
St. Anthony the Great From him that sitteth on the glorious throne to the humble one upon the dust and ashes [3].
From him that weareth purple and the crown to him that is wrapped in sackcloth. There is wrath, envy, unrest, anxiety, fear of death, rebellion, and strife [4].

v Some of those who frequent inns get beds, while others find no beds, so they stretch out on the ground and sleep in perfect peace, just like those who sleep on beds. And in the morning, when the night passes, all rise and leave the inn, each carrying his baggage. So also those who walk in this life: all will leave this life as those who leave an inn, whether they were living a humble life or had wealth and fame. For all of them do not carry with them the earthly pleasures and riches, but take with them what they did in this life, whether good or evil [5].
St. Anthony the Great Even in the time of man's rest upon his bed, the sleep of the night changes his knowledge [5].

v No one can escape its power, neither slave nor free. All human things perish by death: riches as well as honor. The inequality in this present life is enormous. Great is the freedom after our departure.
v Death makes everything void. Not only is there no longer any possibility of supporting evil, but not even the mere sound of evil reaches the ears.

St. John Chrysostom He obtains little or nothing of rest, and afterward he sleeps, and behold, he labors in the visions of his heart as in the day of watching, and is troubled by the visions of his heart like one fleeing from the face of the battle [6].
And at a certain time he needs to wake up and marvel, since he finds nothing that frightens him [7].

entries.section: 1. The fall of man and the heavy yoke of sufferings

paragraphs.text: This is the lot of all flesh, from man to beast, and for sinners there is sevenfold more: [8]

entries.section: 1. The fall of man and the heavy yoke of sufferings

paragraphs.text: Death, bloodshed, strife, sword, calamities, famine, destruction, and plagues [9].

v Death is an exceedingly terrifying thing, but not for those who have learned the true wisdom that is from above. For he who knows nothing of the things to come, but counts death as dissolution and the end of life, rightly trembles and fears, as one passing into non-existence.

But he who learns, by the grace of God, the hidden, secret things of the wisdom (of God), and counts it a departure to another place, finds no reason for trembling, but rather rejoices and is glad, since by leaving this perishable life we go to a better, more glorious life without end. This is what Christ teaches us by His actions, going to His sufferings not reluctantly or by necessity, but by His own will; therefore it is said: "When Jesus had spoken these words, he went forth with his disciples over the brook Cedron, where was a garden, into the which he entered, and his disciples" [6].

entries.section: 1. The fall of man and the heavy yoke of sufferings

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom All these things were created for the wicked, and for their sakes came the flood [10].
St. John Chrysostom sees that, when the wicked man dies, his sins lead his soul to be the secret of its continual rebuke.

entries.section: 1. The fall of man and the heavy yoke of sufferings

paragraphs.text: All that is of the earth returns to the earth, and what is of the waters returns to the sea [11].

v Perhaps you will say: The dead man experiences corruption, and becomes dust and ashes. And what then, beloved hearers? For in this too we rejoice. For when a man rebuilds an old house that is tottering, he first empties it of its inhabitants and tears it down, and then rebuilds it in greater splendor. This causes the inhabitants no grief but rather joy. For they do not think of the destruction that they see, but of the house that is to be built, which they have not yet seen. So also when God does something similar, He brings out the soul dwelling in it as from a house, in order to build a loftier house, and then brings the soul back again in greater glory. Let us not think of the tearing down, but of the loftiness that follows it.
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 2. A struggle between goodness and evil

paragraphs.text: 12 All bribery and injustice shall be blotted out, but faithfulness shall endure for ever. 13 The goods of the unjust shall be dried up like a river, and shall vanish with noise, like a great thunder in rain. 14 The unjust man rejoiceth when he openeth his hands, but transgressors shall come to nought in the end. 15 The children of the ungodly shall not bring forth many branches, neither shall the unclean roots upon the hard rock. 16 The weed growing upon every water and bank of a river shall be pulled up before all hay. 17 Grace is as a garden of blessings, and mercifulness endureth for ever.

Life presents us with a struggle between justice and injustice, and between goodness and evil. But injustice continues for a short time and ends [12]. Faithfulness, however, suffers pains for a while, but it remains forever.
All bribery and injustice pass away, but true faithfulness remains forever [12].

entries.section: 2. A struggle between goodness and evil

paragraphs.text: The wealth of the unjust dries up like a river, and ends like the noise of thunder in the storm [13].

Because of the love of money and the desire to increase wealth, man sometimes resorts to deceit, injustice, plunder, and robbery. If a man thinks that injustice is the easy and quickest way to achieve his material gains, does not his heart become corrupt? What injustice brings fades away, but what faithfulness brings, and the straight way that is used, remains to our account in eternity. It is fitting for us that our hand not reach out to bribery and injustice, for the money and possessions that come by way of evil vanish like thunder that appears and disappears in a moment. It dries up as happens with rain water, which spreads quickly and quickly evaporates.
v My hope is in God. Yes, for I do not draw near (to evil) but pass by: "Trust not in oppression" (Ps 62:10). In order that I may leap upward, I trust in God; is there then injustice with God?...

Injustice may flourish for a while, but it cannot stand. "Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery." You are not rich; do you want to rob? What do you find? And what do you lose? What lost gains! You find money, and you lose righteousness! "Become not vain in robbery"... "Blessed is that man that maketh the Lord his trust, and respecteth not the proud, nor such as turn aside to lies" (Ps 40:4). Yes, you want to deceive; you want to commit fraud, what do you bring upon yourself in exchange for deceit?... For it is neither deceit nor robbery that you desire any longer, nor do you put your trust in these things any longer.

entries.section: 2. A struggle between goodness and evil

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine The generous man rejoices when he opens his hands, but transgressors (of the commandment) shall perish [14].
These words give the believer comfort in the midst of the world's sufferings, for in the midst of evils the believer tastes the righteousness of Christ.

entries.section: 2. A struggle between goodness and evil

paragraphs.text: The offspring of the wicked shall not put forth branches, for they are unclean roots upon a hard rock [15].

The sons of the wicked who walk in the way of their fathers perish because of the evil that they inherited and did not turn away from; they resemble branches that have no root, or whose root has dried up. The children of the wicked are their works (their lack of repentance). When the wicked flourish quickly we grieve over them and weep for them, because the day of their destruction draws near and terrors await them.

The sickle of God's justice takes them by surprise, because their life has dried up, and their continuing has become a corruption to the earth. Our teacher James says: "For the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways" (Jas 1:11).

v "Fret not thyself because of evildoers, for they shall soon wither like the grass." Tell me then, what is the fate of the one who plunders and robs after his departure? Where are his glittering hopes? Where is his awesome name? Does not all this pass away and vanish from existence? Was not all that he had a dream and a phantom?

This is what you must expect in the case of such a man, whether during his life or in the life of him who comes after him. But the condition of the saints is not like this, and you cannot utter the same words about their state, nor say that what concerns them is a dream and a legend [7].

entries.section: 2. A struggle between goodness and evil

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom The harmful weed that grows upon every water or bank of a river is pulled up before all hay [16].
v He is like a gardener who uproots the unfruitful plant: "Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up" (Mt 15:13).
He planted a vine, Sorek,[8] wholly a right seed, and it was turned into bitter and strange shoots[9] (Jer 2:21).
He uprooted it in order to make of it a true vine and "God's husbandry" (1 Cor 3:9) [10].

entries.section: 2. A struggle between goodness and evil

paragraphs.text: Origen Grace is like a garden of blessings, and almsgiving endures forever [17].

Who is the generous man but the believer who opens his hands with love and mercy through the work of the Crucified One dwelling in him? He gives love generously, and his heart is turned into a delightful paradise. "Kindness is as a garden of blessings, and almsgiving endures forever [17]. And as he gives, he is enriched by Christ, the Giver of good things; his soul is satisfied, so he feels no want or need, but finds in Him the divine treasure [18]. There is no goodness that passes away, because the blessing of the Lord is upon it. God brings blessings out of evils, as happened with Joseph the son of Jacob.

18 The life of the laborer who is content is sweet, but he that findeth a treasure is above them both. 19 Children and the building of a city continue a man's name, but a blameless wife is counted above them both. 20 Wine and song rejoice the heart, but the love of wisdom is above them both. 21 The pipe and the lute make sweet the melody, but a pleasant tongue is above them both. 22 Thine eye desireth splendor and beauty, but the green of the field is above them both. 23 A friend and a companion meet in accord, but a wife with her husband is above them both. 24 Brethren and help are for the hour of trouble, but the victory of mercy is above them both. 25 Gold and silver make the foot stand sure, but counsel is esteemed above them both. 26 Riches and strength lift up the heart, but the fear of the Lord is above them both. 27 There is no want in the fear of the Lord, neither doth he that hath it need help. 28 The fear of the Lord is as a garden of blessing, and is clothed with glory above all glory. 29 My son, lead not a beggar's life; for better it is to die than to beg. 30 The man that watcheth for a stranger's table, his life is not to be counted for a life, and his soul is polluted with strange meats. 31 The prudent, well-instructed man will beware thereof. 32 Begging is sweet in the mouth of the shameless, and in his belly there burneth a fire.

True inner joy is the portion of him who fears the Lord and who is marked by a spirit of discernment in his conduct and works. These inner joys are not everything, but they have their living worth in a man's life. They are blessings that God offers to those who walk in His righteousness. Sirach highlights the superiority of these blessings over ordinary delights:
a. The life of the man who is content and who works is sweet, but the inner spiritual treasure is better [18].
b. The blessing of begetting children is precious, but a righteous wife without blame is better [19].
c. A joyful atmosphere is wonderful, but the love of wisdom is more wonderful [20].
d. Spiritual music is sweet, but the pleasant tongue is better [21].
e. The eye desires beauty, but the field of the Gospel surpasses it.
f. The friend and the companion meet, but the meeting of the wife with her husband is in the heart and never ceases.
g. Gold and silver have their role in life, but counsel is a greater treasure than they.
h. The fear of the Lord is like a paradise that keeps a man, and there is no glory that equals it [27].
i. A man may resort to begging, but death is better than it [28].
j. He who desires another's way of living loses his humanity, but the well-instructed man does not desire what belongs to his brother [29].
The life of the self-reliant man and of the worker is fragrant, but he who finds a treasure surpasses them both [18].
The splendor of life is in earnest work and self-giving, but the treasure that surpasses them is divine grace.
Begetting children and building a city establish a name, but the wife who is without blemish is counted better than both [19].

As Ben Sira points to the paradisal life through the heavenly Bridegroom, the Lord of glory Jesus, he proclaims the happy married life [19-13] as a shadow of the heavenly wedding. The wife who has no blemish is counted above the children, because she makes them good and gladdens the whole house.
Wine and music gladden the heart, but the love of wisdom surpasses them both [20].

When the believer hands the steering wheel to wisdom, he enters into a glorious life even in the midst of tribulations, and circumstances, whatever they may be, cannot spoil his inner glory or take away his true dignity. From his young age he bears the marks of the wise elders.

v It is Solomon who says that he longs to make wisdom his bride (Wis 8:2). And in another place he says of wisdom: "Love her, and she will embrace you; embrace her, and she will keep you" (see Prov 4:6, 8). Let us also take her for ourselves as a wife! Let us hold her in our arms, and not let her leave our embrace, and we will not let her flee from our arms. If this bride is always in our bosom, we shall beget children from her (that is, the fruit of the Spirit, not of the flesh) [11].
St. Jerome The pipe and the harp give sweet rhythm (music), but the pleasant tongue surpasses them both [21].
Mar Jacob of Serugh sees that God created man as a praising being, to join the chorus of the heavenly ones.
v Men were created to praise much, and perhaps they may remember the praise more every day!...
The mouth of man is fashioned as though for the praise of the Lord, and he who ceases from praising becomes ungrateful.
Therefore you have a mouth, to praise with it, and to give thanks with it, and to rejoice with it and to bless with it.
Praise, because you have the word that praises, and rejoice, because you have the voice filled with melodies.
Give thanks, because you have the mind and the discernment, and bless, because you have become a speaking vessel and not a silent one.
You were nothing, and mercies made you something great, and since you have come to be, give thanks with wonder; why are you silent?
Enter into yourself and look at your person within you, for in you are found all the wonders of the creating power [12].
Mar Jacob of Serugh The eye desires grace and beauty, but the green of the fields surpasses them both [22].

The eye desires to enjoy the beautiful nature with which God has blessed us, but the green of the fields, which is marked, along with beauty, by fruits of sweet taste, is better. Thus Ben Sira assures the believer that all that God created for us is beautiful, but we must work in the field in order to eat from the labor of our hands.
The friend and the companion meet at an appointed time, but the meeting of the wife with her husband surpasses them [23].

St. John Chrysostom sees that however close the friendship between two men may be, whether as relatives or colleagues or neighbors, it cannot be compared with the relationship of a man and his wife [13].
Brethren and helpers are for days of trouble, but almsgiving delivers better than both [24].

Almsgiving is the practice of works of love and kindness, and not merely material giving. By sin man shrinks into selfishness around himself, but by love he is released, by divine grace, from selfishness to work for the benefit and happiness of his brother. For by love we fulfill the whole Law and enjoy righteousness.
Gold and silver make the foot stand sure, but counsel is considered more valuable than both [25].

Here he urges us to love counsel and to benefit from the wisdom of others more than from gold and silver, as it is said in the Book of Proverbs: "If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures" (Prov 2:4). Is he then calling us to greed or the love of money?

v Must we think that the Holy Scriptures praise greed? It is well known what great efforts and pains the lovers of money endure with patience. How they deprive themselves of great pleasures out of desire to multiply their wealth or for fear that it may diminish. With what great violence they pursue gain, and with what great caution they avoid losses... It is fitting that we too be urged thus in the love of wisdom, so that we seek her with utmost zeal as our treasure, seeking more and more, and bearing many troubles, and abstaining from pleasures, and thinking practically about the future so that we may keep purity and the (divine) gift. When we act in this way we acquire true virtues, because our goal is sincere, and agrees with our nature regarding salvation and true happiness [14].

v It is not fitting but shameful to compare wisdom with money, yet love is compared with love. What I see here is that all of you love money above everything, so that when the love of money issues a command you spend all your effort to carry it out, and you die of hunger, and cross the sea, and expose yourselves to winds and waves... God says: "Love thus, for I do not ask you to love Me more than this. I am speaking to the common people; I am speaking to the greedy. You love money; then love Me with just such a love and no more. Of course, in comparison (with money) I am better. Love Me as you love money" [15].
St. Augustine Riches and strength build up the heart, but the fear of the Lord is better than both.
There is no loss in the fear of the Lord, and no need to look for help along with it [26].

v Those who look upon the loss of money, or children, or servants, or anything else as a calamity, these must first know the necessity of being content with what God gives, and of being ready to give these things back with composure whenever He asks them of us, without troubling ourselves with grief over losing them, or rather over giving them back, so that we may be like those who use for a time what is not their own and then return it (to its owner) [16].
St. Anthony the Great The fear of the Lord is like the paradise of blessing, and it covers a man better than any glory [27].
The fear of the Lord offers a pledge of the paradisal life, which we enjoy on earth until we pass over to paradise in the other life.

v The Church, for the faithful servants of God, who live in self-control, justice, and love for God in truth, is called a paradise (of blessing), overflowing with abundant graces and pure delights (Song 8:5). Even in tribulation such a servant is glorified in patience and is filled with great joy, because God's consolations delight his soul in spite of the many troubles he experiences in his heart [17].
St. Augustine My son, do not live the life of a beggar, for death is better than begging [28].

The talk here is directed to the beggars themselves, that they may become producers and not a burden on society. Begging is a disgrace for those able to work. By this he calls us to seek the divine Law earnestly and diligently, instead of begging from the pagan philosophers.

v The beggar begs because of his deprivation of what is necessary, and because he finds it impossible to obtain these things in an honorable way. Perhaps in such a case you find those who are said to beg for a cure from the Greeks or the barbarians who promise to offer the truth. They lose the glorious and fitting means offered by the Logos, so they obtain abundant contemplation of the truth without danger. But the Logos forbids this manner of seeking, saying: "Lead not a beggar's life, for better it is to die than to beg" [28].

The steward (the manager of affairs) mentioned in the Gospel was ashamed to beg, so he said to the one who owed a hundred measures of wheat: Take thy bill, and write fourscore... (Lk 16:6-7), preferring to reduce the amount of his master's debt rather than to beg in shame, and he was praised for that. Therefore Jesus freed the man born blind from his begging; He gave him sight and granted him the possibility of obtaining what he needed that was necessary for the salvation of his soul (Jn 9:35-38) [18].
Origen When a man looks to the table of another, his living is unreasonable, or his way of life is not counted as life.
He loses his self-respect by the food of others, but the reasonable, well-instructed man guards against that [29].

It is fitting for the believer to eat from the table of his Father, that is, from the Word of God. This table is not strange to us, for we have become members of the household of God (Eph 3:19), instead of begging from the pagans who are strangers to us.
In the mouth of the shameless begging is sweet, but in his belly a fire burns [30].

He closes the chapter with a warning against folly (shamelessness), for the shameless man begs in order to take, but does not benefit from what he takes, because his inward parts burn with fire [30]. This warning is for those who find begging easier than practicing work, especially the young men able to work.
Inspired by Sirach 40
v In my weakness I bowed my shoulder under the heavy yoke of sin.
And by Your love I fly, as by the Spirit, toward the heavens, rejoicing!
I await the meeting with You, O Giver of joy and rest!
You freed me from returning to the dust forever, and lifted me up to the fellowship of the heavenly glories.
v As a wonderful commander and a divine trainer You led me into the battle.
You drew me to Your goodness, and made sin bitter in my mouth.
I find sweet my release from selfishness, that I may practice love with joy.
You turned my whole being into a harp that praises You without slackening.
Your fear has become a paradise; I enjoy blessings and glories.
I no longer beg for the food of the world, for I sit at Your table!
What shall I render to You, O Lord, for the multitude of Your mercies and Your love?!

1 O death, how bitter is the remembrance of thee to a man that liveth at ease in peace among his possessions, 2 unto the man that hath nothing to vex him, that prospereth in all things, and is yet able to enjoy his food! 3 O death, acceptable is thy sentence unto the needy man, and him whose strength faileth, 4 that is now in old age, and is vexed with every care, that despaireth and hath lost patience! 5 Fear not the sentence of death. Remember thy former days and thy latter days; this is the sentence of the Lord over all flesh. 6 And why dost thou refuse that which is the good pleasure of the most High, whether it be ten years, or an hundred, or a thousand? 7 For in the grave there is no reckoning of life.

Ben Sira offers us a realistic picture of how people view death, before our thought was opened to the risen life that became ours through the resurrection of the Lord Christ. For the man who enjoys good health, who has authority and is well off and lives in security, looks upon death as cruel and bitter in taste, while the old man who suffers from sicknesses, frailty, and want looks upon it as a deliverance for him.

O death, how bitter is the remembrance of thee to the man who lives in peace with his possessions, to a man who is not distracted and prospers in everything, and is still strong enough to enjoy his food! [1]

When man concentrates on what befalls him, he looks upon life with a bitter eye. But when he lifts his heart to God, he sees in life a divine gift, and perceives God's plan behind the troubles that befall him, so his soul rejoices in a spirit of hope.

v Death is an exceedingly terrifying thing, but not for those who have learned the true wisdom that is from above. For he who knows nothing of the things to come, but counts death as dissolution and the end of life, rightly trembles and fears, as one passing into non-existence. But he who learns, by the grace of God, the hidden, secret things of the wisdom (of God), and counts it a departure to another place, finds no reason for trembling, but rather rejoices and is glad, since by leaving this perishable life we go to a better, more glorious life without end. This is what Christ teaches us by His actions, going to His sufferings not reluctantly or by necessity, but by His own will; therefore it is said: "When Jesus had spoken these words, he went forth with his disciples over the brook Cedron, where was a garden, into the which he entered, and his disciples" [1].

St. John Chrysostom O death, thy sentence is good for a needy man, weak in strength, who in his extreme old age (decrepitude) is distracted by everything, and becomes stubborn and lacking in patience [2].

Some look upon death as an escape from their financial, physical, psychological, and also spiritual troubles. David the psalmist cried out: "LORD, what is man, that thou takest knowledge of him! or the son of man, that thou makest account of him! Man is like to vanity: his days are as a shadow that passeth away" (Ps 144:3-4). Again he says: "What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?" (Ps 8:4).
v Death is rest, deliverance from the dreadful toils and from the cares of the world [2].
St. John Chrysostom Fear not the sentence of death, and remember those who were before thee and those who come after [3].

If a man looks at those who preceded him, he finds no man on earth who escaped death, and if he looks at those who come after him, he finds that all know perfectly well that they will not live forever on earth. The wise man looks at those who preceded him, and sees the people of God in paradise sharing the praises of the heavenly ones, and their immortal life is blessed.
v Let the death of others stir you up, so that you may have a profitable fear and cast off all slackness, and let you examine your past works, cut off your sins, and begin a happy change [3].

v Consider to whom the departed one has gone, and be comforted. He has gone to where Paul and Peter are and the company of the saints. Consider how he will rise, with what glory and what exaltation. Consider that by your grief and lamentation you cannot change what has happened, and in the end you harm yourself.
St. John Chrysostom This is the sentence which the Lord has decreed over all flesh, so how will you resist the good pleasure of the Most High?
And in the grave there is no reckoning of your life, whether you lived ten years or a hundred or a thousand [4].

If the remembrance of death was exceedingly bitter for many in the ages before the coming of Christ, the One who rose from the dead said: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live" (Jn 11:25).

8 The children of sinners are abominable children, and so are those who frequent the houses of the ungodly. 9 The inheritance of sinners' children shall perish, and reproach shall cleave to their posterity. 10 The children complain of an ungodly father, because they suffer reproach for his sake. 11 Woe unto you, ungodly men, which have forsaken the law of the most high God! 12 For if ye be born, ye are born to a curse: and when ye die, a curse is your portion. 13 All that are of the earth go to the earth: so the ungodly go from the curse to perdition. 14 Men mourn for their bodies, but the name of sinners shall be blotted out.

At the death of a man known to be wicked, the feeling of some people prevails that it is better to forget them, because remembering them is sometimes hateful. Some do not even want to think about them, for they do not deserve that anyone should remember them even in his thought for a moment, and this besides the eternal torment that the wicked meet. On the contrary, those of good reputation deserve to be remembered for a long time [12-13]. This is what moves the Church to hold yearly commemorations of the saints.

It is painful that the children of the wicked often walk in the way of their fathers, but the son who asks the Lord about the way of truth, the Lord grants him His grace, as happened with some kings such as the righteous Hezekiah, whose parents were wicked.
The children of sinners are abominable children, who often frequent the houses of the wicked [5].

Some may ask: Do all the children of the wicked walk in evil like their fathers? And what is their fault? The historical books, and history itself through the ages, answer these two questions, for the books highlighted the following:

a. Wicked kings who begot righteous sons. For example, King Hezekiah purified the land of Judah from the spread of idol worship and its abominations by the hand of his wicked father Ahaz. And Josiah, the last righteous king in Judah, did the same work to purify it from what his father Amon had done.

b. Wicked kings who begot wicked sons, such as Ahab and his wife the wicked Jezebel, who begot Ahaziah king of Israel, and he was wicked. It is often said of the wicked kings: "And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, and walked in the way of his father, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin" (1 Kgs 15:26).
c. Righteous kings who begot righteous sons, such as Asa king of Judah, who did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord and begot Jehoshaphat.
d. Righteous kings who begot wicked sons, such as David the prophet, who begot Absalom, who tried to seize the kingdom and kill his father.

These cases and the like confirm the personal responsibility of every man, so the Lord does not chastise the son for the sins of his father. "The soul that sinneth, it shall die" (Ps 18:4, 20). As for his saying here: "The children of sinners are abominable children" [5], it is like the Lord's saying: "I visit the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me" (Deut 5:9). This does not mean that He visits them because of the guilt of the fathers, but He warns the fathers of the natural consequences, since the children from their childhood absorb the spirit of evil from their fathers, and often they go further in evil. As St. John Chrysostom says, the man who walks in evil recklessly does not care what befalls him, but he is often troubled when he feels that the fruit of what he does will return upon his children and grandchildren. It is as though God is calling them to repentance and to return to Him, if not out of fear of the bitter fruit of sin upon their own lives, then let them listen to Him in order to preserve their children and grandchildren.

St. John Chrysostom says that God threatens the wicked man, whether concerning himself or his children, not in order to carry out the punishment, but that he may turn back from his evil because of fear, as happened with the people of Nineveh, for He said that the city would perish because of their evils, and by saying this He made them resort to God's mercies by repentance instead of persisting in evil.
The inheritance of the children of sinners perishes, and shame cleaves to their offspring [6].
The children blame their wicked father, because on his account they are condemned [7].
Woe unto you, wicked men, for you have forsaken the law of the Most High God! [8]
The true secret of the destruction of the wicked is their forsaking of the Law, which is for the acquiring of wisdom and the enjoyment of righteousness.
v He who refuses to receive the light of the word of God ought to fear the punishment of the eternal darkness [4].
Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles And when you were born, you were born to a curse, and when you die, the curse is your portion [9].

v This does not mean that God created them for destruction, but by their free will they made their life a curse and their death also a curse. The freedom of choice is declared to us through the Holy Scriptures not in human language but in divine. We begin with this truth, that if there were no freedom of choice, man would not use the commandments of God, and consequently would not receive the promised reward. He gives us the commandments so that no one can protest, excusing himself by his ignorance; therefore the Lord said in His Gospel of the Jews: "If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloak for their sin" (Jn 15:22).
St. Augustine All that is of the earth returns to the earth, therefore the wicked go from the curse to perdition [10].
He who chose evil, what he chose returns upon him: the curse and destruction.
Men mourn for their bodies.
But the name of sinners is blotted out because it is not good [11].

While the wicked who persist in their stubbornness mourn for their bodies, which decay by death and rise on the day of the Lord to be recompensed for what they persisted in, behold, the people of God rejoice in hope even in the moments of death.

v Do not fear because you are burdened with a mortal body; let the Spirit be yours, and you will surely rise again... Truly all shall rise, but not all shall rise to life, but some shall rise to punishment and the others to life (Jn 29:5)...

He does not punish you if He sees His Spirit shining in you, but stops the punishment... and brings you into the bridal chamber to be there with the virgins (Mt 12:25). May you then not allow your body (the carnal life) to live in this world, so that your body may live there. Let it die that it may not die! For if you keep it alive here it does not live, but if it dies it lives. This is the state of the resurrection in general. For it must first die and be buried, and then it becomes immortal. But this takes place in the baptismal font, where the crucifixion and burial are accomplished and then the resurrection.

This also is what happened in the body of the Lord, for He was crucified and buried and rose. Let this also happen to us. Then we shall have the mortification of the works of the body, I do not mean the death of man's substance, for this is far from my intention, but the death of his inclinations toward evil things, for this too is life, indeed what is this but life [5].
St. John Chrysostom

15 Have regard to thy name, for it shall continue with thee longer than a thousand great treasures of gold. 16 A good life hath but few days, but a good name endureth for ever. 17 Keep discipline in peace, my children, but wisdom that is hid, and a treasure that is buried, what profit is in them both?
Care for your name, for it endures with you more than a thousand great treasuries of gold [12].
A good life is a few numbered days, but a good name endures forever [13].

It is fitting that we bless God and thank Him, for He created us in His image and likeness. We cherish our name as human beings, for we fell but He did not leave us, but came down to us and granted us union with Him as members of His body.

v We become worthy to be called men when we are marked by reason; for if reason is not present we do not differ from the dumb animals except in the shape of the limbs and the gift of speech. Therefore let the reasonable man know that he is immortal, hating the shameful lusts which are the cause of the death of men [6].
St. Anthony the Great My children, observe the teaching, and live in peace.
But wisdom that is hid and a treasure that is unseen, what profit is in them both? [14]

The believer, by the Holy Spirit, is the voice of Christ crying out to men by every possible means that they prepare the way of the Lord and make His paths straight. This voice is the voice of self-giving love.

v A brother asked Abba Pimen: "If I see a brother about whom I have heard something evil, is it my duty not to let him into my cell? And if I see a good brother, am I to rejoice in him?" The Abba answered him: "If you do good to the good brother, do twice as much for that one, because he is sick."
St. Palladius

entries.section: 4. Things of which one must be ashamed

paragraphs.text: 18 The man that hideth his foolishness is better than the man that hideth his wisdom. 19 Be ashamed of what I say unto you. 20 For it is not good to be ashamed of everything, neither is every thing done with discretion approved by every man. 21 Be ashamed of fornication before father and mother, and of a lie before the ruler and the mighty man. 22 Before the judge and the prince of an offence, and before the congregation and the people of iniquity. 23 Before a partner and friend of unjust dealing, and before the city where thou dwellest of theft. 24 And of transgressing the truth of God and his covenant; and of leaning with the elbow upon the bread; and of deceit in taking and giving. 25 And of silence before them that salute thee; and of looking upon a harlot. 26 And of turning away thy face from thy kinsman, and of taking away a portion and a gift. 27 And of gazing upon a woman that hath an husband, and of being overbusy with his maid, and by her bed thou shalt not stand. 28 And of upbraiding speeches before friends; and of grudging after thou hast given; and of repeating what thou hast heard and revealing what was said in secret.
The man who hides his foolishness is better than the man who hides his wisdom [15].

Sirach begins with an ironic contrast between the wise man and the fool. Ordinarily we expect from the wise man what is useful and beneficial, and from the fool what is ridiculous, but the case before us is unique, for the fool who hides his foolishness is better than the wise man who hides his wisdom. The first, by hiding his foolishness, has recognized his error, and has not exposed those around him to his foolishness. The second, when the Lord gave him wisdom, hid it, so he benefited neither himself nor his brethren [15]. The fool showed his wisdom by hiding his foolishness, and the wise man did not show love by revealing his wisdom. It was not fitting for the wise man to be ashamed of the wisdom the Lord gave him.

Sirach offers us a list of the things of which it is fitting for man to be ashamed. The purpose of this list is that society may not be lax in its principles and its evaluation of things, so that we do not feel ashamed of errors or evils which society, or the holy family, or the man of God must not accept. These shameful things come to about 20 items, and they are:
First: seven items concerning faults in speech or action:
a. Not discriminating in the kind of shame [16].
b. Speaking of fornication before one's parents [17].
c. Lying in the presence of the ruler or the leader [17].
d. Violating the law in the presence of the judge [18].
e. Committing iniquity before the congregation of the people [18].

entries.section: 4. Things of which one must be ashamed

paragraphs.text: f. Practicing injustice before your friend or your life partner [19].
g. Theft before a citizen in your country [19].
Second: four items concerning rashness and impropriety:

entries.section: 4. Things of which one must be ashamed

paragraphs.text: a. Neglecting the right of God and His covenant [20].
b. Breaking the manners of the table [20].

entries.section: 4. Things of which one must be ashamed

paragraphs.text: c. Showing disgust, whether in taking or in giving [21].
d. Silence before those who greet you [21].
Third: four items concerning shameful sexual matters:

entries.section: 4. Things of which one must be ashamed

paragraphs.text: a. An evil look at an evil woman [22].
b. Disregarding the entreaty of one of one's relatives [22].

entries.section: 4. Things of which one must be ashamed

paragraphs.text: c. Taking away someone's portion or gift [23].
d. Gazing at a married woman [23].
Fourth: four items concerning the disruption of friendship:

entries.section: 4. Things of which one must be ashamed

paragraphs.text: a. He who toys with his maidservant [24].

entries.section: 4. Things of which one must be ashamed

paragraphs.text: b. Being ashamed of insulting words directed to you in the presence of friends [25].

entries.section: 4. Things of which one must be ashamed

paragraphs.text: c. Insulting a person after giving him a gift [26].
d. Repeating words and revealing secrets [26].
Be ashamed, then, of the basis of my words, for it is not good to hold on to every kind of shame; not everything is highly esteemed with confidence by everyone [16].

The offenses of which one must always be ashamed are fornication, theft, unfaithfulness, iniquity, not honoring others, gossip, not dealing in taking and giving, silence before those who greet a person, gazing at an adulterous woman, ignoring the entreaty of relatives, toying with a maidservant (a nurse), insulting a friend, insulting one who offers him a gift, or repeating words and revealing a secret [16-27].

A man feels shame when he faces things which society does not accept, whether through an inherited tradition or things that touch the moral life. It is fitting for the young man to know how to evaluate this shame.
Be ashamed before your father and mother of fornication, and before your ruler or leader of lying [17].
Parents often want their children to be pure, so they cannot bear to hear that they practice fornication; indeed, they are not at ease even to hear about fornication from their children.
And before the judge of violating the law, and before the congregation of the people of iniquity [18].

Here he points to the courts that were set up at the gates of the city, which the judge and the elders of the city discussed together and in which they questioned the accused, and also heard the witnesses until they issued the verdict. From the origin of the Jewish synagogues during the Babylonian captivity until the middle of the twentieth century, if a Jew sinned publicly, the Jewish community would summon him before the council to declare his repentance publicly. And in the early Church confession was practiced publicly concerning what the penitent had done, especially concerning public sins.
And before your partner or friend of injustice, and before the place where you dwell of theft [19].

If a man practices injustice before his life partner (husband or wife) or before a friend, the life partner or the friend loses confidence in the one who did this, which causes troubles in family life or with friends.

Likewise, he who steals in the city where he lives, the people of the city keep away from him for fear that he may steal from them, so he feels that he is alone and rejected by society, and has no place in his city.
Be ashamed before the right of God and His covenant, and of evil conduct at the table [20].

Ben Sira links the one who commits a shameful thing in the house of the Lord, where he breaks his covenant with God, with the one who breaks the accepted rules of the table. For in the house of the Lord he is bound by the covenant with God so that the Lord may fulfill His promises to him, and at the table the peoples, especially in ancient times, used to consider eating together a kind of covenant between them, and no one may betray the covenant or lie or plot a conspiracy against the one who ate with him. This concept still prevails in the villages of Egypt, where a person says to his colleague: We have eaten bread and salt together, a sign of the commitment to behave with sincere love and faithfulness.
And of disgust in taking and giving, and of silence before those who greet you [21].

In offering help or a gift to a person, or in receiving help or a gift, it is fitting in both cases, in giving as in taking, to blend the conduct with kindness. For giving without love insults the recipient of the help or gift.
When someone greets a person, it is fitting for this person not to behave like one who is resentful of this greeting, which is a sign of peace and reconciliation (Mt 5:47).
And of looking at a harlot, and of refusing the entreaty of one of one's relatives [22]

With a spirit of discernment a man conducts himself, so that when he greets someone or someone greets him, his eyes must carry personal interest along with the greeting or salutation. And when he is in the presence of a woman along with an adulteress, it is not fitting for him to gaze at her or fix his eyes on her.
And of taking away someone's portion or gift, and of gazing at another man's wife [23].
And of meddling with his maidservant, and do not approach her bed [24].

The rich used to keep slaves and maidservants in their houses to serve them, under the system of slavery. And with the vast social difference, caution is needed, as Joseph the son of Jacob did, whom his mistress, the wife of Potiphar the captain of the guard, loved, and he fled from her.
And be ashamed of insulting speech before friends; after giving, do not insult the person [25]

When one of the relatives asks for something, one must not ignore him as far as possible. He who gives alms to a needy person and has not considered the feelings of the needy, spoils this giving which is without love!
And of repeating what has been heard, and revealing secrets [26].
Ben Sira has already spoken about the revealing of a secret, for it is almost impossible for a person to regain confidence in the one who revealed his secret.

entries.section: 4. Things of which one must be ashamed

paragraphs.text: Then you will feel true humility, and obtain favor before every man [27].
Sometimes when a man feels that he has been wronged, he finds it pleasant to rob the one who wronged him, and counts this a kind of reaction.
It is not permissible for a man to rob anyone secretly even if he has been wronged, but with courtesy and wisdom he should demand his right.

Sadly we sometimes hear that a person is negligent in his work on the plea that he works according to the amount paid to him. The element of faithfulness is vital; it is not permissible to be lax in it under any pretext.
Moreover, it is not permissible for the believer to gaze at a married woman, because he desires his brother's wife.

Here he links robbing the one who wronged him with gazing at his brother's wife, because both acts are secret theft. The first steals from the one who wronged him, and the second steals from his brother his wife through his looks.

Ben Sira concludes his twenty counsels concerning the things of which one must be ashamed by offering the remedy, which is that the believer be adorned with true humility, so that the grace of God may work in him and keep him from these shameful things!
Inspired by Sirach 41

entries.section: Keep me from what is unseemly, and I will seek a speedy meeting with You

paragraphs.text: v Your divine presence turns the bitterness of death into sweetness as I pass through life in Your company!
I do not desire death in order to be delivered from the troubles of life!
But that I may pass over to You and live in Your embrace.
However long my life may be, it is like a single moment passing while I rejoice in You!
v Remove from me the roots of evil, lest the curse overtake me.
Your Law grants me wisdom, so I ask Your grace as my support.
I do not even disdain my body, for it shall rise and share in the glory of my soul.
What concerns me is the glory of Your holy name, for it is my great treasure!
I am bound to Your name, and so I enjoy my inner peace.
v Grant me the spirit of strength with discernment, that I may practice nothing of which I ought to be ashamed.
Let me honor my parents, and give honor to whom honor is due.
Let me not violate even the laws of the world, nor rob any man of his right.
I hold fast to Your covenant, so I enjoy the heavenly table.
May You sanctify my senses and my emotions and the movements of every member of my body.
I am careful to show personal interest in everyone as far as I can, and not to gaze at what it is not fitting for me to look upon.
Let my heart be a faithful treasury that does not reveal anyone's secret under any circumstance.
Grant me Your grace, that I may enjoy humility, which lifts me above all stumbling blocks, that I may soar in Your heavens!

entries.section: 1. Things of which one must not be ashamed

paragraphs.text: 1 Then shall thy shame be in its place, and thou shalt find favour before every man. But of these things be not thou ashamed, and accept no person to sin thereby: 2 of the law of the most High, and his covenant, and of judgment, that the ungodly be not justified; 3 of the reckoning of thy friend with strangers, and of dividing the inheritance among friends; 4 of exactness of balance and measure, and of gain, whether much or little; 5 and of indifferent selling among buyers, and of much correction of children, and of making the side of a wicked servant to bleed. 6 Sealing is best for a wicked wife. 7 And where many hands are, shut up; and when thou dividest, do it by number and weight; and in giving and receiving let all be in writing. 8 Be not ashamed to instruct the unwise and foolish, and the aged that contendeth with the young. Then shalt thou be truly instructed, and commended before all men living.
Do not be ashamed of the following things:
And do not let partiality lead you into sin [1].

entries.section: 1. Things of which one must not be ashamed

paragraphs.text: There are five things which must be supported and not be ashamed of, and they are: 1. Holding fast to the law of the Most High and His covenant [2], and supporting the wronged man even if he is a pagan (Sir 4:9). 2. Sharing equally in the expenses of a journey and receiving what is due to one in an inheritance [3]. 3. Trading faithfully without greed [4]. 4. Behaving with propriety in work, as with the members of the household and the workers (slaves) [5]. 5. Behaving with exactness [6-8].
Of the law of the Most High and His covenant, and of justice, lest thou justify the wicked [2].

It is no wonder that Ben Sira opens the things of which the believer must not be ashamed, and which establish justice without partiality, with the law of the Most High and His covenant [2]. Some of the Jews who were attracted to Hellenistic philosophy were embarrassed to declare their faith in God and denied circumcision (1 Macc 1:15). They became ashamed in an unseemly way, fearing that those of the pagan Hellenistic culture, which prevailed in some societies at that time, would despise the Jewish Law and the covenant with God.

Some fathers and mothers discovered what is called the "generation gap" to a degree unprecedented among the Jews. The young sons were ashamed of the Law and the covenant. This led to a real catastrophe among the Jews in Judea. This is what moved the Maccabees to revolt against this situation, as is recorded in the books of the Maccabees and in the "Antiquities" of Flavius Josephus, the Jewish historian.

The Lord Christ gave a warning against such embarrassment, when He said: "Whosoever therefore shall be ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation; of him also shall the Son of man be ashamed, when he cometh in the glory of his Father with the holy angels" (Mk 8:38). And the two statements [1, 2] agree with the teaching of the Apostle Paul: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek" (Rom 1:16). Something like this happened when the Apostle Paul preached among the Gentiles, and a dispute arose between the believers of Jewish origin and those of Gentile origin. So with all power the Apostle said: "I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ" (Rom 1:16).

entries.section: 1. Things of which one must not be ashamed

paragraphs.text: And of contributing to the expenses of the work, or of companions on a journey, and of dividing the inheritance among friends [3].

After Ben Sira directed the believers toward the law of the Most High and the believers' entry into a covenant with God, he dealt with some practical matters that prevailed at that time. If the Law urges the believers to give more than to take, what is the position of the believer if he undertakes a work that benefits him and some of his brethren: should he be ashamed to ask them to contribute to the cost of the profitable work and to the expenses of the journey that were necessary to reach a gain from which many benefit? Ben Sira affirmed that there is no need to be ashamed of those who benefit from the work contributing to its expenses. As for the lawful inheritance, the believer should not be ashamed to take his share of the inheritance, for each person receives his right, but if someone wishes to give up his right or a share of it to his friends, this is counted a higher degree.

entries.section: 1. Things of which one must not be ashamed

paragraphs.text: And of exactness in the balance and the measure, and of gain, whether much or little [4].

As for a work that a group did and which produced a profit or gain, great or small, no one should be ashamed to take his share of the profit, provided that this gain is not the result of tampering with the balance or the measure or the specifications.

entries.section: 1. Things of which one must not be ashamed

paragraphs.text: And of profit in dealing with merchants, and of much correction of children, and of striking the ribs of the wicked servant until they bleed [5].

It is no shame for a man to practice trade and make a profit, nor to discipline children so that they behave in the house with order and proper arrangement. Truly the talk here about disciplining the wicked servant seems harsh, but it was an important matter in ancient societies that if wicked servants were left without discipline, they committed terrible crimes and ran away.

entries.section: 1. Things of which one must not be ashamed

paragraphs.text: Locking up wealth is good where the wife is not trustworthy, and where there are many hands [6].

entries.section: 1. Things of which one must not be ashamed

paragraphs.text: What does he mean here by locking up, to keep the wicked wife from going out? Perhaps it means that the wicked woman here is one who practices sinful marital unfaithfulness or squanders his property foolishly. It seems from the next statement [7] that the wife is unfaithful with his property; so the locking up here is meant as watching over her so that she does not squander their property.
And if you deposit anything (of money), deposit it by number and weight, and record in writing whatever you take or give [7].
If doubt enters a man's mind that his wife is squandering his money or his produce or his possessions, it is better to record everything so that he does not let doubt take control of him.
And do not be ashamed to instruct the ignorant and the foolish, or the man advanced in years who condemns the young [1].

entries.section: 1. Things of which one must not be ashamed

paragraphs.text: Then you will truly be instructed, and accepted before every man [8].

It seems that the statement here is directed to the leaders in the Jewish synagogues who are committed to teaching and guidance, even regarding the elders who mistreat the young; they must be guided so as to narrow the gap between the old generation and the new. On the other hand, it is fitting for us to realize that there is no man immune from error, even if he is an elder or a prophet. God sent to King David Nathan the prophet to urge him to repent (2 Sam 12).

There is no partiality with God. Although He had established David as prophet, king, and judge, and he had a glorious history of holy life, yet when he sinned he deserved correction. St. Irenaeus says: [God is no respecter of persons, therefore He imposes a fitting punishment on conduct that does not please Him. So it was in the case of David, who suffered persecution from Saul (1 Sam 18) for the sake of righteousness, and fled from King Saul and did not wish to take revenge on his enemy, and sang of the coming of Christ, and taught the nations wisdom, and did everything under the guidance of the Spirit, and God was pleased with him. But when his lust drove him to take Bathsheba the wife of Uriah, the Scripture says: "But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD." And He sent to him Nathan the prophet to point out to him his crime so that he might judge himself and condemn himself, and so obtain mercy and forgiveness from Christ[2],]

entries.section: 2. The father's obligations toward his house

paragraphs.text: 9 A daughter is a hidden sleeplessness to her father, and a care that robs him of sleep, for fear of her remaining unmarried when she is grown, and of her being hated when she is married. 10 In her virginity, lest she be defiled, and be found with child in her father's house; and in marriage, lest she transgress against her husband, or be barren. 11 Keep a sure watch over the shameless daughter, lest she make thee a laughingstock to thine enemies, and a byword in the city, and a reproach among the people, and put thee to shame before the multitude.

There are no obligations for a father like his care for the upbringing of his sons and daughters. Society at that time was occupied with the marriage of daughters. And the responsibility of the household was to prepare the girl for a pure and successful married life.

Ben Sira had before him the first woman in the world, Eve, who brought shame upon her house. Therefore he presented to us some of the concerns of the good father toward his daughter, with love, wisdom, and fatherly firmness.
The daughter is a secret anxiety to her father[3], and his anxiety over her robs him of sleep.
Lest the time of marriage pass her by in her youth, and lest she be hated in her marriage [9]

v The enemy of holiness is always pressing upon the virgins and putting them in trouble, to make them prey when one of them staggers and falls. There are many treacherous people, and besides this they have a rebellious nature.
The (virgin) must prepare for a double battle: first she is attacked from without, and second she is corrupted from within[4].

entries.section: 2. The father's obligations toward his house

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom And in her virginity lest she be defiled or become pregnant while in her father's house, and of unfaithfulness if she has a husband, and of barrenness if she is married [10].
Daughters were a burden on the father, since three things occupied him: her marriage at the proper age, her purity and protection lest anyone assault her or seduce her, and the bearing of children.

entries.section: 2. The father's obligations toward his house

paragraphs.text: Keep a close watch over the stubborn daughter, lest she make you a laughingstock to your enemies, a source of rumor in the city, of ill repute among the people, and a shame before the great multitude [11].

The talk here [9-11] reveals the anxiety of fathers regarding their responsibilities toward their daughters. If she is a young girl in her father's house, he fears that the age of marriage will pass her by and she will become a spinster. He also fears that someone may violate her, and she will become a shame to him. And if she marries, he fears that she will be unfaithful to her husband. And if she is faithful, he fears that she will be barren.

By the Incarnation of the Word of God from the holy Virgin St. Mary, all these fears passed away, for "there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus" (Gal 3:28). And St. Mary surpassed not only all men but surpassed the heavenly orders.

12 Gaze not upon the beauty of any, and sit not among women. 13 For from garments cometh the moth, and from the woman wickedness. 14 A man that doeth ill is better than a woman that doeth good, who bringeth shame and reproach.
Do not gaze at the beauty of any person, and do not sit among women [12].
He did not say: "Do not look at the beauty of any person," but he said "Do not gaze." For the man of God is holy in his looks, but if he is lax and gazes in looking, the grace of God abandons him.
For from garments comes the moth, and from woman the wickedness of a woman [13].
Garments that are not used for a long time are spoiled, as the eggs of the moth hidden in them hatch, and so human life is spoiled by the hidden evils in the soul such as wickedness and deceit.
The wickedness of a man is better than a woman who does what is good while bringing shame and reproach [14].

In many ancient societies there is a hidden contrast that is hard to perceive: ordinarily the man engrossed in his affairs does not practice his wickedness in secret and with deceit, but his words reveal what is within him, while the wicked woman sometimes is such that one cannot perceive what is in her inner intention. This contrast does not apply to every man or woman.
