Some manuscripts have: "A dignified daughter is better than a son who has little shame[5]."

entries.section: 4. The creation of the world glorifies God[6]

paragraphs.text: 15 I will remember the works of the Lord, and declare what I have seen. In the words of the Lord are his works. 16 The sun that giveth light looketh upon all things, and the work of the Lord is full of his glory. 17 Hath not the Lord made the saints to speak all his marvellous works, which the Lord the Almighty established, that the whole creation may be established in his glory? 18 He searched out the deep and the heart, and understood all crafty devices. 19 The Lord knew all knowledge, and looked upon the sign of the age, declaring the things that are past and the things to come, and revealing the traces of hidden things. 20 No thought escapeth him, neither is any word hidden from him. 21 He hath adorned the great works of his wisdom, and he is from everlasting to everlasting, and nothing hath been added, 22 neither is anything diminished, and he hath no need of counsel. 23 How desirable are all his works, and what is seen of them is as a spark. 24 All these live and remain for ever for every need, and all of them obey him. 25 All things are double, one against another, and he hath made nothing imperfect; 26 but the one establisheth the good of the other. And who shall be filled with beholding his glory?

In the second and third parts of this chapter Ben Sira laments the state of the father whose daughter brings upon him shame and disgrace before everyone through her stubbornness toward her husband or her impurity [9-11]. And the young man who enjoys the company of women with a spirit of recklessness and laxity [12-14] becomes like a garment eaten by the moth, and a plaything in the hand of a wicked woman who moves him toward shame and disgrace while he does not care! Now in this part [15-25] he sees the irrational creation moving through the laws of nature, and bearing witness by its movements and works to the glory of God, His wisdom, His providence, and His power.

The inanimate creation, which was not granted reason with its intelligence and abilities, nor the will to move it, works in exceeding harmony and order. The Apostle says: "For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse" (Rom 1:20).

entries.section: 4. The creation of the world glorifies God[6]

paragraphs.text: Creation, with the billions of creatures it contains, great and small, visible and invisible, was not brought into being scattered, but with an exact and wonderful order, into the secrets of whose precise laws the world is still searching up to this moment. Sirach says: "The Most High knows all knowledge, and looks upon the signs of the times [18].

These statements were in the mind of the Apostle Paul: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor? Or who hath first given to him, and it shall be recompensed unto him again? For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen" (Rom 11:33-36).
Ben Sira sees creation as the chariot of God's wisdom, offering it to every seeker of wisdom.

v "All his works are in faithfulness"; what does this mean? The heavens and their order you will find to be "a guide to faith," for they bear witness to their Maker. And if you see the order of the earth, it increases your faith in God. Yet it is not through ourselves, with our bodily eyes, that we believe in Him, but by the power of the mind we perceive the invisible through the evidence of the visible [7].
St. Basil the Great And now I will remember the works of the Lord and declare all His works that I see; by a word of the Lord His works were created, and all are subject to His will [15].
As Ben Sira speaks of God's works in nature, he mentions God's saying or word, for it is written in the Book of Genesis: "And God said, Let there be... and it was so..." (Gen 1:3).

St. Basil the Great shows that creation is the work of the Holy Trinity, so that when the divine command "Let there be..." was issued, it does not mean the issuing of sound waves in the air, but the issuing of the will of our God, with a divine mind; for creation was accomplished by the Word of God, "the Son." And when it is said that the Spirit was hovering, it does not mean that He made a movement in the air. Rather He played "an active part in creation." He is like a bird that broods an egg with its body, and by the warmth of its body offers a vital power that brings life.
v God created by His word animals of different kinds for our benefit, some of which we use as food and some in our service.
But man, God created him to be a witness to the works of God and one who gives thanks to Him for them.

This is what men must strive for, lest they die like the dumb animals without seeing or perceiving God and His works. Man must also know that God is able to do all things, and that no one can resist God the Almighty.
And just as God brought everything by His word from nothing into being according to His will, so (now) He makes everything for the salvation of mankind[8].
St. Anthony the Great The sun gives light and looks upon everything, and its work is full of the glory of the Lord [16].

As St. Basil the Great takes us on a delightful journey with the Creator, he offers us wonderful spiritual touches. We come into contact with the creativity of the Creator, not only to satisfy the needs of His beloved man, but in order to work in him, so that He may set up for him a beautiful, joyful world and a school that refines his conduct. We mention by way of example the following[9]:
a. As the sun gives light, so the saints in ancient times dispelled the darkness of ignorance[10].
b. As the moon waxes until it becomes full and then wanes, so the human destiny succeeds in virtue and fails in turn[11].
c. Some animals discover by instinct the coming seasons and prepare for them; so it is fitting for Christians to look forward to eternity and to hasten toward it[12].
d. Animals walk with bent backs, looking to the ground and to their bellies, but man was created with his head upward that he may care for heavenly things and not earthly ones[13].
The Lord did not enable His saints to describe all His wonders, which the Lord Almighty made, in order to establish the world in His glory [17].
None of the heavenly orders can declare the wonders of God that bear witness to His glory.
He searches the deep and the heart of man and understands their secrets, for the Most High possesses all knowledge, and looks upon the signs of the age [18].

He links the searching of the abyss, a bottomless, with the heart, for as no one can reach the depths of the immeasurable abyss, so the heart of man contains within it a world whose secrets no one can know but the Most High.

St. Basil begins his homilies on the "six days of creation" with the work of God the Creator for the sake of man, His beloved, and at the close of his homilies (especially Homily 9:6 and Homily 11:14) he affirms the necessity of setting out on a journey to the depths of the soul, so that the believer may discover the microcosm, far more wonderful than the outer world. The saint affirms that getting to know the invisible heaven is easier than man's getting to know his own depths. The inner man is a special and precious world into which one must enter with the Spirit of the Holy God, so that we may know ourselves and grow in the knowledge of God.

entries.section: 4. The creation of the world glorifies God[6]

paragraphs.text: He declares the past and the future and reveals the traces of hidden things [19].

entries.section: 4. The creation of the world glorifies God[6]

paragraphs.text: No thought escapes Him, and not one word is hidden from Him [20].

entries.section: 4. The creation of the world glorifies God[6]

paragraphs.text: He adorned His great works with His wisdom, and He is the One who exists from eternity to eternity; nothing can be added to Him, nor anything taken from Him, and He has no need of anyone to be His counselor [21].

The main idea around which the homilies of St. Basil the Great on the days of creation revolve is that the true beauty of creation, with all its systems that seem extremely complex, and its wonderful creativity, can be perceived and realized by returning to the eternal, invisible world that awaits us and welcomes us, as we long for it and look forward to it through the wonderful love of the Creator for man[14]. Therefore, when Rousseau devoted a chapter to the Hexaemeron, he called it: "A return to the ancient homeland," quoting this from (Homily 6:1).

entries.section: 4. The creation of the world glorifies God[6]

paragraphs.text: How precious are all His works, how they sparkle to the sight [22].

The stories of creation as recorded by the philosophers conflicted and contradicted one another, but what Moses the prophet recorded in the Book of Genesis is the fruit of an encounter with God, and his talk comes to kindle our hearts not to know how creation was accomplished, but how we meet the Creator and enjoy the sight of Him, and enter with Him into a shared love!

The world has a beginning and surely has an end, "for the fashion of this world passeth away" (1 Cor 7:31). So while we receive this beautiful gift from the hand of the Creator, it is fitting that our hearts be attached to the eternal Creator, not to the passing creation.
Moses the prophet affirms: "In the beginning God created," for the world did not bring itself into being, but is the making and creativity of the Creator.

entries.section: 4. The creation of the world glorifies God[6]

paragraphs.text: All these live and remain forever for every need, and all of them are obedient [23].

entries.section: 4. The creation of the world glorifies God[6]

paragraphs.text: All things are made in pairs, one the counterpart of the other, and He has made nothing imperfect [24].
St. Evagrius of Pontus sees that prayer also is accomplished in two ways, by action and by contemplation[15].

paragraphs.text: Each one of them strengthens the goodness of the other, so who can have enough of beholding His glory? [25]
Inspired by Sirach 42

entries.section: Let me walk according to Your good pleasure, O my Creator!

paragraphs.text: v My soul rejoices in Your Law and in entering into a covenant with You!
It lifts me up, so that I gladly give up even my temporal rights.
My heart will not turn aside from the faith, whatever the temptation.
I and the members of my household walk with propriety, for You are our leader in life.
v Who is my only daughter whose marriage and chastity and bearing of holy children I care for!
She is my soul, whose dowry You paid on the cross. She dwells in the Church, the holy house of marriage.
And her children are the fruit of the Holy Spirit!
v For my sake You created the wonderful universe, through which I touch Your surpassing love for me.
You created the sun for my sake, so that my soul may be illumined by You.
Your care for all creation is surpassing, how much more what You are preparing for my eternity?
I long to see You in Your eternal glory!

1 The pure firmament is the pride of the heights, and the sight of heaven is a vision of glory. 2 The sun at its rising proclaims by its appearing. It is a wonderful instrument, the work of the Most High. 3 At its noontide it parches the land; who can stand before its heat? The sun is like one who blows a furnace, for what is made in the fire. 4 It burns the mountains threefold, and sends forth fiery vapors, and shines with rays that dazzle the eyes. 5 Great is the Lord who made it, at whose command it hastens on its course.

Jewish writers and astronomers among some nations, such as the Pharaohs and the Greeks, were concerned to explain in various ways the phenomena of the heavenly bodies and the atmosphere, but what occupied Ben Sira was how these phenomena bore witness to the surpassing wisdom of the Creator. Very briefly, Sirach brings out the role of the sun in creation.
a. Its appearing radiates with joy [1-2]; the secret of its joy is the need of the earth, with its plants, animals and man, for it.
b. It shines upon the earth and dries it [3].

c. It shines upon the mountains and makes them like a furnace of fire, and upon the waters and sends forth vapors [4]; the eye cannot fix upon it and is darkened, whereas without it we cannot see what is around us.
d. It seems to be moving from its rising to its setting.

Ben Sira begins by speaking of it as it appears on the horizon, as though it dwelt there and ran from the east to the west. He sees it at its rising as though God sends it to mankind to announce the beginning of a new day. It calls the believer to constant movement and work until the day of his setting from the temporal world. Similar teaching about the sun is found: "In them hath he set a tabernacle for the sun, which is as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, and rejoiceth as a strong man to run a race. His going forth is from the end of the heaven, and his circuit unto the ends of it: and there is nothing hid from the heat thereof" (Ps 19:4-7).
The joy of the heavenly height is the firmament of purity, and the structure of heaven in the vision of His glory [1].

The firmament is called "heaven" from the use of this word for what is lofty and high above the earth[1]. This firmament divides the waters that are above, that is, the clouds, from the waters that are below, that is, the seas and oceans. Besides its literal fulfillment, this division carried a spiritual meaning touching the life of man. If the spiritual man receives at the outset the breaking forth of the divine radiance in his inner depths, it is fitting for him to bear the firmament that divides between waters and waters, so that he receives the waters of the Holy Spirit from above that give life (Jn 4:14) and rises above the waters that are below, that is, in the depths, which are inhabited by Leviathan, the ancient serpent, and the sea monster that wars against the human soul (Rev 12:7; 20:3). Whoever enjoys the release into the firmament distinguishes between the grace of the Spirit and the deceptions of the Evil One.
The sun at its appearing announces its shining; what a wonderful instrument, the work of the Most High [2].
The Pharaohs called the sun the god Ra, and the Greeks the god Apollo; here Ben Sira affirms that it is the work of the Most High.

v Do we not marvel, astonished, at the structure of the sun? For it appears to the sight a small body, yet it carries a mighty power. It rises from the east and sends its rays to the west. And as the Psalmist described its rising at dawn, saying: "As a bridegroom coming out of his chamber" (Ps 19:5). He has pictured for us its splendor and the mildness of its heat at the beginning of its rising for men, so that when noontide comes we often flee from gazing upon it. Its rising is a delight to all; it is like the bridegroom! Consider also its ordering (or rather, the ordering of God, the Maker of its work), how it appears high in summer, when the day is long, giving men an opportunity to work, and in winter the cold increases and the night lengthens for the rest of men... It also contributes to the fruits of the produce of the earth![2]

St. Cyril of Jerusalem v Lift up your eyes to heaven, like him who said: "Unto thee lift I up mine eyes, O thou that dwellest in the heavens" (Ps 123:1). Look to the Sun of righteousness, for when the commandments of the Lord, which represent the brightest of the stars, direct you, you will have watchful eyes. Do not allow the eyes (of the soul) to slumber, nor the eyelids of the eye to rest (Ps 132:4), until the commandments lead you continually. He says: "Thy law is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path" (Ps 119:105).

Truly, if you never sleep while you are at the helm that steers life... you will receive the help of the Spirit, who leads you in a gentle breeze and in safety full of peace until you cross over and reach the calm harbor in stillness and without any harm to you, by the will of God[3].
St. Basil the Great At noon it dries the earth; who can endure its burning heat? [3]
The man who kindles the furnace works in burning heat, and the sun burns the mountains threefold, sends forth burning vapors, and sends out its rays so that the eyes are darkened [4].
Great is the Lord who made it, and at His command it hastens on its course [5].

St. Cyril of Jerusalem sees that the sun at its setting glorifies God, since man rests from the toil of the day, as he says: [Let no one say that the Creator of light is not the Creator of darkness, but remember what is written in Isaiah! I am God, "I form the light, and create darkness" (Isa 45:7). Why are you troubled at this, O man? Why are you displeased at the opportunity given you for rest?! Would a servant be permitted rest by his master if the darkness did not compel him to rest of necessity?! After the weariness of the day we are refreshed by night, and we rise in the morning with our strength renewed after the burdens of the day's labors, thanks to the rest of the night. What is more profitable to man than the night for attaining wisdom?! For in it we often meditate on the works of God, and in it we read the divine sayings and understand them, and in it we especially compose our minds to chant Psalmody and prayer! Does this not happen at night?![4]]

6 And the moon, in all its appointed phases, is the announcement of the seasons and a sign of the age. 7 From the moon comes the sign of the feast. It is a luminary that wanes at its fullness. 8 The month is named after it, and in its changing it increases wonderfully. 9 There is on high an encampment of a host shining in the firmament of heaven.

The moon, which draws its light from the sun, has its own role. The sun announces every morning a new day, and with every setting is a call to rest from the struggle of work, while the moon appears changing, determines the seasons and months, announces the feasts, shines in the heights, and pours out joy amid the darkness of the night.

The sun is like a furnace and the moon is like a lamp, and neither the one nor the other can be dispensed with! The moon is the sign of the changing of the seasons, especially in the religious calendar of the Jews (Ex 12:2; Ps 104:19).

Origen says: [Christ is the light of the world who illumines the Church with His light. As the moon draws its light from the sun and so lights up the darkness, so the Church draws light from Christ to shine upon those who are in the darkness of ignorance[5].] He also says: [The higher we rise to look upon the sunrise from the heights, the better the splendor and the warmth are. So the more our thought ascends and is lifted up to Christ, the nearer it draws to the brightness of His radiance, and we are enlightened by His light in greater splendor and beauty. And as He Himself says: "Turn ye unto me, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will turn unto you" (Zech 1:3)... If we are able to go up with Him to the top of the mountain like Peter, James and John, we are enlightened by the light of Christ and by the voice of the Father Himself[6].]
And He also made the moon to determine the change of the seasons[7], to announce the times and as an everlasting sign [6].
From the moon appears the sign of the feast, that light which wanes as it completes its course [7].
By its name the month is called, and in its phases it increases in a wonderful way.
And it is a vessel[8] that dwells in the heights[9]:
It is a lamp for the hosts on high, shining in the firmament of heaven [8].

The moon moves according to the order that the Lord set for it, and as for its faithfulness in determining the seasons, this is understood among the peoples whose calendar is based on the cycle of the moon, such as the Arabs, the Jews and others (Ps 89:38; 104:19), like the beginning of months (Gen 1:14); it is the beginning of the month for the Jews, and is called by the Jews the head of the month (the New Moon), and it is a symbol of stability (Ps 72:5); it determines precisely the beginning of the feasts such as the Passover and the harvest, and the Book of Numbers mentions how to depend on the moon in appointing such occasions (Num 28:11-15)[10].

entries.section: 3. The stars, the rainbow and the snow glorify the Creator

paragraphs.text: 10 There is the beauty of heaven and the glory of the stars, and a shining world, and the Lord in the heights. 11 At the word of the Holy One they stand to carry out His judgments, and no weariness takes hold of them in their watches. 12 Look upon the rainbow, and bless its maker. Its splendor is exceedingly beautiful. 13 It girds heaven with a girdle of glory, and the hands of the Most High stretch it out. 14 At His command He hastens the snow, and hurls the lightnings of His judgment. 15 And by Him the treasures are opened, and the clouds fly like birds. 16 By His greatness He strengthens the clouds; and the hailstones are broken in pieces. 17 At His glances the mountains are shaken, and at His will the south wind blows. 18 At the voice of His thunder the earth travails, at the storm of the north and the whirlwind. 19 He scatters the snow as birds flying down alight, and its descent is like the alighting of locusts. 20 The eye marvels at the beauty of its whiteness, and the heart is astonished at its raining. 21 And He pours out the frost like salt upon the earth, and when it freezes it becomes like the points of stakes. 22 The cold north wind blows, and the water freezes. The ice settles upon every gathering of waters, and clothes the waters with a breastplate. 23 It devours the mountains and burns the wilderness, and consumes the green like fire. 24 The mist hastens and heals everything, and the dew coming after the heat restores gladness.

The stars in their countless numbers stand like soldiers amid the darkness, serving the will of God [9-10]. They urge mankind to cease worshiping idols and to return to the Maker, the Creator. The greatness of the sun, the moon and the stars brings out the power and wisdom of the Almighty Creator, and rebukes those who worship the beautiful creation instead of its Creator.

entries.section: 3. The stars, the rainbow and the snow glorify the Creator

paragraphs.text: The rainbow [11-12] is not mentioned in the six days of creation, but appeared as a sign of the covenant and of the Creator's care for mankind (Gen 9). Here he speaks of it as encircling heaven with a glorious arc, and the hands of the Most High stretch it out [2].

entries.section: 3. The stars, the rainbow and the snow glorify the Creator

paragraphs.text: He speaks of the snow and the lightning [13]; the snow comes down slowly so that it does not harm men, and He allows the lightning to appear and quickly vanish, so that it does not harm the eyes; while the clouds move in the air like birds [14]. Wonderful is the Lord in His plan for us: He makes the clouds light, as though they fly in the air, and the hail heavy, falling to the earth.
The glory of the stars is the beauty of heaven, a radiant adornment in the heights of the Lord [9].
v Behold, the creatures in the diversity of their forms chant Your praise, and I open my mouth to praise Your might.
Behold, the days and the nights within their bounds are opened and closed to spread Your report in all the earth.
The evenings and the mornings awaken men by their watches and their seasons to praise You with discernment.
The summers and the winters teach the earth by their changes and their courses that You alter its seasons.
The cold and the heat, which go and come for the ordering, tell how skilled You are in Your works.
The hours of the day and the four watches of the night all send up distinct praises to Your creative power...
All the dry land and the earth and its mountains with their hills praise You, and You bear them up lest they fall.
Behold, the heavens declare Your glory by their natures, and the firmament shows the work of Your hands: how mighty You are!
Behold the great tent that Your creative power wove, and spread out, stretched and standing above all directions, and it is filled with Your praise.
The sun and the moon, their rays and their risings, awaken the world with the great procession of Your praise[11].
St. Jacob of Serugh At the words of the Holy One they stand according to His judgment[12], and weariness has no power over them in their watches [10].

St. Cyril of Jerusalem says: [It would have been more fitting for them to be astonished and marvel not only at the order of the sun and the moon, but at the exact arrangements of the stars and the appearance of each star in its due time. From its appearing summer and winter are known, and some of them announce the time of planting and others announce the beginning of sailing. For a man sitting in his ship sails among boundless waves, guiding his ship by looking to the stars. And as Holy Scripture says of these things, "and let them be for signs, and for seasons... and years" (Gen 1:14), and not for the sake of astrology and idle tales[13].]
Look upon the rainbow, and bless its maker, for its radiance is exceedingly beautiful [11].

The rainbow is like a jewel that adorns creation. In the Book of Revelation a rainbow like unto an emerald appears around the throne (Rev 4:3). The Lord gave the rainbow as a sign of His covenant with man, that He would not drown the earth with a flood again. With this divine pastoral work, the rainbow glorifies God with its splendor, exceedingly beautiful.
It goes around heaven with its glorious arc, and the hands of the Most High determine its course [12].
At His command the snow falls, and He hastens the lightning by His judgment [13].
He describes God's care for creation in the following:
a. Through commands: "At His command the snow falls" [13].

entries.section: 3. The stars, the rainbow and the snow glorify the Creator

paragraphs.text: b. Through His appearing: "At His appearing the mountains are shaken" [16].
c. Through His will: "At His will the south wind blows" [16].

entries.section: 3. The stars, the rainbow and the snow glorify the Creator

paragraphs.text: d. Through sprinkling or scattering: "He scatters the snow as birds fall" [18].

entries.section: 3. The stars, the rainbow and the snow glorify the Creator

paragraphs.text: e. Through pouring: "He pours out the frost like salt upon the earth" [19].

entries.section: 3. The stars, the rainbow and the snow glorify the Creator

paragraphs.text: f. Through destroying: "He destroys the mountains and burns the wilderness" [21].

entries.section: 3. The stars, the rainbow and the snow glorify the Creator

paragraphs.text: g. Through ordering: "According to His purpose He subdued the great deep" [23].

entries.section: 3. The stars, the rainbow and the snow glorify the Creator

paragraphs.text: h. Through His word: "By His word all things are done" [26].
Therefore the storehouses are opened, and the clouds fly like birds [14].

In his love for beautiful nature, Ben Sira sees the clouds moving in the heights like birds singing in exultation [14]. And when the hail falls like little grains and covers the mountains so that they all become like a white carpet [16], the eye marvels at the beauty of its whiteness, and the mind is astonished at its falling [18].
He also sees in the rains and the dew that they transform the earth, which suffers from intense scorching heat, into a fertile land, delightful with fruits and flowers.

St. Cyril of Jerusalem says: [Who stored up the air in the clouds, and bound them to carry the waters of the rains, so that they come golden in color (Job 37:22) from the south, now in one order, and now in the form of many circles and varied shapes?! "Who can number the clouds in wisdom?" (Job 38:37), since it is said in Job: Does He "know the separation of the clouds?!" (Job 37:16) LXX. Who is He "that bringeth the wind out of his treasuries" (Ps 135:7), and as we said before: "Who hath begotten the drops of dew? Out of whose womb came the ice?!" (cf. Ps 135:7; Job 38:28) For their matter is water, and their power is like stone! At one time the water becomes snow like wool (cf. Ps 147:16), and at another He scatters it as frost like ashes, and a third time it becomes a stony substance. He rules the water as He wills. The nature of water is one, but its work is manifold in power, for it makes in the vine wine that makes glad the heart of man, and in the olive oil that makes his face to shine, and in bread it strengthens man's heart (Ps 104:15), and it is found in all kinds of fruit that God created[14].]
By His greatness He thickens the clouds, and the hail is shattered into pieces [15].
At His appearing the mountains are shaken, and at His will the south wind blows [16].
The sound of His thunder shakes the earth, and so do the storm of the north and also the whirlwind [17].
He scatters the snow as birds fall, and it descends as the locust falls.
The eye marvels at the beauty of its whiteness, and the mind is astonished at its falling like rain [18].
He pours out the frost like salt upon the earth, and when it freezes it becomes like heads of thorns [19].
The cold north wind blows, and the ice freezes upon the water, and settles upon every gathering of waters, and clothes the waters as with a breastplate [20].
The Lord Himself calls us to flee from the land of the north, as from Babylon, to set out for Zion, where the Lord comes and dwells in our midst (Zech 2:6-10).

The blowing of the cold north wind: since the north winds coming upon the Middle East region are marked by coldness, it points to the attack of the devil and sin upon the believer, to take from him the warmth of the Spirit; it is said: "And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold" (Mt 24:12).

In the visions of Zechariah the prophet, those in Babylon were called to flee from the land of the north to return to Jerusalem, the city of God (south of Babylon). "Ho, ho, flee from the land of the north, saith the LORD" (Zech 2:6). St. Didymus the Blind comments on this call, saying: [He made clear to where and in what city salvation is possible for those fleeing from the harsh cold of the north wind... It is Zion, the holy land, where those who formerly dwelt in it can flee from Babylon in safety... And since the name "Babylon" means confusion, every person who is confused in mind is counted a Babylonian, which must be avoided, by the desire to flee to Zion where the praises of God are sung, for it is the place fitting for praising God, "Sing praises to the LORD, which dwelleth in Zion" (Ps 9:11).]

v We have been commanded to be fervent in spirit (Rom 12:11); this shows that the word of God is a blazing fire. Jeremiah heard from him who gave him the divine revelation: "Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth" (Jer 1:9). And since God is a fire (Deut 4:24; Heb 12:29), it is fitting for the saints to be aflame with the Spirit of God.

(The wicked) are without doubt cold in their love for Him; truly the Lord says: "And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold." And all those who symbolize the opposing power in the Holy Scriptures are always cold. Satan is in truth called a serpent and a dragon (Rev 12:9; 20:2); who are colder than these? It is said of the dragon that he rules in the waters (cf. Ezek 32:2). And in another place He says: "The Lord shall punish with the holy sword the dragon, the fleeing serpent... and shall slay the dragon there" (cf. Isa 27:1). And in another passage: "And though they be hid from my sight in the bottom of the sea, thence will I command the serpent, and he shall bite them" (Amos 9:3).

And in the Book of Job this creature was called king over all the beings that are in the water (Job 41:25). The prophet declares that evils come from the north, especially upon those who dwell on the earth (Jer 1:14). And the north wind is referred to in the Holy Bible as cold, as it is said in Wisdom: "The icy north wind." Without question it is fitting for us to refer these to Satan[15].

Origen v To make the flight easier, he made clear where and in what city salvation is within the reach of those fleeing from the cold, piercing wind (Sir 43:20; Prov 27:16). It is Zion, the holy place, where its former inhabitants from the daughters of Babylon can flee to it in safety[16].
St. Didymus the Blind He (the Lord) destroys the mountains, and burns the wilderness, and dries up the tender grass like fire [21].
The mist restores them all quickly, and the falling dew refreshes from the heat [22].

entries.section: 4. The great deep glorifies the Creator

paragraphs.text: 25 By His word He calmed the deep, and made islands to grow in it. 26 Those who sail the sea tell of its terror. We hear it with our ears and marvel. 27 There are the wonderful and strange works: all kinds of animals, the creatures of the whales.

The ancient Israelites were accustomed to look upon the seas as terrifying (Ps 107:23-32; Jon 1:4-16), while stressing God's power in overcoming the destructive power of the seas. Here Ben Sira brings out the beauty of the islands surrounded by the waters of the seas, with diverse and beautiful fish, and also sea monsters.
According to His purpose[17] He calmed the great deep, and caused islands to grow in it [23].

St. Cyril of Jerusalem says: [In this great, wide sea live creatures without number (Ps 104:25); who can describe the wonder of the fish that live in it?! Who can imagine the greatness of the whales and the nature of the amphibious animals: how they live now upon solid land and again amid the waters?![18]]
And those who sail the sea recount its dangers, and we marvel at the reports that our ears hear: [24]
For there are strange, wonderful works, and diverse varied living beings, and created orders of huge sea monsters [25].

St. Cyril of Jerusalem says: [Who among men knows even the names of all the wild beasts?! Or who can distinguish the physiology of each of them accurately? If you do not know of the wild beasts even their mere names, how do you understand their Creator?![19]]

28 By Him the end is brought to success, and by His word all things consist. 29 We multiply words and yet fall short, and the sum of what is said is that He is the all. 30 What can we do to glorify Him, for He is great above all His works. 31 Fearful is the Lord and very great, and His power is wonderful. 32 Exalt the Lord in His glorification as much as you can; still He is higher. 33 Bless the Lord and exalt Him as much as you are able; for He is greater than all praise. 34 Be extravagant in exalting Him according to your strength. Do not grow weary, for you will never attain to Him. 35 Who has seen Him that he may tell? And who can magnify Him as He is? 36 And there are many hidden things greater than these; for what we have seen of His works is little. 37 The Lord has made all things, and has given wisdom to the godly.
Because of Him (the Lord) His messenger prospers in his journey, and by His word all things work together [26].

The Apostle Paul presents similar expressions, saying: "For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible... all things were created by him, and for him" (Col 1:16).
We can multiply words without reaching the goal, and the sum of our words is this: "He is the all" [27].
God is omnipresent, present in every place and at all times; He is in all things, and He is above all things; He is the all.

v When we come to You, this many speaking that we do without comprehension will be abolished, and You are the One who remains. You are all in all (1 Cor 15:28), and without ceasing we shall say one thing, we shall praise You in the One, we who become one in You[20].
St. Augustine How can we praise Him as is fitting?
For He is greater than all His works [28].

v As we bend our knees with good reverence before the Maker of the worlds, I mean the world of sense and of thought, what is seen and what is unseen, you glorify God with a holy tongue that speaks of what is good, and lips that are not silent, and a heart that does not grow weary, saying: "O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all" (Ps 104:24); to You belong honor and glory and majesty from now through all the ages. Amen[21].
St. Cyril of Jerusalem Fearful is the Lord and very great, and wonderful is His power [29].
Glorify the Lord and magnify Him as much as you can, for He is above all this.
Magnify Him with all your strength, and do not grow weary, for you will not glorify Him sufficiently [30].

v The subject of our meditation in this present life must be the praises of God, because the perpetual loftiness of our coming life is praise of Him, and no one can prepare for the life to come unless he practices it himself now.

Our praise is marked by joy, and our prayers by sighing... Concerning these two matters, one is practiced in the trials and afflictions of this life, and the other pertains to the life to come, in eternal rest and heaven[22].
St. Augustine Who has seen Him that he may describe Him?
And who is able to magnify Him truly as He is? [31]
v In truth, by what understanding can a person comprehend God if he cannot understand his own mind, by which he knows God?[23]
St. Augustine Yet there are many hidden things greater than these, for we have seen but little of His works [32].

As knowledge advances and our knowledge of God's creation increases, we realize that we are on the shore of knowledge, and humanity remains, until the day of its meeting with the Creator face to face, confessing its inability to comprehend all the mysteries of creation and the extent of the Creator's care for it. This inability gives us a thirst not only for knowledge but also for the Creator, all-wise and all-loving.
For the Lord has made all things, and has given wisdom to the godly (those who fear the Lord) [33].

If visible and invisible nature praises God by its obedience to the law that God set for it, then man, who lost the image of God and is no longer in His likeness because of sin, praises God by recovering the lost image and enjoying the wisdom of God, which is a matter of God's delight!
Inspired by Sirach 43

entries.section: Grant me to join the choir of those who praise!

paragraphs.text: v Arise, O Holy One, in our hearts, and renew our souls, that we may join joyfully the choir of those who praise, and our hearts, minds and emotions be drawn toward contemplating You.
v All creation praises You by its submission to the law that You set for it.
Grant us to join even this irrational creation, and in the spirit of obedience to praise Your holy name.
It praises You by working in silence!
Grant us to praise You when You shine with Your light in us, to praise You by our silence together with the purity of our hearts!
Our inner man praises You, by Your Kingdom which You establish within us!
It is the work of Your Holy Spirit.

entries.section: 1. Blessing upon the godly, the famous heroes of faith

paragraphs.text: 1 Let us praise the noble men, our fathers from whom we were born. 2 In them the Lord created much glory, and displayed His greatness from the ages. 3 They were men of authority in their kingdoms, men of name and might, counselors in their discernment, speaking prophecies, 4 leaders of the people by their counsels, and by the understanding of the books of their nation. 5 They embodied in their instruction words of wisdom, and searched into the melodies of song, and recited the poems of the writing. 6 Men of wealth and power, doing peace in their houses. 7 All those obtained glory in their generations, and their days were days of boasting. 8 Some of them left behind a name that tells of their praises. 9 And some have no memorial, and perished as though they had never been, and were born as though they had not been born, they and their sons after them. 10 But those were men of mercy, and their righteousness is not forgotten. 11 The good inheritance continues with their posterity, and their descendants abide in the promises. 12 Their seed and their sons stand firm for their sake. 13 Their seed continues forever, and their glory is not blotted out. 14 Their bodies were buried in peace, and their names live through all generations. 15 The peoples tell of their wisdom, and the congregation declares their praise.
Come now, let us praise the honored men and our fathers [1]; Ben Sira honors the men of faith in the Old Testament, and he bears the same spirit as that found in (Heb 11).

entries.section: 1. Blessing upon the godly, the famous heroes of faith

paragraphs.text: The Lord established His great glory, and His greatness from of old, through them [2].
Ben Sira takes pride in the glory that God gave to the believers, so that they became glorified, and God was glorified by His work with them.
There were those who reigned in their kingdoms, and men who were famous for their power.

entries.section: 1. Blessing upon the godly, the famous heroes of faith

paragraphs.text: They offered counsel by their understanding, and proclaimed prophecies [3].

He began his discourse by declaring the glory of God without mentioning names, to affirm that He who was glorified in the great men of old is glorified to this day in His believers, and will also be glorified in the generations to come.

Ben Sira did not define a particular form for the great ones, but wishes to affirm that the beauty of the holy congregation is that each person works with the talent given to him according to his gifts and abilities. Therefore he spoke of various categories:
a. Kings and rulers with authority [2].
b. Nobles and leaders with power [3].
c. Counselors marked by discernment [3].
d. Prophets who received the spirit of prophecy [3].

entries.section: 1. Blessing upon the godly, the famous heroes of faith

paragraphs.text: e. Leaders of the people, each in his specialty [4].
f. Teachers gifted in the ability to teach [4].

entries.section: 1. Blessing upon the godly, the famous heroes of faith

paragraphs.text: g. Artists in melodies and music [5].
h. Writers gifted in composing melodies and music [5].

entries.section: 1. Blessing upon the godly, the famous heroes of faith

paragraphs.text: i. Rich men generous in giving [6].
j. Men of peace gifted in spreading peace between the leaders and the people [6].
And there were leaders of the people by their counsels, and by their understanding of the teaching of the people, wise in their words of instruction [4].
There were those who composed musical melodies, and recorded poetic writings [5].
Rich men with power, living in peace in their dwellings [6].

entries.section: 1. Blessing upon the godly, the famous heroes of faith

paragraphs.text: All those obtained glory in their generation, and were a source of pride in their days [7].
Ben Sira did not distinguish between one category and another, but sees all the preceding categories marked by obtaining glory, and the holy congregation takes pride in them.

entries.section: 1. Blessing upon the godly, the famous heroes of faith

paragraphs.text: Some of them left behind a name that makes people tell of their praises [8].
God allows certain faithful and successful names to be brought out, whom the people praise, in order to urge the coming generations to faithfulness and work.

entries.section: 1. Blessing upon the godly, the famous heroes of faith

paragraphs.text: And some of them no one remembers; they perished as though they had never been, and died as though they had not been born, and so their sons after them [9].

entries.section: 1. Blessing upon the godly, the famous heroes of faith

paragraphs.text: Yet they were men of mercy, and their righteousness lives with the Lord [10].

We should not wonder if we see some faithful, sincere and successful men who are no longer remembered, as though they had never been, although they were men of mercy and performed works of righteousness in the Lord. This does not mean that they have been wronged, for what occupies God's mind is that they enjoy the eternal glories. In this there is no difference between one whom men glorify because he walks in the Lord with strength, and one whom history ignores as though he had never existed, for all will be gathered in the great day of the Lord as one heavenly bride.

entries.section: 1. Blessing upon the godly, the famous heroes of faith

paragraphs.text: The good that they did continues with their posterity and their children's children [11].

entries.section: 1. Blessing upon the godly, the famous heroes of faith

paragraphs.text: Their posterity remains (faithful) to the covenants, and their children likewise on account of them [12].

What Ben Sira affirms is that those whom history ignored, and whose portion is in the heavenly places, are not deprived of a holy offspring and grandchildren who are glorified in the Lord. These children and grandchildren are not according to the flesh, but by the Spirit.

entries.section: 1. Blessing upon the godly, the famous heroes of faith

paragraphs.text: Their posterity continues forever, and their glory is not blotted out [13].

entries.section: 1. Blessing upon the godly, the famous heroes of faith

paragraphs.text: Their bodies were buried in peace, and their names live through all generations [14].

entries.section: 1. Blessing upon the godly, the famous heroes of faith

paragraphs.text: The peoples tell of their wisdom, and the congregation declares their praise [15].

Ben Sira concluded the introduction "God's men glorify God" with the affirmation that those who receive honor even after their death, and those who do not receive honor, all together as men of God have died, but their story is recorded in the Book of Life, and God is glorified in them through their children and disciples. With this spiritual thought no kind of jealousy or envy will creep in among the people of God, neither in this world nor in the age to come.
16 Enoch pleased the Lord and was translated, and he will call the generations to repentance.
Enoch pleased the Lord, and was translated, as an example of repentance for all generations [16].

The first example of the famous ones, or of the heroes in the Lord, is Enoch, and he came in the list of the Apostle Paul as the second of the famous (Heb 11:5-6). Jude described him as "the seventh from Adam" (Jude 14).

All that is recorded of him in (Gen 5:24) is that he walked with God, and the Lord took him to Himself. He is regarded as the object of God's delight, for he became a lesson to all generations, urging many to a life of repentance in the positive sense, which is meeting with God and walking with Him. He was qualified to become acquainted with heaven, indeed to depart to it.

The expression "Enoch pleased the Lord" here means that he was the object of His delight. He became a model of the repentance of the generations; therefore Sirach began with him the list of heroes. This repentance is the beginning of the process of seeking God. He pleased the Lord to the degree that He took him from the earth, and so he clung to Him completely. Enoch was not a Jew, for he lived before Noah and did not receive the covenant with God through Abraham. Rather, he pleased the Lord by keeping the tradition that humanity had received from Adam and Abel.

All that Enoch knew about the Lord is that He exists, and he strove to seek Him (Heb 11:6). He believed in God through his little knowledge of Him, and made this knowledge the foundation of his life. If the Book of Sirach is the book of faithful friendship, then God delighted in Enoch as a friend of His, and took him to Himself to be with Him!

v Hardly did Enoch feel death at any time within him, and when he was translated to the Lord he let (death) go from his soul, himself. He drove it out by repentance... Rightly it is said that God translated him that he should not see death, since he was no longer susceptible to death, but drove it out and it fled[3].
Origen v Enoch remained in a lofty and divine beauty, and purified his soul with holiness and purity.
And he excelled in a radiant, pure way of life, and pleased God with thoughts full of love.
He was brought up with chaste and pure thoughts, and lived in purity without care or anger.
And he dwelt in the wilderness without worldly movements, and pleased God three hundred years while he was looking upon Him.
He never found in him a fault, in his sleep or in his wakefulness, nor a slack thought inclined to the world.
He continued looking to the Lord every day for three hundred years, and remained in His beauty, and was not stained with defects[4].
St. Jacob of Serugh

17 Noah was found perfect and righteous, and in him was reconciliation in the time of wrath. 18 Therefore a remnant was left on the earth, when the flood came, 19 and covenants were made with him, that all flesh should not be destroyed by the flood.

The second example is Noah, whom he called perfect teleios and righteous dekaios [17]. St. Peter said of him that he was a preacher of righteousness dikaiosyne (2 Pet 2:5). Ben Sira did not mention his fall into drunkenness, but brought out that he was found perfect and righteous, and because of him he and his wife and his sons and his sons' wives obtained salvation from the flood, and the eight in the ark became a symbol of the believers in the Church of the New Testament (1 Pet 3:20-21). God made a covenant with Adam, promising him the salvation that the incarnate Word of God, the second Adam, would offer, then Noah received a covenant with God after the flood on behalf of mankind. And the covenant was renewed with the four patriarchs: Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Gen 9:9; 17:9; 26:3-5; 28:13-15).
Noah was found perfect and was righteous in the time of wrath, when he became a means of reconciliation[5], and because of him a remnant was left on the earth when the flood came [17].

By his righteous life Noah became an object of propitiation for the whole human race. God proclaimed His mercy upon mankind in the form of a covenant between God and men, and declared that He would not destroy the human race with a flood.
Everlasting covenants were made with him, so that all flesh would not be blotted out again by a flood [18].

Ben Sira brought out that one of the marks of the heroic men of faith is that they enter into a covenant with the Lord, and as for Noah, he entered into "everlasting covenants" [18]. He mentioned the word "covenant" in the plural, perhaps because of the repetition of God's covenant in the Book of Genesis (16:18; 9:9-13, 16-17).
v Noah also arose and saw the iniquity of the wicked generation, and wove righteousness and put it on bodily.
He armed himself with uprightness and meekness, lest sin stain his body should it meet him.
He saw how fornication multiplied among the sons of his generation, so he set virginity in array against it to overcome it by it.
He found that everyone had corrupted his way with defiled fornication, so the distinguished one was afraid to approach marriage.
He found that nature had slipped and fallen from what was due, so he arose to stand firm in virginity, rising above nature.
He kept away from marriage five hundred years, because he found that fornication was among the married[6].
He remained in the rank of virginity five hundred years, then married to beget for a purpose.
He alone was good, and by his righteousness he comforted the earth, and after the whole world was ruined he made it inhabited through him.
He distinguished the sacrifices, and set up an altar with whole burnt offerings, and became in his generation the (holy) "remnant" for the world that perished[7].
St. Jacob of Serugh

entries.section: 4. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob glorify God

paragraphs.text: 20 Abraham was a great father of many nations, and no one was found like him in glory. He kept the law of the Most High, and He made a covenant with him, 21 and established the covenant in his flesh, and when tested he was found faithful. 22 Therefore He swore to him that the nations would be blessed in his seed, and that He would multiply his seed as the dust of the earth, 23 and exalt his descendants as the stars, and cause them to inherit from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. 24 And likewise He placed in Isaac, for the sake of Abraham his father, 25 the blessing of all men and the covenant, then confirmed them upon the head of Jacob. 26 He favored him with His blessings and gave him the inheritance. He distinguished his portions, and divided them among the twelve tribes. 27 And He raised up from him a man of mercy, who found favor before all flesh.

Abraham: regarding Abraham's connection with the Law, the Book of Genesis was concerned with the covenant or compact with God concerning circumcision. Here, however, Sirach brought out the following: 1. Abraham became the icon of the Father, since he enjoyed spiritual fatherhood, not for his family only, nor for one people, but for many nations [19]. 2. There is none like him among men in glory [19], so that reclining in his bosom was counted as reclining in the Kingdom of God (Lk 16:22). This is God's delight, that the heart of the believer be enlarged with love for many peoples. 3. Abraham lived before Moses, the receiver of the law, by about 400 years, yet it is said of him that he kept the law of the Most High [20]. As though the Law were older than the written Law that Moses received. 4. Abraham entered into a covenant with the Most High [20]. 5. God promised to bless Abraham's seed and to multiply it as the dust of the earth, and exalt it as the stars of heaven, and give them an inheritance from sea to sea [21].
Abraham was a great father of many nations, and no one was found like him in glory [19].

While Noah had his effect upon the remnant that is on the earth [17], Abraham receives a promise of his great fatherhood of many nations [19]. Both promises were fulfilled, to Noah and to Abraham. For the Church is truly a holy remnant that remains for the Lord, and at the same time embraces all the nations, peoples and tongues.
Ben Sira mentioned the three heroes: Enoch, then Noah, then Abraham.

The first represents God's establishing a personal covenant with the believer, the second the establishing of a covenant on the level of the family (Noah and his household), and the third on the ecumenical level.

Thus the Church began on the level of the individual like Enoch, and grew to include the family, and when the Savior of the world came the doors of the Church were opened to all the nations, peoples and tongues.
He kept the law of the Most High, who made a covenant with him.
He made a covenant in his flesh, and when tested he was found faithful [20].

Abraham enjoyed an honor that no one like him enjoyed (44:19), because: 1. He kept the law of the Most High. 2. He entered into a covenant with God, and He confirmed it in his flesh (circumcision). 3. He succeeded in the test of faith (the sacrifice of Isaac his son). Ben Sira spoke of the testing of Abraham [20], and that not in the covenant recorded in (Gen 15:18), but the one recorded in (Gen 17).

entries.section: 4. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob glorify God

paragraphs.text: Therefore He (the Lord) confirmed to him by an oath that in his seed the nations would be blessed, and that He would multiply him as the dust, and exalt his descendants like the stars in number, and cause them to inherit from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth [21].
The river here means the river Euphrates.
v Abraham arose, a lover of truth and a good servant, and he also formed in his time the front of faith.
He left his country and went out after the Lord as He called him, and left his kindred to draw near to God.
He walked in the land like an emigrant and did not grow weary, because another world was pictured before him to which to move.
He was kindled with love for the Lord as with fire, and with it burned up all the enticements found in the world.
He bound his only son on the altar to become a sacrifice, and thrust the spear of the compassions of his bowels to slay him for the Lord.
He was tried by the fire and the knife, and proved whether he loved more his children or God.
The proof of his love was his binding of his only son...
His wife was plundered, his country far off, and his son bound, and since he loved the Lord he did not suffer in all these things[8].
St. Jacob of Serugh Isaac was God's gift to Abraham; through him he enjoyed the divine promises of his father.

entries.section: 4. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob glorify God

paragraphs.text: Likewise He established the same covenant with Isaac, for the sake of Abraham his father [22].
What occupied Ben Sira in the life of Isaac is that he enjoyed the covenant for the sake of Abraham. This is what he inherited from his father.

The blessing rested upon the head of Jacob, who was called "Israel." Although he was younger than Esau he received the inheritance in his seed, as his twelve sons became the fathers of the twelve tribes.
The blessing of all men and the covenant that He established remain upon the head of Jacob.

entries.section: 4. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob glorify God

paragraphs.text: He confirmed to him His blessings, and gave him an inheritance, and divided his portions among the twelve tribes [23].

What Ben Sira affirms is that Abraham enjoyed the divine covenant, and passed it on to Isaac, then his son Jacob, and the promise was fulfilled in the Church of the Old Testament through the twelve tribes. What occupied Ben Sira in his choice of the heroes was that they serve the people of God, the possessor of the divine promises. Therefore he did not mention in the personality of Jacob, so rich in events, anything except the covenant that God established with him, and what all men enjoyed [23]. As for Joseph, to whom the Book of Genesis devoted a number of chapters, Ben Sira spoke of him in only one phrase, as a helper of his people (49:15).
v Isaac also arose and was brought up in beauty, and trained himself in divine thoughts.
He filled his soul with faith and humility, and was armed with righteousness and uprightness.
He hated strife, and lost his possessions and was not angry, and loved safety while being quiet and virtuous in his works[9].
St. Jacob of Serugh v A person can discover through deep reasoning that patience is the foundation of the virtues.

entries.section: 4. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob glorify God

paragraphs.text: By patience Abraham became the father of the nations [24] (Gen 17:5; Rom 4:17), and the friend of God (Jas 2:23).
By patience Isaac, after the likeness of the only Son, became a sacrifice (Gen 22:2).
And by patience also Jacob carried a staff as a cross (Gen 32:10; Heb 11:21); and he who fled (Gen 27:34), patience made him return full of riches (Gen 32:22-23).

By such patience Job struggled and raised the banner of victory, although his adversaries were many and powerful. And although he was completely naked, he appeared as an armed man, fearful before his wrestlers. Job found himself cast down on the ground, and those who wished to create obstacles (the demons) were roaming around him in the air (Eph 2:2). Those who reviled him put on purple, but he put on sores. But the powers of the heavens counted him radiant...
The poor glorify him; the rich serve him, and all generations fixed their eyes upon Job as a reflection of righteousness.
What need is there of much talk about him? Do you wish to learn the power of the patience that was in Job?

There were three friends who reviled him; they were healthy in body, full of vitality because of the overflow of their temporal blessings. And when they grew weary of speaking each of them rested in turn. But as for Job, he alone had his body covered with sores, grieved in soul. By his endurance he overcame these strong men, and by his patience he quieted the fiery, babbling chatter of those who insulted him, relying vainly on their chatter.
Father Hesychius of Jerusalem Inspired by Sirach 44

entries.section: Show me the glory of Your heavenly bride

paragraphs.text: v Grant me, with the heavenly orders, to await the day of Your coming.
I see all great and strong, because they are faithful in the truth.
There are no longer kings and rulers, counselors and teachers, rich men and nobles, musicians and composers.
All have become kings belonging to You, O King of kings. All are musicians ascribed to You, O Source of joy.
Billions whom history forgot, and behold they are engraved on Your palm.
Many of whom no one knew any offspring, and behold they enter the Kingdom and with them children without number!
Many whom we thought to be children of the devil, and behold at the last moments they renounced their evil father and received You as their heavenly Father, and became heirs of the eternal Kingdom.

1 Moses was beloved of God and men, blessed in memory, 2 and He gave him glory like the glory of the saints, and made him great, fearful to enemies. By his words he made the signs cease. 3 And He glorified him before kings. He commanded him concerning His people, and showed him His glory. 4 He sanctified him by his faith and his meekness, and chose him from among all men. 5 He made him hear His voice, and brought him into the cloud. 6 He gave him the commandments face to face, the law of life and knowledge, to teach Jacob the covenant, and Israel His judgments.

Moses was honored among the saints, opening the door of hope to all believers, for he stumbled on some occasions (Ex 4:13-15; 5:11-23; Num 20:11-12), but he repented and followed God. Therefore God honored him [3] and sanctified him [4].
The Lord raised up from his seed a man of mercy, who found grace in the eyes of all flesh, beloved of God and man, Moses, whose memory is blessed [1].

The Lord raised up Moses from the seed of Jacob, and here calls him a "man of mercy." He was the first leader of the people of God, whom He chose to free them from the slavery of Pharaoh; with boldness he stood before the wrath of God declaring his love for them, when he said: "Yet now, if thou wilt forgive their sin; and if not, blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written" (Ex 32:32). He interceded for them, giving them priority over himself, as a man of mercy who found grace in the eyes of God and in the eyes of men, not only in his own time but through the generations. God loved him and men loved him; the mere mention of him came to be counted a blessing [1].
He made his glory like the glory of the saints, and made him great, so that his enemies fear him [2].
He described Moses as equal in glory with the saints. Look to Moses, whose face shone as a reflection of the glory of God upon him (Ex 34:33-35; 2 Cor 3:13), since he spoke with God face to face.

The Lord gave him awe before his enemies; it is stated in the Greek manuscript that he was honored like God (who sent him). Moses the prophet, by confronting Pharaoh (Ex 5:1), set a pattern for the prophets after him, who confronted kings with courage and without fear, such as: Samuel with King Saul (1 Sam 15:16), Nathan with King David (2 Sam 12:7-12), Hanani the seer with Asa king of Judah (2 Chr 16:7), Elijah with King Ahab (1 Kgs 17:1), Micaiah the son of Imlah with King Ahab (1 Kgs 22:8), Isaiah with Ahaz, and Jeremiah with Zedekiah.
By his words he stopped signs, and the Lord glorified him before kings, and gave him commandments for his people, and showed him His glory [3].

He gave him to work signs and wonders (Ps 15-17), and glorified him before kings. "The LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend" (cf. Ex 33:11), delivered to him the law, which is counted an embodiment of the divine wisdom (Ex 20-23), and showed him something of His glory (Ex 24; 33), and entered with him into a covenant.
He sanctified him for his faithfulness and meekness, and chose him from among all men [4].
He was marked by faithfulness and meekness (Num 12:3), and he owed this to the Holy One who sanctified him with these two traits, and chose him from among all men.
He made him hear His voice, and led him in the dark cloud, and gave him the commandments face to face, the law of life and knowledge, to teach Jacob the covenant and Israel His judgments [5].

The cloud in which God led him points to his entering into the cloud to hear the words of the Lord on Mount Sinai (Ex 19:16-19; 20:21), and He gave him understanding and a holy life (Deut 4:6; 30:15), so that he might be able to teach Israel (Deut 4:14; Ps 147:19).
v Moses also arose and did good with God, and set up a front of faith according to his ability.
He increased in lofty beauty through humility, and drew near to God by faith.
He became beautiful and enlightened until he became a chosen vessel, for prophecy to use abundantly.
He became inward by the love of his soul for God, until He made him like a steward over all His treasury.
He loved the people of the Lord in the time of distress and persecution, so he took their reproach and left the wealth of all Egypt[1].
St. Jacob of Serugh

7 He exalted Aaron the holy one, the like of him, his brother of the tribe of Levi. 8 He made for him an everlasting covenant, and gave him the priesthood of the people. He made him happy in splendor, 9 and girded him with a robe of glory. He clothed him with perfection of pride, and strengthened him with instruments of might: 10 the breeches, the long robe and the ephod, and He set about him pomegranates of gold, with many bells round about him, 11 that their sound might ring at his step, that the tinkling might be heard in the temple, as a memorial for the sons of his people. 12 And He gave him the holy garment of gold and blue and purple, the work of a skillful weaver, the breastplate of judgment, in which are the light and the truth. 13 Its weaving was of twisted scarlet, the work of a skillful workman, and upon it precious stones like the engraving of a signet, set in gold, the work of a jewel engraver, engraved upon it the names of the tribes of Israel as a memorial. 14 And on the turban was a crown of gold, engraved upon it the inscription of holiness. It was an ornament of honor, a work of skill, which the eyes love for its beauty. 15 All these were exceedingly beautiful, and there was nothing like them in the age. 16 No one wore them but one of his kindred, his sons and his descendants in every generation. 17 His sacrifices are burned with fire every day, twice without ceasing. 18 Moses consecrated his hands, and anointed him with the holy oil, 19 and it became an everlasting covenant, for him and for his seed as long as heaven lasts, to minister to the Lord, and to practice the priesthood, and to bless his people in His name. 20 He chose him from among all the living, to offer the offering to the Lord, the incense and the sweet savor, as a memorial and an atonement for his people. 21 He established him over His commandments, and gave him authority over the covenants of judgments, to teach Jacob the testimonies, and to enlighten Israel with His law. 22 Strangers gathered against him and envied him in the wilderness, the men of Dathan and Abiram and the congregation of Korah with sharpness and anger. 23 The Lord saw and was not pleased, and destroyed them with the sharpness of His anger. 24 He wrought wonders upon them, and consumed them with the fire of His flame. 25 And He increased Aaron in glory, and gave him an inheritance. He made for them the firstfruits of the earth, 26 and prepared for them before others their fill of bread. They eat of the sacrifices of the Lord, which He gave to him and to his seed. 27 Yet he did not inherit in the land of the people, and had no portion among them, for He Himself is his portion and his inheritance.

The Book here covers the personality and role of Aaron more than that of Moses, not because he is greater than Moses, but to affirm that God works in the leaders through the generations, especially the priests. It begins here with Aaron as the first high priest, and ends the discourse with Simon son of Onas the high priest, a contemporary of Ben Sira (Sir 50:1-12).

The discourse concerning Aaron as the first of the high priests came in seventeen statements, more than any hero mentioned in this book except the high priest Simon son of Onias (Sir 50:1-21), because this book is considered the only one among the wisdom books that was concerned with the priestly work and liturgical worship.

The poem concerning Aaron came in two parts: his garments (Sir 45:6-13), and the sacrifices that he offers (Sir 45:14-22). The garments of splendor and his glorious robe with the rest of the garments point to the Lord Christ, who wraps Himself with His holy Church, which is without blame, as a garment of His that reflects His splendor upon her and sanctifies her. As for the sacrifices, they point to the unique sacrifice of Christ.

Moses received the Law, which is based on the existence of a covenant between God and the people, so there came to be a need for holiness, which is a gift of the Holy One, enjoyed by the believers through spiritual worship and the priesthood, which is a shadow of the priesthood of Christ. What Sirach wanted from the series of the heroes of Israel is: the emphasis on faithfulness to God in true worship, and unfaithfulness brings death.
He exalted Aaron, a saint like Moses his brother, of the tribe of Levi [6].

Aaron was sanctified like his brother. The role of Moses as a prophet was to receive the revelation from God and convey it to the people, while the role of Aaron as a priest was to lift up the repentance of the people and their petitions and sacrifices to God, and in this their work is completed.
He made an everlasting covenant with him, and made him priest of the people. He blessed him with a splendid priestly order, and clothed him with a glorious robe[2] [7].

Ben Sira stressed that God deposited the gift of the priesthood and the practice of worship with Aaron and his sons. What Ben Sira affirms is that God is the one who appointed the worship of Israel to Himself, presenting His divine blessings to his people; therefore when Dathan, Abiram and Korah usurped the authority of the priests, He punished them (Num 16; 26), for his making atonement for the iniquity of Israel.
He clothed him with perfection of pride[3], and established him with symbols of strength, and clothed him with linen breeches and a long robe and an ephod [8].

And He set around him pomegranates with many bells of gold around him, which rang with every step he took, and the sound of them was heard as he walked in the temple, as a memorial for the sons of his people [9].
And a holy garment of gold and lilies and embroidered purple, and the breastplate of judgment with the Urim and the Thummim, and its weaving was of scarlet, the work of a skillful weaver [10].
And upon it precious stones like the engraving of a seal, set in gold, the work of a jewel engraver, engraved according to the number of the tribes of Israel [11].

The description of these costly splendid garments occurs in (Ex 28), and God gave wisdom to the craftsmen so that they might make them skillfully, as the names of the tribes of Israel were engraved on precious stones, that is, upon his right shoulder and his left, since all the children of Israel come forward to God through Aaron. And the pomegranates served as bells to alert the children of Israel when he moved, as He also adorned him with the Urim and the Thummim, which are precious stones meaning perfections and lights, and the children of Israel used to inquire of God's mind through the direction of their rays (Ex 28:6).
And upon the priestly turban was a crown of gold, in the form of the holy seal, a sign of distinction of honor, made by an expert, a delight of the eyes for the richness of its adornment [12].
There was nothing like all this before him in beauty, and no stranger had worn them before; rather his sons and his seed alone wear it continually [13].
His sacrifices were whole burnt offerings, perfect, offered every day twice without ceasing [14].
The morning sacrifice and the evening sacrifice, which are a burnt offering to the Lord offered on behalf of the people twice daily.

Moses is the one who ordained him, and anointed him with the holy oil, and that became an everlasting covenant for him and for his seed forever, to minister to the Lord, to minister as a priest and bless his people in the name of (the Lord) [15].

St. Clement of Alexandria[4] compares Aaron the high priest with the sinful woman: 1. Aaron enjoyed his anointing with the holy oil, and that became an everlasting covenant for him and for his descendants (Sir 45:15); and the most precious thing the sinful woman had was the ointment that she poured upon the Lord Christ. 2. Aaron wore a crown of gold (Sir 45:12), and the sinful woman wiped the feet of the Lord with the hair of her head, which is considered the crown and garland of a woman. 3. Since she had not yet entered into communion with the Lord of glory, as a sinner she poured out the tears of repentance.
He chose him from among all the living, to offer the offering to the Lord, the incense and the sweet savor as a memorial, and to make atonement for your people [16].

The priests were responsible for offering incense and teaching the people and interpreting the law (Deut 31:9-13; 33:10), and they had the authority and the right to consider difficult cases [17] (cf. Deut 17:8-12; 21:5).
And He gave him authority by His commandments over the judgments of the law, to teach Jacob the testimonies, and to enlighten Israel concerning His law [17].
Sirach makes clear the integration between worship and obedience to the divine commandment, as it is the source of heavenly wisdom.
Strangers conspired against him, and envied him in the wilderness, the men who gathered with Dathan and Abiram and the congregation of Korah in wrath and anger [18].

Aaron exercised the priesthood for forty years, and the Lord confirmed his priesthood against those who rose up against him, namely Korah, Dathan and Abiram, who tried to offer strange fire to the Lord, so they perished with two hundred and fifty of their company (Num 16), and the Lord's confirmation of his priesthood came by way of the almond rod that blossomed and brought forth buds (Num 17:8).
The Lord saw that and was not pleased, so they were destroyed in the wrath of His anger; He wrought wonders against them and consumed them in His blazing fire [19].

Ben Sira referred to the rebellion of Korah, Dathan and Abiram who challenged Aaron and Moses (Num 16:3). This company became a wonder, as the earth swallowed them suddenly with the appearance of a fire that destroyed those who ran after them.
And He increased Aaron in glory, and gave him an inheritance, and apportioned to him the first of the firstfruits, and prepared for him bread from the firstfruits in abundance [20].

The Lord increased Aaron's glory by assigning the Levites to help the priests, and gave the priests a share in the sacrifices (Lev 24:5-9; Num 18:5-9). And since the Lord Himself became their portion and inheritance, the Levites did not inherit a portion in the land of promise (Num 18:20).
For they eat of the sacrifices of the Lord, which He gave to him and to his seed [21].
Yet he did not inherit in the land of the people, and had no portion among the people, for the Lord Himself is his portion and his inheritance [22]

Many ministers lived on a bare sufficiency, yet did not feel want, nor looked for a temporal reward, but enjoyed the divine promise that the Lord Himself is their portion; this is their everlasting inheritance.

28 And Phinehas the son of Eleazar is third in glory, for his zeal in the fear of the Lord, 29 and because he stood up, at the apostasy of the people, with the goodness of the readiness of his soul, and made atonement for Israel. 30 Therefore the Lord gave him the covenant of His peace, that he should be the leader of his people in the holy things, and that to him and to his seed should remain the greatness of the priesthood forever. 31 And He made a covenant with David the son of Jesse of the tribe of Judah, of the inheritance of the kingdom from son to son in his seed, like the inheritance of Aaron and his seed. That He may give you wisdom in your hearts, to judge His people with righteousness, so that their good things may not vanish, nor their glory, throughout their generations.
Phinehas is a Hebrew name, whose meaning is "mouth of brass," and he is the son of Eleazar the son of Aaron.

After that Phinehas the son of Eleazar is third in glory, when he showed his zeal in the fear of the Lord, and because he stood firm at the apostasy of the people, with the goodness of the zeal of his soul[5], so he made atonement for Israel [23].

By his saying "third in glory" he means the third generation from Aaron (Ex 6:25), and he is as the heir in the priesthood in the Old Testament. The source of his honor is his commitment to the worship of God and setting boundaries between the believers and the worshipers of idols (Num 25:1-9). He was jealous with the jealousy of the Lord when the people committed adultery with the daughters of Moab, so he killed Zimri the son of Salu, chief of a house of the Simeonites, with the Midianite woman Cozbi the daughter of Zur, and the plague was stayed, and he received from the Lord a covenant of peace for him and for his sons, and their headship of the priesthood continued until the destruction of the temple in AD 70 [24].

Therefore (the Lord) established with him a covenant of peace, that he might be in charge of the sanctuary[6] and a leader of his people, so that to him and to his seed would remain the greatness of the priesthood throughout the ages [24].
And a covenant was made with David the son of Jesse of the tribe of Judah, but the inheritance of the kingdom passes from son to son only, whereas the inheritance of Aaron is for his seed [25].

When Sirach spoke of Aaron the high priest and Phinehas the priest, he wanted to affirm the distinction between the Aaronic priestly covenant and the Davidic royal covenant, to affirm that the priesthood belongs to one tribe, which is the tribe of Levi, and kingship belongs to the tribe of Judah. The two covenants are complementary, but it is not the right of the priest to sit as king upon the throne of Israel, nor the right of the king to usurp the priestly work. 1. If the tribe of David alone had the kingship, yet its inheritance is handed over from one son to one son, whereas the inheritance of Aaron is not for a son but for his seed [25]. 2. The kingship of Israel and its priesthood appeared in the visions of Zechariah the prophet not as one olive tree but two olive trees (Zech 4:3), so that one tribe would not usurp what belongs to the other. And their integration was fulfilled as a symbol of the Lord Christ, who alone is King of kings (Rev 19:16) and at the same time the heavenly High Priest (Heb 8:1).

The priestly and the royal work shine with light through the oil of God's grace that the people of God may enjoy enlightenment, while the Lord Christ is the light of the world (Jn 9:5) who grants the believers from all peoples to become the light of the world (Mt 5:14). 3. Under the Law the people of God needed the two olive trees together, one at the right of the bowl full of the oil of grace, and the other at its left (Zech 4:3).
