Hezekiah knew that his father was responsible for what had befallen the people because of his calling on Assyria to intervene in the politics of the Holy Land (2 Chr 28:16-21). He began the religious reform to repair what his father Ahaz had corrupted, and cleansed the Temple of idols. The Kingdom of God had priority in the life of King Hezekiah, with the renewal of spiritual wisdom.

Hezekiah dug a channel underground through a rock so that Jerusalem could obtain water secretly from the spring of Gihon. This heroic work is recorded twice in the Old Testament (2 Kgs 20:20; 2 Chr 32:30).
Hezekiah fortified his city, and brought the water into the midst of it, dug the hard rock with iron, and built cisterns for water [17].

Sirach begins with the rebellion of King Hezekiah against Assyria, for which he had prepared himself by fortifying Jerusalem, the capital of his kingdom, and digging a channel in solid rock so that the people might find water when Assyria laid siege to the city. This supported the city during the siege of Sennacherib in 701 BC [18-20].
In his days Sennacherib came up, and sent Rabshakeh and withdrew, then lifted up his hand against Zion, and boasted in his pride [18].

"Rabshakeh" [18] is an Assyrian title whose meaning is perhaps "chief of staff (a body of military officers)" or governor. Sennacherib king of Assyria encamped at Lachish and sent the arrogant Rabshakeh to besiege the city of Jerusalem and to demand of King Hezekiah that he hand the city over to him. But Hezekiah turned toward God in a spirit of repentance, and God sent him the prophet Isaiah to reassure him. The angel of the Lord killed 185,000 of the army of Sennacherib (2 Kgs 19:35).
Then their hearts and hands trembled, and they were in pain as women in travail [19].

entries.section: 3. In praise of King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah

paragraphs.text: And they called upon the merciful Lord, stretching out their hands toward Him, and the Holy One heard them quickly from heaven, and rescued them by the hand of Isaiah [20].

entries.section: 3. In praise of King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah

paragraphs.text: He smote the camp of the Assyrians, and His angel destroyed them [21].

v When you close the door of your dwelling and remain alone, know that you have with you an angel, appointed by God for every man, whom the Greeks call "the spirit of the house." He does not sleep, and sees everything by his constant accompanying of you, and is not deceived, and nothing is hidden from him in the darkness. And know that God is beside you, present in every place, for there is no place or space in which God is not present. He is greater than all and holds all in His hand [19].

entries.section: 3. In praise of King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah

paragraphs.text: St. Anthony the Great: For Hezekiah did that which pleased the Lord, and flourished in strength in the ways of David his father, which great Isaiah, faithful in his vision, commanded him [22].

entries.section: 3. In praise of King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah

paragraphs.text: In his days the sun went back, and he lengthened the life of the king [23].

The Lord gave Hezekiah a sign as he asked (2 Kgs 20:8), to confirm the fulfillment of the divine promise thus: the sun's going back ten degrees (Isa 38:8). Some see that it was merely the retreat of the shadow on the steps that lead to a "balcony" in the palace or that lead to the upper room. And some see that it was an eclipse of the sun that occurred on January 11, 689 BC. The sun is the true measure of time, and in the hand of God, the mover of history and events and time itself, He used it as a sign in the days of Joshua (Josh 10:12), and also in the days of Hezekiah, and when the Lord of glory was crucified, and before His final coming when the sun will be darkened.
And with a great spirit he saw the last things, and comforted [20] those who mourn in Zion [24].

The message of Isaiah was the revealing of the last times, to arouse in the people the spirit of hope, especially concerning the Incarnation of the Son of God and His offering Himself as a sacrifice of salvation. And the writers of the New Testament, such as St. Matthew the Evangelist, quoted much from the prophecies of Isaiah about the person of the Lord Christ and His life and His characteristics and His ministry, especially concerning the mystery of the Cross.

entries.section: 3. In praise of King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah

paragraphs.text: And he revealed what would be to the last times, and the hidden things before they came to pass [25].

The prophecies of the prophet Isaiah were distinguished not only by their multitude, but by their wonderful precision, especially the birth of the Lord Christ from a virgin, and the affirmation that He is the Mighty God, and details about the mystery of the Cross and its message.

The subject of the "Kingdom of God" with Isaiah is not only given priority over any other subject, but he counts it the main element in everything. He wishes to send every believer forth to see and understand the plan of God, not only in his own time but to the end of the ages.

In the view of the prophet Isaiah, the wise seer, the foundation of the believer's life is not the management of his temporal affairs, but that he be far-sighted. Not to be concerned with his needs through tens of years and the life of his children and grandchildren, but to gaze upon what happens until the end of the world and the passing over into the age to come.
Inspired by Sirach 48

entries.section: By Your wisdom You raise up in every generation wise men who challenge the darkness!

paragraphs.text: v I praise You, O incarnate Wisdom of God, Giver of wisdom and discernment and strength and holiness.
By Your wisdom You sent fiery Elijah to challenge the killer of the prophets.
And by Your wisdom You sent Elisha, the wonder-worker, even in his grave his bones raised a dead man!
And by Your wisdom You raised up King Hezekiah, who did not flatter his father but demolished his idols!
And by Your wisdom You sent the prophet Isaiah to support the believers in the midst of corruption, that they might come to know the Savior of sinners.
v In every generation You send men of God, each suited to his time, to save all!
And with every believer You offer gifts and abilities by Your divine plan for the salvation of his own soul and his brethren.
My heart cries to You, saying: We praise You for Your wonderful works in every generation.
O Lord of the harvest, send laborers, for the harvest is plenteous, but the laborers are few.
Reveal to every believer his mission, for the edification of Your eternal Kingdom!
Grant us not to despise anyone, You who chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise!
To You be glory, O You who are wonderful in Your wisdom and Your plan and Your power!

entries.section: 1. Praise of Josiah the righteous king

paragraphs.text: 1 The remembrance of Josiah is like the composition of the perfume that is made by the art of the apothecary. 2 It is sweet as honey in every mouth, and as music at a banquet of wine. 3 He was appointed to turn the people to repentance by his hand; and he took away the abominations of iniquity. 4 He directed his heart unto the Lord, and in the days of the ungodly he established godliness.
The remembrance of Josiah is like a composition of incense prepared by the art of the apothecary; it is sweet in every mouth like honey, and like music at a banquet of wine [1].
No godly king, a man of faith, was found in the seventh century B.C. except Josiah, the great reformer who reigned in Jerusalem from 640 B.C. until his death in the battle of Megiddo in 609 B.C.
Jeroboam the son of Nebat was a byword for evil, and Josiah was a byword for the removal of idols (2 Kgs 22-23; 2 Chr 35:1-6).

The use of music at tables of food is an expression of the spirit of joy, as it was used in the parable of the son who returned to his father (Lk 15). It was as though Josiah, by his walk in the Lord, were sending forth joy and gladness into the life of the believers.

entries.section: 1. Praise of Josiah the righteous king

paragraphs.text: He led in the turning of the people, and he rooted out the abominations of iniquity [2].

Like the writers of Kings and Chronicles, Ben Sira took note of his great role in purifying the Promised Land from idolatry [2]. Ben Sira did not mention the discovery of the Law in the Temple in 622 B.C. (2 Kgs 22:3-13; 2 Chr 34:14-21). Ben Sira highlighted the difficulty of the work in the time of Josiah, since he lived in an atmosphere of great corruption, and his age was called "the days of iniquity."

entries.section: 1. Praise of Josiah the righteous king

paragraphs.text: And he directed his heart to the Lord; and in the days of iniquity he strengthened godliness [3].

entries.section: 2. The wicked kings of Judah and the Babylonian captivity

paragraphs.text: 5 All except David and Hezekiah and Josiah were guilty of transgression. 6 They forsook the law of the Most High. The kings of Judah failed. 7 They gave their horn unto others, and their glory to a strange nation. 8 They burned the chosen city of the sanctuary, and made her streets desolate, according to the prophecy of Jeremiah. 9 For they entreated him evil, who yet was sanctified in the womb a prophet, to root out, and to afflict, and to destroy; and likewise to build up and to plant.
They all sinned one after another, except David, Hezekiah and Josiah, for they forsook the law of the Most High. The kings of Judah failed [4].
Josiah was worthy to be counted with David and Hezekiah, for the three were kings distinguished by godliness and faith.

The secret of the corruption of the kings of Judah was their forsaking of the Law, and consequently they did not cleave to God; so God allowed the chastening of Judah through the fall of Jerusalem into the Babylonian captivity in 587 B.C.
For they gave their power to others, and their glory to a strange nation [5].

entries.section: 2. The wicked kings of Judah and the Babylonian captivity

paragraphs.text: (The enemies) burned with fire the chosen city, the city of the sanctuary, and made her streets desolate [6].
Jerusalem was exposed to ruin, and her streets became as a wilderness, and the enemies also defiled the Temple and destroyed it.

entries.section: 2. The wicked kings of Judah and the Babylonian captivity

paragraphs.text: According to the word of Jeremiah, they entreated him evil, who was sanctified as a prophet while he was still in his mother's womb, to pluck up, to destroy and to ruin, and likewise to build up and to plant [7].

Ben Sira calls us to read the Lamentations of Jeremiah, which he wrote when he saw destruction come upon the city and the people, and the princes, the nobles and the gifted were led into captivity in 587 B.C.

The prophet who was linked to King Josiah is Jeremiah, whose prophetic ministry extended even after the fall of Judah into the Babylonian captivity. Each of them was in bitterness because of the spiritual corruption of the kingdom of Judah. It seems that they both failed in the spiritual reform of the kingdom, yet both remain great in the eyes of God because of their zeal and their striving.

King Josiah died in the battle of Megiddo against Pharaoh, when he tried to support Babylon against Pharaoh, and in less than 20 years Babylon laid Jerusalem waste, and Jeremiah was killed in Egypt, in the land from which Moses had come out with the people to lead them across into the wilderness and to enter the Promised Land.

The prophecies of the prophet Jeremiah are full of sorrow, since the time of the Babylonian captivity was drawing near while the leaders and the people treated the matter lightly and with contempt. This was a burden on his soul. He tried to keep silent but could not (Jer 20:9). The captivity was fulfilled in his days, and he saw the destruction of Jerusalem and its complete burning (Jer 38:14-39:10; 52:12-13; 2 Kgs 25:1-21).

10 It was Ezekiel who saw the glorious vision, which was shown him upon the chariot of the cherubim. 11 For He made mention of the enemies under the figure of the rain, and directed them that went right. 12 And of the twelve prophets let the bones flourish out of their place; for they comforted Jacob, and delivered them by assured hope.

Ben Sira declared that God's care for the people while they were under chastening had not ceased. The people had become like the bones of the dead, but the prophets received grace from God to raise the dead spiritually, just as the bones of the dead Elisha raised the man who was cast into the grave.
Ezekiel himself saw the vision of glory; God showed it to him upon the chariot of the cherubim [8].

Ezekiel is regarded as a shining star among the prophets in the land of captivity. His book begins with the vision of the divine throne, so that God may assure His people that He longs for them to share with the heavenly ones in enjoying His glory; and on the other hand, that He has no need of the Temple which they defiled, nor of offerings and worship, unless their hearts are holy to Him, prepared for His dwelling. And the book ends with the glorious temple of the New Covenant. Thus the prophet Ezekiel prophesied in the land of captivity, opening the door of hope to his people.

He saw the vision of the dry bones that became alive and stood up as an exceeding great army (Ezek 37:8-10). Because the people were driven out of their homeland on account of their idolatrous abominations and their shedding of blood, their cities were turned into ruins in which no one dwelt, and they became like a place full of many bones, very dry. In other words, they became like an open grave holding lifeless bones! This is not a picture of the cities but rather of the people themselves, who were scattered in many places with a broken soul, and became like a valley of death containing dry bones that need someone to raise them from their death, gather them together again and give them life.

Ben Sira felt that the people had come to be in a state of death, indeed that they had become dry bones through their rejection of the divine wisdom and their preoccupation with vain wisdom; but the Lord alone is able to touch these dry bones, give them life, and make them stand upon their feet and set out toward the heavenly Jerusalem. This was fulfilled by the incarnation of the Wisdom of God and His offering of Himself as a sacrifice; and when He was laid in the tomb, He touched the dry bones that were in Hades and set out with them to Paradise.
O that the Lord would enter every heart as into a tomb, to take our souls to His Paradise!
For He made mention of His enemies in a thunderstorm, and did good to those who direct their ways uprightly [9].
Let the bones of the twelve indeed flourish out of their place, for they comforted[1] the people of Jacob, and delivered them with steadfast hope [10].

Ben Sira calls us to take care of the writings of the prophets, such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the twelve minor prophets, as he highlighted before the role of prophets such as Elijah and Elisha.

13 How shall we magnify Zerubbabel? For he was as a signet on the right hand. 14 So was Jesus the son of Josedec; for they in their days builded the house, and set up a holy people to the Lord, which was prepared for everlasting glory. 15 And among the elect was Neemias, whose renown is great, who raised up for us the walls that were fallen, and set up the gates and the bars, and raised up our ruins again.
Ben Sira mentioned three heroes of faith who built the house of the Lord and the wall of the city, and who cared for the word of God and worship.
The processions of return from the captivity were three.

The first procession was in 538/537 B.C. under the leadership of Zerubbabel (Sheshbazzar), the grandson of King Jehoiachin, and Jeshua the priest. Zerubbabel represented the civil authority, and Jeshua the priest represented the religious authority. Cyrus the Persian did not send Zerubbabel as a king with full freedom to act.

It is the procession of liberation from the devil and of ascent to the heavenly Jerusalem under the leadership of the Lord of glory Jesus, as King of kings and at the same time the heavenly High Priest, bearing kingship and priesthood at the same time.
The second procession was in 458 B.C. under the leadership of Ezra the scribe, who dealt with the problem of those married to pagan women (Ezra 7-10).

The third procession was in 445/444 B.C. under the leadership of Nehemiah the governor, who was concerned with building the wall; it was built in 52 days. The walls were dedicated, the Law was read, and the people enjoyed the joy of the Spirit (Neh 1-13). Zerubbabel stood out as a descendant of King David, as a type of Christ, the King of kings. In the second company Ezra the priest stood out as a type of the Word of God and the great High Priest, and in the last company Nehemiah, faithful in his work, stood out as a type of the Lord Christ, who is called the Faithful.
How shall we magnify Zerubbabel?
He is without doubt like a signet on the right hand [11].

He led the first company to Israel (Ezra 2:2); together with Jeshua and his brethren the priests he took part in building the altar for offering the burnt offerings and ordering the worship (Ezra 3:1-9). He was appointed governor and laid the foundation of the Temple (Zech 4:6-10). He labored for the rebuilding of the Temple, so it was called Zerubbabel's Temple, and the building remained standing until the year 20 B.C., when Herod rebuilt it anew.
So also Jeshua the son of Jozadak; in their days the house was built, and the holy temple of the Lord was set up, prepared for everlasting glory [12].
And the remembrance of Nehemiah is lasting; it was he who raised up for us the wall that was fallen, and set up for us the gates and the bars, and built the sites of our dwellings again [13].

He was born in captivity; he was not of royal descent like Zerubbabel, nor of priestly descent like Ezra, nor the holder of an administrative position like Daniel the prime minister; rather, his intense love for God and for his people made him a leader.

He used to taste the wine before the king so that the king might be assured that it was not poisoned. This position was distinguished in the Persian era. The king's cupbearer was often a eunuch, which explains why no mention is made of Nehemiah's family. Ezra preceded him to Jerusalem by about 13 years. Nehemiah was concerned with building the wall despite the opposition of the enemies to it; and he was also concerned with the inner building of the people. Then he returned to Susa, the capital, and did not remain there long, for he went back to Jerusalem as governor of Judah for at least 12 years. He represented true spiritual leadership. What occupied him was the sufferings of his brethren. He learned leadership through bended knees, silence, tears and crying out. He practiced prayer in every circumstance.

entries.section: 5. The men of God before the Law

paragraphs.text: 16 But upon the earth was no man created like Enoch; for he was taken from the earth. 17 Neither was there a man born like unto Joseph, a governor of his brethren, a stay of the people. 18 His bones were regarded of the Lord, and after his death they prophesied. 19 Shem and Seth were in great honour among men, and so was Adam above every living thing in the creation.
No one was created upon the earth like Enoch, for he was taken up from the earth [14].

Now, lest the reader be occupied with the history of the heroes, Ben Sira wished to show that each of the heroes of faith has an excellence in a particular respect that differs from the rest of the heroes.
Enoch was worthy, by his godliness, of a unique friendship with God, so He took him from the earth to heaven.

And Joseph was worthy, by his love for his brothers and his not repaying them for their treachery against him, so he became the ruler of his brothers, who took his bones with them in the Exodus under the leadership of Moses.
And Shem covered his father Noah when he was uncovered because of drunkenness (Gen 9), and Seth was the secret of the consolation of his parents (Gen 4).
As for Adam, although he and his wife Eve sinned, we are indebted to him as the father of all humanity according to the flesh.
And no man was born like Joseph, the ruler of his brothers and the support of his people; and they cared for his bones [15].

The translation of Enoch from the earth is considered the planting of the seed of the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead and the enjoyment of the other life; and also Joseph's concern that his bones be carried to the Promised Land carries a hint of hope in the coming resurrection.
Shem and Seth were glorified among men, and Adam was above every living thing in creation [16].

Seth, a type of the Lord Christ: Many of the Fathers spoke of Seth from various aspects. St. Mar Jacob of Sarug recorded for us a special homily on Seth, in his poetic style that stirs the soul, in 140 lines. Through it the believer feels that God does not leave a believer in bitterness, but with the multitude of sufferings and their bitterness, His divine consolations increase in their sweetness. As St. Mar Jacob of Sarug shares with our first parents Adam and Eve the bitterness of their souls on account of the killing of Abel at the hands of his brother Cain, he touches the wondrous divine consolations that overflowed upon them at the birth of their son Seth. The secret of their consolation is not that God gave them a son in place of Abel and Cain, when they saw death for the first time in their lives and realized how the earthly body returns to the dust. They also saw Cain in great terror, fearing the animals and being frightened even of his own shadow. Rather, they saw in Seth the surpassing love of God and the consolations of heaven, and they understood divine mysteries that lifted their hearts as though to heaven. 1. Seth was a type of the incarnate Word of God, who gladdens humanity by His salvation. 2. Seth stands over against Cain, for the latter is the founder of the earthly city that leads man down toward the abyss, and the former is the founder of the heavenly city that lifts the depths of the believer to Paradise!
v O glorious Son, who resembles His Father as Seth (resembled) Adam, put upon my tongue the beauty of Your mystery, that I may speak of it.
O Son, who consoled Eve by Your mystery and removed her grief, stir my word with Your power that I may recount Your story.
I have suffered because of the grief that befell the house of Adam! My Lord, help me to speak of their consolation by means of radiant Seth.
I had spoken of the great suffering of Abel, and of the curses with which Cain was cursed by God.
I mentioned before you the sacrifices of the two sons of Adam, and the narrative proceeded to the reading according to its order.
I had also spoken of the lamentations of our mother Eve, and of the intensity of a mother's grief over her beloved.
Today it is needful for me to speak of their consolation, and by what cause they forgot their bitter afflictions.
Let me first recount what sufferings overtook them, and afterward I will return to the consolation that made them glad [2].
St. Mar Jacob of Sarug, inspired by Sirach 49

entries.section: How great are Your shining stars!

paragraphs.text: v My soul blesses You for Your wondrous shining, O Sun of Righteousness.
In every generation many think as though the world has become utterly corrupt.
But You fill our hearts with the joy of hope in You.
You send forth Your light in the midst of darkness, and raise up from humanity radiant stars!
In the last period of the kingdom of Judah, corrupt kings succeeded one another, who devoted their lives to the corruption of Your people!
You raised up King Josiah as though he were a censer sending forth pure incense that bears Your fragrant aroma.
When one speaks of him, his mouth becomes a spring of sweet honey.
And when we look at the work of Your grace in him, we realize that You raise up musicians who fill the world with the joy of the Spirit!
v In the bitterness of the captivity, the powers of darkness could not keep the soul of Ezekiel from enjoying the glories of Your divine throne.

entries.section: 1. The works of Simon son of Onias

paragraphs.text: 1 Simon the high priest, the son of Onias, who in his life repaired the house again, and in his days fortified the temple. 2 And by him was founded the double height, the high fortification of the wall about the temple. 3 In his days the wells of waters were dug, and the cistern, like the sea, reached its full measure of overflowing. 4 He took thought for his people that they should not perish, and fortified the city that it should not be taken.

entries.section: 1. The works of Simon son of Onias

paragraphs.text: Simon the son of Onias, the high priest, the leader of his brethren and the glory of his people[4], was the one who repaired the house in his life, and fortified the temple in his days [1].
He also laid the foundation of the wall of double height, and of the strong wall surrounding the temple [2].
In his days a reservoir of waters was dug, a cistern like the sea in its circuit (or borders) [3].

entries.section: 1. The works of Simon son of Onias

paragraphs.text: He dug the great basin in the midst of the temple to supply the needs of the sacrifices, the purification and the washing. In the days of Pontius Pilate this huge cistern was still standing; water was brought to it from outside Jerusalem, and its capacity was very great, and a pumping machine was fitted to it to feed the other reservoirs in the temple[5].
He was concerned for the deliverance of his people from destruction, so he fortified the city so that it might withstand a siege [4].

5 How glorious was he in the midst of the people, in his coming out of the house of the veil! 6 He was as the morning star in the midst of a cloud, and as the moon at the full: 7 as the sun shining upon the temple of the Most High, 8 and as the rainbow giving light in the bright clouds: and as the flower of roses in the spring of the year, as lilies by the rivers of waters, and as the branches of the frankincense tree in the time of summer: 9 as fire and incense in the censer, 10 and as a vessel of beaten gold set with all manner of precious stones: 11 and as a fair olive tree budding forth fruit, and as a cypress which groweth up to the clouds. When he put on the robe of honour, and was clothed with the perfection of glory, 12 when he went up to the holy altar, he made the garment of holiness honourable. 13 And when he took the portions out of the priests' hands, he himself stood by the hearth of the altar, compassed with a garland of his brethren round about, as a young cedar in Libanus; 14 and as palm trees compassed they him about. And all the sons of Aaron in their glory, 15 and the oblations of the Lord in their hands, before all the congregation of Israel. And finishing the service at the altar, that he might adorn the offering of the Most High Almighty, 16 he stretched out his hand to the cup, and poured of the blood of the grape. 17 He poured out at the foot of the altar a sweet-smelling savour unto the Most High King of all. 18 Then shouted the sons of Aaron, and sounded the silver trumpets, and made a great noise to be heard, for a remembrance before the Most High.

Sirach presents to us the person of Simon son of Onias as a wonderful model of a life of worship in holiness, whose features are the following: 1. The secret of his glory is that he meets with God in the Holy of Holies behind the house of the veil [5], and when he comes out he is surrounded by his people in great glory [5]. Thus Ben Sira ties together, in the life of the leader as a lofty model for every believer, a hidden life and a secret meeting with God as in the Holy of Holies, and that he not withdraw from the brethren. There is no contradiction between the glory that he enjoys secretly from God and the glory that shines from him through his love and service for his brethren [5]. 2. The secret of his holiness is that he rises above earthly things, and lives in the pledge of the heavenly things, like the morning star shining among the clouds, and like the moon in the perfection of its light when it becomes full [6]. 3. Wherever Simon son of Onias is found, glory, splendor, surpassing light and holiness do not leave him. Thus Ben Sira sees him in many situations that reveal various aspects of glory and splendor, of which we mention the following:
a. Behind the veil in the Holy of Holies [5] he enjoys solitude and a secret dialogue with the Holy One, and so is sanctified.
b. In the temple he is surrounded by his people in love for them; he serves them, teaches them and leads them in a spirit of love. How glorious he is! [5].
c. Among the clouds he shines like the morning star [6].
d. In the heaven he is like a moon perfect in splendor, in the state of a full moon, all light [6].
e. On high he is like a sun shining with the divine light upon the temple of the Most High [7].
f. In the divine presence he is like the rainbow, the sign of the divine covenant with men, shining in the clouds of the splendor of continual care [7].
g. In the fields he is like a flower among the roses, like a lily by a spring of water, or a cedar tree in the time of summer [8].
h. As he offers incense to God he himself becomes like fire, not to burn a man, but to burn fragrant incense, which points to the ascent of prayers to God.
i. As he uses the holy vessels he himself becomes a golden vessel, that is, a heavenly one for the service of the Heavenly One, set with precious stones [9].
j. In the garden of the house of the Lord he is like the fruitful olive tree, or like the cypress rising to the clouds [10].
k. As he puts on the garments of glory and goes up to the holy altar, the court of the house of the Lord is filled with the holiness that the Holy One pours out upon him [11].
l. When he takes from the hands of the priests the portions of the sacrifice, he sees the priests gathering round him in love, joy and exultation like a garland that encircles him.
m. As he poured the blood of the grape upon the altar, the Lord smelled it as a savour of good pleasure and delight on behalf of all the people.
n. As the sons of Aaron shout with exultation and praise and blow the trumpets of the word of God, this worship goes up before the throne of the Most High.
How glorious he was, surrounded by his people at his coming out from behind the house of the veil! [5].

This statement is probably a description of what the high priest does on the great Day of Atonement (Lev 16:23-25), when the high priest comes out of the Holy of Holies, from the veil, to the inner court. The Church has taken this rite for some feasts. Here he describes the service of the great Day of Atonement, revealing the skill of the high priest Simon son of Onias and the creativity in the service inside the temple. Ben Sira often records what he saw with his own eyes, as he records his feelings of joy and peace in his depths and in the hearts of those around him. He felt as though he had returned to the days of glory that Israel experienced at the completion of the building of Solomon's temple.
In verses 6-10 there comes a series of similes drawn from the beauty of nature, like those found in (Sir 24:13-17), to affirm the spiritual beauty of the high priest.
Like the morning star among the clouds, and like the moon at the full [6].
Or the sun shining upon the temple of the Most High, or the rainbow shining among the clouds of glory [7].
Or like the flower of roses in the days of the first fruits, or like the lily by a spring of water, or the branches of Lebanon in a summer day[6] [8].
Or like fire and incense in the censer, or a vessel of beaten gold set with every precious stone [9].
Or like an olive tree that bears fresh fruit, and like a cypress tree rising to the clouds [10].
v Let us then be like this, like olive trees, laden with commandments on every side. For it is not enough for us to become like olive trees; we must also be fruitful[7].

St. John Chrysostom: v Be like a green olive tree in the house of God. Never lose hope, but be fortified by faith with the flowers of sincerity, so that you may resemble that plant... indeed surpass it in bearing fruit, if every day you bring in a yield, overflowing with the giving of alms[8].

St. Basil the Great: In verses 11-13 he speaks of the morning and evening sacrifices which the high priest offers, which were mentioned before in (Sir 45:14), since the descendants of Aaron offered them twice every day without ceasing. The rites of this offering were known as tamid, that is, the continual offering (Ex 29:38-42). What is recorded in the Mishnah (Tamid 7:2-3) is that the ordinary priests stand around the high priest at the altar, presenting to him certain parts of the animal for the high priest to offer as a sacrifice. In this he resembles what students of the medical college and nurses do as they stand around the surgeon, handing him the special instruments so that he may perform the surgery.
When he put on the robe of glory, and was clothed with the perfection of honor, and as he went up to the holy altar, he made the court of the sanctuary glorious [11].

Moreover, the garment of Christ, or His clothing, points to the Church that clings to Him, for this garment the Lord washed with His pure blood... And as St. Cyprian says: [When the blood of the wine is indicated, what does it mean other than the wine of the cup of the Lord's blood?![9]] And St. Clement of Alexandria says: [The vine produces wine, and the Word offers blood; both bring health, the wine for the body and the blood for the spirit[10]]. And St. Augustine says: [What is this garment which he washes in wine, that is, washes in His blood from sin... but the Church[11].

And when he took the portion from the hands of the priests, standing by the hearth of the altar, a garland of brethren was around him, like a young cedar in Lebanon, and they surrounded him like the trunks of palm trees [12].
And all the sons of Aaron were in their glory, and the offering of the Lord was in their hands before all the congregation of Israel [13].

At the completion of the service at the altar and the ordering of the offering of the Most High Almighty [14], he would stretch out his hand to the cup, and pour out of the blood of the grape; he would pour it at the foot of the altar, a sweet-smelling savour before the Most High, the King of all [15].
Verses 14-15 describe the pouring out of wine [called libations, as mentioned in (Num 28:7-8)], which, as recorded in the Mishnah, was a daily rite accompanied by the blowing of the beaten trumpets.

v Now the blood of the Lord is twofold: one material, which saves us from corruption (1 Pet 1:8), and the other spiritual, by which we are anointed. To drink the blood of Christ is to partake of incorruption (Jn 6:55). But the Spirit is the power of the Word, in the same way as the blood is of the flesh. In the same way wine is mixed with water, and the Spirit with man. The first, the mixture, gives us joy so that faith increases, and the other, the spiritual, leads us to incorruption. The union of the two, that is, of the draught and the Word, is called the Eucharist, a gift worthy of praise, supremely splendid; those who partake of it are sanctified in body and soul, for this is the will of the Father. For man, a composite creature made by God, is united with the Spirit and the Word. In truth the Spirit is united entirely with the soul which depends on Him, and the flesh is united with the Word, since for its sake "the Word was made flesh" (Jn 1:14)[12].

St. Clement of Alexandria: As the Apostle Paul encourages his disciple to strive by the power of the Spirit for the preaching of the truth, fulfilling his ministry to the end with joy, he presented himself as an example, for he strove to the last breath. How wonderful indeed are his words: "For I am being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure is at hand" (2 Tim 4:6).

It is as though the Apostle had gone back in memory to Jacob, the father of all the tribes, who set up a pillar and poured a drink offering upon it and poured oil on it (Gen 35:14). This drink offering was probably of wine, which he offered on the pillar as the dedication of the first house to be set up for God in the history of salvation, as a reference to the gift of the joy of the Holy Spirit that fills the house of God, that is, His people. It is as though the Apostle saw, in the midst of his sufferings inside the prison as he went forth to the arena of martyrdom, that the spirit of divine joy fills the life of the Church through the sufferings of the Apostle.

And perhaps the Apostle, as he speaks of himself as a drink offering being poured out, remembers what the Law required, the offering of two lambs every day, the one in the morning and the other in the evening, while at its offering a drink offering of wine was made for it (Ex 29:40-41). It is as though the sacrifice of the Cross were tied to the joy of the Holy Spirit who is poured out upon the Church through the slain divine Lamb. This is our continual experience: in the liturgy of the Eucharist, as the Church offers to the Father, by the Holy Spirit, the offering of the only-begotten Son, His body given for us, He pours out upon her and within her His divine joy by the descent of His surpassing Holy Spirit! This is what has lifted the Church to sing the liturgy of the Eucharist as a hymn of surpassing joy, the work of the Holy Spirit, the giver of true joy!
Then the sons of Aaron would shout, and blow the beaten trumpets, and make a great sound as a remembrance before the Most High [16].

The sounds of the trumpets which the priests sounded were a proclamation of the beginning of the service or the sacrifice, and they were still in use in the age of Ben Sira (Num 10:2, 10); at that time all the believers would fall on their faces to the ground, and this moving spiritual atmosphere was interspersed with the praises of the Levites, while the people made supplication to the Lord.
"The Most High, the King of all": such a phrase was a hidden preparation for the salvation that the King of kings offers for the salvation of the whole world and not for the Jews alone.

v When our Lord Jesus comes (whose coming was symbolized of old by Joshua the son of Nun), He sends His priests, the Apostles, carrying trumpets of beaten (hammered) metal (Num 10:2; Ps 98:6), that is, the great heavenly teaching of preaching.

Matthew first sounded a priestly trumpet in his Gospel, and Mark and Luke and John also each blew his priestly trumpets. Peter also made his trumpet resound through his two epistles, as did James and Jude. John went on sounding his trumpet in his epistles, and so did Luke when he described the Acts of the Apostles. And finally there came the one who said: "I think that God hath set forth us the apostles last" (1 Cor 4:9); he sent forth thunderings with the trumpets of his fourteen epistles. He made the walls of Jericho, the idolatry that had been invented and the thoughts of the philosophers, collapse from their foundations[13].
Origen

entries.section: 3. Exhortation to give glory to God

paragraphs.text: 19 And then all the people together hasted, and fell down to the earth upon their faces to worship their Lord God Almighty, the Most High. 20 The singers also sang praises with their voices, and in the great house was made sweet melody. 21 And the people besought the Lord, the Most High, by prayer before him that is merciful, till the solemnity of the Lord was ended, and they had finished his service.
At that time all the people would hasten together, and fall with their faces to the earth, to worship their Lord, the Almighty, the Most High [17].

The high priest alone was permitted to pronounce the holy name of God "Yahweh" when he announced God's forgiveness to the people (Lev 16:30). It is recorded in the Mishnah (Yoma 6:2): "When the priests and the people... hear the expression of the name (Yahweh) coming from the mouth of the high priest, they worship, and bow down, and fall on their faces."
And the singers also praised with their voices, and their songs were sweet with varied voices [18].
And the people also prayed to the Lord the Most High with a prayer before the Merciful, until the ordering of the Lord was finished and they completed His liturgy [19].

22 Then he went down, and lifted up his hands over the whole congregation of the children of Israel, to give the blessing of the Lord with his lips, and to glory in his name. 23 And he bowed himself down to worship the second time, that he might receive a blessing from the Most High.
Then he went down and lifted up his hands over the whole congregation of the children of Israel, and gloried in His name (the name of the Lord) [20].

The service reaches its climax when the high priest stands to bless the people with the traditional priestly blessing found in (Lev 9:2; Num 6:24-26). As for pronouncing the name of the Lord "Yahweh," it was not permitted at that time for anyone to pronounce it, but it was replaced in reading by Adonai, except on the Day of Atonement, when the high priest was permitted to pronounce this fearful, blessed name to call down blessing upon the people.
Then they bow down to worship a second time, to receive the blessing from the Most High [21].

The Jews used to repeat the prostrations (metanoias), especially on the great Day of Atonement, which is what the Church does, especially on Great Friday, as she asks for God's mercies through the Cross as an atonement for our sins.

entries.section: 5. A prayer for the peace of Israel

paragraphs.text: 24 And now bless ye the God of all, which only doeth wondrous things everywhere, which exalteth our days from the womb, and dealeth with us according to his mercy. 25 He grant us joyfulness of heart, and that peace may be in our days in Israel for ever: 26 that he would confirm his mercy with us, and deliver us at his time!
And now bless the God of all, who does great things in every manner, who glorifies our days from our birth, and deals with us according to His mercy [22].
May He grant us joy of heart, and may there be peace in our days, in Israel as in the days of old [23]
May He entrust to us His mercy, and may He redeem us in our days! [24]

"May He redeem us" or "save us": the Jews were awaiting the coming of the Messiah, the Savior! And this was fulfilled in the life, sufferings, crucifixion and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ (Eph 1:7-14; Rom 8:22-23).

27 There be two manner of nations which my heart abhorreth, and the third is no nation: 28 they that sit upon the mountain of Samaria, and they that dwell among the Philistines, and that foolish people that dwell in Sichem.
Two nations my soul abhors, and the third is no nation: [25]
Those who dwell on the mountain of Samaria[14], and the Philistines, and the foolish people who dwell in Shechem [26].

The Samaritans built a temple like the temple of Jerusalem on Mount Gerizim near Shechem, south of present-day Nablus, and the temple was still standing in the days of Ben Sira, although the Jews destroyed it in 128 B.C.

The present-day Samaritans still celebrate the Feast of the Passover beside their temple near Nablus. The Samaritans also claim that the line descending from Aaron the high priest has been broken, and that they alone, and no others, preserve an unbroken line descending from Aaron through Phinehas; this is what drove Ben Sira to hostility toward the Samaritans.

29 Jesus the son of Sirach of Jerusalem hath written in this book the instruction of understanding and knowledge, who out of his heart poured forth wisdom. 30 Blessed is he that shall be exercised in these things; and he that layeth them up in his heart shall become wise. 31 For if he do them, he shall be strong to all things: for the light of the Lord leadeth him.
This was added by the grandson, the translator of the book.
Jesus the son of Sirach the son of Eleazar of Jerusalem, who rained wisdom from his heart[15] in this book, I have written an instruction in understanding and knowledge [27].

Ben Sira signs his words, and encourages keeping and following them, for God gave them to him, and they are not from his own wisdom, or a merely human work, or something transmitted from the sages around him in the ancient world such as Hammurabi, Ahikar, Akhenaten and others; so he poured them out upon the sons of his people and withheld nothing.
Blessed is he who guides himself by them, for he who lays them up in his heart will be wise [28].
And if he does them, he will grow strong in everything, for the light of the Lord is his way [29].

What remains now is that they put them into practice, not merely passing them on in their gatherings, banquets and writings, and not treating them lightly either, for he who puts them into practice fulfills his hopes and is able to do all things, because the Lord will be a light to him through the words of wisdom that come out of the Law, also "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path" (Ps 119:105).
Inspired by Sirach 50

entries.section: May You shine with Your splendor upon Your Church!

paragraphs.text: v Grant us, O heavenly High Priest, to enjoy Your Holy Spirit, for He alone repairs Your temple in our hearts.
And He surrounds our souls like a wall of fire that protects us from the arrows of the enemy.
And He makes springs of living water burst forth within us.
v You raise up from our dark souls shining stars, and You send forth in us Your sweet fragrance, and You establish Your covenant within us, and fill us with Your peace.
You accept our prayers as a fragrant incense.
And You plant in us Your cross like an evergreen olive tree.
v Grant us Your righteousness as a garment in which we may be covered.
Set up Your altar within us, and Your Spirit will pour out heavenly joy.
We submit to You, and worship You rejoicing with the heavenly orders.
With pride the trumpets sound within us with Your life-giving word.
Turn our life into an unceasing hymn that we play all the days of our sojourn.
v You are our wondrous Redeemer.
The devil, with all his wiles and evil works, does not terrify us.
Through his wars, however fierce they become, we enjoy the crown of victory.
You are our support, our salvation, our glory and our crown.

1 A prayer of Jesus the son of Sirach: I will give thanks unto You, O Lord and King, and praise You, O God my Savior. 2 I give thanks unto Your name, for You have been my defender and helper, 3 and have redeemed my body from destruction, and from the snare of the slanderous tongue, and from the lips of those that forge lies, and were my helper against those that withstood me, 4 and have delivered me, according to the multitude of Your mercies and of Your name, from the roaring of those prepared to devour. 5 Out of the hands of such as sought after my life, and from the many afflictions which I had; 6 from the choking of the fire on every side, and from the midst of the fire where I was not burned; 7 from the depth of the belly of hell, from an unclean tongue, and from lying words, and from the slander of an unrighteous tongue before the king. 8 My soul drew near unto death, 9 and my life was near to the depth of hell. 10 They compassed me on every side, and there was no man to help me. I looked for the succor of men, but there was none. 11 Then I remembered Your mercy, O Lord, and Your works of old: 12 how You deliver those that wait for You, and save them out of the hands of the nations. 13 Then I lifted up my prayer from the earth, and prayed for deliverance from death. 14 I called upon the Lord the Father of my Lord, that He would not leave me in the days of my trouble, in the time of the proud, when there was no help. 15 I will praise Your name continually, and will sing praise with thanksgiving, for my prayer was heard. 16 For You saved me from destruction, and delivered me from the evil time. 17 Therefore will I give thanks unto You, and praise You, and bless the name of the Lord.

If the book calls for fellowship in praise, on the other hand the believer must offer a hymn of thanksgiving for God's dealings with him personally, as Savior and King. This hymn, or this psalm, comes bearing the echo of many of the hymns found in the book of Psalms, especially the two psalms (Ps 120; 136).
This hymn came as a practical model of thanksgiving for deliverance from the plots of hidden and open enemies.

a. The desire to praise the Lord: Before Ben Sira sets out what befell him, he made clear at the beginning, as at the end, his earnest desire to praise God [1, 12], as though the believer, whether he enters into trials or does not, never ceases in his depths to give thanks to God. Rather, trials, however intense they become, kindle the heart still more to give thanks to God for His works with us in the midst of affliction.
b. Ben Sira's deliverance from certain death [2-6].
c. God's wondrous salvation: when a man feels isolated, with no helper to support him, the Lord reveals Himself in his life as King and Savior.
d. The Lord's response to the cries of his heart [10].
e. His setting out to praise [12].
I give thanks to You, O Lord the King, and I praise You, O God my Savior, and I give thanks to Your name [1].

Ben Sira revealed his longing to praise the Lord, his King and Savior. And in great brevity he enumerated the dangers that befell him and from which the Lord rescued him, for men had forsaken him, and he had drawn near to death; they had threatened him and wanted to devour him.

The secret of praise is the believer's realization of the truth about God, that He is the King of kings, the Ruler of all, and the Savior who loves all mankind. God, in His fatherhood to humanity, will not ignore the needs of any man, and in His work of salvation He is able to give us His divine righteousness in place of our sins and weaknesses.

For You are my fortress and my helper, and You have delivered my body from destruction, and from the snare of the slandering tongue, and from lying lips. And against those who withstood me You were my help, and You redeemed me [2].

He likens the tongue of the slanderer to the bites of a poisonous serpent, which fasten into a man's body and instill their deadly venom in it. God, in honoring man, gave him perfect freedom. But when he abuses what God has given, using his tongue for slander and his mouth for lying and setting snares for the righteous, God does not allow the rod of the sinners to rest upon the head of the righteous (Ps 125:3).
v God may sometimes permit the rod of sinners to strike the righteous, but He does not let this rod rest for a long time. What is the rod of sinners but their power, their dominion and their harm?

St. John Chrysostom: According to the greatness of Your mercy and Your name, from my being devoured as one prepared for eating, and from the hands of those who seek my soul, and from the many afflictions that I endured [3].

Some see that Sirach's song here points to his deliverance from a deadly danger because of false accusations that a man who opposed the truth brought against Ben Sira before one of the kings, and Ben Sira was on the point of being killed.
And from the choking of the flame which surrounded me on every side, and from the midst of the fire which I had not kindled [4].

Through the flame of the fire of an extremely cruel injustice all the doors of human help are closed, so that the Lord may open to us the door of His mercies, and we discover the depth of His love and perceive the wisdom of His ordering of our lives.
And from the depth of the womb of the abyss, and from the unclean tongue and the word of lying [5].
The slander of an unrighteous tongue before the king. My soul drew near to death, and my life approached the lowest part of the abyss [6].
Some see that an unknown person, or several persons, presented to King Antiochus III a report about Ben Sira that he was a traitor to the king.
They surrounded me on every side, and there was no helper. I looked for the help of men, and there was none [7].
I remembered Your mercy, O Lord, and Your work which is from of old, for You lift up those who wait for You, and save them from the hands of their enemies [8].
So I sent up my petition from the earth, and prayed concerning the turmoil that death causes [9].
When all the doors of men were shut in his face, he found in meeting with God, the Lover of mankind, the way of escape from the injustice of the wicked.

I called upon the Lord, the Father of my Lord, that He would not leave me in the days of trouble, when there is no help for me against the proud. I will praise Your name at all times, and sing to Him a hymn of thanksgiving [10].

His speech about God came as "the Lord, the Father of my Lord" [10]. Who is the Father of my Lord? This cannot be understood except in the light of the Christian thought concerning the hypostases of the Father and the Son.

Ben Sira presents to us a practical exercise for enjoying God's answer to our prayer, which is that we mix our cries in the midst of affliction with thanksgiving and praise to God. As Origen says, thanksgiving in the midst of affliction reveals our surrender and our trust in God, the Maker of good things. Thanksgiving in the time of relief cannot be compared with the greatness of thanksgiving in the time of affliction.

v Since danger accompanies the keeping of the commandment, which is our boast, let us remember the saying of the Apostle: "It were better for me to die, than that any man should make my glorying void" (1 Cor 9:15). And he says at greater length in another place: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?" (Rom 8:35). Here we learn, in a stronger expression, to obey the commandments, and how to show our intense love for God, who said: "If a man love me, he will keep my words" (Jn 14:23), and also in other places, so that rest may be poured into our souls...

From these verses it is clear that whoever transgresses even one commandment will be subject to the general judgment, since the Lord declared: "He that rejecteth me, and receiveth not my words, hath one that judgeth him: the word that I have spoken, the same shall judge him in the last day" (Jn 12:48). And the words that followed are more terrifying... (Jn 3:36)[1].
St. Basil the Great: My prayer was heard. For You saved me from destruction, and delivered me from the evil time [11].
Therefore I give thanks to You and praise You, and I bless the name of the Lord [12].
The psalm ends with praise as at the beginning, and in this it resembles (Psalm 145).

entries.section: 2. A poem on seeking wisdom and establishing a school for teaching wisdom

paragraphs.text: 18 When I was yet young, before I went abroad, I desired wisdom openly in my prayer. 19 I prayed for her before the temple, and I will seek her out even to the end. And she flourished as a ripening grape. 20 My heart delighted in her, my foot went the right way, and from my youth up I sought after her. 21 I bowed down mine ear a little, and received her, 22 and found much learning for myself, and I had great profit therein. 23 He that giveth me wisdom, I will give glory to him, 24 for I purposed to do after her, and I was zealous of that which is good; and I shall not be confounded. 25 My soul hath wrestled with her, and in my doings I was exact. 26 I stretched forth my hands to the heaven above, and bewailed my ignorances of her. 27 I directed my soul unto her, and I found her in pureness. 28 With her I had my heart joined from the beginning; therefore shall I not be forsaken. 29 My heart was troubled in seeking her; therefore have I gotten a good possession. 30 The Lord hath given me a tongue for my reward, and I will praise him therewith. 31 Draw near unto me, ye unlearned, and dwell in the house of learning. 32 Wherefore are ye slow, and what say ye of these things, seeing your souls are very thirsty? 33 I opened my mouth, and said, Buy her for yourselves without money. 34 Put your neck under the yoke, and let your soul receive instruction: she is hard at hand to find. 35 Behold with your eyes, how that I have had but little labour, and have gotten unto me much rest. 36 Get learning with a great sum of money, and get much gold by her. 37 Let your soul rejoice in his mercy, and be not ashamed of his praise. 38 Work your work betimes, and in his time he will give you your reward.

He closed the book with a poem arranged according to the Hebrew alphabet, in which he praises wisdom, takes pride in her, seeks her, and also establishes a school for teaching her. This poem corresponds to the alphabetical poem at the end of the book of Proverbs, where Solomon praises the virtuous wife. Ben Sira looked upon wisdom as upon a holy wife, God's gift to His believers. Moreover, the book began with the seeking of wisdom from God, and he closed it with a positive, joyful thought.

The alphabetical arrangement of the poem enables the reader to memorize it easily by heart, and to count it as a personal poem of his own. It is as though what Ben Sira attained of success in his enjoyment of the divine wisdom is not a matter for him alone, but he desires every man to take pride in having attained it.
While I was still young and before the start of my journeys, I sought wisdom openly in my prayer [13].

If he has already spoken of the blessings of journeys for enjoying the good things of others, he affirms here that journeys alone are not enough; rather, while still a young man, before his travels in many lands, he used to pray openly, declaring his need of wisdom! For she is the fruit of prayers and supplications, so that the grace of God may work, and give him understanding to distinguish true experiences from corrupt ones.
Before the temple I prayed for her, and to the end of my life I will seek after her [14].

Since the divine wisdom lifts man up to the holy life, whenever he stood before the holy temple he asked the Holy One to give him wisdom. And whenever he received wisdom his heart was kindled with longing for more of it, and his heart remains so to the last moment of his life on earth! Thus he brings out here two matters of the utmost importance:
a. True wisdom, which is from God, cannot be separated from the holy life; therefore he seeks her in his chamber as he seeks her openly in the holy temple, without shame!
b. He feels that man, however great his wisdom, will never reach the perfection of wisdom, so he continues to seek her as long as he is in the body, until the day of his departure from the world.
My heart delighted in her blossom as in a grape that ripens. And my foot walked in her straight way, and from my youth I searched after her [15].

Ben Sira makes clear to his disciples, when they see what wisdom has poured out upon him of the joy of the Spirit, that it is not something new; rather, from his youth he came to know her and set out on her way and enjoyed, as it were, her flowers that are on their way to becoming ripe grapes. In this he urges his disciples, in a spirit of hope and joy, to begin the journey of wisdom, even if they have not yet enjoyed the ripe grapes, that is, the deep joy; they will attain it so long as they persevere on the way.
I inclined my ear a little and received her, and found much instruction for myself [16].
Here he calls his disciples to incline their ear to the voice of the Lord through the Law, that they may receive wisdom and grow in her through much unceasing instruction.
And I advanced by her grace; I glorify Him who gave me wisdom [17].
As he advanced in the knowledge of wisdom he did not become proud; rather, this knowledge kindled his heart with praise and the glorification of God.
For I resolved to practice wisdom, and I was zealous for the good, and was not ashamed [18].

His continual advance in the knowledge of wisdom drives him to be determined to practice her, not in slackness, but with sincere zeal and with pride in her, without being ashamed of her even if others criticize him.

entries.section: 2. A poem on seeking wisdom and establishing a school for teaching wisdom

paragraphs.text: My soul strove for her, and I examined myself firmly in fulfilling the Law. And I spread out my hands to the heights, and mourned for my ignorance of her [19].

He often links wisdom with the Law, and even with walking in it in earnestness and firmness, for fear of laxity in conduct through preoccupation with dry philosophical thoughts. This conduct is not achieved without God's help and the practice of repentance. For this reason he links his growth in wisdom with spreading out his hands to the heights and weeping over his ignorance and his sins.

entries.section: 2. A poem on seeking wisdom and establishing a school for teaching wisdom

paragraphs.text: I directed my soul to her, and in purity I found her, and for her sake I gained a heart from the beginning, therefore I shall not be forsaken [20].
He links the continual enjoyment of wisdom with purity of hands and heart, that is, purity of conduct and work together with purity of heart and thought.

entries.section: 2. A poem on seeking wisdom and establishing a school for teaching wisdom

paragraphs.text: My heart was stirred in seeking her, therefore I gained a good possession [21].
He affirms that when he speaks of purity of heart, he means the stirring of his whole being to enjoy holiness and to seek wisdom; therefore he counted her possession a great reward.

entries.section: 2. A poem on seeking wisdom and establishing a school for teaching wisdom

paragraphs.text: The Lord gave me a tongue as a reward, and with it I praise Him [22].
"The tongue" here means the ability even to express what is in his heart of sweetness and longing to praise the Lord. This ability is a divine gift and a talent that must be kindled.

entries.section: 2. A poem on seeking wisdom and establishing a school for teaching wisdom

paragraphs.text: Draw near to me, you who are unlearned, and dwell in my school [23].

The word "my school" came as "beth hamidrash," or the house of learning, where Ben Sira used to gather with his disciples as the people of his house, or his family beloved to him. What Ben Sira did is a shadow of the work of the Lord Christ, who chose His disciples who clung to Him.

Schools were attached to the synagogues; and some leaders demanded that there be a school in every village, and every child was obliged to enroll in it, and learning was not separated from worship and the godly life.
The writer lived interacting with all classes, entering deeply into what is for the edification of men according to their various particular circumstances.

v The word of God has been addressed to us. It was declared in order to counsel us, and as the Holy Scripture says: "Receive instruction in the house of instruction." Instruction is given so that we may learn, and the school of instruction is the Church of Christ.

Let us ask ourselves what the purpose and aim of this instruction is: who is it that learns, and who is it that gives the instruction. One learns in order to live well, and the aim of his learning to live well is that he may live eternally. Christians learn with this goal, and the One who teaches is Christ[2].

entries.section: 2. A poem on seeking wisdom and establishing a school for teaching wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine: Why do you say that you are in need of these things, and that your souls are very thirsty? [24]

Ben Sira asks how long the thirst of his disciples has lasted; let them then come forward in a spirit of prayer and drink, for God is ready to give them wisdom. And as it is written in the book of Proverbs: "Come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine which I have mingled. Forsake the foolish, and live; and go in the way of understanding" (Prov 9:5-6).
I opened my mouth and spoke: Acquire wisdom for yourselves without price[3] [25].

Ben Sira affirms to his disciples that they are without excuse, for wisdom is not sold for silver, presenting himself as an example, that he opened his mouth with sincere zeal, longing and faith, and so attained her.

Teaching in the Jewish tradition was free of charge, and the rabbis who taught in the schools depended for their living on other means, and at a later time they worked in trade[4]. It is stated in the Mishnah: "If you learn much in the Law, you will receive a great reward, and the One who is committed to this task (God) is faithful to give you the reward of your work[5]."

entries.section: 2. A poem on seeking wisdom and establishing a school for teaching wisdom

paragraphs.text: Put your neck under her yoke, and let your souls receive her instruction. She is near, so you will find her [26].

Wisdom does not depart from the one who has enjoyed her, but accompanies him in the grave, and rescues him from the claws of Hades. She is near to us, because Christ, the Wisdom of God, establishes His kingdom within us (Lk 17:21).

entries.section: 2. A poem on seeking wisdom and establishing a school for teaching wisdom

paragraphs.text: See with your eyes how I labored a little and found much rest for myself [27].
He urges the reader to submit to the yoke of wisdom, for he himself has experienced great rest under this yoke.

v He who is plunged into countless struggles for the sake of virtue, and attains to her, and accomplishes still more labors, lives to the end like Lazarus, who toiled in many sorrows (Lk 16), and like Job, who was engaged in struggles against the enemy. He says: "Those who are engaged in toil are at rest (see Job 3:17). Therefore the Lord called those who labor and are heavy laden to rest (Mt 11:28).

Now how can it be said of those who labor in good works that they are heavy laden? Because: "They that go forth weeping, bearing seed for sowing, shall come again with rejoicing, bringing their sheaves with them" (Ps 126:6), full of the fruits that have returned to them from their sowing of the seed. Therefore those are said to be heavy laden who have sowed bountifully and reaped bountifully (2 Cor 9:6), and with eternal joy cast the sheaves of spiritual fruit upon their shoulders. So then, he who is saved by God, to whom He offers redemption, labors in this life, and after this lives to the end. He does not see corruption when he sees the wise die.

He who chooses the narrow and afflicted way instead of the wide and broad one: in the time of God's visitation, when those who did not believe the words of God, but walked after the desires of their vain hearts, are cast into eternal punishment, I say that he does not see eternal destruction, perpetual misery. But he says in truth that the wise have been trained in craftiness. And Jeremiah says concerning them: "They are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge" (Jer 4:22). As it is also said: "Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools" (Rom 1:22). "For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God" (1 Cor 3:19).

And because this wisdom makes men fools, God says that He will destroy the wisdom of the wise and bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent. Therefore these false beliefs, which are called knowledge, bring death to those who receive them. But this death is not seen by those who are saved by Him, who is pleased to save those who trust in the foolishness of His proclamation[6].

entries.section: 2. A poem on seeking wisdom and establishing a school for teaching wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great: Acquire instruction with a great sum of silver, and by it you will gain much gold [28].

In verse 25 he speaks of material silver, for wisdom is not sold for money. But here he speaks of it as instruction by the Law, of which it was said: "The words of the Lord are pure words, as silver tried in a furnace" (Ps 12:6). As for the reward, it is the gaining of much gold. This gold points to the pledge of the heavenly life.

entries.section: 2. A poem on seeking wisdom and establishing a school for teaching wisdom

paragraphs.text: Let your souls rejoice in His mercy, and be not ashamed of praising Him [29].

entries.section: 2. A poem on seeking wisdom and establishing a school for teaching wisdom

paragraphs.text: Do your work before the appointed time, and He will reward you in His appointed time [30].

He closes the poem, indeed the whole book, with the thought that whoever earnestly strives to obtain true wisdom enjoys a pledge of heaven, so his soul rejoices in the mercies of God, and he is not ashamed to praise Him without ceasing. As for his reward, it is in the great day of the Lord, when he will enjoy the fellowship of eternal glory, and see God face to face.
Inspired by Sirach 51

entries.section: Let me offer You the sacrifice of continual thanksgiving, O Giver of wisdom!

paragraphs.text: v What shall I ask of You, O incarnate Wisdom of God?
Sanctify my heart and my life, that I may be made worthy of Your free grace!
I praise You in every state, for every state, and in all states, for You are the secret of the joy of my heart, and You sanctify all my life.
v May You accompany me on the journey of my life, so that my heart does not cease to praise You.
My soul thirsts for You, and I hunger for Your wisdom.
May You lift my heart to Your heavens, and pour Your splendor into my depths.
Take me to Your glories day by day!
Until I see You face to face!
